en: The Collection of Works by Jñānaśrīmitra. Homage to the Gurus and to the authors of the treatises.

1. Introduction to the Author of the Commentary: Among the Indian philosophers, there were two renowned masters known by the name Jñānaśrī. Of these two, the one born in Kashmir was the commentator on the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and the translator into the Tibetan language of numerous Buddhist treatises.

Jñānaśrībhadra is one [author], while the other is Jñānaśrīmitra, the teacher of Vikramaśīla born in the Gauḍa country of great renown. Of these two, the second is the subject under discussion here. In some places he is referred to by the name Jñānaśrī, and in others by the name Jñānaśrīmitra; however, in the colophons of his own works, he bears the title *mahāpaṇḍitācāryajñānaśrīmitrapāda*.

His name became renowned as one who adorned [the land]. At the Great Monastery of Vikramaśīla, which was established by Dharmapāla, the sovereign of Vaṅga and Magadha, and subsequently cherished by those born of his lineage, students from lands other than Bhārata arrived for the sake of acquiring various branches of knowledge; having mastered all the treatises, primarily those of the Buddhists, they [studied] under the learned Ācāryas.

Through their spiritual wealth, [the scholars] adorned their respective countries. It is heard that in the eleventh century of the Śaka era, there were four door-panḍitas and two great pillars (*mahāstambha*) in this center of learning (*vidyā-vihāra*). Among them, Jñānaśrīmitra graced the position of the second great pillar.

It is reported that this Jñānaśrīmitra was originally a Śrāvaka belonging to the Saindhava tradition, and subsequently took recourse to the Tantrayāna. At this Mahāvihāra, the Saindhavas were extremely influential; once, they offered tantric texts and a certain image of Heruka as oblations into the fire, yet they were not punished by the king.
Among these people of Sindh, individuals bearing the name Śrīmitra are seen. Their disputes with those from the land of Vaṅga who follow the Tantrayāna are well-known in historical accounts.
Further details concerning Jñānaśrīmitra and others can be found in Tibetan texts. In his own country...

The Tibetan monarch named Hra la Ye śes ’od, who was devoted to the propagation of the pure Buddha-dharma, dispatched his own kinsmen to invite the master of Vikramaśīla, Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa). Having learned their purpose for going to Vikramaśīla and having observed the royal gifts and other offerings, [he realized they were intended] either to gain royal favor or to amass wealth for the sake of the Tibetan country.

At that time, the Master did not accept the journey. Subsequently, when he learned from the Tibetans who had returned for this purpose that the king—who was intent on amassing wealth for the sake of the Dharma—had been imprisoned by his enemies and was facing death in prison, Dīpaṅkara, overcome by compassion, undertook the arduous journey to the land of Tibet for the propagation of the True Dharma. And these were the Tibetans...

They witnessed the growth of Nāropa’s final stage at Vikramaśīla. This very aged master descended from his palanquin, leaning upon the right arm of Atīśa and the left arm of Jñānaśrīmitra. It is also heard that prior to departing for the land of Tibet, Dīpaṅkara had received secret instructions from Jñānaśrīmitra and subsequently practiced them.

From these [facts], Jñānaśrīmitra’s extraordinary eminence at Vikramaśīla is clearly understood. Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna, who was approximately fifty-six years of age, left the land of India in the spring of the year 1141 CE. At that time, Jñānaśrīmitra also [distinguished himself] through his scholarship and the composition of treatises.
It can be inferred that he attained supreme renown;

for from a close study of the extant works of Jñānaśrīmitra, it is known that he cited and refuted by name the treatises of prominent Naiyāyikas, such as Vācaspati. Of Vācaspati, however, the *Nyāyasūcī*—

By his own statement, the time of the composition of the *Nibandhana* is known to be the year 1418. However, scholars were previously divided as to whether this year referred to the Vikrama era or the Śaka era. Now, through meticulous investigation, it has been determined that Vācaspati indeed recorded the Śaka year.

Udayanācārya states in his *Tātparyapariśuddhi* that the view of the elder Naiyāyika Jayantabhaṭṭa was referenced by Vācaspati in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*. Furthermore, it is known from Jayanta’s own play, the *Āgamadambara*, that he served as a minister to Śaṅkaravarman, the sovereign of Kashmir. This...

According to the consensus of those who know historical tradition, Śaṅkaravarman ruled the land of Kashmir from the eight hundred and eighty-fifth year of the Saka era until the nine hundred and second year. However, the *Nyāyasūcīnibandha*, which serves as a supplement to the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*, does not follow that [era], but rather dates it to the Vikrama year eight hundred and eighty-four (corresponding to the Christian year 827–828 CE).

He deserves to be born; however, it should be understood that this refers to the Śaka year 8976–7 [Vṛḥ]. Vācaspati has presented the sequence of his own works in the *Bhāmatī*. According to that, it is understood that even after the two Nyāya treatises, he composed the *Tattvakaumudī*, the *Tattvavaiśāradī*, and the *Bhāmatī*. Therefore, by Jñānaśrīmitra—
It is highly probable that the splendor of Vidyā was directly witnessed by the teacher Vācaspati during his early years;

furthermore, we shall demonstrate later that Jñānaśrīmitra, along with his disciple Ratnakīrti, was refuted in the works of Ācārya Udayana. Ratnakīrti compiled an essential summary of his own teacher’s treatises, as is evident from his own writings.
This has been demonstrated in the *Bhūmikā*. For this very reason, it is possible that Udayana was the younger contemporary of these two.

Between the two renowned masters of Nyāya, Vācaspati and Udayana, Jñānaśrīmitra composed the *Setubandhana*; thus, his greatness and that of his works are extraordinary. As for the time of his composition, it was the beginning of the eleventh century CE.
He would have flourished in my own time.
This Jñānaśrīmitra was exceedingly well-versed in the orthodox (Āstika) scriptures as well as in the Buddhist treatises.

This is understood from the reading of that very work. However, his previously mentioned adherence to the Tantrayāna does not become clear through a close examination of the text. On the occasion of commenting on a specific verse [1.16] in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, he has also demonstrated the view of his own guru.
It is also heard that he accepted discipleship under the master Dharmapāla, who resided on Suvarṇadvīpa. His own tradition—
The indicator [of this] is the verse composed by him, which establishes his specific form:
"Under the command of that lord of kings, Ārya Asaṅga— who brought about the conquest of the god of love— the teacher Vasubandhu, of steadfast intellect, shone forth."
Then Dignāga, having received extraordinary assistance from Kumāranātha,
established today’s faultless state of the works of the authors of the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya.

Thus, by this statement of his own, it has been made clear that [the author] is included within the tradition of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda originating from Maitreyanātha and within the system of Dharma established by Prajñākaragupta. The master Sthiravrata (Stcherbatsky) demonstrated a threefold division among the followers of Prajñākaragupta; among those divisions were Jina, Ravigupta, and Yamāri.
They became renowned exponents. Prajñākara’s disciple Ravigupta resided in Kaśmīra during the time of Jñānaśrī.

It is reported from that very source that Yamāri was a disciple of the Kaśmīrian Jñānaśrī and that his sphere of activity was in Vaṅga; furthermore, it is heard that Jinendra refuted the work of Ravigupta in his own treatise, and that Yamāri in turn refuted the work of Jinendra.

Jñānaśrīmitra, however, mentions a certain teacher named Ravi twice by name with respect at the end of the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*. Bearing this matter in mind, the mutual relationship between Ravigupta, Jñānaśrī, and Yamāri deserves further investigation. All of these [belong] to the tradition of Prajñākaragupta prevalent in Vaṅga and Magadha.

Furthermore, it must be re-examined whether [he] was indeed Ravigupta or not, and whether Jñānaśrīmitra’s position lies between Ravigupta and Yamāri, or rather between Jñānaśrī and Bhadra. As for the final determination in this matter, it is likely to be achieved only through a comparison with the works of Jñānaśrīmitra alongside the Tibetan translations of the compositions of Ravigupta and Yamāri.
2. Acquaintance with Available Works: Considering that some acquaintance with the available works of Jñānaśrīmitra is required here, it is presented in a very brief scope. Introduction.

(1) The work titled *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* is the most eminent among the treatises of Jñānaśrīmitra, being primarily devoted to the proof of the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of all entities. One should not consider this to be merely a specific chapter of another work; rather, it consists of four distinct sections (*paricchedas*). Herein [are refuted] Śaṅkara, Bhāsarvajña, Trilocana, and Vācaspati, who served as pillars of the Nyāya school.

The author has explicitly established that he has uprooted the opinions of others and established his own view; indeed, it is observed here that those various doctrines have been extracted and refuted extensively.
"Whatever exists is momentary, like a cloud; and these entities exist."

Existence (*sattā*) is here the capacity for causal efficiency; it is established by valid cognition (*mīti*) in those things already established, yet that [capacity] is not one and the same mode even at other times.

Otherwise, there would be either a modification or an action, and thus in both ways there is a connection with momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*); therefore, [the capacity] rests upon the object to be proven (*sādhya*).

Thus, in the opening verse, the subject matter of the treatise is summarized. Thereafter, across the four chapters titled "The Property of the Subject" (*pakṣadharma*), "Positive Concomitance" (*anvaya*), "Negative Concomitance" (*vyatireka*), and "The Refutation of the Theory of Causality and Destruction" (*hetukavināśādhikāra*), the doctrine of permanence is demolished through extensive analysis, and the author's own position is firmly established.
Furthermore, the investigation herein is complete in its components and strikes at the very core of the matter.

(2) *Vyāpticarcā*, however, is a treatise dedicated to demonstrating the nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as conceived by the Buddhists. In the systems of Indian philosophy, pervasion is accepted by all schools with the exception of the Cārvākas; nevertheless, there exists considerable disagreement among them regarding its fundamental basis and essential nature. The Naiyāyikas [hold that it consists of] the knowledge of concomitance (*sahacāra-jñāna*) together with the absence of knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra-ajñāna*).

They declare this to be the means for ascertaining pervasion (*vyāpti*); and the Buddhists establish pervasion through identity (*tādātmya*), causality (*tadutpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*). However, in this incidental discussion, the views of Trilocana, Vācaspati, and others have been cited and refuted. Finally, it is concluded that the establishment of the pervasion consisting of the essential nature of the relation between cause and effect arises solely from perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
The conclusion has been presented.

(3) In *Jñānaśrīmitra’s Collection of Treatises*, the *Bhedābhedaparīkṣā* is the shortest. It appears that its subject matter is an investigation into the relationship between cognition (*jñāna*) and the object of cognition (*jñeya*). Some maintain that these two are distinct, while others maintain their identity. Faults have been pointed out for both of these positions; therefore, others adopt the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*). By accepting difference, [they avoid] the fault of the position of non-difference, and by [accepting] non-difference...

Their intention is that by means of this support (ālambana), the defects of the position of difference (bheda-pakṣa) are removed. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is one that favors the position of non-difference (abheda-pakṣa), because if both difference and non-difference were accepted, there would result the convergence of the defects observed in both positions.

(4) Although the secret of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is minor in its outward form, the definition and classifications of non-apprehension as accepted by Buddhist philosophers have been collected from various treatises and discussed here.
Introduction (5):

The discussion on the non-existence of all sounds deserves to be accepted as a supplementary section (*khila*) to the secret of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-rahasya*), because it analyzes the efficacy of the non-apprehension of effects when there is a general absence of sound; and in the case of the general absence of sound, [the non-existence] is not established—

This is the removal of doubt; for in the present context of the non-perception of an effect, its function here consists precisely in establishing the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

(6) The *Apohaprakaraṇa*, which aims at the analysis of the meaning of words according to the Buddhist tenets, is exceedingly profound in its subject matter. To begin with, the primary meaning is expressed by words; therein, exclusion (*apoha*) is understood as a subordinate quality of that [meaning].

The referent is one from the perspective of superimposition, another from the perspective of appearance, or it may be established as something else; in reality, however, there is nothing at all that can be denoted.

This verse summarizing the meaning of the treatise is by Jñānaśrīmitra. It should be noted by those devoted to the study of the *Bauddhādhikāra* that this work has been extensively refuted by Udayanācārya and by Śaṅkaramiśra, who follows him.

(7) The section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*), however, effects a refutation of the eternal Supreme Lord as the creator of the universe. In the first chapter, the views of Śaṅkara, Vācaspati, Vītoka, Bhāsarvajña, Trilocana, and Śatānanda—which establish the world-creator—are presented through their respective words; in the second, there is a general refutation of that [doctrine] from the Buddhist perspective; and in the third, [the refutation continues].
Detailed Explanation:
The author has divided the third chapter of the seven verses dedicated to the refutation of Īśvara found within Dharmakīrti’s *Pramāṇavārttika* into three parts.

(8) Following his own tenets, Jñānaśrīmitra established the determination of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); this work is another name for the *Trikapañcakacintā*. It establishes the causal relation between two properties (*dharma*). [It is] the *Dharmottara*.

Regarding the determination of the number of apprehensions and non-apprehensions within the process [of cognition], there is a disagreement among Buddhists. There is the position of fivefold [perception], whereas Jñānaśrīmitra maintains the position of threefold. In this work, composed both in prose and verse, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is presented in the *kārikās*, while the prose section contains the analytical discussion of that same meaning. Of the treatises of Jñānaśrīmitra, we have only one available in the Tibetan language—
He was instructed.
(9) In the chapter on the Determination of the Yogin, the Master has analyzed the nature of the yogin and his direct perception according to the Buddhist tradition.

(10) The *Advaitabinduprakaraṇa* is devoted to the exposition of the Vijñānavāda with aspects (*sākāravijñānavāda*). Herein, the refutation of the ultimate distinction between cognition and the object of cognition is accomplished.

(11) The *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* elaborates upon the doctrine of cognition with aspects (*sākāravijñānavāda*) with great flourish. It is traditionally heard that Dharmakīrti was the originator of this doctrine, and it was clarified by Prajñākaragupta. Herein, in the introduction to this treatise...

The commentary on this treatise is available, preceded by a demonstration of the consensus of ancient masters such as Nāgārjuna, Maitreyanātha, and Asaṅga. The views of Dharmakīrti and Prajñākaragupta are also presented. This scripture is divided into six chapters: the first contains an analysis of the doctrine of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavāda*); the second discusses affliction and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadāna*); and the third...

The demonstration of the entrance into the Middle Way occurs in the fourth chapter; the elaboration of the non-duality of the manifold in the fifth; and the investigation of self-cognition in the sixth.
Furthermore, in the sixth, the fundamental unity of the Yogācāra Vijñānavāda with the Madhyamaka tenet is reached.

(12) First, the *Sākārasaṃgrahasūtra* is a metrical compendium of the essential points of the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*. It consists of four chapters (*pariccheda*), within which the subject matter of the six chapters of the treatise is summarized.
3. An Investigation into the Authorship of the Present Works:

Here, with the exception of the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, the eleven works have been edited based on a single manuscript. Furthermore, in many instances, the mention of the author's name does not appear in the colophon (*puṣpikā*). Therefore, regarding the single authorship of these present works—

The reason for this acceptance must be clarified. (1) In the colophon of the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, there is no mention of the author. However, in the final verse—where it says, "By him [was written] this work, which has reached the further shore of Jñānaśrī’s knowledge in the three worlds"—it appears that this is his designation. Ratnakīrti, Udayana—
(1) Verses from the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* were extracted by Jñānaśrī under the names of Vādideva and others.
(2) The *Vyāptinirṇaya*, however, is indeed the work of Jñānaśrīmitra, as it is indicated as such in its colophon.
(3) The *Bhedābhedaparīkṣā* is also composed by Jñānaśrīmitra, because it is stated as such in his *Sākārasiddhi*.

(4,5) The author of the *Anupalabdhirahasya* and the *Sarvaśabdābhāvacarcā* is not mentioned, nor is he found elsewhere. (6) The passage situated within the *Apohaprakaraṇa* is explicitly identified by Vādideva as belonging to Jñānaśrīmitra himself.
In the *Syādvādaratnākara*, it is indicated in the *Īśvaravāda* that the author of that very work is also the author of another text titled *Trikapañcakacintā*. Furthermore,
in the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, the *Bṛhadīśvaravāda* of its author is mentioned.

(8) It is known from the Tibetan translation of that work— *Trikapañcakacintāparākhya-kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhi*, composed by Jñānaśrīmitra— that [it consists of] three [chapters] and five [sections]. Introduction.

(9) In the *Ratnakīrti*, the statement “the determination of the yogin (*yoginirṇaya*) is the basis for the proof of omniscience” occurs due to the identity of terminology and the identity of subject matter. (10) In the *Sākārasiddhi*, a reference to the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa* is seen as a work by Jñānaśrīmitra.

(11–12) Based on the colophons, both the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* and the *Sākārasaṃgrahasūtra* are indeed the works of Jñānaśrīmitra. Keeping all of this in mind, observing a uniform style throughout, and having reflected upon a single manuscript, [one may conclude...]

The conclusion follows of its own accord that all these twelve works found together were composed by Jñānaśrīmitra. Along with these, the *Sarvajñasiddhi*, which has not been found, deserves mention as a work of Jñānaśrīmitra; it appears that this too was utilized by Ratnakīrti in his own *Sarvajñasiddhi*. Furthermore, [it is mentioned] by Jñānaśrīmitra in the *Sākārasiddhi* and the *Vyāpticarcā*.

A certain *Sarvajñasiddhi* has been cited, and there is a *Sarvajñasiddhi* composed by Jñānaśrīmitra within his *Yoginirṇaya*; furthermore, in another section of the *Yoginirṇaya*, a half-verse from the *Sarvajñasiddhi* is observed to be extracted. It appears that the very same *Sarvajñasiddhi* composed by Jñānaśrīmitra is being referred to throughout.

From the observation of the statement in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, "But the doctrine of a persisting synthesizer [of experience] during the apprehension of cause and effect will be discussed in the *Anekāntacintā*," it is known that Jñānaśrīmitra intended to compose another work based on the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*). However, it is not certain whether that *Anekāntacintā* was actually composed or not.

4. Regarding the chronological order of the works presented here, the sequence of the texts as found in the manuscript (mātṛkā) has been followed for the purpose of this edition. Although some discrepancies may arise due to cross-references appearing elsewhere, a rearrangement of the order is not justified here because the manuscript is a single unit; furthermore, the text is not complete.

The sequence [of these works] comes from some other source; furthermore, the treatises herein are independent of one another. It appears that even in the *Ātmatattvaviveka* composed by Ācārya Udayana, while refuting the views of Jñānaśrīmitra, the sequence of the composition of the treatises was not followed.
Therefore, a description of the sequence of the texts as established through the evidence of mutual references is presented here.

The *Anupalabdhirahasya*, the *Sarvaśabdābhāvacarcā*, the *Yoginirṇayaprakaraṇa*, and the *Sākārasaṃgrahasūtra* are not mentioned by name in other treatises; therefore, it is impossible to determine their sequential position among the works of Jñānaśrīmitra. However, because they are mentioned in the *Vyāpticarcā*—specifically in the *Apohaprakaraṇa* and the *Īśvaravāda*—they must precede those sections.
The position of the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*: The discussion on pervasion (*vyāpti*) was composed prior to the *Īśvaravāda*, as it is mentioned therein.
It follows that the examination of difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-parīkṣā*), which is mentioned in the *Sākārasiddhi*, was composed before that. Likewise, [the discussion on pervasion]...
[introduction].

The antiquity of the *Apohaprakaraṇa*: Even in the *Vyāpticarcā*, a reference to the forthcoming *Apohaprakaraṇa* is observed. It is certain that the *Īśvaravāda* was composed prior to the *Sākārasiddhi*, because it is mentioned therein. The *Kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhi* was composed before both the *Kṣaṇabhaṅga* and the *Īśvaravāda*, as it is utilized in both works.
The *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa* likewise precedes the *Sākārasiddhi-śāstra*. By the same logic, the *Sākārasiddhi-śāstra* also precedes the *Apoha-prakaraṇa* and the chapter on *Kṣaṇabhaṅga*.
Thus, although the relative chronology has been determined in many instances, it remains difficult to establish a definitive order for the complete sequence of these works.
It is clearly understood that this refers to the Nibandhas.
5. Jñānaśrīmitra’s Style of Composition:

Jñānaśrīmitra’s style is both unimpeded and simple, such that even though the subject matter is difficult, these treatises have become captivating to the learned. They are largely freed from Buddhist technical terminology and, from the perspective of language, [are accessible].

All the earlier masters connected with the Naiyāyikas and other schools, such as Dharmakīrti and Prajñākaragupta, do not surpass Jñānaśrīmitra in terms of stylistic excellence. Jñānaśrīmitra has lightened the inherent difficulty of his subject matter by employing captivating narratives and the like.

This exposition on the elements (*bhūta*) and mental modes (*vicāra*) is seen to have been employed and accepted in many places in the works of Udayana and others. Occasional insertions of popular maxims (*laukikanyāya*) and witty sayings (*kautukokti*) impart a sense of novelty even to subjects that might otherwise be dry. Generally, all the treatises herein abound in critical inquiry; here, one perceives reasoning as if confronting an adversary face-to-face.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: for this very reason, even the employment of harsh words is not difficult to find, much like the talk of a disputant. First, having restated the opponent’s position using their own words, its subsequent disentanglement and refutation through reasoning is the distinctive feature of Jñānaśrīmitra. He was emulated here by his own disciple, Ratnakīrti, as well.

In this regard, even within philosophical treatises, the language in many places appears adorned with the exquisite beauty of poetry, and the employment of poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra) is exceedingly pleasing. Taking a specific verse from Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s *Veṇīsaṃhāra* as a basis:
"By whom our beloved has been dragged away, having torn the sky-tenement [the garment] of her intellect..."
While those of celebrated fame stand here in this assembly,
this Duḥśāsana— who is composed of cruel injustice and a policy of humiliation— has now fallen into the cage of my arms; let him be protected, O Kauravas!

Regarding the "Introduction" (*prastāvanā*), one should look here at the introductory verse of the *Sākārasaṃgraha*, which is devoted to *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Furthermore, that entire treatise is composed in verse. Elsewhere as well, Jñānaśrīmitra frequently employs metrical expression; even there, he utilizes long meters.
The composition was highly pleasing to the reader. It is heard that he was a teacher of the science of prosody (chandaḥśāstra) named Jñānaśrīmitra;
this appears to be true upon examining the present work.
It is also likely that the fame of this Jñānaśrīmitra as a poet was widely renowned. [Subhāṣita...]
In the *Ratnakoṣa*, by the scholar named Jñānaśrīmitra, there are two verses based on a hymn to Lokeśvara:
"Like the mass of snow upon the waves of the Ocean of Milk, churned by Mount Mandara as it whirled with a deep, resonant roar and a firm form of intense speed;..."

May Lokeśvara protect you— he who is encircled by the splendor of a dense mass of his own light, and who dwells on the glorious Mount Potalaka, which resounds with the echoes of the deep explanations of the profound teachings.
If this smallness of the belly and the innate heaviness of the heart were not present,
how could there be such indolence regarding one's own interest, and how could his mind be so devoted to performing what is beneficial for others?
Thus it has been extracted. And many are seen here crossing the deep lake by means of these two sister-texts under the name of the scholar Jñānaśrī, placing hundreds of wonders within their hearts.
He who, having entered within, thoroughly discerns and extracts some hidden essence after long holding his breath— such a person is indeed rare among these.
This verse was cited by that very [author]. It is also likely to be by Jñānaśrīmitra, given that he is seen to refer to himself with the title "Paṇḍita" in his own works.
[This is] prior to Jñānaśrīmitra by Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, an elder Naiyāyika, and subsequent to him by Vādideva and others.
In the treatises on the systems of philosophy, the employment of verses adorned with poetic figures is prescribed.

6. By examining the treatises presented by Jñānaśrīmitra, it becomes evident that his mastery of various śāstras was extraordinary and unparalleled; he drew upon non-Buddhist authors and works as well. He [engaged] with his own Buddhist colleagues and the leading opponents, the Naiyāyikas.

Setting aside other treatises and their authors, he cites them extensively. In these commentaries, there is an introductory section (prastāvanā) using the general designation "Vedas," and specifically, citations are seen from the Ṛgveda and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.

The extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) and even a versified restatement from the *Mahābhārata* have been composed by Jñānaśrī. A collection of potsherds has been seen here, but no further non-existence (abhāva) beyond that has been observed. Therefore, where is the basis for the verbal designation "non-existence," and what is its cause?
This is merely a series of potsherds seen here, which belongs solely to the jar itself.

In the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* composed by Mādhavācārya (p. 226), a verse from the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* beginning with "whatever exists is momentary" (*yat sat tat kṣaṇikam*) is seen to have been cited, preceded by the mention of the name Jñānaśrīmitra. In this compendium, within the section on the Buddhist philosophy (*bauddhadarśana*), the influence of Jñānaśrīmitra is clearly evident elsewhere as well.

Śaṅkaramiśra was familiar with the works of Jñānaśrīmitra; in his *Ātmatattvavivekakalpalatā*, he extracted verses and prose passages from the *Apohaprakaraṇa*, the *Advaitabindu*, the *Sākārasiddhi*, and the *Sākārasaṃgraha*, and discussed them in his introduction. Furthermore, in the *Vādivinoda*, when enumerating the renowned Buddhist masters, Bhadanta Jñānaśrī is also mentioned.

He was remembered by Śaṅkara. At the time of Śaṅkara, the stream of Buddhist scripture was obstructed, because prior to that, the Buddhist monasteries (*vidyāvihāras*) and their textual traditions had already been destroyed.
Jayarāma Nyāyapañcānana, too, in his *Nyāyasiddhāntamālā*, [records] the list of names of Buddhist teachers as seen in the *Vādivinoda*.
He rescues [the text]. However, no evidence is found for the claim that Jñānaśrīmitra possessed a thorough knowledge of his [Dharmakīrti’s] treatises.
Among the Jainas, Vādideva compiled a collection of verses from the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* and the *Apohaprakaraṇa* in his *Syādvādaratnākara*.
Furthermore, he extracted passages from another work by Jñānaśrīmitra as well.

In the *Nyāyāvatāra-ṭippanaka* composed by Devabhadra, the definition of existence (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*) found in the chapter on momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga-adhyāya*) has been extracted, and Jñānaśrīmitra is mentioned by name. Furthermore, in the *Syādvādamañjarī* composed by Malliṣeṇa, [the following] from the *Apoha-prakaraṇa* written by Jñānaśrī—among these five... [is cited].

The citation of the verse beginning with *svaprakāśinīṣu* is observed. This verse also appears in the work titled *Sāmānyadūṣaṇadikprasāritā*, composed by Paṇḍita Aśoka. There is no doubt that Paṇḍita Aśoka is earlier than Jñānaśrīmitra; however, once the authorship of the verse in question has been determined here, [the relationship] with Jñānaśrī will become clear.

The determination of Malliṣeṇa’s relationship [to the author] is established by the late Paṇḍita Mahendrakumāra Śāstrī in the introduction to his *Nyāyakumudacandra*, based on his citation of a portion of a verse from Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Apohaprakaraṇa*: "Exclusion (*apoha*) is not expressed by word or logical mark (*liṅga*) as a positive entity."

It is indicated that Prabhācandra would also be a debtor to Jñānaśrī; however, the verse of Jñānaśrīmitra is indeed different from the one cited, as it is seen in the reading of the *Apohaprakaraṇa*: "The established position is that exclusion (*apoha*) is manifested by both word and logical mark.
The venerable Śāstri has determined the date of Prabhācandra, and he was senior to Jñānaśrīmitra.
It appears so; therefore, even the citation of a verse by the junior Jñānaśrī is impossible for him [Yaśovijaya].

Yaśovijayācārya had no direct acquaintance with Jñānaśrīmitra. In his *Anekāntavyavasthā-prakaraṇa*, he cites a verse composed by Jñānaśrīmitra. Furthermore, [he cites] from the *Nyāyakhaṇḍakhādya* that which was [derived] from the *Ātmatattvaviveka*.

The connection [between them] is well known; therefore, these works of Jñānaśrīmitra have come down there through tradition. Furthermore, Yaśovijaya does not mention Jñānaśrīmitra by name anywhere. There are, however, the *Ātmatattvavivekavyākhyā* composed by Nārāyaṇācārya, the *Ātmatattvavivekadīdhiti* by Raghunāthaśiromaṇi, and the *Ātmatattva-* [vivekatippaṇī] composed by Guṇānanda Vidyāvāgīśa.

Yaśovijaya has extracted the *Viveka* from the *Vivekadīdhiti* in many ways; from these very works, his thorough knowledge of the *Jñānaśrīmitra* [tradition] arises. It appears that even Nārāyaṇa and others lacked a thorough knowledge of the *Jñānaśrī* treatises, whereas Śaṅkaramiśra did possess it. However, Yaśovijaya’s *Kalpalatā* on his [Śaṅkara’s] *Ātmatattvaviveka* was not understood by him.

In this introduction, the mention of Śrīharṣa and Mahāsammat among these treatises is a point of interest for historians; however, no further details regarding them are available. Furthermore, the Pañcālakapāṭha is also mentioned in one place. Upon a close examination of the context...
It appears that here the term *pañcālaka* refers specifically to the long-format commentary (*dīrghavyākhyā*) of Nārāyaṇa.

In Vaṅga, *pañcālī* texts are well known for being composed in a circular format (*parivartin*). Among the Vaiṣṇava Naiyāyikas of Vaṅga, the long-format commentaries of Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya are called "Gadādhara’s *Pañcālī*" (*gadurapā~cālī*).

Conclusion: After a very long period of time, this collection of the works of Jñānaśrīmitra is now being brought to light. In the process of restoring these ancient texts, many individuals have provided assistance in various ways and have offered their encouragement. To all of them, [I offer my] salutation with joined palms.

Gratitude is being made known, and it is remembered again and again that even by a mere mention of the words, "In the ocean, the desired object is obtained by the boat of Jñānaśrīmitra himself," this work was undertaken by a child out of the force of his own restlessness; for even upon hearing [this], fear arises.
If this foremost quality of the ocean of nectar— this ocean whose waves of foam embrace the trembling sky— had not entered its destruction at the edge of that shore, [the world would have perished].
Thus ends the penultimate verse of the treatise *Sākārasiddhi*. May there be peace.

First Chapter – The Section on the Property of the Subject (Pakṣadharma)
[lb] || Homage to the Buddha ||

While the world, which lasts but a moment, is being stretched out by the rays of the Kinsman of the Sun as if by other [forces], you who lament over what is undesirable like those asleep—awaken yourselves, as if by a blow upon the chest! || 1 ||
Whatever exists is momentary, like a rain-cloud; and these entities do exist.
Here, existence (*sattā*) is established as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), proven by valid cognition (*miti*) in those things that are themselves established.
That [capacity] is not of a single uniform nature, nor could it ever be produced by another, nor would it fail to be an action.
Thus, in both ways, the connection with momentary destruction will find its rest in the probandum. || 2 ||

Here, the reason (*hetu*) presented in the first quarter of the verse is a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*). This reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For although there may indeed be a difference in the definition of existence (*sattva*) according to various philosophical systems, nevertheless, in this context, it is precisely the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) that is intended as "existence" and employed as the reason. It is impossible to assert that this [capacity] does not exist in any way, nor is it something that anyone would accept [as non-existent]. For those who cannot tolerate this definition [of existence], [they are refuted by the following].

If they were to state our refutation as being overly broad (*paramavyāpta*), then since those very entities that perform specific causal functions established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the subjects (*pakṣa*) under consideration, there is no suspicion of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*), whether in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*) or its locus (*āśraya*). As for those things which, despite the possibility of their causal efficiency, have not been determined in reality to possess that status, even though they are currently excluded from the subject class—

If, upon subsequent investigation, there is the perception of non-performance (*akriyopalambha*), then another inference will indeed occur. However, in the absence of that [perception], the non-apprehension of the probandum (*sādhyāpratipatti*) is precisely what is intended, just as in the case of other logical marks (*liṅga*).
And they are existent...

If it is argued that, in this way, the proof of momentariness would be non-pervasive (*avyāpinī*), we say no; for it is intended to establish that state [of momentariness] for everything whatsoever that is at any time or in any place useful for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This applies precisely to that which is useful in some instance, since the consideration of specific cases is appropriate to the context. Therefore, there is no exclusion of an undesirable form, nor is there an inability to determine the logical reason (*hetu*), nor...

In all cases, the partiality (*prādeśikatva*) of the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*)—caused by the absence of a single application of inference across every locus possessing the property to be proven—is as in the case of the inference for [the existence of] Īśvara and so forth. By this, it is shown that the various entities whose capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) is certain are the subjects (*dharmin*), and the generality of the capacity for causal efficiency is the logical reason (*hetu*). Alternatively, all these entities, which are the objects of perception and other means of knowledge, are the subjects, and their capacity for causal efficiency is [the probandum].

The reason is "ra" (the letter *ra*). In this regard, because it is impossible to take as the subject (*dharmin*) anything that is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within any inference establishing a positive entity, and because inference operates everywhere only with respect to objects of valid cognition, what other pervasion (*vyāpti*) could there be for the establishment of the probandum? Since the subject is within the scope of valid cognition, there is no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the proof; nor is there an "unestablished nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because in those cases where external causal efficiency is beyond dispute—

There is no concern at all regarding those [objects] that are directly perceived. Even in cases where there is no direct ascertainment of them, the establishment of their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is faultless precisely because they generate a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This occurs directly in the case of perception and indirectly in the case of inference.
Regarding this, some say: "How is it that the capacity of a cause which produces an effect is established only for that [effect]?"

What is the establishment of existence (*sattva*)? If that [existence] is not established, then even the root lacks causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*). Now, just as the seed possesses efficacy in relation to the sprout, so too let the sprout possess efficacy in relation to the leaf, the stalk, and so forth; and likewise, let cognition possess efficacy in relation to another cognition, memory, verbal expression, purposeful activity, and so on, or in relation to its own and others' benefit and so forth.

This might be so: if there were no ultimate termination in the succession of effects, then one could not establish momentary destruction by considering even a single thing that performs some purposeful action; for if every effect were itself ultimately non-performative of purposeful action, then by the consequence that all preceding things would possess that same nature, not even a single thing capable of purposeful action would be established. Thus, there is no lack of proof.

The rebuttal: Furthermore, as for the claim that even if existence (*sattā*) is established through distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no impairment of its being an effect (*kāryatva*), that too is not correct. For if existence is established despite a difference in exclusion, how could "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) also be established? [For it consists in] coming into being after not having existed.

For you, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and coming into existence (*bhavana*) are nothing other than the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Therefore, as long as there is doubt regarding the capacity for causal efficiency, it is impossible to say that "it exists. Furthermore, even the definition of being produced as "the state of depending on the operation of another for the completion of its own nature" is not a property of a non-existent thing. And existence (*sattā*) is indeed causal efficiency itself. Thus, properties such as "being differentiated by a difference in conditions," which belong to existent things, cannot be predicated when the existence [of the subject] is not yet certain.
Thus: 1. [the property] desired in the proof (sādhanādiṣṭa), 2. in the locus (dharmiṇi), 6. or (vā), 7. existence (sattā) [is the probandum]. (ra, ā, asi)

The section on the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), concerning the logical reason of capacity (*sāmarthyahetu*): [a 4] "of the seed," [a 5] "there is no," [ra 4] "desire for," [āra 9] "establishment of existence," [ra 10] "the distinction between the distinct and the distinguisher."

To this it is replied: First of all, sprouts and the like—which appear clearly in a perceptual consciousness that has attained proficiency through specific practice and is entirely free from the suspicion of error—cannot be said to be non-existent, even though their fruit is not seen. Otherwise, there would be no confidence even regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and consequently, due to the absence of any transaction with what is other than the real, the world would be rendered inactive.
The world would arise [from nothing].

Now, if you argue that the very definition of existence (*sattva*) for you is simply the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), then should the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) be stated by means of a definition established merely by convention? If so, then this [definition] constitutes a flaw in your own definition as well.

Let that which is intended to be stated in due order be explained. For us, however, the preparation is not for the sake of establishing its definition, but rather for the sake of proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of that definition. Therefore, the failure to ascertain its definition would only create an obstacle to the proof of momentary destruction regarding the effect. But when another effect is observed, who can prevent the production of an inference regarding that [momentariness] as well, through the same sequence? Now...

Since only that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), it has already been stated that there is no fault whatsoever even if the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are unestablished in what lies outside the subject. Therefore, even when the conventional definition [of perception] is impaired, how much more so in the case of mere non-ascertainment, given that [the object] is supported by the force of a very clear perception?

"In the case of an entity, such as a sprout or similar thing, there is a contradiction with the property of being an effect. With respect to that, the seed and so forth are indeed capable of sustaining the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*); how then can [their] existence be unestablished?
But surely, if sensory perception does not touch upon either the capacity for causal efficiency or any other characteristic of an entity, how can it establish their status as real entities?

Why is it said to be "established"? Even that [is not established], because there is no room for considering other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding whatever is experienced. For it is observed that even without the mention of scriptural definitions, activity directed toward an object—based merely on the arising of a perception conditioned by habituation—is accompanied by non-contradiction; so what can be done in this matter? However, it might be thus: if, in the ultimate sense, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)...

If the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) alone constitutes reality, then by that perception which delineates the object as the locus of its arising—namely, "this arises from that"—it is precisely this capacity for causal efficiency that has been delineated. On the other hand, if the definition of reality is something else entirely, then it is that [other thing] which has been delineated. For example, just as when blue is perceived by a cognition grasping blue, its being composed of the three qualities (*triguṇamayatva*) or some other property not delineated [by that cognition] is not apprehended; thus, it is established that [the latter] does not belong to that [perceived object].

Even in the theory that [the sprout] is an effect, although no other effect is observed when the manifesting agent (*adhyakṣa*) is present, the cause [is established]; [this applies] even to non-existent things such as a cloth and so forth. In the *Ajñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, [it is said]: "The capacity of the object [is established] by means of the seed and so forth. In that case, let the seed and so forth also be [established] simply from the arising of direct perception (*pratyakṣodaya*), just like the effect (*kārya*).

If it is asked, "Why seek causal capacity when [the object] is an existing entity?"—we reply: it is certainly not that we disregard the acuity of perception in the practical engagement with entities and instead follow the objective power [of the cause], for even that [power] is dependent upon perception. Rather, it is to compel the acceptance of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

For the practical engagement with entities produced by perception, according to the sequence described, is common to both what possesses that characteristic and what does not; it is not, however, common to the proof of momentariness.

It prevails by necessity. However, although the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not itself the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastulakṣaṇa*), wherever it exists of its own accord, it necessarily does not enter into the existence of its own nature without bringing that [capacity] along with it. Therefore, it is established that its introduction here is as a means of proof (*sādhana*), and not as the defining characteristic of a real entity.

Thus, even regarding cognition, self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is invariably concomitant with existence; everything is as previously stated. By this also, it should be understood that the establishment of the object's causal capacity (*sāmarthyasiddhi*) remains unimpeded. For when one thing is perceived by another, there is room for the suspicion of error; however, in the case of self-awareness, such [error] is altogether absent. Now, if one were to disagree regarding self-awareness, then [one would have to agree that] even [cognition] inherent in the same object...

If cognition is accepted as being apprehended by knowledge, then—just as in the case of a sprout and so forth—there is no fault whatsoever, since its own nature is presented by another [cognition]. Otherwise, the loss of all empirical activity regarding perceived objects would result in every respect. Now, one might ask: how is the causal relationship between the object and the cognition to be understood, given that the object does not exist prior to its perception?

Is it because of non-apprehension? We reply: it is by virtue of the power of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, the undertaking of determining whether an external object is stable or otherwise occurs only when such an object exists.

Therefore, just as in the case of taking a collection of things that perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as the subject of the thesis, even when taking the entire range of objects within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the subject, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*)—of either kind—regarding the nature of the substratum for the proof of instability.

Now, if it is argued that because the causal capacity of an object cannot withstand analysis in every respect, one should take "everything" as the subject (*pakṣa*)—namely, that "everything lacks causal capacity"—or if one asks what the proof (*sādhana*) is: [we reply] surely, the capacity of seeds and the like for sprouts and so forth is observed; for there is no such thing as the "impossible" regarding what is observed.
Indeed, experience alone is the limit of all that is called the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, how can one who does not accept this be considered an authority (*prāmāṇika*)?

Will you infer fire even from smoke? Would you adopt a behavior toward water and fire similar to that toward wind, heat, cold, or hunger? Or would you rather remain inactive? How is it that you yourself, when an opponent has put forward a proof while falsely attributing a power [to it] that does not exist, are one who—knowing its absence and desiring his defeat—is answered by the presentation of a refutation? Even in that case, you should take care to state only [the fallacies of] "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth.

Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*)? It follows from this that there is no cognition even by means of itself. Therefore, you must say that someone has been deceived by something. But the capacity [of cognition] regarding objects is difficult to deny. If it is fallacious, it is so conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), not in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*).
Let it be as it may, whether conventionally or ultimately; what is the point of insisting on this?

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), under the section concerning the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*),
there is this thought: "Now, if momentariness were also merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtī*), being endowed with a power that is itself conventional, it would not be ultimate (*pāramārthikī*)."

Regarding this, it is said: Here, virtuous persons begin an investigation into the eternal, the non-eternal, and so forth, on the grounds that the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*) is the cause for the fruits of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). For if there were no certainty regarding that [reality], such practice would be impossible. Now, as for that practice, is it the cause of its fruit when assisted by an eternal Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth, or is it independent of Him? It is in regard to such a topic that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—

The entry into the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is for those skilled in critical investigation. Here, if this conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—which is the means to the supreme human goal and which is inseparable from the persistence of causal capacity—is indeed merely conventional, then let momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) also be merely conventional, since we have respect for momentariness precisely because it serves the supreme human goal. What is the use of our investigating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), wherein neither means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor object of cognition (*prameya*) [is established]?

Is there some distinction, such as the conventional practice of the probandum and the probans? Or, if such [distinctions] were possible even in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then the emergence of causal power (*śakti*) would be excluded from that, or momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) following upon it would not attain the status of being ultimately real. However, in the absence of the distinction between means of knowledge and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vibhāga*), whether through the total exclusion of consciousness or through the establishment of pure self-consciousness alone, [there can be no] "residing in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.

Just as at the time of determining existence, the proof of momentary destruction does not cause distress even if it is not [ultimately] real. Therefore, why does one who is terrified that the proof of momentariness is unreal not also fear that the attainment of the fruits of heaven and liberation is non-ultimate?

Consequently, as long as there is the conventional practice of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, so long is it "capable of withstanding examination"—this alone is the ultimate [reality].
The state of being a mere semblance [of a reason] is the fundamental flaw, because any further subtle investigation would be as good as non-existent. Enough of this excessive detail.

By this, it has been demonstrated that everything described by the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, who is fixated on an improper position, after raising a series of arguments to refute the commentator’s [Udayana’s] theory of causality, is entirely useless. For instance, if the utility of such great effort lies merely in pointing out its lack of proof (*asiddhatā*), then what is to be done with this? And as for the lack of proof...

[The objection] has been refuted, because [the capacity] is conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*), since for one engaged in the investigation of the reality of things, [the establishment of capacity] is an inseparable concomitant operation. Therefore, that which was stated—that "consequently, the pervasion [of the production of an effect] by either succession or simultaneity is also unestablished"—is likewise without foundation. Furthermore, whatever [was argued] by him regarding those various doubts, out of pride in his own rebuttal, ultimately [leads to the conclusion of] its conventional nature (*sāṃvṛtatva*).
Because it falls under the category of activity:
"That which is capable of causal efficiency is, in this context, ultimately real" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.3).

This was written after raising the objection that the statement in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, "In whatever way something is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) conventionally, in that same way it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*)," is redundant.

If it is asked: "Why is existence not likewise accepted for universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth?"—and if it is argued that "these lack causal efficacy even conventionally" (*saṃvṛttyā*)—we say no, because the appearance of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is equal in both cases. For instance, wherever the eye functions, there the appearance of a pillar and so forth occurs, unlike the appearance of hair and such to one with ophthalmia; thus, the causal efficacy of the pillar and so forth is established.

Likewise, the cognition of a genus such as "cow" does not arise with respect to buffaloes and the like; nor does the cognition of the conjunction of a whole arise with respect to mere atoms that lack conjunction and so forth. Thus, it is argued that the capacity [of a universal] is understood from this. That too is without substance. For one should not accept or reject something merely because it is a conventional construction (*saṃvṛti*), since that would entail the acceptance even of the conventions of children. Anticipating the objection that "the superimposition of a property (*dharma*) constitutes a distinction," [the author replies]: "Indeed, its capacity (*śakti*) consists in the completeness of its auxiliary factors (*sahakāri*); its incapacity (*aśakti*) consists in their deficiency. Therefore, when there is a deficiency of auxiliaries, it is said to be 'incapable' previously; and when there is completeness [of auxiliaries] later, it is said to be 'capable. Furthermore, the difference between the property and the substratum (*dharmin*) has been established. Consequently, even when capacity arises, the [substratum] itself does not necessarily arise [as something new]. [This applies to] incapacity..."
Even when [the attribute] ceases, there is no necessary cessation of that which possesses it, because there is no essential connection [between them].

All of this should be understood as already refuted by the demonstration of the non-difference between the property and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) in the discussion on *apoha*, since it is the property-possessor itself that exists in such a state through the manifestation and disappearance of its totality and partiality.
Or let there indeed be a distinction between the property and the substratum. Nor do we dispute that auxiliary causes are ineffective;
however, it is not the case that those auxiliaries alone produce the effect, nor does the totality itself bring about the effect, but rather [the substratum] as well.

This is the state of affairs. Since they have already exerted themselves for that purpose, there is no need for further elaboration. And if the very same nature of that entity—which possesses the property of performing its function in its final moment—is present in the first moment as well, then it must necessarily act at that very time;
even the curse of the gods could not prevent it, let alone this [attack] of yours, which is rendered feeble by the agony of a mortal wound.

By mere outcry? For just as, in order to avoid the consequence of [the entity's] destruction due to its being either capable or incapable, capacity and incapacity are conceived as having distinct natures— characterized by the properties of completeness and deficiency— likewise, that nature which consists of the property of non-delayed action cannot be said to be distinct from the entity itself, because it would follow that the entity is a non-agent.
And just as we maintain that capacity and incapacity are two distinct properties, and yet there is nothing in the entity itself due to the arising or passing away of those two,
so too, the property of non-delayed action and the property of delayed action are merely other distinct properties.

"It arises and passes away by virtue of the presence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-sannidhāna-pratyaya*). In that very same way, it is said that there is nothing [intrinsic] to the entity (*bhāva*) itself. Let this be said.
However, let it be granted that for now there is no production of an effect, because that which is considered the cause remains in its identical state.

For instance, just as it is neither the auxiliary causes alone nor the totality alone that is the producer, so too, when the totality is present, there is capacity. If it is argued that this is not so—[if one says] "there is no capacity in the totality"—then [the response is]: "There is capacity in the totality. [If one asks] whether this is a property of the subject (dharmin)—[the answer is] yes. [If one asks] by way of its location—[the answer is] yes. [If one asks] "only by the auxiliaries"—this is not found in manuscript A. For this purpose, it is understood by Gopendra. It is capable. A.

Even the quality of performing an action without delay (*akṣepakriyādharmatva*), once it has arisen, does not produce the entity in question independently; for even if it were a producer, one must admit that the entity itself is the producer. However, the entity in question must also be accepted as the agent. And since its form is not distinct from its previous state, if it performs [the action] now, it should have performed it previously; or, if it does not perform it now, it would not perform it later either.

"To do so" refers to that very state of being subject to defeat. However, if the occasional nature [of the effect] is due to another entity, such as "completeness" (*sākalya*) and so forth, as its cause, then it is logical that the effect is also occasional in dependence upon that. In this way, for every further postulation of an additional property (*dharmāntara*), the entity remains indifferent [to the causal process]. Now, if the property of "non-delayed action" (*akṣepakriyā-dharmatva*) has arisen, but the effect...

In that case, what is this logic? That [capacity] must necessarily be produced by the effect. And since that property of non-delayed action (akṣepakriyā-dharmatva) already existed previously, there would be no occasion for the arising of the effect. If that is so, then the production of the effect is necessarily concomitant with the non-delayed action, and the non-delayed action is necessarily concomitant with the production of the effect; thus, mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) is evident.

Otherwise, if non-delayed action (*akṣepakāritva*) were not necessarily concomitant with the production of the effect, then the production of the effect would not be implied by non-delayed action. And if the production of the effect were not necessarily concomitant with non-delayed action, then it would have to occur even prior to [the state of] non-delayed action. But if they share the same objective, then once the totality [of conditions] has arisen, what is the use of this other property (*dharmāntara*), namely non-delayed action, which has now come into being?

Is it argued that the effect is produced by means of speech? If that were so, the aforementioned defect would not be avoided. For there is no dispute regarding the production of the effect itself; rather, the point to be considered is how the effect can be occasional, given that its own nature—which the emergence of the effect depends upon—remains eternally the same.

Therefore, if this designation "that which has the property of non-delayed action" or "that which produces" is applied by virtue of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how could that [nature] ever fail to produce [the effect] if it existed even previously? Or, if the prior entity—which possesses a nature opposed to non-delayed action—were to persist later, how could the effect possibly arise at any time? Alternatively, what if that very [entity] alone were the sole agent?

This is logical; however, since it is the totality (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer, at a time when other auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) are absent, even a powerful [cause] does not give rise to the effect—what contradiction is there in this? Furthermore, "auxiliary-ness" (*sahakāritva*) was stated on the basis of performing a single purpose, not on the basis of providing a benefit (*upakāra*).
To this, it is replied: if they produce the effect while being conjoined, then that which is characterized by the performance of a single purpose—

Let it be that these [causes] possess the quality of cooperation; who is there to deny it? But how can it be established that the effect must be produced by them acting together? For if the preceding and succeeding effects were identical, then the unavoidable consequence would follow that the entity must be subject to one of the two—either perpetual production or perpetual non-production. Therefore, for those who maintain the doctrine of permanence, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, not a single individual cause.
The object of desire is something else. If it is argued that "it is observed to be thus," [we reply]: for this very reason, the position of stability is not tenable.

[The opponent] says: "Indeed, every reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) culminates in its opposite (viparyaya). Therefore, if the producer were eternal, the produced effect would either exist at all times or not exist at any time at all. But this is not the case; since the production of an effect occurs only occasionally despite [the cause's] completeness, there is a contradiction of its inherent nature (svabhāvabhaṅga)."

Now, if it were observed anywhere that something is eternally and at all times devoid of causes, then the consequence of its being an agent at all times would follow from the admission of its eternity. However, since such a thing never exists, how can such a consequence be urged?

This too is vulgar. For instance, regarding the phrase "if it were eternal," this is its meaning: if that very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity which exists at a later time and is productive were to exist at an earlier time;
or if that very nature which exists at an earlier time and is non-productive were to exist at a later time—then production or non-production would be perceived precisely in that same way.

It might be so. And that being the case, if there were a superimposition of identity upon two things already established, then either production or non-production would necessarily follow as an established fact.
Is there anything contradictory here in saying that this occurs because identity between prior and subsequent natures is possible when [the thing] is eternal? Or, if you think:
"Since identity between the prior and the subsequent is not perceived, how can it be superimposed?"—then the same would apply even in the case of mother-of-pearl.
There can be no superimposition (āropa) by means of silver; for mother-of-pearl in the form of silver has never been an object of perception anywhere.

It is your own established doctrine that the silver which is superimposed must have been perceived at some time, otherwise there could be no superimposition. Thus it is with the [object of] inference.

Even in the case at hand, I do not perceive the identity of the prior and posterior natures; however, the prior and posterior natures being superimposed upon one another are indeed established. Thus, both the performance and non-performance of that superimposition are equally appropriate, just as there is burning when fire is superimposed upon a cluster of *guñjā* seeds.

Thus, Śaṅkara has revealed his own extreme frivolity; for this negation by the Buddhists—stating that "non-momentary things do not exist"—is as irrelevant as the perception of blue and other colors by those blind from birth. Therefore, this remains established: the necessity of producing an effect through conjunction occurs only if there is a stable nature, [otherwise] it is like the daydreams of the unfortunate.

And this being the case, one who rejects the conventional usage of the word "power" (*śakti*) when the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-sākalya*) is present is merely a pretender. Furthermore, what purpose does he fulfill by deceiving others through the mention of something irrelevant and useless, other than [causing] delusion? [This applies to the doctrine of] momentariness—

For it is appropriate for this [opponent] to provide a refutation according to the specific nature of power and incapacity intended by the proponent— who, by superimposing contradictory properties through their respective natures of being capable or incapable, attributes a distinction [between them]. Abandoning that, however, he himself [superimposes] a single identity upon that which has arisen from its own causes, [claiming] the existence of non-existence...

[The opponent] nourishes the meaning of "momentary" (kṣaṇika) through convention (saṃketa); 9. for the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin), there is no power (śakti); 10. thus [he] constructs a rebuttal by means of convention; this is a great skill of the preeminent Naiyāyika, who [argues] that fire exists here because of smoke.

He says that it must be so: even in that case, if someone were to establish the convention of the word "smoke" for a donkey or the like and then deny fire, there would be no fault. For the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādī) maintains that the designation "that which produces" refers to the nature of the cause as being capable with respect to the effect that occurs immediately after it. Nor is this merely a novel convention; for even in the world, [the relationship between cause and effect] is established precisely through the act of production.

This is the conventional usage regarding capacity (*śakti*). Although production occurs only when there is completeness (*sākalya*), nevertheless, a thing is not called "capable" by way of its completeness, but rather because of its production. For even when completeness is present, if it is delayed, the direct conventional usage of "capacity" is absent; yet, since production is observed even when the completeness of specific auxiliary factors has not been definitively ascertained, the convention "this is capable in this respect" is employed.

And such an essential nature (*svarūpa*) is called "power" (*śakti*). Although there is a designation of difference in the expression "the power of this," it is non-different from it, just like the expression "the essential nature of this. Furthermore, that generative nature exists even prior [to the act of generating]; yet, it does not follow that it must necessarily generate, for that would lead to the absurdity of saying "she is both a mother and a barren woman. In this context, even if you were to employ the word "power" in some instance...
If that were done, then the manifestation and disappearance of those two would have no effect whatsoever on the entity. Consequently, what follows for the case at hand?

For if that which is non-different from the producer and the produced form does not undergo arising and passing away, how could there be occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatā*) of the effect? Or, if it is joined with arising and passing away, its difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) remains as before.

If, however, even that [subsequent state] does not produce a distinct form, then its own existence would be severed by its arising and passing away; it would simply be a non-productive entity, which constitutes the destruction of the root. Therefore, you must say: for that which produces something [distinct], there is indeed a difference [between states] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties—namely, the capacities and incapacities of its nature—at different times relative to the effect.

Therefore, as the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* has said: "In that case, there is no contradiction because of the difference in time; just as a crystal is motionless prior to the arising of an action, and that very same [crystal] is subsequently possessed of motion. If it is argued that this is not a valid example because it is something yet to be proven (*sādhya*), we reply: no, for that which is established by means of valid cognition cannot be considered "yet to be proven. Thus, even the distinction [between entities] based on the imposition of contradictory properties remains unproven.

How can one who speaks thus be deterred? Therefore, in whatever manner a contradiction between two properties is observed, it must be accepted in that very same way. Just as a single cause is capable with respect to its own effect but incapable with respect to another effect—and thus the capacity and incapacity of one and the same thing toward different objects are not contradictory—so too, even when there is a difference in capacity due to a difference in time, there is no contradiction in the identity of the possessor of that capacity.

"Because there is no difference between the two cases regarding the establishment by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This too is without substance; for with this [argument], one merely mimics the grandiosity of a mass of beeswax. To explain: indeed, it is not possible to assert that "establishment by means of valid cognition" occurs while setting aside perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). And in that context, perception is nothing other than conceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā-vikalpa*), which has already been refuted.

"Like the exclusion of a real entity. Since there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the reason is indeed positive (*anvayin*). If it is argued that "there is a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*) because there is no contradiction between cognizability (*prameyatva*) and momentariness," we reply: No, for cognizability is not established for anything in the state of momentariness; this is because that which has the property of existing for only a single moment has already passed away by the time of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and furthermore, if what is past were perceptible—
This is a mere consequence; that too is nothing more than a wishful thought. For instance: let there be no apprehension of the past;

rather, the apprehension of the present—which is momentary—will occur by means of a momentary cognition. Therefore, there is indeed no contradiction between being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

Now, if it is argued that because an object is the cause [of cognition], an entity whose existence is required prior to the knowledge [of it] would not be graspable at all if it did not persist into another moment; or else, if it were to persist into another moment, it would simply be non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*)—then is this some royal decree that an object must not be graspable if it is not a producer [of cognition]? Or is this merely its established convention (*samaya*)?

This is the occasion for logic (*nyāya*), not for convention (*samaya*). Therefore, one who is devoted to debate should instruct the opponent by presenting logic, without relying on convention. For if convention were the means of proof, then since everything would be established [by it], there would be no such thing as "logic."
But how could logic, which exists precisely for the sake of refuting conventional consensus, take that very convention as its refuge?

If it is asked: "How can there be apprehension by that which has not yet arisen? And if this were so, would it not lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? [We reply: How, then, can there be apprehension even by that which has already arisen? For a cognition arises while experiencing its object. And that [arising] must be either produced by the object itself or produced by something else; what is the difference? As for the charge of over-extension, it is common to both cases, since the cognition is also produced by the eyes and other [senses]. [The opponent says: "But that [cognition] does not have the object as its..."

If it is argued that this is because [the universal] possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then—surely an object is only designated as such when it is actually being perceived; there is no such thing as an "object" restricted by its genus (*jāti*) that exists apart from perception. Therefore, since it is not an object and thus not being perceived, the reply "it is not perceived" is irrelevant here. For instance, if you say that the sense organ itself is not perceived precisely because of its intrinsic nature, we say no; for yogins do perceive it.

Because [the object] is accepted [as being grasped]. If it is argued that this restriction is made with respect to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), then, in that case, even subtle objects and the like would be grasped by their very nature; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Alternatively, the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produced the preceding cognition [produces] the momentary object.
One should make it possess light and form, so that there may be simultaneous perception.

Now, in the *Ājñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, by him [it is said]:
"Or rather, the cognition produced, restricted to its own object, apprehends only that [object], or [is produced] by the causal complex of that [object]."

Now, for the proponent of cognition with form (sākāravādin), the arising of the awareness of its own nature is held to proceed from the object itself.

In this regard, if there were the apprehension of the past, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and if there were persistence through the moment of apprehension, the establishment of stability (*sthirasiddhi*) would follow—this is what is intended.
