If that were the case, because it results in a contrary conclusion (*viparyayaparyavasāna*), there would be either the establishment of stability for you or the apprehension of the past; thus, it would follow that the cognition of the nature of the object does not arise from the object itself. Thus...

And this being the case, the maxim applies: "One thing has been eaten, another has been vomited. For one who has begun to establish a stable [object], the cognition of forms (sākārabodha) is undermined by its opposite.
Now, if it is merely said that for the Sautrāntika both of these are inconsistent, even that is not the case.

For, according to the position that sensation arises with a form (*sākāra*), even if it persists into the second moment, the manifestation of an object is impossible because the object is insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, the cognition of an object is simply the self-cognition of a nature that possesses a form similar to [that of] the opposite [object]. And thus, there is no need to conform to the present, since the connection with that cognition does not cease even in the case of the past. Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because [the cognition] possesses similarity (*sārūpya*) with the object itself, and not with other objects.

Because of the surrender [of that position]. Nor is it the case that "the maintenance of that view is the subject at hand. For you, however, it is established that even by resorting to that view, the reason *prameyatva* (knowability) is not capable of proving stability;
thus, the avoidance of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy is accomplished. Therefore, regarding an entity of stable form, there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since even a diamond, when struck by the blow of a *siddha*, is shattered in its wings and belly—how much more so, then, the wretched crystal?
Thus, this [diamond], being split apart between its states of activity and inactivity, how can it serve as an example for the absence of contradiction despite a difference in state?

Furthermore, the attempt to establish that there is no contradiction between power and impotence based on a difference in time, just as there is none based on a difference in object, is likewise irrelevant here.

For in all cases, a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a property that acts as an antagonist. Now, the non-performance of another's function is not the antagonist to the performance of one's own function; rather, it is the non-performance of one's own function [that is its antagonist]. Likewise, the performance of another's function is the antagonist to the non-performance of another's function, not the performance of one's own function. Indeed, it is precisely in order to exclude the non-performance of one's own function that one says, "it performs its own function."
Furthermore, perception establishes that which performs its own function as distinct from that which performs the function of another through the difference between entities.

However, perception does not establish identity across a difference in time, because recognition has already been refuted. Consequently, the performance and non-performance of its own function, being the only remaining alternatives, are insufficient to resolve the contradiction.

In the chapter on momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the section on positive concomitance (*anvaya*) begins:
"If it is argued that the performance and non-performance of one's own effect with respect to multiple points of time is contradictory, [we reply: such dependence may indeed exist."

It has already been largely stated that if there were a functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes non-difference between things possessing distinct parts, as there is a difference in their objects, then [non-duality would follow]. If it is asked: "Even for you, what is the proof for the persistence of contradiction if that [non-difference] is disregarded?"—the answer is precisely what was said: "Whatever is capable of producing something at a certain time, that necessarily produces it at that time," and so forth; and regarding the dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), [it concerns] their presence or absence.

Because [the opponent's position] has already been refuted in the context of the production of effects, therefore, for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), the very nature of producing [an effect] is what is intended by the term "capacity" (*śakti*). And if there were a difference in that [nature], how could there not be a loss of the entity?
Nor is this the case here.

And as for what has been prattled by the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*: "Even if it is admitted that the power is distinct from the possessor of power, nevertheless, there is not necessarily a difference between the potent and the non-potent. Why? Because even in your own system, the rule that a difference in attributes necessitates a difference in the substratum is unestablished. And thus, while demonstrating the separate utility of auxiliary causes even when the effect is distinct, it was stated:"

Having written in the *Hetubindu*: "From the lump of clay, from those things whose nature is clay," and so forth; and [having argued] that just as there is no difference in the effect despite the difference in natures such as the essence of clay (*mṛdātmatā*), so too there will be non-difference despite the difference in natures such as being capable or incapable, because the uncontradicted determination is the same—this too has been refuted by the following: for there certainly exist properties (*dharma*) which are mutually...

There are both contradictory and non-contradictory [attributes], but contradiction and non-contradiction do not reside in the attributes (*dharma*) alone. For it cannot be asserted that because Brahminhood is not contradicted by grammaticality, it must likewise not be contradicted by being an outcaste (*cāṇḍālatva*);
indeed, being an outcaste is pervaded by [the absence of] Brahminhood. Nor is it the case that it is not contradicted even by grammaticality. And as in this case, with respect to its own...

The state of being other than a Brahmin who is a yogi creates a contradiction, but not with [the state of] being a grammarian; likewise, the nature of producing [something] is contradictory only with non-production, and not with a difference in the continuum of the entity. However, blueness, squareness, and so forth may encounter contradiction with whiteness, circularity, and so forth, but never with cause-and-effect relations and the like. Therefore, if there were even a scent of contradiction—

Because of their coexistence, the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and the clay-nature must exist as non-different from the same substratum (*dharmin*). Therefore, who with any intelligence would consider it possible that two things which are absolutely opposed—such as that which produces a certain effect and its opposite—could also belong to one and the same thing? If it is asked, "How is it to be understood whether something is contradictory or not? [the answer is: When there is the affirmation (*vidhāna*) of one thing through the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of another, or the exclusion of one thing through the affirmation of another...

Exclusion (*ccheda*) is contradictory to that [affirmation]. Nor can there even be a suspicion of the exclusion of "bulbous-bellied-ness" by the injunction "made of clay," for by the mention of its producer, the non-production of it is indeed excluded, and by the non-production of it, its production is excluded. Nor is there [any change in] color or configuration...

And when the measure [of the causal factors] is equal, equality ought to result for other seeds as well. It has been shown in the discussion beginning with "the cognition of the higher and the lower" (*aparāparapratyaya*) that even when there is some perception of similarity, the only recourse in answering [the objection] is the difference in the power of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).
Therefore, what was stated—namely, "But [the sprouts] born from the same granary... and so forth—is refuted; for [the distinction between them depends on] the seen and the unseen (*dṛṣṭādṛṣṭa*)...

In the transformation of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), there occurs a succession of specific inherent natures (*svabhāvabheda*) in the seed, which—through the cooperative condition of the soil and other auxiliary factors—produces, via a series of transformations, either the initial excellence (*atiśaya*) or the sprout itself. Other moments of the seed (*bījakṣaṇa*) do not possess such power, because they lack that specific nature due to the absence of the preceding causal succession. Is it possible?

To this it is replied: Indeed, in all cases, causes are of two kinds—seen and unseen; this is established for all those who maintain the reality of all things (Sarvāstivādins). The variety [of objects] is not inferred through sound alone. Furthermore, that which is perceived (*dṛśya*) is twofold: having a nature pertaining to this world, and being either visible or invisible.

Each of these, in turn, is twofold—being inherent in a conscious entity (*cetana*) or inherent in an unconscious entity (*acetana*)—thus becoming fourfold. Therefore, the entire causal complex (*hetusāmagrī*) is not perceptible in every aspect to an ordinary person.

The same applies to external things as well.
Regarding entities: for the learned, it is accepted that the totality of all effects arises from both common and uncommon causes.

thus, even when the specific [cause] is not determined, there exists some distinguished cause or utility that is impossible for anything else, [and this is known] in a general sense.

"From the connection with a cause of transformation, there is the determination of a difference in the nature of a member [of a causal series]. Consequently, because such a difference in nature is possible, that very same seed is employed for the sake of producing a specific quality conducive to the generation of the sprout, even through a continuous succession."
Thus it is established that there are no other seed-moments.

It cannot be that of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because even when there is a determination of gross unity and homogeneity through the similarity of form, the subtle internal difference [remains unperceived].

Because that which has not been determined by it cannot be negated. The persistence [of the material cause] is not contradicted; thus, the mutual exclusion of excellence [between cause and effect] has not been established through perception regarding the subject at hand. Nor is it established through inference.

Thus, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by being either unitary or manifold, and either dependent or independent.

Because of the absence of a third possibility; for the negation of one of these two is inseparable from the affirmation of the other. And because it is impossible; for there exists precisely a subverting [reason]. Therefore, nothing is achieved merely by proclaiming what is undesirable.

By this, it is shown that "assistance" is not the meaning of "dependence," so there is indeed no dependence on auxiliary factors for a momentary entity, nor is there the exclusion of both [alternatives].
Now, if "acting together" is the meaning of dependence, even then, if that requires a qualification such as "of that which was previously existing," then...
For that which is momentary, there is no such thing as "non-dependence," because it is independent and undecaying.

Now, if one says "of that which previously existed," then it does not depend [on anything else]; however, since the meaning of dependence is merely the requirement of a cause for that which exists in a combined state, in that case there is indeed dependence, not non-dependence. Even so, there is still no exclusion of both [possibilities].

[20b] Now, if from our perspective there is a state of dependence, then we have established that what is dependent is indeed incapable. Thus, the formal determination is this: that which is incapable with respect to a particular effect is dependent, whereas that which is capable is independent. And in that case, since the affirmation of one follows from the negation of the other, that which is devoid of capability becomes indeed capable.
[This refers to] efficacy. And it has been said:
"It is indeed efficacious"; thus, there is certainly no exclusion of both [states] in the case of momentariness.

This must be so, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the causelessness of the diversity of effects.

This is appropriate for Vācaspati; otherwise, how could a single seed produce an entire series beginning with the sprout, the stalk, the earth-dwelling [root], and so forth? This much alone suffices to resolve the matter. Nor is this an objection, because if the intended meaning were a denial of the production of multiple effects from a single cause according to the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even from a single lamp, multiple effects such as the transformation of the wick and so forth are observed to arise.
It causes one to place reliance on the superintendent of the path, which is entirely the opposite of those [other views].

If it is asked, "How so?"—surely, when an investigation is conducted by placing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at the forefront, beginning with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and then enumerating the remaining ones, once something has been established or sublated by that [perception], no other [means of knowledge] has the authority to either sublate or establish it. This is because of the [nature of] the means of valid cognition...
As for one who transgresses the path, let it suffice to say that the same kind of reply must be given;

however, how could there be a cause for a momentary existence of the earth? For even here, it is not logical to assert a contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), because the moment (*kṣaṇa*) lies beyond the scope of such perception. Even then, if one who is a single causal agent does not become a non-agent...

If [the reason] is pervasion (*vyāpti*), then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of a lamp itself. If, on the other hand, it is argued that "that which produces a sprout is not a cause of earth," then there is an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy. If it is asked, "How can that which is the cause of a sprout be the cause of another?"—is it the cause of the sprout alone, or of the sprout as well [as others], or does it belong to the sprout for now while being uncertain regarding others? And in all three of these positions, [the reason] remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

The fallacies of contradiction (*viruddha*) and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) are respectively difficult to avoid. Therefore, there is no operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*) here. Even the presentation of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) occurs by means of what is accepted by the opponent; however, it is not the position of the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) that a single [cause] is a non-producer of multiple [effects]. Thus, for one who is not a fool, the consequence that the effect must be singular because of the singularity of the entity within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not tenable. Furthermore, when there is dependence upon a cause characterized as a causal complex...

It is established that even for distinct things such as sprouts and the like, there is a conformity to the difference or non-difference of their causes; thus, it does not follow that sprouts and the like must become one simply because they conform to non-difference. For just as sprouts and the like, despite being individual effects, possess both distinct and non-distinct natures, so too the seeds and other factors denoted by the term "causal complex" (sāmagrī), while each acting as a cause, are likewise both distinct and non-distinct.

The difference [of effects] is established by the difference of their causes. Now, if seeds and the like, though distinct in nature, are brought within the scope of a single conventional designation (*ekavyavahāra*) due to some proximity (*pratyāsatti*), then sprouts and the like are likewise so designated; thus, when there is no difference in the cause, non-difference is also established. In that regard, regarding the single purpose of each of the causes—

The state of being a producer (*janakatva*) is the cause for the linguistic convention of "one"; however, the fact that effects are each produced by one [individual cause] is the same [in both cases]. Therefore, why must sprouts and the like be unified? For even when there is dependence upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that much alone is sufficient to account for the conformity to the difference or non-difference of causes. And this is so even for the opponent who understands the term "cause" as referring to the causal complex; [it remains true] regarding difference—

O Dhāriṇī, [this is] verse 6.0. Through investigation (vicāreṇa), there is no [such thing as] "it moves" (veti) [in reality]. There is no [distinction between] proof and refutation (sādhanabādhanayoḥ).
The distinction of moments (kṣaṇabhedasya) transcends the sphere of sensory perception (gocarātikrānta).
That [distinction] is not established by its own difference. It is established [as such].

There is no [separation] between the two; they are indeed distinct. Thus it is not the case that there is no production. Or rather, in the *Ratnākaraśrījñāna-nibandhāvalī*, it is stated that the non-production of the two distinctions is expressed "in accordance with the intellect" (*buddhayanurodhāt*). But in reality, it is like a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
It has already been shown that just as [the collection] is intended to be expressed, so too difference and non-difference—namely, dissimilarity and similarity—are intended to be expressed.

Now, one might object: "Even now, since there is no 'causal totality' (sāmagrī) other than the individual members of the totality, it follows that the similarity or dissimilarity of the effects depends solely upon the similarity or dissimilarity of those very members that constitute the totality. This is indeed so; however, it does not refer to [the similarity or dissimilarity of] those things situated within that aggregate relative to one another.

An examination of similarity and so forth: However, it is like the determination of similarity or its opposite between one army and another army, based on their respective own types while they exist within distinct aggregates. In that regard, if as many things of such a kind—which are accepted as causes and fall within the scope of a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) based on a single causal complex—as exist in one place, were to exist in exactly the same way in another time or place, then that [other] complex would be similar.

And since its effect is similar [to it], by the word "effect" (*kārya*) as well, only the aggregate (*puñja*) is meant. The meaning is that however many and of whatever kind effects have arisen in one place, exactly those many and of those same kinds arise elsewhere as well. However, if there were dissimilarity (*vaisadṛśya*), then the effect, being differentiated by degrees of difference, would itself be differentiated by degrees of difference; thus, it is precisely the aggregate of effects that is differentiated by degrees of difference.

The meaning is "dissimilarity. This same principle applies even when one intends to express mere difference (*bhedamātra*). When there is a contradiction, a different effect arises from a different causal complex; such conformity of the effect to the difference in its causes is what accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If this were transgressed, the consequence would follow that the entire universe is without cause (*ahetuka*), which would lead to logical inconsistency. Not [without] valid cognition...

When the rule that a single cause produces a single effect is transgressed by something already sublated, this Nyāya claim regarding the imitation of both difference and non-difference resembles the report of hearing that milk-rice is delicious from the mouth of a cowherd.
Therefore, a single seed alone produces many things such as sprouts, and likewise, each factor such as earth and so forth does so individually.

Therefore, there is no exclusion of either the one or the many; for this other non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is presented here to refute activity even in the case of momentary things, in order to establish that they are not common [to others] by virtue of their existence. As for the position that [an entity] produces [an effect] through another form, that has already been rejected by us; thus, we do not undertake the effort of refuting the subsequent series of objections against it. And this—

This is stated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*). However, in the play of conceptual construction (*kalpanāvilāsa*), the production of a sprout is not the same as the production of the earth; likewise, being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is not itself being the material cause (*upādānatva*). Thus, even though such a proliferation of distinctions may occur, there is no fault whatsoever in the nature of the thing, characterized by the absence of [intrinsic] activity, because everything is accounted for through its very real form. For this very reason, when the earth and so forth are to be produced...

Since that substrate is already established as a distinct form (*rūpāntara*) of the seed in relation to earth and the other factors, why should we state it again so that the subsequent argument might be effective? Furthermore, since the independence [of the cause] even with respect to auxiliary conditions has already been proven, the entire conclusion of the section is confused for the opponent of unsteady intellect.

Furthermore, those who interrogate [the opponent] by asking, "Is it by the very same form that the seed produces the sprout that it [produces] the moment of the earth? are themselves to be interrogated: "What is intended here by the word 'form' (*rūpa*)? Do you mean those properties (*dharma*) that, like "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) or "impermanence," appear as if distinct while resting upon the bed of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), such as the capacity to produce the sprout or other things?

Even by the term *svarūpa* (own-form), are they "those who have attained conventional usage"? Or is *rūpa* the *svarūpa*, the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic), such that there is no other distinction of entity (*vastubheda*) apart from it, regarding which it is said: "If that which was initially the own-form of the entity does not produce [an effect] later as it did before, and so forth"?

Alternatively, just as the Naiyāyikas employ the term "brother" for one who does not know the name of his master, so too has it been stated that the "form" (rūpa) is merely a designation by its own essential term for what is actually a causal factor (sahakārī). Regarding this, in the first case, there is no room for objection; for conceptual attributes (dharmas), though appearing as if they exist in mutual relation to one another and to their substratum (dharmin), are [merely] imagined.
Because it lacks reality as a mere appearance and cannot withstand valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot in any way function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) for an action.

For although the very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has been made the object of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is the sole basis for determining the accomplishment of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there arises in the conceptualizing mind a determination (*vyavasāya*) of an object as excluded from this and that [other thing].

In discussions concerning the relative strength or weakness [of means], and regarding dharmas, one merely extends a conventional usage by extracting them from their context, saying, "this or that dharma is employed for this action. However, they possess no status as instruments (karaṇabhāva) in any case, because they lack inherent existence. Yet, that which is produced by the speaker’s intention (vivakṣā) is not denied. Just as even in a lamp whose nature is to illuminate with a reddish glow, it brings about the destruction of darkness by its very undivided form—

And they produce a yellowish-piñjara hue; likewise, since this lamp is determined to be of the nature of light, it removes darkness like the moon. And because of its yellowness, it is the cause of the piñjara-hue, like turmeric and the like—such is the conventional usage. Yet, in that case, the states of luminosity and yellowness are not distinct. However, in the conceptualizing mind, appearing as if distinct, one extracts each [quality] separately as if they were different.

The two are intended as being non-distinct in their status as action and instrument [or not so distinct]; yet, by mere intention alone, there is neither the lack of agency nor the differentiation of the lamp. Likewise, although in conventional usage the seed is designated as the "agent" (karaṇa) of the sprout by way of its imagined form as the producer of the sprout, and as the "instrument" (karaṇa) of the earth by way of its production thereof, in reality there is no prohibition against a single entity having multiple objects of action.

Either there is the occurrence of division or there is simply non-action. Therefore, with respect to a form mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the production of many things by means of many forms is a mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and not a reality; yet this investigation must be based on what is real. So, what is the use of this conceptualization—whether it be by that form or by another? Even in the case of conceptual construction, the relinquishing [of the object] occurs through many [means] as a mere convention. And there is no one...

This is a fault. As for the second alternative, it is only possible when there is the perception of multiple particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, even the particular characteristics of the seed are not produced (*kṛtaka*) [in that sense], nor are they obtained [as such]. There is no [such thing as] "its own" (*sva*), nor is there [the notion of] "difference" (*bheda*). Long before that, [it was said] "that" is erroneous; [the word] "not" is absent. [Is it] among those that are consistent? By means of the extraction of the [essential] nature, there is no suspicion.

The number "one" is the object of a single observation. Indeed, for a person whose extent has not been perceived, there can be no occurrence of such questions as, "Is this man to be employed in this task, or is that one? In the third alternative, the meaning would be this: by that very same form through which it produces a sprout, does it [produce] the earth?

By what [auxiliary cause] does it produce the sprout? Is it by that very same one which produces the soil? And when would this be said? Only if, regarding the production of the sprout, a certain auxiliary of the seed were established as having a fixed nature and a definite operation, while another [auxiliary] involved in the production of something else were of doubtful operation. But such a thing cannot be demonstrated.

Now, this being the case, the intended meaning of the alternative is as follows: "Are those very factors—earth, water, and so forth—which are the auxiliaries for the seed in producing the sprout, also [the auxiliaries] for its production as earth? This too is of no use; for since it is well-established that all things everywhere stand in a mutual relationship of auxiliary cause (sahakāribhāva), what is the point of this question? Nor is a subsequent argument suitable here, for even then—

There is a certain connection in the principle that the difference or non-difference of the effect follows from the difference or non-difference of the cause; therefore, those who consider themselves experts in logic merely wish to cause extreme confusion with these useless ravings, which are tormented by the thorn of envy. Enough of this persistence.

Moreover, this manner of proclaiming an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is unprecedented. For an existing entity (*bhāva*) that has unascertained positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with both the probandum and its opposite is rightly considered uncommon, like "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*). Furthermore, by the force of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in the case at hand, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) itself is entirely non-existent; so how could that [non-existence] be an uncommon inconclusive reason?
Is this appropriate? It would have been more proper to state the refutation based on non-establishment (*asiddhi*). And that has already been stated there. Now, if you say:
"It was stated that in the case of momentariness there is an absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*); however, that does not mean absolute non-existence," then [we reply]:
in that case, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), while existing, is excluded from the momentary alone; therefore, by necessity, it must reside in the non-momentary.
Therefore, let there also be the fault of contradiction (*viruddhatā*), since [the probans] is pervaded by that [contrary].
If it is argued that there is doubt because there is an absence of either a sublater (*bādhaka*) or a prover (*sādhaka*) for non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika*) in a direct manner, [we reply:
its very existence—provided it is established as excluded from the momentary (*kṣaṇika*)—is the proof that leaves no room for such doubt. Its existence...
Furthermore, when there is doubt, the very fault is "doubtful unestablishedness" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhi*).

Moreover, since the non-perception of the pervader of the subject (*prakṛtavyāpakānupalambha*) does not lose its capacity even in the case of a non-momentary entity—just as it does not in the case of a momentary one—how can there be the establishment of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*)? Thus, unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) follows in every respect. For it is indeed possible to say, regarding even a permanent entity, that [the capacity] does not reside in the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), regarding the section on positive concomitance (*anvaya*): the production [of an effect] by that which is dependent [on conditions] is impossible because there is no benefit [conferred]. Furthermore, as for whether a stable seed produces the soil in its very same form as the non-producer, or in a different form, and so forth—when [there is] dissimilar soil and so on...

Even a lamp, which is subject to rebuke regarding its production, is likewise non-momentary for you. In that case, it is the same as to whether the modification of the wick and the consumption of the oil are produced by a single distinct form or by different ones. As for the resolution that "the auxiliaries themselves are distinct, and this constitutes a difference in its own nature"—by speaking thus, the other would be the self and the self would be the other; thus, the notion of "self" has now ceased.

Thus, this argument—which is devoid of scripture and logic—is stated out of mere rivalry and inevitably becomes an object of ridicule.

Furthermore, for one who asks about the meaning denoted by the term "essential nature" (svarūpa) while disregarding the auxiliary causes (sahakārin), the answer given by the auxiliary cause is that "even a stable entity does not produce [an effect] either by itself or through another self-nature. Thus, the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi) is necessarily admitted. For even in the case of another [entity], it is that very same self-nature which is the producer, and not the entity itself; therefore, nothing whatsoever is a producer. Consequently, this [proposition regarding] a stable entity—

The general principle regarding two stable [entities] is that it serves as a means for negating action. If that [principle] were firm, then since action would not exist at all, [the argument] would be unestablished (*asiddhi*), because even the fault characterized by the absence of succession and simultaneity could not ultimately be avoided. Even in the case of a stable entity, the cessation of action must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, how could the mere statement of the negation of action in the case of a momentary entity [be effective]?
Would the thesis of "commonality" (sādhāraṇatā) depend upon exclusion? For it is not the case that "commonality" consists merely in being excluded from the probandum (*sādhya*).

Otherwise, why not simply call it "uncommonality" (*asādhāraṇatva*) by virtue of its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)? What is the point of such great effort? If you argue: "But surely, through exclusion from the counter-example, the reason would be restricted to the probandum and thus become a valid *hetu*," [we reply: [the same would apply] through exclusion from the probandum.

In the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it would necessarily be a contradictory reason (*viruddha*); thus, the situation is the same. Therefore, regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is indeed non-establishment even when only the proposition (*pratijñā*) is stated.
Now, if by some other means the mere uncertainty of both [existence and non-existence] regarding existence (*sattā*) is being expressed, then in that case, there is no commonality (*asādhāraṇa*).

However, by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), the production of an effect at a single time is not contradicted even for an effect that possesses other times. Therefore, the production of effects at that time and not at another is established, just like the production of multiple effects in different locations.

And the relation of cause and effect is accessible [to perception]. Just as those two are observed when an effect arises in that same place, so too are they observed when an effect arises in a different place.

Nor is it correct to say that the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an effect—whether occurring at that same time or at another time—with a cause that remains stationary are identical; for even at a different time, that very same cause persists.

Recognition is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since it has been refuted, how could there be the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for effects that occur at different times? Thus, this logic is not the same [as the case of spatial difference]. [This refers] to the proof of difference. For it is not logical that because a bull is unfit for milking, a cow must likewise be so. Furthermore, since the same logic is observed everywhere regarding time and place, they share a common fate (*ekayogakṣema*); therefore, just as in the case of a difference of location...

Is it not said that "there is no difference in the cause," even though the effects possess a difference in time? That too is incorrect. For instance, proponents of eternalism do not accept that the spatial pervasion of an atom is similar to its temporal pervasion; nor is the temporal pervasion of the moonlight similar to its spatial pervasion, and the same applies to jars and other things. How, then, can there be a uniform principle of logic in all cases? No.

Furthermore, even if one observes the same logical principle elsewhere, it does not follow that the case is the same everywhere; for in the present instance, there is no subverting evidence to rule out the possibility of the opposite being true.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that when there is a difference in location due to a difference in material causes (*upādāna*), the relationship between material cause and auxiliary condition (*sahakāribhāva*) is merely intermediate—that too is incorrect. Even if those two states of being material cause and auxiliary condition appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are not real entities as if they were distinct, nevertheless, because such exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are possible for the real entity, there is no unreal determination; nor is this the case through mutual dependence on one another.
There is no contradiction. Just as the status of being both father and son for one person relative to another is not ultimately real, yet there is no contradiction;

nor is there the production of two distinct effects by means of two distinct forms, such that—because those two forms appearing through conceptual construction are unreal—there would be no production of the two. And just as there is no production of two by means of a single form, so too [is there no production of two] when one produces its own effect in its own location and the effect of another.

The difference in location is established even though it arises from a difference in the material causes (*upādāna*), because the effect does not possess a difference in location merely through an imputed difference in its own nature; rather, the logical principle is that by producing their respective locations within their own material causes, the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) effectively produce the effect in a different location. Therefore, it is not the case that a non-different [entity] produces effects at different times merely through an imputed difference in its own nature.
Because difference is established by the force of sublation; for this very reason, the cause does not occupy the same location as everything.

For its status as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritā*) consists in its cooperation with its own auxiliary causes and its material cause (*upādāna*); and since that effect can only occur in the very location of its own material cause, its capacity for action exists only there and not in another location. Thus, how could it have the same location as everything, given that no benefit whatsoever [could be derived from such a claim]?
Even regarding existence?

For instance, just as a cause situated in one place produces effects located in different places, [so too does it produce them at different times].

Nor is there any suspicion of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), because pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established as encompassing all cases. [Objection: But surely, pervasion is established by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the contrary; yet, there is no mention of its presentation [here]. So how is pervasion [established]?

Why is it said that [the entity] is "adorned" (prasādhitā)? This is merely the play of a mind that is excessively wavering and unsteady. For this has been established: that action does not belong to the agent at any other time; rather, it is either the action of another or simply no action at all. Therefore, in both these cases, the connection with momentary destruction—meaning its necessary concomitance (*tanmātrānubandha*)—is inevitable. And since that has already been proven, [the reason] is connected with the probandum.

That causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) is indeed pervaded [by existence]. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, let there be mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*); but how can the absolute exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) be established? It is established precisely through the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is asked, "How is the proof of pervasion established regarding exclusion?"—no, for it is of two kinds.

For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is twofold: that which is positive (*anvaya-rūpā*) and is a property of the agent (*kartṛ-dharma*), which is the necessary presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*dharmin*) possessing the probans (*sādhana*);

and that which is negative (*vyatireka-rūpā*) and is a property of the object (*karma-dharma*), which is the necessary absence of the probans when the probandum is absent. This is according to the principle that pervasion consists in the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) only where [the pervaded is], or the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only there [where the pervader is]. And because of the rule that the establishment of one of these two necessarily entails the other...

It implies the cognition of the second [object]; otherwise, not even one would be established. It is simply that the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs directly in one case, while in the other it is a cognition by way of necessity; on that basis alone, there is the designation of "one. And this being so, although doubt regarding the other might arise prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition in one case, it is subsequently removed by that very [cognition], just as follows:

For those who maintain that there is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary [of the thesis], even though the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubted, it reaches a conclusion where doubt is eliminated by the force of its absolute exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). [The reasoning is:

"This existence, which is in every way untenable in a non-momentary entity, is necessarily restricted to momentary destruction. Thus, because existence entails the presentation of a distinct nature at every moment, even the moment of doubt regarding existence—which had previously arisen—even in the absence [of certainty], [is removed].
It dissolves of its own accord. If it possesses activity, it must necessarily be momentary; for apart from momentariness, existence is certainly not established.

If, however, it were to exist even in the absence of that [cause], then momentariness would not necessarily follow from its presence; thus, there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) either.

How so? Therefore, there is no difference in meaning between "the absolute negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the probans when the probandum is absent" and "the necessary positive concomitance (anvaya) of the probandum when the probans is present. However, the operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is twofold in its conventional usage: primarily and by implication. For this very reason, wherever there is a search for a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) regarding the opposite of the probandum, [there is such a search] regarding the probans.

When the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum exists, the search for the validating means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should also be understood as being indicated by that [concomitance]. Furthermore, by the term "sublation of the opposite" (*viparyaya-bādhaka*), both cases are indeed included. For in the case of pervasion in the form of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is a sublation of the probans when the probandum is absent; whereas in the case of pervasion in the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is a sublation of the absence of the probandum when the probans is present. In the absence of both of these...

The meaning is this: there is no logical impossibility regarding the probans being connected with the probandum. Otherwise, even if the means of valid cognition that directly establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not obtained, if one were to demonstrate a means of valid cognition that establishes the rule of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the probans and the probandum, what obstacle would there be to the establishment of the probandum? For the power of the positive concomitance itself implies the negative concomitance.

Otherwise, the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*) would indeed be unacceptable, because it does not directly demonstrate the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, even if the nature of the negative concomitance is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), if one merely understands that "wherever there is the probans (*sādhana*), there is the probandum (*sādhya*)," then, when the probans is present, the person who is intent upon the expectation of the probandum has achieved his purpose; for [the probandum] is absent when that [probans] is absent.

For if the probandum (sādhya) necessarily exists when the probans (sādhana) exists, then the acceptance of the probans is fruitful. Therefore, both [the presence and absence of the probans] must be investigated through conceptual analysis by the proponent of the probans; and the proponent must demonstrate at least one mode established by valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, regarding the proofs of others, a positive concomitance (anvaya) that possesses a necessary rule is as difficult to find as a negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Thus it should be understood.

By us, however, in the present proof, a positive concomitance (anvaya) characterized by necessity has indeed been demonstrated through the two preceding reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its contrapositive (viparyaya);
and although those two were applied to the cloud, which was treated as a similar instance (sapakṣa), nevertheless, whatever possesses the nature of performing a certain function—

It indeed produces that [effect], and whatever does not produce it does not have the nature of being its instrument; thus, as these two [reasons] proceed, they demonstrate that everything necessarily possesses momentariness through its capacity for action. Therefore, this universal application (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) is the seed for implying the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), just like smoke and other such signs. By not applying [the property of] existence [to the example], one accepts [the subject]; likewise, when one realizes momentariness in that which holds water, the aforementioned inference establishes, by means of a general principle applicable to whatever possesses activity, a pervasion between [activity] and momentariness. In *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is stated that the action may occur either subsequently or at some other time; thus, the definition of these two is declared to be unmixed, as they constitute a sequence (*krama*).

It occurs as follows: although simultaneity is relative to a single action occurring at the same time, while succession is relative to actions at different times, nevertheless, due to the difference in what is being depended upon, there is no confusion between them, just as in the case of a father and a son. Furthermore, by the mention of "non-action," it is intended that—according to different philosophical views—either the non-existence of the entity itself should be accepted in every respect, or its essential nature should remain devoid of action; there is no insistence on this point. In that regard:

Nor is it the case that there is only one [action], for the mention of the genus (*jāti*) is intended merely to express the identity between the preceding and succeeding [moments]. Whether the action be prior or posterior, or again, whether it be one or many, even when the position of a single action is maintained, both do not fail to be designated by the term "successionless" (*akrama*). Even in that case, only the manifold action is real, because the production of an aggregate from an aggregate is what is ultimately real. This is stated [here] merely as a formal objection (*śaṅkāmātreṇa*), not as an actual logical possibility.

Or rather, it is a single expression for a single action. Therefore, since this [action] is also indicated by the term "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*), the meaning subsumed under "non-sequential" (*akrama*) must be understood even from the word "simultaneity" in the treatise. And since this twofold mode residing in the effect is compatible only with the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of the agent, the exclusion of the eternal (*nitya*) is stated through the function of determining absolute non-existence. This is primarily [the case].

The syllable "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), however, like [the term] "eternal" and so forth, is capable of defining exclusion even from that which is momentary. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of indicating that the pervaded exists only there. By this, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity in the case of the eternal, its existence—which is defined by that [efficiency]—is lost; therefore, it rests solely in momentariness. By this, Trilocana’s objection— that by adopting the definition of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and relying on the sequence [of moments], this sequence of momentariness and so forth can be refuted— is rejected as a worthless argument. In the first position, however, the meaning is that for an eternal entity, the state of performing an action as indicated by succession and non-succession is contradictory. This is because of the qualification "by means of succession and simultaneity" (*kramayogapadyābhyām*).

However, if that [agent] is not admitted, then because the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, both [reasons] possess a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdha-vipakṣa-vyāvṛttikatva*).
Just as it is impossible to perceive cause and effect as sequential, so too it is with respect to the effects; thus, there is no perception of sequence, nor is there perception of simultaneity.
As he himself has said: "Nor is there [perception] of simultaneity, because by means of a cognition possessing a distinct form, [objects] with their own specific forms..."

Because simultaneity cannot be established [by those very cognitions]. Simultaneity cannot be apprehended by that many cognitions alone, because if they are not mutually cognizable, their simultaneous existence remains unproven, just as in the case of different mental continua (*santāna*). Nor can a single [cognition] possess multiple forms, because if there were a difference in the forms that constitute its very nature, a difference in the cognition itself would necessarily follow. And if there were such a difference, it would entail the consequence that the cognition is something distinct from its forms.
"The fact that the object possesses that form will not be established.

To this it is replied: First of all, the acceptance of a synthesizing subject (*pratisandhātṛ*) is incoherent, because the cognitions intended as the objects of synthesis cannot withstand the dilemma of being either different or non-different. For if there were non-difference, would it be that very same subject, or would they be the cognitions themselves? In this regard:

And in the first case, [the agency] belongs to the action; in the other case, since there is no agent, what is the purpose of the synthesis? Even if there were a difference, what is the purpose of synthesis for that which is insentient and distinct from the cognitions? If it is argued that the self is the synthesizer because of its connection with cognition—just as one is a seer—then, given the necessary acceptance that cognition alone is the seer and the synthesizer, what would be the use of another [self] connected to it?

What is the point of this borrowed ornament called "suchness" (*tathātva*)? If you argue that it is because cognitions lack agency, then, by that same logic, the conventional designation of that Self as a "seer" and so forth would also be untenable. For if cognition were the seer of either the cause or the effect, then it would be the synthesizer and the conceptualizer of the necessary sequence and its specific determination; and through association with that [cognition], the Self would possess the status of being a seer.

It might be argued that the capacity for synthesis (*pratisandhātṛtva*) is being discussed in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*. However, when cognition has not yet acquired distinction with respect to each particular object, even a connection is not capable of effecting a specific conventional usage— such as "now the knower of the cause," "now of the result," or "at this moment."
Regarding the term "to reconnect" (*pratisandhātā*): if one accepts a specific quality residing within such a cognition, what else remains to be done?

For practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is fully accomplished by that alone. If it is argued, "Without a permanent self (*sthirātmā*), that very cognition would not exist," by whom have you been so deceived? Oh, the power of delusion (*moha*), which brings even such [arguments] under its sway!

For instance, that which is stated as "this cannot exist without that" is indeed appropriate only when the causal capacity has been determined elsewhere through perception and non-perception, as in the case of smoke [in relation] to fire. Or, as in the case of the eye and other [senses], when the collection of visible causes is present but the effect is not seen, and it is later seen, one concludes in a general manner that something else must be required. First of all, the former position is not...

This is clear. Nor is a second [cause] possible. For when the cognition of the effect arises immediately after the cognition of the cause, there is no previously unobserved synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) on the part of one engaged in a definitive judgment, such as "this was seen by me immediately after that," from which the postulation of another [cause] might occur. Likewise, even memory [arises] from experience through some indirect transformation of potency (*śaktipariṇāma*).
[Memory arises] through the door [of experience], from some cause, directly by the power of that maturation.
[Objection: "In that case, how is it that there is no memory for one person regarding the experience of another?
[Response: The word "another" does not establish a relationship [between two distinct entities]; why then is such an objection raised?

In the context of a debate concerning the establishment of a substratum distinct from experience and so forth as the locus of the relationship, to raise an objection by relying on that very [substratum] as already established is irrelevant. For if that were established, the debate would reach its conclusion; what further dependence on another could there be?
Therefore, having removed the subject of dispute expressed as "of another," the question "why is there no memory in experience?"—leaving only this—does not serve the purpose of the present topic.
The point of the objection is indeed formulated correctly: why is it that an experience connected with one body does not give rise to memory in another body?
By saying this, it is effectively asked: why does a seed belonging to one field not produce a sprout in another field?
And what is the logic behind that?

Now, one might object: there is no other proximity between experience and memory than the mere relation of cause and effect; nor is there any such rule regarding the cause-and-effect relationship that the effect must reside in the very same locus as its cause, since we observe the effect of cognition even at a great distance from its object. If this is so, then for the sprout as well, there would be no proximity other than the mere fact of being an effect.

Knowledge, like a seed, might produce [its effect] even at a distance. But surely, how can certain atoms—which initiate the seed and serve as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the sprout—be capable of producing that sprout in another field?
[Is it] by something else? Or by what is immediately adjacent? Or indeed by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone? Or by some other [means]?
In this regard, [the following applies]: 4.0. *siddhādhi* 5. There is no "parī" (exclusion) in relation to 6. *ra* (the reason). 7.

Regarding *vapatā* (the subject), in the chapter on momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), there is the section on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). But for you, because of the absence of such a proximity, its being an effect—which is common to cognition and so forth—[is established] even at a distance.

If it is argued that the production [of effects] is unavoidable, then why do the atoms of the seed function as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) only for the effect that is the sprout, and not for cognition and so forth? For all things are of the same nature insofar as they are effects. Consequently, just as with the sprout, all things would have to be produced in that very location; or else, like cognition and so forth, the sprout too would have to be produced at a distance, since there is no distinction among them in their status as effects.
In the same way, even with respect to the sprout, the seed functions as a causal condition (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); thus,
while the continuity of the series is established in one case, it is not so in the other.
But surely, that very sprout in which the seed-atoms attain the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the sprout itself;

so how can it be urged that their status as inherent causes applies elsewhere than in the sprout? If this were the case, then because the status of being an inherent cause—due to the single essence of being an effect—is difficult to avoid, it would follow by necessity that all [atoms] possess the same form as the sprout and occupy the same location.

It was appropriate that the hope for an exemption bore fruit. For if all effects were indistinguishable by virtue of being effects, then all causes would likewise be indistinguishable by virtue of being causes; thus, the diversity of the universe would be left without protection.

Therefore, even though they possess the nature of being effects, it is not the case that there is only one single mode for all of them. As it is said: "Due to natural difference, in some cases something [arises] from something..."

For you, [the cause] functions as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) in some cases, as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in others, and as an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) in still others;

likewise, for us as well, one effect produces its cause in the very same location, while another produces it in a separated location. Furthermore, some effects are by necessity characterized by arising in the very location of their cause, while others are otherwise. This is the case with respect to a single effect.

The possibility of recognition does not occur elsewhere, even though there is no difference in the nature of being an effect— just as in the case of another lamp or [the case of] cognition. Furthermore, for us, the designation of "material cause" (upādānakāraṇa) applies to that which, according to you, is established as the "inherent cause" (samavāyikāraṇa), provided it is such an effect.

It does not exist elsewhere than in the Self and so forth. And since there is merely the state of being a cooperative cause within such a succession of causes and effects, it is established that even if there is a difference in the process (*prakriyā*), you cannot avoid the fact that such a duality of effects is naturally established (*nisargasiddha*). Furthermore, when such a distinction is possible, that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the production of the effect—

Since it is of a nature to arise only in that [specific] locus, how could it arise elsewhere? Or, how could a cause—which is capable of producing its effect only within its own locus—generate that effect in another place? Likewise, how could this experience, which produces remembrance in its own locus just as a seed produces a sprout, generate that remembrance elsewhere? Or, how could remembrance, whose arising is restricted to the locus of the experience, arise in another place, like a sprout?

Why would the objection regarding the contingency of memory in another body find any ground for application? For in the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*), this [objection] is difficult to avoid, since that [self], being all-pervasive, exists in another body as well by virtue of its very nature of producing memory. Furthermore, the recourse to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) applies only to that which is eternal. If it is asked: "How is it to be understood that the principle governing experience and memory is like that of the seed and the sprout, and not otherwise?"

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, this same principle is determined even in the case of the seed and the sprout, precisely because it is observed to be so; likewise, such a rule of necessity exists between experience and recollection, for indeed, when one body possesses an experience, another form cannot possibly possess the corresponding recollection.

[Objection: But how can the body possess experience? [Response: There is no fault, for there is an intention to express a relationship [between the body and experience] by virtue of its being the locus (*ādhāra*) of that experience, its being the cause (*kāraṇa*) of it, or its having the same causes as it. Furthermore, how does the self (*ātman*) possess experience? If you say "by the power of inherence (*samavāya*"), then surely inherence itself—being desired as the cause of the cognition "it is here"—must be postulated as the basis for the cognition "it is here."

[Objection: There is indeed cognition (*buddhi*) here in this body; therefore, why not assume an inherence (*samavāya*) [relation] as well? [Reply: If you argue that it is because there is no state of being inseparable (*ayutasiddhatva*), since the body and cognition are perceived as distinct entities—surely for two things perceived separately, there is the rule of perception as "this is here," when two objects are observed in an upper-lower spatial relationship without mutual confusion.

The designation of the seventh and first [cases] would be possible as a source of expression; however, when there is no perception of difference at all, how does one who designates "this here" by way of distinction not lose their status as a discerning person? If it is argued that this is because no difference is ever perceived in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), then for that very reason, one must produce—by means of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—the cognition "it is here," which is capable of being brought about through volition.

Inherence is postulated as that which is the basis for the cognition "it is here. However, the establishment of inherence would depend upon the cognition "it is here," and such a cognition could only occur if two things were perceived.
Yet, in no case is there a perception of two things in its object; therefore, this [postulation] is merely one's own imagination and is not a valid means of proof.

Therefore, to apply the designation "possessing intelligence" to a self that does not exist at all mimics the story of a barren woman’s son fashioning a helmet from a horse's horn. For when a thing is postulated for a certain purpose, the very fact that that purpose is accomplished by something else constitutes its non-existence; and since the purpose of the self—such as memory and so forth—is established otherwise, it follows that [the self] does not exist. Thus, it is not one...
An experience residing in one body is capable of producing recollection in another body.
But surely, if [the mind] were momentary, since recollection would arise only in a different body, how could this be resolved?

Or, if one accepts the taking up of another birth, why would the same consequence not apply even to a body intended to be a different continuum, given that the fact of being "other" is no different in either case?

If [you argue that] such a different body produces memory, then for the self (*ātman*) as well, this is difficult to avoid; thus, the same consequence applies elsewhere as well, since there is no difference in their being "other. Furthermore, even if the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of the body is not accepted, its perishability (*āśunāśitva*) is certainly accepted by them; therefore, the fault is the same, out of fear of which the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*) is embraced. Now, regarding the doctrine of the self...

In that case, there is no fault, because the production of memory occurs precisely within the body conditioned by the karma of that self (*ātman*). However, in the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), whose is that karma? For, apart from the body, only a momentary consciousness (*buddhi*) is possible. And for this very reason, it cannot be determined [as the cause] from the observation of the agent-moment [of action], nor can it be established for one possessing consciousness, even in the case of the opposite [position].

That karma which is conducive to pleasure, pain, and so forth would belong to one who lacks the experience thereof; and since the moment that is experienced is not the agent, there would be the additional fault of the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Consequently, no action would be established for anyone, from which the refutation of the aforementioned fault might follow. Furthermore, even this "continuum" (*santāna*), though spoken of, is nothing distinct [from the moments]. Nor...
Since you possess actions that are distinct [from one another], this is like a work of painting without a wall.
Regarding this, the first point is stated here: First of all, it is not a refutation [of our position] that the momentary agent lacks the experience of the fruit of that action;
for a person does not cease to possess fire simply because he has produced it without performing such acts as burning. The final—

Even a single moment is connected [to the result] through a causal series by virtue of being an auxiliary to that action; for it is precisely because of this that one becomes a partaker of the experience.

Furthermore, simultaneity is not possible even between cause and effect, yet it is possible between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara. Therefore, the connection expressed as "this belongs to that" despite their difference occurs solely through the medium of assistance, and such assistance, produced by that [action], exists in its full magnitude for the final [moment].

Furthermore, for the moments situated between those [initial and final moments] and for the moments occurring within that same continuum, the capacity to produce a final moment of such a kind—whether directly or through a succession—arises from that very same karma; thus, their connection to that [result] is mediated solely by way of assistance (*upakāra*). And so, when the established order of all things being connected to karma is maintained, it is only in a body brought forth through the sovereign power (*adhipatya*) of that karma [that the result occurs].

The arising of moments of consciousness and body produced by that karma occurs [only] there, and not elsewhere, because of the absence of such proximity. And while karma is certainly not distinct [from the moment], the description as if it were separate is also made in accordance with conventional usage. As for the moment said to be connected to previous karma, it has arisen as possessing such a specific quality, from which—ultimately—the result of that [karma] arises.
There arises a continuum capable of producing a moment of an enjoyer, as well as a continuum of a body corresponding to that [enjoyer].

Two specific moments of intellect and body, having arisen endowed with the slightest degree of excellence, produce together subsequent moments of even greater excellence; and those moments of lesser excellence, in turn, produce further [moments]. Following this direction, [the process continues] until the characteristic of capacity—

The excellence of the distinction increases through the stages of "taratama" (higher and higher) and so forth, until the arising of that which is capable of the final birth; therefore, it is called "final. Because the intellect and the body—being mutually bound by dependence on a single causal complex—are both distinguished with respect to the subsequent series, there is no room for a second [birth] apart from the first. Even when taking up another birth, as that lifespan and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, they perish.

A subsequent moment of the mind, acting as a cooperative cause for the preceding corporeal moment, produces another body corresponding to it; this, as before, provides assistance to the mind. Thus, there is no room for concern regarding memory or the status of being an enjoyer in another body. Nor is there any need here for a distinct entity called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*)—apart from the very establishment of the connection between moments and their actions—for continuity is established through that very means without any obstruction.

Thus, that [is said] when there is the establishment of the characteristic of one's own intended continuum.

As for what the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* says in refuting this— namely, "No, because proof and refutation are impossible; there is no proof because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth— for there can be no positive concomitance such as 'memory arises from the relation of cause and effect, like the redness [of dye] in cotton'— nor is there negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) such as 'wherever there is no memory, there is no relation of cause and effect'— because it is unestablished (*asiddha*)..."

There is no refutation because you have failed to state the [proper] reason. For it is not possible for subsequent cognitions to have memory of an object experienced by a preceding cognition, because they are distinct from it—just like the cognitions of a different continuum. Thus, the example "like the redness in cotton" does not establish any fault in this argument. This is an unconsidered statement, due to a failure to understand the meaning of the proof (*sādhana*). For here...

In this verse, it is understood that the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is presented as the reason for memory; what then [is the cause]? It is the latent impression of action (*karmavāsanā*).

For a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is indeed the formative influence (*abhisaṃskāra*) produced by action. That which has been infused (*vasitam*) is called "formatively influenced" (*abhisaṃskṛtam*). The bond of the fruit, such as experience, occurs only in that continuum (*santāna*) where the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) produced by the action has arisen, and not elsewhere, because that distinction is absent there. Having thus asserted this:

Regarding the statement "just as redness [arises] in cotton," the intended reason is either the distinction within the continuum of impressions (*saṃskāra-santāna-bheda*), while the probandum is the negation of results such as experience elsewhere; furthermore, it is understood that there is the capacity for those results within that very continuum. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
whatever impression is deposited in a particular continuum is capable of yielding its fruit only therein and not elsewhere, just as...

In the continuum of cotton, the state produced by the conjunction with the substance of dye while in the stage of the seed is capable of manifesting the fruit of dye in the stage of the flower or the stage of the fruit, but not in another continuum.
And this impression (*saṃskāra*) is a mental continuum generated by acts such as giving; thus, it is precisely a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) within the collection [of factors].

This is with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*). For the capacity to yield a fruit within that [specific] continuum is necessarily concomitant with mere conditioning (*saṃskāramātra*), whereas in another continuum there is an absolute incapacity for it; thus, because no other cause is required, in the first case (where each instance is the probandum) there is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). In the second case, however, there is the perception of a pervading contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*): [the presence of the capacity] in its own substratum is pervaded by the contradiction of [yielding] a fruit in a continuum other than its own substratum.

In that case, even if there is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*),
since the nature of being an impression is observed to be pervaded by the production of a result within the very continuum (*santāna*),
if one were to require some other cause for the capacity to yield a result within that continuum, then the effort of constructing an impression would be useless.

It might be argued that if the capacity to yield a fruit existed even in another continuum, then a second effort would be useless. Furthermore, when milk is poured upon a single *āmalaka* fruit, not every *āmalaka* tree will bear sweet fruit. Therefore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is pervaded by the yielding of its fruit only within its own continuum; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). And it is established by scripture (*āgama*) that this refinement is a specific quality of the mind produced by karma, which we accept as such.

The refutation is as valid as the objection, so there is no unestablished reason (*asiddhi*). Nor is there a contradiction, because [the reason] exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), nor is there a failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Alternatively:
whatever is a continuum is capable of yielding its fruit only within its own substratum, just like the continuum of cotton;
and this is a mental continuum—just as before.
This same principle applies even with respect to results such as mindfulness (*smṛti*) and so forth. If this determination were made by way of the continuum (*saṃtāna*),
then [there would be the consequence that] a student could [remember] what was experienced by his teacher and so on.

Even if the lineage were established by means of a connection through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*), the undesirable consequence would follow that memory and so forth could arise [in one person from another]. In this way, it would follow that a son could possess the experience and so forth of his father. Such a lineage is not what is intended here; rather, it is a succession of cause and effect consisting of material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). What, then, is the definition of material cause and its product? It is the state of having a single substratum (*ekādhāratā*).

The restriction [of memory] occurs when there is no cause for doubt; even when there is doubt, the restriction lies in the capacity [for that specific memory]. Indeed, the diverse succession of causes and effects has been established previously, and it was already indicated therein that such a specific sequence is called a "stream" (*santāna*).
Furthermore, this is not the case between the minds of teacher and pupil, or between the minds of father and son; thus, there is no fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) according to logic.

Alternatively, there is the fault of mutual dependence regarding the establishment of the continuity and the appropriation; this must be addressed by demonstrating that [the self] does not depend upon them.
Regarding the establishment of appropriation (*upādāna*):

alternatively, it is the non-erroneous, singular determination [of identity]. Both the original nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformation (*vikriyā*) constitute the characteristic of cause and effect as appropriator and appropriated. Within the continuum of cause and effect, there is the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is the appropriator" and "this is the appropriated."

It should be understood as characterized [by its nature]. However, in the case of arising from a dissimilar cause (*visabhāga*), the characteristic is simply the essential nature (*svabhāva*) itself: the material cause (*upādāna*) is the "original" (*prakṛti*) and the effect (*upādeya*) is the "modification" (*vikṛti*). Alternatively, the characteristic is "the state of being original and modification"; this is an expression emphasizing the abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna-nirdeśa*), like the examples of wood and a sacrificial post (*kāṣṭha-yūpa*) or wood and charcoal (*kāṣṭha-aṅgāra*). Even when multiple things arise, the distinct parts themselves constitute the material cause, just as, for example, the heat of a woman's body [is the cause of her perspiration].
Regarding the cognitions (*buddhi*) of the various limbs, even though they are many, there is a single conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) and a single determination (*ekāvasāya*) as "one person.

Furthermore, for one who discerns the coloring by objects and perceives only pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), there arises the determination within that continuum accepted as a single person: "This is that very same cognition.

However, these [cognitions] do not conform to the entire nature [of the person]; and even if such conformity were possible, the single determination—like [the case of] a different pillar—is an error. Thus it is not [the case].

By this, the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established; however, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) should be understood from the context. Consequently, all that was said—taking as its basis the direct relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as the means of establishing memory—is refuted. Rather, it is faultless to maintain that memory is that which conforms to the specific particulars that serve as the substratum for the relationship of cause and effect.

Furthermore, regarding the proof that "there is no recollection by subsequent cognitions of an object experienced by a preceding cognition because they are distinct, like the cognitions of a different continuum": in this case, is it being denied that the subsequent cognitions—which are the subjects (*dharmin*)—have a connection with a cognition in the form of memory; or is it their very nature as having the form of memory that is being excluded; or is it that they do not possess memory as their result?

Is it being established? First of all, the first position is untenable; for we do not maintain that memory is one thing and the cognition possessing memory is another, such that there would be a negation [of their identity], but rather that cognition is of the very nature of memory itself. If it is argued that at the time of looking for a cow while remembering a horse, that perception of the cow becomes "possessing memory" (smṛtimat), then is that [perception] of the memory itself in that state?

Is a negation intended? If it is merely memory that occurs, then let it be so. If this is not the case, then what is the purpose of this mention of concomitance regarding subsequent cognitions? If it is argued that the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is for the sake of inference—no, because the desired totality of the subject at hand is established, since the negation of memory at all subsequent times is precisely what is intended.
