If it is argued that there is a distinction [of validity] by means of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), has it not already been largely established that this correspondence must be either the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-prāpti*) or the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-vṛtti*)? And if another means of valid cognition exists, let that alone suffice; what is the use of this [correspondence]?

Furthermore, no certain purposeful action is established as something persisting through time, since all such things are accomplished by means of the intellect and the body. Nor is there anything other than these two.

I am the object of cognition. For just as in the case of the recognition "this is that Caitra," where Caitra's body alone is recognized as one and the same across prior and subsequent times by disregarding the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and states, so too is it in this cognition: "I myself am the seer and the rememberer. This is merely a collective designation mediated through the intellect (*buddhi*), just as in the expression: "I who was a fool [am now learned]."

Some [use] the designation "I am wise" by way of the intellect (*buddhi*). Others, however, use it by way of the body (*deha*), as in "I am fair" or "I am fat," because it is well known that a designation for a whole can be applied to a part. Still others use it by way of both, as in "the kingdom was ruled by me" or "my misfortune," and so forth; these should be inferred accordingly. There are also [designations] by way of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*).
These designations—such as "I am happy" up to "I am righteous"—are indeed based on the intellect (*buddhi*), because they do not exist apart from the intellect.

Even the distinct designation "the face" or "the body" [as belonging to me] is intended to express a distinction between a whole and one of its parts, just as one says "the branch of a tree. For this very reason, the expression "I am the face" does not occur.

How then can there be the expressions "my intellect" (*mama matiḥ*) and "my body" (*mama mūrtiḥ*)? [It is] like "the body of a stone-son" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*). In that case, one might also say "intellect-body" (*buddhi-śarīre*); for have we not also seen such usages as "the body of a stone-son" and "the head of Rāhu"? And just as in those cases, despite the absence of a second self (*dvitīyātman*), there is the conventional usage "my self" (*mamātma*), so too, despite the absence of a first self, there is the usage "my intellect" (*mama buddhi-*).

It is intent upon the negation of others, but not intent upon another entity apart from the intellect (*mati*) and the body (*vigraha*).

Regarding those two—the intellect and the body—even when they are past or future, because of their identification with the present [self], one employs such expressions as: "I alone saw," "I alone touched," and "I alone remembered. Therefore, just as in the case of "This is that Caitra," there is a unity of both aggregates across prior and subsequent times.

This is merely a metaphorical expression; it does not imply the apprehension of a distinct entity. If it is argued that in the case of Caitra as well, it is the self alone that is recognized, we say no, because recognition does not occur regarding what has not been previously perceived. For it is only the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*vigraha*) that have been perceived. And although the intellect of another is to be inferred, there is no fault, because through extreme habituation, one observes its functioning as if it were directly perceived (*pratyakṣavat*). This is evident even from the mere sight of a friend or an enemy.
For indeed, no performance consistent with that [nature] is observed there; nor is there any lapse in following the form of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth.

Nor does such performance occur merely upon the apprehension of the body, for that would entail the same [performance] even in the case of a dead corpse. Furthermore, since it is the motivator of all bodily activity, the very perception of the Self by the intellect from birth onwards is itself the seed for the habitual practice associated with it in other lives as well.

[The self] exists as something constantly present. However, there is no such seed of practice for the perception of a self, because every activity culminates solely in the body and consciousness. Therefore, it is precisely the mind and body, which are the objects of the word "Caitra," that are recognized by the recognition "this is that very same one. Likewise, this is merely a recognition of those two alone, which are the objects of the word "I," [expressed as] "by me."

"I have seen," "I have remembered," "I have done," and "I shall be liberated"—these too are merely determinations of unity belonging to those very two [the seer and the rememberer]. Thus, in this view, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) arising in the wake of perception has as its object a state of confidence; yet, if that unity were a mere existence, it would be a non-entity across preceding and succeeding moments. If, however, it has a distinct objective referent, then even while the object is manifest, there arises a mixture of doubts regarding whether it is unreal or real, and thus it remains uncertain.

How can the Vastuka [proponent] establish the self as being established by direct perception? Furthermore, the inference he proclaims— namely, that "the various distinct states such as desire belong to a single related entity because they are the objects of a single unifying cognition (*pratisandhāna*),
just as spectators are the objects of a single unifying cognition regarding a single dancer"— is also a sign of extreme superficiality of mind.

This very point he clarifies: "Indeed, there is no dancer who is a single entity in reality, because she is merely an aggregate of atoms presided over by consciousness. Since the unity [of the dancer] is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and this establishes the validity of the example, who can deny that the unity [of the self] in the case of the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) is likewise established through conventional usage? If it is argued that the example does not hold in every respect, we reply: "That is true."

Furthermore, by whose power could a real unity be established? [If you say it is] because its concomitance is seen in the example, and therefore it is fit for the application of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the purpose; if you say this is merely a matter of desire; if you say it is what has been seen; if you say it is memory; if you say it is also other; if you say it belongs to that; if you say it is the body; if you say it is the culmination—even so, [the argument fails]. There is not even a suspicion that it might be established [by that alone]. Therefore, even according to the *Vārttika*, a common example (*sādhāraṇadṛṣṭānta*) must necessarily be provided by way of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). This is the meaning: and by a non-demonstrated example, the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) is not shown. By [the proof of] establishment, the avoidance of the charge of being devoid of the probandum is achieved. Because a dancer lacks the status of being a whole (*avayavin*) due to being a collection of body, intellect, and so forth, the refutation of her own parts (*avayava*) remains valid in relation to the body. However, with respect to the self (*ātman*), that [refutation] does not yet apply.

It is established; and since there is no sublation by the contrary, there is no peace for the charge of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). For the recognition "this is mine" is, by its nature, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Even if it occurs through the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), like a case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), how could it admit dependence on a single underlying relation?
Thus, just as memory, the connection between action and its fruit, and so forth, are all possible even without a persisting substrate, there is no failure [of our position].

For the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), [the cognition] "it measures" arises; likewise, the cognition of the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) also arises. Thus, there is no stain of suspicion regarding a non-exclusive inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānekānta*).
Śaṅkara, however, out of his loquacity, puts on some kind of dramatic performance. For instance, he suggests that sometimes [the cognition] is preceded by perception (*upalambha*).

The cognition of smoke produces the ascertainment that "this object, grey like the neck of a pigeon, is an effect of fire"; sometimes this [ascertainment] is preceded by the non-perception of those two [fire and smoke] after their prior perception. Non-perception, moreover, being essentially the perception of the counter-positive entity, is indeed of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established in the context of non-perception, it must be determined in that very [non-perception]. Positive concomitance—

The method of perception and non-perception that apprehends negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has also been demonstrated in the investigation of the triad and pentad; let that suffice for now, and we shall speak of the subject at hand. In either case, since each preceding cognition among successive cognitions deposits a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the final cognition is capable of producing the understanding—"this is the effect of that"—just as before.
There is no requirement for one who reconnects [the series] to remain fixed [in that state].

Furthermore, as for what was said—that "exclusion (vyatireka) is not even within the scope of a mere mental wish"—that is an extreme audacity. For it is not claimed that the very same perception which grasps two real entities also grasps their exclusion upon the cessation of those two entities; rather, [it is claimed that]...

It is simply another perception whose nature is the apprehension of an object that serves as the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) distinct from that [other object]. Therefore, what is the point of saying that "that [object] does not exist, and yet there is cognition by means of it," which is illogical? Furthermore, in this way, there is no contradiction with the doctrine of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) regarding the apprehension [of the object].

As for what was also stated—that there are cognitions of the preceding and succeeding moments, and from those two arises a latent impression (*vāsanā*), whereby there is the determination of cause and effect—[this too is consistent].

If it is argued that [this is] a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then is this now some kind of rule being followed, whereby one must speak on the basis of whatever has been suspected?

Is it by you? For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must either be a synthesis of what has been grasped or a superimposition of a form that does not belong [to the object]. It cannot be the former position, because for a person who has not perceived the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there can be no apprehension of the relation between cause and effect; consequently, the specific latent impression (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*) which is the cause of the synthetic cognition would be impossible. Furthermore, if there were synthesis of what has not been grasped, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This [objection] has not been correctly considered; for, since the preceding and succeeding moments, which stand in the relation of cause and effect, are directly perceived through sequential experience, the nature of cause and effect is indeed grasped.

It is only because the effect is absent at the time of the cause that, even when the capacity regarding that object is grasped, no activity toward it occurs due to the non-perception of the effect; rather, it is only upon seeing the effect that one proceeds to act.

Likewise, even when observing the result, it is precisely that state of being its effect which was already apprehended that is subsequently synthesized by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); thus, this conceptualization consists solely in the synthesis of what has been previously apprehended.

Furthermore, since the grasping of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), this [objection] is trivial.

By this, that [objection] is also refuted, which was stated: "The relationship of cause and effect is not established for a latent impression (*vāsanā*) nor for the cause of a latent impression when the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has not been observed; and since the same objection applies there as well, it results in an infinite regress. For it has already been demonstrated that the observation of positive and negative concomitance pertains precisely to the subject under discussion. [As for] the conceptualization of latent impressions—

The establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) occurs solely from the final [moment] among the perceptions and non-perceptions, because activity does not proceed from a solitary perception or non-perception; and because, since a latent impression (*vāsanā*) has the nature of a capacity (*śakti*), its determination is untenable without an effect. By stating that every conceptual construction beginning with those arising from a logical mark consists of the manifestation of a non-entity (*avastu*), it is declared to be a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

Perception is the appearance of a real object (*vastu*), because if its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were absent, that appearance would cease. Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not like this, because its appearance does not conform to the real object. Therefore, conceptual construction is a semblance of perception. However, that which arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it causes one to attain the object exactly as it is determined. Furthermore, a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) being conceptually constructed cannot [be established] by a conceptual construction arising from a logical mark due to the absence of such a mark.

Even though conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from a real entity through a lineage beginning with direct experience (*anubhava*), it lacks validity regarding that entity, because validity belongs to direct experience alone. Furthermore, since direct experience—which would serve as the basis for exclusion (*vyatireka*)—has just been refuted, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), conceptual construction determines its object only when that object is non-existent or its reality is doubtful; thus, existence is non-existent.
A mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or one whose negative concomitance is doubtful is not sufficient for proving momentariness.

Nor is the third alternative [valid]. It is understood that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has also been refuted by the sequence previously stated.

As for what was said—that because the internal organ (*koṣṭha*) is pure, the entity (*vastu*) itself is eternal—what follows from that? The word "of the reason" (*hetoh*) refers to that which is engaged in the refutation of a reason under discussion. And thus, the claim that "there is neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity" (*avastu*) is set aside.

Furthermore, this non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is employed in its own terms, because there is the conceit that being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is pervaded by being a real entity (*vastutva*).

Now, in that regard, how can there be the nature of a property (*dharmatva*) in non-entities, up to and including the son of a barren woman? If there is no cognition (*pratīti*), how can there be conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)? If it produces a cognition, how is it not an entity (*vastutva*)? Nor should mere words be accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, whatever reason (*hetu*) is employed—
If all that is being offered is [the argument], how is it not a case of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)? Thus, it follows that "the fault which is equal for both parties," and so forth.
And if these faults do not apply even to things whose non-existence is certain, then why [would they apply] to something whose existence is not yet doubted prior to the proof?

Will it exist eternally? What, then, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) here? For a valid knower (*prāmāṇika*), the conventional practice of affirming or negating any property (*dharma*) regarding a non-entity (*avastu*) cannot be avoided. If it is argued that these faults do not follow as a consequence, it is replied: first of all, there is no absence of being a substratum (*dharmitva*) for a non-entity. For wherever there is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this very thing," by means of this [awareness] "this is precisely that"—

By means of the suffix *kāra*, there is a substratum (*dharmin*). "In this way" (*evam*) indicates the connection with a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Just as "the jar is blue" [indicates the jar], so too in "the son of a barren woman does not speak," the property of being a speaker is understood to belong to the son of a barren woman just as blueness belongs to the jar; thus, there is no absence of the status of being a substratum (*dharmitva*) in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Only some properties, such as blueness and the like, are restricted to real entities (*vastu*), while others, such as the absence of all designations (*sarvopākhyāviraha*), are not so restricted.

Is there something common to both that is merely non-apprehension (*anupalambhamātra*)? In that case, it is logical to negate the status of being a property of a non-entity for that which has the nature of an entity; however, this does not apply to mere properties (*dharmamātra*), because self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*) acts as a subverting factor. Furthermore, the claim that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) occurs through the absence of cognition is also incorrect. For linguistic convention does not depend on a cognition of both [entity and non-entity] in one and the same manner. Indeed, [the basis] of an entity is its own—

Cognition arises through causal capacity; conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), moreover, is an indirect effect of perception and inference. However, regarding that which is not a real entity (*avastu*) or that whose status as a real entity is doubtful, there is merely conceptual construction. For if, in the absence of causal capacity—and consequently in the absence of those two [perception and inference]—even mere conceptual construction were not established as cognition of that [object], it would be entirely beyond the scope of practical activity (*avyavahārya*). Yet, practical activity is desired; therefore, [conceptual construction must be admitted].
In that case, cognition is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpana-mātra*); and the nature of those two [the subject and object] is precisely what is presented by that construction, nothing else.

Just as the nature of a real entity is only that which is brought forward by perception or inference, so too the essence of a non-entity, or of something whose status as an entity is doubtful, is only that which is presented by conceptual construction and nothing else. Therefore, those who draw out a member from convention (*samaya*) cannot be considered authoritative.

they recognize that very thing as the state of being graspable.

And thus the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* itself says: "For you do not accept that which does not produce another object as being an object of cognition. Nor is a non-entity (avastu) another object; for it is only an entity (*artha*) that is called 'another object' in relation to another entity, and not [a non-entity]."

It is a non-entity (*avastu*). It is merely the negation of its existence. Therefore, because there is no other object [corresponding to it], the non-entity does not depend upon a cognition produced by itself. Consequently, mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is the only refuge here. Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that its nature is nothing other than that which is delineated by the form of that [conceptualization]. Otherwise, the consequence would follow that words such as "the horn of a hare" could never even be uttered.

Thus, how is linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) possible? For instance, having referred to an object denoted by a word such as "the horn of a donkey," one must necessarily predicate something of it—either that it possesses the property of being devoid of succession and so forth, or that it does not possess it; or else, that there is no cognition of contradiction with anything for that which is non-existent, or that it is not a substratum of properties. In this regard, if [one were to say] by means of words such as "hare's horn" or "non-entity" (*avastu*)...

The intended object is not what is communicated; rather, it is something other than the intended object that belongs to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the sound. In that case, when [properties] such as the negation of succession and non-succession are being predicated, of what could they be perceived? And in the absence of such perception, the utterance of the word would result in being purposeless. Yet, there is indeed the linguistic usage of words such as "the hair of a tortoise"; therefore, that [usage itself] is its meaning.

The determination of the object is also that very [conceptual construction]. Even when something is seen, conceptual construction alone is the determination. If this is so, then let conceptual construction alone be relied upon in all cases; what is the use of perception? It is not so; for when an object has been excluded by perception, one must rely on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—whether to establish its reality or to refute it—because only the mere appearance of a form flashes forth in the mind of conceptual construction. However, when the object has been made a direct object of perception...

To the extent that there is conceptual construction regarding a form, to that same extent there is certainty, provided there is no deception due to similarity. Therefore, even with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), mere conceptual construction is the refuge; but with respect to a non-entity (*avastu*), that alone is the refuge. For it is precisely the determination of an external object in the form of that [conceptual image] which is required there, depending upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that is established by conceptual construction itself. However, in the operation of a means of valid cognition, there is no [need for] another means of valid cognition.

There is no dependence on anything else. Therefore, when wise people, through the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that very nature which is delineated by that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), establish—on the grounds of its fitness—the negation of being devoid of succession and non-succession and so forth, what kind of fault could there be in establishing a state of contradiction with a form that is the opposite of that nature? Or, for example, just as the negation of beauty and other qualities in the son of a barren woman is appropriate.

And so, what contradiction could there be in the non-contradiction of reality? This is mere incoherent prattle. For so-called "contradiction" (*virodha*) is not some distinct entity that places its feet upon both sides [of a dispute].

We maintain that the designation of a relation is either intended by us or is logically tenable, such that it would be non-ultimate only if one of the two related entities lacked reality. The meaning of "contradiction" is merely the mutual exclusion of the intrinsic natures of two things regarded as opposed; and this [exclusion] between existence and non-existence is itself ultimately real. For it is not...

Existence does not enter into the form of non-existence, nor does non-existence enter into the form of existence; this very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes contradiction (*virodha*). And that rule establishes even its own self—the contradiction—within the sphere of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-pada*). Likewise, the rule that the eternal does not enter into the form of succession or simultaneity, nor do succession and simultaneity enter into the form of the eternal, is precisely that [contradiction].

Such is the contradiction between those two. Nor can it ever be otherwise; thus, since establishment by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone constitutes ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatā*), how can it be said that because the contradiction is not ultimately real, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "existence" is also unreal? On the contrary, having accepted that the eternal is not ultimately real, everything has been established; therefore, there is no fault. And as for [the argument] regarding the contradiction of an imagined contradictory...

It was stated that [the reason] is a "contradiction with a conceptual opposite" (kalpitavirodhivirodha) for the purpose of negating reality, like the contradiction of a barren woman’s son; yet, in that very context,
this wretched man has not even perceived the grosser fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi)— so let us leave aside the exposure of his vital flaw.
And this is being considered: Is it the case that the very state of being opposed to what is imagined is opposed to reality, or not?
If it is not opposed, then there would also be opposition to what is not opposed to the imagined, and reality itself might [also] exist;
thus, how could the presentation of that [opposition] be conclusive for its refutation? For from the prescription of something that is not opposed, no negation can be established.

Now, if it is contradictory, is that contradiction real (*vāstava*) or unreal (*avāstava*)? In that regard, if the contradiction were unreal, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [calling everything] "unreal. If, on the other hand, you maintain the position that the contradiction is real, then even the contradiction with a contrapositive that is merely conceptualized must itself be accepted as real. Furthermore, observe the display of audacity in claiming that this [contradiction] does not, like ours, denote the negation of its own opposite. For, as it is said:

There is a contradiction between permanence and succession; this is a contradiction with the imagined contradictory, because the permanent is imagined. Or rather, that follows from the reality [of the permanent]. By which, for one connected to a single [entity]... in the state of being a real thing. Here the sequence of the leaves has been corrected. Not the existence of another; in contradiction; the negation of the capacity; but thus; the state of being the contradictory of the contradiction.

Furthermore, what is called "contradiction" (*virodha*) is sought for the purpose of prohibiting the coexistence of two things in one place; it does not, however, consist in the establishment of the reality (*vastutva*) of both. Where, on the other hand, there is the establishment of the reality of both, there—by the force of implication—one thing excludes another thing in a certain location, as in the case of "incompatibility in coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*), as previously stated. But the contradiction under discussion here is...
The result is the negation of the coexistence of two properties within a single substratum (*dharmin*).
In that regard, just as two existing properties are both negated—such as when it is said, "Where there is blueness, there is no non-blueness;
therefore, the blue and the non-blue are not one"—so too are two contradictory properties, such as existence and non-existence, [negated] in a single substratum.

Both are indeed prohibited by way of superimposition (*samāropita*). For it is not the case that the son of a barren woman, who is superimposed upon the mother’s son, need not be negated because he is in reality non-existent; nor is the status of being the mother’s son, which is superimposed upon the son of a barren woman—who is the exclusive object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—not to be negated. Indeed, the mother’s son and the son of a barren woman do not share a single identity; by that much alone, the function of contradiction is fulfilled.

Because this is already established by exhaustion, what is the point of another so-called "contradiction" (*virodha*), which does not even attain its own existence without depending on the properties of real entities?
Thus, where there is permanence, there is no possession of succession or simultaneity; and where there is possession of succession or simultaneity, there is no permanence.

Therefore, in the ultimate sense, that which is permanent cannot truly possess succession or simultaneity. Consequently, even if it were endowed with existence, it could not necessarily be [the cause].

In reality, therefore, existence must rest upon momentariness alone; since existence is dependent on that [momentariness], there is no contradiction in the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) from the fact of existence. Even so, if you wish to enter a corner of a mountain cave and shout—having grasped [the argument] through the sequence of "mother-candy" [i.e., a superficial or deceptive connection] by means of a synthesis of contradiction and absence—then go ahead and shout! But it does not affect the proof we have undertaken.

In the case of an obstruction, you might have some utility; therefore, enough of being overcome by dogmatic attachment. It is correct to say that these contradictions and so forth are indeed real. If you ask, "But surely there is no such thing as contradiction apart from the two contradictory properties of permanence and the possession of succession or simultaneity; what, then, is the reality of this [contradiction]?"—that too is trivial. Since this conceptualization is the cause for the linguistic usage that a real entity has an unreal substrate, what is the point of saying that it has a real entity as its substratum? If...

This [characteristic] belongs to apprehension alone. Therefore, is it only in inference that being grounded in a real entity (*vastvadhiṣṭhānatva*) or validity (*prāmāṇya*) resides, and not in perception?

For it is only by relying on a logical mark (*liṅga*) that reflection upon a subject (*dharmin*) finds its scope. But perception, which does not rely on that [mark], is grounded in a real entity simply because it arises from a real entity and functions through the mediation of that entity; in this same way, inference is also "grounded in a real entity."

1. Thus, let this section on exclusion (*vyatireka*) in the chapter on momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) be understood. Only indirectly is even perception itself [the source of] birth; however, its practical application (*vyavahāra*) belongs to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

[In the case of perception,] there is indeed an intervention by means of a divine [sense-faculty]. In the case of inference, however, both [the object and its locus] are mediated through a succession [of steps]. This is because even linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are mediated by memory, desire, and so forth. Thus, while the fact that [inference] has a real entity as its substratum is a defect in itself due to this lack of directness, in the case of inference alone, this [lack of directness] is distinct from the mediation that occurs elsewhere in relation to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely, the grasping of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The claim that [inference] proceeds by depending on another [perception] is a blindness of the intellect. Even in that case, this property is not common to all other forms of inference;

for in the cases of the non-perception of cause, effect, and pervader, the capacity to produce knowledge arises through the pervasion of the opposite (viparyaya-vyāpti), while setting aside a direct connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum.
Similarly, if "having a real entity as its substratum" were to apply to a specific object through the aforementioned mediation, [it would be valid].

What kind of fault is there, since there is no subverting factor? With respect to the conceptualization of the subject (*dharmin*), however, even that much mediation is not possible; moreover, the proximity is unique because the subject is unified with the form of the conceptualization. For even in the position that [the object] is formless, the false and eternal form has its manifestation dependent upon the conceptualization.

Regarding the subject (*dharmin*): therefore, since the search for the real basis of the subject relies upon a specific proximity, it achieves its purpose even through the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus, there is no fault whatsoever. This very principle should be applied in such cases as: "The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because he lacks consciousness," or "A donkey's horn is not a substance because it lacks substantiality," and so forth; for there is no contradiction regarding a non-entity (*avastu*).
And in the passage beginning with "because it is not an object of cognition" (pratītyaviṣayatvāt), this is the refuge.

If "not being an object of cognition" is intended in reference to mere conceptual cognition (*pratīti*), then there is the fallacy of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*); if it is intended in reference to direct experience (*anubhava*), then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
Such is the capacity to ward off objections of this kind; however, there is no counting of any multitude of fallacies such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth.

By this, the claim that "in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi), the absence of the pervaded (vyāpyābhāva) must be established as something distinct" is easily dismissed; for what is presented as the object of cognition is the nature of the locus (dharmin) itself as a distinct entity, just as the absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness [is established] by the absence of tree-ness on a boulder. Thus, there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) for the non-perception of the pervader under discussion regarding eternal succession and simultaneity.

Because of the demonstration of contradiction. When it was said, "there is a contradiction between succession and simultaneity," he stated this again by way of its pervader: "because of the contradiction with causal efficiency. Nor is there a lack of proof regarding the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because even a non-entity is demonstrated to have the status of a subject (*dharmin*), and because its cognition is demonstrated through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason, in the treatise:

Regarding the general rule that the establishment and ascertainment of a property (*dharmin*) occurs through either direct perception or inference, one should understand that the exception (*apavāda*) consists in the proposition of the probandum and the probans regarding a non-entity (*avastu*)— such as nails and so forth having a nature never previously produced by others, or not being causes for sound and so forth. This is clearly evident.

Chapter Four of the "Examination of Momentary Destruction" (*Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*): Section on the Absence of a Cause for Destruction (*Ahetukavināśādhikāra*).
By means of perception, which discerns positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as between smoke and fire,

the relationship of cause and effect is established between destruction and its constituent parts through the observation and non-observation of the visible. Prior to that, when the cause is present, the non-existent destruction brings about stability.
Even the claim that "for such a duration" is false, for destruction is not perceived as having its own essential nature.

The nature of destruction is not within the range of perception such that, through the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one could establish the stability of an entity for as long as the effect called "destruction" did not exist prior to the presence of the hammer or other causes deemed to be its causes; for since the intrinsic nature of destruction is unperceived, this conceptualization is merely false— how then [could it be established]?
Is stability established through the non-perception of a cause?
If it is argued that the nature of destruction is unestablished because the pot, the mallet, and so forth are indeed perceived, and that there is no such thing as "destruction" within them?
The jar, which was seen as the limit of visibility, is seen here falling; likewise, the hammer is seen, and the collection of shards is seen. Beyond that, no other non-existence is seen.
Therefore, where has this expression "non-existence" been placed, or what is its cause here?
Only this row of skulls belonging to Parigha was seen, now under one's own control.

Even though we examine most skillfully with our physical eyes, we do not perceive any other category of entity here that could be made the object of the scriptural teaching regarding non-existence (*abhāva*). And because of this absence of perception, how can we determine its cause—that by whose absence it could be said that "the preceding [entity] has ceased to exist"? Furthermore, as for the staff which is postulated as its cause, its positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—

Only the series of potsherds (*kapāla-paṅkti*) is observed as following upon the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and nothing else whatsoever. This is presented as an example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): just as this [series] is seen to follow positive and negative concomitance through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*), being [thus] visible—[as it is] seen, [as it is] abundant, [as it is] indeed, [as it is] within the range of experience, and [as it is] observed.

It might be argued as follows:
Let alone the row of potsherds; this destruction of the jar did not exist previously—this is the answer here.
Therefore, let even stability be established; what then is the use of a separate "destruction"?
If that very [non-existence] is called "destruction," then how is it that when another jar is placed there, the term "non-existence" is used? Therefore, even for us, non-existence is established.

This is the meaning: just as it is possible for you to demonstrate that the destruction of the jar does not exist prior to the blow of a swift mallet—because the series of potsherds, which constitute its very nature, is not perceived—likewise, it is also impossible to maintain that there is no acquaintance with a succession of absences. For even absence is not said to be the series of potsherds itself, such that the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) could serve as a basis [for the cognition of destruction].

It would be exactly like that. Now, if it is argued that non-existence (*abhāva*) is also nothing other than the series of potsherds (*kapāla-paṅkti*), then how could there be the conventional usage of "non-existence" when one jar has been removed from a certain place and another jar is placed there, given that the series of potsherds is no longer present? Yet, for someone who perceives some degree of difference and is deceived by the similarity of one [jar] to another, the conventional usage of "non-existence" does indeed occur even in that case.

Even if one determines that it remains in its former state, how can it be that the very row of potsherds is the non-existence [of the jar]? If one applies the term "destruction" (dhvaṃsa) to this situation, it might be possible to say that "previously there was no destruction" because of the absence of the state of being potsherds;
however, it is not possible to say that "non-existence does not exist," for it is difficult to discern due to the presence of another similar object. Therefore:

Even if the prior non-existence of the jar before the blow is possible, our desired point is established; namely, that there is no occurrence of the "non-perception of a perceptible object" (*dṛśyānupalambha*). Therefore, the designation "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) serves no purpose regarding the potsherds. Furthermore, since nothing else is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the mallet, destruction is merely a matter of conventional usage and does not exist as a real entity.

If destruction were not restricted by its own causes, why would there be a restriction in experience such as "the jar has been destroyed at this particular place and time"? Therefore, it is an effect. Nor indeed is there any other cause [for its destruction] than the swift-moving staff; otherwise, it would have occurred even earlier.
Who can prevent the stubborn cognition of a destroyed jar that arises from its destruction?

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*), in the section on Causeless Destruction (*ahetukavināśādhikāra*):
"If that is so, then like any other effect, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) would follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its cause, with its neck wide open—"

The argument is refuted because there is no experience [of destruction] other than that of the action itself. Merely establishing [destruction] through reasoning, one must prove its dependence on a specific cause intended as its basis; however, that reasoning is exhausted, since when a cloud is seen, the sequence of potsherds produced by a hammer or similar instrument is observed.
First, the cognition of a destroyed jar arises through the following convention:

"In this context, there is no factor whatsoever called 'destruction' within the causal complex; nor does this [cognition] exist within that complex, nor has it ever existed before, even when the causal complex was complete."

By the first half [of the verse], the causal complex for the cognition of a "destroyed jar" has been shown; then, by the second half, it is demonstrated that for that which is called "destruction"—which is something additional—there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), nor is its distinct causal complex present, such that both would be replicated. In this regard, the positive concomitance is refuted by the fact that there is nothing here within the causal complex that serves as the cause for what is termed "destruction"; nor, even when this causal complex is present, does it [arise].

The reliance on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, that "this cognition might not exist at some time"—is rejected. Then why, by means of the remainder, is the denial of the notion of negative concomitance—that "this cognition did not exist previously"—not addressed? If this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) had existed previously, this cognition, necessarily arising, would indicate its dependence upon another factor. Yet this causal complex does not exist even previously, because the series of potsherds is incomplete.

Because [the effect] is absent due to the absence of causes such as the striking of a bar, how could there even be a mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? However, regarding the aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by two negations: "this [effect] would not exist even in this [complex]," and "it would never exist. By the remainder [of the argument], the negative concomitance is also made clear.
Thus, since it is demonstrated that the causal complex itself is absent at the time of the absence of cognition, this absence of the causal complex is the absence of cognition.

The meaning is that [the causal complex] is pervaded. However, for one of narrow vision who maintains that every causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—by virtue of being the totality of auxiliary factors other than perception—is itself an "examination" (*parīkṣā*), and consequently asserts that there is no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for it because it is beyond perception (*parokṣa*):

alas, even the causal connection between fire, fuel, and so forth would vanish from smoke and the like, leading to the absurd consequence that the world would be devoid of both purposeful engagement and withdrawal.

Therefore, there is no assumption of an unperceived entity by way of obstructing the capacity of a perceived means of proof; enough with this prolixity. Thus, it is established that for one who perceives the jar, the very experience of the potsherds is the means for determining the destruction of the jar. Consequently, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) has reached its end; it is not capable of establishing destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

If it is argued that there can be no cognition of a particularity (*viśeṣa*) without a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), we say: no, because in the case of an entity (*bhāva*), since destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) occurs at a different time, its status as a qualifier is not established. If the logical mark (*liṅga*) is abandoned, then inference cannot exist, as it would be a mere assertion. How could that which is not even perceived by others—being dependent on a certainty that establishes the object called "destruction"—be designated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) in its own right? Nor is there any other logical mark, because since it is entirely invisible, no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) can be established for anything with respect to it. For this very reason:
That very cognition is resorted to as a refuge for its own establishment; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (anekānta) regarding what is established by inference.

This is because the manifestation of the nature of the qualifier is inseparable from inference itself, and because the cognition of the qualifier and the inference are not established separately—this being the case for whomsoever...

That which lacks the manifestation of its own nature cannot be the cause of a cognition colored by itself, just as the mane of an elephant [is not the cause of such a cognition]. And since there is no manifestation of the nature of destruction (*adhvansa*), this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). The state of being the cause of a cognition colored by itself is pervaded by the very possession of manifestation; thus, if it were to exist in the absence of manifestation, it would be sublated by the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasanga*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddhi*), because [destruction] appears as "this" (*idantayā*).

Because there is no conventional usage regarding the appearance of an external object that cannot be demonstrated, and because there is no dispute concerning that which is to be designated as "this," [the staff] is not established by perception through the cognition of the person with the staff; for even the staff is not established by that cognition. Even when establishing conventional usage for the sake of a deluded person, there is no designation as "this" specifically regarding what is within the range of the eyes.
If it is argued that [an object] is made the object of cognition through a difference in time,
then every entity appears in its own form and not in the form of another, just as an existent does not appear in the form of non-existence.

In this way, even non-existence (*abhāva*), although not appearing as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), certainly appears by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). If it is argued that even for an object within the range of the eyes, there is indeed manifestation (*bhāsana*), and therefore, even in the absence of manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*), it is not a case of non-manifestation at all; we reply: no, for one does not seek manifestation in the form of another, since that [manifestation as another] is already established as being absent. However, when we examine what its own nature (*svarūpa*) is that manifests, we find nothing; yet, the designation as "this-ness" applies only to existent things (*bhāva*).

There is no royal decree [to the contrary]. Therefore, if you were to say that even among existing things, this "thisness" (idantā) is designated only for certain objects that serve as the scope of the eye and not for all, then what could be said in this case? For even the letters *ṭa*, *va*, *ka*, and so on, appear before us, yet they simply cannot be designated as "this. Consequently, as long as an object falls within the range of the visual faculty, it is designated as "this."

The logical principle is this: that which appears as a verbal designation is indeed a conceptual appearance (*pratibhāsa*), whereas that which is devoid of such designation and cannot be pointed out as "this" is indeed a non-appearance (*apratibhāsa*) graspable by the eyes.

Now, if it is argued that even the appearance must be established by means of a specific cognition (*viśeṣabuddhi*), just as the cognition of a man with a staff [is not the same as] the cognition of the staff—

If it is asked: "Just as [the cognition of a staff] occurs even without the appearance of a staff, so too the cognition of destruction, though it is a cognition of a specific quality (*viśeṣabuddhi*), does not occur without the appearance of destruction;

how then can there be a 'sound without appearance'?"—[we reply: There certainly is a transformation (*vikāra*), but it is not of such a kind. For we too must understand through inference the appearance of that which possesses its own continuum, such as a jar and so forth.

If it were so even in the case of a manifestation, then this would follow: "What is it that I see? Even for one who lacks inference, the meaning would have to be understood through the word of a reliable authority (*āpta-vacana*); thus, even without employing any other means, a physician would achieve his purpose. Ultimately, one might even rely upon an oath. For these methods find their scope only in regard to objects that are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).

It is not in the case of knowledge. Furthermore, when one who does not see is made to grasp that he is indeed seeing while experiencing himself [as seeing], this is clearly the "magician's trick" (bhaṇḍavidyā) which deceives even one who is actually seeing. And he who, though not seeing, grasps "I see" by virtue of those words, is indeed a beast among beasts.
For even in the theory that knowledge is imperceptible, that which does not appear [to someone] is established by means of the appearance of something else;
it is not established by logical arguments that "this has an appearance" or "this does not have an appearance."

Therefore, the claim that even the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) is the probandum (*sādhya*) is incoherent. If destruction (*nāśa*), which does not itself appear, is being proved, let it be proved; however, it is established that this is not by means of the cognition of a destroyed jar.
Or, let there be destruction, but it is not that which generates the cognition, just as [destruction] is not the cause of the cognition of a destroyed jar.

Even granting this, we say: let there be such a thing as "destruction," yet it cannot be maintained that its producer—such as a mallet—is necessarily perceived. Just as the experience of the potsherds is not accepted as the cause for the cognition of a destroyed jar because it is not perceived, so too [is it with] the particular (*viśeṣa*). Thus, it is not possible to say [that it is the cause], nor can it be said [to be the cause] in the cognition.

Nor can the convention itself be said to perish by undergoing destruction, precisely because it is imperceptible; rather, it is said to "perish" in such a state when it undergoes a modification consisting in the production of a division [between the object and its name].

By this, those who imagine that the perception of non-existence itself constitutes the non-apprehension of an entity are refuted, precisely because it is merely the perception of the form of non-existence.
Therefore, there is no such thing as "destruction" (dhvaṃsa) that occurs subsequently.
Furthermore, if this world is established as having a different nature at every moment;
By the force of mature reasoning, death may be delayed or perhaps not; what of it?
It might be argued:

"If that [destruction] were not distinct from the entity itself, it could not exist alongside the entity; therefore, being both existent and non-existent, what would be certain about the nature of things? Consequently, this destruction must be a subsequent state of the entity."

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*), regarding the section on causeless destruction: Since [destruction] exists as something distinct from the entity itself, its own cause is impossible; because it is thus [distinct], even the "alteration" (*anyathātva*) produced by that [cause] vanishes—so how could there be moment-by-moment destruction?
"The description of the arising of non-existence from the presence of existence" was stated as "if it [the destruction] were together with the existence.

Here, what is the meaning of "other than destruction"? Is one single existence broken into pieces by it? Or is it merely the production of another existence from this [destruction]? Or is it both the cessation of the prior [existence] and the production of another existence? Or rather, the cessation of the prior...
In that regard, [the opponent asks]: "Does it not consist of a mere measure?
To this, [the author replies]: "Destruction does not cause a single entity to become manifold, because of the contradiction between oneness and manifoldness."
If it is argued that even a single entity does not incur a fault by becoming manifold through a difference in time, [we reply]:
what is gained by the difference in time if there is an absence of internal difference [in the entity] itself?

For this would be the case only if the difference in time were to produce a difference in the entity; however, since the entity remains in its same state (*tādavasthya*), it is like [the uselessness of] *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass.
The first position is refuted by the fact that such [an object] must indeed have been employed as the objective support (*ālambana*).

The second fault is that if [the mind] produces something different, there is no "shattering" (*dalana*) of that [original object]; for if another object is produced, the former one is not destroyed, even when [a potsherd] such as a *karpara* is made.
There would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the jar;
what is the use of its destruction when it has already been split?

If it is admitted that the jar is perceived through another entity, such as its shards, then [the destruction] has no utility. If you argue that its utility lies in the production of that very other entity called "destruction," why then does the cause not produce something distinct from the jar?
Since the jar and so forth arise from the very same cause as the hammer and other instruments, why posit destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as the effect?

By this, the portion concerning the production of something else in the third alternative is also refuted; thus, only the fourth remains: that its cessation is brought about by destruction. Even in that case:

[The answer is: No, for it is not perceived as a destruction, since the thing is observed. This is because of its manifestation.

How can this be explained? If it is claimed that when that [hammer] exists, there is a cessation of the entity called "destruction" due to the non-perception of the object,
then let destruction be the hammer itself, or rather, the fragments themselves.

In both cases, since the intention is to express "when that exists," [the cause must precede the effect]: because the mallet exists prior [to the shards], and because the shards exist simultaneously [with the mallet]. This is like saying, "When the seed exists, the sprout [arises]," or "While the cows are being milked, he has departed. As for "destruction" (*nāśa*), it is either a cessation (*nivṛtti*) known as annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*), or let annihilation itself be nothing other than the mallet and so forth. Enough with a separate annihilation!
Even by means of conceptual construction, since that [object] does not exist even to that extent, it is established that the entity was previously stable.
To this, it is replied:
those two...
As a positive entity, it cannot be the negator of another positive entity;

for a positive entity itself cannot possibly be the negator of another positive entity. And if there is no contradiction with the positive entity, how could there be the cessation or non-perception of something else? To this, the reply is:
The very act of "becoming" (bhava) on your part constitutes the alteration of states of being.
In this matter, there is no efficacy belonging to entities themselves; rather, it is through your own speech that things possess existence or non-existence.

For instance, a "being" (bhāva) is so called because it "comes into being" (bhavati), and its "becoming" (bhavanam)—that is, its arising—is thus admitted. Even when a "being" is defined as that which "exists" (asti), [it is still dependent upon your verbal designation].

Even then, existence (*vidyamānatā*) is the meaning of the term "being" (*bhāva*). That [existence] is indeed accepted as characterized by the reality of its own nature (*svarūpasattva*), adorned with permanence, and so forth. Furthermore, how could that which does not exist—such as a barren woman’s son or a sprout [from a barren seed]—be connected with the act of arising? [The text continues: ...destruction... Now, since the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs through the absence of any description of causal capacity, even *śakti* (potency) is admitted to be a form of existence (*sattva*).

That [existence] is also indeed admitted in the production of its own cognition, and movement without hesitation and so forth is precisely its effect. There is no other [existence] than the inherence in existence (*sattva*) as admitted by oneself, or the inherence in its own cause. Nor must every property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) exist in every entity, nor does the absence of every property of an entity imply that another entity lacks the nature of being an entity (*bhāvatva*). This being the case:

It follows that universals, particulars, and inherence would also be non-existent. Furthermore, the very production of destruction as something distinct from those [categories] is a fault. Moreover, since a real entity (*vastu*) necessarily possesses destruction—meaning it "resides" in it—and performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it cannot be called a "being" (*bhāva*). Alas, what a painful and perverse obsession with dogma this is! Therefore, you have full autonomy in this matter. If you say that destruction must also be a being (*bhāva*), [we reply:]...
If it is argued that even a hammer or the like would be the non-existence of a jar—

since no one indeed treats a hammer or such as either a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative one (*abhāva*)— then [we reply]: surely, if anyone were to perceive even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as arising in some form, specifically as something eternally abiding?

What could one designate as "non-existence"? For we observe that things such as thin smoke, whose forms were not perceived due to obstructions, lack of attention, and so forth, become recipients of the linguistic convention of "existence" when they are subsequently perceived. Therefore, the loss of the linguistic convention of "existence" for this [object] is experienced at every moment solely through non-perception, because its nature is the perception of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). And that non-perception, if it is accepted as being based on experience, is itself an existence.

But if [an entity] were non-apprehensible, then the mention of its "origination" and so forth would be like painting a picture in the sky. However, if both its essential nature and its origination are apprehended, the conventional usage of "existence" follows by necessity; so how could even this [non-existence] be contradictory? Nor is it the case that the term "non-existence" does not apply even to a mallet and the like, for that [non-existence] is established through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*). Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). For just as:

By proximity, the very entity called destruction (dhvaṃsa) is said to be the cessation of the jar; there is no obstruction of that [destruction] by either the shards or the iron bar. Furthermore, their mutual opposition is most plausible precisely because of the excellence of those two [shards and the bar] through even the slightest portion known as "perception. For if the conventional usage of the "absence of the jar" were to occur while those two exist, this would result in an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), as the grounds for such a designation would be fully established. It is not so.
Furthermore, one entity is certainly not opposed to another entity; otherwise, how could "cowness" [not be opposed] to "non-cowness," or "fire" to "cold"?
Moreover, opposition is known to be of two kinds. Among these:

If that coexistence were simultaneous existence, then it would belong only to two entities, like fire and snow; for the determination of non-coexistence occurs because an entity whose causes are unimpeded does not exist when another entity is present. And it is evident that this possibility does not apply to existence and non-existence.

10. [The following] are the names of the chapters: 1. On Non-existence; 2. On the Refutation of the Manifestation of Appearances; 3. If [it is argued that] there is no exclusion of one by another when their definitions exist in a state of mutual exclusion... [from the *Ājñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*].
Indeed, the function of contradiction characterized by definition (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*) is not the sublation of an existing entity, but rather that of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*);

for that which is characterized by definition pertains only to the establishment of two properties (*dharma*). It is only when an entity is already established that [contradiction] occurs with respect to that entity.

Alternatively, there is the negation of the confusion and intermingling of intrinsic natures by means of a non-entity. Therefore, just as blue does not become non-blue because the two possess mutually exclusive intrinsic natures, so it would be for the pot and its destruction as well. Yet, this alone does not establish the desired conclusion, because the pot’s state remains unchanged even when the mere proximity of a mallet occurs.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a jar, a thunderbolt, and so forth, because there is a contradiction between two properties alone, there is merely a difference in that which is superposed upon them; however, since the destruction of the jar consists of existence and non-existence, they are themselves contradictory—how then could they coexist? [Response: No, for it is between existence and non-existence that...

The mutual exclusion between two things occurs only between two properties (*dharma*) by virtue of their being positive (*bhāva*) and negative (*abhāva*) in nature; for there is no non-existence (*abhāva*) of that which is occupied by existence (*bhāva*), nor existence (*bhāva*) of that which is presided over by non-existence (*abhāva*), just as there is no identity between a jar, space, or a lotus. What mutual exclusion could there be between these two entities consisting of the destruction of a jar, which are themselves properties? Only their mere contradiction (*virodha*) is not denied.
It is only when there is the exclusion of one by the other that there is the operation of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*).

Therefore, it is only between two properties (*dharma*) that there is mutual exclusion. If it is asked, "How is this so in the case of blue and non-blue?"—the meaning is simply that for blue and non-blue to exclude each other, they cannot be identical. Thus, even in this manner, it is only a contradiction between properties (*dharmavirodha*) that is established.

It is thus clarified: otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-coexistence even for blue and non-blue garments when combined, just as in the case of snow and fire. Yet, even then, identity (*tādātmya*) does not exist at all.
If it is argued that the location (*deśa*) of the blue and the non-blue is indeed distinct, let it be distinct; however, this does not constitute a contradiction between the two entities themselves.

To that extent, the purpose is fulfilled by the difference in location (*deśabheda*). Otherwise, even water and fire, when combined in that same way, would result in a continuous state of existence; for contradiction becomes effective only through the exclusion of infinitesimal points of space (*sūkṣmadeśa*). For this very reason, in the perception of a contradictory [property], the locus (*dharmin*) is the gross location itself, conceived as such. Likewise, it is said that "blue is contradicted by non-blue."
The meaning is simply that "blue" is not "non-blue.

However, if there were a direct contradiction between the subject (*dharmī*) and its property (*dharma*), then wherever non-blueness exists in a subject, blueness would not exist there. Yet, as in the case of another gem, such as *tapanīya* (gold), destruction likewise [exists].

Even though it consists solely of the property of being an existent (bhāva-rūpa-dharma-mātratve), the meaning is simply this: a jar possesses the property of existence (bhāva-dharma) and is not non-existent, nor does it possess the property of non-existence (abhāva-dharma) and thus is not existent. Therefore, [there is] stability... and here there is no sublation of one thing by another thing.

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the section concerning causeless destruction (*ahetukavināśa*) states: By means of the established property of non-existence (*abhāva*), it is simply the case that a jar which was existent is designated as "non-existent," but the existent jar itself is not being removed. However, in the case of the removal of existence (*sattā*), there is everywhere an operation of mutual exclusion (*sahānavasthāna*). But how can non-existence be a property (*dharma*) of the jar? Of what [is it a property]?

Furthermore, let this property (dharma) be [the absence]; since it is accepted as a property, it necessarily implies a locus (dharmin). If you say, "Let it be the surface of the earth itself," then what follows? Is it intended that the surface of the earth itself is non-existent?
Surely, the absence of the jar—which is related to the ground through the relation of the sublated and the sublator—is said to be merely a property of the ground.
If it is argued that [non-existence] does not exclude the ground (bhūtala), let it be so; let that property merely not exclude the ground.

Just as the presence of a blue object is not contradicted on a ground that possesses non-blueness—which is the opposite of blue—so too, even on a ground possessed by an absence that is considered the opposite of a jar, the presence of the jar would be non-contradictory. Therefore, the relationship between what is to be excluded and what excludes is established merely through mental presumption.

This is the state of affairs. Therefore, it is logical that the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), which manifests the absence of a jar on the ground by way of its relation to the jar—the substratum of the ground—causes that absence to be treated as a property (*dharma*) of that [ground]. However, with respect to what has been determined (*adhyavasita*), there are [the categories of] correspondence and its opposite. Thus, a property that is contradictory by way of mutual exclusion brings about the non-existence of its own opposite—which is precisely non-existent—within the locus of its own property.

It causes the conventional usage [of difference], but it does not actually bring about cessation; thus, it is precisely the cause for the conventional usage of difference regarding the substratum (*dharmin*). In this way, in the case of water and fire and so forth, the heat or coldness of their touch becomes the object of the conventional usage of contradiction through the mere reflection upon their own nature—even from a distance—by virtue of possessing mutually opposed forms, without depending on the actual removal of one by the other. However, non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is the [negation] of the existence of one by means of the other.

The determination [of contradiction] is made simply from the observation of cessation. Therefore, if contradiction is intended as "incompatibility through non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*), then let the cessation of existence and perception be established for an entity; however, this applies only to two entities, not to an entity and its absence.
But is it not the case that contradiction is intended as "incompatibility through non-coexistence" in the sense that when one thing exists, the other ceases? And that—

If it is argued that since the existence of an entity is obtained even through another entity, the restriction that [the relation] belongs only between two entities is not tenable—[we reply: it has already been stated in this regard that the phrase "when this exists" is difficult to establish in the case of non-existence. Furthermore, establishing the nature of non-existence in this way is useless, because even in the case of two entities, there is no contradiction [between them], and since the contradiction is established by means such as a mallet, the destruction (dhvaṃsa) is redundant. Now, if...

If a contradiction defined by essential characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*) is intended, then since that [contradiction] is fulfilled simply by the non-confusion of intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*), the persistence of an entity in its state is unavoidable.
Furthermore, under the view that contradiction is characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), an opponent cannot be opposed by a contradictory factor that has not yet arisen.

If it is argued that there is obstruction [of the effect] at the very moment [of the cause's existence], then for this duration of time, the entity would coexist with the prior non-existence of its obstruction. Alternatively, if the operation occurs at the very moment of production, even so, the entity—having destruction as its concomitant factor while being produced—would establish its own effect, namely bondage;
from that follows cessation. Thus, coexistence is unavoidable. Even if one disregards the establishment of the moment of bondage, in its own continuum—

Because destruction occurs immediately after the moment [of existence], coexistence even for a single moment is established. And how can this be endured by one possessing consciousness—that a thing's existence and non-existence should occur in one and the same moment?
Moreover, by accepting simultaneous non-existence, [destruction] produces another destruction, just as fire [produces cold].

Even by means of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), that which has fallen away must be turned back; thus, since that [destruction] would have to produce another destruction in order to counteract its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, even in a hundred human lifetimes, no one could ever engage in the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "non-existence.
Now, as for the second contradiction: where there is existence (*bhāva*), there is simply no room for non-existence (*abhāva*). For this very reason...

The nature of contradiction in its technical sense (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*) is that when two contradictory properties reside in a single substratum, there is no room for the other; thus, destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) simply does not arise. If it is argued that, by the power of a cause, how could [an entity] exist after having been non-existent, and therefore destruction must necessarily come to be—[we reply: no, for it is impossible to postulate the efficacy of a cause regarding an object that is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As long as the breath of an entity moves, there is not even a scent of non-existence. Otherwise, if two properties considered contradictory were to coexist in a single substratum for even a moment, what would "contradiction by mutual exclusion" mean? For indeed, let it be granted that they exist by the power of causes; however, the coexistence of existence and non-existence in a single thing is difficult to avoid. For that [thing] is an existent...

Established as it was before, the entity would not cease merely because one is weary from the exertion of its production. Furthermore, the function of the hammer and such [causes] is simply destruction.

Even if there were a function in both cases, what need is there for destruction? Nor can it be brought to cessation by destruction alone, since destruction has no operation prior to its own arising. Therefore, the coexistence of the persistence of the entity and the arising of its non-existence is established, just as in the case of a mountain.

If it is argued that [the cause] will be refuted later by destruction, just as fire destroys fuel, then this person— fearing the refutation consisting in the undesirable consequence of the coexistence of existence and non-existence, yet accustomed to fallacious reasoning— merely utters a lamentation later regarding that destruction. Later, by destruction...

Whether existence (*bhāva*) is refuted or not, the consequence that existence and non-existence (*abhāva*) must coexist follows; thus, the very position [of your argument] is undermined. What is the point of further searching? Moreover, if existence were established as something that must be destroyed by destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), then it would be evident that this is an operation of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*); thus, the primary point [of your argument] is lost. For the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra-virodha*) is indeed under consideration—
He proceeded to explain. Then, due to forgetting the context, he interrupts [the argument], [saying]:

If it is held that there is a contradiction, then the operation of removing one while the other remains established cannot touch the tangible object; thus, their non-coexistence is protracted.

Now, since the jar and its destruction—which depend on the strength of their own respective causes—are brought together, existence and non-existence are maintained for a long time within a single substratum; thus ends the discussion of contradiction.

Now, if it is argued that there is no such fault because the entity, being constrained by its own destruction, ceases to exist even before its own arising, and destruction subsequently comes into operation; and if it is further argued that this is not an operation of simultaneous non-existence (*sahānavasthāna*), we reply: it cannot be so.
For [this would apply] only when a thing is already established.
Even though it occurs subsequently, destruction is merely its servant;
for as long as this [destruction] has not yet occurred, the entity itself remains more powerful.
However, it has already been explained that this operation [of the hammer] applies not only to non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) but also to mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*).

Nor does a future entity possess any capacity [to act]. If you argue, "In that case, let it cease by itself," then what is the use here of another factor such as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or a hammer? Furthermore, if there is a dependence upon its proximity, the meaning of the word "by itself" is rendered empty.

Just as it is said that "the sprout arises by itself depending on the seed," the fact that it depends on that [seed] is not thereby avoided. If, on the other hand, this is indeed an avoidance [of dependence], then one should not say "depending on that. Furthermore, since the probandum would be established by that much alone, what is to be done here [by the argument]? [Otherwise,] it would follow that even prior [to destruction], an entity ceases by itself without depending on its destruction, a hammer, or the like.
The establishment of cessation [is as follows]: since destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere entity and independent of any other cause,
there is a contradiction between this [position] and the two [conceptions of] object and failure.
If, according to you, there is no co-existence even for a moment— just as between cold and fire—
then simultaneous destruction would now result in the occurrence of another destruction.
Even that which is an adversary leads to another form of decay; thus, destruction occurs in no way whatsoever.
But when the object exists, then, because it has mutual non-existence as its nature,
at that time—
Let there be the mere absence of destruction, or let it occur through the power of causes; however,
its natural cessation occurs through destruction when it does not arise.
If the meaning itself is already more powerful, what need is there here for another [argument] when it has already been diminished?
Thus is the summary verse.
