8. Regarding this [question] in the *Ājñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*:
"If it is asked how the negation of an entity (*bhāva*) occurs through the production of its non-existence (*abhavanotpatti*), [the answer is:
because the production of non-existence itself constitutes the negation of the entity, by virtue of its being incompatible with coexistence. Such is the statement.
It has been shown that [the opponent's position] is characterized by a lack of understanding regarding the contradiction between these two.

For this very reason, one who asserts that "the claim that existence remains in its original state despite the production of non-existence is the talk of a fool" clearly besmears only himself with ashes blown back by the wind; thus, being submerged in great delusion, he should be understood as an object of pity for the great ones.

If it is thus that non-existence (*abhāva*) is designated by you, what is its intrinsic nature? If it is not a real entity (*vastu*), then why does this not indeed contradict existence (*bhāva*)? Or how is the establishment of these two contradictions [of existence and non-existence] possible, and what is their cause? If an entity is both occasional (*kādācitka*) and non-occasional (*akādācitka*), why is it not designated as such at the same time? Or why is it not [perceived] later just as it was before?

If it is argued that the production of a succession of moments is impossible because there is no contradiction between coexistence and non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna-virodha) at the time of production,
and furthermore, since non-existence is not a real entity, even the mutual exclusion (parasparaparihāra) between existence and non-existence would result in being unreal—
precisely because the opponent’s position is thus incapable of withstanding scrutiny.
Therefore, it follows that the mere fact of falling away from that [state] is the occasion for conventional usage;
however, the subsequent designation of the object is contradicted, yet its "birth" is not. What need is there for a cause?
Precisely because of that contradiction, there is no conventional usage of it even once; and due to the exhaustion of the cause, there is no arising.
If the obstruction were real, then the reality of the mutual destruction of their inherent natures would necessarily follow.

The definition of its essential nature is that it is "mere cessation of an entity" (bhāvapracyutimātra), designated as a non-affirming negation (prasajyapratiṣedha). In that negation, they maintain that the reality is the negation itself; thus, it is called "mere cessation. To the doubt, "What indeed is this so-called 'cessation'—is it a third kind of negation of an entity? it is stated that it is "called prasajya. Furthermore, that is an object of mere conventional usage, and not an object of direct experience.

Otherwise, it would be a real entity (*vastu*) itself. Furthermore, not everything that is conventionally designated by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) is a real entity; for if it were, even things such as a donkey’s horn would entail the status of being a real entity, and because it would be impossible to establish a conceptual construction that lacks a real basis (*nirvastuka*). And that [conceptualization] occurs through the property of the manifestation of non-existence (*abhāva*).

"It is indeed contradictory"—this is the response to the second question. Is "existence" (bhūti) the capacity for the purpose of being, or its abiding in its own nature? In either case, because they are of mutually opposing forms, they are contradictory by the mere fact of their exclusion; thus, the established definition of contradiction as a state of mutual exclusion has been stated.

In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the section concerning causeless destruction (*ahetukavināśa*):
Now, mere disappearance (*pracyutimātra*) is nothing at all; how then could it be contradicted by anything? Precisely because it is merely disappearance...
To some extent,
however, existence (*bhāva*) is indeed contradictory to that which is the opposite of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), for that very reason;
yet this contradiction is not a mutual physical obstruction (*anyonyapratighāta*).
It is not like the non-abiding of existence (*sattānavasthāna*), but rather merely the non-penetration of one another's forms.

And since that [non-penetration] exists even between the conceptualized and the experienced, there is no fault. As for the question "Why is a cause required, since mere disappearance might at times lack the nature of being?"—this is answered in the fourth [chapter]: for it is [the entity] that emerges again in some form.

If it were to be postulated as a "non-existence" (*janaka*), would it be occasional or would it exist at all times? Or would it not exist at all? Among these, since the position that it exists is rejected, it does not exist at all. Yet, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is occasional, because such usage does not occur at the time when the positive entity (*bhāva*) is present. How is this so? Precisely because of contradiction. For non-existence is the opposite of existence; its nature is privation and it is a conceptual inversion. How, then, could it be conventionally designated at the time when the positive entity is present?

For an entity that possesses the nature of becoming—whether it be causeless, produced by a cause of becoming, or created by another cause—might indeed exist even at the time of its manifestation and would thereby attain a linguistic convention (vyavahāra) following upon that existence. However, when its existence is absent, there can be no linguistic convention following upon existence. But as for the contradiction inherent in the latent impressions (vāsanā), there is an awakening of those impressions upon the perception of a real object by one who possesses certainty.
How could [non-existence] function due to a lack of [the object]?

Therefore, as long as there is the determination that "this very thing exists as its own nature," there is no opportunity for the conventional usage of non-existence, even if momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) were real. However, when, by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an entity is established as having the property of existing for only a single moment—

When one ascertains that "this is its intrinsic nature," then at the second moment, simultaneously with the moment of the material cause (*upādāna*) of that object, one employs the conventional expression of its non-existence. However, when that means of valid cognition is not obtained, the conventional expression of non-existence depends solely upon the observation of transformations such as shards;
this is the resolution in the fifth [chapter]. In the sixth [chapter] as well, there is the arising of the causal vehicle (*hetuyāna*) in the form of a continuum of homogeneous moments.

This is what is meant: in the case of the spontaneous cessation [of a series], because of the dissimilarity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in each preceding moment due to the presence of a hammer as a cooperative cause, a barren moment is produced; thus, the material cause (*upādāna*) is exhausted, and consequently, no further [moment] arises. Furthermore, that entity by whose action a certain barren moment is established—which results in the non-reconnection with another moment of the same kind—is itself [the cause] of that [cessation].

Since it is established that one state (*bhāva*) is the opposite of another, this constitutes the determination of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*). Therefore, even in the seventh [verse], by the fourth quarter, although the mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*) between an entity (*vastu*) and a non-entity (*avastu*) is a form of contradiction, nevertheless there is no loss of its reality (*tāttvikatva*).
For there is never any commingling of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-sāṃkarya*); this alone is the meaning of the contradiction of properties (*dharma-virodha*). Precisely for this reason—

The mention of "stability" (sthiti) is intended primarily to indicate a restriction; by this, the third alternative is also refuted. Therefore, it is established that what is called "destruction" is neither of the nature of a positive entity (*prasajyātmā*) that would require a cause for its production, nor does it entail these aforementioned defects.

Furthermore, regarding whether an object is perishable or otherwise: if it is perishable by nature, its destruction is brought about by causes;
however, in the case of its arising, causes that are not the cause of its destruction are useless. Conversely, if it is imperishable by nature, those [causes] are incapable [of destroying it].
If that is the case, then what is the purpose of causes in the production of things that are either destined to come into being or not?
For it can be said that if an object is destined to come into being, the causes of its birth are redundant; if it is not destined to come into being, they are incapable [of producing it].

And thus the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* says: "That is not so, because it would follow that the doctrine of causes is abolished, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is possible in every case. For instance, does that which exists by virtue of a cause have the nature of coming into being, or rather the nature of not coming into being?
If the first position is held, then it comes into being by itself, because it has that very nature; thus the cause is redundant. In the second position..."

For that which is incapable—such as a rabbit’s horn, whose nature is non-existence—cannot be produced by anything whatsoever. Likewise, causes such as cutting or burning must be seen as untenable, whether one holds the position that the object possesses that nature or does not possess it, due respectively to its futility and its incapacity. Thus, since all possible causes are refuted in this manner regarding these [alleged] causes, [there can be no production] of liberation and so forth.

Regarding the claim that "the effort of hearing the scriptures is useless," one is here questioned as follows: Why this approach, which is like striking at the root with an axe? It is said that in no case whatsoever, when something is presented as a reason, should a fault characterized by incapacity or futility be asserted. However, that is incorrect; for indeed, the futility of an axe is observed in the case of what can be cut by a fingernail, and [the futility of a fingernail] in the case of what can be cut by an axe.

There is an incapacity on the part of the fingernail. Likewise, regarding that which is to be accomplished by Devadatta alone, Yajñadatta’s activity while acting as Devadatta’s assistant is useless; yet, when deprived of him, there is an incapacity. When the causal complex of fire and fuel is present, the donkey’s contribution to the smoke is useless; when it is absent, there is an incapacity. Or, where there is the bolstering of what is already established (*siddhasādhanapoṣaṇa*), there is futility (*vaiyarthyam*). [In the case of] the unestablished (*asiddha*)—

"Incapacity" refers to the presence of any one of the contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacies. As for those who maintain that "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) is also included among these, their effort yields no fruit; for the fault of futility (*vaiyarthya*) cannot be denied in any way as a defect of the reason (*hetu*), and because even a probative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*) acts as a causal factor toward cognition. Furthermore, if incapacity and futility were not considered defects...

Since there is no refutation of the reason other than [the one already stated], everything would be established by anything whatsoever. [Variant: Or rather,] the cause of birth is purposeless. [The concluding construction is: "In the case of future existence, the causes... [Variant: *tataṃ* (ra); *tad* (ā) is not present;
*pakṣa* (ā) is not present.]

Now, if it is argued that the refutation based on the alternatives of "having that nature" or "not having that nature" is invalid, that too is incorrect. For regarding a lamp, whatever reason is adduced— whether for its being an illuminator or for its being a cause of darkness— is it not defeated by either futility (*vaiyarthya*) or incapacity (*asāmarthya*)?

Furthermore, as for what he himself says—that even the example of light and so forth is untenable—it is as follows: first of all, in our view, the oneness of the lamp and its light is not established, nor is their having a single cause. For it is our settled doctrine that after the substance has arisen, qualities such as light arise from a different set of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*). That too is irrelevant, because:

Even though the quality of luminosity (prakāśa) arises immediately after the substance has arisen, nevertheless, that very substance, once produced, does not depend on any other cause for the perfection of its own form; nor does the subsequent quality of luminosity depend on anything else for its nature as the quality of luminosity— thus, there is no failure of the illustrative example.

Now, if it is argued that even the form of a substance (dravyarūpa), prior to its inherence in the generality of substantiality (dravyatvasāmānya), is neither a substance nor a non-substance; then, in that case, the position must be that this form of a substance is either known through the generality of substantiality, or else it becomes the object of conceptual construction (vikalpa) and verbal expression as "a substance. Regarding the first alternative, there is no fault; for it is precisely from the generality that it is a substance.

For it is the established position that [the universal] must arise from some source by means of its own nature, such that once born, it does not require any further cause for its existence. Even in the second alternative, there is no fault whatsoever; for that which has the nature of a substance is indeed already born even prior [to the cognition], since the production of the cognition and the verbal designation of the substance arises precisely from the universal (*sāmānya*). Nor does this much require any other cause for its existence. Indeed, [this is not like] by means of an effect...

Regarding the causal factor's operation through its own objective capacity (*sāmarthya*), that capacity is either unestablished prior to it, or the cause exists while that capacity is present; in that case, the effect itself would have to depend upon another cause. Furthermore, even when the quality of illumination (*prakāśaguṇa*) arises later as something distinct, at that time, [the object] would already be endowed with the quality of illumination.

Since the lamp is already complete, why would it require another cause for its existence such that the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) would be undermined? Therefore, one who relies on invalid means of knowledge cannot defend the system by bolstering its methodology. Rather, according to experience, the example is exactly as intended.

For there is no perception of a distinction based on the presence or absence of connection with a universal (sāmānya) in the first and second moments; nor is there [such a distinction] in the substance—

As for the claim that there is an experience of difference between two universals (*sāmānya*), since this is already established otherwise in the context at hand, there is no insistence on this point. Therefore, manifestation is not produced as a manifestation by its own cause; once it exists, it does not depend on another cause, because that would be redundant. Furthermore, it is established that [the cause] lacks the capacity even to render it dark.

"Now, it is observed that a white cloth (*śuklam ambaraṃ*) is being colored by means of the application of a dye-substance (*rāgadravya*). In that case, why is the objection regarding the uselessness and incapacity of the dye-substance—not its having the nature of redness or not having that nature—not raised against the cloth? If this is asked, [the answer is: No.

It is not intended that this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) applies in all cases; rather, the refutation of the reason (*hetu*) is first undertaken by way of the conceptual constructions of "having that nature" (*tatsvabhāva*) and "not having that nature" (*atatsvabhāva*), as an absolute negation of impossibility (*atyantāyoganiṣedha*). Consequently, wherever this refutation can be established, it enters into the state of being a valid refutation. What is the point of further deliberation if there is a difference in reasoning?

And likewise, what is this so-called perishability? Is it momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), or existence for a shorter duration? Is imperishability, too, [defined by] remaining forever for an exceedingly long time? In every case, if an entity that arose from its own cause were destroyed by something else within the duration of its existence, then it would not have arisen with that very duration of existence. For indeed, [if it were destroyed], it would not last for a year—
"It is well said that its two natures—being permanent and being perishable at day's end—are mutually contradictory.

But surely there is no contradiction: it remains for a year in the absence of a cause of destruction, yet perishes momentarily when an intermediate cause of destruction is encountered. Indeed, there is a contradiction only if there is no room for the qualification 'if' (yadi) in the determination."

Regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): for example, if smoke were possible upon the falling of a leaf in a certain place, it would necessarily be embers; otherwise, however, it would be a cluster of *guñjā* seeds—thus there is no difference in their intrinsic natures. Similarly, if something perishes during the day, let it be that it was produced by a cause limited to that very time; but if it perishes after a year, let it be that it was limited to that duration. However, two mutually contradictory natures cannot coexist in a single place.

[This is] a synthesis. For in that case, it is not possible for [the object], while perishing, to remain for a year, or for both [states] to exist by way of successive halves. Alternation (*vikalpa*), however, belongs to knowledge itself as its nature of doubt; it is not a property of the real entity (*vastu*). Therefore, a real entity possesses only a single nature and is not joined with another contradictory nature. And this persistence for a day and so forth deserves to be determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is true.

Or not? This has been considered while tentatively accepting [the opponent's position], because it is difficult to rely on the efficacy of a cause when that is contradicted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, even if there were non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatā*), it remains established that as long as there is a limit to its duration, another cause lacks efficacy within that interval, and beyond that, it is futile. Even in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), [it is futile] at that very moment.

It is evident that nothing can be accomplished by a cause of destruction; for since the thing itself ceases to exist in the very next moment, there is no purpose served by a cause of its non-existence. Furthermore, such a cause would be entirely incapable regarding something that is eternal.
Therefore, when destruction is to occur, no cause whatsoever can escape the consequences of incapacity and futility.

But when it concerns another object, such as a potsherd, that very same hammer is not tainted by those two defects, because the potsherd comes into existence immediately after the operation [of the hammer]. Likewise, in the case of the substance of passion (*rāgadravya*), which arises immediately after that operation—[provided] there is conjunction (*yoga*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the red garment": there is no lack of capacity [for the word to function], nor is it redundant. As for the exclusion of the pale *caṇḍātaka* (tattered garment), who indeed would exclude that?

Even when the substance of the garment is one and the same across two states, there is still no escape from that fault. For even in its red state, it does not follow that it is purely white. Therefore, if at that time too the substance were purely white, then [the redness] would not exist.

The term "opportunity" (*avakāśa*) refers to a substance of passion that is not yet capable [of manifesting]. However, in the case of one already colored by passion, it would be redundant if it were merely expected to be colored by that [new] degree alone. Therefore, since a fault arises only upon the expectation of stability, such a thing is a transgression of convention (*samayāparādha*), not a fault of the object itself. For when the previous [state] is naturally suppressed, the fault is successfully avoided by producing a cloth newly colored by the substance of passion in dependence upon its material cause (*upādāna*). It is not so [in the other case].

If you say it is the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), surely that very point is what is being investigated: what kind of actual state of things is it? Must the opponent here be convinced by drinking from the vessel [of poison]? Why then is it stated so abruptly that "this is the actual state of things," given that the reliance on the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been refuted?

Furthermore, the denial of the occasional occurrence of destruction has already been stated.

Furthermore, if non-existence were the qualifier, then since a distinct entity can arise from its own causes alone, and since the perception and conceptualization of distinction are established by presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), what is the use of non-existence? Moreover, that which is experienced as distinct is a contradiction of distinction. Now, if there is neither distinction nor non-distinction without non-existence (abhāva), then what is the operation of the causal factors (kāraka)? Where even a single [element] is not perceived and manifests under the name of non-existence (abhāva), pervading its own [domain], there it is called a "succession" (paramparā).
If falsehood has already begun, what is the use of secrecy here? This is precisely what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa writes when he says:
"Is a cognition, by its very nature, excluded [from others] or not excluded? If it is excluded, then exclusion is redundant;

What is the meaning of "in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*)? Does it mean "without exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), or rather "by means of a form distinct from exclusion"? It is not logical to say "without exclusion," because exclusion is an eternal property (*nityadharma*). For a substratum (*dharmin*) is designated even without that property which occurs only occasionally; for example, a person is designated as "not wearing earrings" (*akuṇḍalī*) when he is without his earring, due to its destruction.
"Previously it was not destroyed. Nor can an entity ever be devoid of its exclusion from other entities, just as there is no cow devoid of "cowness," nor fire devoid of heat.
Now, if you intend that it is excluded by means of a form distinct from the exclusion itself, then that is exactly what we accept.

Because difference is admitted. Nor is exclusion (vyāvṛtti) thus purposeless. If a person is wealthy because of wealth that is distinct [from himself], does it follow from this that wealth becomes useless? Therefore, the claim that even mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) is indeed a separate entity from a positive thing (bhāva) is also refuted. For this objection was certainly not raised while conceding that exclusion exists as a real entity; rather—

The meaning of the objection is that since exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is useless—due to both incapacity and redundancy within the cognition of exclusion—it cannot be established by means of that [cognition]. In this regard, "redundancy" is stated in the first position, while "incapacity" is intended in the second. Furthermore, the point is as follows: if an entity possessing an excluded nature has arisen from its own cause, then by that [nature] produced...
It must be understood that [the object] is indeed excluded by its opposite.

For it is not a mere whim on the part of the object, nor has it been determined by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that even when all other conditions for cognition are complete, it should not produce its own cognition in the absence of that [exclusion]. Nor is it a property of the cognition produced by it, that it should exist without such [an exclusion].

This so-called "grasping at the non-grasping of that" is merely an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) belonging to that [object]. Since the cognition of an exclusion can occur in another way as well, it should not be postulated.

Now, if an entity has arisen without having excluded [its opposite] from its own cause, and having arisen, it possesses a mixed nature, then how could that very non-exclusion of what has arisen produce a cognition of exclusion? Thus, it is incapable. In this way...

Furthermore, within the context of this objection, having established that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is already proven, what is the use of [positing] its being a permanent property and so forth? For this does not address the issue of avoiding the futility mentioned in the first position. To explain: since exclusion is postulated by the force of the cognition of exclusion, and that cognition of exclusion is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), what is the point of this postulation? Such is the objection regarding exclusion.

The proponent of the reply [states]: "Dharma is eternal; therefore, it is impossible to be without it. But what connection is there between this and that? For as long as the exclusion [of the object] is distinct from the exclusion itself, there is no occasion for the argument that the cognition of the excluded object is otherwise inexplicable (anyathānupapatti) except through its very persistence; so why discard that and engage here in a mere statement of a philosophical tenet?

Nor is it proper to state that "it has not perished prior to destruction," because the difference [between the entity and its destruction] is unestablished. Furthermore, regarding the claim that "an entity is not devoid of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), if the exclusion is not ultimately different [from the entity], this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because even in the case of the example, it is impossible to demonstrate a difference between the cow and fire by means of "cowness" and "hotness," which consist of the exclusion of non-cows and non-hot things, since such a difference is unestablished.

Furthermore, regarding the second alternative proposed here by him—namely, whether exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) occurs through a distinct operation—that is already refuted by the very fact that such an [external] operation is not admitted; for what is intended to be expressed is the meaning: "it is cognized as excluded by its own nature," which is to say, "it is cognized as having a form excluded from everything else. Nor has the objection regarding the futility of the first [alternative] been avoided, as has already been stated. Nor [is it resolved] by the example of the wealthy man.

Because there is no rule for establishing a distinct exclusion [of one thing from another], and because it does not depend on relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)— as in the case of "one possessing wealth" or "the door"— there would also have to be a conventional usage of relation for other qualifiers, such as "having a staff" or "being white. Therefore, there is no such thing as "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*),
since things arise from their own causes already mutually excluded from one another.

The same applies even to that which is separated by an interval of time. Nothing at all is produced by a cause of destruction. Thus it is said: "If there were anything to be produced, another [cause] would depend upon it" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.579).
Thus the principle is established. Why this needless grinding of what is already ground?
Non-existence is not a distinct category of entity (anyapadārtha) in the sense that "destruction has arisen today";
rather, non-existence is restricted to its own specific time and does not exist at any other time.

Because of the possibility of a difference in designation: [57b] what exactly is this excluded entity that should now be designated? Regarding the exclusion by way of negation (*paryudāsavyudāsa*): if it is further asserted that even the possibility and perception [of an object] depend solely upon convention (*samayamātra*) with respect to that which is intended as non-existent, then this is indeed a real non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and not a negation by way of exclusion; thus there is no fault. However, this person who fancies himself a knower of logic, having transgressed that very method established by reason, [asserts that] the capacity for existence, perception, and causal efficiency belong to non-existence as its actual nature.
They must be accepted. And what further calamity, endless indeed, could there be than this—that he says:
"For origination is not the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāva*), such that its cessation, while occurring, would be an entity; rather, it is non-origination."

Furthermore, regarding the claim that origination is held to be characterized by the cessation of its own nature (*svarūpa*) in the case of destruction, rather than being characterized by the relation to existence of what was previously non-existent or by inherence in a cause; even in that case,
it is simply the cessation of the very nature itself that is everywhere called "origination."
But by throwing it into the category of "inherence," that too has been lost by the deluded.

Since inherence itself does not exist, how can there be a relation with existence (*sattā*) and so forth? Or, even if such a relation were granted, origination would still consist solely in the acquisition of a previously non-existent nature; however, the presence or absence of other factors, such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), are neither the cause of its establishment nor its sublation. Furthermore, regarding the effect as well—

What is the meaning of the statement that there is no connection with existence for an entity that was previously non-existent? Does it mean that what was previously non-existent simply does not come into being? Or does it mean that even afterwards it lacks existence? In either case, how can it have the status of an effect, like a sky-flower or a lotus in the sky? Let there be the existence of what was previously non-existent, but let there be no connection with the category of "existence" (sattā).

Is it not the case that "existence" (*sattva*) and "being" (*sattā*) are not different in meaning, and that "conjunction" (*yoga*) is a relation? In that case, what is this principle: that there is a conjunction with existence (*sattva-yoga*), but no conjunction with being (*sattā-yoga*)? If you say that "being" is called the "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*), and that even in its absence one is later said to "be" by virtue of mere existence-in-itself (*svarūpa-sattva*), then if that existence-in-itself is ultimately real (*tāttvika*), [the same problem remains].

If being an effect consists in that much alone, what further function remains to be performed by another [cause] for any other effect? Or, if it is merely figurative, then how can destruction itself possess the status of an effect? For surely, even if the term "subsequent existence" is applied figuratively to the son of a barren woman, his status as an effect is not real.

By this, it is demonstrated that the appearance in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is pervaded by non-falsity; for if the object were situated otherwise, the appearance would cease to exist due to the absence of its pervader in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and thus it is pervaded by being situated exactly as it appears.

The third quarter [of the verse] establishes the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). The fourth quarter refutes its non-establishment (*asiddhi*). For if an entity were identical across prior and subsequent times, then because it would lack any other form than the one perceived, the form belonging to another place—even if it existed at a different time—would necessarily manifest; thus, there would be no occasion for seeking another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its state in another place or time.

Furthermore, there is an inquiry as to how that object exists now in another place or at another time, wondering whether it has perhaps been sprinkled with the essence of passion; for such an investigation is observed when there is an occasion for the possibility of its occurrence. And such a possibility does not exist for that which has already been made an object of perception. Nor can it be asserted that there is no determination even when something is seen, provided that it is thus desired to be known.

Just as there is no determination of momentariness regarding a form such as redness due to the absence of prior habituation, otherwise, even upon seeing it later, there would be no arising of a determinative cognition (*avasāya*).
Therefore, the absence of that determination arises precisely from its non-appearance [at that time].
Now, even if the object appears as pervading the three times, regarding its own related particulars of time and place—

If it is argued that "the non-appearance of the ten types of relations (*daśāntara*) does not constitute a sublation, because even when a momentary entity is perceived, the non-appearance of other entities related to it—such as cause, effect, or conjoined things—is equally present; therefore, it is indeed logical to seek further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to those other related entities," we say: this is not so, because since [entities] possess place, time, action, qualities, and so forth, their difference [from one another] is not established.

However, let there be no appearance of even a related entity that is distinct [from the object]; therefore, having excluded all other momentary states, it is established that every object appears only through a form encompassed by a single moment.
For as long as a dissimilar state, such as a red color and so forth, is not present, for that duration they are unified.

And let there be the apprehension [of the object]. That too is not the case; for immediately after the characteristic of seeing, when the eye moves swiftly, even regarding similar objects, a doubt of error actually arises in subsequent moments, whereas such doubt is impossible regarding things that have been directly perceived.

Therefore, that seeing which occurs immediately prior to the movement of the eye is not momentary, because for an ordinary person, there is the possibility of a doubt of error regarding the final determination.
To establish a connection, that perception must necessarily arise for two or three moments to be effective;

therefore, how could there be a loss of manifestation for a form lasting two or three moments during its first moment, such that a distinction between the second and subsequent moments could be established? As for one who holds that [the object] exists only until the very moment immediately following the first moment of observation—

When the eye moves, there arises the conceptualization of objects; for that [eye], the expansion of the investigation into the subversion of all other moments is difficult to restrain. [The text contains the following variants:

Therefore, in this chapter on momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga), there is the section on causeless destruction (ahetukavināśa).

If it is argued that this is not possible for anyone, what is the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) here? And if it is asked what the establishing proof (*sādhaka*) is here, it is said: if the search for a proof occurs immediately after the moment of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), then there are two kinds of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception (*pratyakṣapṛṣṭhaja*): the conceptualization of "merely what was seen" (*dṛṣṭamātra-vikalpa*) and [the conceptualization of] "this is the cloth. It is simply: "This cloth has been seen."

Furthermore, regarding the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) in artificial and non-artificial gems, pearls, and so forth— wherein similarity must be excluded from the object—

this delusion (*bhrānti*) of the dull-witted common person (*pṛthagjana*) is set aside by the excellence of practice, which has been established as the general rule. Due to the gradation of intensity in its arising, when the limit of the brevity of time is reached, even immediately after the moment of perception, this [delusion] arises.

The negation of what is impossible to conceive cannot be established by mere perception. However, regarding a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has just been perceived, its arising immediately after the perception is set aside by the difference in causal conditions (*sāmagrī*). For instance, those whose conceptual constructions have become habitual through the beginningless continuum of *saṃsāra* act toward or desist from even a directly experienced object based on conceptualization—especially in the case of pleasure and pain.

How could all those who seek the attainment [of liberation] and the avoidance [of suffering], whose mental continuums are constantly perfumed by the practice of investigating the means to that end, fail to experience the state of non-conceptuality when the cause for it—namely, the experience of that object—is present? They would surely experience it, were it not for three reasons: sometimes there is no habituation to the withdrawal of conceptualization; sometimes there is attachment to other things; and sometimes there is [the absence of] ultimate...
Due to delusion, there might be a manifestation [of conceptualization] through such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that gives rise to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) delayed by a long interval.

However, in the absence of that [delusion], the arising of conceptualization immediately following the moment of perception is indeed established. Consequently, with respect to all moments of the object that are devoid of that [initial] perception, the mind’s oscillation in the form of doubt—such as "is this red? and so forth—is just like [the doubt] regarding a series of remote moments.

Even when [the object] is made the focus of reflection in the second moment, how could there be no room [for this]? Nor is it the case that such is so even in the manifestation of perception. Therefore, the entire mass of objects enters into the manifestation of direct perception as if already encompassed by the moments [of its existence].
Hence—

It might be argued as follows: This [argument] would be tenable if perception were momentary; however, since perception extends over multiple moments, there is scope for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) when that which extends over multiple moments appears. Therefore, how can the apprehension of a single moment be established? It is replied: First of all, does [perception] extend over multiple moments because they are useful for the production of its own nature (*svarūpa-niṣpatti*), or...

Is it [perceived] as a whole, or because that which is produced in a single moment is itself stable? Regarding these, the first alternative is impossible, because cognition—being devoid of the nature of a composite whole—cannot arise in fragmented parts. Furthermore, if those parts, which are distinct moments, possess the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then there would be as many perceptions as there are parts; thus, with respect to the first perception, the same dilemma remains.

However, if the nature [of the object] is indivisible (*aparicchitti-svabhāva*), then even when aggregated, it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Indivisible determination" (*akhaṇḍaśaḥ paricchitti*) means the complete determination of the entire entity as a whole by means of the aggregate. Even then, the entire entity is merely a fragment determined in the first moment, because that which has not yet entered into it is distinct from it. Otherwise, the entire universe, being perceived sequentially, would be a single entity.

It might be argued that all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed one and the same direct perception. To this it is replied: [the text] does not exist [in version A]; or rather, [the word] "or" (*vā*) is thus [placed]; [the term] "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) does not exist [in version A]; here, page 137 is missing [in version A]; [the reading] "at the conclusion" (*sāyaḥ*); [this is from] the *Ajñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*.

Even in the second position, is it that of one whose activity has already been completed? Or is it that of one whose activity is completed by pervading another moment? In the first case, since its very activity consists in the grasping of the object, there is no room for the arising of conceptual construction by that much alone; let the [perception] itself exist in another moment or not. And this being so, whether the eye or the object moves, [the fault remains].

The claim that perception remains inclined toward grasping its object is an unprecedented approach. For if it remains in a state of non-grasping, there is no liberation from the opportunity for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) merely by that much. Furthermore, the position that [perception] is stable cannot be maintained on the grounds that what was previously grasped is not subsequently grasped; for it is utterly unworthy of credence to suggest that perception remains even while failing to grasp the sensory object presented before it.

Likewise, the notion that the operation [of cognition] persists even when unaccomplished is difficult to believe. For, unlike other effects, cognition has no operation distinct from its very arising. And even if this were the case, it would still be a well-spoken statement—just as before—that perception, having arisen upon the proximity of the sense organ and the object, "apprehends" its previously unperceived domain at the time both [the object and the cognition] are being examined.

"Enough with these excessively persistent false conceptualizations"— this is indicated by the fourth quarter [of the verse], which refers to the reversal of the occurrence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that was previously hinted at: namely,
that whenever any form whatsoever capable of being determined appears, it does so at that very moment as something variegated, red, or otherwise.
A means of knowledge that has ceased does not desire to manifest therein;

for when [an object] is appearing at that moment— just as taste is [not perceived] in the appearance of color— another means of knowledge is required, which depends upon the determination of its prior state.

Thus, by the perception of the pervasion of the contradictory, it is established that the manifestation of direct perception reveals the very nature of an entity as lasting for only a single moment. Furthermore, it has already been explained in the section establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) that its nature does not exist outside of that manifestation.
Therefore, it is not [the case that] its establishment is unestablished.

Consequently, its perishability is established by perception; and it is treated as such by inference, supported by other means of knowledge, once the direction of the reasoning for the determination of momentariness has been indicated by perception.
In this work on the exposition of conventions established through implication, there is no prolixity for the wise;
yet even that [work] was composed by the preeminent teacher Ravi, while those of small intellect— due to their lack of understanding of reality— have vomited forth falsehoods with natural loquacity.

nor [is it established] by depending upon the path of the teacher Ravi.
Since our method concerns the apprehension of moments (*kṣaṇika*),
and since the consistency with the statements of the *Bhāṣya* is as follows,
we have not sung [of it] here for fear of an irrelevant prolixity.

Enough, then, with this insistence on incidental discussion. It remains established that there is no such thing as "destruction" distinct from the iron bar and other such instruments, which could be accomplished by a hammer or similar tool and, by its non-occurrence at the time when those instruments have not yet fallen upon it, fulfill the desire for the permanence of an entity.
"Śaṅkara, with ease, [overturned] these firm pillars of the altar of Dunitāśrama— Trilocana, Nyāyālaṅkāra, and Vācaspati."
By whatever merit I have acquired through uprooting this momentary destruction [of worldly existence],
may this person attain the glory of wisdom that reaches the further shore of the three worlds.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Destruction Without Cause," is completed. 4.
