|| An Inquiry into Pervasion ||
[1b] Homage to the Blessed One, who is free from passion!

Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and the like by fire and the like—established through perception and non-perception—is explained as being characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). For the earlier opponents maintain that the nature of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) consists merely in the observation of smoke where there is fire and its non-observation where that [fire] is absent.

They postulated this. In that regard, even if seeing and non-seeing were merely accidental, they would occur only once; therefore, it requires repeated occurrence. If it is argued: "But even with repeated occurrence, deviation (vyabhicāra) is observed in the case of a jar, an unchaste woman, and so forth";
what does this matter? Is it said that an inference must still exist even there, or rather, that it should not exist in the case of smoke and such as well?

The first position is refuted precisely because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The second is also refuted for the very same reason of non-deviation. For there is no harm to smoke simply because something else deviates; surely, just because a particular poison is undesirable, other food should not be abandoned either! If cessation were achieved by that much alone, what would be the point of seeking its production, or of perception which is useful for its ascertainment?

If its origination (*tadutpatti*) were also apprehended solely through perception and non-perception, what fault would there be? Let inference itself function through such a distinction; thus is that [origination] sought. And that distinction is established by way of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and non-deviation. In the absence of deviation, the capacity to convey the object of knowledge (*gamakatva*) exists by that much alone; the origination [of the effect from the cause] would then be useless. And in the case of deviation—

Even a hundred instances of its arising are not capable [of establishing it]; therefore, the search by means of proximity is fulfilled by conjunction alone. For this very reason, conjunction is called the cause, as in "smoke is the cause, not the effect. Trilocana, however, says: since perception and non-perception have particulars as their objects, how can the two [establish] universals?

What is the cognition of a relation? If it is argued that the relation between that which is excluded from non-fire and that which is excluded from non-smoke is indeed cognized, then of what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that the object? It cannot be that of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its object is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Nor can it be that of inference (*anumāna*), because inference is preceded by that [perception]. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "relation" that is excluded [from others]. Now, if [it is argued that] perception—

The subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), having perceived a difference, determines non-difference; that alone is the universal (*sāmānya*). Even so, the object of conceptual constructions is not the real entity itself, but rather the apprehended form (*grāhyākāra*), and that is not a real entity. Since the real entity remains entirely beyond the reach (*parokṣa*) of those [constructions], how could there be a grasp of its relationship? For us, however, the mind—aided by repeated observation—[grasps] the relationship among members of that same class.

It is apprehended; therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire. If it were to deviate from that, smoke would transcend its relation which is free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Thus, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that removes the suspicion of the reason’s presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is precisely perception (*pratyakṣa*), known as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), which has as its cause the absence of a limiting condition that meets the criteria for perceptibility. Consequently, the natural relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is established.

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, however, Vācaspati’s elaboration is as follows: namely, that the relation between smoke and so forth with fire and so forth is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), but not the relation of fire and so forth with smoke and so forth; for those [fires] are perceived even without smoke and so forth. But when there is moist fuel—

When they experience a connection, they are then connected with smoke and so forth. Therefore, the connection of fire and the like with wet fuel and other such conditions is produced by adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*), and is not inherent (*svābhāvika*). Consequently, it is not invariable. However, the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is inherent, because no such adjunct is perceived. [2a] In some cases, there is deviation...
Because it is not perceived; for the postulation of that which is not being perceived is untenable.

Nor is it logical to claim that an unperceived *upādhi*, even if suspected due to the absence of both proving and subverting evidence because it is unfit for perception, would obstruct the inherent nature of the connection [between the middle and the major terms].

And since it has been said, "For those who perceive no restrictive factor, doubt must necessarily arise" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.324), the demoness of uncertainty, having found its opportunity, will not cease its spread by overstepping the boundaries of worldly means of valid cognition.

If one were to think "it does not exist anywhere," no one would ever act; for in every case, there is some possibility of some harm arising in some way. And because the apprehension of potential harm is a necessary factor for the desisting of prudent people—even since death is observed at times despite the consumption of wholesome food and drink—therefore, one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative means of knowledge must entertain doubts in accordance with what is observed, and not otherwise.

Even in the case of something never seen before, doubt necessarily depends upon the recollection of specific characteristics; it does not arise from a lack of recollection. Furthermore, recollection cannot occur regarding that which has never been experienced before. As it was stated by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*, and likewise by him himself in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*:
"An apprehension devoid of a means of valid cognition is not [justified];
for he who, out of delusion, might imagine an obstructing factor even though it has not arisen," (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 2.60).
In all worldly transactions, he who is of a doubting nature shall go to his ruin.
Thus, having searched diligently for a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and not finding one, we understand that it does not exist and conclude that the relation is innate (*svābhāvika*).
This might be so: if an innate relation were to exist between one thing and another that is not its cause, then everything [would be related to everything].

Everything would be connected by way of its own nature, and everything would be understood from everything. If, on the other hand, the effect of one thing were different [from it], [then there would be no pervasion]. (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā, p. 138, Vyāpticarcā)

Why is it that everything does not arise from everything, given that there is no difference in their being "other" (*anyatva*)? Consequently, that same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains. If it is argued that the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities are not subject to questioning—such that even though there is no difference in their being "other," only certain things are causes and only certain things are effects—is this refusal to question intrinsic natures not equally applicable to those things that are not related as cause and effect, provided there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*)?
Thus, this [objection] is also trivial.

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), moreover, is this natural connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) apprehended? In the case of connections perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is by direct perception. For instance, when one first perceives the connection between fire and smoke as being together with moist fuel, [it is apprehended by direct perception].

In that case, is the relation between the two natural or conditional? Furthermore, it is impossible to determine whether the relation of smoke is conditional while that of fire is natural, or whether the relation of fire is conditional while that of smoke is natural.
For fire without fuel is observed in cases such as a red-hot iron ball even without smoke; therefore, fuel is its condition with respect to smoke.

It is determined that the relationship [between smoke and fire] is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). For, since a particular instance of smoke is never perceived without fire, and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating an unperceived limiting condition (*upādhi*), doubt—which depends on the recollection of specific features—does not arise regarding something previously unperceived. Alternatively, if it were to arise, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), resulting in the cessation of purposeful activity by discerning persons.
The intrinsic relationship is determined.

This determination is not mental, for if the mind were to operate toward external objects independently, it would follow that there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf. Furthermore, if its operation depended upon repeated observation, it would result in the introduction of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the mind is not the instrumental cause [of perception].

Thus, the mind itself is mental. This being so, there is nothing that is not mental, because every cognition (pratyaya) depends upon a specific cause that serves as its unique basis for being designated as "mind."

Since even here, in the designation of those respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), frequent observation (*bhūyodarśana*) exists as the uncommon cause, another means of valid cognition has arisen. Therefore, just like the discernment of the true nature of various noble gems, it is the sense organ itself— assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by frequent observation— that [perceives] the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) of smoke and so forth, according to the proponents [of this view].
It is logical that [inference] is a grasper.

Thus, in the case of those things whose relations are known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it should be inferred that those very other means of valid cognition—assisted by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) according to their respective natures—are the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the natural relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*). And therefore, reasons (*hetu*) that are thus connected with their own probanda (*sādhya*)...

If [the reasons] were to exist without the probandum, they would deviate from their very nature; thus, where they are observed with the aid of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) to have eliminated doubt regarding the absence of the probandum, they necessarily establish their own probandum. Furthermore, there is no possibility of an essential (*svābhāvika*) necessary connection between "being the son of Maitra" and such qualities as "darkness of complexion," because the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for darkness of complexion is the specific transformation of food and drink.
Because [the property of] being Maitra’s son is not a prover with respect to the relationship of existing [in him], since that relationship is already established;

by this, examples such as "the fruits at the top of this tree are ripe because they originate from this tree, like a fruit already tasted," which involve adventitious relationships, are also explained. Therefore, that whose relationship is natural and necessary is a constituent part of inference.
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*,

it is established that [a reason] such as "being smoke" or "being produced" is valid, whereas that which is adventitious (*aupādhika*) does not constitute a limb of inference (*anumānāṅga*), such as "being his son" and so forth.

To this it is replied: what is called "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) consists in the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) there, or the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only there; thus, because it is understood as a property of the agent and the object respectively, it is intended as being of two kinds—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—since otherwise it would be useless for inference. For if, in a general sense, it were merely that when the probans (*sādhana*) exists, the probandum (*sādhya*) necessarily exists, [then it would not suffice].

It is established that when the probandum is absent, the probans necessarily does not exist; thus, by specifying this distinction, there arises the expectation of the probandum where the probans exists, and the absence of the probans where the probandum is absent. However, when the aforementioned rule does not hold, and there is the suspicion that something may be a probans even though it lacks the probandum, how could there be any scope for inference? Therefore, regarding inference—
In the case of falsity, the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be understood as being strictly necessary; its establishment cannot be achieved through mere repeated observation alone.

For just as there is the possibility of a single instance of correspondence occurring by chance, so too can there be a negation of correspondence occurring by chance even over several occasions. And just as deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed upon seeing a single instance of coexistence, it does not follow that [the relation] holds everywhere.
Furthermore, the suspicion that there is a rule of constant concomitance between them arises precisely because deviation is observed even after repeated observation; thus, it cannot be refuted.
As for the [alleged] deviation...

The claim that inference is precluded by the observation [of deviation] is not tenable. For instance, whose observation of deviation here serves as the cause for obstructing inference? Is it the observer’s, or the author of the treatise’s, or anyone’s at all? In the last case, what has happened to the observer such that he would not perform an inference?

Otherwise, since another person would have achieved their purpose simply by directly perceiving those respective objects, why would they necessarily seek out inference? Furthermore, it is unworldly to claim that one who has asked the author of a treatise might infer fire from smoke despite not having perceived the relationship between them. For the cognizer, however, even if a deviation (vyabhicāra) exists, it does not necessarily come within the range of perception; for it is not the case that wherever there is a deviation, [the deviation] is right there [before one].

At that time and in that place, it necessarily enters into the realm of cognition. Furthermore, one cannot conclude that what is not being perceived simply does not exist, because it may be seen even after an absolute lapse of time, and because its presence is established for those who have not yet developed a subverting cognition, due to its proximity to death. Consequently, even if there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the perception of the cognizer is possible. It occurs.

If one remembers what was taught— that inference occurs only when there is non-deviation (avyabhicāra) and not otherwise— would such a person proceed with inference based on a certainty regarding that non-deviation, or would they refrain from it? Since certainty cannot be achieved through mere non-perception, non-deviation remains unestablished and thus doubtful.

It is like the case of a proven reason (*siddhahetu*). In that regard, according to the first position, one could infer even from a camel; however, according to the second, one could not infer even from smoke.

For there is no distinction whatsoever at the time when one observes the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between what is present and what is absent. Therefore, if one suspects that even frequent co-observation (*sahopalambha*) between a camel and a deceptive person is merely accidental, why not suspect the same for smoke and fire?
The same applies here. Now, even when a camel and a donkey are observed nearby as independent entities, I observe the discussion of pervasion (*vyāpti*):
with the desire to know whether one, being driven away, follows after the other like a calf follows a cow, I proceed accordingly.

One acts accordingly: when fire is removed, one perceives the departure of smoke, and when fire is present, one perceives the occurrence of smoke. If it is argued that, therefore, deviation is possible for the camel at other times but not for smoke, [we reply that] it is indeed qualified.

In that case, the kind of perception and non-perception that establishes the origin [of smoke] in relation to smoke does not exist in relation to a camel. For instance, when one cognizes the absence of smoke upon the absence of fire, then—preceded by their joint observation—the non-perception of smoke when only fire is absent is employed for the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Otherwise, in the absence of joint observation, the removal of glowing coals—which are indistinguishable from fire—and the mere removal of the flame would not suffice to establish the non-existence of smoke.

It does not exist at all; for what kind of understanding of a relationship could there be in the case of the absence of a donkey [inferred] from the presence of a camel? Even if they are observed together, if it is the removal of fire accompanied by another object, then there is no certainty as to whether its prior existence was caused by the existence of the fire or by the existence of the other object. However, if there is merely the absence of fire, it is easily understood that its prior existence was indeed caused by that [fire’s] absence. This is also the case when...

The existence of smoke in the mere presence of fire: even then, it was previously necessary to observe the smoke after first observing only the fire, having not observed both together beforehand; otherwise, if only the fire were brought and smoke already exists there—as in the case of a camel—where would the establishment of the invariable relation (*pratibandha*) occur?
Furthermore, even when fire accompanied by other objects is brought, there is no certainty as to which object's absence was responsible for the prior absence of smoke.
But when only fire is perceived, it is logical that [the absence of smoke] is conditioned by its non-existence.

Thus, the non-perception of one thing is said to be qualified by the prior perception of another, which depends upon a previous observation; and that prior observation is itself qualified in relation to the two aforementioned types of non-perception occurring at a later time. The same applies to cases preceded by non-perception.

A distinction must be inferred in perception, such that in its absence there is no certainty regarding a camel or similar animal. Relying precisely upon that distinction between perception and non-perception,
the conventional operation of perception and non-apprehension, as well as its object— the nature of two entities— is called the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Furthermore, that which is dependent on what is not [yet] dependent is also necessarily bound to it by way of its arising from that. For instance, when only that [first factor] is removed, the association with a second [factor] is also negated; thus, it is evident that the latter is dependent upon the former. This should be understood in the same way regarding the removal of the first factor alone; otherwise, since the removal of the second would still be required, how could there be a removal of the first alone? Therefore, it is precisely by way of its arising from that [that dependence is established].

Pervasion is said to be established by means of perception and non-perception, and not merely by seeing and not seeing while devoid of those specific features. And when there is dependence on those specific features, since fulfillment is attained through a single occurrence, there is no further need for repeated occurrence. For just as one does not require another cognition beyond the mere apprehension of concomitance—which produces lack of confidence—through a single instance of seeing and not seeing, so too [is it here].

Since the causal relationship between two specific types of entities has been established through perception and non-perception, there is no need for it to be inferred through a series of intermediate steps; the process is completed by that much alone. If it were not so, and one were to determine a different genus (jāti) through similarity and the like, then the person must be considered a discerning cognizer. However, if there is merely concomitance, doubt arises regarding that very genus, and not otherwise.

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even when there is mere concomitance (*sahacāra*) serves as its well-nourished seed. Furthermore, the analogy of poisoned food does not apply here for the sake of pacification, because other types of food are of a different nature than poisoned food; however, in this case, that which is the predominant causal factor is [the poison].

The definition of concomitance (*sahacāra*) implies that smoke possesses the very same nature as its cause; it does not share a commonality with curd-rice and the like, which may be poisoned. Thus, there is a distinction. Furthermore, without "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), there would be no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) at all, because in the case of distinct entities, non-deviation itself consists in the fact of being produced from that. Therefore, to claim that origination from that is delayed relative to non-deviation is entirely illogical. Consequently, [the mark] is indeed an effect (*kārya*).

Smoke is the cause of fire because it implies an invariable concomitance through its production from that [fire]; it is not a "conjoined" (saṃyogin) indicator, as that would merely refer to their coexistence.

How then is the example of the camel and the donkey given, since there is no conjunction? Let satisfaction be found in the abundance of observed instances of the conjunction between a maidservant and a water-jar. Or rather, even in the case of the camel and the donkey, there is a restriction of their presence at that time and place, just as there is for the crane and the water.

The claim that "it may be so from perception" is of no consequence. Therefore, it is established that when another object is to be known, there is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), and the proof of its existence is based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). Regarding the objection raised by Trilocana, we say: as for the statement that "perception has particulars as its object," does this mean that the particular itself is also its object?

Now, if it is indeed a particular (viśeṣa)? In the case of the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda), there is no obstruction to its having a universal (sāmānya) as its object; so why would there be no scope for perception and non-perception regarding two universals? But as for the exclusion of connection with another (anyayogavyavaccheda), is this stated by relying on our own established tenets, or according to the actual nature of things (vastuvṛtti)? For us, both [types of exclusion] are valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and have both as their objects, because the apprehended (grāhya) and the...

By way of distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*): for that which appears in a cognition is the apprehended, whereas that toward which it [the cognition] operates is the determined.

In that regard, for perception, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the apprehended and the universal (*sāmānya*) is the determined; for inference, however, it is the reverse. Therein, the perception of the means of proof (*sādhana*), although at that very moment it observes a moment for one seeking causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), has the universal as its object insofar as it refers to the continuum (*saṃtāna*).

Furthermore, in the section concerning the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), even when there is the perception of a single individual instance, it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object because it takes all individual instances of the same class as its domain. This is because one experiences a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) arising from the force of that perception, which includes within itself the entire collection of instances excluded from everything other than those—such as the cognition: "By me, through direct perception, smoke was determined to be born from fire. This is just as, upon seeing a mere color, [one determines] color and taste.
Perception has as its object a jar, because it is observed to be a determinate cognition regarding a specific aggregate of odor and touch;

nor is there such a thing as a "universal" (sāmānya) that is entirely distinct [from particulars], but rather the unique particulars themselves (*svalakṣaṇa*), whose differences are not distinguished from one another, are called a universal. However, when their differences are distinguished, each is a unique particular, and thus they are designated by the very word "particular" (*sva*). Therefore...

Although things possessing their own unique characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are entirely distinct from others, do not become objects by way of being apprehended because they do not appear [in cognition], nevertheless, they cannot be avoided as objects by way of being determined (*adhyavasāya*). Thus, how can there be an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)? Furthermore, the claim that the object of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) is merely a non-entity is stated only through ignorance of the established tenets of others, because both synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and inference have real entities as their objects insofar as they depend upon determination (*adhyavasāya*).

The rest is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*). Now, if you maintain the position that [the object exists] "in reality" (*vastuvṛttyā*), that too is incorrect; for it is impossible to bypass the twofold nature of objects, consisting of the distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*), which applies to all cognitions. Indeed, the very validity (*prāmāṇyam*) of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is what is exceeded [by this claim], as is the investigation into pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The duality of objects, however, is established everywhere. In that regard, first concerning inference: since a real entity does not appear [in cognition], it is only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is determined; yet, what is grasped is the form of the cognition itself. This point has been thoroughly examined by us in the *Apoha* chapter, and thus it is not introduced here. Furthermore, even if the form of cognition is not admitted [as real], how can it be excluded when it has arrived through the force of the real object?

For there can be no such thing as cognition without an appearance; and since it is established that in inference what appears is not the external object itself, its own form (*svākāra*) is necessarily [the object]. If you argue that this form may be false (*alīka*), even so, when that [form] appears, the external is both the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determinable (*avaseya*). Thus, since the duality of objects is established, why this insistence? Likewise, in perception as well, only a certain individual (*vyakti*) appears and is apprehended; but all—

At the time of perceiving the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), [the object] is determined through its own class (*sajātīya*); for if it were not manifest [at that time], even if there were a determination, the very scent of the established perception of the connection would be utterly dispelled.
As for what was said regarding apprehension by means of the mind or by the sense organ aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—that is as follows:

This is now investigated. First of all, there is the repeated sensory perception of individual instances of fire and smoke. There also arises a reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*) born from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that perception: "This [smoke] is always perceived only in conjunction with this [fire]; so, is this concomitance between these two eternal, or is it merely adventitious, like that of a friend? For one whose power of reflection is weak, even the cognition of the necessary connection (*hetunāntarīyakapratīti*) [is not established].
It occurs; and the performance [of the action] conforms to that. However, no further manifestation of knowledge is perceived here.

Therefore, the observation of multiple instances has merely been made an auxiliary by means of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); it is not possible to state that which is under discussion [thereby].
Furthermore, the claim that it has as its object all individual instances of a single class, including the final one, is a mere fantasy, because those individuals do not appear [simultaneously].

Because of its existence; even doubt, occurring immediately after that, cannot be determinative of the relationship precisely because it is a doubt. And as for the subsequent [cognition], even though it has the form of a certainty, it belongs only to one devoid of *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness). Thus, what confidence can there be in the object of knowledge (*prameya*) presented by that which is called "perception"? For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) not born from a logical mark (*aliṅga*) conforms to the object exactly as it was previously engaged by the operation of perception.

The arising of an entity does not occur through independence, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, previous perceptions, which are satisfied by mere concomitance—like the concomitance of wind and sunlight—do not penetrate any specific distinction; how then could they be capable of establishing its correspondence with reality? Even if that were the case, those [perceptions] alone would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein, whereas this [present cognition] is merely a recollection (*smaraṇa*) serving as a means of valid cognition.

It is well said that [the relationship] is being pointed out. It should not be argued that there is no difference between wind and sunlight regarding the subsequent cessation of their co-existence, because the intended non-difference is relative to the time when no deviation is observed; furthermore, as has already been stated, even in this case, the certainty of non-separation is untenable. For as long as the non-arising of smoke prior to the operation of fire remains present in the mind, it is precisely for that long...

The discernment of a distinction arises from another instance of co-occurrence; therefore, it is only logical that if there were deviation from that [co-occurrence], smoke would transcend its relationship with fire as being free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Otherwise, just as when one previously perceives mere co-occurrence and subsequently observes fire without smoke, one postulates a limiting condition for the relationship between fire and smoke in a general sense, so too [would one postulate one] for smoke in the absence of fire.

In the case of the apprehension of an entity, there would have to be the postulation of another limiting condition (*upādhi*); therefore, what could have what kind of relation—whether adventitious (*aupādhika*) or intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)? For it is not the case that when two friends see one thing, they do not also see the other [simultaneously].

There is no such possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). For, since the existence of Maitra is not contradicted even in the absence of Caitra, his fitness for being seen does not vanish even when he has entered a cave in a mountain; however, in the case of smoke, there is certainly no arising at all without fire, and thus no such possibility exists. By that much, the relation of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) alone becomes the refuge [for inference]. And that [relation] is not established by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*).
This has already been stated.

For this very reason, it is impossible to assert that the relationship between a cow and "cowness" (*gotva*) is innate, because there is no perception of its arising [from them], and there is no distinction from other co-occurring factors. Nor is it [innate] due to the observation of co-occurrence—

Furthermore, this is not evident through perception, because neither part [of the causal complex] is individually apprehended. Therefore, what is the point here of introducing a distinction between the "intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*) and the "conditional" (*aupādhika*) theories?
Moreover, regarding the capacity to indicate [the effect], since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause, there is no fixed rule that one cause produces [the effect] while depending on another.

However, the effect is restricted by the causal complex and is thus restricted by each individual member; therefore, it is established that the effect itself is the logical mark (*liṅga*), and not the cause.

Because smoke is observed when fuel is present near fire, fuel is established as a *upādhi* (limiting condition) specifically with reference to that particular instance. Furthermore, if fuel were to serve as the *upādhi* for the connection of smoke with fire, it would necessarily be perceptible; however, since it is not perceived, it is said to be non-existent. Is fuel alone, then, the ultimate *upādhi*, such that its perceptibility is restricted? For it is indeed fuel that is intended as the requisite factor in the connection.

Furthermore, an *upādhi* must be defined as either a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) or a specific property of the nature itself (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). Now, a distinct entity is not necessarily perceptible.

Consequently, even in the case of the connection between smoke and fire, there might exist an *upādhi* that is simply not observed; how then can one conclude that it does not exist at all on the basis of non-perception, such that the establishment of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) could be achieved?

Now, if there were another distinct entity to be depended upon, how could there be such a rule that the existence of fire is necessarily determined by smoke alone? Is this not precisely what is being investigated: whether, when smoke exists, fire must necessarily be present, or not?
For perhaps, depending on some other factor as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), there might be smoke without fire; what, then, is the definitive cause for certainty in this matter?

Therefore, it is correct to say: how could smoke, whose arising is entirely dependent on fire, ever accept existence in the absence of that [fire]? Furthermore, this non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is unestablished. For just as fire is not connected with smoke without fuel, so too smoke is not connected with fire without that [fuel]; thus, the status of being a limiting condition is the same for both.

If it is argued that the establishment of the condition (*upādhi*) is that smoke is obtained through the presence of fuel when fire is already established, whereas for smoke that is not yet established, its natural connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is established because its very existence is caused by that [fire] and thus it does not deviate from it— even so, this amounts to nothing other than "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), and that alone is the natural relation. Nor is it as has been stated—

It is perceivable by the mind and so forth; nor is it sublated by the non-perception of a visible limiting condition (*upādhi*). Thus, it is established that in the case of the suspicion of a limiting condition, there is no exclusion of smoke from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Regarding fuel (*indhana*), it is present in both cases. However, in the treatise *Vācaspatya*, while discussing pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is stated that in the relationship between fire and smoke, fuel is indeed observed as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); but as for smoke...

In the case of the relation with fire, there is intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), and the sublation [of the opponent's view] occurs through the mere non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). And in that regard, the reason is "because no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed anywhere. Regarding this, it is considered: does this reason prove the non-perception of the limiting condition, or is that very non-perception the proof for it?
Is it a sublater of the limiting condition itself, due to the lack of strength in the non-perception of an existing [condition] which gives rise to doubt about intrinsic nature?

In the first case, there is no utility; for the existence or non-existence of cognition is not to be established by another cause, because it is of the nature of self-cognized awareness or another [mental] perception. Furthermore, since there is no perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), non-perception is already established. Thus, even when no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed, the lack of utility of the reason must be stated. If it is argued that "utility" consists in establishing conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), we say no, because there is no disagreement on this point.

Because mere non-apprehension is already established, the third [alternative] is also not tenable. If the first [non-apprehension] lacks the capacity to prove negation when it is devoid of the qualification of being "perceptible," what kind of capacity could the second possess? If it is argued that "deviation" (vyabhicāra) is intended only in the case of the perceptible, then it does not apply everywhere or at all times. Consequently, since there is no deviation anywhere, [the connection is] natural (svābhāvika).

Your [argument] is incorrect. For if one were to assume non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) merely because deviation has not been observed in some instances, then such an assumption would apply to fire as well by means of smoke, or even to Caitra and Maitra in relation to one another. And if this were the case, it would follow that there could be no confidence even in a relationship based on intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika-sambandha*).
Therefore, non-deviation must be sought in every single instance. Consequently, even regarding the object of inference, as long as the probandum (*sādhya*)—

As long as one does not establish [the relation] through perception, one cannot realize the absence of deviation; thus, inference is rendered useless. Furthermore, in the theory of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), the doctrine of "inherent nature" (*svābhāvikavāda*) was resorted to in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding smoke;

and this inconclusiveness arises from the suspicion of deviation. Therefore, if there is no deviation due to inherent nature, it must hold everywhere; and because there is no deviation everywhere, it is inherent.

The statement "you [must rely on this]" involves mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, for one who holds that the very cognition of the production of one universal (*jāti*) from another universal at a single instance constitutes the cognition of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) everywhere, this undesirable consequence does not apply; for it is logically established that such an admission occurs only when there is a requirement for repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Just as there is a requirement for something else when doubt arises during a single observation, so too is there a requirement for doubt at other times as well. Thus, they are mutually entailed.
Thus, there is an objection regarding the observation in all cases. However, if one were to show a restriction on the number of times [the cause is observed] even in that instance—as we do:
"Having first not seen them, one who sees them in succession knows the state of cause and effect;
or, having seen them, one who does not see them in succession [knows it] by their being otherwise."

Thus, if there were a rule of three repetitions for the individual instances of perception and non-perception, but only one repetition for the totality, then it would be well-established by that much alone. However, since the word "repeatedly" (*bhūyas*) does not have a fixed number, how could one who follows the definition reach completion with a certain amount?
And if that were impossible, one would never produce an inference; thus, the science of definitions would be useless. But in the case of memory—

To instill proficiency in the mind, some degree of philosophical exposition will proceed; yet therein, nothing is lost by the absence of a fixed limit of quantity, just as there is no fixed temporal limit for a seed to produce a sprout. Likewise, even in the case of the manifestation of the true nature of a noble gem, there is no fixed limit to the number of observations required, because what is intended is merely the disclosure of the distinctions between its subtle forms.

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, regarding one who has entered a dark chamber [to perceive] luminosity and so forth, or like a pair of conjoined twins (*yamalaka*): in the case of smoke and the like, however, no distinction in form (*rūpa*) is intended, but rather a distinction in essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For just as, even though there may be hundreds of observations previously [made], there is no [perception of] the two forms—blue and its opposite—[as distinct].

[The senses] are capable of determining specific differences; however, prior to observing deviation, there is no determination of any difference in form between two things—one possessing deviation and the other not—even when they are present together as distinct objects. In the case of smoke, however, it has been stated that even the mind does not perceive any distinction in its form, because its occurrence is dependent upon fire. For this very reason, its non-occurrence is established through the operation of perception and non-perception.

However, with respect to form, even in the case of smoke, the very same initial perception that occurs remains exactly the same up to the final moment; it does not possess any distinction like that of a gem.
If the cognizer is free from doubt regarding deviation in such a perception, then there is no need for a second perception either.

[This is] dependence (*apekṣā*). But for one who is suspicious, there is no conviction even through a hundred observations; thus, what is the fate of those who mutter the syllables of your mantra, saying "repeatedly" (*bhūyaḥ*)? Therefore, even one who has observed non-deviation a hundred times remains full of doubt beforehand.
As for that lamentation like a person in deep sleep—"because the postulation [of an object] is impossible even for that which is not perceived"—that is [merely] wailing.
Even for a child, this is improper; for conceptualization occurs only regarding that which is not being perceived, as in the case of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), and so forth.

The distinction, however, is that some conceptualized entity accords with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while others do not. Indeed, a jar that is currently being seen is not called "conceptualized.

Therefore, the conventional usage of conceptualization applies only to things that are not being perceived, though in some cases it may occur through the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) and the like.

Because no subverting factor is observed, the determination of existence is firm; however, for the critical investigator, it is merely partial. Therefore, if deviation were ever seen even in the case of smoke, it would indeed have been seen; what room for doubt could there be then? But when it is not seen, let there be no determination of its existence as a certainty—since that would exceed the bounds of valid cognition—but how can the partial mention of its existence be prevented? Now, if the intention is this: "No."

If you argue that non-perception is intended only in that specific case, but not elsewhere—such that one does not suspect [the absence of fire] regarding something else that is not perceived—is it not true that deviation from fire has indeed been observed in the case of gold and other such things? Let there be satisfaction with that. Or, if you say it is not seen in smoke, then has "manhood" ever been seen in a post, such that one would suspect it in a post? If you say it is seen in what is characterized by verticality, then here too, [it is seen] repeatedly.

[The concomitance] is seen only in another instance that accompanies [the probans]. For this very reason, such statements as "nor even when not being seen" and so forth are contradictory. It is unworldly to claim that one must observe the [probans] only in that very place where its deviation is suspected. Therefore, even if a deviation or a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not observed in the class of smoke, it is impossible to perceive it due to its unobservability. This doubt now—its own...

A doubt regarding actual existence necessarily obstructs the certainty of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*). Furthermore, since smoke is a signifier by virtue of an intrinsic connection, how could it be grasped as a signifier if that [intrinsic nature] were not certain? For a reason is not a signifier merely by its presence in the subject (*dharmin*); it cannot be a signifier even when there is doubt regarding its presence. And that which proceeds despite a doubt regarding something...

Even if that [invariable concomitance] were absent, [the cognition] would still proceed; thus, by discarding the notion of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that anything else—just like smoke—could serve as a means of knowledge (*gamaka*). Therefore, the restriction of certainty (*niścayapratibandha*) is in fact nothing other than the restriction of essentiality (*svābhāvikatvapratibandha*), because without certainty, the factor that constitutes a means of knowledge is itself ineffective. Consequently, in the case of smoke where fire is absent...
"A discussion of pervasion must necessarily be undertaken by those who do not perceive a restrictive factor" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.324).

Thus, this [absence] is difficult to transcend if one does not rely on its production. Nor is there any reproach for overstepping the boundaries of the world of authoritative persons (prāmāṇika) in this way;

for no one asserts uncertainty regarding the domain of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nor certainty where there is an absence of a means of valid cognition—just as you yourself assert the certainty of non-existence despite the absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa) regarding the upādhi. For this very reason, there is no room anywhere for the demon of doubt when there is an absence of a means of valid cognition.

This is because it has already been conceded. If you say that something can still be said even regarding the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then if there is a face, let it be said that it exists. However, if one speaks while adhering to the characteristics of accepted means of valid cognition, then the answer is excellent. But if it is otherwise, then it must be stated by the other party alone; we have no occasion [to intervene], for that which accepts a means of valid cognition results in certainty.

Since the acceptance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of certainty regarding its object—a domain where no disagreement exists—how could the demoness of doubt ever find an opportunity anywhere? You may simply say that the definition formulated by you is not a valid means of cognition; however, that very point remains to be examined. Furthermore, it is the principle of those who follow authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) that even an unperceived limiting condition (*upādhi*) must be excluded from smoke.

If it is argued that this constitutes a violation of worldly practice (*lokyātrā*), we say no; for those who accept valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) have already prohibited the authority of sublation (*bādhādhikāra*) regarding an unperceivable object due to its unsuitability for perception. Otherwise, the proofs for God, heaven, and so forth would be as good as dead. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because [the existence of the omniscient one] is established through the valid means of inference and scripture (*āgama*), we say no; for once an object has been previously sublated by non-perception, inferential and other such means of proof cannot operate. This was established in the proof of the omniscient one (*sarvajñasiddhi*).
Therefore, this mere non-apprehension, which results from the discrimination between the preceding and succeeding [moments], is the means for establishing certainty.

Consequently, since there is no room for doubt regarding the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is incoherent to claim that one would not act toward anything at all. Nor is it the case that one simply does not suspect [the existence of an object].

There is activity, because activity is unavoidable when there is doubt regarding the object, as in the case of eating palatable food and drink. But for one who cites this as an example of doubt regarding what is useless (*anarthaka*), it remains unexplained whether the object of the doubt is beneficial or harmful; what more can be said than this? Moreover, this is not the subject at hand, for the subject under discussion is whether or not there is doubt regarding the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vṛtti*), and that has already been addressed. Now, this intention [of yours] is manifold.

Because smoke is observed to be non-deviant from fire, there might arise this harmful doubt that "perhaps smoke could exist even in the absence of that [fire]"; and since that doubt is an obstacle to action, it must be dispelled. Thus, the meaning is that one should simply establish the cognition of the natural (intrinsic) relationship, just as one proceeds with eating and drinking after casting aside the fear of death. If this is so, then it is logical that even a doubt regarding the purpose is a factor for action.
Furthermore, based on the observation of concomitance, non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is indeed common, just as food and drink are for life.

If you say, "We speak of such a thing as a doubt regarding harm (*anartha-saṃśaya*)," then that very doubt is what prompts action. How then can it be said that one would not act at all? Or how could even a doubt regarding harm be a factor for desisting? And this may occur even when there is occasional deviation.
It is the same as [the argument] that occasional giving and begging are not [necessarily] connected; thus, the establishment of smoke’s natural relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*) is well-founded.

Furthermore, the suspicion regarding what has been observed was already refuted previously. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "viśeṣa" (particularity) and so forth is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
— *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, 172.172 *Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary reference to a verse number (172) and the title of Jñānaśrīmitra’s collected works.*

This is stated by the words "tad uktam" and so forth; taking up the authority of the Master (Dignāga), this is the entry into the fire [of certainty]. For it is said: "As long as subverting cognition has not arisen, doubt is without foundation" (*Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, verse 2.60).

Thus: if, while an object is being written down, a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) has arisen, or if there is a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what room is there for doubt? For doubt is of the nature of uncertainty (*saṃśaya*), whereas a proving or subverting factor brings about a definitive determination (*ekāntāvasāya*). Or, if it is intended that no subverting cognition such as "timira" (visual disorder) arises with respect to the sense organs, that is irrelevant; for [the absence of subversion] does not pertain to the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of smoke and so forth.
Success is suspected, but [it is suspected] on account of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
What indeed is the meaning of "lacking proof"? If it is intended as the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), then what is the point of the suspicion?
Or is it the object being delineated by the suspicion—does that [object] exist in that very place or elsewhere? Even if elsewhere, is it in something of the same class (*sajātīya*)?

Or [is it] merely another? First of all, the first position is not consistent with the context. Even if it were so, then regarding the cognition of that other [object], the means of proof—whether it be mental perception (*mānasa*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—is not exhausted by this [objection]. Furthermore, it has been stated that the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the suspected [object] in the present case serves precisely to prove that suspicion. [This applies] elsewhere as well, by means of a similar [instance of] valid cognition...

The meaning of this state of affairs is as follows: if it is suspected that smoke’s dependence on fire is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in respect to its belonging to that same class (*tajjātīya*), then does that "belonging to the same class" refer to the individual (*vyakti*) or to the universal (*jāti*)?

First, with respect to the individual, "belonging to the same class" refers to another instance of smoke itself. And if, in that case, its non-dependence on fire were cognized by valid cognition, then—

Since smoke is excluded from pervasion precisely because of deviation, it becomes a "common inconclusive" (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason; what, then, is the point here of introducing doubt for the sake of [establishing] the exclusion of the reason from the doubtful counter-example? If you ask, "Even if fire is not known [to be absent], why should there be doubt simply because of non-deviation from that which is not dependent on fire? [The answer is: because the absence of deviation is not established by mere non-perception, since only a non-perception of something perceptible establishes its absence.

Because [the relationship] is established through the capacity for proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, there is room for the suspicion that [the concomitance] is merely one of frequent co-occurrence (*sahacāra-mātra*), which is fallible and not determined to be infallible. However, with respect to the universal (*jāti*), the universal of smoke is indeed distinct from any other universal; it is of the same class (*sajātīya*) through some proximity (*pratyāsatti*) such as being a substance (*dravya*).
Consequently, when it occurs in the intended subject (*pakṣa*), its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in water and so forth has already been ruled out. And this alone is logical.

[The opponent’s] position: In the investigation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding smoke, since the determination proceeds by unifying smoke that is spatially and temporally remote, it is appropriate to observe the perception of doubt regarding a different class [of things], for even by that much, the requirement that memory be preceded by experience is not lost.
[The author replies: This is trivial; apart from the first position, this syllable is neither expressive nor applicable there.

For one who perceives no sublation (*bādhaka*), even the state of being a doubt is merely the prattle of a child. Indeed, it has been stated that the perception of sublation is contradictory to doubt because it consists of certainty; for a sublater does not have uncertainty as its result. Therefore, since we maintain that there is no doubt where there is the absence of existence, how could [the cognition] consist of that [doubt] in all worldly transactions? Or, if...

What is intended here is not that the discussion of pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself imagines a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding smoke’s dependence on fuel, but rather a doubt concerning its lack of necessary connection (*apratibaddhatva*) with fire.

"It should be understood that the subverting [reason] was stated because of its contradiction with the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nevertheless, to say 'one might imagine' (*utprekṣeta*) is contradictory;

for the meaning of *utprekṣā* is conceptual construction (*vikalpana*), and it is not the case that the conceptualization of doubt itself—which is already of the nature of conceptual construction—is what is under discussion here.

However, 'production' (*janana*) would be appropriate. Even then, the qualification 'unborn' (*ajāta*) is purposeless, because it is incoherent to speak of the production of that which has already been born. Now, [the opponent says]:

The meaning is that even if something has arisen, though it be non-existent and unreal, yet suspected—such as [the claim] that fire does not depend on fuel and so forth—one might imagine a subverting proof contrary to it, or bring it forward by mere imagination alone. Even then, if one were to speak thus after having established that unreality by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then everything would be well. And for this reckless person, there is no means of proof other than verbal abuse.

If the status of being a fit object for censure belongs only to one who postulates something beyond what is commonly established, then why would it not also apply to one who, in the case of a theory of pervasion established merely through observation and non-observation, postulates an intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) and so forth in order to dispel the suspicion of its occurrence in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)?

Furthermore, for him who asserts that this very relation is perceptible by the senses—thereby contradicting its being graspable by the mind—or who asserts that it is knowable and so forth, thereby contradicting the existence of an omniscient being; or for him who asserts that the meaning of words such as "Urvashi" is something other than what is well-known; or rather, for him alone who has devised this unprecedented weapon of abuse, which is capable of shattering the multitude of Buddhist doubts: [The verse follows: "The relation between word and meaning is not grasped by the senses, because it is not perceived when the sense-organ is in contact with its object, like color and so forth. [And the commentary: This is not a valid reason, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, the relation between a word and its meaning is not perceived even when the sense-organ is in contact with its object, because it is supersensible (*atīndriya*), just like the relation between a substance and its quality. Or else, the relation between a word and its meaning is indeed perceived by the sense-organ, because it is an object of cognition (*jñeya*), just like color and so forth. Thus, since the reason is inconclusive due to the presence of a counter-example, the proof is refuted. Furthermore, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it proves the opposite of what is intended. For the non-perception of a relation when the sense-organ is in contact with its object is established only for supersensible things; therefore, the fact that the relation is not perceived when the sense-organ is in contact with its object proves precisely that the relation is not supersensible, but rather that it is perceptible by the sense-organ. Consequently, the reason contradicts the very nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpaviruddha*). Moreover, the reason is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the desired conclusion, for it establishes that the relation is perceptible by the sense-organ, whereas the proponent intends to prove that it is not. Furthermore, the reason is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyaviruddha*), for it establishes that the relation is perceptible by the sense-organ, whereas the property to be proven is that it is not. And finally, the reason is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the pervasion (*vyāptiviruddha*), for it establishes that the relation is perceptible by the sense-organ, whereas the pervasion is that whatever is not perceived when the sense-organ is in contact with its object is not perceptible by the sense-organ. Therefore, the reason is indeed contradictory. Furthermore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject, because the relation between word and meaning is not actually perceived when the sense-organ is in contact with its object. Thus, the reason is unestablished. Moreover, the reason is unestablished because it is impossible for the relation to be perceived when the sense-organ is in contact with its object, since the relation is supersensible. It is appropriate that [the proof] first undergoes destruction.

If you argue that this is desired because it arouses doubt, then surely [the proof] is already defeated by arousing a doubt that had not arisen previously; consequently, why would it not also be defective for arousing a certainty—brought about by either a prover or a refuter—that had likewise not arisen before? [The same applies to] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)...

If you argue that certainty is difficult to overcome by force, then in its absence, doubt would likewise be difficult to overcome; enough of this overly prolix discussion. Therefore, how could anyone who is not insane claim that the raising of a doubt regarding something other than the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs through the consideration of what precedes and follows? For if certainty, which is bound to a means of valid cognition, were to occur even in the absence of that [means], for what purpose would one exert effort?

Is the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) an effort on the part of the discerning person, or is it the toil of the authors of treatises for the sake of refuting misconceptions regarding them? Therefore, since doubt necessarily arises when the means of valid cognition are absent, how can it be dispelled merely by [your] disapproval? Even if this is so, nevertheless, because there is no other recourse and because one generally observes concomitance in worldly practice, yet fails to observe it even once—
Having rendered the deviation—depicted by conceptual construction and consisting of an unfulfilled doubt—as if non-existent, one must proceed with certainty alone, not with doubt.
To this it is replied: Does the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) truly exist as established by valid cognition (pramāṇa), or not? If it does exist, it is necessarily...
Is its object otherwise? If you say "no," then everything would collapse without effort, because there would be no room for either proof or refutation;

this has been analyzed at length in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅga*. Even if it exists, if its object were not restricted, then it would simply exist [without purpose]; this too has been explained extensively in the treatise.

Furthermore, one who desires heaven and the like cannot be said to follow the Vedas or God as a matter of necessity, for otherwise it would follow that even the killing of a Brahmin could result in attaining those goals.

Therefore, since it must necessarily be admitted that this [cognition] exists and has a restricted object, being established by the aforementioned means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), the absence of any other alternative for the establishment of certainty is unproven; for without that [certainty], there can be no natural [connection].

Because the establishment of a relation [of pervasion] also lacks a substratum. As for the argument beginning with "when they are sought with effort," we understand that even there, the search for deviation is itself the search for a limiting condition (*upādhi*), since it is impossible to establish a limiting condition without deviation. Therefore, as long as smoke is observed, the process of determination remains incomplete because it is undermined by the suspicion of deviation; thus, it has been said that [inference] has no scope.

This is the conclusion. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of the phrase "being sought with effort"? For if one has only brought [the object] within the range of observation on a few occasions without deviation, what kind of certainty (*nirvṛti*) could there be regarding another instance? As for that which was boasted—"it might be thus"—that too is pithless. For when a nature is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its own inherent character—
[This is] the objective support (*ālambana*). However, the determination of the nature of a thing does not occur solely by the force of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*).

Therefore, if the doctrine of intrinsic nature is [invoked] regarding the causal relation (*hetuphalabhāva*) established by the means of valid cognition—namely, perception and non-perception—which apprehend the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) of a fixed object, then what has been gained for an "essential connection" (*svābhāvikasambandha*)? In that case, having mentally discarded the causal complex through which that [connection] is perceived, one [seeks it] elsewhere as something merely co-existent (*sahacarita*).

When there is no perception of a distinction between the two [the universal and the particular], the means of perception itself is the most remote; and if one depends upon that causal complex, then its very production is what constitutes it.

What is the use of this boastful changing of names? In this interval, the process ending with apprehension—aided by the sense organ through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—is already refuted by the previous objection.

And as for this [definition] of doubt, it is that doubt which arises from the perception of a commonality, the non-perception of specific features, and the recollection of specific features, depending upon the observation of those specificities.

Thus, not wishing to admit the doubt that would undermine the definition [of perception] as stated in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.17, he raises the following question: Is it because of the fear of undermining the definition that one must maintain that no cognition of two forms can arise regarding what is not an object of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or rather, is it intended that even if there were two forms, this would not constitute a doubt?

Now, there are these positions: [first,] let there be doubt from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), or let there not; however, we nevertheless engage with it as a state of doubt because our own defining characteristics have perished. Regarding these, the first position is impossible: for when there is an absence of both conclusive proof and refutation regarding a form delineated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—such as the thought, "Is this true or not? like news of a beloved’s arrival tomorrow—a conceptual construction that delineates both sides [of the doubt]...

For even by the command of a king, one is unable to prevent [the arising of a cognition] at birth; for while bodily and verbal activities can indeed be forcibly altered—even when the mind is otherwise—by means such as fear, the transformation of the mind (cittavivarta) cannot be so altered, as it arrives through the gateways of valid and invalid cognition. However, this may be the case: because a single part is perceived more frequently, that limb appears as if fully developed, whereas another does not due to its absolute lack of frequency.

The portion [of the object] is as if diminished; yet, in the absence of such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), both [aspects] remain common to it. Just as in that house, the state of being twofold—whether the crow exists or does not exist—does not depart at all. Therefore, the claim that "that alone is the object of doubt" is also untenable. Otherwise, [if it were so], it would be distinguished from both erroneous cognition and correct knowledge by their respective determinate forms.

If there is no doubt regarding the discussion of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then why is this a fourth category? Therefore, let this fault belong to the definition itself for one who does not grasp it; the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) cannot be altered. For this very reason, even the final [category] is not useful. It is a cognition that relies upon both parts.

If [the relationship] is established merely by depending on the necessity of the action, then since the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) is not thereby established, what is the use of your reliance on doubt and conventional usage? Enough of this childish talk!

As for the refutation of the mental [cognition], let it be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); why exert such effort even here? Regarding the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*):

However, [the claim that] its capacity to convey [the object] is established merely proves what is already established; for it has been established that this [capacity] is characterized solely by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). And thus, since the efficacy of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is undermined, other means of knowledge (*māna*) that rely upon it should be understood as sterile for the purpose of establishing a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) regarding the nature of the object of perception. Rather, it is the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*)—namely, inference—that must be inferred.

In the absence of that [essential nature], it is impossible to exclude its occurrence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), just as the fact of being a son cannot exclude the possibility of dark complexion. Furthermore, the rebuttal that there is a lack of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) here because of the presence of the limiting condition (*upādhi*)—namely, the specific transformation of food and drink—is not tenable, because there is no certainty regarding the specific transformation of food and drink being a limiting condition. For instance, smoke does not arise from mere fire when fuel is absent.

Thus, by means of smoke, fuel related to it is called a *upādhi* (limiting condition). Similarly, if someone born of Maitra were observed to be dark-skinned despite the absence of the intended transformation of food, that would be identified as the *upādhi*. In that case, what is the use of speaking of an *upādhi*, since it would suffice simply to say that "being the son of Maitra" is not a prover because of its deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? But this cannot be maintained.

How, then, is this determined? Is it because of Maitreya’s own vow (*praṇidhāna*) in a previous birth that seven or eight sons who were seen to have dark bodies were not born? What is the proof for this? In that case, one might suspect a similar vow on the part of the mother or even the sons themselves. Furthermore, if the merit and the vow of those [parents] were not firm, then even a difference in diet would [be a factor].

The capacity [of the reason] is thus established. In that case, the doubt as to what causes their dark complexion does not provide any occasion for an inference based on a suspected *upādhi* (limiting condition). What is the use of determining that? Now, the final proof of dark complexion has reached its conclusion: having burst open the belly of the "son-of-a-bard" argument—which excludes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), rests upon the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and possesses an uncontradicted object—it renders that [alleged] reason a non-reason (*ahetu*).

How was it that you were not afraid while raising the demon of doubt? Therefore, since there is no evidence establishing a necessary connection between being his son and being dark-complexioned, and since non-existence cannot be established by the mere absence of observation regarding the lack of darkness, it is best simply to say that [the reason] is not a cause; what is the use of this useless internal argument concerning "limiting conditions" (upādhi)?
Furthermore, it must be admitted that "doubt regarding the exclusion from the counter-example" (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) is indeed a real defect of the logical reason (*hetu*);

for otherwise, it would be impossible to remove the status of this reason—which is otherwise beautiful in all its parts—as a valid probans. Moreover, if this were not admitted, what kind of "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) could one possibly perceive in the reason "being composed of earth" (*pārthivatva*) when it is invoked to prove that a diamond (*vajra*) can be scratched by iron, such that one would refuse to accept the inference?

[Objection: "But sir, since the sinking of an iron tip is observed in wood and other materials whose constituent parts are loose, and since a diamond is firm, that very [firmness] is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

[Reply: It is not so. Indeed, we do not perceive any difference between a hundred-edged [iron spike] and a crystal by way of their having dense constituent parts, such that an iron spearhead, which is not obstructed by the sun-gem (*taraṇimaṇi*), would be obstructed by it. —From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

This might be so: it is indeed observed that iron, when struck by a thunderbolt (*vajra*), is repelled. But surely, an inference is not directed against one for whom a proof or a sublation of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) has already functioned; rather, it is directed against one who merely takes the "hundred peaks" as the subject (*pakṣa*). How then can there be an inference [of pervasion] for such a person, given their lack of awareness of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) and their reliance on an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*)?

It has already been stated that even in the case of a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), this must be refuted. Now, if it is argued: "Even if no other limiting condition (*upādhi*) is determined for the earthen substance, there will nevertheless be some specific property inherent to it (*svāgata*) which serves as the limiting condition, and because of it, there is no 'scratchability by iron'"; then, in this case, the demoness of doubt (*śaṅkāpiśācī*), having found her opportunity, would pursue even smoke, thinking: "There is also some specific property inherent to smoke..."

It will exist, by which it will exist even without fire. But surely, though we search with effort, we do not perceive a specific characteristic (*svagata-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in smoke; yet in the case of a diamond (*vajra*), which is earthen, we understand [its distinction] from its capacity to cut metal. Well then, is that capacity to cut metal [the result] of a purposeful application once inference has proceeded, or is it by chance, or rather—

Is it by means of inquiry (*jijñāsā*)? In the first case, since the accomplishment of a great purpose arises from inference, you would likewise have to resort to another such inference. Yet, there is no such labor as that required for the determination of a painting when it occurs by chance. Or, even if that [painting] were not an inference, how could another be? Inquiry, moreover, would have no scope at all. For instance, in the case of clay, wood, or stone—

Since no deviation has been observed—even among millions of kings who have witnessed the sinking of iron [into water]—among those with sharp discernment, the certainty of an intrinsic relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is established; thus, for one whose doubt regarding deviation has been dispelled by the inference from the written record, how could there be any room for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) preceded by that [doubt]? Otherwise, even upon perceiving smoke wafting from a mountain slope from the top of a palace, through repeated observation...

For one who possesses the cognition of an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*), there would be only a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) even in that case, not inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, inference is excluded in every respect. When a correspondence has occurred on a few occasions, inference from smoke follows at a later time due to the ascertainment of the intrinsic relation; it does not follow throughout one's entire life as in the case of "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*). Thus, [the opponent] is one of praiseworthy intellect.
Now, if it is argued that even though [the object] is earthen (*pārthiva*), because a gradation of hardness is observed, the cessation of its capacity to be scratched might also be possible;

thus, despite a great degree of agreement [with the general rule], there can be no inference of earthenness and so forth—whereas in the case of smoke, no such gradation of independence from fire is perceived?
Well then, when one says "it would depend on fire," what must be stated is precisely the exclusion of fire. And where there is absolute exclusion [of fire], [smoke does not exist].

In that case, there will necessarily be a perception of the degree of prior disconnection, as in the case of a man and his shackles. However, at the end—even in the case of smoke—this will occur for only a few moments; yet, unlike the mere conjunction of two separately established entities such as a man and his shackles, smoke is produced from fire itself, so there is no suspicion of disconnection even at the end. But this applies only so long as one does not touch upon the specific distinctions [of the relationship].

Śaṅkara: Therefore, because the mere non-perception of the nature of fire—which excludes [other] fires—in smoke or in earth, or of the property of being scratchable by iron, along with the frequent observation of the opposite, is common to both cases, there is no establishment of an essential relation fixed to one side;
and since there is no determination of the presence of adventitious conditions (upādhi) regarding the probandum, inference is either equally valid or equally invalid.
