When, however, in the case of smoke, the discussion of pervasion concerns the very fact of its being produced from that [fire] as the proof of pervasion— since there is no difference between them— it is not by way of being earthy or being scratchable by iron; nor is it identity, because it is unestablished that "this [smoke] has the nature of being scratchable by iron" (i.e., that being scratchable by iron is its very self).

Because it is impossible to demonstrate an inference that would subvert [the pervasion], just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Furthermore, since perception functions only with respect to specific classes (*jāti*), the establishment of pervasion occurs only in those cases where "scratching with iron" is observed among all the various classes of earthy things, and not elsewhere. Therefore, while reasons such as "smoke" or "being produced" are [valid], [reasons] such as "being the son of that [specific person]" or "being earthy" have a doubtful counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣa*).

The fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is that which is excluded [from the locus of the probandum]. Likewise, [the reason] such as "being produced from the same branch" is [fallacious], because, in view of the contact with wind and sun that occurs at the time of the first growth, there is a suspicion that ripening might be absent even in something produced from a single branch. Thus, if repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is the means for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) through some other object, then since exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not established merely by its non-perception, for those [who hold such a view]...

Furthermore, because deviation is observed, smoke and other such signs do not establish the probandum through an unerring [reason], since their exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

As for the doctrine of "intrinsic nature" (*svābhāvika*) and so forth, it must be avoided like smearing one's heart with impurity; for it has been demonstrated that it merely serves to appropriate the views of others at first glance by propounding some extraneous meaning based solely on the passion of the *Ḍiṇḍika* sect.

Therefore, in the case of difference, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is precisely the cognition of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). And that [cognition] occurs only through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*). Let it be that the cognition of pervasion is the cognition of "origination from that" in the case of difference; however, it does not [occur] through perception and non-perception, because perception is restricted to the apprehension of the present moment, and non-perception has that same nature. And as for that which is superimposed—

It has been stated that, in relation to fat (*vasā*), the sensory cognition (*akṣadhi*) possesses the quality of being distinct from all other members of its own class; even there, what is called "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is nothing but a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, the claim that perception becomes universal in scope by virtue of that [determination] is merely a borrowed ornament. It would be better to accept that it is precisely a conceptual construction—having as its object two universals characterized by all individual instances of both [fire and smoke], namely "smoke is [an effect] of fire"—that grasps their existence.

If it is argued that [conceptual cognition] is either a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) or a distinct form of perception (*pratyakṣāntara*), because it apprehends what was previously unapprehended and because it exists at the time of the operation of perception—this too is without substance. For even in conceptualization, the state of having all things as its object is merely a matter of determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) and recollection; this is because there is no manifestation of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), since only one’s own internal form appears by way of merely following the shadow of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Therefore, what kind of distinction does this [conceptual cognition] possess?

Is it from perception? The determination of the object in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is established solely in relation to the subsequent series of mental events, such as the self-corroborative awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that conforms to itself. In perception (*pratyakṣa*), however, there is a distinction in that it includes even that conceptual construction; yet, the contact with all things does not occur in either case. Furthermore, it has been discussed that there is no other mode of apprehension [than these two].

Therefore, in conventional practice, it is unavoidable that even through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), the establishment of objects remains unrefuted; and since this is common to both perception and conceptual thought, even the nature of mental convention applies when the relationship of cause and effect has been made an object of direct perception.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is merely memory; it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, perception (*adhyakṣa*)—by way of a single part—is appropriately established as grasping the whole through contact with it, thereby apprehending all members of its own class; this is not the case for conceptual construction, which by its very nature lacks contact with external objects. Therefore, it is established that the proof of the essential relation of pervasion (*svabhāvavyāpti*) regarding the nature of cause and effect occurs precisely when there is the possibility of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
The treatise titled "An Investigation of Pervasion" is completed.
This work is by the great scholar, the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra.
Examination of Difference and Non-difference
[16] || Homage to the Buddha ||

With the desire to avoid the refutations that apply specifically to each individual position, the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), which is maintained by some, is now examined.

In this regard, does this [position] have the nature of a conjunction of both, or is it of the nature of the absence of those two? If it is an absence, is it a mere negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or is it another positive entity through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? Furthermore, is that [other entity] a third form distinct from the two under discussion, or—
Is it something entirely unprecedented?

Regarding that, in the first position, are these very same difference and non-difference—which were previously swallowed by the net of various defects—now asserted as residing in a single entity, or are they two different things? If they are the same, then since those defects necessarily persist, your admission is futile.

Even if there were difference, just as that [fault] was a defect, the quality would likewise not persist. Indeed, thinking, "I shall avoid the fault of the consequence of separate cognition—which arises in the position of difference—by resorting to non-difference," you have accepted non-difference even within difference. And if that very non-difference, which sublates the perception of separateness, were now brought forward, then its avoidance would consist merely in a single shared fate (*ekayogakṣema*).

Because of this inclusion, it also entails the non-occurrence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, if one were not to entail this by way of its being distinct [from them], then for that very reason, one would also not establish the negation of its separate apprehension.

Now, even if the result of non-difference is the sublation of separate apprehension rather than the inherent nature of the exclusion of other words, nevertheless, the admission of duality is fruitless. The same should be said regarding the position of difference (*bheda*) as well.

Now, the sublation of separate perception is indeed the fruit of non-difference, whereas the occurrence and cessation of other words is the fruit of difference itself; for even that [difference], being possible, must necessarily produce its own effect. Likewise, the dependence upon another means of knowledge is the fruit of difference, while the sublation of separate perception is the fruit of non-difference.

It is said: Both [difference and non-difference] are observed to be the effect of both. For difference, there is the fault of the consequence that it must manifest separately, and the dependence on another word is a merit. For non-difference, there is the fault of the consequence that it must depend on another word, and the lack of separate manifestation is a merit.
Therefore, in this case, one must remain merely by extending the operation of another word through difference; however, regarding the second effect—

A counter-blow must be expected. Even when producing an appearance together with that which is non-different, what causes the distinction in the counter-blow directed toward another effect? [This distinction arises] either because entities conform to your own intention, or because attachment and aversion toward qualities and defects occur spontaneously, or because of a difference in time between the two natures and their effects.

In that case as well, is the sequence of qualities and defects fixed or unfixed? Regarding the first alternative, in the case of either difference or non-difference, only one's own position—offering merely its own quality and remaining untouched by any defect—will prevail. Nor will any defect be brought against it.
Thus, why has this adherence to duality been made by one ignorant of the authority of the Self? Furthermore, because entities are devoid of consciousness, they cannot conform to an intention.
For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable. Let there be affection and so forth toward inequality; however, that [affection] is for the sake of benefiting the Self—

It might be so; however, nothing has been subtracted from these [entities] by virtue of being the signifier or the signified, nor has anything been added by the distinction of their appearance or by the other. Nevertheless, the use of the terms "quality" and "defect" is made out of deference to you. Consequently, even if that were the case for something devoid of such conformity, it would matter nothing. Or, if there is no conformity, consciousness has already been explained [as being impossible].

It might be argued that, just like the operation of the collection of instruments which is the cause for the arising of sound, the conformity to intention occurs by its very nature (*svabhāva*). Even so, the acceptance of duality is nothing but a failure to grasp the truth. For it has already been stated: why not simply assume such an operation for a single nature alone?

Nor is the proposal of a third alternative tenable. For if there is a difference between the two natures due to a difference in time, then when there is difference, there is no non-difference; and at the time of non-difference, there is no difference. Thus, there is never an avoidance of the opponent's fault. In that case, just as in the case of a thing that is either different or non-different, the effects such as synonymity and so forth—which presuppose absolute difference or non-difference—cannot be established.

In the same way, two natures do not obtain when there is a difference in time, because of the absence of their opposites. Nor can there be a negation by means of what is yet to come, because that is not a real entity. Therefore, the difference between the time of that [negation] and the time of the effect must be sought as a refuge. In that case, as soon as the difference, having established its operation through a different word, begins to bring about a difference in appearance, it is immediately obstructed by the necessity of being subsumed under non-difference.

Thus, who indeed—unless it be you, whose sole domain is audacity—being confounded by logic, would venture to propose such a thing as being composed of hands? For there is only a difference in time between two natures; and for what object is that [difference] difficult to find?

Indeed, it is not logical for that [difference] to belong to the very same thing, because even in that case, each [nature] individually lacks a consideration of a cause for its temporal distinction. It is not so.

This would be logical only if [the sequence] were tied to a single inherent nature; even then, there would be a fixed order in the production of effects regarded as qualities or defects. However, since there would otherwise be the consequence of falling down a precipice without any restriction, it is clear that one whose heart is captivated by mere whim does not perceive anything at all and thus deserves to be disregarded. For we do not perceive any cause here other than his desire. Moreover, when—

If the admission of difference occurs after [the prior state of] difference, then what could prevent the second effect of non-difference—which subverts separate perception? If you say "by difference," no; for if that difference arises at a later time, then yet another must be sought to remove its own share of defects, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is by the prior [difference], then if it possesses such power as this...

How could that which is subsequently presented non-differently not indeed produce a non-distinct appearance? Therefore, it must be considered: if the latter sublates the former in relation to the former, why should it not do so in relation to the one even earlier? Consequently, each instance must be examined individually regarding the distinction or non-distinction of its two effects.
Therefore, it is groundless to claim that there is either an exclusive rejection or acceptance of both difference and non-difference [between the universal and the particular].

Consequently, it would follow that for a single entity, there would simultaneously occur distinct appearance and non-appearance, simultaneous production and non-production, and the application and non-application of different words, and so forth.

Furthermore, there is not even a scent of experience regarding the distinction between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the substratum of the adjunct (*upādhimat*). Nor, upon the destruction of the individual instance (*vyakti*), is there even a trace of destruction [of the universal].
The universal is not accepted by the opponents [as existing] in its own form.

If it is argued that it is indeed intended [to exist] in the form of the individual (*vyakti*), then surely "in the form of the individual" is intended to mean "in its own form"; otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless. This [discussion] concerns the consideration of difference and non-difference regarding its very own form.

Regarding the objection that this is a "reductio ad absurdum" (*prasaṅga*), what has been resolved by this? Or, if no other form of its own is even possible for it, then whose is the inquiry into difference and non-difference? Thus, properties (*dharma*) are established as being without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). But surely, even if non-difference were possible for that which is different, we do not perceive the futility of another word [to express it]; what can be done about this? If that is so, then even though the limiting adjunct is different, the manifestation (*prakāśa*) is not different from it.

If one says, "What can we do about this?", then there is no fault even in the doctrine of non-duality (*ekāntavāda*); nevertheless, resorting to the dualistic view (*dvaitamata*) is futile, because in the end, the stretching out of the feet [to avoid the consequences] cannot be avoided. Is it merely excessive exertion that remains, or is it mere boastfulness? Or perhaps it might be argued that for one who accepts identity (*tādātmya*), when the opponents point out faults such as the recurrence of other words and so forth—

If that [non-difference] follows as a consequence, then the possibility of difference is the rebuttal. Furthermore, in the case of difference, when one brings about a distinction in appearance, it is impossible to establish non-difference within a doctrine of absolute monism (*ekāntavāda*). Nor is this a mere "stretching out of the feet" (i.e., an easy evasion), nor does it entail the fallacy of both positions. For when difference was previously established, and once the faults associated with it have been uprooted, non-difference is then established.

If it is argued that there is no harm even if there is no finality due to such a continuous succession of repetitions, then it follows that the subverting or proving property being presented by you does not function through its own inherent capacity alone. Furthermore, if the application (*upanaya*) were not expressed in the form of speech, then even your fire (*uṣarbudha*) would not be a subverter. By this, for the sake of the present context—
The argument that "it is not accepted" is also refuted; for it cannot be said that poison being consumed for the sake of survival does not kill.
Therefore, this recourse to both positions out of a desire to avoid both [consequences] is like a pair of iron shackles for those of dull intellect.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has a specific cause alone (*tanmātra-nimitta*) necessarily occurs when that [cause] is present; for example, the arising of cognition, which has as its cause only the totality of conditions such as the eye and so forth. And the aforementioned collection of defects depends solely upon difference and non-difference; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Being caused by that alone is pervaded by independence from other factors; furthermore, even when those [other factors] are possible, their absence [of the effect] would be contradictory to that [dependence].

Since it would follow that [the appearance] would be independent, the fact that [the appearance] has as its sole cause that [non-difference], which is excluded from the opposite by the perception of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), is restricted to the case where that [non-difference] exists; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. Nor is the [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*), because of this dependence on that alone. For no cause for simultaneous arising is logically possible other than mere non-difference, nor is any [cause] other than mere difference possible if the distinct manifestation is to be perceived.

If it is argued that, even though there is a difference between a glowing iron ball and fire, or between milk and water, the non-distinction of their manifestation is established as being dependent on something else— no, for the context concerns non-erroneous sensory cognition; in that case, one would be apprehending two distinct entities as if they were one.
How can knowledge be called non-erroneous?

By this, the appearance of two moons has been explained. Now, if the thought arises that "this single object has come into being, produced by the causes of both [the real and the unreal]," then there is no deviation at all; thus, its dependence on that alone is established. This might be so.

Even for that which depends solely on its constituent taste (*tanmātra*), its existence is necessarily contingent upon that [taste], just as bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) arise from pungent and sweet substances respectively.

This is incorrect, because substances can produce effects both similar and dissimilar to their tastes even when considering potency (*vīrya*) and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*); thus, bile and the like do not invariably follow the mere presence of a specific taste.
The Examination of Difference and Non-difference is completed.
The Secret of Non-apprehension (Anupalabdhi-rahasya)
In this [work], a clear compendium is made of that very same non-apprehension— which, though scattered throughout the established doctrine (siddhānta),
is here restricted to its formal nature (rūpa).

When negation is the probandum, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the third logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, if that [non-apprehension] were merely the absence of apprehension, how could it be the cognition of anything, or the cause of a cognition? And how, moreover, would there be a cognition of it itself? Therefore, like "that which is not to be eaten" and so forth, non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of something else by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

In that case as well, if it were the negation of another in general, then it would follow that everything belonging to a single entity, such as Kapila, is negated. If you argue that the negation of identity with respect to everything is indeed intended, then the negation of its location is likewise unavoidable. Thus, this is the distinction:

For when there is a restriction of the cognition regarding an object of knowledge, that cognition may or may not exist; however, non-perception is not accepted as the basis for the establishment of the knowledge of the absence of something else.

When something is being experienced, the phrase "of which there might be a cognition" serves as a negation of remoteness in terms of space, time, and intrinsic nature. By the word "necessarily," the deficiency of other conditions for perception is excluded. By this, it is shown that the existence of a thing consists in its being known as having attained the status of a perceptible object. Therefore, there is no consequence of negating everything. And when, upon the experience of something, there would necessarily be a cognition of another thing—

The cognition of that very [object] is desired because it is capable of initiating a continuous stream of the ascertainment of the non-existence of any other second [entity]. By this it is stated that there is not merely an absence [of the object], but rather, through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is the cognition of another specific [entity]; for here, by the force of the phrase "of that very one alone," otherwise the non-existence would not be established, since the perception of the other would remain unprohibited.

For example: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived. This is like saying "someone [does not see] something. In this context, the phrase "of the perceptible" (*dṛśyasya*) should be understood as referring to a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) and the completeness of all other conditions for perception. The phrase "because of non-perception" (*anupalabdheḥ*) means "because of the perception of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*). And that counter-correlate is either the locus of the reason—the ground—or something else perceived by the same sense faculty.

Is it associated with cognition, or something else? This follows from the general statement that when a locus is being perceived, the object to be negated must necessarily be perceived. In that case, if the presence of a jar on a patch of ground is the probandum, then that very ground is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); what need is there for anything else? But when the locus is the sky, even then it is that very space known as "light" (*āloka*), or else some other indeterminate object such as a jar.

But in the case of the negation of tangibility, this very same [principle] applies. In *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, by this, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) as that which is associated with a single cognition has been explained. However, in some cases it is otherwise; for example, when one is devouring a lamp, [the argument] "there is no taste here because of the non-perception of a perceptible object" takes touch itself as the counter-correlate. For if both [taste and touch] were present, there would be no restriction to a single form.

The proximity [of the sense organs] is like that of a beverage. If that is so, why is there no perception of taste even when seeing a form from a distance? Because for those separated by space, there is an absence of fitness for apprehension, since the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile senses function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). And it has been said: "When one thing is being experienced, that which is necessarily experienced [along with it] is indeed perceived. Nor is there a negation of form during the experience of taste, because at that time too, its [the form's] defining characteristic—

Because of [their] connection. Thus, even in the perception of sound, there is no negation of form (*rūpa*). For in darkness, although form exists, the cognition of sound does not invariably accompany its cognition.

In light, however, there is no negation of that which is actually being seen. But as for the negation of an unperceived object that is nonetheless perceptible (*yogya*), even in that case, there is no [negation].

This is a fault, because it does not abandon its defining characteristic. By this, it is shown that when a temple or similar structure is being perceived, the non-existence of the drum or other sounds belonging to that specific location is established without necessarily depending on the cognition of another sound. And as for the claim that there is no rule for their simultaneous perception—that is not the case even for a portion of ground and a jar; for even in those two cases, there is an absence of a rule for the perception of only one form while the other exists, since perception applies there as well.

It is the same: there is no distinction as to whether a single cognition is invariably concomitant with the apprehension of another [object], or invariably concomitant with another cognition that apprehends it; likewise, whether it is produced by a single sense-faculty or otherwise. [This applies to] the absence of a lamp for one who lacks its form.

Even if, ultimately, it were similar to another cognition or even to a conceptual construction, in reality, it is only a real entity—namely, darkness—that can come into contact with a single cognition along with a lamp; what need is there for anything else? This is true even in a room shrouded in deep darkness.

But surely, even when there is a specific nature [of the object], the proximity of other conditions constitutes its fitness for perception; and although that [fitness] serves as the cause for cognition by a different sense organ, it is not utilized in the ascertainment of the conditions for cognition by that different sense organ. Therefore, when a negation is made regarding the doubt of another's proximity of conditions, how can there be a negation of the perceptible—even ultimately—by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that possesses a determinate form?

For it is not only the cognition by the same sense-organ that is established as being dependent on the presence of other conditions; rather, there is also the experience of a specific state of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) characterized by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
This occurs when there is no specific difference in the nature of the sense-organ.
In cases such as sound or a lamp, another illuminator is required; however, in that regard, for one who has previously heard or seen [an object],
whose senses are directed toward that very state, and who is wise, by whom can the establishment of its absence— not based on some cognition devoid of its form— be prevented?

What, then, is the utility of apprehending another cognition? For the absence [of that first cognition] is established simply by the non-arising of a cognition of it during that state. Or how can there be a negation of anything else based on a sensory cognition whose object is different? To this it has been said: "There is no capacity for non-existence anywhere," and so forth. Therefore, another cognition is not relied upon to ascertain the excellence of the sense organ; rather, [the certainty arises from the following].
1. Here the reading is not omitted.

Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the secret [means] for generating the conceptualization of the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). In that regard, just as a cognition of that which is in contact with the same sense faculty [as the locus] leads to the ascertainment of the absence of another [thing],...
It is capable; likewise, another [cognition] as well, while existing, is non-deviant and devoid of the form of the cognition of another object—there is no difference whatsoever.

If one asks, "How so? it is because there is no efficacy here in terms of desire or lack of desire. Rather, for whatever [cognition], there is that which follows its positive and negative concomitance—

The term *kāra* refers to the acceptance of the relationship of cause and effect between those two. Just as the cognition [of a surface] is followed by the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the conceptual exclusion (*apoha*) of other things due to the restriction to the single form of "ground," so too, for one casting a glance at a lamp, that cognition [of the lamp] occurs through the cognition of the absence of taste due to the restriction to the form of touch alone. For there is no distinction between mediation and non-mediation in the arising of these two.

Likewise, for one whose nose is directed toward pure water that is free from any adjuncts, even though there is no contact or visual perception, there occurs a mere conceptual construction; and although no other odor is being experienced, by means of a cognition having the form of "odor," [the object] is empty of that form.
In that case:

If it is argued that this [cognition] is inferential (*laiṅgika*), we say no; for there is no intervention [of a middle term] for one who is in a state of repeated practice (*abhyāsadaśā*). Indeed, when the very apprehension of X is itself the certainty regarding X, that is not inferential, but rather established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), as in the case of "blue is not yellow. And in the case of water present before one, for someone whose conceptual construction takes the form of merely attending to the nose, there arises the certainty that "there is no odor."

If the mere absence of the cognition of fragrance is not a proof because the experience of a determinate conceptual form is not its cause, then let there also be no experience of blue for the cognition of the absence of yellow. Or rather, for one who maintains that perception possesses an active causal power (*pauruṣa*), this difficulty is unavoidable even in other cases. And that very same perception is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with respect to the object to be negated, as has already been stated. And that [perception] is confused (*mūḍha*).

The logical mark (*liṅga*) is that which, with respect to a cognizer, determines the absence of a particular property in accordance with prior convention. However, for one who is not deluded and possesses [the knowledge of] absence, this determination—which is free from subsequent doubt—is indeed stable; thus, it is said to be "initiated by perception" (*pratyakṣapravartita*).

Now, it may be objected that no linguistic usage regarding non-existence is produced by perception, nor is perception said to be fruitful by way of ascertaining the absence of an object, but rather only by way of ascertaining the absence of cognition. It is only through that [ascertainment of the absence of cognition] that it includes the ascertainment of the absence of the object; thus, it is said to be "produced by perception. And although that [ascertainment of the object's absence] arises from the capacity of that [perception], it is subsequently overcome by doubt, leaving one deluded.

The inferential [non-apprehension] is as follows: for an object, unlike cognition, there is no necessity of being of the nature of light; thus, since its existence is not contradicted even by its being unseen, the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the refuge [for proving its absence]. However, for one who is not deluded, there is the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the existence of a perceptible thing is pervaded by being an object of perception.
Some say that the former person is "deluded" due to an inability to make this distinction.

That is incorrect. For just as cognition is non-luminous and non-abiding, so too is the external object; therefore, like that [cognition], it possesses the practice of non-existence that cannot be avoided by perception. It is only by its very nature that cognition is "visible," whereas externally, something is visible only in some way and at some time. In that regard, for a cognizer possessing a specific degree of practice, [the external object appears] just like the generality of another cognition.
Even regarding a specific case, how can the fact that the establishment of a negation occurs instantaneously through perception alone—a process experienced repeatedly—be denied?

If it is argued that this is because inference is possible in reality according to the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, [we reply: even the ascertainment of the intended fitness (*yogyatā*) is produced by perception.
This is trivial; for the aforementioned doubt does not arise solely through external agency.

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it could not be said that "this non-conceptualized perception, whether as the nature of seeing or as the nature of the seen, precludes the conceptualization of non-perception within sensory cognition during the perception of a conceptual construction. Therefore, even regarding a cognition, there may at times be a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of another cognition.

Even regarding an object, certainty (*niścaya*) is a state of doubtlessness within that which has been reflected upon; thus, the establishment of the capacity of perception or anything else occurs through a division of states (*daśā*), and not through a division of genus (*jāti*).
Now, one might object:

If it is argued that by the passage beginning with "ekopalambhānubhavāt" (PV 4.270), the very capacity for the negation of another cognition has been stated, and that experience is likewise exactly so— [we reply: no, for it is as one says, "I do not perceive this."

Just as [an object] is experienced through direct perception, so too for one who possesses [mental] cultivation (*abhyāsa*), the thought "this does not exist" arises instantaneously; however, for one lacking such cultivation, there is simply the absence of cognition, which constitutes the certainty. Through that [absence of cognition], however, there is the absence of the object; it is with reference to this that it is so described in the treatise (*śāstra*). The same should be stated regarding [the absence of] co-occurrence in a single cognition, effort, and so forth. Therefore:

"Those of great intelligence determine all aspects from the very first moment," so it has been said. Furthermore, effort is required at various points for those of duller intellect. Therefore, for those of sharp intellect, [the object is known] from perception alone.

Just as in the case of distinguishing between a gem, silver, and so forth, the conventional usage of their negation is likewise unavoidable. Furthermore, non-existence (abhāva) does not possess a physical form such that it must be directly perceived through a nature distinct from other things; rather, it is something to be conventionally designated. And because its form is uniform, it is indeed capable of being clearly designated by direct perception (pratyakṣa). As for one who, due to a lack of acuity, doubts even when a determination of non-existence has occurred at first glance—

One initiates the conventional usage of this [non-perception] by following its mere non-apprehension; however, one who is less proficient than that, being doubtful even regarding the non-apprehension of the perceptible, proceeds by means of the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). But for one who is not deluded, there is no proceeding by means of this.
For it is precisely when there is a lack of proficiency in perception that inference is sought; and that proficiency is established through the generation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Moreover, in that case, there is greater clarity due to the absence of deliberation (*vimarśa*).

However, the Cārvāka, while accepting the existence of separate non-existence (*pṛthagabhāva*), has shown that perception (*pratyakṣa*) has no function in negating it, because perception is joined with a dependence on the capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthya*). Furthermore, the determination of apprehension for perception is not based on certainty (*niścaya*) in the same way as it is for inference (*anumāna*).

Rather, it is by virtue of appearance. And its very possession of a determinate form is the manifestation of the absence of anything other than that. Therefore, the secret of non-apprehension is that the capacity of perception to function as a conventional expression of absence is difficult to deny; however, the claim that "negation occurs everywhere because of non-apprehension" is not [the case].

It is not a rejection of perception, but rather that there are only two means of establishing a positive proof (*vidhisādhana*), such as [the following]: this negation of odor in water is established by perception itself due to non-interruption, and is not inferential (*laiṅgika*). Furthermore, what here is the mark (*liṅga*) that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) with respect to the absence of odor?

If it is argued that it is the non-perception of the effect, namely cognition (*jñāna*), then this is appropriate when the cognition that grasps [the object] itself is the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*); however, when...

That is indeed perception; for if, at that time, the absence of what is perceptible were not the non-perception of the perceptible, then let there be no [non-perception] even of a jar. This [position] is merely the fruit of deceiving oneself regarding the nature of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, if this proponent says this without ascertaining the integrity of the sense faculties, then it follows that even a present odor and so forth would not be perceived.

Furthermore, it should be understood that [the non-perception of the effect] is sufficient for establishing [the absence of the cause]. It is inconsistent to say that one applies the non-perception of the effect with effort when the cause and so forth are merely possible through inference (*parokṣa*), yet now hesitates even when they are possible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) out of fear of even a trace of error. Therefore, this remains established: when X is being perceived, that which necessarily must be perceived is non-different from it.

Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the cognition of either something else that is perceptible by the senses or something that is not perceptible by the senses. And this [non-apprehension] establishes only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), because otherwise [the object] would be established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that purpose, it was stated that [non-apprehension] is the basis for the stability of the persistence of the absence of cognition; however, it is not the basis for the certainty of separation. And just as the single cognition of two things that are invariably perceived together serves to negate the other, so too [is it here].

He says "or not" regarding the two [cases] of "necessarily not being perceived together. The meaning is: where, with respect to an object of cognition (*vedya*), the notion of one would necessarily not exist [upon the presence of the other].

For example, as in "this is blue; it is not non-blue. Here too, it is precisely conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is to be proven. By this, the contradiction characterized by the state of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti-lakṣaṇa-virodha*) has been explained.
[Objection: But is this not already covered by the principle that "when X is not being cognized, it is possible for Y to necessarily exist [in relation to X]"?

For even an invisible object, when being negated through identity, is negated only as having been conceived as visible; otherwise, one would have to admit a distinction between the visible and the invisible on one's own account. So what is the point of this separate statement? [Reply: If that is so, then...

Alternatively, this non-existence (*abhāva*) characterized by destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is explained as follows: the meaning is that even when a cognition has arisen, it necessarily ceases upon the presence of a certain object of knowledge. And such necessity is logically appropriate only for non-existence when there is a sublation of existence, as in the case:
"There is no cold here because of fire. By this, opposition (*virodha*) characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is also explained.

If it is argued that non-perception is necessarily [due to] darkness, and therefore one does not necessarily embrace a contradictory [reason], we reply: this definition does not depend on a single perceiver, but rather applies generally. Furthermore, there is the perception of form even in the absence of light by certain individuals, or it may be possible for others through the use of special ointments and the like. However, the rule [of non-perception due to darkness] holds only regarding the destruction of existence (*sattoccheda*).
Thus, there is no fault. But one might object: even here, if cold were present, the cognition of fire would not be restricted to a single form;

so how is this different from the previous case? It is not so, because the negation is intended to apply to that which is accessible through touch. In that case, even when activity occurs, it is impossible to ascertain that the cognition of cold has necessarily ceased once the fire is perceived; yet this is not contradictory, as such a cognition occurs at other times.

Because it is intended [as such] in Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Nibandhāvalī*. If that were so, then because its operation would be mediated by the recollection of a previously grasped contradiction, there could be no determination of non-existence through perception. Let it not be; for even when there is such mediation, it is simply the cognition of the contradictory that constitutes non-existence.
Since the factor of certainty does not belong to others alone, there is no injury to the basis for establishing non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Nor is it accepted here that this merely establishes conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); thus he says: "But in the case of memory, it is dependent on another;
therefore, here even non-existence (*abhāva*) is to be proven. And when that is established, conventional usage—characterized by the stability of its ascertainment—also [follows]."

The meaning is that it is merely that [absence]. Likewise, in the case of the negation of a cause or a pervader (*hetu-vyāpaka-nihave*), "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is also the probandum (*sādhya*). For example:

"There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," or "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of a tree. For in these cases, the mere perception of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogi-pratyakṣa-mātra*) does not—without depending on the recollection of the previously established knowledge of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—bring about the ascertainment of the absence of smoke or the *śiṃśapā*.
It follows that even there, the establishment of the conventional usage of proving non-existence [is achieved].

Thus, these are now the reasons for negation: the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Likewise, there are two reasons for affirmation; thus, five reasons would result. No, because of non-perception—

Because they share a common substratum and are therefore one. Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is of two kinds: that of oneself and that of another. For the cause and the pervader, there is only the non-apprehension of their own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). For another—that is, for an effect or for the pervaded—there is what is called the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). For just as the perception of one thing is itself the non-apprehension of another, so too is the apprehension of the nature of something [the non-apprehension of its absence].

Since the very perception [of an effect] is called the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpaka) of the cause with respect to the pervaded (vyāpya) effect, there is no difference in reality due to a difference in designation. Therefore, the negation of everything is by means of the non-perception of essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi) alone; thus, there are only three types of logical marks (liṅga).
By this, the non-perception of the effect of a capable cause is indicated as being nothing other than the non-perception of its essential nature.

It should be understood [as such], because the word "cause" (*hetu*) is explained as having the sense of a logical mark (*liṅga*). For example: "The causes of smoke do not exist here with unimpeded capacity, because of the absence of smoke. How, then, is the case of "there is no sensation of frost here because of fire" included under the perception of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*)? In this case as well, there is the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) consisting in the perception of fire, which is the contradictory of cold—the pervader.

That acquisition (*labdhi*) of the pervaded, namely the sensation of cold, is called the "perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*); thus, there is no fault.

Although it could also be described as the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), it is designated in that way for the purpose of demonstrating its nature as the cognition of a contradictory counter-correlate (*viruddha-pratiyogi*). In the same manner, the "perception of that which is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇa-viruddhopalabdhi*) and others are to be explained. In every case, it is indeed non-existence (*abhāva*).
The object to be proven is not established by perception; rather, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is based upon that [non-perception]. Now, one might ask:

how can there be a linguistic usage of non-perception in cases such as the "perception of the contradictory" (*viruddhopalabdhi*)? It has been stated in this regard that the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) itself is the non-perception of the other. Furthermore, the counter-positive is of two kinds. Among these, when the counter-positive is a contradictory entity...

In that case, the employment of a contradictory term establishes the very word "perception" (*upalabdhi*) as the required factor. However, when the remaining counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is understood as non-perception (*anupalabdhi*),
the words "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) or "visible" (*dṛśya*) being employed function, in relation to the object of negation, as the word "non-perception."
It designates [the object]. Thus, while its being perceived in one place is understood, its non-perception elsewhere is implied; since that reality is indeed one and the same, there is no fault.
And when the contradictory counter-correlate is such that the negation of the second, which is itself beyond perception, occurs, then for that too—

Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not necessarily perception alone; rather, it is also inference. For a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is considered to be that which, by its own existence, removes the existence of another. And who can prevent such a thing from being so even if it is imperceptible? However, when the counter-correlate is necessarily perceived together [with the object], there is a negation of only that which is capable of being perceived; thus, in that case, there is necessarily a requirement for perception. This is not the case when [the object] is being inferred.

If a jar were present in a particular location, it would necessarily be perceived; since perception lacks the capacity [to establish its absence] and inference lacks a rule of necessary connection (*ārambha-niyama*), how can there be a negation?

If you argue that there is no negation because this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa-mātra*), we say: no, for even in that case, when the form of the conceptual construction is being experienced...

It is said that even externally, one may experience a desired location provided there is no impairment of the sense faculty's capacity. However, it cannot be maintained that when an external object is being conceptualized, a second [object] would also be cognized. Why should it not be the case that even when an external object is being conceptualized, another object in that same location would certainly be perceived? For the cognition of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) does not constitute the perceptibility of something else.

It is not a basis for planting [a seed of cognition], but rather a cause for the arising of the ascertainment of non-existence because it is a real entity (*vastu*). And since that [status of being a real entity] belongs to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as well, what is the distinction?

If you say it is out of deference to common practice (*pratipattyanurodha*), then deference should also be shown toward that which is associated with a single cognition; thus, it is not the case in the instance of water.

For we observe that the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs even when only a remnant of smell is perceived in fire, or of taste in wind, or of form in the remaining elements; or, as in those cases, it is simply due to the non-perception of the effect, which is the cognition [of the object]. Since this is the same elsewhere as well, what is the use of [the condition of] being associated with a single cognition? If it is argued that the non-perception of the effect negates only a capable [cause], then [we reply]: in that case, smell and so forth, though present, would not be perceived by the sense organs in water and the like.

"It is not perceived due to a defect [in the sense organs]"—this indeed is the great fruit of the labor of the scriptures. For even when the cause of a defect is not perceived, one might still doubt, imagining that it has been overwhelmed by something like a "yogic power" (yogādi); but why would one not doubt regarding the non-perception of an object on the ground, even when the senses are sharp, if one imagines that such non-perception is caused by that [overwhelming factor]? Therefore, during the stage of practice, worldly transaction proceeds precisely through the persistence of that state [of non-perception].

But for the Master of Logic (Nyāyanātha), there is neither a challenge nor a concession following conventional usage; rather, it is out of a display of boldness (*prauḍhi*) to show that even with such an interpretation, there is no impairment of our own definition—just as when all things are cognized and their nature determined by a single cognition, that very [cognition] is "omniscient. And in conventional usage, just as one perceives something associated with a single cognition, so too does one perceive its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Since the ascertainment of non-existence is observed to be common [to all] and non-erroneous, the apprehension of something associated with a single cognition is not required; rather, it is logical that the very perception of its own form through conceptualization— precisely by means of such repeated practice— is the means for proving the negation of the other.
And in the state of refuge,
from the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

Because the capacity of direct perception is observed, in this way, even the apprehension of something remote that is contradictory establishes the absence of its opposite through the nature of inference. For example, "There is no cold here because of smoke"—thus should the apprehension of the effect of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-kāryopalabdhi*) be understood. For instance:
"There is no frost here because of smoke. This is to be explained as a synthesis at the time of formal application (*prayoga*).

In reality, however, "there is no cold in fire" is not a single formal argument (prayoga), as in the case of "there is no frost in fire. For that which is contradictory to a pervader is indeed contradictory [to the pervaded]; for example, "fire exists because of smoke. The remainder should also be inferred in this manner.
If the non-perception of the nature of a cause, etc., is the non-perception of another's cause, etc., in the form of a relative negation (paryudāsa), [then it is a valid reason].

How, then, is it [stated] regarding things that lack any designation (*nirupākhya*), such as "the son of a barren woman has no consciousness because of the absence of sentience"? In that case as well, the perception of the mental image (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*) itself as being devoid of sentience constitutes the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). And the perception [of the subject] through the exclusion of the property of being a speaker constitutes the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*). Indeed, all non-perceptions (*anupalabdhi*) ultimately resolve into reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).

And because there is a determination [of the object] through the means of proof for its negation, it is designated as distinct; thus, there is no fault. Nevertheless, one might ask: "Since negation occurs directly through the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) according to the sequence already stated, why has the Master made it figurative by describing it as indirect (*paramparayā*)?
[The answer is: If the non-perception of the visible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is intended as the negator of the very object to be negated, then it is figurative. But if...
If it were merely a figurative statement, one might ask: "What is the contradiction in saying that even for another [person], that [negation] is primary?

Furthermore, in that case, the negation would apply only to what is perceptible, as far as possible, and not to others—such as the Omniscient One or the Dispassionate One—who constitute the primary human goal; thus, their inclusion there is for the sake of the task at hand. But in reality, whether it be that [Omniscient One] or anything else...
The non-apprehension of that which has been described is the means of proof.
The Secret of Non-Apprehension is completed.
An Investigation into the Absence of All Words

In this context, some establish the non-existence of all sounds by means of the non-apprehension of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*). They argue that, because there is no connection with a single cognition, there is indeed no occasion here for the non-apprehension of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). For in this [latter case], three things must necessarily be stated:

the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) consisting in the negation of something like a jar, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the result (*phala*). Among these, by virtue of the qualification regarding a perceptible object—

There is no non-exclusion of [objects] such as *piśācas* (demons), because taste is [inherently] connected to the cognition of color through its nature of being experienced in association with a single cognition. Nor does there follow the defect belonging to the position of non-existence (*abhāva*), for the establishment of perception is presented as having practical efficacy (*vyavahāra*) as its fruit; and that [establishment] is possible only when there is a substratum for the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). For it is precisely that [substratum] which, by being invariably concomitant with the absence of other counter-correlates, possesses the capacity to generate the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that non-existence.

The proof would then be as follows: for a fool, the non-apprehension of that which has that [sound] as its nature is the means of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence; this is logical. However, when the non-existence of all sounds is to be proven, not a single object associated with a single cognition can be found; therefore, there is no room for such [non-apprehension] here. For that mass of sounds, while present in the intended location, is incapable of failing to initiate its effect, namely cognition; thus, regarding the effect—

The point is that even in a negation, existence (sattā) is negated precisely as it is without qualification. Here it is considered: sound is not heard merely by its own nature, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing even for one who is deaf.
Therefore, it is only sound when assisted by the acuity of the sense organ that possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of hearing. And that [capacity] is the acuity of the hearing...

When there is an absence of contact with a single cognition, it is difficult to ascertain [the non-existence of an object]; therefore, the negation of a jar depends upon the perception of its location.
Consequently, while enumerating the qualities of the sense organ, one ascertains that the non-perception is due solely to the fault of the jar, just like the case of mental attention (*manaskāra*).

The establishment of the sense organ through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is impossible because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). Nor can it be apprehended by another sense organ, because it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, its effect is nothing other than perception itself. And when that [perception] is established, the non-perception of the effect is itself unestablished. Since it is unestablished, the [reason's] inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) is proven; for even when an object exists, non-perception—being possible due to a defect in the sense organ—is not necessarily determined by its absence.
If you say: "It is not that the word does not exist; rather, we say that it does not exist as something capable of producing the cognition of it," then this [is what you have said].

The conduct of a quack physician is as follows: first, having accepted a desired remedy characterized by boldness, he subsequently proclaims its incurability once the opponent has demonstrated the truth regarding the fact that what was proposed as a means was not actually a means. Indeed, this non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is stated as a proof only when the absolute non-existence of something is intended to be known; it is not [the proof] for the absence of the capacity to produce cognition.

Regarding this inquiry: if the failure of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has somehow been understood in this way, why then is the failure of the object of cognition (*prameya*)—the very basis of what is to be known—not accepted? It would be better to simply seek another means of valid cognition; why is it proclaimed that [the object] is simply unprovable? For it is not so.

It is not possible to reject the absence of the sound of a nearby drum for one who is deaf while it exists for one who is not deaf, because this would entail the absurd consequence that there is no distinction between the deaf and the non-deaf.
If it is argued that there is a distinction made by hearing—namely, that [the sound] exists before and does not exist after—it is not so; for if [the sound were different] from its prior state...
Since this [capacity for hearing] is indistinguishable from the power of hearing, how could there be no hearing when sound exists? Otherwise, it would not exist even previously.

If it is further supposed that it exists in a dissimilar state, then one should not have confidence in hearing either, because such a distortion is possible. In that case, there is no difference between non-hearing and the hearing of what is non-existent. Ultimately, from where does this reversal of capacity arise?

If this is argued, then the question "Why is there an absence of that [sound] in the middle? remains the same. Therefore, this is simply not a valid position; even though the sound exists at that time, it is not heard. When considering what the proof for this might be, it has already been stated that the non-perception of an effect is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the proficiency of the auditory organ is difficult to ascertain.
But how can this be difficult to ascertain for one who has begun to listen and possesses the strength of keen sight, hearing, and memory?
For even if [the mind] were momentary, a dissimilar state is impossible in the absence of other dissimilar auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*).

Indeed, those conditions that cause a modification of the sense faculties—such as disturbances of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) or physical blows—have their powers determined within their own continuum.

The causes for the confusion of the mental continuum are indeed easily perceived; but how could those that remain unperceived ever withstand the suspicion of being distinct from their own source? For one who suspects that even a subtle cause—such as the intervention (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a powerful being—is the cause of such a transformation, what confidence can there be even in hearing [the teaching]? Therefore, even when an error of the senses characterized by disorientation regarding the directions (*diṅmoha*) is seen to have been produced by an unperceived cause, [the rule holds] provided that no well-known cause is present.

Just as the non-alteration of the state [of the senses] is not established for the sense organs by virtue of their characteristics—otherwise, it would follow that the cognitions based upon them are erroneous—why is this not likewise reckoned even now? Let there be no total collapse of all conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
However, the reliance on the presence of the state of practice is common [to both]. For it is not the case that for one who is deaf, the power of hearing has ascended to the ear...

We maintain that even in the case of [the self] not being heard, there is no certainty of its non-existence, because there is simply no certainty regarding its strength. This applies equally to anything else whose strength is unmeasured.

For when those who have slept through the entire night wake up, even though they do not see [the objects], we observe that their cognitive activity proceeds without error as they experience that state; so what occasion is there for one who is awake to suspect that his own self is otherwise?

Therefore, is there a negation of this state of being (tādavasthya) or of its determination (tadvyavasthā) because of the absence of a well-known cause, or because of the absence of its defining characteristic? If one who maintains that the basis for perceptuality in seeing, hearing, and so forth depends on the state of practice intends this state of being to be established by convention, then neither the state of being of the sense organ nor the state of being of the cognition restricted by the causal complex [is established], with respect to their common capacity.

Or rather, consciousness alone is taken as the refuge, and that very same [consciousness] exists even in the state of not hearing; so how could there be an absence of sound, given its non-exclusive nature?
If it is argued that self-awareness belongs only to the nature of cognition itself—no, for this is merely a discussion regarding the absence of all sounds.
When objects are of a single nature, conducive to a single purpose,
and exist without division, there arises a single cognition directed toward all those objects.

Even regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is a single conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of "I," and there is a functional utility (*upayoga*) toward a single object—such as speaking—in which they are mutually dependent.
This principle is well-established in the case of things designated as "pot" and so forth, consisting of form, taste, and the rest; otherwise, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible.
Now, it may be argued that perception of the body does not follow the intellect. This is true with respect to their individual forms, such as form and taste.

Divadeva: Generally speaking, however, it is stated that [the self and the cognition] are objects of a single cognition, so long as there is no insistence on their distinction. But when there is such analysis, they are said to have separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the two propositions—that Caitra is perceived and yet the cognition is not directly perceived—are not contradictory.
For this very reason, even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I am in that state" follows from direct experience and has everything as its object.

If it is argued that this is an error—no, for since there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), the status of an error is unestablished. Therefore, because it is possible to ascertain that the auditory power previously perceived remains in that same state, the non-hearing [of the sound] is due solely to the fault of the sound itself; thus, even through the absence of cognition, the non-existence of the object is established with certainty, and there is no contradiction of the subject matter. Such, then, is the complete set of conditions for the definition of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

What is the purpose of applying the designation "non-perception of the effect"? It is because a sound that has attained a particular state—namely, the completeness of other causal conditions—is negated precisely through its non-perception.
Even so, if another designation were used, who would be the negator even when negating a jar? For the sound, just like the jar, is merely [an object of negation].

It is said that even by means of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), a negation is established as the probandum (*sādhya*). If it is argued that negation by such [non-perception] is logical because of the possibility of association with a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*), then in that very case, in relation to what is there an "association with a single cognition"? For in the perception of color, taste is not negated precisely because it has reached the condition of non-perception due to being at a remote location; this is because the sense of smell functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*).

Regarding the senses of taste and touch, since their status as sense organs is established by the aforementioned sequence, what is the need for dependence on association with a single cognition? It is not so, because light, which is distinct from the sense organ, must be depended upon there; for that [light] arises and ceases depending on external causes easily available outside.

Since the property of being a "common object" (*janadharma*) cannot be established by the mere persistence of its own nature, for that purpose a connection within a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*) is required; this will also serve as an auxiliary factor even in the cognition of the excellence of the sense organ (*indriyasādguṇyajñāna*). Thus, it is established that where the capacity for apprehension is independent of light, there is no requirement for a connection within a single cognition. And that [connection] is indeed required in some means of proof (*sādhana*), because without it, there would be a contradiction.

In cases where there is doubt regarding the accomplishment [of the proof], there is no attachment to other defects. Furthermore, when something that has attained the fitness for perception is negated by non-perception in some instance, that [fitness] exists, such that a correlative would necessarily be required. Even where this [correlative] is required, it is solely for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) in the negation of an object whose cognition depends upon light. And it is not by this much alone—
In Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Nibandhāvalī*,
there is no requirement for that [dependence] in every case; for dependence on destruction is not a means of establishing pervasion in every instance of proving momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
This is required in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If this [reason] must indeed depend [on such a condition], then what need is there for the qualification "perceptible" (*dṛśya*)? For there is no deviation from perceptibility in anything that is associated with the same cognition as the subject. Indeed, a *piśāca* has no association with the same cognition as anything [else]. Thus, the single object [of the cognition] is of two kinds—

If it is argued that there is no discussion of a different purpose because the *pīti* (joy) occurs in a single application—no, for the distinction [between them] is not unmanifest due to their relationship as general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*).

For conjunction (*saṃsarga*) does not deviate from the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), whereas the mere qualifier certainly deviates from it. Therefore, conjunction is brought forward for the sake of establishing the qualifier; however, the qualifier is not capable of attracting conjunction, even in the case of a word (*śabda*).

Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). And thus, since the position [of the opponent] would be destroyed, what would be the point of the effort? Therefore, what is called "coexistence in a single cognition" is proclaimed only with reference to the specific example under discussion, and not as something to be required in all cases of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

For, while the negation of the jar is the subject at hand, let that direction [of the argument] serve to establish the qualification; indeed, the definition of one's own non-perception is simply "that which is perceptible is not perceived. Thus, both in the definition and in its formal application, there is the presentation of mere non-perception of that which meets the conditions of perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*); and in the treatise, when demonstrating the sublation of the contrary, [it refers to] the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the presence of other causal conditions.

The impossibility of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) when [the object] possesses a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) is being demonstrated; otherwise, one would have to show that the relation with the causal factor (*prayojaka-aṃśa*) exists everywhere, just as it does with the qualifier. However, since identity (*tādātmya*) is negated only after having accepted its perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*), this is merely a failure to state the qualifier, and not a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*), unlike the case of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) known by the learned. Or, if there is a specific statement of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)... in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)...

[This is] for [the sake of] one who [holds such a view]. Therefore, even for the Lord of Logic (Dignāga), there is no necessary intention to depend on a relation with a single cognition in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Moreover, if this were so, he would have stated that everything is subsumed under the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) alone, since the non-perception of an essential nature is but a part of it. Furthermore, he would have established the system of all means of valid cognition within the inference from effect, except for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Therefore, just as there is no establishment of an inference from effect regarding the object of sensory perception, why would the author of the treatise also establish non-perception of effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) regarding that which is not grasped by it? For just as there is a fear of the collapse of the system of perception in one case, so too is there [a fear of its collapse] in the other case regarding the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). Or, just as the effect is a logical mark (*liṅga*) for what is imperceptible, so too is [the effect] for the imperceptible—

It is equally valid that there is thus a non-apprehension of that [other cognition]. Just as this very Blessed One, even regarding the absence of another cognition within ignorance, employs it in conventional discourse by means of the non-apprehension of the perceptible. As he said:
"When there is the perception of a conceptualization whose nature is perceptible, it precludes the conceptualization of non-perception in sensory cognition."

In that case, what is the correlate within a single cognition? Furthermore, if this is accepted, then even the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) becomes unestablished; thus, the very position under discussion is abandoned.
For the absence of the body of cognition cannot be known through the non-perception of an effect alone, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Moreover, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), being restricted to a single form, necessarily implies the determination of the absence of anything else—provided it exists for one who holds a contrary view.

Since the discussion regarding the absence of all sounds would have to be experienced through another cognition, non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) alone is the refuge in conventional practice, as if it were external. However, there would be no utterance of the qualifier; indeed, there is no other way. And since that [non-perception] is also absent when there is a requirement for a relation (*saṃsarga*), the reason is "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).

Therefore, it is impossible for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) to function without violating the rule that it depends upon association within a single cognition. If it is argued that this rule applies only with respect to external objects—no, for even there, there is no underlying basis [for such a restriction]. For if a capacity exists internally, why should its manifestation not be possible externally as well? Indeed, the nature of objects is manifold.

Regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): therein, first of all, the self-nature requires nothing more than the capacity for manifesting in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, sound, odor, taste, touch, darkness, and light require nothing more than mental attention (*manaskāra*) in addition to that. Furthermore, the specific forms (*rūpa-viśeṣa*) residing in objects such as jars generally require even illumination.

Likewise, just as there is apprehension (*upalabdhi*) in the case of their affirmation, why should there not also be non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) of their intrinsic nature in the case of their negation?
Would it depend on a distinct collection [of causes]?

In that case, just as in the first instance there is no utility in the sense organ remaining in its original state, so too in the intermediate cases there is no utility in its being associated with a single cognition.
However, for one who depends on something additional to those [causes], such dependence is indeed logical. Therefore, just as if a cognition were to exist, it would necessarily be perceived—

The implication is: "Is it because of the persistence of the state of the sense faculty? For if taste and so forth were present, they would certainly have been perceived by me through that faculty remaining in its original state;
thus, it is indeed possible to ask whether they are associated with a single cognition. Therefore, even regarding external objects, the possibility of such a restriction is far-fetched;
or, if one were to accept it, one would have to expect it for cognition as well.

If it is argued that even in that case there exists a connection with a single cognition based on the single perception of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), [we reply: surely there is no such thing as a single perception called "self-awareness," because that, being merely a property (*dharma*), is distinct in each individual instance. Furthermore, if you are satisfied with the designation of a "single cognition" by relying on a universal (*sāmānya*), then the same consequence would apply even to objects grasped by different sense organs, or even to the objects of self-awareness and sensory cognition. This applies to whichever two...

If it is argued that there is no deviation from mutual perception between two existing things, and that such a rule applies there, [we reply: this restriction does not apply even to two forms (*rūpa*), since a *piśāca* is not perceived in a location. If it is argued that [the rule] certainly applies to two specific instances (*viśeṣa*), yet a fault in the general case (*sāmānya*) does not infect the particular instance—[we reply:
even so, the same consequence would follow for sound and space, or for sound and mental attention (*manaskāra*). For space is not perceived.

Alternatively, the perception of sound in a sentient being is subject to deviation from the perception of mental attention (*manaskāra*). Since there is such deviation, the non-perception of the effect would result in the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the requirement of dependence on a single cognition is not all-pervasive, and this [requirement] is easily available for other cases as well; so enough with this dispute.

Moreover, this co-inclusion (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*) of two cognitions is something entirely unprecedented; for there is no primary [co-inclusion] due to the absence of a single substratum, nor is there a secondary one because they are not subsumed under a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*). If it is argued that "being subsumed under a single sense-base" is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), then why is "co-inclusion in a single cognition" not likewise declared to be an indicative mark? However, both of these have been stated with reference to the example of the jar under discussion; thus, one should not be dogmatic. (*Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*)

For just as the non-deviation from mutual perception is observed through their inclusion within a single sense-base (*āyatana*), so too it is logical that through their association within a single cognition there is likewise a dependence solely upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
And what is the counter-correlate of what? It is that between which a perception restricted to a single form establishes the ascertainment of the absence of the other.

It is possible to say that [one] can perceive [the other]. And of which two things is there such non-perception? Of those two for which the perception of one is invariably concomitant with the non-perception of the other;

for when both exist, a cognition restricted to only one form is impossible.
