Therefore, in relation to specific time, place, state, and continuum, they are established as mutual counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), because their simultaneous attainment of consciousness—characterized by similarity—is impossible.
Having done so, it is precisely because of this that the cognition restricted to the single form of those two is able to establish the conceptual exclusion (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*) of the other;

thus, such a non-existence is said to be established by perception. That very certainty, for the sake of one who is deluded, is the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) whose nature is the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*); and since the capacity for apprehension is possible for things existing at the same time, there is also the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on that usage.

Since the establishment of both the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the result (*phala*) is already accomplished by the mere refutation of other positions, what is the purpose of including the requirement that they be apprehended by a single sense-faculty?
For this counter-argument applies whether the objects or cognitions— or both cognition and object— are apprehended by one or by multiple sense-faculties.

And since this [argument] is common to all and is beyond reproach in establishing non-existence, what need is there for compliance with it? For just as the cognition of the floor and the jar, or the single-form perception of them, is sufficient to produce the ascertainment of their absence due to its non-deviation from other direct perceptions, so too is the mere perception of touch at the time of eating a lamp by one who has perceived both [the lamp and its function] while drinking a beverage and perceives them to remain in that same state.

In producing the ascertainment of the absence of taste, or in establishing the determination of the absence of a nearby touch through the mere self-awareness of the form of one's own conceptual construction, [the cognition] is indeed capable.
For that awareness of the conceptual construction does not deviate from the perception of a touch that exists at that time; nor is there another—

The capacity to produce a certainty regarding the absence of a second [entity] elsewhere, based on the non-deviation of perception, is nothing other than that [perception itself]. Nor is the "direct perception of absence" anything distinct from the capacity to produce a certainty of absence; for absence does not possess a physical form by which it could be directly perceived. And when, through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the counter-positive itself is the absence, then its establishment through perception is indeed primary.

Thus, it is logical that in all cases the result is practical efficacy (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, this counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) does not exist for anyone with respect to things remote by nature and so forth, such that someone’s perception would be capable of manifesting its absence. Nor, in this way, is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) said to be a mere cessation [of cognition].

But Bhaṭṭa [holds that] even in the view of *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation), one establishes non-perception as a means of knowledge by perceiving "anything else" without depending on the aforementioned counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); thus, in his system, the exclusion of things such as *piśācas* is logical. However, the perception of color is spatially remote from the taste located in that same place;
it does not fulfill the aforementioned requirement of being a counter-positive. Furthermore, the presence at the tip of the tongue does not deviate from non-perception in the case of absence.

Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the discussion regarding the non-existence of all [other types of] non-perception. For this very reason, it is stated that the inclusion of the non-perception of effects (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth within the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) occurs through an indirect succession, because such counterparts (*pratiyogin*) do not exist.

Therefore, the definition of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is simply the non-perception of that which has attained the state of being fit for perception. And since this [non-perception] results in the conventional (*vyavahārika*) absence of that which is established as being capable of the aforementioned cognition, there is no contradiction with either the *Nyāya* or the *Śāstra*. As for the mention of "being apprehended by a single sense-faculty," it should be understood as being made solely with reference to examples such as a jar.

It is established as follows: when one perceives the absence of a drum or the like in a space characterized by darkness or light, or in a temple or similar location that is being observed, then either that very space—colored by the assistance of its uniform aspect—or the cognition itself which has become the object of such a cognition, constitutes "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).
This is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the object to be negated or of the cognition thereof, which is necessarily preceded by the arising of a perception [of the locus].

However, for one whose eye has not turned away [from the object], the taste and so forth, or the cognition thereof, ultimately consist of the mental attention (*manaskāra*) which is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the knowable object; and the awareness of that [attention] is also an exclusion. For even that [awareness] is not possible for one with keen hearing unless it is accompanied by the arising of verbal perception, provided it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

However, there is no authority for a negation [here]. Rather, as long as the perception of sound connected to a specific location does not deviate from the perception of rasa and so forth, or from the awareness of the form of a conceptual construction, then the exclusion (paryudāsa) must be stated in relation to the word for that specific location; for it is impossible to state a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) with respect to another thing characterized by non-deviation from the mutual perception of one another. And therefore, as before, [this is] perception—

The establishment of non-existence is achieved; and it is proven that even in the case of sound, conventional usage as a result arises solely from the non-perception of what is perceptible. Thus [it is established].
Even in the absence of a single cognition,
there is no attraction of the undesirable because its activity is not obstructed.
Because it depends upon the counter-correlate.

In the case of words, lamps, and the like, it has been indicated that for the attainment of the completeness of conditions such as light, there is a dependence on manifestors that exceed the mere birth [of the object]; this applies to both the word and the cognition.
However, for a consciousness that perceives in such a manner, its mind is one that has previously heard or seen something similar.
For in other cases, one's own non-apprehension is indeed the cognition of something else that is empty of forms such as sound.
If the persistence of the sense organ is not established,
then there is no capacity for the non-perception of the effect;
if the persistence of the sense organ is established...
The result [of this] is not the non-perception of an effect;
rather, in the case of essential non-perceptions (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), there is necessarily a requirement for [the perception of] cognition. (Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī 198)
How can there be the establishment of contact for you, even in the state where cognition is the effect?
If this restriction applies only to external objects, then what causes it even there? For the status of objects is diverse, due to the suitability of specific locations alone.
Just as the sublation of a cognition lacking illumination does not constitute a distinction [from valid cognition] unless it is stated otherwise,
so too, in certain cases, there is sublation even while disregarding the associated [object].
However, there is no fear for Bhaṭṭa regarding the nature of that [negation], for its counter-positive is simply the cognition of the object;
thus, even that state of being a counter-positive—
In secret, there is indeed no deviation from what was witnessed.
Therefore, it is a single cognition itself that constructs the conceptualization of the non-existence of another;

non-existence is not something to be cognized by perception, since it is nothing other than the certainty produced by that [cognition]. Only when there is the aforementioned counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is sense-perception capable [of apprehending it].
Such is the status of the thing: that it consists in the determination of its non-existence.

Now, it may be argued that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) alone is what is associated with the same cognition, because direct association with a single cognition is intended as the primary sense due to the acceptance of the theory of *sākāra* (the cognition possessing the form). Therefore, by implication, the word "one" (*eka*) stands as an indicator of mere non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, its application as "one" is solely in reference to the single genus of perception (*pratyakṣa-ekajāti*). Nor is this merely a matter of terminology, for such conventional usage is observed, just as in the case of "a single grain of rice" (*eko vrīhiḥ*).
It is said that "being complete brings about abundance. Therefore, even where it is stated that "it is seen as associated with a single cognition," the meaning is precisely this:

that there is a mutual non-deviation from direct perception. However, the state of being within the same sense-base (*ekāyatanabhāva*) should be explained as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), depending on the context, just as in the case where "the location and the cognition thereof constitute non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).

And therefore, since in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the "basis of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisamāśraya*) is said to be precisely the "basis of that which is associated in a single cognition" (*ekajñānasaṃsargisamāśraya*), how could this so-called "association in a single cognition" be non-pervasive? True, it is so;
[this is] because of the state of being situated in a single cognition with the dark [object], in every age...
If it occurs to you that there is no harm [in this],
then let there be a self-evident negation of *dhvani* as something devoid of all constituent parts.
The discussion regarding the absence of all sounds is untenable, because mutual non-deviation from perception is possible even in the case of some sound, whereas the other [sound],

being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is impossible. For one who considers the co-occurrence within a single cognition to be restricted to the counter-correlate, their own non-perception serves as the negation of the subject at hand.

What dependence on another [factor] is there? Therefore, in proving the non-existence of all sounds in a suitable location, one need not resort to the non-perception of the effect, which is cognition;

for this is established by the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone. However, since darkness and light, situated in mutually exclusive locations, easily come into contact within a single cognition produced by the same sense organ, they remain at a distance when it comes to the section concerning the proof of their non-existence.
Because intrinsic nature is not perceived, there is no consideration of another means of proof.
The investigation into the non-existence of all words is completed. 6.
The Chapter on Apoha.
The established position is that exclusion (apoha) is revealed by words and logical marks;
this is proven in order to establish that all phenomena are inexpressible.

"Stability" (*sthiti*) means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*). By the phrase ending with "is made manifest," it is stated that *apoha* is the denotable object (*abhidheya*) here; by the remainder [of the verse], the fruit of its establishment is indicated. Alternatively, the meaning is that this is for the purpose of establishing the principle (*vyavasthā*) that *apoha* is manifested by words and so forth, as formulated by the Teachers (*ācārya*). In either case, the establishment of *apoha* is intended primarily to demonstrate that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible.
This is what has been stated.
But is it not the case that this claim—that exclusion (apoha) is manifested by words and logical marks—is contradicted by experience?
For instance, when one understands from a word or a logical mark that "there is fire in this mountain region," the cognition is observed to delineate only a positive form.

The statement "it does not exist without fire" merely indicates an exclusion (*nivṛtti*). Furthermore, regarding that which is sublated by experience, there is no consideration of other means of proof, because the efficacy of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) rests precisely therein, as they originate from it and have it as their fruit.

Indeed, the arising of another means of valid cognition is not independent of the assistance provided by perception; nor is one's purpose fulfilled merely by the arising of another means of valid cognition.

As long as there is no experience of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the object presented by that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), another means of valid cognition—being seized by incapacity and futility when independent of it—is itself nothing at all; thus, it finds no scope whether for sublation or for establishing what has already been established. So how can it be said that exclusion (*apoha*) is the object of words and the like?

Now, even if there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "I cognize an absence," nevertheless, the very mention of the object that has ceased is itself the mention of the absence. For there is no cognition of a qualified entity that does not involve the cognition of its qualifier. Therefore, just as the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is a conceptual cognition because of the manifestation of a common form—even in the absence of a conceptual construction such as "I cognize a universal"—[so it is here].

If it is argued that the cognition of others is likewise, and that the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti-buddhi*), projected by a ceased conceptualization (*pratyaya*), extends the conventional usage of the apprehension of exclusion (*apoha*);

[we reply: well then, if the establishment of the cognition of a universal is based on the manifestation of a common form in the manner of a positive entity (*vidhi-rūpa*), what has come of the establishment of the cognition of exclusion when the mind does not manifest the form of an absence? Therefore, "I perceive exclusion... [is untenable].

Even in the absence of a mental aspect such as "I understand," if there were a manifestation of the cause for cessation, who indeed would deny the established status of the cognition of cessation? Otherwise, if the conventional usage of that cognition were based on its appearance [even without the aspect], then it would follow even in a mind having the form of a cow— *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.
Let it be called "the cognition of a horse. Now, it was argued that the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti*) is included as a qualifier;

even so, if the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) takes such a form as "excluded from non-cow," then let there be its inclusion as a qualifier. However, the cognition is "cow" (*gauḥ*). And in that case, since the specific characteristic consisting of exclusion, though existing, is not manifested therein, how [can it be a qualifier]?

Is this the established rule for its cognition? If so, it follows this: how can there be such a principle that the positive element (*vidhi*), even while manifesting, does not have an objective status, whereas the exclusion (*apoha*), even while not manifesting, does?
And likewise, how can that form which is not determined by determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) be their object? Nor [is it an object] in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The term "ascertainment" (*niścayana*) refers to that which does not manifest [as a positive form]. Since that which is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*) manifests within the internal domain alone, it is said that there is also an exclusion of the other (*parāpoha*) regarding it;

this is what is called its cognition. Even in that case, the exclusion (*apoha*) possesses only a mere relationship [to the object], whereas the positive form itself appears directly; thus, one is not liberated from the aforementioned fault. Furthermore, in this way, even perception would unavoidably have exclusion as its object, especially in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For one who perceives a single exclusion while delineating it as distinct from all others, conceptual cognition— just like perception which grasps a positive form (*vidhyākāra*)— has only a positive entity as its object, not the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). As for that which is excluded from others, or that in which others are excluded, it is simply the external object itself, distinguished from things of a different class.

It is said that the form of cognition is "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). Therefore, this [theory] serves no purpose, because by the name "exclusion" it is actually a positive entity (*vidhi*) that is intended to be expressed; nor does changing the name of a thing cause its essential nature to change. Consequently, in accordance with experience, let the external object itself, which is of a positive nature, be what is understood from words and so forth. Furthermore, regarding this point, the treatise states: "There are two means of establishing a positive entity, and one for negation."
This is the reason:
by this [negation], a negation that does not admit any portion of a real entity (vastu) as its object is established;
however, even regarding a real entity, through the first two [types of negation], there is an exclusion (paryudāsa) by way of affirmation.

[Pravā. 4.262] And if, as in the case of the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), there were a cognition of mere non-existence even from another logical mark (*hetu*), then it would follow that difference does not arise from non-perception (*anupalambha*); consequently, the entire systematic framework based on the classification of logical marks would fall into disorder. Thus, how could there be *apoha*?
Since it is said that [the object] is manifested by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*), he says "sthitih" (the established state). This is merely a conventional arrangement;
the meaning is that exclusion (*apoha*) is primarily the object of words, and this is not the actual reality (*vastutattva*). If one asks, "What then is the actual reality here? [it follows].
1. Now, the section from "atha yadyapi" up to "tatpratītivvyavasthā," which concludes this [work], has been extracted from the *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī*, page 53.
2. "That which is of a positive nature... does not have exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object"; compare *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī*, page 53, lines 19–22. 3.
From the ninth leaf to the sixteenth leaf, the reading is extremely unclear.
In the section on Apoha,
it is primarily the positive object that is expressed by words; therein, exclusion (apoha) is understood as a subordinate quality of that [object].
One meaning appears through superimposition, while another is established as the literal sense; in reality, however, there is no meaning at all.

This is the summary of the meaning of the section (*prakaraṇa*). Indeed, it is not possible for a treatise (*śāstra*) to exist by disregarding direct experience (*anubhava*); thus, while introducing [the topic] in the form of a positive injunction, it cannot be denied that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises. This is the meaning of the first quarter-verse (*pāda*). Because there is no dispute regarding its connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), it is not [discussed] therein.

[The word] "by means of words" (*śabdaiḥ*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that [the object] is also "conveyed by means of logical marks" (*liṅgaiḥ*) and "made an object of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpaiḥ*). This being the case, let alone the status of exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable meaning, even its mere systematic establishment is lost. For that established state is also twofold: through proximity (*sannikarṣāt*) and through the causal factor (*prayojakāt*). In this regard, although all phenomena (*dharmas*) are inexpressible—

Having raised the objection that it has been stated that the presentation of "tva" (the abstract suffix) is the motivator [of the cognition], and not some kind of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), he says: "In that case, there is apoha.

For when a positive entity (*vidhi*) is primarily presented, apoha is indeed understood as a subordinate element by virtue of being its qualification. In this regard, "by way of being subordinate to it" refers to the contact with the object (*artha-sannikarṣa*). "It is understood" refers to the contact with cognition (*pratīti-sannikarṣa*). Consequently, it is both connected to the object and being cognized.

Exclusion (*apoha*), although it is the primary object of cognition, is said to be the denotable meaning (*abhidheya*) principally by setting aside the positive injunction (*vidhi*), because of the stated purpose. Alternatively, it is understood only as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and not as the primary [meaning]; thus, those who maintain that exclusion is directly expressed are refuted.

And although it was stated that there is no mention of words such as "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), nevertheless, there is certainly no non-cognition of exclusion when it functions as a qualifier.

For the word "cow" (*go*) and others are applied precisely by excluding what is not a cow and so forth; as the treatise states: "And the application [of a word] is such that one excludes that from which [the object] differs," and so on. For just as when the word *indīvara* (blue lotus) is applied to a blue lotus, its cognition does not involve the manifestation of blueness [as something separate].
Likewise, when the word "cow" is applied to that which is excluded from non-cows, the manifestation of the exclusion of non-cows (*agopoha*) is unavoidable upon the cognition of a cow.

As for those who raise the objection that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) in the process of establishing the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) of the word "cow" through the exclusion of non-cows— an objection they consider as dull-wittedness characteristic of common folk— [we reply as follows].

How do those who maintain that the convention applies to the universal (*sāmānya*) or to the possessor of the universal (*sāmānyavat*) see themselves as being freed from this fault? For it is not intended that the "universal" refers to the universal in its mere abstract form—since that would lead to the absurd consequence of applying the word "cow" even to a horse—but rather it is intended to refer to the universal of cowness (*gotva-sāmānya*). And yet, if [the convention] were applied to that universal of cowness...
1. *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, p.

54.20–4: "Or, if the convention of the word 'cow' is [established] in that which possesses [the universal], then the same fault applies when the object is the referent; for if the individual cow is not cognized, the universal of cowness—"

Because of [the lack of] full comprehension; for if there is no full comprehension of the universal "cowness" (*gotva-sāmānya*), there is no full comprehension of that which is denoted by the word "cow. Now, if the convention were established by such syllables as "the word 'cow' [applies] to cowness or to that which possesses it," then there would be a fault. However, when—by means of context and so forth—one points to a single individual object standing before one, which resides in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as a form common to all individuals scattered across different places and times, [then there is no fault].

If one determines the practitioner [of the convention] and establishes the convention "this is a cow," then, since he employs that very common form which he perceives in that instance by means of the word "cow," how can there be the fault of mutual dependence? And as for the statement that the convention applies to "cowness" or to "that which possesses it," this is merely a restatement of the established doctrine of commentators; it is not the actual sequence of instruction given by those who establish the convention. If you argue thus: [The response follows: This is not so. For if the convention were established solely with respect to the individual (vyakti), then because individuals are infinite and distinct, the convention could never be grasped. Furthermore, if the convention were established with respect to the universal (sāmānya) alone, then because the universal is eternal and omnipresent, it would follow that all things—such as jars and the like—are denoted by the word "cow. Therefore, the convention is established with respect to both the universal and the individual together. Consequently, when the convention is grasped, the cognition of the object arises from the word through the mediation of the universal, just as the cognition of fire arises from smoke. Thus, there is no fault of mutual dependence. As for the claim that this is merely a restatement of the commentators' doctrine and not the actual method of instruction for the convention-makers—that too is incorrect. For even if the convention-makers do not explicitly state, "This is the universal, this is the individual, and this is their relation," they nevertheless apply the convention to the object characterized by the universal and the individual. Otherwise, the convention would be impossible. Therefore, the convention is indeed established with respect to the universal and the individual together. Thus, the objection regarding mutual dependence is refuted. Furthermore, the statement that the convention applies to "cowness" or to "that which possesses it" is simply a way of expressing the same fact through different terminology; it does not imply a difference in the underlying reality. Hence, the position remains consistent.
If that is the case, then this fault applies only if the word "cow" (gośabda) is defined as being "that which excludes the non-cow" (*agavāpoḍha*)—that is, if its nature is proclaimed in such a form.

But when the convention is established as "this is a cow" for a listener who has determined, through the context, that the intended individuals are the objects of a single uniform conceptual reflection (*ekākārapratyavamarśa*), then what room is there for a fault? For he [the listener] [perceives] all [cows] lying upon the bed of his own conceptual construction (*svavikalpatalpa*).

One who understands individual cows as excluded from non-cows— without depending on a single [negative] letter— as being themselves excluded from all individuals of other classes and denotable by the word "cow," employs those very individuals by means of the word "cow" wherever he apprehends that exclusion from other classes.

To that extent, the statement "the word 'cow' [denotes] the exclusion of non-cows" is merely a restatement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), not a description of the manner of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), as intended.

Because, when the word "cow" functions, the remainder [of the meaning] can be expressed by the word "non-cow. Furthermore, that common form excluded from heterogeneous classes—which appears as the universal (*sāmānya*) in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or as the very self of the individual (*vyakti*)—will be determined later.
Thus, it is established that there is no circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). And this is established just as, upon hearing the word "puṇḍarīka," one understands a white lotus.

Even upon hearing the word "cow," when there is a cognition that excludes non-cows, the proponent of the universal (jāti-vādin) must necessarily admit that the cognition of the positive entity (vidhi) is inseparable from the cognition of the qualifier, namely apoha. Furthermore, the distinction is that while the two [the universal and the exclusion] do not appear directly as mere traces of a relationship, they are perceived through the primary and subordinate relationship [of the qualifier and the qualified]. Alternatively, the word *guṇa* may denote a property (*dharma*), referring to the positive form which has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its property.
Because it is perceived.

Regarding the similarity between two superimposed external objects produced by the exclusion of others—which belongs to the third form—Vācaspati, while refuting it, says: "And you do not admit that exclusion is a property of the particular (svalakṣaṇa); therefore, that [position] is indeed faulty. Now, as for the future...

If it is argued that this is intended merely for the sake of conventional expression (*kīrti*), even so, it serves no purpose; for it is precisely the relationship between subject and predicate (*dharmidharmabhāva*) as established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that is accepted [as the basis].

What remains is only the question: why is there not a designation by way of affirmation alone, or else why does the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) not follow that even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be treated as having the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*) as its object?

To this we reply: In this context, a certain established rule may, by relying on a mere fraction of the true nature of things, be formulated otherwise for a specific purpose, even though it exists otherwise; as, for example, in the case of the self and its origination. For origination, indeed, belongs to an entity characterized by prior non-existence. (Tattvārtha-ṭīkā, p. 684)
The section on *apoha* [states]:

A property belongs only to that which exists; nevertheless, by resorting to a mere trace of the reality characterized as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it is established as "non-existent" in order to avoid the suspicion of the doctrine of pre-existent effects (*satkāryavāda*). Or, for example, as in the case of the single [verse]: "Who else shall experience the karma performed by this very person? [This is said]...

Relying on the designation of a continuum (*santāna-prajñapti*), the deception regarding the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done is for the sake of removing delusion. Likewise, even now, the expression of the object of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is established as being merely an exclusion (*apoha*)—the object of conceptual construction—even though there is an understanding of an inseparable connection, in order to dispel the suspicion that one might accept the denotability superimposed upon a real entity by another. Therefore, it is not by means of a positive injunction alone.

This is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). However, when exclusion (*apoha*) alone is the primary meaning of a word, then it is a superimposition (*āropa*); in that case, even a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is put forward.
As it has been said:
"First, the primary meaning is expressed by words."

However, since there is no dispute regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not correct to establish [the matter] in this way. It has already been stated that in that case, there is no excellence consisting of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For the scripture says, or rather:
"It delimits that [object], and thereby excludes what is other than it," and so forth.
With respect to the object of negation, however, the operation of negation is indeed set forth there by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).

In the case of the *prasajya* (non-implicative) negation, the so-called "non-grasping" of a positive occurrence is simply the capacity to produce a conceptual construction of absence based on the experience of a determinate form.

Likewise, in the case of conceptualizations regarding injunctions (*vidhi*), the capacity to provide the performance corresponding to the tantra is itself the apprehension of the prohibition; and there is also the capacity to produce the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that "fire has been perceived by me. Furthermore, in the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the apprehension of the prohibition in both cases consists simply in the perception of the determined nature [of the object]. Both of these are intended by the author of the treatise; in some instances, he employs the *prasajya* [negation] in accordance with the context.
Under the heading of negation (*pratiṣedha*),

there are statements such as "there is nothing whatsoever in form" and so forth; however, in some cases, there are those based on exclusion (*paryudāsa*), such as "because it establishes a mere entity that is excluded from what is not of that nature" and so forth.

But there is no single fixed rule. Therefore, that which the commentator [Śāntarakṣita] and Trilocana—who was eager to introduce that very meaning for the sake of establishing his own theory of Apoha—stated, namely that "the Teacher is inferred to be one who favors absolute negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha)," has been refuted. Furthermore, there is no loss of the conventional usage of qualifiers due to the absence of difference, because such usage is produced by intention (*vivakṣā*), as in the cases of "Rāhu’s head" or "cowness is a universal."

Because it does not fall into error. Furthermore, even you yourself must indeed employ the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the absence of a jar and a location, or between the absence of a *piśāca* and a pillar. If you ask, "How can this be so for us, who maintain that negation is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?"—it is not now a matter of defining the essential nature of non-existence, but rather a matter of defining its cognition (*pratīti*). And that [cognition]...

They cannot be denied. Even in the case of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) view, since the prescription of that [one thing] itself constitutes the negation of the other, there is no loss of cognitive validity (*pratīti*).

Nor is there any loss regarding the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because this very sentence demonstrates the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the positive and negative prescriptions. (Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, 206)

Therefore, even the objection regarding contradiction is not flawed; for there is a contradiction with existence by its own nature, not with the absence of another, since they coexist. Thus, it is rightly said that in that case, exclusion (apoha) is understood as a quality of that [positive entity].

Alternatively, this very exclusion of others (*anyaniṣedha*) is the quality of that expression of meaning; therefore, it should be understood that "it is conveyed by that. The application of words is such that a treatise (*śāstra*) proceeds by avoiding what is other [than its intended object]; otherwise, its usage would be purposeless. By this, the fact that exclusion (*apoha*) is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) has been demonstrated, as well as the avoidance of the charge of non-pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*). This is the path.

In the case of "he approaches Śrughna" (*śrughnam upatiṣṭhate*), this same [principle] applies with respect to the alternative paths under discussion. With respect to undesired locations that are the opposite of Śrughna, it is Śrughna alone [that is intended].

Because there is no interruption, as in the case of a forest path, he indeed "approaches" (*upatiṣṭhate*). By excluding [the possibility of] a caravan, a messenger, and so forth, the restriction to "only the path" is easily established. If it is argued that the meaning "only the path" is already understood from the pointing out by the index finger (*tarjanī-nirdeśāt*), [we reply: it serves to exclude other [possibilities].

And it is indeed accepted that [the object] exists. Furthermore, the use of a term even when its meaning is already understood is clearly observed in common usage, as in "he is coming" (*abhyāgacchati*) or "two Brāhmaṇas. For just as there is a question such as "Which path leads to Śrughna?"—intended to exclude other paths, persons, and so forth—the answer is likewise "This is the path. For in every case, it is precisely that which is marked by the doubt of the person to be informed who is the object of the injunction.

Regarding the phrase "the two negations": if exclusion of others (*parāpoha*) is not apprehended at the time of hearing the word, how could there be activity by way of avoiding what is other? Consequently, one commanded by the words "Tie up the cow" might even tie up horses and the like.

As for the claim that, although the nature of the cow is not [explicitly] perceived at the time of its cognition, the exclusion of others is subsequently determined through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), [we reply as follows]:

This view is incorrect, because even for the first [hearer], no sequence of cognition is observed. For one who has mastered the convention at that time, when told "Bring the cow," does not resort to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) upon seeing another [animal] turn away. Nor is it logical to have a certain determination of the cow if there is a cognition of something else mixed in with the word "cow. Or, if such a cognition were to occur, how could presumptive testimony arise even subsequently?

For a cow is perceived as being accompanied by the exclusion of other forms; how then could it be capable of establishing its own non-mixture with those others? Therefore, the cognition of "cow" is called a cognition that excludes the non-cow. Consequently, the very time of the cognition of its own object is the time of the cognition of the exclusion of other objects, just as at the time of perceiving the moon when the word "moon" is employed, there is also the perception of its whiteness. And just as when whiteness is perceived, what kind of [cognition] is there of the moon...

The same applies to the cognition [of a cow]: even when there is a cognition mixed with the form of another, what kind of cognition of a cow is it? Nor is it possible to apprehend an object as being neither mixed nor unmixed, because even subsequently its capacity [to function] remains impossible to establish. Therefore, it is not best to rely on the capacity of the object for the sake of understanding a negation.
Furthermore, as Vācaspati said: "Individuals possessing a genus (jāti) are the domain of conceptual constructions and words;

and the form of those [individuals] which possess that [genus] is differentiated from what does not belong to that genus. This means that because it is understood through its object (*arthataḥ*) that [the individual] is excluded from what is of a different class, one is prompted [to act], such as by the command, "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*).
(Compare *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*, p. 55, lines 6–9).
2. *Tulana*, same page 54, line 14–15; *Tattvārtha-ṭīkā*, page 684.
3. *Tattvārtha-ṭīkā*, page 684, *Apoha-prakaraṇa*.

The claim that one does not bind horses and the like is also refuted by this very argument. For even if the universal (*jāti*) is added as something additional, if the form of the individuals remains excluded from those of a different class, then since they become the objects of words and conceptual cognitions precisely through that form, how can the appearance of their exclusion from what is not that [class] be avoided? On the other hand, if the form of the individual is not perceived as excluded from heterogeneous classes, [then the objection stands].
Or, if it is argued that this is a clarity regarding the universal (*jāti*), how can there be an understanding of it even in terms of its meaning? This has already been largely explained.
Now, if the universal is by its very nature excluded from others, then it must have existed previously as well; thus, it was not capable [of producing cognition] before.

If that were so, how could it produce it later either? For the requirement of the auxiliary factor of remembering the convention applies only to the association with a name, and not to the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīya*).
The notion that [the cognition] depends merely on perception, like that of a child and so forth, is trivial.
Alternatively, "quality" (*guṇa*) means that which is multiplied or practiced; thus, it signifies here a primary attribute (*upādeya-dharma*).
Consequently, that very quality—namely, exclusion (*apoha*)—is the principal element in those words; by virtue of that state, exclusion itself is present in words denoting positive entities.

It is said to be the object (*gamya*), not the injunction (*vidhi*), even though it manifests, just like a subordinate element. For indeed, because it depends on non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*) in all cases of heterogeneous things, and because it depends on perception (*dṛṣṭi*) in some cases of homogeneous things, the treatise states that "exclusion" (*apoha*) is connected with the verbal testimony (*śruti*). Furthermore, even when both [the positive and the negative] appear, since there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) corresponding to the appearance, and since the exclusion of others is necessarily a positive entity, exclusion alone is the primary element.
As for that treatise which states: "The contact with the form of the object occurs in sound when it effects a separation;
for that [contact] truly exists therein."
[Pravā.
3.132] Furthermore, in the case of words expressing non-existence, it is precisely because the entity does not exist. As the treatise states:
"Because of the absence of form, the words for non-existents do not denote form."
Those [exclusions] are established as being beyond number, for they are the indicators of exclusion.
[Pravāraṇāvāda 3.184–5] Thus it is said.

Alternatively, when that exclusion (*apoha*)—or rather, the form excluded by way of *paryudāsa* (exclusion-by-contrast)—is the denotable object, those words for which the quality consists in the negation of defects denote that very excluded object as their state. For example:
Because cessation lacks intrinsic nature, there is no conceptualization of another state;
and since the error [regarding] the cognition of a universal is likewise [unfounded], it is not a defect.
[Pravā.
3.168–9] Thus, the reasons for establishing exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object, which are being stated in the treatise regarding exclusion, are as follows: [Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī].

In the case of words denoting positive entities (*bhāvavācin*), those factors which oppose the primary manifestation [of the object] must be inferred. It has been stated that this very distinction is the primary one in the context of words denoting non-existence (*abhāvavācaka*). By contrast, he indicates that in the case of words denoting positive entities, this distinction is secondary (*amukhya*) because it functions as a subordinate element (*upasarjanatayā*). Indeed, this must be understood specifically: in words denoting non-existence, the exclusion (*apoha*) is the very referent of the word (*padārtha*); whereas in words denoting positive entities, it is the exclusion of the referent from others.

Exclusion (*apoha*) and the referent of a word (*padārtha*) are distinct; the difference between these two is merely verbal. If the status of exclusion as the denoted meaning is established based on such a [conventional] foundation, yet the actual object itself is declared to be the primary [meaning], then alas, the doctrine that all phenomena (*dharma*) are inexpressible has come to an end, and the very purpose for which this undertaking was begun has been undermined—this is what is indicated.

Regarding the claim that the determination of apoha as the primary denotation is for the purpose of negating the superimposition of a real entity upon the word-meaning—even there, one’s own position accepts the denotability of the object itself, while something else is taught to the opponent; anticipating the objection that this is a great lack of discernment, he says:
"And the object is one," and so forth.

This is the meaning: for an object (*artha*) is indeed twofold—external and internal—since no other exists. Of these, first, the external object is established as denotable solely through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not through the vivid manifestation of its specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*). If one asks why this is so, it is because of experience itself. For instance, in the case of perceptual consciousness, objects restricted by place, time, and state appear with perfectly clear forms.

Particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) appear and are experienced [in perception], but not so at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). For at the time of conceptualization, the object of experience is some form that appears as excluded from dissimilar classes, yet as if intermingled with the forms of others, as if indistinct, and as something unfamiliar to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As the treatise states:
Because an object does not appear in the cognition of one whose senses have not been diverted [by another stimulus] through the word, just as it appears when it is directly perceived.

If it is argued that there is a difference in appearance for the very same object due to the difference in means— since in one case the sense organ is the basis for the cognition, while in the other case it is the word and so forth?
Regarding this, it has also been said:
"The basis for the various cognitions of that single object is indeed distinct;
how then can it possess a single nature that appears in diverse forms?"
[Pravā.

2.235] For two mutually contradictory forms, one clear and the other indistinct, cannot belong to a single entity, such that one would appear in sensory cognition and the other in conceptual construction; for if that were the case, it would follow that the entity itself is divided. Indeed, there is no division other than that of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

1. *Tulana-ratnanidhi*, p. 55, lines 16–17. 2. Cited from the same work, beginning at line 18: "The *apoha* treatise [states]: 'The distinction between things is not a distinction other than the distinction in appearance; otherwise, the three worlds would be a single entity.'"

Now, one might object: even when there is a difference in clear versus unclear manifestation regarding a single tree located in distant or near places, there is no actual difference in the tree itself, because there is no difference in its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, it is only a difference in manifestation assisted by a difference in causal efficiency that serves as a differentiator. Since there is no such difference in causal efficiency here, how can there be a difference in the object—such as a cow or the like—of the cognitions produced by the sense organ and the word?
If you say this is so, we do not say that a difference in appearance is necessarily restricted to distinct objects;

rather, it is necessarily restricted to the absence of having a single object. For instance, whatever appearance is contrary to the direct perception of a certain object does not have that same object, just as the appearance of a cloth is not the same as the apprehension of a jar, or as [the appearance of blue] is not the same as the apprehension of a conch shell.
It has a yellow appearance. Thus, at the time of conceptualization, the appearance is contrary to the appearance of the direct perception of the cow;

this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For having a single object is pervaded by the non-difference of appearance, as is observed in the case of what is seen by the left and right eyes. If, however, there were no such pervasion, then even another direct perception might have a contrary appearance, [and thus] the thing...

And it would thus possess two forms; yet since neither of those two exists, there is indeed a pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, when cognition arising from distinct substrata is made the subject (*pakṣa*), its opposite—the difference in appearance—is established. Therefore, wherever there is a difference in appearance accompanied by a difference in causal efficiency and so forth, there is a difference in the real entity (*vastu*), as in the case of a jar and a cloth. However, when that auxiliary factor is abandoned, [cognition] necessarily results in having a single object.
One who says that [the cognition] "avoids" [the object] is simply mistaken here; it is merely an erroneous appearance, like the appearance of yellowness in a conch shell.

If you argue that even in that case, the conch shell itself is the object—then it is poorly stated that a cognition which does not touch upon its whiteness has the conch shell as its object. If you say that it cognizes the conch shell alone—that is not so, because nothing beyond that [yellow appearance] flashes forth as the "conch shell alone. [The opponent asks: "What about the back [of the conch]?"...

If it is argued that [the cognition] flashes forth within a future conceptualization (*vikalpa*), let it be so; however, it is not established that the appearance of yellow has the conch-shell as its object when it is free from conceptualization. Likewise, even the perception of a globular form on a distant mountain peak does not have the tree as its object in the absence of specific features such as leaves—which are capable of determining distinctions like *pippala* and so forth; thus, this case is equivalent to the one under discussion. Furthermore, this is because there is an absence of any difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the like.

If the object were not distinct [from its appearance], then even in the case of a single [cognition], should the manifestation of perception not be erroneous, we would say that the manifestation of something else is indeed the error. This same logic applies equally to the appearance of yellow and to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a cow. Now, one might object:
"In some cases, the superimposition (*āropa*) of something occurs due to a certain similarity; however, this is not the case with the manifestation of a conceptual construction."
If it is argued: "A certain mixed form has been perceived even in another birth;
from where, for whom, and by what superimposition does this error arise?"—then this is yet another fault of yours:

that you claim the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is exclusively the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and not the domain of anything else, such that even a cognition lacking an external object cannot be called an error.

However, for us, the point at issue is established simply by the fact that it does not fall within the scope of that [cognition]. If you argue that "it is precisely that which appears otherwise, and therefore it is indeed its object," [we reply]: since there is no entity existing apart from the form presented directly before one's perception, it must be so.
1. *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, p.

55: "In whose [view] does the status of the agent of 'misapprehension' (*anyathākhyāti*) reside? That [object], however, is not apprehended at all; enough of this prolixity. Therefore, it is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
The principle is that there is a manifestation within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, what Vācaspati said— namely, "And even though verbal and perceptual cognitions have real entities as their objects, there is no identity of cognition,
because the distinction between mediacy and immediacy is established through a difference in their causes"— is not pertinent, because a mediate cognition [does not have] a real entity...

Because it cannot be established that [the object] is within the range of sensory perception. As for the distinction in causes based on the state of being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*), its purpose is fulfilled simply by the absence of grasping an object within the range of the sense faculties.

If you argue: "But since you yourself have stated that if [cognition] had a real entity as its object, it would follow that there is no difference between cognitions, therefore, by the very fact of avoiding that consequence, it is established that [cognition] has a real entity as its object; and since there is no other reality, it must have that [entity] as its object"—we say: not so. For, regarding the appearance (*pratibhāsa*)— [12a]

Since you establish pervasion by asserting that [the cognition] does not have that [external object] as its object due to the heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) [of the causes], this reductio (*prasaṅga*) is our own. For us too, this effort is directed precisely toward the disruption of the pervasion. When a difference in appearance is possible, brought about by a difference in the causes, how could there be a pervasion based on having that [object] as its object? And when would even this be appropriate? Or, [how could it be established] merely by the fact of having that as its object, [regarding] the cause—?

A pervading distinction can be demonstrated; however, that does not exist here, because the distinction of causes fulfills its purpose merely through the non-perception of the object itself. Now, if it is argued that this manifestation of difference is possible even from a difference in causes despite the objects being identical, then let the identity of object also be possible for the cognitions of the *gāndhāra* and the sweet (*madhura*) notes.

Since a difference in causes is possible even there, there is confidence in the identity of the object because both the non-conceptual and the conceptual [cognitions] possess the mere apprehension of "fire-ness. But if it is argued that in those cases, there is no apprehension of "being a Gandhāra" or "sweetness" in the two cognitions of those two, alas, what great obstinacy! For this is the result of an absolute difference in causes regarding the single object.

Reassurance will arise again at the end through the mention of the actual object. In the case of doubt regarding a difference in the nature of the cause, there is a mention of a subordinate property such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*). But in the case of absolute [non-existence], it is a property common to all; therefore, the [figure] does not have that [doubt] as its sole object.
Furthermore, there is a persistence of the unreal property of sweetness (*mādhurya*) even in the *gāndhāra* [note].

If it is argued that its sweetness is of a different kind, then even the "fire-ness" attributed to a conceptual construction (vikalpa) would be something else entirely. Furthermore, even when two things are perceived as having the same form, there can be no identity of object between the appearances of their internal attributes, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver;

for the appearance of mother-of-pearl does not have silver as its object, nor does the appearance of silver have mother-of-pearl as its object, even though both are perceived as sharing a common whiteness.

Therefore, just as in the conceptualization of fire, even though the thing itself appears, there is no cognition of the object "donkey" because the subordinate property of "donkey-ness" does not appear; so too, even though the subordinate property of "fire-ness" appears, there is no appearance of another substance because the specific form of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear—this is the logical principle, since the substance "fire" is nothing other than the particular itself. Consequently, there is a difference in the cause of the cognition.
Let there be a distinction between the two appearances; however, it is established that neither of these two appearances has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.
Therefore, it is proven that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words and the like. (Compare *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*, p. 56).

Furthermore, in the section on Apoha (Exclusion), if affirmation and negation were themselves of the nature of exclusion (*apoha*), their very utterance would be impossible. For these two must belong either to a substratum (*dharmin*) or to attributes (*dharma*),
such as "the tree exists or does not exist," or "the tree is blue or not blue."

Among these, the first position is not tenable. For a tree, which is restricted by its existence or non-existence, is denoted by the word "tree. Thus, in the position that it is restricted to existence, the statement "it exists" is redundant, while "it does not exist" is contradictory; in the case of defining it as non-existent, the opposite would apply. Furthermore, upon hearing the word "tree," there is an expectation for both affirmation and negation; therefore, this [referent] denoted by the word "tree" is common to both existence and non-existence.
The principle is that the appearance is not an external tree.

As for the fact that in the *Nyāyadarśana*, the author of the *Tātparyaṭīkā*, having introduced the view that the individual possessing the genus (*jāti*) is the denotable object by his own words, immediately thereafter states: "Nor is it untenable that the word-meaning, which is the genus, is common to both existence and non-existence; for that [genus], in its own nature..."

Even though it is eternal, because it rests upon many individuals scattered across space and time, the universal (jāti) is common to both existence and non-existence, and is thus capable of being connected with "is" and "is not. For the existence of a universal consists in its connection with a present individual, while its non-existence consists in its connection with past and future individuals. Because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) regarding existence and non-existence.

As for the lamentation that [the universal] is either common to all or otherwise established [as non-existent], there is no damage to the present subject by that much; for one who places the burden on the universal (jāti) has themselves admitted that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not denotable. Moreover, since it is expressed by a word prior to the use of words such as "exists" (asti), the universal is indeed denoted by the word as a present individual.

The possible positions are: [the universal] is connected with its instances, or connected with past and future instances, or connected with both, or unconnected. Not even one of these provides a refuge against the clever objections of the opponent. For in the first position, there is a restriction to existence;
in the second, a restriction to non-existence. Even in the third, if it were to have the status of existence or non-existence due to its connection with existing or non-existing instances—

The word *hāra* (necklace) is a mental construct (*manoratha*); likewise, the word should express those very substrata by which its connection with present individuals is designated, as well as those by which its connection with past and future individuals is designated. For otherwise, it would not be expressed as being connected to both sets of individuals.
And that being the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that words such as "exists" (*asti*) would never be employed.

Now, suppose this thought occurs: "That form which is related to both individual instances is indeed expressed by the word; however, there is no cognition of the two types of individuals related to it. For the cognition of one related entity does not necessarily entail the cognition of the other related entity, unlike the case of the cognition of a son and so forth. If this were so, then in the absence of the cognition of the related entities, the relation itself could not be perceived.
Nor is there cognition [of the relation] from that alone;
for, the awareness of a relation residing in two things does not arise from the perception of only one form.
The cognition of the relation occurs only when there is the apprehension of the essential natures of both.
1. *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* (Ṭīkā), p. 684; likewise, *Ratnākaraṇibandhana*, p. 56, lines 11–16, in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*:
"Therefore, just as in reality even a son, when his relationship to his father is not ascertained, is perceived merely as a human being..."

The refutation of the fourth position is as follows: [the opponent argues that] just like a jar, a substance (*vastu*) which is a collection of universals (*sāmānya*) is perceived independently, and thus it is not perceived as having the nature of a universal. Even in that case, since there is no implication of the relata, the non-employment of words such as "exists" (*asti*) is established; for when that independent entity is being determined, the employment of words such as "exists" must occur only through its own presence or absence.

Not [the existence] of another. For even when a relation is established, the application of words such as "exists" does not occur for one thing based on the presence or absence of another related thing. Indeed, even if Maitra is determined to be Caitra’s son, he cannot be said to "exist" or "not exist" in relation to Caitra’s presence or absence; how much less so in the case of a universal that lacks such a relation? The relation in that case is of a different kind.
If one asks: "What kind [of nature] could it be?"—whatever it may be, that which has not ascended to the level of cognition is merely like a non-existent fiction (*asatkalpa*).

Therefore, the application of words such as "is" (*asti*) to that which is perceived as being like an iron rod—[a bare particular]—cannot be logically connected with the existence or non-existence of other things, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, since its own nature (*svarūpa*) has been established as persisting eternally, the word "is" is redundant, and the contradiction with the word "is not" remains as it was.

Therefore, the fact that the appearance in conceptual cognition is common to both existence and non-existence is neither "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) nor is it an absolute certainty for proving an external object. For the fixed determination of objects is pervaded by having a cause; and no cause other than the proof of the existence or non-existence of the object is tenable, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, in the absence of that [cause],...

Since the possession of an object (*viṣayavattā*) does not exist in the absence of its pervader, and is thus restricted precisely to the proof of existence or non-existence, it is pervaded by that [proof];

how then could it subsist in that which contradicts it? Whatever cognition has an appearance common to both existence and non-existence with respect to a certain thing, it does not possess that thing as its object, just as the cognition of a cow does not have a horse as its object. And [the cognition in question] has an appearance common to both existence and non-existence with respect to the external.

"The cognition of the conceptualization of a tree" is an observation of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For that which is incompatible with the establishment of existence or non-existence—which is the pervader of being the object of that [cognition]—is the state of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), which consists in the failure to establish it. Thus, there is indeed the same fault even when speaking of an individual as possessing a genus (*jāti*); if the cognition of the individual is established, whether the genus is additionally perceived or not, there is no escape from that fault.

As for what has been stated by the Kaumārila followers— that because a thing possesses parts (*sabhāgatva*), there is no fault of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), since "treeness" is understood from the word as being undetermined regarding existence or non-existence, and it is then connected with one of those two as apprehended through another word— even in that case, if "treeness" is intended to mean a universal (*jāti*), then it is refuted by the very same critique [of universals]. On the other hand, if it is [meant] as something where difference and non-difference are not yet considered...

In that case, "treeness" is necessarily determined by its presence or absence; and since this has already been indicated by the word [“tree”] itself, what further purpose is served by words such as “exists”?
It might be argued: even though it is so determined, the word has only enjoined the factor of treeness, not the factors of existence or non-existence.

If this is argued, then is the difference between those two parts conceptual or real? If it is conceptual, then [the phrase] "this is a necessary pervasion" (niyamavatī vyāptiḥ) is the final construction [of the argument]. Cf. *Ratnākaranibandhana*, p. 56, ll. 18–21.

It is thus established that verbal cognition, which appears as if directed toward a real entity such as a cow, cannot have a real entity as its object. If it were real, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "tree" and "existent" would be untenable, just as in the case of a jar and a cloth; for the logical principle is that two properties must reside in a single entity.
The refutation of those who hold [the view] that perception is [the sole means of knowledge] will be stated later. The position of both difference and non-difference has also been refuted elsewhere.

As for this argument—that the manner in which words convey their objects is not like that of perception, such that there would be no need for words like "exists" (asti) and so forth as if they were seen [by perception], because the means of valid cognition possess diverse powers—that too has been refuted by the critique of the appearance of distinctness when there is a single object. Therefore, if...

The presentation of an object through direct perception would appear in the same way as it does through verbal expression; and since [the object] does not exist [in that manner], it cannot be said to manifest its own nature. Therefore, this diversity of capacity among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is caused solely by the difference in the way they apprehend the essential nature of the thing, and not by a difference in appearance even when the object is one and the same, because the unity of the object is contradicted by the very difference in those appearances. Thus, this remains established: [The original Sanskrit text: *pratyakṣārthapratipādanaṃ śabdena tadvadevāvabhāsaḥ syāt, abhavaṃśca na tadviṣayakhyāpanaṃ kṣamate | tadasyāpi vicitraśaktitvaṃ pramāṇānāṃ vastusvarūpānubhavādhyavasāyamātrakṛtameva, naikārthatve’pi pratibhāsabhedakṛte, tadbhede ekārthatāyāḥ pramāṇabādhitatvāditi | tasmādavasthitametanna...* [The English translation: The presentation of an object through direct perception would appear in the same way as it does through verbal expression; and since [the object] does not exist [in that manner], it cannot be said to manifest its own nature. Therefore, this diversity of capacity among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is caused solely by the difference in the way they apprehend the essential nature of the thing, and not by a difference in appearance even when the object is one and the same, because the unity of the object is contradicted by the very difference in those appearances. Thus, this remains established: (Note: The final portion of the provided text appears to be an incomplete sentence or a transition to another argument.)

If one expresses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), affirmation and negation would be impossible; thus, the employment of further words would be redundant. Nor [is it possible] for the properties (*dharmas*); for since the subject is presented in its entirety by the word "tree"—just as in the case of perception—what room is there for another word to effect the affirmation or negation of qualities such as blueness, or for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to do so? This is true even in the case of perception.

If it is argued that dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is observed [in the case of conceptual construction], let it be so; however, this applies only to that [conceptual construction] whose object is an unpracticed nature, because it is itself non-ascertaining (*aniścayātmaka*). But as for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is itself of the nature of ascertainment (*niścayātmaka*), what need is there for anything else when it grasps its object? Furthermore, there is indeed dependence on words, logical marks (*liṅga*), and other factors. Therefore, there is no apprehension of the actual nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*), but rather only the experience of the arising of a conceptual construction that imitates the shadow of a single property (*ekadharmacchāyā*).
It is established. It is not established, for properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from one another and from the substratum (*dharmin*).
Thus, even when the tree is cognized by means of the single property of genus, there is no cognition of it as possessing other properties;
therefore, why should the comprehension of other properties—such as being blue, moving, or very high—not depend upon distinct designations?

That is incorrect; for if, despite the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) through its difference [from others], there were no cognition of its properties (*dharma*) by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), then let it not be so by means of the sense organs either. Now, if it is argued that—by virtue of the power of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) on the part of the sense organ—the properties that participate in the contact of inherence and so forth also become objects of cognition when the substratum is in proximity, then this same [power] belongs to the logical mark as well.

The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed not deficient even by a fraction. Now, although for a word there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) with its denoted object (*vācya*), a proximity characterized by the relation of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is certainly accepted; for in the absence of that, the consequence would be the non-existence of the cognition of the denoted object itself.

Or, once the cognition has occurred, what need is there for conjunction and the like? And this [is true] even for those who rely on a natural relationship (*svābhāvikasaṃbandha*), as in the case of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

It is the same regarding the cognition of the object (*vastu*). Nor is there any suspicion of an intervention that would obstruct the basis for activity (*pravṛttinimitta*) when cognition occurs through the medium of a word;

for according to you, the individual (*vyakti*) as possessing the universal (*jāti*) is apprehended from the word all at once. If, however, there were a sequential awakening of each [element] one by one, the cognition of the individual as possessing the universal would never occur. Furthermore, no sequence of certainty is ever perceived. Therefore, let the universal be cognized as something additional.

Indeed, when an individual (*vyakti*) is perceived as the locus of attributes (*dharmin*), it cannot attain its own stability without conveying the qualities, actions, and so forth inherent within it. Otherwise, even in the case of perception, the cognition of other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) would be without a basis. [From the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*:
If this is the case, one might ask: let there simply be the communication of the individual by the word; what is the point of accepting its association with limiting adjuncts?

In that case, must entities now abandon their intrinsic nature out of fear that your own position would be rendered futile? Let this other fault of yours remain, whether it exists or not; however, one cannot remain without first establishing the cognition of things related to an object through the means of knowledge, just as in the case of the sense organs. If you argue that such a thing is observed to happen only with the sense organs and thus there is no such consequence for anything else?

If that were the case, then since grass-fire has been observed to be capable of producing smoke as an inseparable concomitant of the process of transforming its fuel, a fire of *khadira* wood would not be so [capable]. However, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists generally in both cases, there is no distinction. Therefore, if there is an absence of transformation in the *khadira* wood, then that is not smoke at all, but rather a mass of dust stirred up by the wind; nor is there a fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) there.

However, suppose there were a towering mass of rays from a heap of radiant ruby jewels; if that were smoke, and if that were fire, then there would necessarily be a transformation in the *khadira* wood. Likewise, if this is the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) and the word is its means of proof (*sādhana*), then there is inevitably the fault of cognizing a property (*dharma*) that resides in that [subject]. If, on the other hand, there is no cognition of a property residing in that [subject], then it is neither a cognition of the subject nor [is it a valid proof].

A word is that which makes known its own substratum (*dharmin*). Whatever is a means of cognition is necessarily a means for the cognition of its own properties, just as a sense-organ is. Furthermore, both the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and the word are occupied with being means for the cognition of that which is intended to be beyond perception; such is their essential nature (*svabhāva*), which serves as a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) reason.
But this is not the case [for the word], because the word requires another inferential mark. That which is not a means for making known the properties inherent in something else is not [that thing].

That [cognition] generates knowledge of its own intrinsic nature; for example, the word "cow" does not cause the cognition of a horse, nor does a horse cause the cognition of a donkey, and neither the *godhūli* (dust at sunset) nor smoke causes the cognition of their own respective subjects as possessing some other property inherent in them. Thus, in the case of the contrary [position], there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Since there is no possibility of perceiving something devoid of genus, quality, action, and so forth even in a dream, the perception of a non-existent thing [occurs] through a cognition of another property that arises from the mere existence of that [non-existent thing].
Thus, in both applications [of the reason], there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). For the dispute regarding universals (*jāti*) and so forth concerns only their difference.

As for the term "inherent" (*samaveta*), even on the view of non-difference, it refers to the fact that things appearing as distinct in a conceptual cognition (*kalpanābuddhi*) do not manifest separately. Therefore, let there simply be non-difference among the properties (*dharma*); for if the cognition of the entity itself is admitted in every respect, the cognition of the properties [is necessarily included].

Since the objection is difficult to avoid, what is the point of accepting a distinction that contradicts experience? Universals (*jāti*) and so forth are simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity.
As for the statement by Bhūṣaṇa—that "that which is related to a nature is not itself the nature"—if that were the case, then [the universal] would be unrelated [to the entity].

"You yourself [have said] that it is not the case that a thing is established by itself. That is incorrect. In the very expression "essential nature relation" (*svabhāvasambandha*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*) intended is that of some entity, and there is no difference between the two. For if there were a difference, the claim that one is the essential nature of the other would be unworldly.

How then can you avoid the objection that "that very thing is related to itself"? Otherwise, the use of the genitive case in the expression "this is its essential nature" (*asya svabhāvaḥ*) would be untenable.

[This is] because it follows [from the opponent's own position]. Now, if it is argued that there is no fault at all because "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers precisely to the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, when one reflects upon the intrinsic nature of the mere thing (*vastumātra*) after having analytically separated out the universal and the rest—then indeed, this [nature] cannot be said not to be the intrinsic nature of the thing alone.
And that very [nature] is what is intended by the phrase "that which is related to an intrinsic nature," since by the word "related" (*saṃbandhin*), the universal and the rest are intended.
The Chapter on Apoha:

Therefore, since that which is not different [from another] is nevertheless shown as distinct through conceptual construction, the conventional usage that "this is related to that" is difficult to avoid.

And as for what Vācaspati [says]: "When this [substance] qualified by one adjunct, namely existence (*sattva*), has been apprehended, there is no apprehension of it as qualified by another adjunct; for it is the nature (*svabhāva*) of the substance that is qualified by the adjunct, but the adjuncts or its state of being the qualificand are not its nature"—that too is indeed floating away. For the apprehension of another adjunct was not attributed [to the cognition] on account of non-difference (*abheda*); even in the authoritative treatise (*ākara*)...

For, by prioritizing a distinction based on the gateway of causal efficacy (*kāryopakāra*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving all aspects [of the object]. However, it has been stated that there is no difference between powers (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*); thus, even this [objection] has not touched upon our position. Furthermore, as for the refutation offered there by Bhūṣaṇa—namely, that the perception of the sun and so forth would entail the perception of the entire mass of things that are benefited by them—[this too is irrelevant].
