That which was stated is the result of not having fathomed his intention; for this is the underlying point: having yourself established the refutation of inherence (*samavāya*) that you will later state, you, the preeminent Naiyāyika, maintain that at the time of perception, when the connection with the sense organ occurs in the substrate (*dharmin*), there is a cognition of the properties (*dharma*) such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth precisely through their being assisted [by it], because the power that assists them is non-different [from the substrate], despite the admission of a difference between them.

It must be so; for there is no restriction whatsoever upon anything that possesses distinction if it provides no assistance. Thus, by way of establishing the non-difference of capacities, he says: "If those [capacities for the assistance of the property] were distinct, what would they do for it?"
There would be no benefit from them, and likewise, there would be an infinite regress.
[Pravā.

3.53] Thus it is said. As for the claim that "capacity" (*śakti*)—whether innate, natural, or adventitious—is distinct from the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*), and that this [completeness] is the objective basis [of cognition], that has been refuted. In the chapter on Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*), it was established that capacity is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing as it engages in causal activity.

This has been refuted. Furthermore, the claim that assistance—whose nature is the production of a common effect—is possible even for that which has no effect, has also been demolished in that very same context.

In reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between the "effect" (kārya) and the "beneficiary" (upakārya). However, in conventional usage, "effect-hood" (kāryatā) is attributed to the production of something previously non-existent through the process of affirmation and negation. But in the case of what was previously conceived as the object [of an action], "beneficiary-hood" (upakāryatā) is asserted due to the experience of a specific change. Yet, in ultimate reality:

To say that something is both "previously situated" and "now distinguished" is indeed contradictory. Therefore, when considering this matter from the perspective of a genus (*jāti*) held to be stable, the conventional usage of being "benefited" (*upakārya*) rests solely upon the state of being an effect; whether this is in reality due to a single essence (*ekārthatā*) or otherwise, there is no fault. Thus, since proximity characterized as "benefit" must necessarily be accepted, there is no deviation from experience regarding those things benefited by the sun and so forth.
[14b] What follows by implication is common to both of us.

1. Compare *Ratnākaranibandhana*, p. 57, ll. 16–19; 2. Compare *Ratnākaranibandhana*, p. 57, l. 23. In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, Vācaspati states: "And the natural relation between an individual and its universal does not depend upon any assistance."

In this context, what is called "intrinsic" (svābhāvika) is not some relation distinct from those well-known [types] such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth; rather, it is merely a conventional distinction based on the fact that, while the existence of conjunction and the like is subject to deviation or non-deviation regarding the related terms, there is a difference in their mode of occurrence. This is designated as "intrinsic" and "extrinsic" (aupādhika) only by way of definition. An investigation into this matter should be sought in the discussion on pervasion (vyāpti). And just as...

Just as there is an innate relationship between the individual and the universal because the former is never found apart from the latter, so too there is an innate relationship between the universal and the individual for the very same reason of non-deviation;
for without particulars, a universal could not exist, being like the horn of a hare.
According to this principle, since there is no other proximity between these two [the universal and the particular], and since inherence (*samavāya*) is a mere conceptual construction,

even if there were a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary— as in the case of water and seeds— the rule of non-deviation would be untenable for those addicted to the admission of difference, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For in the case of a benefit, it must be either the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a specific quality thereof.
The phrase "inseparable from that" (tannāntarīyaka) alone serves the purpose of non-deviation; it does not mean "only there," and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, if that [inseparability] were absent, there would be two ways to avoid that [over-extension]: by resorting to the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) or the power of inherence (*samavāyabala*). The first position is not tenable, because it would entail the subversion of any perceived capacity whatsoever in any given case. For instance, a perceived efficacy is seen in fire, artisans, water, and so forth.

The non-deviation [of smoke] from the fire-pot, the crane, and the deity is due solely to the dependence upon time, place, and so forth; this is the distinction. Thus, by asserting that even when there is difference, non-deviation arises from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone and not from causal efficacy (*upakāra*), one has necessarily excluded [the necessity of] capacity. Furthermore, the second position is impossible, because *samavāya* (inherence) itself does not exist. For *samavāya* is accepted as being established by the cognition "this is here."

That cognition has already been refuted; moreover, it cannot be accepted by those whose vision is clouded by the mass of darkness consisting of the grasping of conventional designations (*saṃketagraha*), because that would entail the absurd consequence of everyone achieving all their goals. This is because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise under the sole control of mere desire. Furthermore, for other people, that cognition does not exist at all regarding any point of dispute, due to the absence of its cause: namely, the two things whose forms are unmixed with one another.

For manifestation is the cause of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that discriminates between the meanings of the locative and nominative cases, thinking "this [manifestation] is the cause here";
this is because, even when water is present in a jar, for one who perceives only the jar, that manifestation is absent despite the presence of the entire collection of other causes.

Furthermore, for one in such a state, [the cognition] occurs subsequently merely upon the perception of the second [object]. And since that appearance of duality does not exist anywhere in the domain of *samavāya* (inherence), the object of that conceptualization is precisely the domain of the conceptualization of *saṃyoga* (conjunction). For one who is not insane, there is no cognition of "this is here" where both [objects] are not perceived while excluding their non-self-nature, as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit.

[The reason is] the non-perception of the concomitant. Furthermore, there is no experience of the universal and its possessor through a distinction in the appearance of the forms of "self" and "belonging to self";
thus, there is a non-perception of the cause. Since the causal relationship between the two intended [terms] is established—just like smoke and fire—there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, those who by means of the word *svayaṃkṛta* (self-made) postulate a different meaning are merely following the track of a horse's scale; this very point he will state [later].
The chapter on Apoha; and these words such as "the cloth is here in the threads" are themselves composed by [Dignāga]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.149)

Thus [it is said]. Now, it has been stated that even an object consisting of two natures is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition; how then is it not the case that there is an appearance of two natures? Therefore, the non-perception of the cause is unestablished. This is a most wretched argument. For regarding an object accessible through direct perception, the instruction of another is not authoritative. If you argue that the appearance is likewise [non-dual], then this follows: [15a]...
While these five fingers are clearly manifest in direct perception,
he who perceives a sixth finger here as common to them all is like one who sees a horn upon his own head.

Thus [it is said]. For we, possessing only the physical eye (*carmacakṣus*), even though we open our eyes very wide and examine [the matter] a hundred times, do not perceive anything else; whereas for you, through the grace of a deity unseen by others, such an appearance may indeed occur, yet for another person, the establishment of such a cognition does not occur in that way.
Therefore, one who declares that "only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is to be seen—that which, being one, reveals itself to many observers as common to all"—[is speaking thus].

It appears that even Trilocana views [the universal] as if with another eye; for he says: "Even though a genus (*jāti*) is perceived, because it does not exist in a location separate from the individual (*vyakti*), it is not seen as distinct from the individual, unlike one individual from another. In this statement, by saying "the genus is seen, but not as distinct," he implies that it is necessarily within the range of perception as non-distinct. And just as it is grasped by perception...

The entire object belongs to you alone; indeed, there is no application therein of either a sublater (*bādhaka*) or a prover (*sādhaka*). Consequently, the description of the justification—that the persistence of the cognition (*pratyayānuvṛtti*) will differentiate the universal from the individual—is without foundation. Furthermore, it is not rightly said that a tactile cognition differentiates touch from smell and so forth; for there is no [cognition] that grasps even the non-difference between smell and touch.
[Objection: It is perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*). [Response: In that case, let it be explained that "it is not seen as distinct" means "it is not determined as distinct.
Even so, when it is said that "the universal (*jāti*) is being seen," is it intended [to be seen] as distinct or as non-distinct? If it is as non-distinct, then there is determination (*vyavasāya*).

Let it be either through difference or non-difference; what is the use of considering this, since non-difference is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Or, is it intended that [the object] is seen as different? That, moreover, is impossible, because the absence of a difference in appearance has already been stated. If you say that the difference in appearance is established by reasoning (*yukti*), then this is shameful; for:
"That which does not appear [to someone] is established by means of what appears to another;
that 'this appears to him' or 'this does not appear to him' is not within the scope of logical proof."
1. "It is not established by means of logical arguments"—this is the reading found in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* [Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya, pū:
111], in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.
This has been analyzed by us in the section on the absence of causeless existence.

Furthermore, if it is admitted that even when there is an appearance of a single form, another appearance can be established through reasoning, then the statement "fire is not hot" would not be sublated by perception, because an appearance of non-heat is also possible there in individual instances.
[It is] like the appearance of [the universal] *jāti*.

If it is argued that there is no parity because there is no proof for the appearance of non-heat in fire (*citrabhānu*), even so, let there be doubt; how then can perception be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the non-heat, and how can there be an absence of proof, given the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*)?

If you argue that the reason (*hetu*) is non-deviant because [the property] exists, then even deviation occurs either directly or indirectly through perception itself; and it has already been stated that in such cases, a contrary appearance cannot be negated. Furthermore, if the proof of non-hotness is not established due to the defect of the reason—namely, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*)—then the observation that "fire is not hot" would not be valid.

This is a flaw in the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), because it is not sublated by the fact of [fire] being non-hot. Nor is the proof (*sādhana*) perception (*adhyakṣa*). For that which is hot is simply hot; it is not both hot and non-hot. Therefore, even one who is unwilling must admit that the experience of a determinate appearance necessarily sublates the appearance of anything else; otherwise, there would result a confusion of practical activity (*pravṛtti-saṅkara*). And thus:
For it is not as if one sees this fire, and so forth. Therefore,
that which is asserted by those fallen into the flood— that when a convention is made regarding individuals possessing a genus (*jāti*), then wherever there is the perception of the genus,
there is the cognition of its being denotable by that word— this merely mocks the empty sky, for [the genus] is distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because [the relation] is not perceived even in a dream. For this very reason, that which was previously asserted—the claim that conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) possesses validity because it joins the substrate (*upādhi*) and the possessor of the substrate (*upādhimat*) when they are grasped in their mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*)—is refuted, since there is an absence of the perception of both [related entities]. Therefore, the non-apprehension of the cause is not unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, what is the news regarding "inherence" (*samavāya*), given that there is no such cognition as "it is here"? And this [notion] of the manifestation [of an individual] by means of the universal (*jāti*) is baseless.

Is it an essential (svābhāvika) relation? And thus, even if the proponent of difference between the limiting adjunct (upādhi) and its possessor (tadvat) is difficult to avoid, then even in the case of proximity characterized by assistance (upakāra), since only that which occupies the same location is perceived, the capacity of the perceiver of the object remains the same; therefore, the avoidance of deviation regarding subtle things that provide assistance is identical.

Therefore, since the nature of the entity is cognized in its entirety even through the medium of a single property, what room is there for affirmation or negation by means of another word? Why, then, persist in using the mere word "tree" alone? Consequently, what basis is there for the determination of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), or the distinction between the universal and the particular? However, when...

When there is a dissolution of a pun based on a single meaning, either a single suggestion (dhvani) operates, or else it is a mere indicative mark (liṅga); for you, there is no expressed entity whatsoever that remains distinct.
In this chapter on Apoha,
by the denotation of which there occurs a comprehensive understanding through the power of the thing itself,
a word thus possesses various fruits while having a single substratum.

[Pravāṇavāda 3.128–30] For when a real entity (*vastu*) is the object of expression, it is impossible to establish either its affirmation or its negation in its entirety. However, when— due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the beginningless habituation to false conceptual constructions— a cognition itself, characterized by the form of the exclusion of one thing, arises from the awakening of certain latent impressions...
When [the cognition] attains its arising, then what room is there for the aforementioned defects, which would otherwise exist if there were no capacity to grasp the actual object?

For instance, when "tree" is uttered, by virtue of the appearance of a form common to the *dhava*, *khadira*, and other species, the universal (*sāmānya*)— which has the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣāpoha*) as its ultimate reality— is [perceived].

It is established that this form [of the object], because it possesses distinctions such as being non-rejected, non-appropriated, existent, and substantial, depends upon the employment of other words; thus, within a single substratum (dharmin), there occurs grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with words such as "existent," "blue," or "moving"— which function like the basis for other attributes— and furthermore, in accordance with the requirements of cognition, when there is a need to indicate a specific distinction, there is a designation of difference such as "the existence of the tree."

The relationship between qualifier and qualified is established in both ways. This being so, just as in the case of a tree, increase and decrease are observed through contact with water and fire, and because of the superimposition of identity, there arises the cognition: "This very same tree has become like this";

and even though there is no arising of those properties that are capable of such connection, the tree is determined as if it were connected to them—so too it is in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even when other properties do not appear, that which has the form of a tree is perceived as being capable of such [a cognition]; and in such formulations as "the blue is not fruit-bearing," that very same entity appears as if undergoing increase and decrease, and is determined to be so. An external object, however, does not undergo increase and decrease even at the time of the utterance of a word, as it does when in contact with water and the like. And this [phenomenon] would not be tenable if the object were external, since it occurs exactly as it appears.

Because [the referent] is identical with itself, and because it does not appear as having the nature of its qualifiers; for this very reason, even in relation to distinct qualifiers— as in "Caitra has a cow" or "Maitra has no horse"—
there is no occasion for the employment of another word, since there is no external appearance of increase or decrease produced by those qualifiers.

Therefore, this is merely a play of the intellect (*buddhilāsa*). In cases where such a confusion occurs through a traditional lineage that is invariably connected to a reality excluded from others (*paramapohita-vastu*), people who have achieved their desired purposeful action do not exert effort to infer such a specific distinction, nor are they capable of doing so; thus, worldly practice remains uninterrupted. Even when there is a discrepancy, they do not establish that "this is false," nor do they do so at any other time.

Since even the authors of the treatises maintain that external objects are not the domain [of words], what need is there to mention others? Therefore, it is established that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not within the range of words and the like.
Having apprehended a single substratum as the locus of various excluded properties,
this primary cognition— which appears to involve effort and expenditure in the process of establishing or negating each one— deludes people just as they themselves are being deluded.
"Having attained fulfillment through the aspect of reality (*tattva*), one does not regard even the boat as [something to be clung to]. Having said this,
[the author] concludes with this summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*.

Nor [is it] the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For instance, in the sentence "Cows are grazing on the northern bank of the river," from words such as "cow" (*go*), there appear the dewlap, horns, tail-hair, and so forth—surrounded by the forms of the syllables—as if they were almost unified because there is no reflection upon their internal differences; yet that itself is not the universal.
For it is said that "cowness" (*gotva*) is empty of color, shape, syllables, and form (PV 2.147).
Yet nothing else appears [in its place], like space; otherwise, there would be no distinction between the conceptual constructions of "cowness" and "horseness."

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). For that very thing, which consists merely of a blazing and radiant form, though entirely distinct from all individual manifestations (*vyakti*), is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) when it is unified with them by means of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It is not, however, the universal itself that is the cause of their mutual conformity, because [the universal] exists elsewhere as a form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*).
Indeed, the treatise states:

And how could that which is non-different from cognition proceed as a distinct object? Furthermore, in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is it," "this is like that," or "this is a cow"—which arises immediately after sensory perception and is intended to be produced by the sense organ and the object—there is no appearance of a distinct object. Rather, it is as if a unified, non-empirical form appears within the self.
One joins [the notion of "pot"] to a mass appearing before one; likewise, because that external object does not exist, this is merely an error, like the appearance of [illusory] hair.

If it is argued that this is so because of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), [we reply: surely, in the case of a mass of hair, there is no such subversion, since there is no resistance when one extends the hand with effort and so forth.

There is a contradiction; however, in the present case, if there is a sublater, that very experience of the manifestation of the manifestor is the sublater—what is the use of anything else? It has already been stated that it is simply the incapacity of people to discern [the truth]. Or how is it that the absence of resistance by the hand and so forth is still not a sublater? For those very horns and such things, when situated in their proper places, are of indistinct form and have no established location or state.

Particulars, possessing infinite forms due to distinctions of place, time, and so forth, appear even today as if they were intermingled; since these are subject to fixed constraints such as resistance, what kind of distinction could there be between them and hair and the like, such that one might claim there is no sublation here?

Therefore, let this be merely an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of the intellect itself in that form through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), or rather, let that form be simply non-existent.
Or let it be known that the individuals themselves appear otherwise by means of the exclusion of dissimilar differences;
[this is] the *Apohaprakaraṇa*, page 58, lines 1–4, of the *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā* (Commentary on the *Tattvasaṃgraha*), based on the *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*.
Or let it be called a lapse of memory; in any case, this report of a "universal" (sāmānya) with respect to an external object is nothing but an error.

Furthermore, since it arises from the experience of an object present before one as "this," it ought to be [considered] valid. Now, the causes of error—such as cataracts, rapid motion, or spinning—which produce a distortion of the sense organs, have indeed been enumerated; yet not even one of these is present here.

How can this error be accidental? Or do you think that those [causes] belong only to non-conceptual error, while this is a mental error? Even that [mental error] is based solely on the perception of similarity between the superimposed object and the locus of superimposition;
thus, since there is no distinction from that [non-conceptual error], how can even a mental error exist? Indeed, every error is based solely on similarity.

Indeed, it cannot possibly occur even in another birth without the perception of something similar; and since nothing with a mixed form has ever been seen even in another birth, how could there be such a superimposition? Oh, what great human prowess! For instance, if its lack of an objective basis cannot be avoided by the method already stated, then whether it produces the conventional usage of error or not, that much alone [is sufficient].
Since the point is already established by the nature of things (*prakṛtisiddhi*), why this insistence here?

Furthermore, that which was stated regarding its being "accidental" (*ākasmikatva*) is incorrect, because even you must necessarily admit a difference in the causal complex (*janakasāmagrībheda*). Otherwise, how could the sense organ and the object—which are observed to be restricted to producing non-conceptual cognition—produce conceptualization?

Does it produce [the conceptualization] by itself? Therefore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), its capacity being augmented by the recollection of the previous perception of the object-mass, produces a conceptualization;

thus, it indeed produces a cognition that is without an external object (*nirviṣaya*), because the nature of conceptualization is established as being objectless with respect to that [perceived] portion. Consequently, it is better [to hold) that [the conceptualization] is indeed distinct from the experience which has a vivid appearance, just like a conceptualization of a different class.
It is better to say that even the conceptualization of a similar class [is not established]; therefore, the establishment of a universal (*jāti*) does not occur through perception.

Nor does it occur through inference, because—just as in the case of fire and smoke—it is impossible for anyone to grasp a causal relationship solely on the basis of what falls within the scope of perception. Rather, regarding the production of cognition in general, there must be another cause [beyond] those causes already observed.

That which is to be depended upon, like a sense faculty, might sometimes be established if one could demonstrate the absence of the intended effect—namely, cognition—at a time when all other causes are present. However, this is not possible in the case at hand. For when one would show the absence of the cognition of "cow" either in another individual body or in the interval between them, that absence of the cognition of "cow" is accounted for simply by the absence of the individual cow-body itself.
How could it imply dependence on another entity such that there might be the expectation, "This is indeed that very cowness"?

[Objection: But surely, the term "cow-body" [is applied] precisely because of the universal *gotva* (cowness); otherwise, even a horse-body would be a cow-body. [Reply: If this is so, then the universal *gotva* must also [be derived] from the cow-body itself; otherwise, even horseness (*turagatva*) would be cowness. This is the same [logical difficulty]. It is not [the case that one is primary].

Furthermore, it is not possible to ascertain the existence or non-existence of an invisible universal anywhere, just as one cannot ascertain such things regarding a physical body; therefore, this argument amounts to nothing.

Now, it might be argued that if there were no cognition of "cow" in a horse due to the absence of the Bāhuleya individual, then there should likewise be no such cognition in a Śābaleya [individual], since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not persist anywhere. It is true that the particular characteristic does not persist; however, just as it [persists] within its own class—

In a cognizer who possesses the memory of perceiving other individual cows (*piṇḍa*), the capacity to produce a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of that form exists equally for Bāhuleya and for Śābaleya as well. Therefore, it is not just a single cow-individual, but rather all such [individuals] that ascend into conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
[These are] the clusters. Therefore, there is no cognition of "cow" with respect to a horse.

But surely, capacity (*sāmarthya*) is power (*śakti*), and thus it is the universal (*jāti*) itself that is being spoken of. For is that power distinct from [the individual] or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, then, like the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would not be inclusive; thus, nothing else would be capable [of producing the cognition]. Now, if it is distinct—another...

And if it is common, then there is a dispute only over the name, as it is simply "jāti" (universal). To this it is replied: That [jāti] is indeed non-different with respect to each individual object; for if one entity possesses a nature capable [of producing effects], what kind of fault does another entity that exists in the same way bring about? For according to you, even though the *jāti* is one, it is the cause for the production of uniform cognition and verbal expression, while the other [the individual] is likewise so by its own nature.

Because there is no absence of other types [of causes], so too for us, the individual (vyakti) is also an independent cause by its very nature, even though it is distinct. That nature of the individual, however, is constrained by a succession of causes.
As for what Trilocana says—that the inherence (samavāya) of universals and particulars, such as "horseness" and "cowness," resides in their own substrata—[that is not the case].
The claim that "the universal (sāmānya) is the cause of the designation and the cognition" has already been set aside by the refutation of inherence (samavāya).

Alternatively, if inherence itself is the cause by its very nature, there is no damage to the illustrative example. Furthermore, it is not the case that the universal and inherence possess mutual causal power through the postulation of their acting together; for in that case, even a single entity would be a producer by its own nature, which would mean [the universal] is not a universal.

A funeral libation has been offered to the theories of [inherence as] denotation and cognition; for since the capacity of seeds and other causes to produce their own forms depends solely on the presence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), their productivity by way of their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) must necessarily be asserted—thus, reliance upon inherence (*samavāya*) is a mere mockery. Nor does the arising of a cognition with that form occur from other causes alone in the absence of the operation of that [inherence]; otherwise, [the following would occur]:...

Even if one considers why there is no production [of the universal] through its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) when a recurring cognition arises—even for that which has a circular form—such a reflection would utterly uproot the theory of the universal (*jāti*). Furthermore, even if the universal were held to be accidental (*āakasmika*), that same fault would apply. Thus, for one who accepts the universal because it is pressed upon them by the "noose around the neck" (the aforementioned fault), the universal itself must perform its function within the recurring cognition in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), without being superimposed, out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that individuals belonging to other classes must be accepted [as denotable], how can this be resolved by means of inherence (*samavāya*)? Furthermore, whether that [inherence] acts as an auxiliary factor or not, the universal (*jāti*), being independent of the individual and possessing its own inherent capacity by its very nature, produces the recurring cognition;
for since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be questioned, it cannot be stated—without the command of kings—that it is the individual [that does so].

By this, his attempt at reasoning—namely, "How can this recurrence of cognition, which follows a recurring entity, be possible in the case of individuals that are absolutely distinct and which follow the state of being objects of exclusionary cognition?"—is also refuted;
for there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of universals (*jāti*), which, though mutually distinct, are perceived as recurring through a recurring cognition. Now, if...

If it is argued that since universals (*jāti*) are not perceived, how can there be a recurring cognition, and therefore there is a deviation [from the rule]? No, because this would contradict your own tenet.
(Compare *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*, p. 58, l. 20–25, *Apohaprakaraṇam*).
Because it is established by this sequence: for indeed, the recurrence of a cognition is adduced to prove the existence of a recurring entity;

and that [recurrence] is inseparable from the absence of a recurring entity if there is no establishment of a recurring entity—who, other than one possessed of dullness, is able to bear this contradiction? Furthermore, the fallacy of deviation remains exactly as it was even regarding imagined universals (*jāti*); what more is there to say here?
[Is it] by perception?

Now, if a restriction is stated regarding objects currently being perceived—no, because even there, due to the absence of a subverting cognition that contradicts the contrary, a necessary connection (pratibandha) is untenable. Furthermore, since deviation is observed in general, there is a seed of doubt regarding other cases as well. And if...

The avoidance of the fallacy of deviation from the universal is made in relation to specific visible objects; in that case, one should not say: "That recurrence of designation and cognition among distinct things is caused by a recurring entity, just as the recurrence of designation and cognition as 'thread' occurs among flowers, so too the recurrence of designation and cognition as 'cow' occurs among distinct cows. For [the recurrence of] designation is based solely on a visible cause.

Because the persistence of the conceptual cognition (*pratyaya*) is pervaded by its being based on a persistent object, there is a rule regarding its coming to rest. And this is logical; for indeed, even in the case of a sutra, the persistence of the conceptual cognition of the sutra does not occur with respect to things that have not been made objects of vision. Since conceptualization, when accompanied by an object, is established as having the effect of seeing the object—apart from inference—it follows that, by the non-perception of the cause through the method of contraposition (*viparyaya*), the persisting [conceptualization] is negated.
The pervasion of the recurrence of designations and cognitions by an entity rests solely upon the fact that they have a perceptible cause, provided that they have an entity as their object;
however, this rule does not hold when there is a dispute regarding the fact that they have an entity as their object.
Furthermore, as for the sublation of the contrary argument stated by him—that the recurrence of designations and cognitions ceases from something...

"In some cases, [the cognition] arises as having a cause, and there is no other cause," and so forth. That is not correct, because it has already been established that the continuity of denotation and cognition occurs even without a recurring [universal], due to the necessity of accepting a specific nature [defined as] "exclusion of what is not of that form" (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*). Therefore, just as the universal "cowness" or "horseness" exists precisely by excluding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal...
The persistence of verbal designation and cognition occurs through some form of proximity; let it be the same for individuals as well.

By this, when the persistence of verbal designation and cognition is to be proven regarding a recurring entity, both [the reason and the example] are to be understood as inconclusive—since the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) serves as the subverter of the contrary (*viparyayabādhikā*) in establishing its pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, even "proximity" does not exist...

It is not distinct from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For just as "cowness" is excluded from the generality of "horseness," so too are "horseness," "substancehood," and the like; and just as one individual cow is excluded from what is non-cow, so it is with this [exclusion] as well. Regarding the verbal prolixity concerning its difference or non-difference, the answer is the same as in the case of "capacity" (*śakti*). Consequently, those objects which are mutually proximate through their exclusion from what is not themselves—

Immediately after the perception of one among them, the others produce a continuous cognition; it is this very capacity that does so, not a universal essence (*jāti*). Otherwise, since that [universal] would exist even in a single instance, auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) would be useless.
[Pravā.

3.164] This is to be understood from the *Sahakārivāda* in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). And that proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is a causal succession (*kāraṇaparamparā*).

The phrase "yāte" (having gone) has been explained immediately above. Furthermore, a specific causal proximity must necessarily be admitted, because only certain individuals serve as the substratum for a universal, while others do not. Otherwise, if it were otherwise, the statement that "the effect possesses a restricted universal due to the restriction of the causal complex" would provide no defense for the *Bhūṣaṇa*.
And this being the case,
what is the use of a genus here?
For when the difference is equal, it is by virtue of some proximity that a genus extends [to certain things].
Or rather, let that very [form] alone be the basis for the cognition of the word, and nothing else.

[Pravāraṇāvāda 3.161–2] Furthermore, regarding what was stated by him here— “Another effort has been made elsewhere: for it is not the case that, by whatever proximity a staff, a thread, or the like extends to a certain place and not elsewhere, that very same proximity [would account for] the state of being a ‘staff-bearer’ or a ‘threaded [crystal]’ in the case of a person, a crystal, and so forth” — [it is refuted as follows:]...

"Let there be a basis for conventional usage; what is the need for a staff, a string, and so forth? When would this be appropriate? Only if some capacity established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) were to be denied in some instance. For instance, the proximity of a staff or a string to a person—which depends on causes such as the cognition of approaching—is established by perception and other means of knowledge as the cause for the [staff or string] appearing in the person, just as it is in a crystal; and likewise, the appearance of the person or the crystal [in the staff or string] which is conjoined with them—

Furthermore, for a cognizer who possesses the recollection of convention (*samaya*), the cognition of "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is established as being based on the Buddha [the staff]; likewise, this cognition of "cow" is not observed to follow the presence or absence of the entity "cowness" (*gotva*). Rather, it is merely like groping in the dark with one's hands, thinking, "There must be some such basis for the cognition of 'cow'. In that case, if by some other means that must necessarily be accepted...

If that is established, why is it said that there is no sublation [of the claim], and what is the use of this more cumbersome conceptualization? Otherwise, having imagined even that, one could not avoid imagining hundreds of useless things. However, if—as is observed in the case of a person and so forth—the proximity of a staff and such is seen to conform to the presence or absence of the cause of approach and so on, and it is also observed in the case of a person and so forth that [the proximity] follows upon the proximity of the staff and such—

The cognition of "staff-bearer" and the like conforms to the existence, non-existence, or absence of the staff; likewise, the function of the causal complex consists solely in the restriction of the genus (*jāti*) itself, and not in the unifying reflective awareness (*ekāmarśa*). If it were the case that this genus itself were experienced as possessing the function during that unifying awareness, then the fault would belong to one who denies it, since this [genus] is merely a conventional designation (*samaya*) established by demonstrating that it transcends actual experience.
Thus, how could that [objection] regarding its futility possibly apply even to the staff and so forth? In this manner, one should infer the refutation for other similar cases as well.
1. Cf. *Ratnākara-nibandhana*, p. 59, lines 9–17.

Now, the inference is as follows: whatever is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇagrahaṇa*), just like the cognition of a man with a staff (*daṇḍijñāna*). And this cognition "this is a cow" is indeed a qualified cognition; thus, by implication, it is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). For in the example, the qualified cognition is established as the effect of the experience of the qualifier. To this, the following objection is raised: does the qualified cognition follow immediately after the apprehension of a qualifier distinct [from the qualificandum], or...

Is the probandum the state of being inseparable from the experience of the qualifier alone? In the first case, the perception of the subject (pakṣa) subverts [the argument], leaving no room for the application of the proof, because there is no appearance of both [qualifier and qualified] in a perception that grasps a real entity. Furthermore, the reason "being a qualified cognition" (viśiṣṭajñānatva) is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since it is observed even without the apprehension of a distinct qualifier, as in the case of [the cognition] "possessing its own nature" (svarūpavān).

Or [one might say], "the pot" or "cowness is the universal. However, in the second case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because—just as in the case of "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*)—the relationship of qualifier and qualified is accepted by resorting to an imagined distinction, such as "the individual possesses the universal cowness" (*gotvajātimān piṇḍaḥ*); for the linguistic usage "this is a cow" is produced by an experience that excludes the non-cow. Thus, in verbal and other cognitions, there is no external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Or else, there would be the appearance of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); yet it has been demonstrated that a universal is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) should be considered in the same manner.
If this is so, how then [is it]?
In the section on Apoha,
it is first stated that the primary meaning is expressed by words.

Is the treatise thus endowed with logical consistency? No; for it is not that [the Self] which is propounded by it, nor is there any logical connection such as "when that [treatise] is known, that [Self] is revealed. To this he says:
"due to superimposition" (adhyāsataḥ).

The conventional usage of an object is twofold: by way of appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and by way of determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, in this context, even though there is an absence of appearance, the status of being an object is stated for the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) excluded from others (*parāpoha*) solely by means of determinative judgment. And thus, because one acts toward the very thing (*vastu*) itself through that determinative judgment, even on the basis of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Now, what is this so-called "determinative judgment" (*adhyavasāya*), which is distinct from conceptual construction? [For] "the conceptually constructed" and "the determined" are not different in meaning.

Because of its being [the object] of conceptual construction? Then how is there this distinct designation, "by means of determination (*adhyavasāya*) from conceptual construction" (*vikalpāt*)? Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is excluded from others (*anyāpoḍha*), does not appear clearly in conceptual construction. What logic is there in saying that [the object] is determined by conceptual construction, such that the object of conceptual construction is established as being dependent upon determination? Moreover, the external world is not the object of conceptual construction, yet it is apprehended.

Furthermore, it is difficult to establish a connection between this [conceptual cognition] and the word; moreover, since that [particular] does not exist in the self, there is no such thing as a conceptual construction (vikalpa) at all—so what is there to consider regarding its object? And if activity were to proceed from a word when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended, it would follow without distinction in all cases, because there is no difference since everything remains unapprehended. Consequently, even the attainment of the desired object would not occur.

"By necessity," [it follows] that there is also a subversion of inference. Regarding this, it is said in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*: "It is true that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) have a single object; however, the word 'conceptual construction' [refers to] sound and so forth—"

The [conceptual] construction (*yojanā*) has as its cause the grasping [of an object]. Determination (*adhyavasāya*), however, has as its cause the fitness for engagement even with respect to what has not been grasped.
And although the entire universe is ungrasped, nevertheless, engagement is restricted to specific objects because conceptualization possesses a restricted form.
For entities possess restricted potencies; their natures are established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and they are not subject to the objection of a confusion of potencies.

It is like the arising of what was non-existent (*asadutpatti*). For even though everything is non-existent therein, it is only from a seed that a sprout arises, because its capacity for that [arising] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that very case. Likewise here too, how could the capacity—established by valid cognition—for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of fire to engage specifically with the object fire when one seeks the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of fire and possesses the memory of it, not be subject to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
And by considering proximity, the blazing, radiant form belongs to the real object as much as it does to the manifestation of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

To that extent, the power of the conceptualization of fire to prompt activity resides in that [fire] alone, and not in water or other things. Nor do we say that activity occurs through the superimposition (*āropa*) of similarity, which would allow for the opportunity to criticize the process of superimposing the external upon the form, or the form upon the external. What then? It is one's own latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)—

That cognition, arising solely by virtue of its own maturation, extends its activity toward the external even though it does not perceive the external; thus, it is indeed erroneous. As the treatise says:

And there is no delusion regarding place in cognition, because the arising of a consciousness is identical [in both cases], since a consciousness of that kind is not admitted elsewhere than where it actually occurs. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.13)
Thus, it is not that activity occurs through superimposition (āropa) as in the case of silver and the like; rather, it is due to the restriction of power bound to the arising of such a form.

This is just as the rice seed is the material cause (upādāna) for the rice sprout—the effect (upādeya)—even though the latter arises without any continuity [of the former], because the stability of the persistence of "rice-ness" and so forth has been refuted by the critique of permanence. Nor does the investigator, while determining the non-perception of an object, [fail to see it].

The consequence of non-activity is avoided; for even in the case of perception (*darśana*), activity occurs when it is accompanied by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and the attainment of that purposeful action is contingent upon the necessity of the object’s existence. And just as that necessity is established by perception through its connection with the real entity, so too is it established indirectly through a specific conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*); thus, inference is not an infinite regress. However, in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), because there may be doubt regarding the object, even the attainment [of the goal] is uncertain.
In that regard, there is no fixed rule. Therefore, "determined" (*adhyavasita*) means that even though it does not appear [in consciousness], it has been made the object of activity.

Consequently, even if it does not appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), the fact that the external object is determined is not sublated. This very point is the meaning of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, as well as the apprehension of their non-difference. And therefore, that [external object] is not cognized by that [conceptual cognition].

It has been demonstrated that the objection—that there is no appearance of non-difference—is untenable, because the demonstration was established with respect to the object itself. And just as the determinate cognition "fire is here" gives rise to physical activity, so too does the cognition "fire is perceived by me" give rise to verbal activity; this is the section on Apoha.

It produces this; it also produces a mental [cognition] in the form of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) having that very form. This being so, just as there is the certainty "this object has been grasped by conceptualization," so too is there the [certainty] "it has been conjoined with a word," because the form of the word flashes forth just like a trace of the form of the object. Therefore, for as long as a person possesses the conceit of grasping the object, for that long there is the grasping conjoined with the designation.
Even for one who possesses pride, the determination of conceptual construction (vikalpa) occurs solely in accordance with the resulting conviction (avasāya), and not in reality.
And it has been said:
"There is no connection with words anywhere, whether externally or in the mind."
Again, a fragment of the form of an object flashes forth, interspersed with the appearance of the perishable.
Although both of these are merely the determinations of the intellect itself, they are placed upon the external and upon words; therefore, there exists the state of conceptual construction (vikalpa).

For this very reason, the qualification "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is employed in the definition of perception with respect to the empirical subject whose mind is withered by pride regarding that [perception].

Even in the Sūtra, there is a distinction made by stating "from conceptual construction through determination" (*vikalpād adhyavasāyena*). Furthermore, in that context, this term "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is not used as a designation for the conceptual construction itself as the substratum (*dharmī*), but rather for the act of determination residing therein.

Regarding the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the dharma: this is the meaning. Even when [the object] is not seen, there is a certain dharma called "fitness for engagement" (*pravartanayogyatā*); through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), activity proceeds by means of that.

If the object is known and established through determination (*adhyavasāya*) by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), then the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object is also obtained; thus, it is logical that "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*) consists in mere determination.
Therefore it has been said, as the author of the Bhāṣya stated:
"And the single object is denoted through superimposition."
"How is it that it has that [unseen result] as its object? Because it impels one toward it.

As for the objection, "How can there be an impulsion toward something unseen?", the lion’s roar—that "impulsion occurs everywhere precisely toward the unseen"—has not been elaborated by us here for fear of making the text too voluminous.

Thus, regarding the statement "because one acts through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within one's own appearance," here too, there is a determination of an "object" (*anartha*) that is actually one's own appearance, as before; whereas "object" (*artha*) has been defined as something external capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). By its exclusion, the "non-object" (*anartha*) is the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*). In this way, it should be understood as both "a real entity" (*vastu*) and "non-existent" (*asat*). And this has been made clear by the words of the *Vārttika* itself: 228. *tasmād arthāvabhāso 'sau na tv artha eva kathyate / jñānaṃ hi viṣayākāram uktaṃ tan na ca tad bhavet // yadi syāt tasya nirbhāsaḥ pratyakṣaṃ syāt tathā sati / na cārthasya parokṣatvaṃ kathañcid upapadyate // tasmād arthāvabhāso 'sau na tv artha iti niścayaḥ /* (PV III 397–400) "Therefore, this appearance of an object is not said to be the object itself. For it has been stated that cognition possesses the form of the object; yet that [external object] could not exist [as such]. If it were so, its manifestation would be perceptible, and thus the object's state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) would never be possible. Therefore, the conclusion is that this appearance of an object is not the object itself."

In the *Sākārasiddhi* within the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, [it is stated]: "The engagement of inference is through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object; thus, 'inference of the determination of the object' is the meaning. However, as for the commentator’s explanation here, it should be rejected exactly as it appears in his *Apohasiddhi*, for fear of excessive prolixity.
This was not raised by us.
If, then, the external object is the denotable [referent] by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), how is it so for the form of the cognition?
As the treatise says, beginning with "it" (*yat*), and so forth.

The referent of a word, established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless predispositions, is the subject (dharmin) which is threefold, based on existence, non-existence, or both. [Pramāṇavārttika 3.204–5]

Thus [it is said]. For even regarding the form within cognition (*buddhyākāra*), determination (*adhyavasāya*) cannot be predicated, because that determination is established only with respect to the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*).
And since that object belongs exclusively to the external world for one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), he says:
"Another object, the denotable, appears."
1. Of Dharmottara:
[The word is bound to the conceptual reflections that reside therein;
because it does not reside in anything other than those, the word is said to perform the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).]

"That reflection of an object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct from the word—[even that is not the nature of the object; it is an error arising from latent predispositions]. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.164–5)

The meaning is that the mental form (*buddhyākāra*) is other than the external object. Since in a cognition produced by sound and so forth, only the mental form appears, that alone is called the "object" (*viṣaya*), just as visible form is the object of the eye; it is not, however, [the object] by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). And it has been said:
"The referent of a word is stated according to how it is perceived, even though it does not exist [externally]."

[Pravāraṇā-vāda 3.83] Thus it is said: "But it is 'non-existent' because it does not exist externally as it appears; and this is because the inquiry is undertaken from the perspective of the external world. This very meaning is expressed by the statement: "Because it is not real according to its conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and because it is not conceptually determined according to its actual reality (*tattva*)."

Since "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is a synonym for "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), it is established that [the object] rests upon the meaning according to the manifestation of the conceptual construction. Even in the case of the manifestation of non-existent objects and so forth, the meaning is simply their external non-existence in accordance with how they are perceived. Furthermore, even the state of being an error is only in relation to the external world; thus, all this constitutes the section on Apoha (Exclusion).

It is unconfused. However, it is not correct to assert the non-existence of that which is the object of self-cognition on the grounds of its being of the nature of cognition, as is the case with the appearance of hair and so forth. For this very reason, even though it is expressible, there is no proof by way of affirmation (*vidhisādhana*) of either the form or the external object in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
For indeed, by conventional truth alone it exists externally; however, even by conventional truth, it does not exist as a [real] form.

For there can be no application of affirmation or negation by means of words and the like toward an object that is free from doubt, self-cognized, and [already] present as a mental form, because such an effort would be redundant and incapable [of producing a new cognition]. Nor can it apply to an external object that does not appear in conceptual construction; for if the object is not apprehended, of what could there be affirmation or negation? Therefore, just as an external tree is the denotable object of the word "tree" through the process of cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), [so too is the case here].

It has been established that it is precisely through such determination (*adhyavasāya*) that the affirmation or negation of an external object is conventionally expressed. Even when an investigation is conducted by taking some mental form from a particular context through another conceptualization (*vikalpa*), even then, the affirmation and negation pertain only to the external object on the basis of that conceptualization.

"For one who discriminates regarding the object, it indeed falls away"—such is the scripture (*śāstra*). Therefore, in reality, there is neither affirmation nor negation for either; for according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti*), it pertains only to the external.

And [the object] is difficult to avoid; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of conventional linguistic usage (*saṃvyavahāra*). 1. Only that which is superior in terms of its nature (*dharmottara*); cf. *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*, p. 60. 2. "It has no form whatsoever"; *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.30.

By this, the statement made by the commentator—that affirmation and negation have as their objects an external reality that is superimposed—is an unworldly and non-scriptural assertion belonging to the logicians (tārkika), and it is hereby refuted. For no systematic arrangement is possible without relying upon the two truths: the conventional and the ultimate. In this regard, this [superimposition] cannot be the conventional truth, because that consists of worldly conceit, and such is not the case for the world.

Furthermore, there is no disagreement that the object of a word is established as external—whether enjoined or prohibited—and that this pervasive basis for engagement and withdrawal is a mere conceit (*abhimāna*). People do not touch upon the externality and so forth of what is superimposed, nor is this [superimposition] the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For injunctions and prohibitions do not apply to that which is inexpressible, and scripture states that nothing whatsoever is expressible in an ultimate sense. The direction of reasoning (*tarka*) is likewise no different.

Furthermore, affirmation and negation do not apply to that which is not an object of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), nor is there determinative cognition from a word regarding anything other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—this is proclaimed by you yourself. Therefore, what follows for affirmation and negation [applied] to superimposed externality? And all systematic establishment proceeds through appearance and determinative cognition without touching upon reality. In that regard, neither the superimposed nor the superimposed externality [is real].
It is not the object of appearance, nor is it the object of non-determination. In that regard, what is superimposed does not touch upon appearance, as [stated] in *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, p. 12.

Thus he says: the superimposition, which occurs at the same time as the experience of the mental image (*ullekha*), is itself non-manifesting and has a non-entity as its object, namely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For this very reason, even its externality does not manifest, because it is a property of that [conceptual content]. As for the object of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), since it is restricted solely to external particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it does not belong to these two; so enough of raising this issue.

Even that which is called "superimposed" (*āropita*) is said to be merely imagined (*kalpita*); and the activity of imagination consists of two things: the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and its determination (*avasita*). Therefore, from where could this separate category called the "superimposed" arise? Consequently, it is appropriate to consider conventional and ultimate reality solely as having external support for the forms of cognition (*buddhyākāra*). And when there is a desire to express such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), what need is there for these tortuous and difficult paths?

Enough with this excessive persistence regarding the "basis. This remains established: it is by means of determination (*adhyavasāya*) that the external [object] is expressed, whereas it is by means of the appearance of the mental form (*buddhyākāra*) that the status of being denotable by words is asserted. Now, one might object: "If you explain it in this way, you have accepted the denotability of the entire mass of both types of objects;
how then is this introduced for the purpose of establishing that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible? To this, he says:

"It is established" means that this is merely a formal arrangement made with a view toward another purpose, namely that expressibility (vācyatva) exists through mere determination or mere appearance. And thus, for one who grasps the external objectification as merely a formal establishment of its reality—

To that extent, it is said that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, as excluded from others, is the object; this is intended to exclude the collection of adventitious attributes (*upādhi*). Similarly, the statement that the form excluded from others is the nature and object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is intended to exclude all external [objects], but not to imply that the status of being an object rests within the [conceptual construction] itself;
thus, there is no contradiction.
But why is this so? For even though the status of being an object is established in various instances, the intended rest is not there;
rather, the intent lies in the refutation of anything else. Thus he says:
"In reality, no object whatsoever is to be expressed."

Thus it is said: For a manifestation accompanied by determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) brings the object of knowledge into the state of being an objective domain for cognition from the perspective of conventional practice, just like perception. Indeed, a mere manifestation—whether devoid of determinative cognition or its activity already occupied by another determinative cognition—is not capable of establishing the object for one desiring purposeful action, just like the touch of grass brushed against while walking, or [the appearance of] water in a mirage.

Nor is it a mere determination devoid of appearance, just like the superimposition of water. Therefore, the determination of an object, which is pervaded by its fitness for purposeful activity, is sublated when both [appearance and determination] are absent due to the absence of the pervader; thus, when one is excluded while the possibility of both is restricted, that [determination] is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). In whichever cognition something does not appear, or by whatever...

That which is not ascertained is not the object of that [cognition], just as a horse is not the object of the cognition of a cow. Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in verbal cognition, nor is the form of the intellect (*buddhyākāra*) ascertained by it; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Even though, in the case of extreme familiarity, it is observed that something may become an object of activity through mere appearance alone, [this does not apply here].

In the *Apohaprakaraṇa*, it is likewise stated: "Nevertheless, that very [cognition] is a result of practice (*abhyāsa*) and not without a determinative judgment (*avasāya*); thus, the determinative judgment itself possesses that human agency.
Therefore, since that which is not determined by a person does not arise from practice, the qualification [‘by one who has practiced’] must be required."

Now, one might object: even in the case of perception, there is no determination (*avasāya*) of the apprehended moment, but rather of the continuum (*santati*); and since this [continuum] does not appear [in perception], how can it have an object? For neither the moment nor the continuum exists [as such in perception]. In inference, however, there is indeed examination (*parīkṣā*).

Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for which some object could exist through the possibility of both [internal and external]; thus, this [notion of an object] is impossible. Therefore, if it were established that each [means of cognition] individually possesses its own object, then everything—whether external or internal—would have to be expressible as an object. To this, it is replied: He states the determination of reality (*tattvavyavasthā*): the status of being an object occurs precisely through the possibility of both; it is merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*).

In relation to the *hārikā* (the concealer), it is conventionally designated as "reality" (*tattva*) only in dependence upon a lower concealer; for when one enters into the distinction between moments, conventional usage is lost, and from the perspective of the conventional, there is no absence of momentary decay. Thus, since both [convention and reality] cannot coexist in what is perceived as ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), there is no fault. Furthermore, it is certain that for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is a grasping of the non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized.

If it is argued that the fire is indeed determined as being "thus" because it has appeared [to perception]—no, for the error regarding that appearance has been dispelled by the recollection of another appearance. And just as direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is capable of demonstrating that the appearance of the real object is indeed other than the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), so too there is no [appearance] other than the appearance of direct perception; therefore, the appearance of the real object finds its rest in that very [direct perception].
It is better to exclude the appearance of an entity belonging to a different class [from that which is intended]. Therefore, it is rightly said:
"Nothing at all is to be established or expressed in reality.
Alternatively, even if there is no expression of another entity, the exclusion (*apoha*) is understood therein as its qualifier.
The status of exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object is indeed accepted. Nevertheless, he asks how there can be the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmānabhilapyatva*), and replies:
"In reality, no object whatsoever is denotable.

This is the intended meaning: first, according to the position of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), like a positive entity, its status as a denotable object is produced merely through cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*).

You [are not so], because [the object] does not appear [in the cognition], unlike in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, in the case of the *prasajya* (negation) position, there is no difference between the mere exclusion of one thing and another time; nevertheless, since that [exclusion] is not the actual object, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Or rather, whatever is stated in the treatise—therefore, this is established: conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have as their object the differentiation (*viveka*) of all words—and thus, by means of the conclusion itself, he demonstrates that they are grounded in the object.
"No object whatsoever is expressible in reality"—
this is stated because expressibility is shown to exist only through appearance and conceptual determination within the conventional realm;
thus he says "in reality."
This is the meaning: that which was concluded in this treatise as "only exclusion (*viveka*) is to be expressed" does not have "exclusion" itself as its expressed object;

rather, just as the statement "non-existence occurs" has the sense that "existence does not occur," so too the expression "the expressibility of exclusion" [refers to the non-expressibility of the opposite]. Thus, regarding expressibility...

This is the meaning of *apoha*. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that this very point has been made clear by the treatise itself through such means as the classification of the three types of logical reasons (*hetu*).
Thus, to the question of how *apoha* can be the denotation of a word, the answer is: "By virtue of being its quality (*guṇa*), according to the aforementioned sense. Now...

The question is: why are the mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) not denotable? The responses are given in sequence: because of the absence of both the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and the appearance (*pratibhāsa*). However, when the inquiry is "what is denoted by words?", then [the answer is] based on appearance and the determination of the object; or, having distinguished between "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) and "as it stands in conceptual construction" (*vikalpastha*), [it refers to] that which is other [than the particular].
The sixfold form [of the response]—namely, that the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) excluded from others is nothing at all—is stated as a series of replies.

Therefore, the establishment of the fact that words and logical marks have exclusion (apoha) as their object is intended to demonstrate that all phenomena are inexpressible; this is the summary of the meaning of the first verse.
Let there be this elaborate discussion regarding exclusion (apoha) for those who are clever; however, my concern is the failure of the true nature of things to manifest.
If that [nature] is not firmly established, everything is lost without effort.
But when it is firm, there is indeed well-being by that much alone.
This illumination of the direction [of this work] has been provided by us in detail for its justification; however,
the full extent of it should be sought in the source itself.
Scattering [the enemy] like cotton blown by the wind.
The *Apohanakaraṇa* is completed.
The Discourse on God (Īśvaravāda)
Summary of the Prima Facie Position (Pūrvapakṣa)
I bow with all means of valid cognition to him whose teaching is unimpeded, who proclaimed that the world is a manifold creation of karma and is devoid of a sovereign creator.

Here, the counter-argument of others is as follows: "The mountains and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are preceded by an intelligent agent, because they are effects. Whatever is an effect is seen to be preceded by an intelligent agent, such as a jar. And these mountains and so forth are effects; therefore, they are preceded by an intelligent agent. Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*), for even for the Buddhist, the Vindhya, Gandhamādana, and other such [mountains] are effects.

There is no dispute regarding its being an effect (*kāryatva*). Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is impossible to demonstrate any deviation of an intelligent supervisor (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhāna*) from any effect whatsoever. Furthermore, because it is not sublated by perception or scripture (*pratyakṣāgama*), it is not "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). And because there is no counter-reason (*pratihetu*), it is not "neutralized by the presence of an opposing argument" (*prakaraṇasama*). Therefore, by this [reasoning], that which...

That which is established is to be accepted by the wise, just like that which is established by other means of proof. Nor should it be asserted that because the effect is not beloved by the intelligent as much as the reason is in all cases of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it lacks probative force; for while this [effect] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is absolutely excluded from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) such as space and so forth.
For there are three classes of entities: those with an intelligent agent, such as pots and the like; those without an agent, such as space and the like;

and those whose agency is doubtful, such as mountains and the like. Among these, "being an effect"—which exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa) such as pots and does not exist in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as space—is a reason characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin). As it occurs in the remaining cases, it necessarily brings about the presence of the probandum (sādhya). Even though...

Furthermore, according to the views of the Digambaras and others, atoms are indeed effects even though they are non-existent; nevertheless, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the non-existent is certainly accepted. And thus:
"If there is no cessation [of the cause] in that [effect], why is the operation of the cause desired?"
"For the *vipakṣa* is characterized by not being the locus of the *sādhya*";
such indeed is the treatise (*śāstra*). And there is no impairment of its status as a *vipakṣa*.

What is the use of this effort to prove their existence? Therefore, there is no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the aforementioned agent and the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*). The same logic should be applied to [the reasons] such as having an origin (*utpattimattva*), having an insentient material cause (*acetanopādānatva*), persistence, and activity. Here, in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, Śaṅkara, raising the Buddhist objection, states that [the property of having an intelligent cause] does not follow merely from the fact of having an origin.

[This] is established. However, if that which is observed in palaces and the like—whereby the notion of having been made arises even in one who does not observe the act of making—were exactly the same in the case of the earth and so forth, then there would be an inference of an intelligent agent here as well. It is not [established] by the mere similarity of the word "being an effect," because deviation is possible therein; for [the notion of being made] does not arise from anything other than [an observed act].
Because they are non-different due to the identity of their verbal designation,

it is logical to infer fire from whiteness; likewise, because the earth and so forth have insentient material causes, one may infer a creator for them as well, just as in the case of a jar and similar objects.

If you say it is inference (*anumāna*), then in that case, since objects such as jars—which are transformations of clay—are preceded by a potter, it would follow that an anthill must also be inferred to be preceded by one. As it has been said:
"That which is established as being of such a kind," and so forth.

[Pravā. 1.12] "The triad of Vārtikas. This has been stated by one who has not ascertained the opponent's intention. For instance, there is the presence of existence when there is the presence of an intelligent cause, as in the case of a jar and so forth, and the absence of it when there is the absence of production and so forth, as in the case of space and so forth. And that [relationship], being thus well-established as an inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—

Only where [the effect], such as earth and so forth, is perceived, there alone does that which is bound to the capacity for its production generate it for those who know it. But this is not the case with qualities such as paleness, because they are observed to deviate from fire while inhering in a different genus. Likewise, independence in actions has never before been observed for instruments and objects when they are not presided over by an agent possessing effort; rather, [such independence is observed] only in all cases when they are presided over by an intelligent being.
Thus, because there is the perception of the production of palaces and so forth.

Vācaspati, however, having introduced the concept of an essential (svābhāvika) relation, says: "In this case as well, the effect-ness [of smoke] has an essential relation with an agent who possesses knowledge of the material cause and so forth; for since no limiting condition (upādhi) is perceived, the charge of deviation (vyabhicāra) is unestablished. Furthermore, it has already been stated that grass and the like are included within the subject (pakṣa). Moreover, it has also been demonstrated that one must not merely engage in speculative conjecture (utprekṣaṇa). Therefore, by nature..."

If that which is connected with its own probandum were to exist without the probandum, it would necessarily deviate from its very nature; thus, supported by such *tarka* (reductio), and having the doubt regarding its occurrence in the absence of the probandum removed, the [reason] observed in the mountain and so forth is capable of establishing its own probandum—so what is the use of personal prejudices? As for those [reasons] such as paleness, the transformation of a mango, or "cowness," they are [established] through perception itself, because they consist in the inherence of a different genus (*jātyantara*).
