However, those are not valid reasons because deviation has been observed; for instance, the whiteness found in snow and other things, which inheres in a different genus, deviates from fire. Likewise, the modification of clay, being preceded by architects and others, deviates from the potter.

In this same way, it should be understood in other cases as well. Therefore, the distinction there is as follows: that which is the specific form of smoke consisting of white substance—1. For this, the *Vārtika-saptashlokī* should be consulted; 2. cf. *Tattvavaiśāradī* 4.1.21, "A Summary of the Pūrvapakṣa" in the *Īśvaravāda*.

That alone is the cause of fire, because its non-deviation from it is observed there. On the other hand, a mere pale substance produced from a cause distinct from fire—which is actually different despite being non-different due to a similarity of words—does not lead to the inference of fire, because its deviation from that [fire] is perceived there. This should be applied similarly to the products of clay and so forth. However, regarding the generality of "being an effect" (kāryatva), which is characterized by the state of coming into existence after having not existed previously...

Its existence in mountains and the like is indeed established; however, they say it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not proven. But since that [connection] has been demonstrated in the case of smoke and so forth, it is logical that inference from it follows.

Vittoka, however, says: This may be so. There can be no certainty regarding non-deviation (avyabhicāra) merely by observing [the reason] in similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), because a rule of non-deviation is impossible for that which does not possess the nature of the effect (atadātman) and does not arise from it (atadutpatti). Therefore, this "being an effect" (kāryatva) is not a valid proof, as its negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful.

To this it is replied: there is no doubt regarding the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because the causal relationship—which is established through the means of perception and non-perception (*upalambhānupalambha*)—is proven for the cognition of an effect and for the cognition of [the cause], just as it is for smoke and fire. It is only the specific effect whose production from that [cause] is established, not the general category of effect; just as, for example, in the case of smoke and so forth, there is no certainty that the property of being a real entity (*vastutva*) and the like is produced by fire and the like.

If it is argued [that there is a distinction], we say no, because there is no specific reason [for such a distinction]. Since perception and non-perception are accepted as the means of proving that [the effect] arises from that [cause], there is no distinction between the generalities of the probandum and the probans; thus, just as with a specific effect, the fact that a mere effect depends upon a basis for its awakening is established.
Furthermore, it is not the case that "substantiality" (*vastutva*) is also an effect of fire, since it is perceived thousands of times even in the absence of fire. Therefore, just as...

Since an effect such as a cloth is observed to possess a material cause (*upādāna*), another effect is likewise established as being so; and since that very effect, such as a cloth, is observed to have an intelligent cause (*buddhimaddhetuka*), even an effect whose agent is not perceived is established as being preceded by an agent.

This is because, just like the material cause, the agent also exhibits positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the effect. Therefore, just as an effect cannot be without a material cause...

And thus, it cannot be suspected that an effect could exist without a creator; nor should such a suspicion be entertained, because for every effect in general, the existence of a creator is established by the very same reasoning as the establishment of material causes and so forth, since there is no distinction between them.

As for what is said—that a different kind of effect alone is pervaded by an intelligent agent, such that from the sight of which even one who has not observed the act of creation forms the notion of its being made—and that this is unestablished in the case of the oceans, mountains, and so forth; [we ask]: what is this "notion of being made"? Is it a notion of the means (*sādhana*), or a notion of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)? As for the notion of the means, it is already established for you, since you admit that the variety of the world is born of action (*karma*).

Now, the opposing position [is as follows]: by that, the following meaning results: this "productness" (*kāryatva*) perceived in earth and so forth is not capable of inferring the probandum (*sādhya*), but rather it is something else entirely, because it does not generate the cognition of the probandum. And this is not logical, because it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference.
For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could indeed say: "This smoke is not capable of inferring fire, but rather it is something else."

Thus, for one who perceives the probandum (*sādhya*), no cognition of the probandum arises. And so, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum is not established; nor is the cognition of the probandum established as long as the means of proof is not established. Thus, it is quite clear that there is a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*). — *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

Śaṅkara also said: "Nor does the reason (hetu) become unestablished (asiddhi) for someone due to delusion when there is an absence of the cognition of the probandum (sādhya), because that would result in [the invalidation of] all inferences."

The author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*, however, says: "If it is perceived as being produced (*kṛtaka*), why is there not the cognition that it was made (*kṛtabuddhi*)? It is not the case that everyone has the cognition that things like palaces were made;

rather, just as the cognition that old palaces and the like were made arises only for one who knows the pervasion (*vyāpti*), while those who are ignorant of the pervasion have the cognition that they were not made, so it is with the earth and other elements—there is no difference whatsoever. [Puruṣa...]

If it is argued that the cognition of being "made by an intelligent agent" does not arise with respect to the earth and so forth, as it does with respect to palaces and the like, [we ask]: is this the case for those for whom an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well-established, or for those for whom it is not? Even among those for whom it is well-established, is it for those who lack the memory of having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), or for others? First of all, for those whose memory has not failed, the cognition of being made by an intelligent agent certainly arises; even in the world, the universe is observed to be diverse.

There is a common recognition that [these things] were created by some creator (*dhātṛ*). However, for those who are confused regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and its recollection, the notion that they are produced by a person does not arise even in the case of certain palaces and such; yet, this alone does not mean that these are not man-made.
Furthermore, since the Mīmāṃsakas lack the notion that the Vedas are produced by a person, it follows that [the argument against human authorship] applies there as well.

The reasons stated for the proof, such as "being a sentence" and so forth, would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) which was stated for the purpose of establishing impermanence would also be unestablished; for the kind of "being produced" and so forth observed in jars and the like—which is not perceptible by the ear—is not present in sound. Therefore, this discrepancy between the example and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) exists in all inferences.
It is equally a sublation of the inference regarding Īśvara alone.

In the *Mañjarī*, Trilocana further states: "How do you establish that birth is pervaded by being preceded by an intelligent agent, given that it exists only in things such as jars? If you say, 'Because they possess the cause of the cognition of having been made,' then you must specify that particularity of jars and the like by virtue of which, through a distinction not possible in the case of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), only jars and the like produce the cognition of having been made, and not the great elements."

First of all, there is no distinction in the perception of the agent and the action, because it is admitted that even one who does not perceive the action forms the cognition that [the object] has been produced.

If it is argued that the distinction lies in the dimension of magnitude (*mahattva-parimāṇa*), that too cannot be the case, since such magnitude is observed even in the great elements (*mahābhūta*) due to the plurality of causes, their own magnitude, and specific arrangements. Nor should it be said that the distinction is simply "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), for [this would fail to account for] that which is characterized by inherence in its causes (*kāraṇa-samavāya-lakṣaṇa*).

Because manifestation is no different even in the case of earth and other such things; nor can any distinction other than these be discerned even by Śakra, on account of whose existence it could be said that jars and the like alone are the causes for the cognition of being "produced," while earth and the like are not.

Vācaspati, however, says: "Let your honor examine this more precisely here: is the specific point the fact that [the production of things] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent? Or rather, is it the observation of that [agent], which is said to be absent in the case of mountains and the like? If it is the former alternative, that is certainly accepted by those who maintain that the body, the world, and so forth have an intelligent cause; for [otherwise] there would be no cause."
A summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*):

"Surely no one other than a fool would claim that the existence or non-existence of an effect is not governed [by a cause]. Now, is it the final position (*caramaḥ kalpaḥ*) that [the cause] is merely perception (*darśanam*)?"

In that case, for one who perceives no causal activity, the conception of an agent cannot arise. For it is only that very jar which is seen to conform to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with fire that is its effect, not one found in the marketplace. If you argue that because a member of that class is seen to conform to the positive and negative concomitance of that [agent], another member of that class—even if its own conformity to such concomitance has not been seen—is likewise [the effect of that agent], then alas, [this leads to] production...

Since a clay pot and the like follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an intelligent agent, other things as well—such as the body and the world—being likewise characterized, cannot be set aside by mere force.

If it is argued that "a pot of its kind arises without being preceded by an intelligent cause," then surely beds and such would not have that [intelligent agent] as their cause, because they do not belong to the class of pots. Alternatively, if it is held that whatever belongs to a certain class follows the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent...

It has been observed that even things of that same class which do not have their positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) perceived are caused by an intelligent agent. Why, then, is it that buildings and the like—which belong to the same class as effects—are not seen to be caused by an intelligent agent, such that the body, the world, and so forth, which possess the property of being produced, would not be so? Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever based on belonging to that same class.

Even if there is a doubt, or even if some unspecified particularity exists, what is intended by one who points out this particularity? Is it the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the generality of being an effect (*kāryatvasāmānya*), or rather that of a specific effect (*kāryaviśeṣa*), or perhaps the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "mere effect" from an intelligent agent (*buddhimatkartṛ*), or merely a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? And what follows from this?

If it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*)—the mere fact of being an effect—is unestablished (*asiddha*), that is not so; for in the case of the earth and so forth, as with jars and the like, it is established for both parties (*ubhayasiddhatva*) by virtue of being produced through the operation of a cause. If, on the other hand, it is asserted that a specific kind of effect, such as one residing in a jar, is unestablished in the subject (*pakṣa*), then there is no harm here, because the specific variety is not adduced as the reason (*hetu*). However, if it is claimed that the general property of being an effect (*kāryasāmānya*) deviates from its agent (*kartṛvyabhicāra*), [then...]

That which is intended to be established cannot be proven because it is not observed in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since even grass and the like have been included within the subject (*pakṣa*). If it is argued that the proof consists in the demonstration of the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the probandum and the example, that is not so, because such dissimilarity is easily found everywhere.

"Another [author] says: Thus far, the natural connection (*svābhāvika-pratibandha*) of the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) with smoke and so forth has been established. Now, for the sake of pleasing the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists), even subverting proofs (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) are stated. Indeed, we do not suffer from a lack of subverting proofs; however, we say that this is not the correct logic. In that regard, first of all, this very thing is the subverting proof:"

The proof is the fact that [the effect] never arises from a person even once. For example, according to the Buddhists, in the inference regarding fire (*citrabhānu*), if smoke were to arise in another place or at another time from another cause even in the absence of fire, then fire would not obtain its own existence even once in those observed places and times; for if it does not exist when they [the effects] occur, it cannot be their cause.

A restriction [of cause and effect] is logical, for otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, since everything of that nature would not have that [specific cause] as its cause, it would never arise from it even once. Yet it does so arise; therefore, such a thing is not produced by anything other than that. This is established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary [position]. [Note: 1. In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, in the work *Bandhasiddhi*: likewise, for us as well, if some effect were to arise from something else even without the superintendence of an intelligent agent, then alas, it would never be produced by an intelligent potter or the like; yet it is produced from him, and therefore it is born of that [intelligent cause].
This is one subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Or, for example, even for the Buddhists, it should not be suspected that smoke arises from something else, because if it had an indefinite cause, it would follow that it is causeless (*nirhetuka*). And as for that which is causeless—
An effect must be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent because it would not depend on anything else if it lacked a cause;
for it is only through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.
"In the same way for us as well"— this is the second subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
And this being the case, just as this rule of yours is established— that "this smoke [is that which follows] the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with fire"— [so it is for us].
A "creator" (vidhāyī) is a specific kind of entity, namely fire, which is the producer of smoke. Therefore, if that smoke is being produced by it, then it is indeed the effect of fire;

likewise, for us as well, whatever is preceded by an intelligent agent is its effect, and that person is the one who produces it. Similarly, if there were no conscious supervisor, there could be no activity of insentient things toward any effect whatsoever.

If there were cessation [of activity], then there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-interruption of causal action. For instance, if the activity of insentient things occurred by their own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), then, because their operation would be devoid of intention, activity would occur at all times. Indeed, the destruction of activity occurring without cause is not logical. Consequently, there would be no cessation of the effect. Alternatively, if there were indifference (*audāsīnya*), then activity would never occur at any time.

Because there is no distinction [between the atoms]. We consider it logical that they are set in motion at times by a presiding agent possessed of effort, but not by something insentient; for the latter lacks the capacity for activity and cessation dependent upon will. This is the third subverting proof. Here, indeed, the state of being an effect is pervaded by the presence of occasional causes, [and] occasional causes—

And the presence [of causes] is dependent upon the operation of an agent, as is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just like the presence of a loom, thread, and so forth.

In the contrary case (*vipakṣa*), there is no occasional existence of the presence of causes; for an insentient entity cannot bring causes into proximity, and if it were capable of doing so, it would follow that even in the case of a jar and other such things, the operation of an agent would be unnecessary. Consequently, by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*)...

The fourth subverting proof is that the property of being an effect, when excluded from the contrary class, is pervaded by having an intelligent agent as its antecedent; thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.

Likewise, the consequence of there being no restriction regarding place and so forth is a subverting argument. For it is thus: the property of being an effect [would otherwise] involve a restriction of place, time, and material cause.

If [the world] were produced without a conscious agent, it would not occur with restriction to specific places and so forth. For by the will of a creator, it would arise in a particular place and be excluded from other places; in the absence of such a [will], it would exist everywhere.
This is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).

The establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is as follows: when "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), it is pervaded by the state of being invariably concomitant with that which possesses effort (*prayatnavannāntarīyakatva*); this is the fifth subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
As for Śaṅkara’s argument that there would be no spatial or other restrictions on all effects if they arose from operations devoid of intention;

likewise, there is no distinction whatsoever between the causes of the earth and so forth and the causes of palaces and the like, by which these [former]— while being operations devoid of intention and independent of effort— could possess such [intentional] activity characterized by specific restriction.

Vācaspati, however, raising the argument for God (Īśvara) in the *Kaṇikā*, says: "If, on the other hand, insentient things were to produce an effect without being presided over by a sentient being, then they would produce it wherever they happen to be situated; thus, an effect characterized by a specific restriction of place and time would not be observed. Since its birth is dependent upon the conjunction of causes, the effect is not produced by the individual causes alone."

If this is argued, [we reply: True; however, from what does the very conjunction (*samavadhāna*) of the causes arise? If it is argued that it is due to a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) whose maturation is occasional, [we ask: But how can this [unseen merit], being itself insentient, bring the causes together in their proper manner? Indeed, sticks and other such tools situated anywhere do not, by the force of a specific unseen merit alone, [function] without the effort of a potter.

They either come together with one another, or, being already present, they exercise control over the effect. Therefore, since the production of an effect is pervaded by the conjunction of its causes, and since that conjunction is impossible in the absence of a conscious perceiver, the production of the effect—by the exclusion of the pervader—is excluded from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) and is thus pervaded by having a conscious perceiver as its antecedent. Thus, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established.
If it is argued that this being the case, let there be the establishment of a mere agent, but how can he possess omniscience, since its concomitance is absent in the illustrative example? We say: no.

Regarding this, Trilocana says: "This is not so; for it is not a creator characterized by specific attributes that we intend to prove, but rather the general property of being a creator. And when that general property is to be ascertained, those specific attributes with which it has a real connection—namely, the characteristics of directly perceiving the material causes and so forth—must necessarily be ascertained as well."

Because if that [specific instance] were abandoned, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the generality of the probandum (*sādhyasāmānya*). Nor can it be abandoned, because the generality of the probandum pervades the properties of earth and so forth. Furthermore, the material cause (*upādāna*) consists of four atoms; the actions consist of the forms inherent in all *kṣetrajñas*; space and time are the instruments (*upakaraṇa*); and the recipient (*sampradāna*) is characterized by all *kṣetrajñas*.

And the purpose is characterized by the experience of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). One who perceives all this through direct perception is an agent who has directly perceived the entire differentiation of the universe and is therefore omniscient. Furthermore, no positive concomitance (anvaya) preceded by a formal presentation [of a reason] is shown in an example, such that there would be the occurrence of a host of defects like non-concomitance (ananvaya).
1. Nyāyakaṇikā, p. 215–6; 3. "Indeed, this... Nyāyakaṇikā; 2. "Of causes, mutually... Nyāyakaṇikā.
4. From this very [reasoning], Oṣādevanyāya, Jñānaśrīmitra’s Collection of Treatises (*Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*):

It might be argued that just as there is a sequence of binary atoms (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth for the arising of the great elements, there is likewise a sequence of binary atoms and so forth for the production of a jar.

Because no distinction is perceived, this potter, while making a jar, also makes a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Yet the potter does not perceive its material cause or its instrumental conditions through direct perception. Therefore, the following [proposition] is inconclusive: that whoever is the maker of something knows its material cause and so forth.

To this it is replied: there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) only if the potter were the creator of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). For the potter does not create every factor that serves as a constituent for the production of the ultimate composite; rather, the nature of being a creator is defined by the employment of causes whose causal efficiency has been observed. Therefore, even the dyad—like the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—is itself a probandum (*sādhya*), since its creator is subject to doubt.

Thus, that general object of inference (*anumeya-sāmānya*) which is desired to be established by the proponent (*sādhya-vādin*) cannot be refuted by the opponent (*dūṣaṇa-vādin*). However, that particularity (*viśeṣa*) which is intended to be refuted by the opponent is not what is intended to be established by the proponent of the general object of proof. What then? When the general object of proof is to be ascertained, [the proponent establishes] a particularity that possesses a real connection (*vāstava-pratibandha*) with it.

Success arising by force is not overlooked. Thus, the Teacher, considering that specific success depends upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), stated this objection: "To whatever extent the means of proof extends toward an object, so too does the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
If this particular [object] has not been made an object of the means of proof, how can there be its establishment from it? Or, if it is being established, how can it not be an object?"

If it is argued that [the universal] is the object [of inference], then how could it not be touched by the occurrence of defects residing in its own substratum? That objection is refuted; for this would only be the case if the proponent of the proof admitted that the establishment of the particular depends upon the proof itself. However, the Naiyāyika does not rely on the establishment of a particular as being dependent on the proof. What then? [He relies on] the particular which is drawn forth by the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the general property to be proven (*sādhya*).

Success [is achieved] as follows: for instance, the Buddhist, through the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), relies upon the proof of selflessness (*nairātmya*) because of a real necessary connection (*vāstavapratibandha*).
For if the self were eternal and omnipresent, one would not be able to infer momentariness with respect to all things.

Even the Mīmāṃsaka, while determining a single whole (avayavin) through both seeing and touching, [necessarily] ascertains these [concomitant facts]: the plurality of the sense organs, the restricted domain of the sense organs, that the sense organs have the apprehension of their own respective objects as their inferential mark (liṅga), that the cognizer possesses the means of cognition, that there is a substratum of qualities distinct from qualities such as odor, and that the conscious being has unrestricted objects [of perception].

Just as one relies on the meaning [of a treatise], so too do the Naiyāyikas rely on the specific thesis (*sādhyaviśeṣa*); thus everything is the same, except for their dogmatic attachment. Therefore, omniscience is established.

Vācaspati, however, says: "This might be so. Having an origin is pervaded merely by an agent who knows the material cause and so forth; this [pervasion] is observed in jars and the like, and it would lead to the inference of such an agent for the earth and other elements. But how could [the property of] being preceded by an agent possessing eternal knowledge of all objects be established?
For this is not observed in jars and the like, which serve as the instances."
1. Tātparyaṭīkā, p. 954: A Summary of the Pūrvapakṣa on the Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda).

[Objection: But if this is so, how can the inference of the means such as the eye from the perception of color and so forth—which is of the nature of an action—also be established? For it is not the case that...

Actions such as cutting and the like are observed to have the sense organs as their instruments, because they are seen to have axes and similar tools as their means. Now, even though the fact of having the sense organs as their instrument is not perceived in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), it is established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). For the nature of action (*kriyātva*) residing in the perception of color and so forth leads to the inference of that very instrument which is capable of accomplishing that perception; and axes and the like are not so capable.

"Capable"—by the force of this property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), this establishes the eyes and other sense organs as distinct from axes and such tools, even though they have never been perceived before.

This is the same in the present case as well. For indeed, the simultaneity in the production of effects characterized as immeasurable, occurring in indefinite directions and locations, consisting of sensory objects, supersensory things, living beings, and stationary objects, cannot be established unless there exists either omniscience or an eternal [consciousness]. Certainly, such a thing...

Supreme Lordly knowledge (*pārameśvara-jñāna*) cannot be an effect produced by a body, senses, and so forth; for prior to the production of the body and other such things, that [knowledge] would be insentient, which would entail the further postulation of another Supreme Lord to produce the effects of that earlier time. And thus, rather than postulating a multitude of such supernatural entities—thinking "prior to that," "prior to that"—it is better to postulate a single supernatural quality: the eternity of consciousness (*buddhi-nityatva*). By this very [argument], [the eternity of consciousness applies to] the body and the senses...
The hypothesis of permanence has been refuted. By this, that which some say— namely,
"although everything possessing structure and so forth might be established as having an intelligent cause—
it follows from where that there is a single creator for structure and the rest?"— is also answered.
[As stated in the *Vidhiviveka*, p.

219], that too has been refuted. Their desire to negate the existence of an omniscient being would succeed only if those with fleshy eyes were capable of seeing atoms, individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), or the latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*) inherent in them; but this is not the case. Therefore:

Many beings distinct from ourselves who perceive supersensible objects must be postulated; therefore, it is better that there be only one such being, for the sake of parsimony in postulation (*kalpanālāghava*). Thus, it is established that the existence of such a Lord is proven by the very fact of [the world] being an effect, aided by its subsistence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Or, let it be that from this [argument] there is established merely a creator who is omniscient regarding the material cause and so forth; however, the establishment of a specific distinction for one whose second name is "the Excluded" (the Opponent) follows from the inference by elimination (*pāriśeṣyānumāna*). For instance, the creator who is omniscient regarding the body, the world, and so forth, cannot be one whose intellect is non-eternal or not all-encompassing, because it would follow that such a creator would lack knowledge of the material cause and so forth of those things. Indeed, one of such a nature [who lacks such knowledge] is not omniscient regarding their material cause and so forth.

Just as we and others are seen [to possess knowledge], this [Lord] is also one who knows their material causes and so forth; therefore, it is so. Indeed, no one other than such a Lord is capable of knowing the infinite distinctions among atoms and the distinctions among the latencies of karma (karmāśaya) inherent in individual conscious beings (prati-kṣetrajña). — *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

Vittoka, however, argues that just as by the observation of smoke, through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), a specific location such as "being within a bower" is cognized—even though it is not pervaded [by smoke]—so too is the agent; thus there is no fault. Therefore, God (*īśvara*) is precisely such a specific person established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How then can the Blessed One, who teaches a doctrine uncontradicted by valid cognition, be one who maintains that the world is not governed by a Lord?
The summary of the prima facie argument in the section on the doctrine of God is completed.
A Brief Refutation in the Section on the Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda)

This is a brief discussion consisting solely of refutations regarding the doctrine of God, intended for those who are weary of extensive treatises that require the commentaries on the *Vārtika* and the *Saptashloki*.

In this case, although the proponent has shown a great deal of mere concomitance of the effect with the intelligent agent, and has also shown its absence in some instances where that [agent] is absent, nevertheless, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, it might still be an effect even if it were not preceded by an intelligent creator. Thus, due to the lack of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), the reason "being an effect" is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) when proving an intelligent creator, as its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. It is not [a valid reason].

Nor can the mere observation and non-observation of the probans in the similar and dissimilar instances suffice as a proof for the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which is denoted by the term "invariable connection" (*pratibandha*)—consisting in the necessary presence of the probandum when the probans is present, or the absence of the probans when the probandum is absent;
for such pervasion is observed even in cases where a future deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is subsequently perceived. Is this current non-observation due to the absolute non-existence of deviation?

Furthermore, for one who merely observes concomitance and possesses a reflective disposition, it is simply impossible to determine that [the relation] is due to the absence of the convergence of the causal complex for perception.
For this very reason, even Vācaspati’s proclamation of an "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvikasambandha*) is a mere verbal flourish, as it lacks any meaning beyond that.

Because of nourishment (*poṣaṇa*). For when, upon repeated observation, no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is perceived, there is an inherent determination (*svābhāvikavyavasthā*). And this non-perception of deviation is said to be merely the non-observation [of it] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). As for the claim that deviation is not established due to the non-apprehension of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), in that case there exists nothing called a "limiting condition" that functions as a visible mark (*dṛśyacihna*) such that its non-apprehension could establish the practice of non-deviation. Rather, [The text continues: ...but... (kiṃtu) [the argument proceeds].

The postulation of that [intrinsic nature] arises merely from observing deviation; and because that [deviation] is not observed, there is intrinsic nature. Since there is no distinction [between these two positions], nothing is gained by the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikavāda*), for it is sufficient simply to state: "A reason is that which is repeatedly observed together with the probandum, and where there is deviation, it is not a reason. All of this has been analyzed in detail during the discussion on pervasion (*vyāpti*); in some cases, what is called "obstruction" (*pratibandha*) refers to something other than [the mere absence of deviation].

That this [invariable concomitance] is established through the proof of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) without [the necessity of] that origination (*tadutpatti*), should be understood from that very source. By this, those who rely on the systems of Śaṅkara and Vācaspati are refuted.
Let it be, then, that even for one who possesses effort, the connection of the effect with its cause is characterized solely by that origination, just as in the case of smoke.

By Vahninā, as stated by Vittoka: For instance, prior to the activity of the potter, although the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth are present, the effect called "pot"—which has reached the conditions for perception—is not perceived; yet it is perceived immediately after his activity. Thus, since the relationship of cause and effect is established, how can there be any doubt regarding its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? True, in this case, the [distinction between] the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class—

There is no doubt that this is indeed the case; for here, because the nature [of the objects] is admitted as being suitable for perception and non-perception, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the unperceived operations of a person by means of trees, *vīraṇa* grass, and so forth, which are manifested [by those operations]. Grass and the like are included within the subject (*pakṣa*), and not by that which is itself the subject alone—[as stated] in the collection of works by Jñānaśrīmitra.

If it is argued that this constitutes a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), we say no; for there is no logical principle for taking as the subject (*pakṣa*) that which has already been refuted. Otherwise, even in cases such as "Fire is not hot, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), making it the subject would be the only recourse. For it is said:
"Since the statement of a reason applies to what is doubtful, that which is [already] excluded is not a locus for the reason."

This is the principle [of Pra.vā. 4.91]: non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is said to be simply perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to one counter-entity (*pratiyogin*) in relation to another counter-entity. Therefore, even that which is sublated by non-apprehension is indeed sublated by perception. However, with respect to the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is inference (*anumāna*).

Nor is there any room for another [inference] when an inference has already been sublated. For that [non-perception] establishes the absence only of that which has acquired the qualification of being perceptible; however, since "intelligence" (buddhimattva) is common to both those with perceptible and imperceptible bodies as well as others, it is impossible to establish a restriction on its perceptibility. Thus, how can an intelligent agent be denied in the production of grass and such things by mere non-perception? Therefore, it is proper to take this as the subject of the thesis (pakṣa) due to doubt.
If you say this, it is like guarding a cow after it has already been sold.

For, by granting scope to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) as means of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), the acceptance of their having a visible object (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) follows by necessity. Indeed, neither perception—which establishes positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—nor non-perception—which establishes negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—can function with respect to that which is invisible (*adṛśya*). Therefore, since there is a distinction [between the two], [the relationship] consists of positive and negative concomitance through perception and non-perception.

One who enters into the state of being cause and effect is not able to transcend visibility for that which is to be proven; and since visibility is found even in fixed grass and the like, there is a deviation, making it a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
Now, might he not grasp the pervasion through the wonder of non-deviation by means of an effortful agent who is beyond the scope of perception?
Let him grasp it; however, for him, reliance upon perception and non-perception is not superior. But surely, without depending on the qualification of "visible" and "invisible," a discerning person—
Is the apprehension of pervasion [established] by mere verbal testimony? It is not so; for even by that much, there is simply no room for a pervasion established by perception.

For how could that [pervasion], which is restricted to an object whose nature is exclusively perceptible, have as its domain both the perceptible and the imperceptible? Indeed, that which is perceptible and that which is imperceptible are of entirely distinct classes due to their extreme difference in nature—whether characterized by remoteness or otherwise—even though they may share common properties such as being the objects of a single cognition. Therefore:

Perception, having proceeded by accepting a single genus (*ekajāti*) among visible objects while remaining ignorant of other reports, demonstrates that very same pervasive property (*dharma*) as common even to that which is qualified;
for although an object remote in space or time is not visible, it nevertheless possesses the capacity for such visibility through its belonging to the same genus.

Or rather, this is a refutation by means of perception directed only toward that which is spatially remote (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*). For if all other [possible objects] were excluded, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would not exist at all, because it would terminate solely in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), as in the case of smoke and fire, or trembling and wind. Just as the pervasion established by perception—which operates by taking as its primary object a blazing, radiant form capable of its own activity—is not common to both the seven-flamed fire and the digestive fire in the stomach.

It culminates in form; otherwise, even regarding a form that is intended [to be real], one who doubts it—like [doubting] the difference between grass and other materials—would not proceed with a one-pointed mind toward obtaining the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by it. Or, as in the case of a deficiency in the causal connection (*pratibandhavaikalya*), for one who reflects that "there is no internal heat" (*jaṭharyatva*), this is a brief refutation in the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda-adhikāra*).

There would be activity. Or, just as the pervasion of the wind in causing the unfolding of sprouts—established through perception—is determined not by its ungraspable form, but results in a form common to still air, otherwise one who even now infers the wind from the trembling of a young leaf would certainly act with movements and cessations corresponding to a tangible gale; so it is with the Person (Puruṣa) as well.

The apprehension of pervasion established by perception occurs only through the exclusion of those things whose forms are invisible. Therefore, if under the guise of perception there is merely the proof of what is desired [by the proponent] and not actual perception regarding both visible and invisible universals, then due to the absence of pervasion, the reason possesses a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever determination of causality is produced by perception does not terminate in a nature that is both visible and invisible, just as one who excludes the common form of fire produced from the stomach (*jaṭharaja*) and ordinary fire (*jātavedas*). And this determination of causality regarding the intelligent being (*buddhimat*) is produced by perception;

thus, there is the apprehension of a property pervaded by what is contrary to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). For being produced by perception is pervaded by having a visible object, whereas in the case of an invisible object, it is not.

Because of [the nature of] activity, its opposite— namely, the state of having both visible and invisible objects— is pervaded by the state of being restricted to the form of either visible or invisible [objects].

Furthermore, if one intends to express a pervasion merely by means of "intelligence" (buddhimat), setting aside the qualification of "visible and invisible," then when one demonstrates the absence of the pot's effect in the absence of an intelligent agent for the sake of establishing negative concomitance (vyatireka), at that time, regarding the visible and invisible...

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the non-existence of mere consciousness devoid of qualifiers established? For the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) has jurisdiction only over the negation of that very [perceptible]; otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the presence of] grass and so forth.
No.

Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) whose object is only a perceptible person (*dṛśyapuruṣa*) is capable of serving as a means for establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of mere intelligence (*buddhimātra*), because the absolute difference between their objects is manifest. Otherwise, even in the case of the production of grass and so forth, non-apprehension whose object is only a perceptible person would become the cause for stabilizing its deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For [non-apprehension] does not enter into the acquisition [of the probandum] when there is a cutting off [of the reason].

It is logical that [the reason] must be an escape [from the contrary]. Therefore, on the view that excludes the qualification of the perceptible object (*dṛśyaviśeṣaṇa*), because there is no means of apprehending the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is a lack of pervasion; consequently, doubt remains as to whether the reason is excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Nor is the manifestation of the absence of both [the reason and the probandum] in space the means for grasping the negative concomitance, because the absence of the effect is determined to be caused by the absence of the operation of an intelligent agent.

Because [otherwise] it would be untenable. For when all other causes are present, the absence of the effect in the absence of that specific factor alone can be understood as being caused by the absence of that factor—just as was considered in the *Trikapañcakacintā*. However, in the case of two factors, the mere cessation [of one upon the other's absence] is easily found even between those that stand in no relation of cause and effect.
Furthermore, regarding the ether (*vihāyas*): is the absence of "being an effect" due to the absence of the operation of an intelligent cause, or rather due to the mere absence of any cause at all?

What is the definitive conclusion? If that were the case, every effort [to prove the existence of God] would be fruitless. For even as for positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there remains a doubt: is it grasped as being between "effect in general" and "cause in general," or rather between [effect] and a cause qualified by a specific person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇena*)?

Now, if this particularity is indeed perceived—just as [the nature of] fire is perceived in smoke—then how can it be avoided? If that is so, since a particularity consisting of a visible body is also clearly apprehended, how can it be avoided, just like the radiant form of the sun? Therefore, that...

If it is argued that the specific property (*viśeṣa*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the effect, let it deviate. Even in the case of the effect, just as in the case of the cause, let the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) be restricted solely to those observed specific properties, since it is observed even in palaces and the like, just as it is in jars; what is there for us to lose? This [argument] is stated while disregarding the refutation [of the opponent] by closing one's eyes like an elephant. In reality, however, [the proof rests on] perception and non-perception...

Since it is impossible for either of the two [the positive and negative concomitances] to function with respect to the two [the mountain and the pot], there is neither positive nor negative concomitance. Furthermore, while "being an effect" exists in the case of the mountain and so forth, positive and negative concomitance do not touch upon an agent who transcends perception. And because there is no other category besides those consisting of being produced by such an intelligent agent and its opposite, this is simply an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*), like the property of "fragrance" and so on. Therefore, by means of perception, [the relationship of] the mere effect...
Thus, it is established that there is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇa*).

And since these [cognitions] proceed toward the apprehension of the causal relation by means of a reference to the universal (*jāti*)—specifically regarding the effect characterized by perception and non-perception—and not merely by a reference to the effect-in-general; for it is in this way that the operation of perception and non-perception occurs.
Immediately after such a specific object of a blazing and radiant nature, an object arises that causes the throat and eyes to become affected by a coating of whiteness;
it is in this manner that the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect occurs, excluding all other classes of cause and effect.
It functions by indicating precisely two distinct classes [of entities]. This is the universal rule everywhere regarding the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect;
however, we observe that this particular case involves a transgression of the established principle due to deference to Īśvara.

What, then, would be the fault here if perception were to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of all effects by an intelligent agent— setting aside distinctions such as those between grass and other fuels— just as it apprehends the pervasion of mere smoke by fire, setting aside distinctions such as those between mountains and other substrates? For in that case, just as the apprehension of pervasion occurs through the inclusion of a mere subtle intermediate genus within the smoke, which is a specific class of effect produced by fuel, and not [through its specific individuality], so too [would it occur here].

Likewise, let there be [the same] for cloth and so forth, even though they possess intelligence. Or, just as you desire to grasp a pervasion of "merely that which possesses existence" by including within it the various classes of effects—even though they are extremely dissimilar—so too you should grasp it by means of fire.
For how could the operation of sensory perception itself assume two different modes of activity in both cases? Because of the observation of deviation...

If it is argued that this distinction is produced by perception (*darśana*), then in that case, perception and non-perception—so long as they have not ascended to the level of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*)—are as ineffective as the touch of grass while walking; thus, there must necessarily be a corresponding reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Yet such a thing does not exist.

For no one, when the activity of perception and non-perception is engaged in grasping the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of fire, smoke, and so forth, [perceives] a class of effects.

Having experienced the mental resolve that "it arises from every fire," and subsequently observing deviation—since other effects are perceived or found even without fire—one determines with certainty that "this [smoke] alone is produced by this [fire]. However, immediately thereafter, through another instance of perception and non-perception, one grasps the universal: "from this fire and so forth, this smoke and so forth [arises]."

The synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*) is experienced as that which makes manifest two specific features, thereby serving as the vessel for the conventional usage of the relationship between cause and effect. Regarding the refutation in brief of the doctrine of God (*īśvara-vāda*) within the scope of direct perception, there is no distinction whatsoever between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And when, from something situated in another conceptual construction, such as a thorn, [there is a sudden...]

"Distress" (*vyathā*) refers to the cognition that apprehends the relation of cause and effect, which is established by direct perception preceded by non-perception; it is the absence of deliberation regarding the observation of deviation manifested by that [cognition], because conceptual constructions cannot exist simultaneously. Thus, even in this case, the linguistic convention "this effect, such as having a broad base and belly, belongs to this artisan," proceeds by setting aside intermediate subtle distinctions. However, when [it concerns] a cloth—
When one observes even a cart or similar object being produced from a person, the non-contradictory cognition arises: "This too, and that too, is produced by a person."
Furthermore, what is this so-called "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*)? Does it refute mere inference only when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is already established?

Or does it establish that the pervasion itself is false? Even in this latter case, does it do so while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion is still manifesting by its own power, or does it do so by undermining the validity of that very cognition—either with respect to all objects or only with respect to a restricted one?

Is this restriction due to the power of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), or because perception operates only in that specific case? First, the initial position is not tenable due to contradiction. For it is not logically consistent that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a reason—characterized by its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum—and the absence of inference caused by the possibility of the probandum’s absence should coexist; furthermore, there would be a lack of confidence in pervasion elsewhere as well.

Thus, it should be understood that while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) maintains its status as a valid authority, the attempt to demonstrate the falsity of that pervasion is likewise incoherent. Furthermore, if the validity of the means of cognition grasping pervasion were to fail in every instance, then fire could not even be inferred from smoke, because there would be no other means of cognition to grasp the pervasion. What, then, will be the refuge for the inference of God (*īśvara*)?

Furthermore, when the scope is restricted by one's own whim, the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be rendered a mere wretched instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that remains indifferent; thus, in reality, nothing would be either a valid reason (*hetu*) or a non-reason (*ahetu*), because there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of being able to arbitrarily subvert the pervasion even in the case of smoke. Moreover, how can there be a restriction of scope for perception, which is the very locus of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since it is only that [perception] which, functioning within a restricted genus, grasps pervasion?
Is it not the case that both [the cognition of pervasion and the cognition of deviation] have all things as their object, since they possess neither less nor more capacity?
For the apprehension of pervasion and the perception of deviation would both have the same object; what, then, would now be the means of proof and what the non-means of proof?
Or, let us grant for the sake of argument that, due to your own constraints, the valid cognition (pramāṇa) that brings about the awareness of sublation has a restricted object.

Nevertheless, the realization of sublation does not indeed occur all at once for those things characterized by deviation, but rather sequentially. At that time, since there is no direct observation of deviation even among those things that deviate, smoke possesses no distinction from them; consequently, it would either again lack the status of a reason, or else everything else would also possess the status of a reason.

Nor should it be said that there is no confidence in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding smoke because of the observation of deviation in all other cases; for if that were so, immediately after grasping the pervasion in smoke, one would not be able to infer fire from smoke on the slope of a mountain rather than a tiger, due to the requirement of waiting for the observation of deviation elsewhere. And this [waiting] is impossible... [248]... by means of observations of deviation elsewhere.

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is held that the certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*) rests [upon this]. For even the objects of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are infinite; since human life is shorter compared to the time required to perceive those things situated at a distance in space and so forth, therefore, like the observation of deviation, it is restricted—

The apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs without exception only with respect to the object itself, because the pure conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) functions through differentiation. For this very reason, only natural conceptualization (*svābhāvikavikalpa*) has the authority to grasp the relation of cause and effect, not that which is adventitious (*aupādhika*).
Indeed, there exists a conceptualization common to children and animals that depends solely on the knowledge of bare perception (*ālocanājñāna*) produced by the pure object.

That is called "pure" and "essential" (*svābhāvika*), by virtue of which even animals— determining that only there are the means for allaying hunger, thirst, and so forth— again proceed toward it or withdraw from it accordingly, whether through association or non-association.
And there exists a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by a perceptual cognition accompanied by the recollection of linguistic convention, such as [the cognition of] soot from a lamp.

The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that "this is blue, fit for dyeing and so forth," as held by worldly people, is said to be conditioned by such [prior] factors (*aupādhika*), being produced from experience aided by the recollection of previously perceived causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Yet, at that time, no discerning person determines that "by this very conceptualization of blue, all blue things such as lamps are produced. Rather, it is only that which is preceded by a conceptualization corresponding to the mere perception of lampblack.

[27a] A thing (*vastu*) is fit for the application of the word "lamp" due to its connection with a universal (*jāti*), or because of a specific nature (*svarūpaviśeṣa*); it is that very same thing which performs the function of a lamp.
And regarding the basis of deviation (*vyabhicārālambana*), it has been stated:
likewise, in the case of smoke as well, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following convention—such as "this white thing is excluded"—is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Thus, it implies snow and the like by virtue of their being effects. However, when the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is pure, it is only the genus of smoke (*dhūmajāti*) that manifests; therefore, the exclusion of snow and so forth from the pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on that alone is not a sound basis for deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This should be understood. Similarly, even the conceptualization of an effect (*kāryavikalpa*) is everywhere merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). For that which is blind regarding its own production depends upon the operation of another. [End of] Effect...
Since [the cognition] arises from sensory perception aided by the recollection of a convention (*saṅketa*), it is not a factor for the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect.

Therefore, although— just as when one sees the arising of a jar from a person— the conceptual construction "this jar is from him" is easily available, and likewise the conceptual construction "this is the effect of that" is also easily available, nevertheless, because there is an absence of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), the status of being its effect cannot be established for that whose nature is based upon such [convention].
But let it be granted that [the conceptualization] of that which has been made an object of natural conceptualization [is indeed conceptual].

However, is it not observed that even regarding an object within the scope of pure ascertainment (*śuddhāvasāya*), there occurs a conceptualization produced by the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketasmṛti*), such as "this jar is man-made," because of the mention of its name? Therefore, that too would result in being adventitious (*aupādhika*). [Reply: No, for there is no recollection in the mere conceptualization of that [name].

Because it is not the primary cause; for its capacity lies solely in the manifestation of the denotative aspect. And although the arising of an indivisible conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which transcends the forms of both the signified and the signifier, occurs with the assistance of memory, nevertheless, by way of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), its operation is said to pertain to that [denotative aspect] alone, just as the potter’s operation is said to pertain to the state of being made of clay alone. [This applies to qualities such as] whiteness, which is an effect inherent in a different genus.

However, the conceptualization of a dharma—without the recollection of prior operations such as grasping the relationship through convention—is impossible for a pure determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), as was briefly refuted in the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*);

for [such a cognition] achieves its purpose merely by indicating the universal (*jāti*) alone, like that of a child and so forth; therefore, the function of perception has as its object only that [particular].

Thus, [the definition of] pervasion (*vyāpti*) is faultless. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of pervasion produced by perception and the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) have entirely distinct objects.
If it is argued: "In that case, the establishment of the 'common inconclusive' (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy through the observation of deviation would be untenable," [we reply: indeed.

This would be the case if there were a uniformity of intellectual acuity among all people. However, one of dull intellect, even when a specific universal (*jāti*) has been presented through perception by means of similarity and so forth, might—due to the conceit of grasping a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—unite it with another universal and thereby claim to have established an inference. Then, another person of keen intellect points out the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and demonstrates that the pervasion is difficult to grasp. Therefore, the status of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason remains common [to both].

Just as when smoke has appeared, even though it is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one who recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— which grasps the connection with fire in its rising and abundant form— and thereby infers fire from a mass of dust blown by the wind, is prevented from falling into error by the presence of steam, which is known to be deceptive due to its similarity to smoke; for that reason as well, it is established that the pervasion is grasped by direct perception only with respect to a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*).

For if perception were to grasp the necessary connection as being restricted to a single class of smoke, then it would be appropriate to superimpose that form upon another object based on similarity, and to exclude it due to deviation from other similar things. But when the apprehension of pervasion occurs in every case within the class of effects, then what is the need for dependence on similarity? If, then, the connection is indeed restricted to a specific class by perception—

How is it that the cognition of conjunction— though entirely heterogeneous even to jars, pots, walls, and the like— leads one to infer the application of a common dyeing agent, such as the processing with turmeric and other substances? Or how is it that the intellect, though entirely heterogeneous, infers [itself] as an instrument by virtue of being an action, since its operation is observed in the act of cutting performed by axes and other tools?

If it is argued that even things such as Mount Kailāsa and the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), though extremely heterogeneous, will lead to the inference of a conscious agent (Puruṣa) because they possess common properties such as being effects, we say: not so. This is because it is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) that makes [the pervaded] known; it is only with respect to that [pervader] that one should consider whether [the probans] is of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*). Furthermore, the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—in relation to the object to be produced (*nirvartya*) or the object to be modified (*vikārya*)—is of two kinds, namely, that which has the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*).

And [there is] the form of a property (*dharma*). In that regard, when there is an origination of something entirely new in every respect, it is called the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the substratum (*dharmin*), as in the case of smoke and so forth. And in that case, another instance of smoke is indeed of the same class (*sajātīya*), while any other entity is of a different class (*vijātīya*). But when there is the determination of the origination of a different property belonging to that very same thing previously existing, then it is called the pervasion of the property (*dharmavyāpti*), as in the case of heat in water; and in that case, another instance of heat—
Thus, it is the property itself that is of the same class [as the effect], and there is no longer any dependence on the genus of the substratum (*dharmin*).

In the same way, passion (*rāga*) too, disregarding its difference from substances such as a jar or a mat, indicates the refinement of the substance of passion solely by virtue of its own dependence upon an effect of its own kind. For this very reason, regarding its particularities, there is in some cases contact with saffron and in others with turmeric.

[The creator] is thus inferred. However, in the case of pre-existing things such as mountains and clouds, the person [to be inferred] is not intended merely as one who brings about their "product-ness" (*kāryatva*) and so forth;

rather, he is intended specifically as one who produces them anew, just like a pot and the like. And at that time, [the properties] such as product-ness are [inferred] from smoke, just as its whiteness and other qualities are.
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is stated:

"Even if there are properties inherent in a different class [of things], they are entirely ineffective because they lie outside the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, the apprehension of the pervasion regarding the factual subject (*dharmivastu*) does not depend on a mere proximity of properties; nor does the [apprehension] of the subject from the pervasion of the property [depend on such]."

[The author] speaks of "belonging to the same class" (*sajātīyatā*). And it has been stated that the distinction between what belongs to the same class and its opposite is made with respect to a single pure reflective awareness (*ekavimarśa*).

Therefore, even when there is a difference in nature (*vaijātya*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), such as passion, [qualities like] being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth do not possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum]. Otherwise, the undesirable consequence of inferring fire from white matter would be difficult to avoid; for the objection based on deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has already been refuted.
Regarding the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the inference is as follows: That which occurs only occasionally (*kādācitka*) when its [own] causes are present must depend upon other causes;
for example, a sprout [occurs occasionally] when water and earth are present. And cognition (*buddhi*) occurs only occasionally when the object, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and light are present.

This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). In the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), namely the case of independence (*anapekṣatva*), occasional occurrence is contradictory because it would entail non-occurrence at all times.

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through sublation (*bādhaka*). The determination that "whatever is dependent on something else is a sense-faculty" does not allow for the inference of a cause by means of the property of action (*kriyātva*), nor does perception grasp the pervasion. Furthermore, perception must necessarily be held to apprehend a universal (*sāmānya*) only by way of presenting a distinction between classes (*jātibheda*) brought forth by innate conceptualization (*svābhāvikavikalpa*); otherwise, when [the object] is [apprehended] by perception—

When a convention is established—such as "this is a jar"—after demonstrating a single pervasion (*vyāpti*), does that [convention] then enter into the entire universe as possessing properties such as being an effect? Or is it restricted to a specific domain by observing deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? Or does the instructor himself, by negating [the convention] in all other classes, bring it to rest upon a fixed domain? Or is this convention not even concerned with a general object at all?

The same should be understood regarding the distinction between the classes of denoters (*vācaka-jāti*). However, the word "effect" (*kārya*)—being applied merely to that which arises in dependence on another within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) without depending on direct perception—is not restricted to a specific instance. If, however, even that were applied to what exists in direct perception as "this is an effect," then it too would be restricted to a specific instance, since it would possess other synonyms for that same object.

Therefore, the very apprehension of the specific class and individuality of the body is the natural function of perception. And if perception, though directed toward a distinction between the effects and their classes, were to take as its substrate merely the effect in general, then—when operating upon a cause—it should likewise ascertain the cause in its mere generality; why then does it rely on a specific cognition of the material cause and so forth? Therefore, if this is not [the case] according to your view—
The inclination toward probability applies to the observer in both cases: this [observer] must either rely upon a generality or rely upon a particularity.

If he relies upon a generality, then since the inference of a cause is from an effect, what talk can there be of establishing an Īśvara? And if he relies upon a particularity, then because a pervasion by the mere fact of being an effect is unestablished, it is therefore logical that based on experience, one should infer a specific cause for a specific class of effects.
He demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by stating "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever perception apprehends a causal relationship has its operation restricted to a specific class [of objects], just as [the perception] of fire and smoke. And this [perception] which establishes the pervasion of the effect by an intelligent agent is likewise [restricted]. Its own...
This is a reason based on existence (*bhāvahetu*). It is not inconclusive due to the suspicion of its functioning otherwise, because that is refuted by the non-perception of a cause.

For indeed, a difference in causes is the cause of a difference in effects; otherwise, it would follow that everything is without a cause. Furthermore, there is no cause for this [creation], as has been briefly refuted in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).

There is a distinction [between them] because they arise from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the object, the sense organ, light, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the suspicion that the example might be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), [the response is]: whatever is perception, that necessarily apprehends a universal (*sāmānya*) by means of a specific genus (*viśiṣṭajāti*) alone—just as the perception that grasps deviation [is a perception], and the perception that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*) is likewise a perception; this is simply its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). This very point constitutes the non-conclusiveness (*anekānta*).

The rebuttal: Even regarding the two cases of "intelligent agent" and "effect," this very same formulation applies to the substratum (*dharmin*) where the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped. Alternatively, in both instances, whatever perception grasps a relation does so by means of a specific universal (*viśiṣṭajāti*), as in the case of the signified and the signifier;
and the perception that grasps the relation between cause and effect is likewise as before. Therefore, if this [perception] is in fact entirely...
The collection of effects is invariably concomitant with effort; nevertheless, because the classes of effects are infinitely diverse and mutually distinct,

and because the apprehension of pervasion must be sought for each specific class, it is rightly said that the inference of that [effort] is direct only so far as the class of effects preceded by a person has been delimited.
"Established as such," and so forth.

And thus, it is fire alone that is the basis for the inference in all those effects—such as smoke, ash, embers, cooking, clearing away, observing, or injury—wherever the perception that establishes the necessary connection has occurred; it is from that very [perception] that the inference arises, and not from anything else. In this way...

We accept that inference from an effect is valid even in the case of things such as temples, water-jars, palaces, chariots, and fine silken garments—which, though in fact produced by human agency—is restricted to those very types of objects in which the activity of a person has been previously perceived. However, regarding the class of rain-clouds, mountains, and the like, since their operation cannot be ascertained, what talk can there be of inference? For it is possible that they belong to an entirely different genus.
Because the pervasion is not apprehended, and because the effect whose pervasion has been apprehended is not observed?

Even the inference based on the perception of the creation of pleasure-mountains and the like upon actual mountains is not supported by logic, since its application falters; for that [creation] is equal to a mere name.
Furthermore, if a Lord were established by means of multiple similar human actions, [the argument would fail].
What talk can there be regarding the cognition of equality in the fruit, since from what cause could there be a state of distinction?
Thus is the intermediate verse.

Furthermore, one might ask: what kind of class of effects (*kāryajāti*) is pervaded by an agent possessing effort? Anticipating this, it is stated for the sake of brevity that because of its infinity, there is a certain class of effects such that upon seeing it, even one who perceives only causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) forms the cognition that it was "made" (*kṛtabuddhi*). In this context, "forming the cognition that it was made" does not mean the cognition of a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), nor does it mean the cognition of the specific probandum (*sādhya*) under discussion—namely, the knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth—but rather it refers to the nature of weavers and the like.

The cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*). And because of its absence, neither the non-establishment of your reason (*hetu*) nor the establishment of the probandum under discussion (*prakṛtasādhya*) is intended as being direct;

rather, this is a demonstration of absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*). And by means of that, the non-establishment or the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason is precisely what is intended.
— *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

For instance, the cognition of a craftsman—such as a potter—arises with respect to things like temples seen in an empty city, but not with respect to things like Mount Malaya or the ocean. The intention [of the argument] is that the presence or absence of such a cognition of a craftsman does not occur without an absolute difference in genus (*jāti*). If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were not grasped, or if there were a lapse in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) for recollection, this [cognition] would not arise even in the case of a temple and so forth; [this would apply] equally.

The cognition of an artisan [arises from this]. Therefore, just as the cognition of fire arising from smoke, but not arising from a donkey, necessarily establishes a distinct genus for the donkey relative to smoke, so too does this [cognition] establish [a distinction] for Kailāsa, the thunderbolt (kuliśa), and so forth, relative to those entities whose status as products of human effort is firmly determined.
If it is asked, "How, then, is the very absence of inference to be understood? [The answer is:

because even in a dream there is no suspicion that a thunderbolt could arise from a potter; otherwise, the world would not experience the misery of drought caused by the trampling of weavers' feet, nor would one terrified by the invasion of a foreign army desire to flee across the mountains and oceans.
Thus, it would attain its manifestation. If it is argued that another factor, standing in the place of the weaver, must necessarily be expected there—[we reply:

no, because when the production of the effect is identical, it is illogical to search for a cause of a different genus, since the accomplishment of the goal is achieved by the weaver alone. For even in the case of another cloth, there is no expectation of anyone other than the weaver.

If it is argued that there is indeed a dependence on a specialized artisan regarding a particular type of cloth, we grant that this is so; however, as long as there is a firm recognition of a single genus (*ekajāti*) across other pieces of cloth, it is for this very reason that the artisan is merely conceptualized as a *kuvinda* (weaver).

In the absence of such a recognition, there is doubt regarding its being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). But mountains such as Meru and Mandara are not [recognized] by anyone as having a single... of human origin.

[They] possess reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Thus, one who out of deceit denies the extreme heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*) of these [effects], which is established by direct perception (*adhyakṣasiddha*), must accept that there is an absence of inference based on a common artisan.
