And once the difference in genus (*jātibheda*) is established, the kind of effect such as a jar, which is known to be dependent upon a person, is not like the kind of effect such as an embryo or an infant; and since this [latter kind] is not pervaded by a person, the non-establishment [of the reason] is established.

And there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) in both cases. This being the case, those objections which function by way of failing to produce the cognition of the probandum under discussion are cast far aside.
Consequently, we do not assert that the reason—such as "being an effect" (kāryatva)—is unestablished because of the absence of a cognition of the specific probandum under discussion. What then?

We assert that it is unestablished because of the absence of a cognition of a craftsman similar to a weaver in the case of Mount Mandara and so forth, and thus the status of being an effect belonging to the same class as cloth and the like is unestablished.

There is no fault whatsoever in [the argument] being the absence of a cognition of the subject at hand (*prakṛtasādhyabuddhivedhuryam*). Furthermore, since it is accepted that—in relation to what is to be accomplished by a weaver—there is simply a lapse in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and for recollection, there is no room for the alternative views proposed by the *Bhūṣaṇa*. The mere perception of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is certainly not what is intended [here]. For those whose recollection has not lapsed, the cognition that the earth and so forth were made by a person indeed arises. This, however...
It is far-fetched.

For the non-establishment of the negation of the notion of "being made" (*kṛtabuddhi*) as formulated by the Buddhist is what is intended to be stated here; and that is not impossible, because by the term "notion of being made," the intention is to refer to the artisan's cognition. This is the manifestation of the absence of the notion that [the world] is made by a person (*puruṣa*).

Furthermore, a detailed refutation within the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*) is useless; this investigation into the refutation applies only when that [God] is already accepted. In that case as well, the phrase "for those whose memory is unimpaired" is incoherent, because an absolute difference in nature (*atyantavaijātya*) is established, and since no pervasion (*vyāpti*) is perceived from anything other than the ocean and so forth, there is a failure of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) for recollection.
Because it is impossible to remove [this doubt], for this very reason, what confidence can there be in the mere prattle that "the world was created by someone"?

By the very fact of refuting the objection regarding the non-establishment of the understanding of the specific probandum under discussion, the argument beginning with "and likewise in the case of the Vedas" has already been rejected.
However, if the Mīmāṃsaka were to demonstrate an absolute difference in kind (*vaijātya*) between the Veda and human speech and the like, then what [of it]?

Is it to be defeated by mere convention? Yet, there is no distinction between those two [the word and the object] based on their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or their power (*śakti*). And so, having recited that pair before someone who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), tell me, what kind of distinction could the listener explain regarding which [belongs to which], or do you not see the removal of poison and so forth performed by mantras such as that of Garuḍa?
Thus, this follows: therefore, [the cognition] is one, as it conceives its own specific cause as being distinguished precisely by a particular effect.
Just as one perceives that the mere effect of fire is pervaded by its cause,
another does not recognize that the effect belongs to that same class and has that very thing as its cause;
alas, this is a particular kind of darkness even regarding perceptible objects for those who claim to be wise.

Or rather, since speech— which exists as something distinct from the person yet participates in his existence— cannot be differentiated from other speech, there is no distinction between Vedic words and other words capable of possessing their own nature;
furthermore, they equally indicate supersensible objects, and there is certainly no greater reliability in one than in the other.
The Veda does not rest without reaching the status of being authored by a person.

If that were so, what need is there to speak of the human origin of the cognition restricted to those specific classes found in objects such as jars, clouds, and thunderbolts—objects which transcend the scope of investigation and possess absolutely distinct genera? Furthermore, whatever has been alleged as a proof for [the world's] impermanence is also outside the bounds of logic; for it is only when perception is authorized to cognize the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) that such [a cognition] occurs regarding a homogeneous class.

An Investigation into Relative Strength: Regarding impermanence, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) occurs through inference by its very nature, because the proof that subverts the contrary (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*) applies to "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) alone; thus, there is no requirement for a specific genus (*jāti*) therein. However, it must be considered whether that proof is capable or incapable of establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding "the state of being produced" in general, unqualified by any specific genus. If it is capable, there is no contact with any fault.

Therefore, it is not correct to claim that the pointing out of a difference there by means of the word "pot" constitutes a statement of dissimilarity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the thesis (*dārṣṭāntika*). This is because, since the two properties (*dharma*) are extracted from the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), the substratum is nothing other than the reality of the properties themselves;
thus, the statement of a difference between them has as its only meaning a difference in the mere substratum. (From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*)

If it is argued that even here, in the case of effects which are the subjects (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "being produced by a person" while the reason (*hetu*) is merely "being an effect," and thus there is no distinction whatsoever; we reply: what is the meaning of this statement that "merely being an effect" is the reason? Does it mean that, primarily, because the cause—such as saffron and the like—is operative only with respect to the coloration of the property itself, it is stated thus? Or rather, [does it mean] in its entirety?

Is it because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established regarding the effect, as in the case where "the mere state of being smoke" is the reason? Just as all smoke is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), so too is every effect produced from the activity of a person; such is the certainty. Both of these [arguments] have been refuted. However, the statement that "the mere state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is pervaded by impermanence" is an indication of the nature of things (*bhāva*) alone, insofar as whatever is produced...

The meaning is simply this: "everything is impermanent. When the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been applied to this point and the fact that sound is produced has been established, the objection—"Since a jar, which is produced, is seen to be impermanent, how could sound be otherwise?"—is rendered entirely without scope. It is precisely this meaning that is elucidated by the method of stating, "this is merely a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*)."

For just as, in the context of the discussion on essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason, the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) and the proving property (*sādhana-dharma*) are established as distinct with respect to their forms as they appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍha-rūpa*), so too is the substratum (*dharmin*), such as sound and the like; for there exists no other substratum possessing those properties. Nor [is this distinction] elsewhere.

In the proof of the impermanence of sound by means of a produced object as the property (*dharmin*), the impermanence of sound is established. Yet, one who brings about a distinction in that *dharmin* by treating it as having the nature of a jar or a word, and then articulates a refutation, is defeated through the mere distinction of the *dharmin*. However, in the case at hand, because of the misconception that [the reason] is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the mass of effects—standing in the place of smoke—is distinct from the person to be proven, just as fire is distinct [from smoke]. It is merely...

It is not like fire, which exists at that very same place and time; rather, it must be determined as being present at the place and time of birth, just as fire and the potter are inferred from ashes and a jar, respectively. Therefore, just as when one presents the argument "this jar is preceded by a potter because it is a jar," the potter—who is present at the time and place of its production—is determined even though the jar itself is the actual logical reason (*hetu*), so too is it in the case of proving the existence of the *puruṣa*.

The object itself (*vastu*) alone is the reason (*hetu*), not the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*). This being so, by one who asserts that effects such as mountains (*kṣoṇīdhara*) are dissimilar to effects pervaded by a conscious agent (*puruṣa*), a dissimilarity of the *sādhana* (the probans) has been pointed out, not a dissimilarity of the *dharma* (the property). For in that case, the locus (*dharmin*) is precisely the place and time of its own arising; and no one can claim a dissimilarity between the place and time of a jar (*kalasa*) and the like, and the place and time of Mount Kailāsa and the like.

By means of which [reason] there would be an exposure of its similarity to the property (*dharma*) [of the subject], therefore—just as from the mere form of fire one infers fire—an exposure of the similarity to the property of the probans (*sādhana*) serves to demonstrate either non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). To say "of the subject" (*dharmiṇaḥ*) is, however, a confusion on the part of others. This very point is what is meant by "the nature of being an effect" (*kāryatva*) being such that...

In a temple or similar structure, it is perceived as being pervaded by a person, whereas such is not the case in the Yugandhara mountain range and the like; this is the direction in which the point is taught.

The meaning is that whatever class of things a temple belongs to is pervaded by a person, but the Yugandhara range does not belong to that same class. Furthermore, because of their absolute dissimilarity, only a similarity in terms of the word "effect" (*kārya*) is stated, but there is no deficiency in the exclusion of non-effects (*akārya*) in any respect. As for pervasion, however, regarding the effect—

We maintain that "tva" and so forth are not included therein; for this very reason, similarity by way of mere existence (*sanmātra*) is not useful, just as [similarity] by way of having form (*mūrtatva*) and so forth is not useful in the inference of fire.
This is a brief refutation in the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).

Mañjarī’s objection, however, is misplaced. For by stating that the very genus (jāti) of jars and the like is established as being pervaded by a person (puruṣa), he intends to express merely a doubt regarding other cases. Furthermore, the notion of being "made" (kṛtabuddhi) refers to the cognition that it was produced by human agents such as potters;
and the absence of that [human agency] has been made the response when there is a difference in genus (jātibheda). Since that [absence] is admitted by both parties, it leaves no room for dismissal.
And it has been demonstrated that this is not possible without an absolute difference in genus (*atyantika-jāti-bheda*).

Thus, it should be understood that Vācaspati’s search for a specific distinction is prompted by an ignorance of the subject matter and its purpose, arising from a deficiency in cultivated intellect (*kṛtabuddhi*). For if "cultivated intellect does not exist" is intended to mean "the intellect regarding the present probandum does not exist," [then the following applies].

In this dispute regarding cognition, one must consider: why does that [cognition] not occur elsewhere, such as on a mountain and so forth, due to the absence of that [cause]? However, when the cognition that "it was made" is absent, it must be stated that the cognition that "it was made by a similar artisan" is also absent;
and in that regard, there is no dispute. Furthermore, the purpose is to demonstrate the absolute dissimilarity (*atyantavaijātya*) of clouds and the like compared to jars and other such objects.

That is impossible to avoid. Therefore, how can there be a cognition of the probandum under discussion from something that is absolutely distinct from those [instances] from which the pervasion was grasped? This being the case, everything of this sort simply collapses. Furthermore, since the pervasion has been refuted for the mere fact of having an origin, alas, [the argument] beginning with "that which has an origin" and so forth is shattered by the staff of a later time. Thus, for one who has observed the pervasion in a jar—

It has also been stated that when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped even in the case of palaces and the like—as being preceded by an intelligent agent—then it is established that their genus (*tajjāti*) is likewise preceded by such an agent.
Furthermore, having raised the objection, "Of which genus [is it]? the reply is: "Of which genus is it? It is not seen to be so [in the case of the subject]."

That too has been refuted by demonstrating that even for a universal appearing through innate conceptualization, there is the capacity for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of perception. Therefore, although the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding things of that same class is difficult to avoid even in the case of a form appearing through adventitious conceptualization, there is a great distinction [between the two cases] because such a form is rejected when it comes to the apprehension of pervasion.

For this very reason, even the conceptual constructions regarding "wealth" (*vitta*) and "fragrance" (*oka*) amount to nothing. To explain: if our question concerns intentionality, then a specific class of effects characterized by temples, jars, and so forth, is understood to require an intelligent agent; for through these, one infers a craftsman of a similar kind who has experienced the activity of making them while they were out of sight. However, that [specific class of effects] is not established in the case of the oceans, mountains, and the like. What remains, however, is merely the state of being an effect (*kāryatvamātra*).

We ourselves continue to proclaim with even greater force that [the cause] is not pervading; therefore, reflect on this: what is the use of these conceptual alternatives? Furthermore, it is even more wretched to claim that the specific property (*viśeṣa*)—by virtue of which the class of effects is distinguished—is itself of an unascertained nature, for it is impossible to deny the mutual dissimilarity of classes of effects established through perception. Pervasion, however, pertains to the specific class of effects.

Let it be that this applies only to the mere performance of a function; one ought to reflect upon this at first glance. Otherwise, how could he himself have avoided [the objection] by relying on deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the fact that "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) does not entail the production of the effect of fire? It has already been made clear that there is no dispute concerning the fact that cognitions of deviation have a restricted class as their object. Therefore, [the definition of a real entity is established] through the perception of form, causal efficiency, capacity, and so forth.
The most eminent [work] in this world of diverse forms is the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*.
It is certain that this [subject] has perceived a single, extraordinary form solely through the grace of Īśvara; therefore,

even the previous example of a material cause (*upādāna*) offered for him, based on the confusion regarding its pervasion (*vyāpti*) over all effects, is not tenable, because in that case as well, the operation of perception cannot be established.

Because it is the object of innate conceptual construction, and because the material cause possesses the nature of being both visible and invisible. If one asks: "In that case, is there no pervasion of the collection of effects by the material cause at all? Or rather, should it be accessible through another means of valid cognition? There is doubt in both cases, even regarding that which exists.

Because it is possible that no instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or a subverting inference (*viparyayabādhakānumāna*) has been cited, there is currently an absence of a conclusive reason (*ekāntahetu*).

Therefore, this universally established tenet (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*)—that every origination possesses a material cause (*sopādāna*)—persists without contradiction; and as long as we observe an effect, our practical consensus (*vyavahāra*) is likewise without dispute that it must possess a material cause. Furthermore, there is no cognition that extends to the very limit of all effects.

For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), doubt is difficult to ward off even by the slightest contrary element. Furthermore, since it is certain that cognition is the material cause (*upādāna*) of cognition, and because one consciousness does not have another consciousness as its material cause, this is established and thus is not contradictory; therefore, even if the determination of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established from the perspective of the final tenet (*siddhānta*), there is no harm. However, let it be that it is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nevertheless, in this case—

It may be argued that, in this case, the reason "having an insentient material cause" (*acetanopādānatva*) might be suspected of being unestablished in one part of the subject (*ekadeśāsiddha*); such a conclusion would indeed follow, so what can be done? However, once a subverting proof (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*) is obtained, even that [suspicion] would not arise. This [objection] is merely an instance of there being no example at all in the theory that perception establishes a pervasion over the entirety of the effect-class. Therefore, because it has been established that the operation of perception is restricted to specific types of things (*jāti-viśeṣa*), [the reason is not unestablished].
Is even the argument beginning with "due to the absence of a specific cause" thereby destroyed?
As for the effort of another [author] in presenting a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary, regarding that as well, the first two [points] constitute a sublation;
for just as in the case of smoke, once its production from that [cause] is established, the perception and non-perception that prove it must be specific—

Because activity is established by virtue of the category of "birth" (jāti), it is possible [to infer] only a specific effect such as a jar. And thus, if it were produced without an intelligent agent, it would not occur even once; or, if the cause were indeterminate, there would be no cause at all.
Therefore, since there is no proof that every effect arises from a person, that which is an effect must have a person as its antecedent.
Thus, this too is without foundation.

Nor does there follow the undesirable consequence of an uninterrupted stream of effects; for even though there is no constant presence of that specific state of the cause—which depends on its own causes and has the transformation of *adṛṣṭa* as its auxiliary—the occasional nature of effects is logically established. It is in relation to this [specific state] that even the Lord, despite possessing eternal power, is not considered an agent [at all times]. For if there were a restriction to a single state, there would be no activity of other causal factors.
One would have to desire a means for cessation; yet that does not exist, because [cessation] is a transformation like the increasingly swollen state of a seed.
This is the final remark regarding Śata-ananda.
A brief refutation in the section on the Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda).
Because it is impossible for them to abandon their long-standing habitual tendencies (*paramparāparicaya*). Or, let there be a restriction to a single state for God;

since His will is also eternal, the non-cessation of effects would remain in that same state. But if it were non-eternal, and if the manifestation of this [will] at some time were dependent upon something else, what kind of fault would there be if the collection of effects were likewise dependent upon that? In that case, even regarding the sequence of effects such as jars and so forth—
Is it by the will of a person? For one could argue that whatever [cause] this sequence depends upon, that very same [cause] must also exist for jars and the like.

That is incorrect, because it is impossible to deny a cause whose causal capacity has been observed through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, in the case at hand, since there is an absence of valid cognition, one merely relies on the fact that the effect is occasional; since this can be explained otherwise as well, how can a person [be established as the cause]?
What is the necessity for an effect?

If it is argued that since the occasional existence of things such as jars is seen to be dependent on a person, the same must be true for other effects as well; then, in that case, mere observation and non-observation alone would have arrived as the proof for pervasion (*vyāpti*). What need is there here for a subverting argument against the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*)?
By the phrase "through the audacity of his eloquence," the third [objection] is also refuted.

As for what is said—that the certainty [of a cause] depends on the presence of the cause and the possession of intelligence—even in that case, one must say the same regarding the mere observation [of concomitance]. Furthermore, no subverting argument against the contrary has been stated. And if one takes recourse to perception and non-perception, then all [objections], such as the inconclusiveness due to the causal complex of mud, water, seeds, and so forth, which are affected by wind and other factors, remain to be addressed.

It must be understood that the causal complex (*kāryavat*) is accompanied by this [concomitance], and that only a specific causal totality (*sāmagrī-viśeṣa*) is fit for pervasion (*vyāpti*). This extends up to this point.

Therefore, the establishment of pervasion between the causal totality and the person is not achieved; for, since there is no possibility [of the cause existing] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) due to the non-perception of the pervader, the fourth [reason] is also refuted.
By this much alone, even the hollow prattle of Bṛhaspati has been cast aside.

For it has already been stated that the absence of a specific state is the seed for the non-production of extended things. Even though it is observed that the staff, the wheel, and so forth meet with a person, and that the undertaking of an effect occurs when they are accompanied by human effort, nevertheless, this is not the case everywhere or at all times.

The same fault remains, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the restriction "it is exactly thus," since even the conjunction of causes—which pervades the production of the effect—is dependent upon an intelligent agent, and thus its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unproven. Furthermore, just as the occasional occurrence of effects depends solely on specific states of other causes, so too is the case with the subject at hand; thus, the fifth [argument] is reduced to ashes.
Furthermore, it is shown in the treatise that this is a proof establishing the occurrence of mere causes.

By this very [argument], even what was stated by Śaṅkara— that "there is no distinction whatsoever," and so forth— is reduced to a mere literary composition, because all means of valid cognition that establish a necessary connection have been exhausted. And although there is no distinction between the causes of palaces and the like and the causes of mountains and the like insofar as their operations are devoid of intention, nevertheless, if there were a difference based on whether they depend upon or do not depend upon an agent possessing effort (prayatnavat), [then the argument would hold].

What is the fault? It is just as, despite the lack of distinction in their being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), there is the distinction between being scratchable by iron and not being scratchable by iron. Furthermore, even though there is no distinction in their being devoid of consciousness (*nirabhijñānatva*), a distinction among these [atoms] must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, how could there be an absolute difference in the nature of their effects (*kāryavaijātya*)?
Therefore, if that potency, even while depending on effort, were capable of [producing] the primary effect as well, what harm would there be?

Furthermore, it is not observed that even for an agent, the accomplishment of a material effect occurs from mere volition alone without the operation of hands and other limbs; so what need is there to mention mountains and the like, which transcend such [human] agency, in the case of mere volition?

If it is argued that hands and other organs are also set in motion by volition (*samīhā*), we reply: it has already been stated that even volition is incapable of doing anything with respect to an object that is already situated, provided there is an absence of activity such as lying down and so forth. Therefore, by whatever power the causes of mountains and the like—having cast aside dependence on the activity of hands and other organs—are not obstructed in their causal operation despite being devoid of intention, by that same power [they produce effects] even without volition.

Who could have faith that they would not transgress? For when, at the time of the appearance of smoke, a rising and thickly formed object is conceived as being produced by fire and fuel, its determination through the absence of one [cause] does not lead to a suspicion of its existence even in the absence of the other; this case is exactly like that.

But if the acceptance of a body [is granted], then the Lord (Īśvara) has been effectively proven by the wise as being limited, non-eternal, manifold, and non-omniscient due to possessing such qualities. By this very fact, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth. For, based on the statement "not of those who are unguided," etc., one does not touch upon any means other than mere observation and non-observation to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [reason]; and that has already been answered. And if...

Observation and non-observation alone are the refuge [of proof]. In that case, just as the performance of an action is observed in one who possesses volition, and thus an inference of one possessing volition is accepted when an effect exists; likewise, since corporeal action is observed only in one who possesses hands and so forth, why is it not determined that the person is inactive when the operation of hands and so forth is impossible? Indeed, there is no lack of validity in the reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*) or in the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

There is a certain distinction. If, however, one were to set aside mere observation and non-observation and there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) restricted to a single [subject], then there would be a cognition established by that one; but in its absence, there is merely a mutual contradiction between those two, not a sublation (*bādhā*), because they are of equal status—this is the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy according to the opponent's intention.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not possess the activity of its own limbs is not observed to be capable of producing a material object, just as a potter is [incapable] when his hands and other limbs are withdrawn from activity. And there is no activity of one's own limbs in the case of the Person (*puruṣa*) under discussion; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Nor is there a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), according to the logic of the chapter on momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Therefore, in reality, another refutation alone is appropriate.

If it is asked, "What opportunity is there for a counter-reason (*pratihetu*)?", we say: no, because this [counter-reason] is presented for the purpose of demonstrating that frequent observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is not a factor in establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*). For if frequent observation were the means, then even such a case [as the counter-example] would be possible; thus, since the methods for grasping pervasion are untenable, it is established that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Or, let it be granted that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs in some way; even so, the hope for the proof of God (*īśvara*) is not fruitful, because there is no certainty regarding the restriction of the intelligent probandum (*sādhya*) to oneness. For if its oneness were established, then its eternality, omnipresence, and omniscience would follow—this is a brief refutation within the section concerning the doctrine of God.

Success [in this argument] would merely superimpose the conventional usage of "Lord" [onto the cause]. However, when it is conceivable that a multitude of effects, characterized by different places and times, has been produced by a plurality of agents exceeding any number, then how can there be omnipresence or eternity? And if [the agent's] establishment consists only in knowing their own respective objects, materials, and so forth, where is the omniscience?

Now, if it is argued that when many [agents] act with distracted minds, the non-production of the effect would follow, and there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its total disappearance; we reply: this suspicion might indeed apply to the activity of multiple lords (īśvara) who possess qualities such as omnipotence individually;
however, in the present case, it is stated that not even one such [lord] is established. Furthermore, numerous beings of limited power [cannot produce] a single or multiple effects.

Indeed, they are seen to begin and bring [the work] to completion. Now, one might argue: "Even in many cases, there must be a single predominant factor, or one that is more powerful—like a master builder or a general; therefore, agency belongs to that one alone, since the others merely follow it. To this we say: No, for even in those cases there is no such rule, as some independent beings, acting according to their own respective purposes, may still collaborate on a single entity or the like.

Because it is observed that even there, it is not the case that only a single first instigator exists, since the longing in the hearts of many cannot be prevented, and because even a lowly person may be an instigator. Therefore, just as in the case of bees, honey-flies, and the creatures of an anthill, by means of small living beings, [the mountain] Maināka and others were brought into being.

What need is there to speak of the possibility of a single agent performing an action for the sake of the entire universe? In that regard, mountains and other such things, whose origins are unobserved, have their conscious agents already inferred by the mere fact of their existence. Furthermore, those small creatures, knowing the extremely minute material cause—the substance of earth and so forth—knowing the instruments, such as pleasure and the like, knowing the recipient of the gift, which is the self, and knowing the purpose, which is the pleasure of continued existence and so forth, act with full awareness.

They would proceed like the creatures in an anthill. Furthermore, even if [the existence of a creator] were established, supervisors would not necessarily be visible, either because their diverse powers and actions project [their presence beyond perception] or because they are remote by nature. As for those things produced by human agency whose production is witnessed in this life, such as trees and the like, there is no doubt there at all. However, even those entities existing in the vicinity of the Vindhya and Yugandhara mountains, whose operation by a person is not seen, are likewise [produced by agents], whether they be *piśācas*...

If [the world] were possessed of agents by means of countless presiding deities of such types and so forth, who could possibly be omniscient? Furthermore, if space and time are indeed distinct [from one another], how can they possess omnipresence and eternity? Nor is there any subverting inference, functioning through the force of real entities, that would counteract such a doubt.
But is it not the case that even you yourselves have not accepted this? It would be better for one who postulates such an extremely difficult hypothesis.

If you argue that the postulation of a Lord (Īśvara) alone is simpler (*lāghava*), that is true—if this were merely a matter of setting aside one hypothesis for another. In that case, we would indeed favor your proposal. However, as long as you do not abandon the pretext of inference (*anumāna*), we must necessarily apply ourselves to a rigorous examination. Now, if it pains your heart to think that the Narmadā and other rivers were fashioned by a lowly, uncountable number [of beings]?
It is even more so because they were created by a single bodiless being (*aśarīra*). Therefore, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone is the most powerful;
the state of the object exists exactly as it establishes it. For this very reason, that [valid cognition] is examined with firmness, and there is no concession whatsoever to trivial matters.
(Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali, 260)

Let the arrangement of the world be created by beings— whether small or large, invisible or visible, equal or superior in power, independent, or accompanied by single individuals regarded as primary— forming boundless herds that know only their own respective tasks, whether gross or subtle, singular or multiple, such as the material causes and so forth, and who are included within the six states of existence; however, let there not be a single creator of this.

Nor is there an exclusion of the reason from the Buddhist [position], because he does not accept it in that way; for if there were exclusion from even one [of the two positions], it would follow that the reason is excluded from both.

Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta*), there is no dependence upon the acceptance of another. This is because there is no contradiction in abandoning mere acceptance. Thus, when "merely possessing intelligence" (*buddhimattvamātra*) is the probandum, since [the property] characterized by knowledge of the material cause and so forth is inseparable from it, [the reason] directly [establishes] the material cause and so forth—

Alternatively, the proof of the desired [conclusion] through the establishment of a creator who possesses supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) is not conclusive, because it is not established that every causal activity has a single creator. Furthermore, if one were to prove merely a creator who possesses knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, it would be futile, like the stories in the *Mahābhārata* and similar works. Therefore, since there is no other means of proof, the intended proof of [the Lord] endowed with qualities such as omniscience must proceed from this very [argument]; thus, the refutation should be stated specifically with reference to that, as it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Thus, it is established that [the definition] is "the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the statement beginning with "to whatever extent the comprehension of the object... and so forth is difficult to refute. Even though the establishment of a particular [property] is drawn forth by the connection with the universal of the probandum (*sādhya*), its proof remains dependent upon the means of proof (*sādhana*) alone; for the means of proof is presented solely for that purpose, and there is no other means of proof.

For even for a Buddhist, the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is indeed dependent upon proof. If the proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) were to achieve its purpose even in the absence of selflessness, then what would the establishment of selflessness have to do with the proof of momentary flux? As for you [the opponent], however, having set aside the establishment of omniscience and so forth, you have instead established a specific distinction characterized by the knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so on.

It is not the case that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is demonstrated in the example preceded by the introduction of the self (*ātman*); thus, [your objection] is irrelevant. Even if that concomitance were perceived directly, the necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatva*) of the general property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) must still be demonstrated. And that is impossible, because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the substratum of all actions as a single entity.

For this very reason, Vācaspati’s own pretense at proving omniscience has also been refuted by this same argument. However, once an omniscient creator is established, our effort in determining the oneness of that creator becomes subject to censure; therefore, we shall desist. As for the negative inference (*vyatireki-prayoga*) that he [Vācaspati] states:

That too has been refuted precisely because singularity is not established, since it has already been demonstrated that even if cognition is impermanent and has all things as its object, the perception of the material cause and so forth is still possible. As for the resolution offered by Vītoka, it is like [the inference of] the exclusion of a mountain from smoke; however, [it fails to establish] the five-colored crest of flames of fire.

It would follow that even a cloth could be inferred [as having an agent]. If you say there is no such capacity here [in the case of a cloth], then in that case as well, the capacity lies precisely in the exclusion of non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavaccheda*). Even if an effortful agent is established for a mountain, since its oneness is not certain, how can the proof of omniscience be established?
But surely, because even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is an effect, its agent must necessarily be one who perceives the atoms which are its material cause.

[He] must be sought after; yet it is not possible for those with the fleshly eye to be so [as He]. Otherwise, what offense have we committed against you, such that in the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*) there is a brief refutation, while we ourselves do not exist in that manner? Therefore, if a creator who perceives beyond the senses is necessarily accepted, it is logical that he be none other than God (*īśvara*). That too—

Whatever [is said]: for even the capacity of the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is not common to all, since we observe an excellence of sensory acuity even among those far inferior to us, such as vultures and the like. Furthermore, by virtue of a particular power of karma, some who are extremely minute might even perceive atoms (*paramāṇu*), just as ants perceive odor-atoms that are beyond our range. And...

For those who perceive that subtle [object] consisting of the mere elements (*tanmātra*), would there be the apprehension of another subtle object separated by space and time, or rather of every gross object?
In neither case is there any hope for establishing the existence of God on that basis alone.
No.

If that is so, let there be the possibility of perceiving the atom; but how could there be such a possibility regarding all the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) and the specific *dharmas*, *adharmas*, and latent dispositions (*āśayas*) inherent in them? Not at all. For in the example of the potter, the performance of an action is not seen to be pervaded by a complete knowledge of the nature of the *kṣetrajña* and so forth; rather, its accomplishment is held to occur through the cognition of the recipient (*sampradāna*) and the instruments (*upakaraṇa*). And that [cognition] is impossible.

Because [the intended meaning] cannot be established through the force of the context, since the cognition of that alone is sufficient according to the sequence already stated; and because, since the object (karman) is intended as oneself, its status as the recipient (sampradāna) is unavoidable—just as in the expression "he builds a house for himself. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a logical deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the requirement for the cognition of a recipient.

If it is argued that another person who knows the recipient must exist there as the one being inferred, we say no; for since deviation is observed, the fact that the agent's knowledge of the recipient is necessarily concomitant [with the action] is unestablished, and thus the possibility of inference is absent. Furthermore, its status as an "agent" cannot be relative to the inferred object. For if this were so, it would follow that even the potter would not be the agent [of his own action], and due to the absence of a graspable pervasion (*vyāpti*), the state of inference remains as before.

[The opponent's] arguments are as follows: Therefore, since whatever constitutes agency necessarily depends upon knowledge of the recipient (*sampradāna*), one must also accept that one's own self is the recipient.

Nor is he [the Lord] capable of knowing the nature of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), setting aside even the recipients well-known in worldly usage, nor those comprised by the term "instruments" for the sake of the various latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) and their objects. Consequently, just as a potter, though not knowing them [as such], is a knower of his instruments through his very knowledge of the staff, the wheel, and so forth; [so too is the Lord].
Even if living beings were to be inferred in such a manner, they would still be perceived through the knowledge of their own hands, faces, and so forth.

Whence, then, could there come this comprehensive knowledge of the nature of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and the distinctions between its respective merits (*dharma*) and demerits (*adharma*)? Furthermore, for one who is bodiless, what connection can there be with the activity of one's own limbs? And of what sort could even the attainment of perfection (*siddhi*) be for one who is bodiless? For it is only when unity [with the body] is established that one is a possessor of a body.

Since a limited being is not capable of all actions, there is no hope for the accomplishment of a bodiless state (*aśarīra-siddhi*) by implication; furthermore, it has been stated that [the creator's] oneness is difficult to establish.

Moreover, even if one were bodiless, since instruments such as the rod, the discus, hands, and faces would be impossible, it follows by elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the knowledge of instruments must consist solely in the knowledge of the various latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya-bheda*). This is for the sake of elegance. [This is so] because even space, time, inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth, which are included among the instruments, are known through that [knowledge].
Because one’s purpose is fulfilled by the mere knowledge of that [object].

But what is this distinction, such that for one in that state there is knowledge of the instruments [of action] through the knowledge of direction and so forth alone, and not through the knowledge of *dharma*, *adharma*, and the like? If it is argued that there should be knowledge of both, that is incorrect; for [the knowledge] does not extend to every instrument...

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, it is observed that an agent must necessarily know the object of knowledge. However, we do not maintain the certainty that the cognition of the instrument [of action] occurs solely through the cognition of direction (*dig*) and so forth, such that a specific inquiry could be made; rather, because other instruments are possible, there is no resting place for the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

To this it is said: Just as among various agents—whether superior or inferior—a state of "knowledge of instruments" is observed through a succession of absences of tools such as the staff, the wheel, the shuttle, and the loom, but rather through other external instruments such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; is it the case that this [state] remains even today in that same way?
Or must it be by taking up merit and the like? This is indeed a doubt. However, if there were no other instrument, then the explanation would be by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

It would be fitting [to say he shines]. And when there is doubt regarding the path to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), what could such a person—who is designated as "Lord" (*īśvara*)—do for us, being devoid of wealth?

Therefore, even if he were bodiless, there would be no drawing forth of knowledge regarding *dharma* and so forth; how much less so when that [bodilessness] is unestablished? Let it not be [claimed] that he serves as an instrument.

It is argued that the knower of dharma and so forth must necessarily exist as its effect; for since the agent is the perceiver of the form and other qualities of the effect, and he is God, this too is hollow. For those who perform acts such as giving and non-violence perceive them merely in their own nature; they do not become God by that alone. Nor is another person established as a knower of that [dharma] through its effects. Furthermore, the determination of something as dharma or adharma applies even to the one who performs it.

It is not necessarily so, as in the case of a potter. For those who perform such actions, since there is no certainty regarding their true nature (*tattva*), the certainty of that true nature—on the grounds that it is an effect—cannot establish a creator who is none other than Īśvara. Indeed, even the determination of what constitutes merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) remains a correct one whose very existence is still doubtful. How, then, can there be hope from that? For [the agent] is of a nature characterized by volitions (*saṅkalpa*) whose suspicion of error has not been dispelled.

Furthermore, because they accept [the existence of] divine beings, those who remember their past lives, and so forth through the gateway of scriptural authority (*āgama*), even they possess at least a slight understanding of the connection between right action and its fruit. Yet, this alone does not suffice for sovereignty.
Thus, since God is unproven, the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all living beings are not merely instruments (*upakaraṇa*) for Him, but rather the actual causes [of their own results].
Thus, for the wise, the meaning of the first verse is that which is to be accepted regarding the diversity of the world.
The refutation of Īśvara is completed.
The Seven Verses on the Vārttika (Vārttikasaptaślokī)

If [the reason] is established in terms of activity, structural configuration, specific purposeful action, and so forth, then there is either the proof of what is already accepted, a lack of proof, or doubt regarding the example. (12)

That which is established—namely, the arrangement and so forth—which follows the presence or absence of an intelligent controller, is joined with that [controller]; therefore, it is from this that [the controller] is inferred. (13)

It is not logical to infer [the presence of] fire from something that is established as distinct in its actual entity, merely because it is non-different through the identity of the word, as in the case of a white substance and so forth. (14)
Otherwise, because a potter produces some modification of clay such as a jar and so forth, it would follow that even an anthill is his creation. (15)
Because it follows from the probandum even when the effect is established by means of a general property as the reason,
the fault of stating a distinction based on a difference in related entities is considered "balancing the effect" (kāryasama).

Because one observes a commonality of the word for something well-known in another class of beings, it is not logical to use that as a proof [for the same thing], just as the presence of horns does not prove that speech and other such things possess "cowness. (17)

Since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, they do not exist anywhere [independently]. However, if the establishment of an object were to follow from their mere existence, then everything would be established for everyone. (18)
In the first chapter of the *Pramāṇavārttika*, within the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*), this is the commentary on the seven verses of the *Vārtika*.
I bow with full conviction to Him whose teaching is unimpeded, who proclaimed that the world— devoid of an independent creator— is a manifold variety produced by karma.

Having established the negation of eternal validity, the skillful author, demonstrating that invalidity resides in non-eternal entities, says: "This path removes the portion of delusion regarding that specific aspect."

Even if one has personally refuted the arguments of another, if there is no satisfaction in merely citing the name of the author of the *Vārttika* when those arguments fail to connect, then it is better to exert one's effort through a further description of that very argument itself.

Whatever is an effect is preceded by an intelligent agent, just as a pot; and the earth, mountains, and so forth are effects. Alternatively, whatever is not preceded by an intelligent agent is not an effect, just as space; and trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth are effects. Thus, in meaning, this is the reason based on being an effect (*kāryahetu*). Likewise, [the reasons] consist of having non-conscious material causes (*acetanopādānatva*) and performing purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Since it is to be established that [the object] possesses a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts and that it has the property of engaging in causal activities after having remained stationary for a time,
how can it be said that [the cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge even with respect to what is impermanent?

And this proof is indeed common to both the eternal and the non-eternal. However, when proceeding toward the demonstration of non-eternality, the opponent’s search for valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) would proceed; the mention of the word "non-eternal" is merely for the purpose of introducing that [proof]. It is not, however, that we maintain the Blessed One to be non-eternal in an absolute sense. For instance:
The one, all-pervading, omniscient, and eternal Lord known as Īśvara, who is the sole basis of consciousness and the creator of the world,
is accepted as the authoritative means [of knowledge] and is to be sought by those desiring heaven and liberation.

To this it is replied: Is the desire to establish the excellence of the Supreme Person—who is the abode of the multitude of qualities taught by these very reasons—accomplished by these reasons alone, or rather by the force of other reasons? In that regard, the first position is not tenable. For instance, a proof establishes only as much of the object as it pervades; it does not establish anything beyond that. Indeed, an object is not pervaded merely by one's wish.

The capacity of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) extends only as far as its own efficacy reaches; however, the establishment of an object occurs by means of that [cognition] to the extent that the means of valid cognition is capable. Furthermore, even though being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth is pervaded (*vyāpta*) by having been preceded by an intelligent agent, it is not capable of producing a cognition restricted to [the agent's] oneness and other such qualities, because no pervasion is perceived with respect to those specific attributes; otherwise, there would be a contrary form [of pervasion].

This is because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that even certainty [would be undermined]. For no one, having perceived smoke pervaded by the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*), is able to infer a fire characterized by a beautiful mass of five-colored flickering flames.

[Objection: "But even so, by the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), one indeed infers a specific qualification of place and time; likewise, for one who has perceived that being an effect in the case of a mountain and so forth depends upon the superintendence of an intelligent agent, the desired conclusion will be established by the logic of a *siddhānta* based on the locus. [Reply: No, because the capacity [of the reason] is untenable. For just as by fire associated with this particular place and time...

In the inference from smoke and so forth, the capacity [of the reason] lies in the fact that what is being produced does not possess the same place and time [as the cause]; however, we do not perceive such an impossibility—such as the trees' inability to be arranged in rows—without [postulating] a conscious agent endowed with qualities like unity and omniscience. Therefore, even if the establishment of the potter's capacity to produce [the jar] occurs by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), it cannot support the specific [conclusion] we desire.
Enough!
Surely, if one who is capable of creating mountains and the like has been established as the *siddha*, what else is being sought?
Why then is there satisfaction with a mere denoter (*vācaka*) whose denoted form (*vācyarūpa*) remains unestablished? For in this way, the intended subject matter at hand cannot be proven.

For the operation of production is nothing more than the state of being invariably antecedent to the effect about to arise; and this [operation] is established as common to both the insentient and the intellect (*buddhi*), and is not restricted by specific qualities such as non-omnipresence. Therefore, with respect to the intended probandum, there is nothing gained by a mere verbal assertion.

But who indeed asserts that mountains and such things are preceded by an omniscient being? Rather, suspecting that they mean "they have an intelligent cause," [the author] says, while inwardly mocking the proof:
"In regard to activity after remaining still, specific structures, purposeful action, and so forth..."
Regarding the phrase "the desired conclusion is established":
for it is accepted that the entire aggregate of things is produced by both common and uncommon karma; and since karma is insentient by nature, [this applies to] omniscience.
The sense is: what undesirable consequence for us do the oceans, mountains, and so forth bring about when they remain unestablished as causes?

Furthermore, if the intention were that the probandum consists merely of those [general properties], then since no contradiction would be established, there would follow the absurdity of the futility of presenting the proof. Therefore, it is only a specific property as it has been presented that is the probandum by this [reasoning]. And it has already been stated that the power of the proof does not extend to that [specificity]. Let it be so.

In that case, since such establishment would arise from another means of proof alone, he says "or non-establishment" (*asiddhir vā*) while pointing out the absence of certainty with respect to the second alternative.
The meaning is that there is neither another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor another logical reason (*hetu*) by which this certainty might arise. Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows:]
Since perception is impossible because [the object] is beyond the senses, inference must be invoked; and for that purpose, he says, with reference to every reason:
"In the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*), the commentary on the *Vārtika* on the seven verses states, 'or there is non-establishment' (*asiddhiḥ*)."

For, although by the aforementioned inference a conscious being who is the creator of all things is established in a manner common to all disputants, there is no reason that indicates any specific attribute which is not unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), with the exception of mere existence (*sattā*). This is because there is no occasion for an inference regarding a property that exceeds mere existence. However, since existence itself implies momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), he speaks [of it] in contrast to permanence and unity (*nityaikatva*).

"Or non-establishment" means the establishment of the opposite. For, just like [the proof of] non-dharma and so forth, since refutation is intended here even regarding the eternal by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), just as in the case of the opponent's proof, the mention of "non-eternal" results merely in the introduction [of the argument]. [The reason is] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*).
At midday,
it is said that the example is unestablished;
because pervasion does not exist in the ultimate sense, there is no perception [of it] in the example, and therefore, by means of that, no property whatsoever—
It is stated that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. However, even if all cognition exists, there is no realization of its being a pervasive [property]. Why? He says:
"Because there is doubt regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)."

Thus, because it is impossible for one with limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) to ascertain [the object] in its specific nature as a reality, the aforementioned means of proof do not establish [the existence of God] either directly or by the logic of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established incidentally), nor through any other means of proof. Thus, the absence of any proving instrument (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) is established; and since the desired conclusion is established regarding that which lacks those specific qualities, [the opponent's position fails].

Alternatively, when reasons such as "being an effect" (kāryatva) have been put forward, he states that there is a proof or a lack of proof based on the distinction between the generality and the particular of the probandum (sādhya). In that regard, since the proponent's position is already established through the well-known fact of being an action (karma), proving what is already proven (siddhasādhana) is evident; thus, demonstrating the absence of concomitance (anugama) regarding the particular—which would otherwise lead to a lack of proof—he says:

"Or there is non-establishment [of the reason] in the example, or else doubt," where "of the probandum" is understood from the context. In that regard, since a potter and the like—who possess qualities contrary to omnipresence and so forth—are established without dispute, there is non-establishment of the intended [probandum] in the example. Alternatively, if it is intended that the portion of the self distinct from the body possesses omnipresence and so forth, despite being by nature difficult to distinguish [from the body], [then the following applies].

"Such is the opinion; nevertheless, let there be doubt—what is the point of insisting on this matter now? This is the sense. "The probandum is already established by the general [definition]" (*sāmānyasiddhasādhyatā*), as stated in *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* (268).

Therefore, because the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhya) or because its probandum-property is doubtful, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) of "being an effect" and so forth with the probandum in the example;
thus, due to the very non-establishment of the specific [reason], the inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) is a fault of the logical reason (hetu).
Now, even in the case of the concomitance of smoke—

"There is no concomitance in the particular, and in the universal there is the proving of what is already proven"—this is the same logic [applied here]. Therefore, for these two [the particular and the universal], validity is not restricted to one or the other, nor is it anything else. If it were restricted? That would not be a sound consideration. For, inference does not attain its status as valid cognition while disregarding the establishment of the particular.

Siddham. But that specific qualification (*viśeṣa*)—characterized as the mere exclusion of non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavacchedamātra*)—may exist either as distinct from that [subject] or not, as in "there is fire here because of smoke," or in such a form? In that regard, if the first [type of distinction] were denied, there would be a repudiation of inference itself, since even the establishment of what is distinct is rooted in it. Nor can that [first type] be refuted without following the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). [For] it is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)...

For if that which is established as being invariably concomitant with something were to be separated from the subject (*dharmin*) by its very existence as a self-nature (*svarūpasattā*), while not showing it to be inseparable from that [concomitant], then— unless one is dealing with the context of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) where dependence on time and so forth is excluded— it would indeed be separated. As for the second type of establishment, however, since it is to be proven by that alone, even though it does not occur without the pursuit of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), which is necessarily tied to the apprehension of the specific quality produced by that [reason], [the reason remains valid].

It is not capable of negating inference in general, because even by establishing the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) through a property that lacks those specific features [of inference], that [negation] has already achieved its purpose. However, there might be a negation of a specific type of inference, such as when someone, intending to infer a peacock with a five-colored crest,

employs the proof "there is fire here because of smoke," and is then met by another with the objections of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and lack of concomitance (*ananugama*).
In that case, one who asserts that even inference would not exist here because of the total abolition of smoke when challenged, might indeed appear wise;

yet it would not be the case that inference itself is abolished, for at that very moment, the inference of the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*) is being accepted by him as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore:
The refutation [of the other positions] is based solely on the exclusion of non-connection with the subject (pakṣāyogavyavaccheda).
As for the others, the refutation consists in the fact that they either prove what is already established or lack positive concomitance (anvaya).
It is not held that these two [reasons] are fixed as either fallacious or non-fallacious; rather, their status is twofold depending on the difference in the object of inference.

Similarly here, having accepted the exclusion of the impossibility of being presided over by an intelligent agent (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhāna*) in the case of the ocean, mountains, and so forth, it is quite logical to urge that for one who raises an objection against these [reasons] with respect to some other intended specific qualification, there would follow the total destruction of the inference regarding the flame of a lamp.

There is no annihilation of inference. Therefore, it is correct that validity or invalidity is not restricted to a single [universal] category with respect to specific types of inference, but rather depends on the particular case; this is not so in a general sense.
This concludes the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda). 269.
Now, one might object: "Even now, since difference is established without depending on continuity (*anvaya*), what prevents it from being established in another instance of difference? [We reply:
Indeed, there is no establishment whatsoever that is devoid of continuity. For continuity as a universal (*sāmānya*) is incapable of remaining without drawing forth that particular (*viśeṣa*).
Nor can it be claimed that it necessarily possesses this power with respect to every other particular, as was described previously.

Otherwise, an inference based on [the presence of] five-colored tufts of hair and so forth would be difficult to avoid. Here, the objection regarding impossibility (*asambhava*) and so on applies equally even to a person possessing a single-pointed mind (*ekacittatva*). A similar formulation of such an inference applies there as well. Therefore, one who asserts a specific distinction must necessarily demonstrate a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); since that is absent, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when proving merely "one possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat-mātra*).
And thus it is established that this is a case of proving what is already proven (siddhasādhana).

It might be argued as follows: "Intelligent" does not mean merely possessing consciousness, but rather one who is cognizant of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, or one who possesses effort (*prayatna*). Since such a being is established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of effects like jars and the like, the fact that "being an effect" is perceived even in the case of the mountain and other such things establishes a creator of that very same kind; thus, neither of the two aforementioned faults applies. For instance, he is cognizant of their material causes and so forth...

If it is argued that "the Omniscient One is thus [one], and being restricted by place and time, a distinction between them (multiple omniscient beings) could not be capable of accomplishing the collection of effects when they are brought into operation; therefore, attributes such as eternality and omnipresence are also established for Him," this is like the hope for fruit and enjoyment from a tree whose roots have been severed. For these qualities are established only if His oneness is established; otherwise, for one who exists at different places and times...

If it is possible for many agents to produce a single effect, whose are these powers and so forth? And since each would only know the scope of his own respective activity, whose omniscience could there be?
If unity were established, then the entire range of what is to be proven would be encompassed; yet there is no basis whatsoever for the certain determination of that [unity].
It exists. Nor is its existence established by the use of the singular number [in the word "creator"], because one who is capable of fashioning earth and so forth has not been proven;

for there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If such a connection were established, how could an opponent disregard that which possesses proven unity? However, this may indeed apply with respect to a genus (*jāti*), as in the case of fire inferred from various successive instances of smoke; thus, there is no insistence on a specific individual. Furthermore, even in the case of a variegated painting...

Just as the existence of a single creator is established through the persistence of similar lines and so forth, the oneness of that [creator] is established by the persistence of specific qualities across different effects; for no such persisting entity is actually perceived. Furthermore, the properties being observed—such as "being an effect" or "being an entity"—cannot prove oneness, just as in the case of a painting; for even when other qualities are possible, there remains only doubt as to whether the creator is one or many who are similar.

Furthermore, even in the absence of that [direct perception], is there a single certainty? This is certainly like painting on a wall—that is, when there is no certainty regarding non-difference, omniscience and so forth are nonetheless determined.
But the other says: "In this very way, you too must understand [the object] through the production of an effect. How? Through the contradiction of many..."

If the minds were independent, there would be mutual contradiction and a lack of mutual awareness of intentions favorable to one another; consequently, there would be a non-production of effects simultaneously, as well as the undesirable consequence of the destruction of what has already been produced. In this regard, it is considered here by many that the non-production of simultaneous effects [arises] from [the nature of] the instruments, and thus [the causes] belong to different times.

The intended meaning is that there is no production of effects for [multiple] locations, or else the position is that it belongs to a single great composite whole (mahāvayavin) in the form of a mountain and so forth.

In that case, we see no contradiction in production even when multiple [causes] act upon a single [locus]. For just as there is activity on the part of one, so too might there be for others, as in the case of an anthill. If it is asked, "With what purpose in mind do they act?"—the answer is: no, because their activity is manifold.

Because of the inability to determine the specific cause for the activity of minds other than one's own, it would be impossible to persist in the inquiry as to what the Lord himself intended; or rather, such an inquiry could be sustained by those capable of discerning the sublation of others' intentions and so forth,
but not by the Lord, who is of a gentle nature.

Nor can a rule of mutual pervasion among many [causes] be established, since we observe the construction of anthills by ants alone. If it is argued that such a thing is possible for humans due to their competitive striving (*ahamahamikā*), [we reply: even those who possess discernment and undertake a single task exist; thus, when one massive object is produced in succession by others of that same kind in great abundance, [the rule fails].

Since [the simultaneous production of multiple effects] is possible, what consideration do we have for human agents? Nor has the simultaneous production of things such as the Yugandhara mountains ever been observed anywhere, by virtue of which one might suppose that the capacity belongs to a single individual. Furthermore, even among humans, it is impossible to maintain a rule of non-contradiction through competitive rivalry (*ahamahamikā*), because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in a person without mutual conflict. Therefore:

This is merely a conjecture and does not follow the path of valid cognition; thus, it deserves no serious consideration, whether as the claim that "the manifold cannot be produced by a single [cause]" or as a mere recollection of conventional doctrine.
But surely, even in the case of many [causes], there must be a single predominant factor that is more powerful, like a master builder or a general?

If it is argued that, therefore, agency belongs to that one alone because the others merely follow him—[35b] we say no, because even in that case there is no such restriction; for we observe that some independent beings, acting according to their own respective purposes, may still collaborate on a single task, such as building a house.
Furthermore, there is no rule that in such cases only one must be the primary instigator, since many may simultaneously have such an impulse in their hearts.

Because there is no one to prevent it, or because even a subordinate factor can be a motivator; yet mere [motivation] does not constitute primacy, as that would contradict common worldly experience. Furthermore, even if a massive undertaking were possible through innumerable caravans—each consisting of countless individuals acting as architects—what kind of fulfillment of desire could possibly result? By this, [the notion of] a primary agent among the creatures of an anthill is also refuted.
The objection regarding the assignment [of parts] has already been answered.

Furthermore, just as a specific arrangement of components such as comfortable cushions is perceived in a palace being constructed by many people following a single design, it is not so in the case of [buildings] composed of masses of irregularly placed large stones.

Even in the case of mountains, by that same reasoning, they too would have to be preceded by a single predominant Puruṣa; therefore, since multiple operations are incapable of being sublated when producing each individual Kailāsa and so forth, how could they be sublated in the case of entities situated in various distant places and times?
In the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), there is the commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī*.

If it is argued that "the proof of unity [of the self] is established through scripture," this is merely like performing a protective rite (*rakṣābandha*) with poison for one who has fallen ill from a combined affliction;
it is not at all a refutation directed toward the Buddhists, whose minds are solely adept in investigating scripture. For if scripture were accepted only after critical examination...

Therefore, since this very moment is the time for examination, why insist on it now? Or, if it is independent of examination, then let the establishment of all desired objects proceed from that alone; what is the use of this addiction to presenting inference, which consists of nothing but the labor of effort? For it is indeed arduous.

The endeavor to purify the cause is easy for those whose intellects are devoid of subtle penetration; however, the attainment of one's desired goal through the mere recitation of a portion of the scriptures is difficult for them.

Furthermore, even this very proponent, while establishing the authority of the scriptures, [argues that] if they were not authoritative, [there would be no distinction] among all those in the stages of life.

As for the argument that "corroboration" (*saṃvāda*) is not a valid means of knowledge—because if it were not a means of knowledge, it would be possible for there to be even a lack of corroboration due to the cognition of some invalidity, and because the rule of corroboration is applicable only to means of knowledge such as perception and the like—it follows that the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are not non-means of knowledge, since they serve as instruments for producing corroborated knowledge for all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*), just like perception and the like; thus he recites this five-membered syllogism (*pañcālaka*). That too [is refuted].

It is employed precisely within the assembly of disciples; for indeed, what is called "corroboration" (saṃvāda) would have to be either consistency with another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or causal efficacy (arthakriyā), and neither of these two applies here, as in the case of [the statement]:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads."
"He knows all, yet there is no knower of him" (cf. Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).

In the sense of such statements as "The one God existed, generating heaven and earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.5.11), or in rites such as the Agniṣṭoma which are means for attaining heaven, there may be some possibility for someone [to have such a realization].

If it is argued that, just as for one member of an order (āśramin) there is the conviction that "there exists a single, all-pervading, eternal creator of the world," so too is it for another, and their practice conforms to that—then we reply: this conviction of theirs must either originate from that same scripture, or from another similar source, or consist of a mere accidental conceptual construction; it cannot, however, take the form of perception or inference, because [the creator] is not...

Because there is the possibility of even ascetics providing an opportunity for error, perception and the other means of knowledge are not faultless when it comes to other persons. However, knowledge based on scripture would not exist for one who does not respect it; or rather, it might arise through the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from practice in another life, but not for anyone else—this is logical. In that regard, this is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it could occur whether the object exists or does not exist.

[This is] due to repeated practice and [the resulting] production. By virtue of its originating from that [scripture], it is said to be consistent with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for since it originates from such [a source], that [other cognition] would also lack validity. This is the principle: "that which is unestablished cannot be proven by what is unestablished.
Therefore...

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, this is merely a recollection of such a tradition, namely that "there exists someone of such a kind. Furthermore, we understand that even the term "āśrama" (stage of life) is a mere designation; consequently, the qualification "of all those belonging to the stages of life" (*samastāśramiṇām*) is unestablished, because no consensus is established with the Buddhists, the Digambaras, and others.

Furthermore, since even one with a contrary understanding may possess some degree of agreement, the presentation [of such agreement] is not fruitful. For this very reason, the absolute cessation of disagreement—which would establish validity—is unproven;
for validity might even arise from the power of a common delusion that has persisted since beginningless time among those in the [four] stages of life (*āśramin*), so this argument is trivial.
Therefore, even regarding a single object such as Mount Mandara,

among those who possess effort and who perceive the various parts that are the objects of the activities of countless persons, who is the "knower of all"? Furthermore, if such things are produced by beings situated in different places and times, how can [the creator] possess attributes such as eternity and omnipresence?

Nor is there any room for knowledge of an unseen portion [of the effect], since it is observed that even without such [an agent], a potter brings about the production of the object of his own activity.
