Furthermore, there is no logical connection whatsoever to the consequence that what is produced by many must necessarily be destroyed; thus, when unity is lost, the inevitable conclusion regarding omniscience and so forth is not accepted. This being the case, this [argument] is likewise entirely groundless.

As it has been said: "Even if they were many and omniscient, because they would be the makers of everything, there would be no proof for their simultaneous engagement in effects restricted by specific place and time," since a single substratum for both omniscience and action is not established. For this very reason, the consequence that the admission of "many" and so forth would result in the abandonment of "one" is not a valid objection; for if it were established that there are many who are both omniscient and all-powerful creators, then the refutation of "one" [would indeed follow].

The instrument itself would become useless, and a far greater effort would have to be admitted. But when a multitude of beings—like the creatures in an anthill—is brought together as the producer of each single effect, while remaining untouched by the primary qualities (guṇas), then what loss is there? For it is not those very [qualities] that are [the producers] at that time.
"They should be sought after by those desiring heaven and liberation"—
by this [statement], even that which some think, namely, that God (Īśvara) must also be manifold just like your own omniscient ones, is also [refuted].

[The opponent’s position is] untenable, because not even a single basis for all [cognitive] activities is established. For us, however, the establishment of omniscience does not proceed from every single activity, but rather from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). And since that practice is possible because conceptualizations of all forms to be directly perceived are possible, it follows a "possibility-inference" (*sambhavānumāna*).
Thus, the proof of such omniscience—just as it might belong to one, so too could it belong to another—is accepted; therefore, there is no fault.
If it is argued that "then all creation will come about through practice alone"—no, because it is impossible.

For instance, the production of stationary beings or the attainment of the state of mobile beings is not the fruit of practice. Even when imagining the construction of other remaining replicas, one might think, "let it be thus," but one cannot say, "let this very thing which is currently perceived be so."

The certainty that forests and such things are not so [independent] arises because inference based on possibility does not apply when there is a specific objective. Even in that regard, in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), it is difficult to find [a solution]; for the practice of that [meditation] is dependent upon the excellence of external requisites, and thus it is not as easy as the transformation of the mind alone (*cittamātraparāvṛtti*).

[Objection: Determination [is sufficient]; what is the use of craftsmanship when there is dependence on excellence of power and assistance? If it is argued that "it is without proof that he lacks the capacity without that [craftsmanship], because we see it to be so elsewhere," [we reply]: No, for the construction of the body while in the womb and so forth occurs according to a perceived sequence.
Because of [the lack of] attainment, that [agency] must necessarily be devoid of power; nor is there any certainty regarding a path for the sake of acquiring such power.

Or, let it be granted that there is the accomplishment of pervasive craftsmanship and that "practice" is included by the word "etcetera"; even so, he says: regarding the causes such as the arrangement [of parts], there is either the proof or the non-proof of the desired non-agency; it is indeed non-proof, because of the absence of utility.

For the hells and such have no utility whatsoever for the practitioner who seeks experience; even in the creation of mere instruments of pleasure, there is no purpose. Since one's own supreme good can be attained through effort, those [hells] would otherwise exist [as obstacles], or else living beings would not experience happiness. At most, for those ignorant of that path, the instruction of it alone is a source of grace; therefore, for that purpose, the path—

The practice of direct realization alone is superior; thus, there is no practice [of other means] due to their futility and lack of certainty. If that is so, one might ask: even if there were practice of knowledge regarding every single atom, or even if all instruments were employed, why would there be no harm? To this he says: "in the case of the knower of all things," or else, there is doubt regarding the illustrative example.

Thus, because the position of the "omniscient through application" (*upayukta-sarvajña*) is what will be primarily discussed; or else, the meaning is that in that case there is doubt regarding futility and lack of determination, rather than a certainty of non-existence. Furthermore, since "enunciation" (*uddeśa*) is defined as presentation elsewhere [in the context], it does not share the same status as the opponent's view.
Consequently, even if those possessing effort are established by the reasons under discussion, there is no damage to our position.

If it is argued: "Is it not indeed undesirable to you that the Gandhamādana mountains and so forth were produced by a multitude of beings possessed of effort? Therefore, since no other cause is possible, an intelligent agent who is excluded from multiple [causes] must be established as the sole creator of all effects; and thus, he also revives such qualities as omniscience. This is not so, because a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the object and the desire [of the agent] is untenable. That—

Since the negation [of the probandum] from multiple [alternatives] once it has been established is not a means of proof; and if the opponent should somehow not accept this, then he must be propitiated through prostration, sweet words, and so forth— this is not the proper method, for even a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is not applicable against an independent [opponent].
For there is no lack of clarity in its destruction, nor is multiplicity intended for it.
"Because its operation results in the opposite [of what is intended].

Now, in either case, it is indeed undesirable for the opponent; for the entire world of sentient beings is not held to be a cause by way of effort, but rather solely through the sovereignty of karma characterized by consciousness. Therefore, [the reason] is not invariably concomitant with effort.

If it is argued that the probans— whether being a single effect or multiple effects— places [the subject] in proximity to an agent possessing effort, and thus serves as a means for establishing exactly what is undesired [by the proponent], then is this probans now set forth merely to establish something undesired by the opponent, or rather to establish one's own thesis? And in that case, regarding what is desired by the opponent...
He says this in order to state that there is no result whatsoever from the presentation of a proof regarding whether the self is established or unestablished:
"Whether there is the establishment of what is desired or its non-establishment, in regard to persistence, activity, and so forth.
The sense is that this is identical for both sides, because it is based on the statement of a member of the proof and thus results in futility (*ānarthakya*). Nor does the opponent...

Thus it is for the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādī*), because the two-fold undesirable consequence being leveled against him would be [merely] a pretense of beauty. For his own undesirable consequence—namely, the very reality of the world’s being eternal, unitary, and omniscient, which is relevant to the present context—is what he has begun to establish, not just anything at all. If this is so, then even when a proof is presented, one must state what the basis for its non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—
that there is a lack of positive concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to particulars—

even though there may be non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding the positive concomitance with respect to attributes such as being omnipresent or omniscient, according to the circumstances, nevertheless, by way of oneness...

Let it not be that, upon the establishment of a single agent possessing that one effort, the entire probandum is established. Anticipating the objection that a single potter is seen to be the maker of many jars, pots, and so forth, [the author] states, in the context of the example, while establishing the positive concomitance even in the case of unity: "In the example..."

Thus [it is said]. The term "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) carries over. This is the intended meaning: it is not the case that because a specific effect such as a jar or a pot was made by one person, everything must likewise be so; for in those cases, the activity of multiple potters and others is clearly perceived. Therefore, how can there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a single active agent for effects that are actually observed? Alternatively, is there some single being called a "potter"?

This collection of material cognitions is the object of designations such as "potter" and so forth, or it is a composite of hands and feet. The meaning is that, in reality, by which single factor does the perception of a pot or the like become an object of experience?
Now, what is the point of this insistence? Whatever kind of thing is seen to be the object of a single conventional usage, such is [the nature of the entity].

If a single creator, whose very nature is composite, were established as one who knows the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth of everything, he would be established as omniscient (*sarvajña*). Therefore, even if other qualities are set aside, his worthiness of being accepted is justified by that much alone, as he proclaims both types of human goals (*puruṣārtha*); thus, there is no flaw here. Even in this position, all these reasons—such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so on—are rendered inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) by that very [omniscient being].
Intending to demonstrate the inconclusiveness [of the reason], he says: "This is not a commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of Īśvara."

"Or there is doubt" means that the subject of the doubt is the "probandum" (sādhya). This is because, although there is the state of being an effect due to its being a mere composite and its possession of configuration and so forth—just as in the case of a potter—there is nonetheless an absence of being preceded by an agent possessing effort; or else, even in the absence of such an agent, that [state of being an effect] may still exist. In that regard as well, another [instance of] an agent among the causal factors is desired.
Or else, there would be non-comprehension due to infinite regress.
But surely, that which is insentient by nature requires an agent possessing effort for its own production and for producing another;
yet since that [agent] is itself the substratum of such an intellect, what need is there for anything else? For insentient things like jars do not require illumination.
Thus, there is no rule that one manifestation must necessarily depend upon another manifestation.

If that is so, then why does this collection of factors—consisting of the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth—which is designated as the "potter" and possesses effort, not depend on something else?
Therefore, whether conscious or unconscious, a collection [of causes] arises or produces [an effect] by its very nature, depending upon another consciousness.

If it is argued that [the agent] must go [to the object], there would be an infinite regress. Alternatively, if the group of conscious beings is held to be independent of any other consciousness, then properties such as "being an effect" residing in things like jars—which are invariably concomitant with an intended agent who is the opposite of what is desired—would be established; they could not maintain their status without being undermined by the fault of contradiction. However, if such a form of superintendence is accepted, [the argument fails] because of the extreme remoteness of their essential natures (*svabhāvaviprakarṣāt*).
Even when [the cause] is obtained, if there is the possibility of its operation, these [reasons] do not possess the property of being invariably concomitant with the opposite of that [operation];

thus, due to the absence of negative pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*), there would be an absence of the contradictory convention (*viruddha-vyavahāra*). Even then, if someone skilled in the investigation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not take care to establish the determination of cause and effect, then at present—
Let it rest for now that [the argument] has begun;

what is the use of this persistence? For if one persists, there is the consequence of introducing gross defects that contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or else, even so, there would be non-establishment (*asiddhi*)—thus, the opposite proof will be applied. Therefore, with internal pride, like an elephant closing its eyes, the [opponent], like a submarine fire (*vāḍava*), [remains silent].

Just as he has accepted God as the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the production of all effects, so too, having considered this [analogy], and fearing an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if a conscious being were to require another conscious being, he relies on that very [God]—because He is never non-deviant—and states the doubt: "Now, even though the potter possesses effort, it is not directed toward his own body, but rather toward the jar and such; therefore, why does he not [exert effort] toward the accomplishment of his own body?"

If [it is argued that] it must depend on something else, then why would even that which is intended as God—not being in his own body and because of the contradiction of acting upon oneself—not depend on something else? Yet he does not depend on anything. Therefore, since whatever produces an effect, such as a product, is presided over by one possessing effort, this [argument] is contradicted by that very [example]; thus, doubt is established.

[Objection: But since he has no body at all, how can this [argument] be inconclusive? [Response: This is the result of forgetting the context. For, in the vicinity of demonstrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), you yourself have accepted a conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) unity in the potter and thus admitted that the world is created by such a conventionally unitary person; this is our point. However, if it were indeed real...

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, oneness that is contradictory to coexistence with the body is being maintained; therefore, one must not introduce a merely conventional oneness as a pervading property (*vyāpaka*) in the example for the effect and so forth. Nor is there any fruitful hope for establishing such [oneness] in reality through that which is concerned merely with names. Not so.

Indeed, having perceived an effect such as a specific verbal expression associated with a boy who is metaphorically designated as "fire," one might infer some ultimate fire. If it is argued that there is a single, unerring cognition regarding the person as a whole [who is the substratum], then what, in this case, constitutes the directness of the metaphorical designation?

He asks: "Is it not so? It is said that the conventional designation of one thing as another is common to both cases. Since the parts [of the body] sublate [the notion of] corporeality, the error of the single-determination must be recognized; for even if there were a whole (*avayavin*) possessing existence, this collection—consisting of the whole as the body, its parts such as the hands, and the intellect—or else the collection of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, is established as being non-ultimate, being denoted by a single term.
[Regarding] the presiding controller:

it might be argued that the person (*puruṣa*) alone is the presiding controller there, or the agent; and that he, having attained distinction from the body and so forth, is one and only one—if this is your position?
Even when an effect arises from a collection of visible causes,
another unseen factor is postulated; yet even in that case, having set aside what is seen, it is that very same [unseen factor] which is [the cause].
The manifold, the impermanent, non-increase, and various forms of delusion.
First of all, it has been stated that the very existence of the unperceived is difficult to ascertain here because of innate discrepancies in inference.

Furthermore, its status as a cause is to be established by perception accompanied by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible; and that [status] belongs to that [cause] alone through the exclusion of other perceived things.
Otherwise, if activity were possible even for hands, feet, and so forth, the same fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) would recur, as those too could then be inferred as causes.

Otherwise, even the inference of a person (puruṣa) would be without a basis. By this, the conceptualization of the continuum of consciousness (caitanya-santāna) as a single person is refuted; for its power is perceived only when accompanied by hands, feet, and so forth. Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the reality of the cause must be inferred from the effect, just as fire with its fuel is inferred from smoke.

If it is argued that pervasion is apprehended by consciousness alone and not by anything else— no, for it is impossible to make such a distinction on the basis of an identical logical principle. Therefore, this [consciousness] can only express its causality as being non-different from the intellect and the body, by means of the exclusion of other possible connections (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), so that one might be able to infer it solely through that [non-difference] without obstruction, given its ultimate identity.

And [it would be] impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*). This being the case, to set aside the collection of causal factors (*kārakasamudāya*) whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been observed, and to postulate some other cause altogether—this is another instance of contempt. Furthermore, if that [other cause] were somehow a single entity, then the entire *Saptaślokī-vyākhyāna* in the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*) would be rendered fruitless.
We perceive this entire world as being like the clamor of bees attracted by the fragrance of a lotus in the sky—the notion that there is only one "vehicle" (yana) to be conceptualized.
Therefore, enough with the introduction of a self distinct from the body and so forth; consequently, the pervasion of a single, effortful agent is not primary.

Because, in reality, it is impossible for a potter or any other agent to possess oneness; and since, if one were to rely on a conventional [agent], there would follow an inference of exactly such [an agent], the reason—such as "being an effect"—would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) by that very [example]. Thus, it was stated that there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
But even so, such [an agent]...

If the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, by what means could there be deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? And if it is established, what would deviation accomplish? If you argue that "from deviation follows non-establishment," then since there is no deviation when there is non-establishment, on what basis can one determine whether there is non-establishment or establishment? Furthermore, since properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) are real attributes of a thing, the substratum (*dharmin*) must itself be a real entity.

The objection that [the reason] ought to exist is not valid, because we have begun to demonstrate—by means of a sequence that avoids contradicting our own accepted tenets—that this is so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Furthermore, there exists a relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the three modes of the probans (*sādhanatrairūpya*), and between the probans possessing those three modes and the intended probandum;

for in that case, when the probandum exists, there is no absence [of the probans] in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Thus, by virtue of being established through one's own acceptance, it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasiddha*).
This is called the "common inconclusive" (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) [reason],

because of the statement that "the opponent's admission is a factor for the effect. Indeed, it is logical that the opponent's admission is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), since [the proponent] proceeds precisely to refute it.

Therefore, this [reductio] does not have a self-standing reason (*svatantra-hetu*) as its basis. Furthermore, the result of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) is precisely its reversal (*viparyaya*). However, if one’s own position were not established by valid means of cognition (*apramāṇatva*), there would be no utterance of words at all; for speech is the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself through inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). And since the proponent has not, by this [reductio], manifested the three characteristics (*rūpatraya*) as perceived by himself, the statement of that proponent constitutes a "defeat" (*nigraha*) due to the utterance of a non-essential member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

The appropriate position is that it is indeed the pointing out of a fault in the other [opponent's] argument; this is established. Alternatively, he says "or there is doubt regarding the example" in order to raise an objection concerning the employment of a single [reason] for the sake of establishing a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
[Pravā.

1.12] Thus it is said. First of all, there is simply a lack of proof regarding the instrument in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Or, even if it were proven, there would be doubt as to whose [instrument] it is for the sake of which the example is adduced; that is to say, [there is doubt] regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases. For it is not observed in the example.

Thus, the cognition of a pervaded-pervader relationship (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) does not arise for just any entity whatsoever, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); rather, it arises from the establishment of an essential connection (*pratibandha*). And since there is no such basis here [in the case of the world], agency (*kartṛtva*) and the like, even if established in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), do not extend to a self necessarily restricted to oneness, because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary. [Therefore,] an effort-endowed agent—278...
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*,

it is stated that even though properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) are indeed certain, they are merely "doubtful reasons" (*saṃśayahetu*) when proving a single creator, because their exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) is doubtful.
And Śaṅkara himself has said: "The non-deviation of the status of having an insentient material cause from the unity of the agent [is not established]," and so forth.

As for what he further says—that there is no deviation of the status of having an insentient material cause merely by virtue of being presided over by one possessing effort—that alone is of no use in the present context; for [the proof] was previously shown to be dependent upon the establishment of the property that serves as the locus of the dispute.
Because of the demonstration.
Thus ends the first section.

Having thus stated the refutation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to a specific probandum (*sādhya*), he speaks while reflecting on how to state it even with respect to "merely that which possesses effort" (*prayatnavanmātra*):
"In cases such as activity after remaining stationary, specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*), purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and so forth..."
Either the desired conclusion is already established, or it is unestablished, or else there is doubt regarding the example.

Thus: "Dṛṣṭānta" means a "seen end" (dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ), which is to say a "established conclusion" (siddhānta). This is because pervasion is established by mere effortful [inquiry], and because a real entity cannot transcend the nature of being either one or many. When [arguments] such as "acting after having remained stationary" have been put forward, there is doubt regarding the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): does the proponent's desired proof hold in the case of unity, or is there merely a lack of proof in the case of multiplicity, or rather is there no pervasion at all?

"In both cases" is the meaning of the question. Here, the answer has already been given immediately following [the previous section] by means of the discussion on proving non-difference and by pointing out that the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. Therefore, only the third position remains; for indeed, there is no production of an effect even without the application of effort.
While this is being considered, let us examine some potential subverting arguments (*bādhaka*). How, then, could there be a necessary rule (*niyama*) regarding the effect and so forth in that case?

If it is argued that the subverting argument is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the lack of restriction by time, place, and so on—that is incorrect; for even when there is an absence (*vyatireka*) of a particular state of the cause—which possesses restricted power, does not exist at all times, and whose presence depends upon its own causes—the absence of the effect is still possible.

It is possible to establish that [the effect] is invariably concomitant with effort. Since it is in every respect independent of a cause, this subverting argument, being applicable, would prove the pervasion of the effect by the cause in general; however, it does not [prove it] by means of a specific cause, namely one possessing effort.
But surely, what is called a "cause" everywhere is merely a collection, and that [collection] does not exist when the factors are in a disjoined state. And their conjunction...

If [the effect] were to exist without dependence on effort (*prayatnavant*), it would necessarily be eternal. The same must be said regarding place as well. Consequently, that very same undesirable consequence of restriction by place and time follows. If you argue: "Since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth—which are impossible due to the absence of their pervader, namely 'being produced by the causal complex independent of consciousness'—are instead pervaded by 'dependence on one possessing effort' (*prayatnavad-apekṣatva*), [therefore there is no such restriction]," then in that case, that effort itself—

If [the cause] were momentary and localized, then the entire collection of effects would exist only at that single moment and in that single location; therefore, it must be admitted as eternal and all-pervading. Consequently, the very same restriction regarding place and time remains applicable even now—so what is the point of accepting this [new theory]? Furthermore, if it produces [effects] by depending on the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), it would produce them determinately; however, the unseen merit does not belong to insentient things.
Regarding the phrase "locana" (the eye):

if it is argued that, in that case, the causal conditions—aided by the ripening of that unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—will necessarily produce [the effect] even without the eye, so what is the use of consciousness? For one who speaks thus, it would follow that even the potter and others are useless; for even in that case, [it is not the case that they are unnecessary].

There is no unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) that acts as an auxiliary cause; nor is it the case that [the effort is fruitless]. Therefore, the opposite is true: whatever constitutes a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it does not render human effort fruitless without depending on an unseen factor, just like the collection of thread, a lump of clay, a stick, a wheel, and so forth. Furthermore, the causal complex that produces mountains, oceans, and the like [is such a case]; this is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). For the rendering of effort fruitless is indeed its independence from that [effort].

That which is to be negated is established in the case of the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth. Therefore, that which is contradictory [to it], namely "dependence on effort" (*prayatnāpekṣatva*), is pervaded by "being a causal complex" (*sāmagrītva*), because that [complex] is an effect of effort.
To this, it is said: if it were established through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*) that the causal complex is an effect of effort, then this would be correct. But it is not.

And it is not so, for even in that case there is no subverting argument against the contrary [position]. For just as an effect—because its presence depends upon its own cause—is conceivable as not occurring at all times due to its dependence on a particular state of that cause, why should the same not apply to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)?

Why, then, would the consequence of its eternal existence be urged? Therefore, if the causal complex, with the suspicion of its occurrence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) unrefuted, were to depend upon effort...

One should restrain [this objection]: what kind of offense has been committed by [the reasons] such as "being directly produced" (*sākṣāt-kāryatva*), that upon their presentation, one who is in doubt should resort to the "collection of causes" (*sāmagrī*) as a refuge?
If it is argued that clay and so forth are seen to come together only from a person, then the effect (*kārya*) must also arise only from one who possesses effort (*prayatnavat*).

Why is it not said that [the potter's] pride has been perceived? And just as, even though some effect is seen to belong to one who exerts effort, there may still be the suspicion that another effect might belong to an intelligent being despite setting aside [the current case], so too, what purpose does the postulated totality of causes (*sāmagrī*) serve? Therefore, this is equivalent to what was not stated [previously]. Consequently, even by inserting the totality of causes into the midst [of the argument] regarding jars and the like—

In that case, it is precisely the observation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that must be accepted as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This being so, it is sufficient to establish that the effect itself is invariably concomitant with effort through direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). What is the use here of the pride of adducing a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Alternatively, it may be that direct perception and non-perception, according to the sequence to be described, are capable of apprehending only a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*).

Would it not be established that "mere effect" is pervaded by "that which possesses effort"? To that end, one resorts to the refutation of the contrary (viparyayabādhā). If that is so, then even in the case of a causal complex (sāmagrī) being an effect of that which possesses effort, those same means of perception and non-perception (pratyakṣānupalambha) are the refuge;
thus, it is logical to conclude through universal induction (sarvopasaṃhāra) that such a collection is produced by that which possesses effort. And so:
There can be no arising from that which is distracted, nor can there be accumulation from that which is devoid of consciousness;
if this were so regarding an entity, would not this same defect apply equally even to an eternal body?
If it is argued that, in the case of that [eternal body], there is a restriction of time by depending upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then what is the use of the mind at that time?
Even in the case of a jar and other such objects, the artisan's labor is not fruitless; nor is this the reverse of that.

If, because it is seen in a jar and so forth, there is an inclusive extension (*abhividhi*), why is there a contradiction in the opposite case? Is it not accepted that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through perception and non-perception?
If this were so, then if their object is indeed a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*), such being the case...
If it were thought that an arrangement arises from consciousness, what certainty could there be regarding anything else?
Thus are the two summary verses!
This concludes the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).

Nor is it correct to argue that if another causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were not preceded by that [divine intellect], then this [complex] should likewise not exist; for [it is not so], since it is not the case that all...

For even though properties are all-pervasive, they are observed to exist only in certain locations, just as the property of being scratchable by iron exists only in earthy substances, or as the state of having a body preceded by a prior [birth] is not established in every effect. If it is argued that there is no omnipresence because of sublation (*bādhaka*) in those cases, then when such sublation does not manifest, by what means can doubt be dispelled? For indeed, one's own opponent’s [position] is not subject to sublation in other contexts, such as in other sets of causal factors or in other types of effects.

Regarding the dependence on volition (*cetanā*), just as you maintain that it must necessarily exist in every class of entity, there is no proof for this. Furthermore, just as you observe a dependence on an intelligent agent in some cases, so too the opponent observes that a property seen in one instance does not pervade those of a different class. Therefore, in some instances, there is [the observation of] being scratchable by iron and physical activity.

The non-observation of a subverting proof (*bādhakādarśana*) is indeed useful for the opponent as a means of establishing doubt; otherwise, it would follow that doubt itself would be baseless. Furthermore, it is not a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason that has now begun to be stated, such that the non-displayal of a subverting proof in this case would serve as a subversion against the respondent; rather, it is precisely the state of having a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*). And that is established.

Because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established by mere observation in the example, as there is no other basis [for such a conclusion]. By this, the following argument is also refuted: that because the causes of the earth and so forth possess restricted activity while being insentient, they must be presided over by an intelligent agent, just like the causes of a palace and similar structures. This is because even insentient things, such as time (*kāla*), exhibit restricted activity that does not necessarily entail the presence of an intelligent agent.
"Because, just like that [effect], there is an absence of a means of valid cognition [to establish it].

Nor does the consequence of the non-cessation of effects present a logical connection, because the possibility of a single power being maintained across entities has been set aside by the occurrence of differences in intrinsic nature produced through the conjunction with successive conditions (*pratyaya*). Therefore, by raising a doubt regarding the unity of the agent...

By means of the same logical principle (*samānanyāyatayā*), he states the following in order to refute— by way of a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason— the very impediment to cognition that has been introduced for the sake of satisfying his opponent:
"In the cases of staying, activity, specific configuration, purposeful action, and so forth..."

"Establishment or non-establishment of the desired [property] in the example. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction. When these [conditions] are present, there is either the establishment or the non-establishment of that consciousness which is desired, in the example—that is, in the subject possessing the probans—in the case of a jar and in the case of a tree branch respectively. Therefore, it is clear that these [reasons] function in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

This refers to the state of being (*bhāva*). By this, the following alternative possibility is rejected: that if it is impossible to state a sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*) as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth, then—just as with smoke and the like—the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) between effort and effects such as sound will occur through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
This is because, even in the absence of such effort, the effect arises; thus, there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) itself, as has been stated.

Now, one might object: "Intelligence (*buddhimattva*) is a property common to both visible and invisible bodies; since it is not observed to be operative in the production of trees and the like, how can its absence there be known? For non-existence cannot be established by mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). This is correct. [As stated] in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*: 282.

If it were intended that the pervasion [of consciousness] occurs by means of pure cognition alone, which is devoid of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of a visible body— if you say, "Certainly so," then in that case, with reference specifically to the negative concomitance (vyatireka) as in the case of smoke,
he says: "Or else there is doubt."

Thus: when the absence of the jar prior to the potter's activity is to be understood, then the absence of the jar caused by the absence of the probandum would not have been cognized, because of the doubt regarding the absence of the probandum. For pervasion was not sought by a mind conditioned by such a physical body, whereby a negation could be established through a specific non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

However, [this occurs] merely by means of effort. And just as at the time of the birth of a tree or similar things, the negation of its possibility is impossible, so it is even now; thus, even if that [tree] were possible, the absence of the jar which is being considered cannot make one understand that the self is caused by its absence. Therefore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

If it is argued: "It is indeed correct to say that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful when there is doubt regarding the presence of the probans in the absence of the probandum; however, the non-existence of the jar prior to the activity of the potter is not something that is doubted," that is incorrect. For the proponent of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must demonstrate that the negative concomitance of the probans is necessitated by the negative concomitance of the probandum. And that [necessitation] depends upon the absence of the probandum—

Alternatively, it was not shown even by himself because of doubt; or, because there is doubt regarding its nature even in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), there is no distinction [between the two cases], since in both instances that [subject] with its qualification remains doubtful. For this very reason, the fact that the subject (*dharmin*) possesses both the doubted probandum and the doubted probans is stated to be a defect of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If, however, only the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*) were stated without regard for the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), then this would be correct; yet even so, there is no apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Otherwise, having established pervasion through perception and non-perception, when a trembling produced by a means of proof for the "wind-injury" theory is made common with a trembling caused by massaging and the like, then—

If one considers that the wind is motionless and, by its very nature, impossible to obstruct through contact, and thus avoids it, [the opponent] would be unable to prevent [the objection]. If it is argued that because a specific qualification is established there, there is indeed no deviation (vyabhicāra), then from what source is this specific qualification being established by that [reason]? Furthermore, the word "obstruction" (upahati) will have a corresponding object, just as [the term] "activity of the bodiless" (aśarīravyāpāra) does, provided it is not contradicted by perception.

If it is argued that this is because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is described through the apprehension [of the absence of the probans], that too is equally applicable to you. Just as for you, when the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is avoided by means of invisibility in relation to such a mere desert, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established precisely because of its invisibility at the time of grasping the pervasion—so it is for you as well regarding consciousness alone in one devoid of a body. Therefore, even when there is doubt regarding its absence...

In that way, there might be the conceit of grasping a pervasion based merely on the absence of the effect; likewise, even when there is doubt regarding the absence of an untouchable wind, the absence of trembling is established, and thus there would be a pervasion.
This concludes the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*).
Now, if no one establishes pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the body-possessor alone, nor even by means of one devoid of a body, but rather by mere consciousness (caitanya) itself—

and since that [consciousness] exists even at the time when there is a body, because the universal must necessarily exist when a particular instance is possible— then the apprehension of pervasion occurs in relation to that [consciousness].

It remains restricted to the universal alone, just as [the concept of] fire does not enter into the specific nature of another fire; this same point applies to the inference of wind. Furthermore, no conscious person infers the wind from mere trembling alone, because even when there is a determination that [trembling] is omnipresent, the capacity of the means [of proof] to establish [wind] is not perceived. For it is not the case that because "kingdom" is desired, one performs the naming of it [based on that desire].

Even though it arises immediately thereafter, it validates the proponent of that means; or rather, the probans "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), although in reality lacking a constituent part of the proof, is presented as a pervader for the sake of establishing impermanence.

Therefore, satisfaction is not found merely through internal purity or the actual state of the object of cognition; rather, the excellence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is what is investigated.

Furthermore, in establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of trembling by mere air, there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary; for it must necessarily be accepted that perceptual non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is capable of including within its scope even that which is remote in terms of nature, place, or time—provided it is capable of becoming an object of its own range—and not anything else. Otherwise, just as in the case of grasping the pervasion, there would be deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Otherwise, even the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would result in being restricted solely to that [pure consciousness]. Therefore, just as positive and negative concomitances concerning particulars are established as having as their object only the pure consciousness that is beyond the scope of perception and other means of knowledge, why is it not likewise established that even the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding particulars has as its object only that [pure consciousness]? For it cannot be maintained that "one enters upon obtaining [the object], and one withdraws upon its destruction."

It is logical that fire, although spatially and temporally remote, being of the same nature as that [smoke], is as if present; for, by its very nature, it attains entry [into the cognition] through its suitability for perception and other means. Consequently, because of the single determination of that [fire], everything being apprehended as the pervader of smoke is not defective; however, the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) is not so determined because of its unsuitability for such [perception]. For this very reason:

The activity of one who is free from doubt toward fire as intended [by smoke] is logical; otherwise, even if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were grasped by the sense of sight (*āśrayabhuja*) despite its being unamenable to direct perception (*pratyakṣāyogya*), that pervasion of smoke would be established as having as its object only the generality of fire (*dahana-sāmānya*)—whether amenable or unamenable to perception.

Consequently, one might hesitate regarding the specific form intended [such as fire from grass], and with a mind not focused solely on obtaining the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by that [specific fire], one would not act.

Or rather, just as in the case of an obstruction or a deficiency [of causes], there would be the occurrence [of an effect] even when the state of being digestive fire (*jāṭharatva*) is absent, provided one does not perceive it; but this is not the case. Therefore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that rests upon a specific nature does not establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a general sense.

However, having come to apprehend the pervasion of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) by "impermanence" (*anityatva*) through a means of valid cognition that sublates the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—

Since it functions by means of mere existence (*bhāva*) unqualified by any particularity, one apprehends it only as a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, no one who acts on the basis of something produced (*kṛtaka*) can possess a cognition that is intended to be both eternal and one-pointed;

therefore, it is established that even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which culminates in a universal does not grasp a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of a particularity. And it has been stated by Śaṅkara, the follower of Nyāya: [that]...

"A valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) pervades as much as the range of objects," and so forth. A valid means of cognition whose activity depends upon a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot establish the pervasion of anything by an intrinsic nature other than that [specific one], just as, for example, a cognition that serves as a sublater of its opposite [cannot establish the pervasion of existence by non-existence]. (JNĀ 284) *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 284.1–285.3: "Furthermore, it is not the case that a valid means of cognition does not establish the pervasion of something by another thing merely because it is not observed in some instances. For if that were so, then even the inference of fire from smoke would not be established, since smoke is not observed in all instances of fire. Nor is it the case that the pervasion of a probandum by a probans is not established simply because the probans is not observed in all instances of the probandum; for if that were so, then even the inference of impermanence from the fact of being produced would not be established, since 'being produced' is not observed in all impermanent things. Therefore, the establishment of pervasion occurs through the observation of the probans in at least one instance of the probandum, and through the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 285.3–286.1: "Moreover, the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum is not established merely by the failure to observe it in some instances. For if that were so, then even the non-existence of a rabbit's horn would not be established, since its non-existence is not observed in all cases. Rather, the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum is established by the observation of the probans in at least one instance of the probandum and by the certainty that the probans could not exist without the probandum. Thus, the pervasion is established by the observation of concomitance in presence and the non-observation of concomitance in absence. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 286.1–287.1: "Furthermore, the pervasion is not established by mere verbal convention or by the authority of scripture alone. For if that were so, then the pervasion between 'being produced' and 'impermanence' would not be established for those who do not accept such conventions or scriptures. Rather, the pervasion is established by the force of reality (*vastubalapravṛtta-anumāna*), which is based on the observation of the essential nature of things. As it has been said: 'The pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in the presence of the probandum and by the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 287.1–288.1: "In this regard, some argue that the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in all instances of the probandum. But this is incorrect, for it is impossible to observe the probans in all instances of the probandum, since the probandum is often beyond the reach of the senses. Others argue that the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in a single instance of the probandum and by the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. This is the correct view, for it is sufficient to observe the probans in at least one instance of the probandum to establish the positive concomitance, and to observe the non-existence of the probans in the absence of the probandum to establish the negative concomitance. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 288.1–289.1: "Thus, the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in the presence of the probandum and by the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. This is the essence of the method of establishing pervasion. Any other method would either fail to establish the pervasion or would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, one should rely on this method when establishing the pervasion for the sake of inference. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 289.1–290.1: "Furthermore, the pervasion is not established by the observation of the probans in a single instance of the probandum if there is doubt regarding the possibility of the probans existing without the probandum. For example, the pervasion between 'having a body' and 'being subject to death' is not established by the observation of it in a single instance, such as Devadatta, because there is doubt as to whether someone with a body might be immortal. However, the pervasion between 'being produced' and 'impermanence' is established, because there is no reason to doubt that the probans could exist without the probandum. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 290.1–291.1: "In conclusion, the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in at least one instance of the probandum and by the certainty that the probans cannot exist in the absence of the probandum. This is the definitive rule for establishing pervasion in valid inference. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 291.1–292.1: "Those who claim that the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in all instances of the probandum are refuted by the impossibility of such observation. Those who claim that it is established by the observation of the probans in a single instance without the non-observation in the absence of the probandum are refuted by the possibility of error. Therefore, the method described above is the only reliable way to establish pervasion. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 292.1–293.1: "Thus, the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in the presence of the probandum and by the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. This is the foundation of all inferential knowledge. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 293.1–294.1: "Regarding the statement that 'the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in all instances of the probandum,' this is a misconception. For if the pervasion were established by such observation, then the inference of fire from smoke would be impossible, as smoke is not observed in all fires. Moreover, if the pervasion were established by the observation of the probans in a single instance without the non-observation in the absence of the probandum, then the inference of impermanence from being produced would be invalid, as there is no certainty that being produced does not occur in eternal things. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 294.1–295.1: "Therefore, the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in at least one instance of the probandum and by the non-observation of the probans in the absence of the probandum. This is the correct method for establishing pervasion. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 295.1–296.1: "In this context, the term 'non-observation' (*adarśana*) refers to the certainty of the non-existence of the probans in the absence of the probandum, not merely the failure to observe it in some instances. It is this certainty that establishes the negative concomitance. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 296.1–297.1: "Thus, the pervasion is established by the observation of the probans in the presence of the probandum and by the certainty of its non-existence in the absence of the probandum. This is the definitive rule for the establishment of pervasion in the science of logic. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 297.1–298.1: "Any other definition of pervasion would either be too narrow (*avyāpti*) or too broad (*ativyāpti*). Therefore, one should adhere to this method when analyzing the relationship between the probans and the probandum. *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī* 298.1–299.1: "Furthermore, the pervasion is not established by the observation of the probans in a single instance of the probandum if there is a suspicion of deviation. For example, the pervasion between 'having a body' and 'being subject to death' is not established by observing it in Devadatta, because there is a possibility that someone with a body might be immortal. However, the pervasion between 'being produced

[The inference] depends on a specific [nature] of the impermanent, such as the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Or, for example, perception and non-perception depend on a specific nature of the intended object, as in the case of smoke [in relation] to fire by way of its common form, namely that of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*). And since perception and non-perception function by depending on a specific nature, there is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) [of trembling] by the wind; this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), like the lightness of the wind (*mātariśvan*).
Because there is an absence of activity [of the means of knowledge] through perception.

Nor is there an inconclusive [reason]. For the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) by some [means of knowledge] is pervaded by the fact that the operation of that means of knowledge depends upon that specific nature; otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) and a confusion of activities. And that which is contrary to it...

The occurrence [of motion] depends upon a nature other than that; therefore, the meaning of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that perception and non-perception—which depend on specific intrinsic characteristics—do not establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of trembling by mere wind, which is common to both stationary and moving things. Consequently, there is no inference of wind from trembling in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

Moreover, there is no conceptual construction for establishing your own tenets that does not follow this [same logic], nor is there any basis for its invalidity that is not brought forward by your own inference. Consequently, if, in order to establish the pervasion between an effect and a conscious agent— just as between fire and smoke— you resort to perception and non-perception as the means of proof, then the operation of that [perception]...
With respect to the nature of the competent [cause], there is an inevitable deviation [of the effect] from one who possesses effort, by means of mere effects such as grass and the like. Now,

if it is claimed that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) with a conscious being that is beyond the scope of the marvel of deviation, then, just as in the case of the birth of a great tree and so forth, it would be impossible to exclude the operation of a mere conscious agent prior to the activity of a craftsman.
When a jar or the like is excluded [from non-existence], for whose absence could its own absence be determined, such that it would be established as being pervaded by that [absence]?

Thus, because its exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is doubtful, the reason is once again inconclusive (anaikāntika). Previously, this was established by the proponent himself by demonstrating the lack of a subverting proof (bādhaka) in the contrary case, without regard for the distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible; now, however, by the very admission of the proponent, it is [refuted] by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) desired by him.

The distinction is that, in comparison with that [specific case], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established. Furthermore, it has been stated that the subverting argument against the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhaka*) would lead to the cognition of pervasion through the reason alone, and not through the cognition of its qualification as "possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat*).

Now, one might object: since trees and so forth have been made the subject (*pakṣa*), how can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them? For the aggregate of existing things (*bhāvarāśi*) is indeed threefold.

[The subject] is of three types: that whose agent is doubtful, that whose agent is intelligent, and that which is agentless. Among these, having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception in the case of a jar and the like—which have an intelligent agent—one applies the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) to a mountain and the like, which are subjects of doubt, and thereby proves the existence of an intelligent agent.
This [subject] cannot, however, be a locus of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

As for what was said— that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*)— that is incorrect. For that which is the very object of deviation cannot possibly be the subject (*pakṣa*), according to the commentary on the *Saptaślokī-vārttika* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).
"Because a reason is stated regarding what is doubtful, a reason that is excluded [from the subject] lacks a locus," according to this principle (*Pramāṇavārttika* 4.91).
Consequently, it is appropriate to take only the mountain and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*), since their creator is doubtful; not trees and the like.

A fourth category must be admitted: that which has a non-conscious agent. Since, by the requirement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no perception of [an agent] in the production of things such as trees—which are held to be perceptible—how can they be made the subject (*pakṣa*)? Let it not be that the universal fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is thereby eliminated.

If an imperceptible creator is postulated to prevent the presence of "being an effect" in the counter-example (vipakṣa), how can pervasion (vyāpti) be established when it is devoid of the proof of negative concomitance (vyatireka)?
Furthermore, sublation (bādhā) consists in the restriction of the cause to its mere nature; it does not establish pervasion through differentiation.
Nor is even a portion that moves within the domain of deviation capable of being made the subject of the thesis.
Thus is the summary verse.

But even so, how can there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), given that space (*ākāśa*) is possible as a locus for apprehending the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? As it has been said: "The presence of production and so forth in jars and the like occurs when an intelligent cause exists, and their absence occurs when it is absent, as in the case of space and the like. And since that well-known inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is perceived precisely in earth and other such things, [therein resides] the agent capable of producing them—

"The intellect produces that [knowledge] for one who knows it"—this means "due to its production and so forth," which signifies "due to its being an effect" and the like. To this, it is replied: the establishment of the probandum does not occur merely through an example, whether by similarity or dissimilarity, because such a possibility exists even in the case of a mere chance encounter. Therefore, what is called an "illustration" (nidarśana) functions only by way of recollecting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) when it has been grasped but forgotten.
It is useful as a cause, not merely by its own presence.

And that necessary connection (pratibandha) would either be remembered in the sky after having been grasped through another means, or it would be established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whose locus is itself. Of these, the first alternative is already discarded, because [the connection] was previously [grasped] only by the intellect (dhī) which has the visible body as its limiting adjunct (upādhi).

Or, even in the case of a jar and the like, this is due to the presence or absence of the means for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, the latter [alternative] is impossible;

for instance, even if the absence of both [the potter and the clay] were observed in the sky, since it would be impossible to ascertain that one absence is necessitated by the other—and because Viśvarūpa is not present there—what relationship could be understood between which two? This would apply even to the case of a camel and a donkey.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] grasping the relation of cause and effect. If it is argued that such a cognition occurs when accompanied by the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) elsewhere, [we reply]:
surely the very meaning of "concomitance" is co-observation; and since that exists even in the case of a camel and so forth at some time or other, your established rule is not tenable.
And that [cognition]—the intellect—...
The meaning of concomitance (*anvaya*) is not the perception of one thing together with another; rather, it is the presence of the one occasioned by the possibility of the other.

If it is argued that this [relation] exists between "being my effect" (*matkāryatva*) and [the probandum], but not elsewhere—[we reply: no, for the fact that the absence of one is occasioned by the presence of the other does not arise from the operation of that [other].
(Jñānaśrīmitra-nibandhāvalī 286)

Since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is distinct from the attainment of existence (*sattā*), and since this prior non-existence cannot exist without the operation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), once the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been ascertained through perception and non-perception, what kind of doubt could there be regarding the status of cause and effect?
Thus, it is merely the recollection of the connection between their cognitions that is enjoined "in the sky" (i.e., is utterly baseless); therefore, this belongs to the first position alone.

Furthermore, what is this? Is it merely that your honor has revealed whether the Lord is manifest or unmanifest, or is it a case of being made a captive? Even in the inference from smoke, the same principle applies: having observed the possibility of both in one instance, when the activity of one is absent in the sky, the absence of the other is observed, and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped. If this is indeed the logic, then for those who desire that, it would be without foundation.

This is a hatred for the subject at hand; by dissolving it in this manner, even the inference of fire is lost, and the establishment of the subject itself is all the more remote, since—even by a donkey—following the stated sequence, one would abandon the hand [of proof] regarding that very fire. But when another possibility exists there that is not impossible for the subject, then why resort to "hostage-taking" as a refuge?

If it is argued that, in that case, the operation of perception and non-perception is resorted to only out of fear of such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and not because that [operation] itself constitutes the convention (*samaya*); then, being thus, you yourself must undergo an oath (*kośapāna*) as to whether or not this burden of over-extension has been placed upon you—
namely, that one who, setting aside perception and non-perception, infers the cessation of smoke from the cessation of the operation of fire in the sky.

Having grasped [the pervasion], one asserts it; however, for such a person, since even a mere thing would cease its operation therein, the pervasion would be established by that as well—this is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Likewise, there is the case of one who, setting aside both perception and non-perception, demonstrates the absence of the status of being an effect (such as a jar) in the sky due to the lack of activity by a specific person capable of perceiving it, and thereby [asserts] the pervasion of this [subject].

One might think that because the exclusion of mere personhood applies there, there would be pervasion by that as well; likewise, because the exclusion of being a different effect applies, there would be pervasion by that too. We see that this is clearly nothing but an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and not a logical principle (*nyāya*). Since deviation is observed in the case of smoke in relation to a donkey and so forth, it is not reasonable to say that pervasion exists with respect to "thing-ness" (*vastumātra*) alone, nor with respect to "mere personhood."

However, since no deviation [of the reason] is observed, this will not be a mere pointing out of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it is not the case that the observation of a sublation (*bādhaka*) in one instance among things subject to the same logic produces doubt in another instance as well. If, indeed, the observation of the cessation of both [the reason and the probandum] in the sky were the establisher of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then even in the case of real fire and smoke, there would be no sublation; but since it is sublated there, how could it be otherwise elsewhere?

Could it be a means for establishing a definitive conclusion? Nor can it be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of what has been made the subject (pakṣīkṛta). For making something the subject is not a matter of magical power; rather, it is the firmness of the grasp of pervasion (vyāpti). And if that [firmness] were merely the absence of both [the probans and the probandum] in space (nabhas), then its firmness would have vanished due to the apprehension of a sublation (bādhaka) therein; thus, even if there is the subjectification, the suspicion of deviation remains.
[The opponent] says: "Let it cease.

If you argue that space exists as the locus of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then even when smoke arises from fire, would that same [space] be the occasioning factor, lest an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occur?

In the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), there is this commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī*: "If it is so, why has another [objection] not been refuted by you? For even here, the observation of a sublation (*bādha*) draws forth a further doubt."
Such is the summary.

Therefore, the pervasion is not established by the absence of the two [fire and smoke] in space; rather, the observation of their non-existence in that case would serve as the cause for remembering the pervasion already grasped. And it has been stated that no means for grasping such a pervasion is possible. Consequently, it remains established that even if there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is absent, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In reality, however, just like negative concomitance, positive concomitance—

That [cause] is also indeed difficult to find. For when something is beyond the range of perception (*pratyakṣāgocara*), it is impossible to ascertain that the absence of an effect is due to its absence; thus, for such a thing, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is utterly out of the question, because it must be graspable by perception. Indeed, perception, even regarding an object remote in space or time, is capable of functioning toward that which is currently being observed.

It has already been stated that one should not conceive of pervasion by including something that is spatially remote in nature; therefore, having disregarded mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a "blindfolded elephant" attitude, the refutation was stated solely on the basis of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In reality, however, there is neither positive nor negative concomitance, because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not [invariably] concomitant with mere effortful action when that is what is to be proven.
Or, in order to show that it is indeed a conflict (*raṇa*), he says:
"or else, it is a doubt" (*saṃśaya*).

With respect to what is suitable for perception and so forth, it is the "inconclusive due to being common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*); with respect to mere consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), it is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "If an effect produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) conditioned by the body is established, then an effect produced by the intellect alone is certainly established as well—just as that which is produced by a *śiṃśapā* tree is necessarily produced by a tree, since the particular does not exclude the general. How, then, can it be said that there is a lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? If this were the case, would there not also be negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in relation to that? What loss is there for us in accepting that the probans "being an effect" possesses both positive and negative concomitance with respect to the intelligent agent (*buddhimat*)?

Is this not so? It has been stated here: if one were to conceive of [the relationship] through such positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then even when fire is inferred from smoke by means of a form residing in the digestive fire or in a *citraka* tree, one who doubts that fire would not proceed with the intended one-pointedness of mind, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not the case that whatever form of an object is possible there is necessarily pervaded by the effect, as is known through perception.

It is determined, however, with respect to *adhyavasāya* (determinate conceptualization). And since *adhyavasāya* is indeed performed by a person (*puruṣa*), [the word] "by an intelligent being" (*buddhimatā*) refers specifically to that qualified subject; for it is precisely in such a sense that the word *puruṣa* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*). It does not refer to mere consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) independent of the activity of hands and so forth; for even though mere consciousness exists, it is indifferent (*udāsīna*) at the time of grasping the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Because activity proceeds only toward a specific [object], even though the word is general in nature, it implies only the specific object under discussion, just as the term "fire" implies [the fire] that pervades [the mountain]. And that determination (adhyavasāya), following the operation of perception, would project only that form which is suitable for it externally, and not even that which is unsuitable for it, such as the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) or [fire from] grass (*tārṇa*). In this same way, there is a pervasion by the Person (*puruṣa*) of something as well.
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, it is stated:

"The negation of mere cognition (*buddhimātra*)—which is devoid of the limiting adjuncts of a body and is unfit for that [function]—would indeed occur; however, there is no negation of the distinction between the 'donkey' (*khara*) and so forth. This very logic applies everywhere regarding the apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of perception."

[42b] If it is argued that for one who perceives smoke produced from a piece of agallochum (aguru) due to contact with charcoal, there would be the undesirable consequence of its concomitance even without fuel and so forth, because it is perceptible— do you mean to say that perception, disregarding the restriction of the objects of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), should be understood as having concomitance with whatever it happens to encounter wherever it occurs? It being thus...

If that were the case, the established distinction between valid reasons and fallacious reasons would be destroyed, resulting in the proof of everything by everything; thus, the search for specific means of proof would be fruitless.
Now, if it is argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by perception even by transcending what is accessible to it, that is unproven. For even when...

When perception, even with respect to an object suitable for its own operation, excludes the universal by taking into account internal differences and thereby apprehends the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then what need is there to mention that which is utterly heterogeneous and unsuitable for its own operation? Nor is our position that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by everything that is perceptible; rather, pervasion is established precisely by that which is perceptible. Otherwise, [the rule would apply] even to donkeys and the like.

It would follow that there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with smoke-pots and the like. What more than this? Why, then, is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) here dependent solely upon internal distinctions and not merely upon the suitability for perception? For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which requires the proximity of perception and so forth merely to awaken latent impressions (*vāsanā*), cannot—given that its arising form is indeterminate—introduce a specific, fixed particularity.

True; for this very reason, there is an application of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a means of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In that regard, just as non-apprehension serves as an auxiliary in the determination of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between fire and smoke, or between a person and a jar—establishing a threefold exclusion of possibility (namely, that the smoke was previously present, produced from elsewhere, or arrived from elsewhere)—for otherwise it would be useless.

Likewise, if one were to establish [the pervasion] through the lineage of donkeys or through the lineage of mere cognition, then indeed there would be pervasion by those two as well, and not otherwise; for it has been determined many times in the treatises that pervasion is not established by perception alone, nor by non-perception alone, but rather by perception and non-perception acting as mutual auxiliaries— this we have also stated in our *Trikapañcakacintā*.

Regarding the phrase "something [else]": even in the case of a connection with a *gadaṃbha* (a type of plant) or similar things, it provides no assistance to that [non-perception]. By this, the absence of the operation of non-perception with respect to a particular instance of smoke is explained; thus, there is no objection whatsoever against one who speaks in this manner. As for that which is within the range of perception...

He describes the pervasion established by that [non-perception]: "The absence of the apprehension of pervasion belongs to that [person] only with respect to that object; thus, the logical position is untenable.
Consequently, this very objection applies to him alone. If it is argued that [the pervasion does not exist] for him either because of the absence of the operation of non-perception—[we say] no;

for even in the case of what is perceptible, for one who asserts a pervasion established by that [non-perception], there is a desire for a pervasion established by it even in the absence of the operation of non-perception.
In the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), there is an explanation of the *Vārtika-saptaślokī*:
"Who is there to oppose him? For if he were ashamed, how could he describe that activity which is by its very nature beyond direct perception?
Moreover, since the ass is excluded simply by seeing the cause—an intelligent agent who knows the material and other factors—what is the use here of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)?"
In that case, you would be describing pervasion (*vyāpti*) only by means of what is actually perceived, and not by means of what has transcended the path of perception;

nor has pure consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), divested of the limiting adjunct of the body, ever been apprehended anywhere. And if the determination were based solely on the force of perception—such that a body presided over by pure consciousness is seen to produce jars and the like, and thus there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) involving a donkey—then [your position holds].

How is the rejection of non-apprehension [as a means of proof]? If it is argued that "only general properties residing in the pervader (vyāpaka) are the establishers of pervasion, because for others, due to the observation of deviation, there is room for doubt elsewhere; thus, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) with a donkey," then [we reply]: surely, the "observation of deviation" is the observation of the presence [of the probans] even in the absence of that [probandum]. Thus, in the absence of the operation of non-apprehension, there would be a lack of proof.

The act of "bringing forward" (upanīyamāna) demonstrates that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) itself functions as the means of establishing the probans (*sādhanāṅga*).
