Furthermore, if you, troubled by the suspicion of its operation upon a particular (*viśeṣa*), resort to a universal (*sāmānya*), then even in the case of [the argument] "because of being conscious," which is common to a clod of earth and the like, and which is fit for proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)— since it excludes the particular who is cognizant of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth— it would likewise [be fallacious].

Or let it state the pervasion by means of a cause in general; for if this were the case, every opportunity for doubt would be entirely eliminated. However, by disregarding this much generality and insisting instead on a specific [cause] such as one who knows the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth—yet not even disregarding that [generality], but rather [insisting] "just as it is observed"—what efficacy is there here other than stupidity? [This is the view of] the proponent of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
In whatever kind of generality there is scope for doubt, it is precisely there that the operation of perception and non-perception occurs; where there is no doubt, there is no such operation.
Thus, no one can, by their own will, introduce or remove a pervasion (vyāpti); it is established by valid cognition alone.

There is no fault, because [the cause] is handed over [to the effect]. But does he not see that even when asserting the entire mass of effects to be produced solely by the cause, there is the apprehension of the operation of perception even with respect to what is perceptible? He certainly sees it, because that is accepted on the basis of scripture which sublates any contrary view.
However, he establishes that perception and non-perception apply only to a mind associated with a specific body;

for even in the case of desire, when the activity of the hands and so forth ceases, the effect is absent, and it is precisely through that [activity] that the aggregate—which is the object of the designation "potter" and so on—is treated as perceptible. This, however, is not the case for a mere mind accompanied by effort alone; even then, the positive concomitance is established through inference.

It will be understood. Furthermore, there is no requirement for it to be perception alone. The determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) must be made through apprehension and non-apprehension; and as for that apprehension, whether it takes the form of perception or inference, there is no insistence on this point.
Here it is considered: is that very mind, conditioned by the body and possessing effort, what is denoted by the term "mind-only"?

Is it accepted [that the cause is the same], or something else? If it is the same reality (*tattva*), what is the use of inference, since there would be no dispute once it is established by perception? Furthermore, by that [perception], positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established, and its non-deviation from the mere effect is made manifest. If it were something else, there would be the fault of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
(From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, p. 290)

Because the purpose of an action such as speaking is fulfilled by the embodied agent alone, and one does not accept a pervasion (vyāpti) even with that which is inferred [by him], because—as in the previous case—there is no certainty regarding negative concomitance (vyatireka). If that is so, then the pervasion of smoke by fire is not with fire restricted by place, time, or state, but rather with fire in general; and since that [fire in general] is distinct from the fire actually perceived, there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the conceptual alternative.

If it is argued that because a fault is common to both sides, the pervasion must be stated by means of a generality (*sāmānya*) devoid of such specific features (*viśeṣa*), and that the same applies here as well—[we reply: even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that smoke is pervaded by its form as it exists in the stomach and so forth.
Therefore, it is not the case that only the generality is employed in the pervasion, nor is it the case that the specific feature is simply rejected.

Because inference from smoke would be utterly abolished, and because there would be doubt regarding activity toward the intended flame; therefore, if one’s own arbitrary will alone were not the means for establishing and delimiting [objects], then, in the process of determining the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), some generality must be sought through implication— even by perception, which proceeds by way of acceptance— as something that has been excluded, such that perception does not apply once that particularity is transcended.

Just as when one moves away from a blazing, radiant form, there is the perception of the pervasion of smoke; however, even something accepted by perception may be rejected by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), as in the case of a cooking pot and the like, by virtue of its capacity.

For that [non-perception], while establishing the absence of the effect in question in the absence of fire, demonstrates the distinction between the presence and absence of that [effect] being necessitated by the presence and absence of the fire.

By excluding [the presence of] forest and so forth through the exclusion of non-concomitance (*ayogavyavaccheda*), even a proof that functions to establish that [specific] effect necessarily establishes the causality of something else as well— provided that in the absence of that [other thing], it does not occur of its own accord. However, in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), when non-existence is established through a non-apprehension that functions to sublate prior existence and so forth, and the absence of the existence of multiple entities is proven, then that which is perceived by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) as being present in the proximity of the nature of one specific entity is [also] perceived as such previously.

Because the absence [of the effect] is manifested as being necessitated by the absence [of the cause], when establishing that [the cause] is the cause of that [effect], whatever has been rejected by perception due to its incapacity for activity is indeed rejected.
Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the gastric fire and so forth; nor is there a rejection of a nature differentiated by differences in time, place, or state.

Because it is accepted that everything is directly perceived through its own fitness for arising; nor can it be [established] by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), for it is logical that non-perception—by not occurring when there is an absence of a nature dissimilar to that [effect]—rejects the status of a cause belonging to a different genus, but not that of the very same [cause], otherwise its reliance would be useless. Now, even in the absence of a nature distinct from place and so forth, this smoke is observed; it is not [the smoke] of something distinct from place and so forth.
Because it is unified with the form perceived through a single uniform reflective cognition, [the object] exists apart from that which is of a nature not capable of being seen.

For this very reason, that alone is denoted by the word "mere fire," even when a distinction is drawn from what is perceptible. Furthermore, because there is no difference—[it remains] non-different even when the distinction from the perceptible is extracted.
[The opponent says: "But surely even that which is remote in space and so forth is simply incapable of being perceived. [The author replies: True, but only in some cases and at some time.
However, that which is remote by its very nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*) does not contradict its occurrence through a distinction between acceptance and rejection, owing to its absolute dissimilarity.
Therefore, just as a proponent of inference must pursue a universal (*sāmānya*) in order to avoid non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) or impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), so too,

in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), the commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī* explains that even a universal distinct from the perceived particulars (*dṛśyaviśeṣa*) must be rejected in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This being the case, just as...

It is logical that pervasion and the determination of identity [of the cause] occur through a subordinate generality (avāntara-sāmānya) that is perceptible, while excluding the generality of fire (*vahni-sāmānya*) which is imperceptible; it does not occur through mere effort (*prayatnavanmātra*), because that is refuted by perception.

In this regard, one who, out of delusion, seeks a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through another means of knowledge is questioned regarding whether [the cause] is identical to or different from [the effect].

Regarding the refutation of that position, it has been stated that there is a logical consistency (samādhi). Therefore, when one desires to grasp the pervasion (vyāpti) through perception and non-perception, and there is a requirement for a generality (sāmānya) suitable for that purpose, the result is that the desired proof is either established or not established in the case of examples such as a jar or a tree;

thus, the effect (kārya) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to being common to both sides. However, by means of mere sentience (caitanya), which is unsuitable for that purpose, neither of the two—positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka)—can be ascertained.

It is appropriate to state that the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are doubtful, as expressed by the phrase "or there is doubt. This follows from the context of "the establishment or non-establishment [of the probandum]. By these two terms, existence and non-existence are denoted. As it has been said: "Apprehension itself..."

"Non-existence is the non-apprehension of existence. Therefore, since there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of that which is intended as the probandum (sādhya) in a subject (dharmin) possessing the reason (sādhana) such as "being an effect"— namely, whether it exists merely through the agency of an effortful agent or not— and because all things are included within those two categories of being governed by such an agent or not being so governed, it is logical that the reason suffers from the fallacy of being an uncommon inconclusive (asādhāraṇānaikāntika) one, as neither positive nor negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) can be established.

But even so, let there be non-exclusivity (anekānta) as well; why is mere positive concomitance (anvaya-mātra) rejected, given that the operation of cognition alone is observed in the production of an effect? In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of positive concomitance of smoke with the common form of "belonging to the stomach" (jāṭhara), because the operation of fire is observed [in digestion]. Consequently, its negative concomitance (vyatireka) would also depend upon that, and thus the aforementioned fault remains. As for the rejection of perception, however—
It is common.

Now, if it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because smoke exists even in the absence of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) and so forth—since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) remains—then why is the production of a pot not also proclaimed by one who lacks the skill of craftsmanship, as in the case of Mount Kailāsa? Or, if [the argument concerns] the generality of the skill of craftsmanship—

Is there no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) here? Even in that case, since it is by virtue of being merely a burner, nothing is gained by introducing the individual instance (*vyakti*). However, with respect to the universal (*jāti*), since that [burning] occurs at other times as well, how could there be the presence of smoke even in the absence of that [universal]? Now, if you argue that the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is stated by positing a universal distinct from the observed particularity—namely, "merely being a burner"—then, in relation to that [distinct universal], how can there be positive concomitance? For it is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as qualified [by that specific universal].
Is it because [the relationship] is established upon the birth [of the cognition], or because a deviation is impossible in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?

Furthermore, as for the objection that one might suspect the ascertainment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through perception with a similar instance—[we reply that] not everything of the same genus is inferred; for since what is perceived is of a different genus, even an imperceptible thing is inferred by means of perceptible individuals such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

The claim that the collection of the eye and so forth, as well as the upper and lower portions of the moon and the earth, have been [established] in that manner is also most wretched. For instance, inference is not devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*); and pervasion is the cognition of a universal through a universal—[as stated in] the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

How could it be that [the opponent's] non-concordant inference (*asamāna-anumāna*) is consistent? Furthermore, that [inference] is of only two kinds: either from perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), or from a subverting proof of the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka*). In both cases, the inference is only of that which is of the same class as what was observed in the example. Otherwise, to take up a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a property of one class and then infer something of another class would be a great lack of discernment.

For even in the case of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), it is precisely that same general property of motion which has been observed to be the cause for reaching another location that is ascertained in another substratum; how, then, could there be an inference of a dissimilar property? If it is argued that this refers to a specific internal distinction established by capacity with respect to a difference in substrata, then that is equivalent to stating the unproven (*anuktasama*). Indeed, no proponent of inference [accepts such a thing].

One who does not desire any further qualification beyond that [mere presence] is capable of establishing a probative inference. If such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) were also present in the inference for God (*īśvara*), then the desired conclusion would be established through the proof of that mere qualification; why then would anyone harbor resentment toward it?
Nor is it reasonable to say that, with respect to that mere qualification, one cannot infer a common genus in every case.

In some cases, even when the inference is of a different class (*asamānajāti*), it is described in that same way; moreover, the distinction consisting merely of that [object] exists in every inference.

Since in the case of an inference based on what is "seen specifically" (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa*), that very [specific object] is determined even in respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), one should not say that in all cases only that [universal] is inferred, because the consideration of "sameness of class" (*samānajāti*) is grounded in difference (*bheda*).

But that [point] is indeed irrelevant. For it is not the case that everything which is not perceived is inferred. If you speak with reference to the means of knowledge for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—as in the case of fire—then inference would apply everywhere to perception alone, because no other means of knowledge operates except in cases where it is specifically prescribed. Alternatively, if you speak with respect to the sublation of the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka*), then one should not say that there is no difference from the proof of fire.

Regarding the phrase "of the inference of God": it would be more appropriate to say "because of proving [something] that is impermanent. This too is so. Therefore, because it does not penetrate the subject matter under discussion, this [objection] is trivial: namely, that "not everything perceptible is inferred.

However, with respect to the time of inference, everything that is remote (*parokṣa*) is indeed inferred, and there is no disagreement regarding that; thus, [your objection] is equivalent to what has already been stated. Furthermore, the sense organ cannot be directly inferred from cognition, because the necessary invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is not apprehended. [Rather, it is inferred] from the effect of cognition...
However, in certain cases, the proclamation regarding the senses—that they possess a dependence on causes distinct from the presence or absence of their own nature—is merely a hollow sound.
In that regard, just as a dependence of the same observed kind is established for spokes and so forth, so too are the upper and lower parts established in the case of effects such as jars;

This is merely an illustration; enough with further elaboration. One should not overstep established consensus by relying on [mere] authority.
In the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), there is an explanation of the *Vārtika-saptaślokī*;

and that authority is of only two kinds for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*): either through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), or through the sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*).
Because these two have the nature of perception and inference, and because certainty cannot be attained through any other means, there is first of all, according to the stated sequence,
a pervasion of the general effect by the cause, and of the whole [of the subject] by the particular, through the force of the sublation of the contrary.
Because [the cognition] does not touch upon the distinction between that which belongs to the same class and that which does not, based on perception and non-perception—
since it follows the sequence beginning with the negation of prior existence and so forth— the cognition of origination, like that of smoke and the like,
conforms to the principle "from such a thing, such a result arises"; thus, there are two types of universals.

This is the sequence for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception: "This [object], which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived; its perception is perceived. Here, "this" refers to smoke and so forth, which appear as a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) due to their belonging to a single class, by means of the exclusion of other classes of effects and the exclusion of other classes of causes, such as fire. "Its" refers to fire and so forth.

This is the meaning. Consequently, when there is a mutual distinction between cause and effect—each being distinct from what belongs to its own class and from what belongs to other classes—there occurs an activity preceded by such reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*); otherwise, such activity would be useless due to either incapacity or redundancy. For instance, [the cognition] "this is that entity" arises through the exclusion of the mass of non-effects, or through the exclusion of other effects.

Would it be determined that [the universal] conforms to the particular entity (*bhāvānuvidhāyin*)? In the first case, the meaning "these entities are restricted to this [universal]" would not hold, because this would be a distinct entity; for if there is an absence of a single form (*ekākāra*), a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of a single form is impossible. If it is argued that this is unproven because one is able to say "this is an effect" or "this is a configuration" by means of a commonality such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), we reply: here...

The cognition that establishes existence and non-existence arises in two ways: having as its object the substratum (*dharmin*) and having as its object the attribute (*dharma*), because the effect is twofold by way of being produced or modified. Among these, the former—taking recourse to the determination of the arising of the whole entity—takes as its object the substratum itself, which is embraced within a specific form; and although it is differentiated by distinctions of time, place, and so forth, it makes its own nature the object through a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).

It is called "having that as its object" because it brings about [the cognition]; for it sets aside even a possible property that is incompatible with the distinction of that specific form, just as whiteness and so forth are set aside in the case of smoke and the like.
However, in a case where another property arises while the locus (dharmin) remains exactly as it was, there belongs to the property alone—

The statement that "positive and negative concomitance [are established] by means of reasons" refers to the object as a property (*dharma*). Furthermore, this [cognition], setting aside the specific form (*ākāra*), takes the mere property as its objective basis, just like [the cognition of] passion and so forth. For people such as weavers and dyers—who experience a complete difference in form, action, and so on—are not satisfied merely by inferring the connection with some other substance possessing the quality of color (redness) whose capacity has been observed, [but rather they infer the specific dyeing substance itself].

The first [point]: It has the very form of the object as its refuge (*ākāra-śaraṇa*), because it arises as the very self of the object. For just as an object arises from some cause as colored by a specific form, so too is it experienced by sensory cognition produced through the power of that [object], and subsequently brought within the range of conventional usage by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). — *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

How is the exclusion of the specific form (*ākāraparihāra*) achieved? Precisely for this reason, when a person perceives a particular instance of smoke or a jar whose origin is not perceived in one location, if at that very moment the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through a specific logical argument (*yuktibheda*), then the determination of its cause arises in that very place, and not elsewhere—even if one were to consider the observation or non-observation of deviation. Subsequently, however, one may set aside the specific form once the property-bearer (*dharmin*) has been established.
[If it is argued that] one perceives only the arising of properties (*dharmamātra*), [we reply:

in a jar or similar object that is already established, the arising of mere properties such as "being an effect" is not observed; nor is this admitted in the case of mountains and the like, such that—disregarding the form—one could infer a cause for that alone, just as one infers passion. Therefore, the configuration (*sanniveśa*) remains [as the necessary factor].

If it is argued that [the pot] arises from the potter within that very [clay], we say no, because even immediately [afterward], the clay is not perceived as being devoid of its configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

If it is further argued that such a thing [devoid of configuration] did not exist previously—that which was the object of the designation "pot"—then, in that case, that very configuration must arise from the person; thus, there is no pervasion by that alone.
Nevertheless, if human action were directed toward the general category of shape,
then even the application of turmeric powder would be the producer of color alone.

But even so, does this not still result in a contradiction regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) being grasped in another individual instance, since it is not a perception of what was previously established?

For it was just demonstrated immediately prior that, by the force of that [pervasion], there is indeed inference in that case. And yet, on that basis alone, the mere fact that a letter arises from safflower is not proven;
for the ground for deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is weak. What, then, is established here?
Therefore, even in the case of a quality, there is an apprehension of its own genus just as in the case of a substance;
yet, inference does not arise from that [quality] when it is already established beforehand, nor from the color of saffron.

For how could there be an inference of saffron from passion, since the specific qualities [of the color] are not perceived? Furthermore, it is even more remote [from inference] based on color alone. And just as with color, the manifold distinctness (*vaijātya*) of shape (*saṃsthāna*) is also an object of experience. Therefore, in these two cases, the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) through a restriction of genus (*jāti*) in a single instance, or through non-restriction in the individual (*vyakti*), is not fixed to one [alternative]. Consequently:

Just as the reality (*tattva*) of color persists through various types of colors and shapes even while following along as a universal (*sāmānya*), it remains entirely external to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*).

Likewise, it is impossible to say that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists previously in a non-entity such as a "person" (*puruṣa*); for if that were so, it would follow that there is a prior absence of all capacity, which would result in the production of something unprecedented (*apūrvotpatti*). Thus, causal efficiency also [belongs] to a specific [entity], following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) with the person.
Thus it is established that [the cognition] conforms to the individual [particulars].

Therefore, even a cognition of pervasion whose object is a property (*dharma*) does not follow after a universal (*sāmānya*). However, when—by virtue of the context of the "reason as effect" (*kāryahetu*)—it has the locus (*dharmin*) itself as its object, then it relies upon a commonality of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the form exactly as it was perceived.

Just as, in the case of the cause, there is a perceptual cognition that determines pervasion by means of a universal whose specific nature is restricted [to that cause], so too, in the case of the effect, there is a perceptual cognition that determines being pervaded by means of a universal whose form is restricted [to that effect]; thus, there is no doubt.
This is the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*).

Otherwise, just as in the case of the effect, why would an active cognition— having excluded specific attributes such as being intelligent and so forth— bring about what is intended regarding the cause? Therefore, just as with the cause, one must likewise be able to ascertain such a specific form in the effect as well.

In this regard, even if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) were to exist in things such as the ground—which are external to that [perceived] form—it would be entirely useless when stated, because, in relation to the operation of perception which grasps the cause and effect within the domain of the property (*dharma*), a mere similarity of properties (*dharmamātra-sāmya*) is of no consequence.

For it is not that very form, nor the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), etc., that serves as the cause for manifesting that similarity. Therefore, by this, such a similarity does not serve any purpose whatsoever.

It nourishes [the understanding] elsewhere than in the case of words whose application to their effects is non-metaphorical. For that [word], having established its convention (*saṃketa*) with respect to an object that requires only the operation of another [factor] for the sake of its arising—while setting aside the phoneme /a/ and so forth—is not subject to contradiction. As for a property that is perceived as being pervasive through another means of justification, it is precisely there that the operation of perception occurs at the very moment of its own arising, like destruction (*nāśavat*).

There is no contradiction, for one requires a similarity in form and so forth that is clearly manifest, whereas when there is a difference caused by location and so on, there is the determination of dissimilarity.
Therefore, due to the absence of a single cause, when there is a dependence upon individual perception and non-perception, these entities—

The determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be established in this very manner: that [the probans] follows the cause of this [probandum]. However, since it is not yet possible to employ every individual instance of the effect, the [determination of pervasion] remains restricted to each single case among all types of effects. And that [individual case] is impossible, because [the concomitance] cannot occur either successively or simultaneously. For instance, their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) does not occur all at once, even when all types [of effects] are present.

For it would follow that the very seer of vision disappears [from view]; or else, a distinction [between them] could not be ascertained, because certain factors such as the substratum, light, and the body cannot be excluded. Furthermore, this observation of everything in every way is not possible within the span of a single human lifetime.

Since the effect is devoid of an end, how can there be completeness when there is dependence on only a few [factors]? Indeed, even if a greater portion [of the factors] is present, there is no fulfillment of the cognition of pervasion (*abhividhi*); for it cannot be asserted that "whatever is an effect is necessarily thus," though it may be said that "it is only this much."

Furthermore, as for the claim that an investigation (*vicāra*) proceeding with respect to one [object] establishes all entities as being of such a nature, this is said with reference to its operation through a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*), because it relies on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by excluding [specific qualities] such as shape (*ākṛti*) and so forth. For it has been stated that the very function of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is restricted to the apprehension of a single genus (*jāti*). Now, even there, since various internal subdivisions are possible, is it not the case that "this is thus"?

Thus, there is a lack of confidence because one is unable to express [the distinction]. Or, if it is argued: "In this case, by disregarding the difference and relying on another universal such as 'smoke' (*dhūma-jāti*), when engaging in practical discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*), what fault could there be even if one resorts to the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) with respect to other universals? We do not, by our own will, disregard any universal or place any particular universal forward. Rather, conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) is preceded by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). As it is said:

One presents objects either as distinct or non-distinct; in that same way, we enter into the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect. However, if that [cognition], having encountered a particular nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*), differentiates its operation among distinct things by means of capacity and incapacity for sublation—whether in a subtle or gross state—then what is there for anyone to do? Its transformation (*vivarta*) alone is to be considered. In this regard:

Just as smoke, even though it possesses internal subdivisions, brings to mind a similarity that excludes other classes [of things], so too does it [bring to mind] the heart in respect to every effect.

Since the presence or absence of the conformity of a single configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and so forth is directly perceivable by each individual, no further basis for a definitive conclusion is required here;

otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion regarding designation, purposeful action, and functional application. Therefore, in no cause whatsoever is there a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—whether successive or simultaneous—of all types of effects that could be established through perception and non-perception.

What is the use of these two [space and time], since it is possible to establish [the pervasion] otherwise? Therefore, this statement by those who claim that all effects are pervaded by space and time is merely a disclosure of their own intention, like the proclamation of a post on the road as being a man. This being the case, it is clear that these two are useless, for mere desire would suffice as the means of proof. Consequently, the cognition "this [effect] arises from these [two]" serves only to exclude other types of causes.

By its very exclusion, it attains agreement with the fact that [the cognition] has only the effect as its object; therefore, setting aside the doubt regarding the knower of the material cause and so forth, he says:
"Or else, there is doubt."
The establishment of what is desired for others does not occur through the refutation or the proof of another, nor through mere cognition or effort;
there is no positive concomitance when proving a specific desired [property], whereas a means of proof that tolerates doubt regarding the counter-example is indeed a valid proof.
If the probandum is perceptible, there is indeed deviation; if it is not perceptible, then the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.
Nor is there positive concomitance (*anvaya*), for as with the negative concomitance, pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not exist specifically in one case and not in the other.
