Second Section.
If this is so, and even if pervasion exists, it is impossible to ascertain; what then is the correct position here? Behold:
the effect, for its part, belongs to many classes, while the producer is observed to be a single, insentient entity.

In the case of that which possesses various divisions, there is no cognition of one restriction even when another division exists. Whatever is known as having a single cause by virtue of its genus, that alone is its constituent part; therefore, this is not the case otherwise, and there would be an over-extension. Nor is this method accepted in the case of the example for the probandum.

Indeed, the production of various kinds of effects is not restricted solely to that which possesses effort (*prayatnavat*), for even fire and other such things, when situated within a diverse collection of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), are observed to perform a variety of actions, such as producing smoke, ash, embers, heat, cooking, clearing away [obstacles], burning, and causing injury. At most, there is a dispute regarding whether these are governed by the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of one who possesses effort; however, there is no [dispute] concerning the fact that a single [entity] is present therein.

Once a rule is known, it is logically consistent for that knowledge of the rule to apply even to other effects, as was stated previously. Therefore, however many modes are ascertained as having a single cause, that many are suitable as means of proving that cause, whether it be conscious or otherwise. Otherwise, smoke whose pervasion by fire has been grasped [would also imply] ashes and the like, which are not familiar as its effects, even though they coexist with fire in damp fuel.

One would infer fire [from smoke]. But this is not the case; therefore, the distinction between those classes (*jāti*) and the grasping of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), each being required separately, uproots inference by means of the grasping of that [pervasion] wherever it may occur through whatever [subject] it might be.

Who, indeed, says this—that one should infer by means of whatever [subject] the pervasion was grasped in some particular instance? [This is untenable because] it is based on a single property (*ekadharmānu-*).

Is it because of the absence of the reason (*hetu*) due to the lack of its occurrence? For at that time, ash cannot be the means of proof because of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), nor can smoke be so because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

If it is argued that even in the case of a jar, a potsherd, and so forth, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) itself—though other properties do not persist—would serve as the reason when present in the inference, we say no;
for "being an effect" has also been extensively proven to be non-pervasive prior to that. In that regard, just as Mount Meru [is not the cause] at the time of the potter's activity...

There is no difference whatsoever in the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether it concerns a rule characterized by a deficiency of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, or likewise the fact that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) exists even though it lacks such a rule—just as in the case of a donkey producing smoke [where the concomitance is not established]. Therefore, one who has apprehended the pervasion in a specific effect such as a jar cannot infer the pervader from "being an effect" in general across all things; nor can one do so merely by the instrument for apprehending the pervasion.

How can one avoid the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by claiming that [the logical reason] transcends having different loci through its fixed rule (*vyavasthā*)? Therefore, there is no utility in the mere persistence of a single property. By whom, moreover, have the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*), being a real entity (*vastutva*), and so forth—which are possible in smoke—been utterly destroyed in ashes? If it is argued that even though these exist, they are deviant (*vyabhicārin*), then surely [the reason] is indeed deviant.

Precisely because of the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), for there is not even a trace of it in the case of pervasion. Furthermore, since that absence of pervasion is not excluded even by the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is unavoidable in that case as well. Non-observation due to proximity might, however, result from remoteness.
—From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

It does not follow from that alone that the [logical reason] is non-existent, because the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) which constitutes its very root remains as it was. If, however, there is deviation (*savyabhicāra*) even when there is pervasion (*vyāpti*), then it is all the more so when there is no pervasion; enough, therefore, with this false obsession. Thus, even if a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is intended as a proof (*sādhana*) while disregarding mere pervasion, why not likewise take a property common to the mountain and other such things?
If one disregards this, the same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains;

nor does this principle apply even to jars and the like, which are treated as being on the same footing as the probandum, for in those cases too, we perceive the potter’s activity in the case of the supporting stand, the bowl, the jar, the water-pot, and so forth, and accordingly, this [effect] is also produced by him.

Thus, perceiving it in this way, we determine that operation to belong only to those modes whose actions are well-known; otherwise, one would not escape the aforementioned faults. Therefore, even if in the ultimate sense this entire collection of effects is invariably concomitant with an effortful agent, nevertheless, from the perspective of the functioning of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the agent] himself is incapable of producing anything.
Whatever arrangement and so forth are established as following the presence or absence of a presiding agent, that [agent] is what is inferred from them.

Thus: "Because of the perception of this [configuration], even one who does not observe an agent forms the cognition that it has been made, like the arrangement of temples and so forth seen in an empty city" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.13).

And that [reason] is unestablished; this is what was intended. If it were observed as such in subjects (dharmin) like mountains and so forth, then it would be proper for this proof to establish the desired conclusion.

Is it not the case that for us there is indeed the notion of being produced (*pauruṣeya-buddhi*) everywhere? That notion of being produced is itself the notion of what is to be proven (*sādhya-buddhi*), and thus the rule that "inference is [the cognition of] what is to be proven" holds, since for some person, in some way, even in those cases [of mountains and oceans], that notion is absent. Furthermore, what is meant by the "notion of being produced"? Is it the notion of mere effect (*kārya-mātra-buddhi*), or the notion of being produced by a person (*puruṣa-mātra-buddhi*)? If it is the notion of mere being produced, then that is established even for the Buddhist in the case of the oceans and mountains.

Furthermore, because it possesses parts, its very nature as "produced" (kṛtatva) consists precisely in the possibility of its being commenced by those parts. Now, if you argue that the cognition of being produced is actually the cognition of human authorship—that is, it is simply the cognition of what is to be proven (sādhyabuddhi)—and that this is what is called inference, then how is it not a contradiction to say that because of the absence of that [human authorship], there is no inference?
For such a statement would be untenable.

As it has been said: "Nor does the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*) arise for anyone simply because of a lack of cognition of the probandum due to delusion, for that would entail the consequence of such a fault in all inferences. And as for this which is stated: "Such properties as being an effect and so forth are denied in the case of mountains and the like"—this is the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* in the section concerning the doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*).

Even in that case, we do not perceive any distinction between Mount Kailāsa, a water-jar, and so forth, on the grounds of their being effects (*kāryatva*) or the like. And it has been said: "Nor is there any distinction whatsoever among the causes of the earth and so forth from the causes of palaces and the like, by which these [latter], while being devoid of intention, could—being independent of effort—possess such [causes] through an activity characterized by specific determination; for [this would not be possible] for those not presided over by an intelligent agent."

The independence of instruments possessing the nature of being tools in their respective actions is preceded by perception; for in all cases, such as the construction of palaces and the like, the production [of effects] is observed only when they are presided over by an intelligent agent.

To this it is replied: this "established cognition" (*kṛtabuddhi*) was not stated with reference to those whose intellects are permeated by an adherence to philosophical tenets (*siddhāntābhiniveśa*), but rather with reference to ordinary persons proficient in worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*). And for such a person—who possesses the recollection of the previously perceived invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*)—when there is an absence of the primary cause (the perception of the probans), such a cognition indeed arises in places like a temple; however, it does not arise in places like Mount Malaya or the ocean.

Therefore, the existence and non-existence of this cognition cannot be established without positing a difference in genus (*jātibheda*), for otherwise, the same would follow even when two [different kinds of] smoke are perceived. Granted, this is indeed a cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*); but who says that this [cognition] is the basis for the inference of that [probandum], or that its absence results in the absence of that [probandum] in the case of the mountain and so forth? Rather, it is for the purpose of indicating the mere difference in genus.
The presentation of existence and non-existence is for the sake of awakening someone of dull intellect, with respect to people of equal standing.

For once such a distinction between types [of things] is established, one would not be able to claim that the perception and non-perception occurring in one case is capable of proving a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in another.

Therefore, the establishment of the probandum does not follow from a reason that lacks a necessary connection (*apratibaddha*), such as mere co-presence (*sanniveśa*); and since a reason that is connected is unestablished (*asiddha*), how can there be inference? Thus, even when this is introduced for the ultimate purpose of negating inference, what is being stated is simply that the absence of that [inference] does not follow from the absence of one [specific instance].
Now, even so, because another inference fails to arise, it follows that for another [person] as well, it ought not to exist.
And how could that [contradiction] be consistent? For it has been stated: "Nor from delusion," and so forth. That is incorrect;

because when there is the possibility of an identical causal complex (*sādhanasāmagrī*), it is impossible for the result (*sādhya*) to be restricted to one [of two cases]. Whatever possesses a specific causal complex must have a result no different from that [complex]; just as two locations possess the same collection of fuel, fire, and so forth, which are the common means for producing smoke.

And there is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*): "The person who is engaged in conventional practice with you possesses the same causal complex for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and for establishing the means of inference as those who are mutually indistinguishable. For even for you, perception and non-perception alone are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the necessary connection, operating through the agency of temple architects and the like; and this is common to the opponent as well.

However, the uncommon means of valid cognition that subverts the contrary would be difficult to infer; and it has already been shown that even you do not possess such a means. Therefore, if attachment to your own position does not cloud your mind, then let that very [lack of proof] be the proof.

If it were common to others, then for that [author] as well, an inference of human authorship would be unavoidable even in the case of Mount Meru, Mandara, and so forth, which belong to the assembly of the gods; yet this is not the case. Therefore, when the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of one thing with another occurs—*Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, 300.

For one who possesses the recollection of the [necessary] connection, that which is seen does not constitute an inference, nor is a connection established for it with respect to that object; this is like one who, while recollecting the connection between smoke and fire, fails to infer fire upon seeing a donkey. And there is no inference of a person in places such as Malaya or Himālaya by a conscious person who possesses the recollection of a connection with a temple or similar structure; thus, there is the non-perception of the effect (kāryānupalabdhi) regarding the recollection.

In the case of following the cause, when other conditions such as the primary [cause] and so forth are possible, he establishes the deficiency in making [the object] the objective domain by means of the proof that establishes the prior connection; and this [deficiency] does not exist even for that which possesses internal differentiation, unless there is a distinction of a different genus, as in the case of a donkey.

However, if there is a failure in either the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or its recollection (*smaraṇa*) regarding smoke, this desired conclusion is not established. To ensure that, there must be a correct apprehension.

In that regard, if there is a failure in recollection, one would not infer even from within a temple (*devakula*). Furthermore, a failure in apprehension is impossible with respect to perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because it has been stated that there is simply an absence of the capacity for a single unifying conceptual judgment (*ekapratyavamarśa*). Otherwise, even those seeking water from clouds and such would have to depend upon potters, architects, and the like. If you argue that even in that case another person occupies the place of the architect, just as someone occupies the place of the potter—no, for when there is no dissimilarity in the class of the effect (*kāryajāti*), there can be no dissimilarity in the causal capacity (*kāraṇasāmarthya*).

Because indifference [toward other causes] would be untenable; otherwise, one would not find satisfaction even with a potter alone when another jar is required. Or else, the farmer would remain in the misery of drought that cannot be remedied by the efforts of a potter. Thus, such a distinction between classes (*jāti-bheda*) is indeed established. Therefore, since the uniform reflective awareness (*ekākāra-pratyavamarśa*) is untenable, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established through perception does not incur the fault of being difficult to grasp, as it has a specific object; for this reason, inference—
Even if [the object] exists, since a distinction in the excellence of the universal (*jāti*) is unestablished, there would be the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanadoṣa*).

Consequently, because the apprehension [of the object] as it truly is is established, where there is no inference, there is simply no apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). If it is asked, "How then is the absence of inference in such a case to be understood by people?"—it is from what has already been stated.

If you argue that we perceive the pervasion [of agency] by mere sentience alone—not by that [agency] restricted to specific states such as being a potter—and therefore this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not apply; for even one who desires rain-clouds might, in the course of crushing the legs of a potter, [mistake him for a cloud], or one terrified by the invasion of a foreign army might long for the protection of the great mountains and oceans—then what fault is there in grasping the pervasion precisely by means of that which is restricted to those specific states? What is the point here?

Should it be said? There is no concern for you, whose intellect is marked by the flaw of partiality toward your own school; rather, the concern is for the world. If it is argued that even the world does not understand [the object] through that [inference] because of its fallibility, then in that case, one should not perform an inference even from another jar.

If it is argued that there is no fault here because deviation is observed elsewhere, this cannot be maintained unless there is a dissimilarity between the two classes (*jāti*). Therefore, why not simply say that the perception which grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) operates only with respect to a specific class, and thus the inference of its operation does not apply elsewhere? What is the point of introducing the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this case? Furthermore, [the role] of perception must necessarily...

A determination of a specific class must be sought; otherwise, even perception—which has as its object that which is not subject to deviation—would not be restricted to a specific class, and it might thus encroach upon another object such as a pot. Such being the case, that same fault would persist. This is the explanation of the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) within the section on the doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*).

If it is argued that this is because [the mind] is presided over by another jar, then surely, while the mind is wandering through an object already presided over, how could it avoid that very same [object]?
However, this fault does not arise if both [the jar and the mind] have fixed objects. But now, regarding the specific object [of the jar] by means of perception—

The presentation of an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not fruitful by way of [the opponent] accepting it. However, for the sake of instilling a memory regarding the specific scope of the object of the means of valid cognition that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is employed against one who is deluded. But pervasion, which extends everywhere, is not made restricted to a fixed object by means of deviation. Nor is there a mere refutation of inference, precisely because of the reasoning already stated. Therefore:

It is established that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by means of a specific subject (*viśiṣṭaviṣaya*) through the potter and so forth, because perception functions only with respect to a single genus (*ekajāti*), depending on whether or not deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed. Thus, even when there is a desire to apprehend pervasion by means of "consciousness" (*cetana*) alone, since no deviation is observed, [the pervasion holds] for whatever genus...

It is also established that when perception operates upon an object, that very object is proven to be pervaded by it. Therefore, how can one who asserts a pervasion in a general sense not deserve censure for merely repeating a convention? However, if a person desiring to grasp a pervasion relies on another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) instead of perception, then this fault does not apply; but that [other means] must be examined—

This is the truth. If, through the grace of the Lord, a perception arises for this disputant that is uniform in every respect by abandoning the manifold forms of the world, and if that [perception] is unique [to him], it cannot be a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). There is no difference whatsoever between one who possesses a body and one who does not, provided both possess effort, regarding the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of perception with respect to the properties of action; for this reason, one who seeks water [must rely on common experience].
If, by following the example of the potter, one were to infer the absence of inference based on what he has produced, then even if there were a possibility of [inference] through another mode,

the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would recur, because there would be no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) based solely on the difference in genus (*jātibheda*). Therefore, the absence of inference therein— established as being caused by the difference in genus— demonstrates that inference is restricted to specific genera.
Whether it be the distinction between castes (*jāti-bheda*)—
which is established by human inference based on specific caste characteristics— or even the fact that [the world] is established by experience,

one who out of deceit denies these, [denies] the next world as well, since its existence is inseparable from the distinction between castes, which is established by the absence of such activity [as seen in the case of a potter].

Because there is no inference [establishing] that it has been made by someone; otherwise, the emergence of an inference would entail the fallacy of a "jāti" (reductio ad absurdum), as it is said: "If there were such a thing as a conjunction distinct from both the post and the crow, it would be visible, and the world would perceive this third entity.
Likewise, if the kind of arrangement seen to be preceded by an intelligent agent were exactly the same as that found in clouds and the like, [then the inference would fail].
It might be argued that even for the world, there could be the notion that it was created by a person, just as in the case of other jars.

But this is not so; it has been stated that this distinction is caused by a difference in their genus (*jāti*), since no other cause exists. Therefore, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of configuration (*sanniveśa*) is established as being invariably concomitant with a supervisor (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), [it is that] from the observation of which [the presence of a supervisor is inferred] by one who does not observe the act of creation...

The word "api" (also) is used here for the purpose of avoiding the burden of enumerating various types [of inference] categorized by different synonyms; for in that context, both "the cognition that [a thing] was made by a person" (*puruṣakṛtabuddhi*)—which is either an inference from effort or an inference from the activity of a potter and so forth—are applicable. (Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, 302)

According to the sequence previously stated: the absence of an inference for a potter is itself the *liṅga* (probans), because it consists of the causal complex that proves the negation of merely one who possesses effort; or rather, the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the knowledge of that [absence]. This has been elaborated while following the wishes of others.
But the world follows what it observes: whatever kind of thing it sees as preceded by a person, it perceives that very thing as being produced by such a corporeal being alone.

The cognition that "it was done" does not even scratch the doubt regarding the cessation of the body; thus, the cognition that it was done remains established only as a conclusion reached through inference by fellow human beings. Even when, due to the power of some supernatural accomplishment (*siddhi*), someone perceives a demonic illusion (*āsurī māyā*) and a certain impression arises even regarding something immovable—thinking, for instance, "this too has been created by someone, or by some means, or somewhere"—[the same principle applies].
Even then, it appears entirely as if colored by hands, feet, and limbs; certainty, however, remains far off.

Moreover, that [appearance] would not be possible if there were a single genus [of cognizer], just as smoke and a jar do not arise from fire and a potter [respectively]. Nor is there even a mention of [a cognizer] devoid of the activity of hands, feet, and so forth. And yet, for this reason alone, there is no denial of inference by those who advocate momentariness and other such views.

It is possible [to say this]. However, we maintain that inference—which relies on the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) preceded by perception and whose operation depends on specific universals (*jāti*)—is not possible for either the common person (*laukika*) or the investigator (*parīkṣaka*), because it is common to both.
And although the second [type of inference] is indeed also common, nevertheless, due to the lack of familiarity with a certain object, there is an exceedingly intense...

For those of subtle intellect, this [inference] is possible even for conventional usage, as it depends upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). In that case, although it lacks the capacity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), an inference may be employed based on a pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped through another inference that sublates the contrary, relying solely on worldly consensus; thus there is no fault, just as there is a specific proclamation of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) among people. Therefore, it consists of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*).

It is entirely logical that one who has formed the cognition [of something as "produced"] establishes a distinction between types of entities based on existence and non-existence. Even if "one who has formed the cognition" (*kṛtabuddhi*) means one who has merely formed the cognition [that it was produced], there is still no fault. Nevertheless, what is called "producedness" (*kṛtatva*) consists in having its own birth dependent upon the operation of another; and this is not established through direct perception in things such as mountains, in the same way that it is established in things such as trees. It is merely accepted by the opponent.
But [if it is argued that] it is established as independent, then in the context of establishing [the self], it is certainly not an auxiliary factor (*anaṅga*).

Therefore, when inference is resorted to as something already established, is it based on what is observed to be of the same class (*dṛṣṭasajātīya*), or is it based on something in any way whatsoever?

In the latter case, if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—which consists of a succession of moments characterized by a continuous stream of causal capacities from beginningless time—is determined by its restricted location...

If it were established by such [a person], what hope could there be for the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a Person? Rather, that auxiliary factor should be one of a kind observed [in the world]. For, setting aside the distinction made by the superintendence of sentient and insentient beings, even if one were to attribute the activity of a Person to the arising obtained through the conjunction of an extensive multitude of causes—since that conjunction is determined to be dependent upon him—the insentient...

For even the mere fact of being a foot (of a syllogism) has its purpose fulfilled according to the traditional sequence; it would not draw in the specific feature under discussion. This very state of being an effect is what is known in the world, and since that is not established in the case of mountains and the like, how can there be an avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*)? [Note: 1. *māmālimālacayato* is found in the manuscript. 2. *kāraṇāṅgo rikta* is found in the manuscript.]

In this section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), this commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī* is a direct proof of non-establishment; however, it is for the purpose of establishing heterogeneity (*vijātīyatva*). It does not concern the mere fact of being an effect (*kāryatvamātra*), but rather [the nature of] everything.

The meaning of this is as follows: what is it that—established by the presence or absence of a governing agent, and by the conformity to [specific] arrangements such as shape—is seen such that even a person who perceives no action develops the cognition that something has been "made"? Therefore, if you maintain that the cognition of being "made" arises even for a thing possessing parts, yet it does not so arise for the world (the universe), then a difference in nature (*bhinnajātīyatva*) is established between them. Otherwise, even in the case of a potter and the like, [the same distinction would apply].

The world would perceive [the Veda] as being pervaded by mountains and the like; thus, as before, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, it is established that, due to the difference in genus (*jāti-bheda*), that which is produced by a person is perceived as something entirely distinct from [the Veda] through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
P.

Regarding the statement that there is no distinction whatsoever in the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*): even though *kāryatva* is a property common to all things, if it is intended that its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through perception (*pratyakṣa*), then—even though it exists—it is effectively as good as non-existent, as has already been explained. However, if one intends to express a pervasion by consciousness (*cetanā*) based on the mere fact of coming into existence after not having existed (*abhūtvābhāva*), while disregarding specific distinctions, then one must likewise disregard the operation of perception.
"Let another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be the refuge"—even this [is not tenable]. Or, in its absence, there is nothing at all, even if it exists as an effect.

As for what he said—"Nor is there any distinction among the causes of the earth and so forth," etc.—that too serves only to delude common folk; it cannot be a means for understanding the intended meaning. It is just like [inferring] diamonds and stones by their being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*).

Establishing the property of being scratchable by iron (*lohalekhyatva*) against one who doubts it, he says: "Nor is there any distinction between thunderbolts and [ordinary] wood, stone, and so forth, by which these [thunderbolts], while being earthen (*pārthiva*), would be devoid of the quality of being scratchable by iron. For the state of being earthen has never been observed in things that are not scratchable by iron; rather, the state of being earthen is observed only in all those things, such as jars and trees, that are admitted to be scratchable by iron. It is the same in that case.
Even what is under discussion appears to be merely a construction of words.

For just as all persons, by virtue of being devoid of independent purpose, are perceived to engage in the undertaking of actions dependent upon others, so too do things possess the nature of being scratched by iron due to their earthiness. And just as that is so, there is much to be observed.

Just as there is no other way here either, so too in this case: one might suspect whether this quality of being inscribed on a wall is invariably concomitant with mere earthiness, or whether, despite being earthen, it depends upon some further specific condition. Similarly, even when many instances have been observed, the same doubt arises:

is it simply that the non-conscious requires consciousness for its causal activities, or is it rather that it requires something specifically related to the object of the activity? The logic is identical.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no distinction [between causes] because they are all equally capable of being apprehended as a single conceptual unity by disregarding their subtle internal differences—just as in the case of fire and the like—then, due to the resulting lack of distinction even among effects, it would be impossible to avoid the absurd consequence that the construction of a palace could be produced from a mountain peak, just as smoke is produced from fire. If God were accepted [as the cause], this might occasionally be otherwise; however, if He were the cause at all times, [the aforementioned absurdity would follow].

In the opposite case, there would be the undesirable consequence of even a rice seed being denied the capacity to produce a rice sprout, or else the production of a palace interior would be prohibited. If it is argued that [the capacity] exists despite an absolute difference in genus, by relying merely on the property of being devoid of intentionality—that too is a delusion. (From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, folio 304)

Thus it is; for indeed, no common property whatsoever is difficult to find. Nor does that much imply that things possess both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), because that would entail the absurd consequence of poison and nectar performing the same function. What undesirable thing could there be? Or rather, disregarding the commonality of being unintentional—which cannot be avoided—even in the case of the construction of palaces and such, by what power based on a distinction of intrinsic nature...

If there were even a prohibition of the restriction [of effects] depending on the effort produced by that [cause], which would cause an absolute difference in the effect—what kind of fault would there be?
This phrase "there is no such thing as a distinction" and so forth is intended to mean this.
Therefore, because there is no way to grasp a pervasion characterized by various distinctions, and because doubt remains unremoved, even in one's own heart...

Such a rambling argument is merely a defense of one's reputation based on an inability to provide convincing proof. Consequently, with respect to the necessary connection established by perception, that kind of arrangement and so forth which is proven to be pervaded by an intelligent agent is not present in mountains and the like;
and that which *is* present there has not been proven to be so pervaded. Thus, the reason is either unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

By this, [the author] addresses what Trilocana said: "Now, what is this 'cognition of having been produced' (*kṛtabuddhi*)? Is it the cognition of the means (*sādhana*), or the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*)?

First, the cognition of the means is already established for you, since you accept that the diversity of the world is born of action (*karmaja*). If, on the other hand, it is the latter alternative, then the meaning is this: the 'effectness' (*kāryatva*) perceived in these things such as the earth and so forth is not capable of serving as an inference for the probandum."
But [if you say] it is something else entirely because it does not produce the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), that is not tenable, because it would entail the destruction of all inference.

For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could just as well say: "This smoke is not capable of inferring fire; rather, it is something else entirely, because it does not produce the cognition of the probandum in one who perceives the probandum. And thus, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum has not arisen.

It is refuted [by the following]: "It is established; as long as the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established, so long the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not established"—thus, the mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is quite clear.
For this is not a direct statement of non-establishment; rather, it is because there is no cognition of something already accomplished for one engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārika*).

Even for one who remembers the pervasion of jars and the like in the Indus region and elsewhere, there is no single genus [for all things]; thus, this would merely prove a difference in genera. Consequently, it is entirely logical that there is either a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) or an inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) by way of the pervasion of a specific genus. And in that case, the absence of the cognition of "producedness" (the reason) means both the absence of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the absence of the cognition of the probans (*sādhana*), which has been fully established.

As for what the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* said: "If it is perceived as being produced, why is there no cognition of it as having been made? Even in the case of all palaces and such, the cognition that they were made does not arise [in everyone]; rather, the cognition that they were made arises only for one who knows the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding ancient palaces and the like, while for those who are ignorant of the pervasion, there is only the cognition that they were not made. It is the same with the earth and so forth; thus, there is no distinction. [Response: This is not a valid point. For even in the case of palaces and the like, the cognition that they were made arises for those who know the pervasion, whereas for those who are ignorant of the pervasion, there is only the cognition that they were not made. There is no difference in this regard between the earth and other such things. Furthermore, since the cognition of being made is indeed present in some cases, the absence of such a cognition in others cannot serve as a reason for the non-existence of a creator. Otherwise, one would have to conclude that because the cognition of fire is absent in water, fire does not exist at all. Therefore, the argument is flawed. Moreover, the cognition of being made is established through the perception of specific qualities (*viśeṣadharma*), such as the particular arrangement of parts, which is observed in objects like palaces.
Since such qualities are also observed in the earth and so forth, the cognition of them being made is likewise established. Thus, there is no lack of distinction.
If it is argued that the cognition of being created by a person is not possible in the case of the earth and so forth, as it is in the case of palaces and the like—[we ask:

is this regarding those for whom an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well-known, or those for whom it is not? Even among those for whom it is well-known, is it regarding those who lack the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or others? First, for those whose memory has not failed, the cognition of being created by a person certainly arises in the world.

For indeed, there is a conviction among the deluded that this diverse world was created by some Creator (*dhātṛ*). However, because the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigrahasmṛti*)— as explained in the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* commentary on the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*)— does not arise even in the case of certain structures such as palaces, it does not follow from that alone that they were not made by a person.
[The reason] is "being produced" (*kṛtatva*).

Furthermore, since Mīmāṃsakas do not even entertain the notion that the Vedas were created by a person, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) cited there to prove human authorship would likewise be unestablished (*asiddha*). Moreover, regarding the [reason] "having an author" (*sakartṛkatva*) which was stated for the purpose of establishing impermanence—

The proof has been stated; yet even if it exists, it would be unestablished (*asiddha*). For the nature of being ungraspable by the auditory organ (*aśrotragrāhyatva*), as seen in jars and the like in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, does not exist in the same way in sound. Therefore, this dissimilarity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) is common to all inference and is not a sublation (*bādhaka*) specifically for the inference of God (*īśvara*); thus, that [objection] is also refuted by this very point.
Furthermore, regarding what was conceptualized with reference to the cognition of the probandum—namely, "Is it [the case] for those who possess well-known inference?

and so forth—we reply: What kind of person is he to be called who, having once observed the production of a temple pinnacle and the like during the activity of a master builder and such, infers human agency at a later time upon seeing that same pinnacle and so forth, even though the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well known?

Does he possess memory or not? In the first case, it has already been demonstrated that for that very person, there would be no cognition of human agency regarding mountains and the like, because this would entail the same inference [of agency] being applied to a potter as well. Therefore, how could there be a rule of necessity regarding the existence of such [agency] for those whose perception is unimpaired?

For that very reason, even the notion that "the world is diverse" and so forth does not arise from the power of remembering a grasped pervasion; rather, it arises from the influence of doctrines originating from other perceptions.
Because it is non-existent for those who do not hear [the argument], like a contradictory statement;

however, [the objection] beginning with "but for those confused about pervasion" (*vyāptivimūḍhānām*) is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, the example is even more flawed, because it merely demonstrates a difference in genus (*jātibheda*) regarding the absence of the cognition that [the reason] has been stated. Nor is there an existence or non-existence of that [cognition] depending on the proponent or the opponent.

It has been stated that this is a matter of reflection (*cintā*), for a conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) may arise otherwise through one's own persistent attachment (*abhiniveśa*). However, with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this reflection is undertaken from the standpoint of conventional discourse (*vyāvahārika-adhikāra*). Now, consider this: for someone who is ignorant of the conventions of the Vedas and so forth, yet hears Vedic sentences and another work composed as their imitation—even while examining it skillfully—what kind of [understanding] might they have? Reflect upon this.

The determination of specific distinctions—such as [the difference between] a jar and a thunderbolt—is due to humans perceiving the causes of all types of things; for if one were to postulate perceptual differences for words that are themselves perceptible by nature, it would lead to the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) that this would apply even to smoke and other such phenomena. Therefore, whatever exists follows the presence and absence of the person [who perceives it]. Thus, those things which partake in the existence [of the word] remain dependent upon the presence and absence of the person.

There is no possible difference between other speech and the words of the Vedas, for both possess the nature of being composed of articulate sounds; they are equal in their indication of supersensuous matters, and since confidence is necessarily established in one of them,
the Veda therefore does not rest without reaching the status of being human-authored.
If that were so, what room would there be for the existence of that [Vedic authority] in mountains and such things, which are directly perceived as being of a different nature? This follows:
when a difference in nature between worldly and Vedic sentences is possible, the Mīmāṃsaka cannot be defeated by mere convention alone.

Nor can "the state of being a statement" (*vākyatva*), whose pervasion is not established by perception, serve as a refuge in that case. As for what was said regarding "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), that has already been examined and will be further considered immediately below. [Objection: Even so, although that [pervasion] exists, since properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) are observed in an effect that is pervaded by that [agency], they might also exist elsewhere. Just as a jar and the like are invariably concomitant with an intelligent agent (*prayatnavat*), so too might the mountain (*pṛthvīdhara*) and other things be so. If this is argued:

But has it not been stated here that, although "being an effect" and so forth exist there, they are effectively indifferent because their pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped? Therefore, even when one analyzes other effects, not even a touch of effort is obtained; only the mere word "effect, effect" remains unanalyzed. If that very [word] is now being sought as a refuge by your long-lived self through another door, then—
Since no direct refutation has been heard, [the author], demonstrating that even that [criticism] is for the most part like the ravings of crows, says:
"In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, one [verse] states:
'Only by conceiving a specific effect as distinct does one [attribute] a specific nature to the cause...'"

Just as one might vainly imagine that the mere effect of fire is pervaded by its mark (smoke), another fails to understand that such an effect must indeed have that [fire] as its cause; alas, this is a particular kind of darkness even among the learned regarding an object of direct perception!
It is not logical to infer [a property] from a word that is established as distinct in one particular object, merely because of the identity of the word,
as in the case of inferring fire from a white substance.

[Pravāraṇavāda 1.14] By this, that which was also stated is refuted: "Nor can the probandum—the fact of having an insentient material cause—be established here through superimposition based on a mere similarity of words;
for, just as in the case of 'producedness' [proving] 'impermanence' and so forth, the connection here too is real. And it is not...

The claim that "the distinction between the universals (*jāti*) of two subjects or two properties everywhere precludes a real proximity (*pratyāsatti*), because it would follow that there is no proximity between 'producedness' (*kṛtakatva*) and 'impermanence' (*anityatva*) due to the difference in their universals, such as 'sound-ness' and 'pot-ness'"—that too is without foundation. For we do not assert the superimposition (*samāropa*) of insentience or having a material cause upon mountains and the like; rather, those [attributes] alone, by virtue of being excluded from the scope of pervasion (*vyāpti*), are as good as non-existent.

If it is asked: "If one kind of insentient material cause (*acetanopādānatva*) is established as requiring a conscious agent (*cetana*), while another kind is observed in mountains and the like [as being independent], what is the basis for this distinction? [The answer is: It is caused by limiting conditions (*upādhi*). If it is further asked: "Is this not the case even for two properties belonging to different substrata (*dharmin*)?"—[we reply: No, because of the disparity. Insentient material causality is like smoke, due to the [erroneous] conceit that it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); yet no one [actually perceives such a relationship] for that [case].

He states the difference based on the difference between the substrata (*dharmin*): "But when, because they have non-conscious matter as their material cause (*upādāna*), mountains and the like are intended to depend upon a conscious being, then the state of affairs is such that 'smoke, by virtue of being smoke, possesses fire. This being the case, a distinction must be admitted between the two instances of smoke and the two instances of 'smokeness' (*dhūmatva*);
so how can there be parity? If you say, 'Let it be exactly thus,' we say no; for the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is indeed what is differentiated."

In the section concerning the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), the commentary on the *Saptaślokī-vārtika* states: "It might even break the end [of the chain]; and this 'difference'—characterized by being excluded from a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*)—does not touch the smoke as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), such that it would divide what belongs to itself, just as [the property of] being the material cause of insentient things does not divide jars, clouds, and so forth; thus, this is not a valid objection."

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that we have never observed a difference in properties based on a difference in the substratum (dharmin)? [We reply: When a property is brought forward as the basis for the operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes a necessary connection (pratibandha), then even if the class of the substratum (dharmijāti) appears as distinct, it does not constitute a sublation [of the connection], provided that it is non-different from that [property].

However, when there is a difference in that [substratum], another property residing therein—even if it is itself non-different—appears as if it were distinct and thus does not establish [the connection].
This is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even one seeking water would have to search for a potter.

If it is argued that this is not so because clouds are seen arising in the sky even when that [potter] is absent—[we reply: no; why can the projection of that wind not be conceived as originating from that very source, just as a jar originates from a potter? Furthermore, since only the quality of "bearing water" is observed in both cases, there is, as in that [previous] instance, merely a difference in terminology.

It is established that it is likewise here as well; for the ascertainment of an impediment occurs only when there is a restriction to the essential nature of the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatva*) consists in the absence of such a restriction, which is contrary to that.

For an ascertainment bound by a means of valid cognition, if it were to occur even when the actual nature of its object is transgressed, it would be produced by both valid and non-valid means of cognition.

It might be so; however, it is not thus, and therefore there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because this follows from the operation of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). Thus, in this case, since the deviation of whiteness from fire has been observed, this is a refutation of the example being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyaśūnyatā*). For this very reason, it is not an inference; due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the result here in both cases is uncertainty. But [this does not apply] to fire and... [smoke], which possess established pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The argument is deficient in its proof because of the deviation [of the reason] from the two pale objects; for as long as pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established, it is impossible to prove a refutation of inference, since deviation itself would be untenable.
Indeed, pervasion consists in a universal inclusion; in the absence of that [inclusion], how could there be the relation "the presence of that [effect] when that [cause] is present"?

Thus, the meaning is as follows: Just as there is no inference of fire from paleness because the latter lacks an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) with it—and that lack is manifested by way of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—otherwise, one would have remained at ease even while accepting an inference in that case. And that deviation demonstrates that all properties common to both the nature of the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-viṣaya-svarūpa*) and its opposite are invariably unestablished as being concomitant.

Because there is no obstacle [to the argument] being drawn from the aforementioned commonality; likewise, just as there can be no inference of a conscious controller even from mere "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth, therefore the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed beneficial to the opponent. Thus, it is established that by reflecting upon the true nature of the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the probans such as "being an effect" is necessarily qualified by such an *upādhi* (limiting condition) regarding the intellect (*dhi*). And of such a [qualified]...
Since the distinction in proximity is indeed real, it has fallen into the state of being a mere name.
Therefore, even though the fact that a difference in the substratum or genus is a differentiator of properties is established, how can there be a denial of that in all cases?

If the meaning is that what constitutes a differentiator in all cases is denied, while in some cases it is also a non-differentiator, then that is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). As it has been said:

For the establishment of those two [the pervader and the pervaded] depends upon the nature of the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This being the case, there is indeed the persistence of difference; and in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, the contact with properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is treated as non-sublating. For even in that case, pervasion cannot be established by the force of perception (*pratyakṣa*), but rather through an inference that sublates the contrary (*viparyayabādhakānumāna*), since in its absence the inference is not accepted.

If, then, the proof of the pervasion of a mere property (dharma) designated as "coming into being after not having been" by means of the property of "having come into being and then ceasing to be"— which excludes the specific difference in kind (jātibheda) of the subject (dharmin)— is like the kitchen and so forth which prove the pervasion of smoke by fire, then what follows for the case at hand,
where the method of grasping pervasion is established precisely upon the exclusion of specific differences in kind in reliance upon the operation of perception? However, if...

In the present case as well, it might be argued that the properties residing in the actual thing to be proven—such as "being an effect" and so forth—are what must be understood as having the pervasion; if that were so, this would not be a fault. However, it has been shown that since even these two types of means are impossible, the pervasion is indeed untenable. In that regard, the proof that subverts the contrary (viparyaya-bādhaka-pramāṇa) consists in the impossibility of those [properties], because we observe that only certain "Buddha-fragrances" (bauddhagandhi) apply such effort. And yet, it is not...

Having discarded attachment to that [position], because it can be stated regarding the subject at hand; and in another passage, by means of the verse beginning "Is there eternal existence or non-existence? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.34).

The venerable author of the *Vārttika*, providing relief by indicating— through the force of the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the contrary— that there is a necessary connection between the mere effect and the mere instrument when specific qualities are set aside, observes that the opponent, who asserts pervasion based on mere observation and non-observation, relies upon the strength of perception and non-perception in establishing that [pervasion]. Having identified this reliance, he sets forth a refutation based on the distinction of logical categories (*jāti*) in order to refute it.

It should be understood that, therefore, because the distinction between classes produced by the operation of perception is extremely clear, it has been stated that even resorting to a mere name is of no avail.

Alternatively, let there be a difference in genus between mountains and the like on the one hand, and jars and the like on the other, on account of which it might be said, "It is established that [the effect] is of such a kind," and so forth.
But as for pleasure-mountains and the like, they are human-made and belong to the same genus as those; why then should they not have the same cause as them?
What follows from this? The meaning is as follows: whatever is a mountain is entirely of human origin, just like a pleasure-mountain (krīḍāśaila) and Mount Kailāsa, which is a mountain.
In this manner, examples such as small streams and great lakes should be applied to rivers, oceans, and so forth; thus he says:
The meaning is this:
regarding the phrase "of that which is well-known when there is a difference in the object," and so forth,
it refers to the inference of [an agent] from the perception of the construction of things such as mountains, which are seen to be like those created by a playful architect (Viśvakarman) and others.
Nor is it supported by logic, since its course is faltering; therefore, that [argument] is equal to a mere name.
This is the commentary on the Seven Verses of the Vārttika in the section concerning the doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda).
Furthermore, if these mountains were established as being created by many similar human beings...
What is the news regarding the means for attaining the Lord? What has been undertaken here, and what has been completed?

If a difference in genus (*jāti*) were established, one might fulfill this hope by following the logic of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established as a corollary); however, if there is no difference, even that remains without foundation. For, according to both experience and accepted doctrine, the existence of a creator of something of a different genus is not established by the presence of another pot of the same genus; thus, the two [the jar and the world] possess distinct genera, and it is not their mere identity of name that brings about a common cause.
Anticipating the objection— "What is this restriction that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only through the two aforementioned modes and not otherwise?"— he says:
"Otherwise, because a potter produces certain modifications of clay such as jars and the like, it would follow that an anthill is also his work."

The sense is this: even by pursuing the matter very far, no method for establishing a necessary connection (pratibandha) can be found which, while avoiding the undesirable consequence of a universal concomitance with all earthen objects on the part of the potter, would establish a universal concomitance with all effects.

For when a potter is capable of establishing a pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the mere effect, what obstruction to his power is there in establishing its specific quality—that it is made of clay? Or, let it be that the apprehension of pervasion occurs through these two modes alone. As for what was said:
"Not by way of differentiation, due to the force of the subverting argument against the counter-example," and so forth.

Fearing that it might otherwise be the case, he says "otherwise," etc., considering the possibility— though already mentioned by way of a different illustration— that one seeking rain-clouds might go in search of a potter.

For when one establishes pervasion (vyāpti) in a general sense— even while proceeding with the aim of refutation— how could one then infer a potter from an earthen object, since only a cause in general would be established? Even when, by means of a specific reason in relation to perception, there is a pervasion of a specific effect such as a jar— which is produced by the operation of a specific agent, namely a potter— with that specific agent, even then...

Whence could such an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) arise? Even when, in a general sense, the particular depends upon the mere determination [of the universal], this [over-extension] remains even more remote. However, if the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) were established otherwise than it actually is—such that the universal [is inferred] from the particular—then how could there not be the over-extension of inferring a potter from a clay object? If such an over-extension occurs even from something entirely dissimilar with respect to its effect, such as a jar, then how [could inference be restricted]?

By what small degree [of difference] would it not be proximate? And thus, even with respect to a homogeneous thing (*sajātīya*), when compared to a perceptual determination that follows internal subdivisions, there is no inference because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has not been ascertained; so what need be said regarding a heterogeneous thing (*vijātīya*)? To show that this is a case of the "stick-and-cake" maxim (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*)—namely, that for one who has observed a pervasion (*vyāpti*) in something extremely heterogeneous, [inference is impossible]—the term "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*) is employed.
