In the case of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it either establishes the absence of certainty regarding the intended restriction, or it establishes that the [reason] falls outside the very categories previously stated. Furthermore, what is called "deviation" either extends an obstruction to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped in a general sense with respect to a specific object, or it demonstrates that there was no grasping of pervasion at all; or else...

Even though the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, he refutes inference alone; for this very reason, it is asserted that "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhita-viṣayatva*) is also a defining characteristic of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Regarding these positions: in the first position, there is a lack of confidence everywhere, since even elsewhere one would have hope for the probandum (*sādhya*) solely by virtue of that [pervasion], and that [hope]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

Even if [the existence of a creator] were certain, there would still be doubt regarding other cases as well—such as the suspicion that someone might have violated [their chastity]—and for that very reason, the apprehension of that [certainty] would be useless.

In the second case, however, there is no distinction regarding the conscious being; for just as the pervasion of the general class of effects with a potter is grasped through perception and established as not subject to deviation, so too is it with respect to mere consciousness. In that case as well...
Because there is no difference in the operation of perception [in either case].

But in the third case, since pervasion must already exist for inference to be set aside by a deviation (vyabhicāra), this is a most grievous succession of logical inconsistencies. Only in this position does the following consequence arise: if this probans here has not remained deviating from the probandum, then...

It establishes what is to be established (*sādhya*). And this [establishment], which is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavidhura*), cannot be accomplished by anyone other than one who has direct perception of all objects (*sarvārthasākṣātkārin*).

For he alone—either [identifies] that very subject (*dharmī*) which does not reside within such a middle [of the class], or else he makes it the object of inference by placing it within the scope of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). However, if all counter-instances (*vipakṣa*) are not seen, the doubt that "this [subject] might also reside right in the middle of those" would not be removed.

Therefore, the very logic already stated is worthy of being adopted; furthermore, the fact that deviation (vyabhicāra) exists only serves to prove the difficulty of grasping pervasion (vyāpti). Thus, a pervasion consisting of mere effect is simply untenable with respect to a specific cause under consideration.
If, once the pervasion has been grasped, there is a contradiction or a lack of confidence, [the inference fails].
If that [logical] apprehension does not pervade [the subject], and if there is no distinction for the intelligent person,
then— given the requirement for non-sublation— it is impossible to observe all counter-instances;
therefore, the rule of apprehension certainly does not apply to the mere result.
This is the summary. Furthermore, if it is held that one first apprehends a pervasion (vyāpti) whose object is all things, and then,
by virtue of a sequence of subverting arguments (bādhaka) regarding each respective class, establishes its own pervaded [specific instance] therein;

In the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*), the commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* states: "Is it not inferred that among various classes [of beings], there exists a sequence of means of accomplishment? For why would the wise enter such a state—which is a ground for exertion, incapacity, and doubt?"
This is an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).
"The uncountable" (*aparigaṇita*) refers to the domain of the operation of entities, whereas "the most uncountable" (*aparigaṇitatama*) refers to the domain of non-entities (*atviṣaya*).

In that regard, who—having repeatedly observed the deviation of each individual member of the multitude of classes of effects that do not belong to [a specific cause]—would [conclude that a cause produces] only its own class of effects?

Is it possible for an infinite operation to be capable of restraining the cause? And this being the case, that very thing whose deviation is not directly perceived would be incapable of being a signifier (*gamaka*) for him. If it is argued that this is not so because doubt is possible—no; for in that case, he might achieve certainty regarding some supersensible (*atīndriya*) object. For perception, which has been established as having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, operates toward the production of an activity directed toward a specific class of things.

If it is asked, "What is the doubt?"— then, in that case, when one follows the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as an antidote to the occurrence of such doubt regarding the higher and lower universals (*jāti*) pervaded by that [effect], the point established falls under the third quarter [of the verse]. Therefore, it is not possible to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of all effects by an intelligent cause through a specific reason.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "Whatever [is produced], etc.
Alternatively, it has been stated that it is not possible to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of an effect by mere effort independent of a body.

"Because it is refuted by perception," and so forth; he concludes that very point with the words "it is established," up to "this [agent] is one who possesses a body and so on, and is a controller. The remainder is easily understood. And such [an agent] is [refuted] by the sublation of perception and so forth—

The intended meaning is that [the reason] has the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, one might object: "Since sentience is observed even in that which possesses a body, it is possible for it to exist elsewhere as well;

thus, just as an effect and so forth are established as being pervaded by an embodied being, they could likewise be established by an 'intended' [sentient being]. To this, [the author] replies—shattering the desire for proof based on what remains as a mere name according to the previously stated logic—with regard to the difference in entities such as jars: "Of that which is well-known in the case of jars and the like..."

Furthermore, it is not logical to infer [the existence of] that which is intended to be non-different from the *tanmātra*—such as the word "that" (*tat*) denoting a potter and so forth—since it has been set aside in view of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, he asks: "How indeed [could there be an inference] from a thing considered to be pervaded? This implies the contextual point that [inference] is impossible.

"Like the substance *pāṇḍu* and so forth, [it leads to the inference of] fire"—this is the intended meaning. If an inference were made based on the mere similarity of words for something that is not actually identical, then why would there not also be an inference of smoke (the bearer of smoke) from something merely similar in name? Now, in that case, it depends upon the knowledge of a specific effect-nature (*kāryasvabhāva*). [From] the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

If it is argued that perception is not called inference because it excludes the pervasion by another [property], then why would perception not also exclude that [inference] by excluding mere consciousness? By this, when even a visible effect is set aside by perception, what need is there to mention something beyond the range of vision, such as mere consciousness? Let it be granted for now regarding the pervaded—
In relation to that [the limited], there is indeed division, because it is perceived as such in the world, and because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Anticipating the objection—"But what fault would there be if this rule did not apply in relation to the all-pervading (*vyāpaka*)?"—he revives the previously stated consequence by means of a different formulation, beginning with "otherwise," etc. "Of the anthill" (*valmīkasya*) means "of the creature living in the anthill."

"Produced by that" means produced by a potter and so forth. This is the meaning: if, having ascertained pervasion even through a specific instance, one were to infer a mere conscious being (*cetanamātra*) as a general property, then—since the production of jars and such is restricted to a potter who is a conscious being—one would have to infer that even an anthill is the agent of a jar and so forth. For just as a jar and the like are made by a potter...

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in the mere fact of being conscious during the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), that [person] too would be subject to inference. Likewise, why would there not be an inference regarding one dwelling in an anthill, as he is no different from others in terms of consciousness? And if, when the pervasion is grasped by means of an embodied being, another embodied being is excluded, then what can be said of one who is utterly dissimilar? Moreover, multiplicity is of no use here, because even a single self possesses consciousness.

Thus is the reference to Vālmīki. By this, the implication of inference regarding smoke and the like, as well as the digestive fire and so forth, is made clear. And in the discussion on deviation (*vyabhicāra*), everything should be repeated as before.

Regarding what was stated—that the arrangement and so forth acquired by an intelligent agent are not established in the case of oceans, mountains, and the like, and that even where they are established, they are not pervaded—this might be the response: "But surely this is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), because it involves a conceptual distinction between different properties (*dharmabheda*). Therefore, just as when it is argued, "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar," someone says: "If the property of being produced residing in a jar is the reason, then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of sound."

However, [the reason] "being included in sound" (*śabdagata*) is contradictory because it is absent in the collection [of things] such as jars and cloths, which are impermanent. Now, if the view is that [the reason] does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) just as it does not in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then it is the inconclusive reason called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*). Yet, by that much, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not truly incapable of proving impermanence; likewise, this [reason] is also not so. For instance, by the statement "that which is established is not pervaded," there is a contradiction due to its non-existence in the similar instance.

Furthermore, it follows that even in the case of exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the reason would be rendered "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). Now, if you argue that this is not actually a flaw because it conforms to the specific purpose at hand, then it would follow that even "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and other such reasons would fail to be proofs, and there would be a contradiction with the author of the Sūtras; for he has declared this very objection to be a flaw under the name "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*). As he said:

The objection that the probandum is unestablished on the grounds of even a slight difference in the nature of being an effect is called "balancing the effect" (kāryasama); this, moreover, is threefold according to the intention of the speaker.
The reading found in the *Mātṛkā* is "How many are absolute?
In the commentary on the *Vārttika-saptaślokī* within the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*),
it is stated that difference is merely a figurative designation (*upacāra-mātra*), and the threefold nature [of difference] is shown according to the intention of the speaker.

Thus, both of these [positions] are devoid of substance; for, first of all, the first position has already been refuted. Indeed, it has been stated that when the essential nature [of things], as presented by the means of valid cognition that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), is non-different, then even the related entities (*saṃbandhin*) that appear to be divided have their difference shaken off.

These [appearances], though appearing as such, are not subverting [evidence]. However, when there is a difference [in the subject], properties such as being an effect—which, although non-different from that [subject], appear as if they were different—are not establishers of its pervader. Furthermore, two methods for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) have been shown.

In that regard, if, by the force of a subverting argument against the contrary—as in the case of perishability [establishing] the state of being produced—[it were established] that even by an intelligent agent, [properties] such as being an effect are not invariably concomitant...

If there were such a grasping of an entity (*bhāvagraha*), then since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would have functioned with respect to mere configuration (*sanniveśa*) and so forth—just as it functions with respect to mere coming-into-being after not having been (*abhūtvā bhavanamātra*)—who could rightly excel in providing a proof by differentiating [the subject] through a distinction of properties? Thus, it is appropriate to call this a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*). However, if, by virtue of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), both "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "configuration" and so forth are pervaded (*vyāpta*)...

In that case, who could prevent the status of being a probans (*sādhanatva*) from applying even to sound (*śabda*), on the grounds of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth? For the operation of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is already fully established through the very delineation of specific universals (*jātiviśeṣa*). Otherwise, even properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in smoke would be established as invariably concomitant with fire without being restricted by specific universals, which would lead to an unavoidable [absurdity].
They should attain composure without resorting to a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum). Even the introduction of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding another matter is a most trivial counter-argument.
For in that case, since the proof is established precisely where no deviation is directly perceived, how much lightening of the burden of defects is there?

Furthermore, it has already been explained that for one who has previously grasped the pervasion of smoke having only a single effect, there can be no inference of it from other effects of fire, such as ashes, because even in dreams no deviation [of smoke from fire] is found. Therefore, with respect to the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must admit that the properties which differentiate the various classes of subjects (*dharmin*) are indeed differentiators themselves. How then can this be called a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*)? [End of] Nyāya...
But for the author of the Sūtras, the opponent [Vādin],
when the effect is used as a probans even in its general form because it is concomitant with the probandum,
the fault of "balancing the effect" (kāryasama) is considered to be the assertion of a difference based on a difference in the related term.
[Pravā.

1.16] This is the meaning: when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) pertains specifically to a qualified object, disregarding the operation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), then let the statement of a difference in "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth—based on the difference from other universals (*jāti*) that serve as its correlates—be considered a fault, for it is established by logic (*nyāya*). Even when...

Even when the proof is carried out by relying on the general property of "having come into being after not having existed" (*abhūtvā-bhāvitva*) as a common feature, because it is supported by the sublation of the opposite through the probandum such as destruction, there still remains the fault of asserting a difference [in the reason] due to the difference in its relata, since [the reason] is observed in some cases— [as stated in] *Pramāṇajñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

Without considering the circularity [of the argument], it is stated that this is regarded by our teacher as "equal to all other cases" (*sarvakāryasama*). However, at another time, this is considered a fault of the proof (*sādhana*); thus, there is no fault [in our position]. Now, one might object: "Even so, it remains unestablished that pervasion (*vyāpti*) encompasses all instances.

But to that extent, it is not the case that the probandum (*sādhya*) itself is unestablished; rather, it is only that the apprehension of pervasion has been carried out in accordance with the opponent's own tenets.
However, for us who exert effort, it is only the form perceived through examples that is determined as being pervaded; just as, having determined smoke seen in a kitchen to be dependent on fire,
one enters into the generality residing in the property to be proven, even while [observing] smoke in the subject of the thesis.
Just as, having perceived smoke where fire has been seen—as in a kitchen—one infers fire in that manner;

so too, although pervasion is established only for things of the same class as a jar and the like produced by an agent, one is able to state that "wherever effect-ness is observed, there is agency. And since the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not contradicted even in this way, what is the insistence on a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*)?

If you ask, "Of what [is there no grasping of pervasion]?"—if you mean "of the proof that the original means of proof is useless"—then it follows quite clearly that one takes the pervasion from one genus and performs the inference from another genus. This would be the case only by relying on the identity of names for the pervaded and the mark; and if that were so, the actual entity as the mark would not have been stated, but only the mere application of words such as "effect" and so forth.
And that is incorrect; demonstrating this, he says:
"For one who exerts effort, because of the observation of a commonality of sound established in another class [of things]."
It is not logical to establish [the existence of] speech and so forth on the basis of "cowness," as in the case of horns.
[Pravāraṇāvastu 1.17].

Now, one might object: "The term 'effect' (*kārya*) and so forth does not refer to mere sound (*śabdamātra*), because it is possible for the universal (*sāmānya*) of 'having come into being after not having existed' (*abhūtvābhāvitva*) to be present [in them]."

The word "cow" (*go*), however, relies merely upon subjective preference (*ruci*) regarding heaven and so forth, and does not function by following any [fixed] object; thus there is a great distinction.

This too is indeed subject to sublation (*plava*); for it is not established that the mere fact of coming into being after not having existed is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) with effort, such that its following [that effort] could be the result. And if it were established, then that very [invariable concomitance] would constitute a universal application (*sarvopasaṃhāra*); so what is the use of this?

Is it avoided or accepted? Therefore, even that [universal] which introduces differentiation through the distinction of causal classes does not involve any real continuity of the entity; we see that one has merely resorted to a proof consisting of words alone. Consequently, there is no difference between this [proof] and the proving of horns by means of "cowness" (gotva) in the case of a horse or the like.

Thus, this same verse applies to the example as well. And in that case, if one wishes to avoid the objection regarding the inclusion of all instances (*sarvopasaṃhāra*), the phrase "in another class" (*jātyantare*) should be construed as "of fire which is well-known to arise from smoke of a different kind. However, when one determines the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by unifying all forms of smoke into a single form through the force of a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), then there is no mere similarity of words; that very [fire] is what is pervaded.

The commentary on the *Vārtika-saptaślokī* within the section on the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*) in the *Mātṛkā* states, "It is not internal, nor is it internal-adjacent" (*nāntaravan nāntarīyakam*).

This same meaning applies here as well; therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Nor is it possible to perceive the futility of the original reason (*maulahetu*) in this manner; for indeed—

Although the cognition that "wherever there is a probans (sādhana), there is a probandum (sādhya)" functions in a general manner, it is capable of taking as its basis the specific distinctions of intended place, time, and so forth. Therefore, in order to make a particular [instance] the object of engagement or avoidance, one would not be able to proceed without relying on the property of the subject (pakṣadharma). Thus, how could the fundamental member [the thesis-statement] be fruitless?
Therefore, for one who avoids the universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) in establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), even smoke would not be an inferent of fire;
thus, for one who desires gain, there is the destruction of the very root. For it is not the case that fire is perceived as pervaded only at the specific instance where smoke is produced.

Even in another location, there remains only a similarity of words, namely that "this too is denotable by the word 'smoke' and that [other] is also [denotable by it]"; thus, there is no distinction between this case and the proof of horns for a cow by means of its voice. Now, one might ask: even so, what kind of proof of horns for a cow could this possibly be, since it is itself sublated by direct perception?
If you say that what is excluded is called "the reason lacking a locus," we reply: True; it is a great gain for us that such a conjecture is even possible for you.
It is truly remarkable that for one who negates in this manner, the hope for establishing the probandum—even by means of mere nomenclature—should utterly vanish.
Furthermore, regarding that which corresponds to one's exertion in the treatises:
for one who perceives that there is no means of proof for the "peak of words" when it is swallowed by pride,
how can the establishment of the probandum be desired through mere nomenclature?

Since even the cowherd women do not believe this now, he—who is thus striving to make them believe it—offers a reply in jest that is appropriate to the situation; by means of his "inference from horns," he characterizes all such improper inferences as mere sophistry. For when even fire and other things can be inferred from donkeys and the like, then [all inference is undermined].

The underlying intention [of the opponent] is: "Whose non-cognition is it, and for what reason? At most, let there be no direct contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣa-bādhā*). But surely, when the process involves the necessity of ascertaining that which pervades [the subject], based on the application of a term common to both the pervaded object and its pervader, what room is there for the inference of fire from a donkey?
For words such as 'smoke' or 'ash,' which are common to objects pervaded by fire, cannot possibly apply to a donkey. [Reply: No.
And as for the point that [the probans] is established through the similarity of the word even by means of terms such as "vastu" (entity) and so forth,

this has already been refuted by the very statement "in the case of eating things such as pale-colored substances" (*pāṇḍudravyādivatāśane*); nevertheless, seeking to satisfy [the opponent] from another perspective, Jñānaśrīmitra says in his *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*:

Since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, they do not exist anywhere [independently]. However, if the establishment of an object were to occur through their mere presence, then everything would be established for everyone.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "just as.

By this, it is shown that even in the case of donkeys and the like, words such as "smoke" (*dhūma*) and so forth cannot possibly apply as long as there is no intention regarding convention (*samaya*).

Consequently, the absence of inference (*anumāna*) is also strictly limited to the period before the application of words such as "smoke. Once they have been applied, however, what [remains] to be proven?

It has been stated that [the reason] "obstructs" [the object]. However, this is not the case when establishing a real entity (*vastu*). For it is said [in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.18]: "The [reason] does not [function] with respect to the object of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)."
The possibility of absence [of concomitance] arises;
for since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, where indeed do they not exist?
But when the goal of that state is accomplished, everything is accomplished for everyone.

However, when the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is intended through the operation of a thing that is invariably concomitant (*pratibaddha*), the establishment of everything—like sound and so forth—is not merely a result of audacity; rather, the sense is that the establishment of everything follows from the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in reality itself. Thus, if one speaks of pervasion based solely on what is observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then an establishment that depends merely on the similarity of words results in nothing but non-establishment (*asiddhi*); this is the point regarding the real [nature of things].

One who seeks the means of establishing the nine categories that lead to success must establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is universal (*sarvopasaṃhāriṇī*). Yet, neither of these two types of pervasion can provide a valid basis for inferring an intelligent agent from [the existence of] structural arrangement and so forth. Or, even if that much were established, the specific qualities desired would not be proven; for this reason, the name "Lord" (*īśvara*), which is being asserted with great effort by those seeking the highest good— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...is merely a designation for something whose nature is unknown. Furthermore, since the inference of an intelligent agent from the mere fact of being an effect is seen to fail in cases such as mountains and stones, it cannot be considered a valid means of knowledge. [This concludes the Discourse on God:
The Establishment of the Relation between Cause and Effect.
Some maintain that the nature of cause and effect is established by three kinds of perception and non-perception, while others say it is established by the pentad. (1)

The principle is that the causal relationship is established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). In this regard, some maintain that its proof is threefold: either two successive perceptions, both of which have both [cause and effect] as their objects and are assisted by a prior non-perception in general; or else, two successive non-perceptions, both of which grasp both [cause and effect] in general and are assisted by a perception. Others, however, [hold it to be] that...

They say that the fivefold [means of knowledge] have a fixed sequence, such that the final three are necessarily accompanied by the first two. For even when the first three are present, an unambiguous cognition does not arise for the perceiver; however, once the final two are obtained, it is established. Indeed, the relationship between cause and effect is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): therein, positive concomitance is understood through the triad, and negative concomitance through the dyad.
Success is well achieved by means of the group of five. The sense is that if there is doubt regarding even one of those two, uncertainty is difficult to dispel.
Here it is considered: if there is no prior perception [of the object], then from another source there may be union and so forth.
It does not negate; what is the use of that subsequent negation?

For non-apprehension is sought precisely for the purpose of establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by means of two types of non-apprehension. And that [negative concomitance] must be established by this [non-apprehension], which subverts the existence of that which is intended as the effect in the absence of that which is intended as the reason. Furthermore, that existence is conceived in three ways: its presence in that very location, its arrival from elsewhere, or its production from a collection of factors distinct from it.
If it is argued: "In the absence of such sublation, what purpose does this [negative concomitance] serve? It has no utility in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Rather, it merely provides assistance to the perception that grasps positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," then we reply: Is it not understood by sensory perception (*akṣaja*) itself that "when this exists, that comes to be"?

And since that is established by direct perception (*adhyakṣeṇa*), what is the use here of non-perception (*anupalambha*)?

[Objection: Is it by way of assistance? [Reply: Well then, is that prior non-existence—which is of the nature of the opposite of existence divided into three types—established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a mere absence (*abhāvamātra*), or as something else? In the first case...
This follows: "When this exists, that comes to be;
otherwise, it is impossible"—this very [formula] constitutes the negative concomitance (vyatireka). ||3||

It does not abide there, nor is it born from another, nor has it come from elsewhere; for if an effect could exist when [the cause] is present, then it would not exist when that [cause] is absent, nor for anything else. (4)

And this is established by perception preceded by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); therefore, nothing is achieved by the latter two [reasons]. For even that [perception] establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) only by subverting the presence of the effect there in the absence of the cause, its production from something else, or its movement elsewhere through other effort; it is not the latter two [reasons] themselves that do so, because even with a hundred [of them], the absence [of the effect] would not occur in the absence of that [perception]. And that—
[If it is argued that] since [the non-existence] was established by one [person], there is no need for another;
or if the thought is that the first non-apprehension cognizes mere non-existence,
then [it is merely] mere non-existence.
Even regarding awakening, the prior [cause] is useless;
since this [awakening] has already occurred, what remains of that [prior cause]? ||5||

If there is the cognition of mere non-existence (*abhāva-mātra*), then what could have concomitance (*anvaya*) with what? Even the cognition of concomitance in the form "when this exists, that exists" is merely a chance occurrence; it is an obstacle to utility because it leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, however, there is the cognition "this [non-existence] belongs to this [thing]" prior to its operation, then that very same threefold alternative (*trayo gati*) arrives; what remains [of the other options] such that the final two would not be rendered futile?
If it is argued that [the negative concomitance] is not established because of deviation in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
then why is the same not said regarding the operation of mere perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself? (6)

For the sake of which [the relationship] was previously sought: indeed, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), when taken individually, are subject to deviation; therefore, it is said that they together constitute the causal relation (*hetu-phala-bhāva*). Consequently, the possibility of each one occurring even where the effect is absent does not constitute a refutation; this is the same for both of us. Regarding the phrase "of three kinds" (*trividha*): therein, the three positions beginning with "remaining in that very state" (*tatraiva sthiti*) have been set forth. In the *Mātṛkā*, the word *bheda* is difficult to read; the reading should be *bhaṭa-pāṭha* (or *dad-pāṭha*).
It has been established. Therefore, the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is achieved;
hence, the first [member] is not useful for the last two, nor are the last two useful for the first. This is established. It is not established.

For it is incorrect to claim that although one realizes through the first [cognition] that "this was not there prior to its operation," one does not yet ascertain that "its non-existence is caused by the absence of its operation," whereas this is ascertained by the final [cognition]; for the inefficacy of the first cognition remains exactly as it was.
Moreover,
because it does not exist apart from those [elements], its non-existence is determined by the subsequent [analysis].
Since that same logic applies equally, why has it not been accepted by the Easterners as well? (7)

For even the statement "it did not exist prior to this activity" indicates its non-existence solely through the absence of that [activity] itself, as has been stated: because of the rejection of the threefold nature of existence, it follows by implication. Therefore, if there is no certainty by means of the former, let there be none by the latter either. In that case, for one who perceives that the former merely brings about the presence of the non-existence of both, and that the latter does not bring about the non-existence of the one, how can there be confidence in the latter?

Even in the absence of that [invariable concomitance], the objection regarding the impossibility of a second non-existence remains equally applicable in the case of the contingency of production. Now, as for the smoke produced immediately after the contact of fire and a donkey...
It is said that even when the jar is absent, its absence is experienced by the former [cognition];
and when both have disappeared, their disappearance is also experienced by the subsequent one— thus there is a succession of ever-newer means.

The refutation of the fivefold classification: If it is argued that this being the case, there are three [possibilities], not two, we reply that even by the latter [classification], it is not possible;
this much alone is stated. But what is the use of this discussion regarding whether there are two or three?

If it is argued that there is a utility [in the two-fold classification] because certainty is impossible in the absence of either of the other two, then the former [classification] is established precisely at the moment when non-perception occurs solely due to the absence of the reason (*hetu*).

Why is it not accepted that [the third moment] is also capable? If it is not, it has already been stated that this is because it is entirely useless; otherwise, one could just as well say that perception consists of three moments rather than two. Furthermore, for the proponent of the five-moment theory, since there is no distinction due to their occurring at the same time, only the first non-perception (of smoke) is admitted. And since that [non-perception] exists even when the fire and the donkey have departed, it remains [present] even now in comparison with the subsequent non-perception of smoke.
It is indeed duality.
Moreover,
having previously not seen [it], one who perceives it sequentially understands the state of cause and effect.
Or, if it were perceived, one would perceive it gradually; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. ||8||

Because there would result an endless search for further and further perceptions and non-perceptions of preceding and succeeding [moments] in order to refute each successive doubt, one may establish the triad [of means of knowledge] as one pleases. However, once the middle [moment] has been established through perception, there is no utility whatsoever for the two types of non-perception; for when another [possibility] is suspected, there is no confidence in either of the two, and since that distinction is accomplished by one alone.
Therefore,
when positive and negative concomitance have been ascertained through perception and non-perception,
what kind of doubt could there be regarding the established relationship between cause and effect? (9)

If they were distinct entities, then those two [the absence and the locus] would themselves constitute the nature of that [absence]; furthermore, there would be no certainty of their cognition, since [the absence] is established in both ways [as either a positive entity or a mere negation]. It might be argued that such an arrangement is possible precisely because of the firmness of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, it is only appropriate that the non-perception apprehending that [absence] should transcend the perception whose object is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For the very nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its object (*prameya*) is indeed that of being invariably related (*nāntarīyakatva*).
It establishes firmness, not multiplicity, for multiplicity is seen even in fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

And since the non-perception of the perceptible alone is sufficient to prove absolute non-existence in the absence of that [object], what is the point of running further? For in that case, not even a trace of smoke could be expected. But one might object: "In the absence of many [causes], in whose absence would smoke not have arisen?"

If it is argued that [the non-existence] must be ascertained, for this very reason perception apprehending positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is required; for if this non-existence were caused by the absence of something else, one would not take its occurrence into account. Thus, even when the ascertainment is preceded by the apprehension of positive concomitance, since many possibilities exist, when the inquiry arises—"Is its existence caused by the existence of what?"—it is through non-perception that one determines that its existence is caused by the absence of that specific thing.

The state [of the subject] is now dependent upon that [other] state; thus it is established that the former state also belongs to this [subject]. And in that case, when each one is either introduced or withdrawn, it is possible to apprehend it in such a manner. This being so, there is the capacity for establishing the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of either the preceding or the subsequent [term];
however, it remains a settled point that when there is the introduction of many [terms] and so forth, there is no capacity for either of the two.

Furthermore, this arrangement of five categories is not all-encompassing; for it is established that in the case of ashes, fire, a water-pot, and a potter, the latter is absent, while in the case of water, its receptacle, and so forth, the former is absent. Indeed, when one has observed the stability of a flood of water behind a dam and then observes the presence of that water upon the presence of the dam, the determination of the causal relationship between the two occurs independently of the former [fivefold] classification.
It is exactly so; likewise, it should be understood that in other cases as well, [the cause] depends upon a triad.
Now, one might object: "Why not assume that when smoke is seen in the proximity of fire after having previously been unseen, it produces something else entirely by depending on the fire?
Even so, the fire would still possess the status of a cause, just like the fuel. If that is the case, then for anything else that occurs by chance—

If it is argued that the establishment of the causal relationship would mean that even a donkey or similar animal could be a cause of smoke, and consequently, one might infer the donkey from the smoke— well then,
is there a certainty regarding the donkey’s causality in the same way as there is for fire? Or is there direct perception and non-perception [of the donkey] in that case as well?

Because neither of the two [alternatives] is possible regarding the occurrence [of the effect]. Nor is there recourse to the three [reasons] for the purpose of negating anything else; rather, it is for the sake of establishing [the cause]. And since that [cause] is established, the non-negation of anything else is not at all a sublation. As for its not being an inference, that is simply because the causality is not ascertained. There can be no certainty even of the suspicion that "the donkey produces [the smoke] sometimes depending on fire," because of the contradiction.

Because that [cognition] is of the nature of doubt, its negation also occurs only through the investigation of that very [cognition] and not of anything else; thus, such idle chatter is misplaced. But even so, since the restriction "fire alone is the cause" is untenable, the situation remains precarious. For fire is not the sole cause, as other factors have not been excluded, and because fuel also possesses causality from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor is it the case that...
It is not a valid objection to say that [the reason] is merely a cause, because smoke might still occur even if it has not yet begun; for all three types of exclusion (vyavaccheda) are established.
To explain:
With respect to the totality [of causes], there is the cutting off of another;
with respect to the substance, there is the non-connection of capacity; and in the case of an action, it is established as being absolute. || 10 ||

For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by fire is denoted in its entirety by the word "fire," then [the statement] "that very thing" constitutes the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). But when it is the substance of fire itself that is meant, if "causality" refers to capacity (*yogyatā*), then [the statement] "it is indeed a cause" constitutes the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). If, however, it refers to the action itself, then [the statement] "it certainly comes to be" constitutes the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).

This is established. Furthermore, since this entire process can only be accomplished through the threefold method of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), it is appropriate that the explanation by the venerable Bhaṭṭācārya be followed in this section;
for the Lord Vārtikakāra himself [has stated so].
The production of a jar by a potter, of ash by fire, and of a wound and so forth by a weapon and the like—this is precisely the position of one who speaks thus. (1)

But how is it that, despite the lack of distinction in their being effects, one does not infer fire from ash as one does from smoke? It is not so, because [the inference] is intended with respect to place, time, and other such factors. For instance, [fire] arises for the sake of something...
Furthermore, another cause is required for the persistence of the continuum;
that [continuum] depends upon time.
4. Furthermore, it is illogical because it is irrational (*ayuktatvāt*).

In that regard, [the production of] a jar, ashes, and so forth, depends upon other factors at the very moment of their birth; for this very reason, there is a continuous succession (*prabandha*) that depends on external objects.

Regarding the cases of deficiency (*vaidhurya*): since the time of the presence of the cause can be ascertained only in the past and not in the present, there is no confusion regarding activity and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of subsequent [causes] such as smoke or light—which, depending on specific conditions, may or may not require a continuous series—there is no fault because they bring about the interruption of the stream due to a lack of material cause (*upādāna*), being independent of anything else, and thus they pertain precisely to the present. With reference to this:

Even if the effort to hear the latter two [works] of the teacher Dharmottara should bear fruit, the restriction to five [works] would still remain incomplete at that time; therefore, since there is no dependence on anything else in the case of non-perception preceded by perception, the first [work] alone is superior.
The *Ekādaśaślokī*—the establishment of the causal relation based on the three kinds of perception and non-perception, compiled by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra—is completed. 7.
