The Chapter on the Ascertainment of the Yoginī.

Whatever is meditated upon becomes clearly manifest at the culmination of the intensity of that meditation, just as the form of a beloved woman appears clearly to a lover. And the properties of things, such as momentariness and selflessness, are indeed meditated upon by one who seeks the supreme human goal. Here, this is considered: let there be mental clarity through meditation; however, regarding objects that are real or unreal—
Since the clarity arising from meditative cultivation is common to others as well, it is impossible for it to be necessarily non-deviant; how then can there be validity?
Thus, how can the cognition of a yogin be considered perception?
If it is argued that because there is no suspicion of deviation regarding the cultivation of an object established by inference, the cognition born thereof [is valid]...

If it is asked, "How can there be room for doubt regarding knowledge?"— let alone any hope for the efficacy of inference or human testimony— even through perception, after grasping lightning, thunder, and so forth, there may arise a cognition that is produced at the culmination of intense cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and possesses a very stable form of that object, provided that one has not reached the limit of application toward a contrary cultivation (*viparīta-bhāvanā*). And since that object has already vanished, how could [the cognition] be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a thing brought forward by a means of knowledge?
Even if it is within the range of perception, why should there be confidence in its correspondence? For even before the sun has set, there is no fixed duration for the persistence of fire;

the same applies to the ocean and other such things. Furthermore, a lack of similarity (change) is observed in trees and the like over very short periods of time, and in mountains and the like due to fires, thunderbolts, and so forth. However, a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is restricted to that single state which one has entered and focused upon.

The claim that "it is a clear manifestation" is an error with respect to its object due to the difference in its form; thus, it possesses neither validity nor the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*).

Furthermore, when even a common plowman, having inferred the consumption of sacrificial offerings, makes them vivid through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), that is not the cognition of a yogi because it lacks an ultimate reality as its object;
otherwise, it would follow that this is merely another type of direct perception.

To this it is replied: First of all, this immediate objection is not even possible. For cultivation (*bhāvanā*) would either occur spontaneously due to the onset of passion, grief, and so forth, or it would be undertaken intentionally by a discerning person in accordance with a specific purpose. In that case, since there is an absence of any talk of a supreme purpose, the mere burning or cooking [of an object] is accomplished simply by approaching that location through fire inferred [by other means]; it is not [directly] touched.
Even in the case of a real object, the cultivation [of a mental image] is fruitless; for when something previously cultivated appears vividly, it is an error with respect to that actual object.

The same applies to a cultivation brought about by grief and the like. Therefore, how could there be any connection to the contingency of it being another form of perception? Or, let us grant for the sake of argument that such a cultivation of an object occurs—like the cultivation of a horn on one's head. Nevertheless...

In the view that [this cognition] is an error (*bhrama*), it is included within *yogijñāna* (the knowledge of a yogi) alone; for yoga is indeed *samādhi*, characterized by one-pointedness of the mind, so there is no fault. However, when the form of a horn appears clearly, as in the case of "the earth is a *kṛtsna*" and so forth, it is indeed not a perception (*apratyakṣatā*) because it lacks a real objective basis (*nirālambanatvāt*). As the *Vārttika* states: [text follows].
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is stated therein:

"That which is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is consistent, like an object previously determined—that is accepted as perception born of cultivation (*bhāvanāja*); all others are distortions (*upaplava*)."
Furthermore, regarding that meditation which— whether the object has ceased to exist or possesses another form— is practiced as having a stable form,

and for which you have established the lack of a real objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), this may be acceptable within the framework of meditating on a conceptualized entity, but it does not apply to the actual nature of things.

Regarding the side of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): one has begun to cultivate the properties of things, such as momentariness and so forth, which become manifest through world-weariness (*saṃsāra-vairāgya*). Now, since a discrepancy is observed even in a single object that has been purified by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the clarity produced by cultivation, what confidence can there be in any other [object]? For, apart from purification by valid cognition, there is no basis for confidence even in this [cultivation].

And is it because of the incapacity of that [cognition] to have a necessary conclusion through correspondence? That is not so, because there is a distinction based on whether the object is stable or unstable. For an unstable entity is seized by destruction and transformation, and thus there is no correspondence; however, the properties of an entity, such as momentariness and so forth, are never interrupted, and therefore the manifestation directed toward them is always possessed of an objective support (*sālambana*).
[The opponent says:

But even this is not tenable. For there is no such thing as "momentariness" and so forth that exists as a real entity (*vastu*); or, if it did exist, it would follow that it is eternal, and thus everything would collapse without effort. Furthermore, if it is not a real entity, that itself constitutes the state of being without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*). Therefore—

In your view as well, what is called "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatva*) refers to the very collection of momentary entities (*bhāvarāśi*) when their internal differences are not perceived; they are spoken of thus by setting aside other distinctions. This being the case, even the phrase "cultivation of momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvabhāvanā*) has the same meaning as "cultivation of the multitude of momentary objects. To that extent, those very same things, while being cultivated, become manifest; thus, the same fault remains. Now, as for [the claim] that even though they are non-different from momentariness—
Do these two not appear as if they were separate? Even so, because of the mental determination (*adhyavasāya*), they are cultivated as if they were actually present in the object;

thus, there is no escape from that fault, since it is impossible to cultivate them with a sense of detachment. And so, the very form of this cultivation is the realization that "this entire collection of objects is of a nature that is constantly disintegrating."

How, then, can there be an avoidance of contact with a real entity even in the case of the cultivation of the reality of things (*vastutattvabhāvanā*)? And if there were such an avoidance, it would be merely the cultivation of another non-entity, not the cultivation of the Dharma. True. Even though the object is implied in a general sense by the cultivation of the reality of things, nevertheless, there is no manifestation of that [object] as such, because the intent culminates solely in the reality itself. For it is the cultivation of reality itself, when becoming manifest, [that constitutes the goal].
It is the path for departing from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). For it is not the actual perception of a beloved woman’s body that brings about the contraction of passion;

rather, it is its very nature as impermanent, suffering, and so forth. Therefore, because the intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward that [nature] alone, it is that which becomes clear through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not the object itself.

[Objection: But even if the intention is directed toward that [nature], what is the connection between the claim that the property of the object (*vastudharma*) becomes manifest, yet not the object itself? Through meditative cultivation, both [the property and the object] are [manifested].

[If it is argued that it is] because of being embraced [by the cognition]? Or what kind of manifestation could there be of a mere property (dharmamātra) that does not touch the substratum (dharmī)? This is merely painting the sky;
indeed, it does not produce even a farmer’s conviction.
[This concludes] the Section on the Determination of Yogins.

This is not a fault, because we observe that even while not touching upon the manifestation of the substratum (*dharmin*), there is a manifestation of the mere property (*dharma*) alone. It may be argued that there is simply no vivid appearance without depending on proximity to the object. However, "manifestation" for that [property] consists in the sudden flashing forth of its respective form within the cognition of it, occurring instantly without depending on effort when the object is present; whereas dependence on proximity to the object [applies] to...

It does not perish, precisely because it is its very nature (*dharmatva*), just like the quality of being pleasant (*priyatva*) and so forth. For instance, in the case of the bitter taste of the *nimba* tree and the like, the cultivation of the perception of pleasantness is seen to become increasingly clear. And yet, that [pleasantness] is not an inherent property (*dharma*) of the *nimba* itself; nevertheless, through the cultivation of that [perception], even the *nimba* tree—whether remaining in its place of origin or present on the tip of the tongue—becomes vividly manifest, provided there is no intensity of application toward the cultivation of the opposite [perception]. Nor is it the case that once [the perception] has become clear...
Even this state of being dear is perceived as something incidental; it does not exist independently of the experience of the nimba and so forth.

Rather, whenever there is an experience of the nimba and so forth, at that very moment the state of being dear suddenly becomes the object of experience. It is not experienced as something repulsive as it was previously—this is precisely what is meant by the manifestation of this quality (dharma).

For just as, even when an object such as a beloved woman becomes manifest, there is no manifestation of reality (*tattva*) established by convention, so too, even through the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), there is no manifestation of the object; what fault is there in this, given that both are mutually non-deviant? If it is argued that "belovedness" is not an external property because it is unique and because it is produced by cultivation—of whom [is it a property]?

Furthermore, is this quality of being dear and so forth, which is to be personally experienced (*pratyātmavedyatva*), impossible to deny? If you say it belongs to cognition (*jñāna*), what logic is there in the claim that the externality’s state of being dear, when cultivated, becomes manifest within the cognition? Even the form of the mental cultivation "this is superior to the *nimba* tree" does not mean that the cognition itself is superior. Moreover, if it were the case that the manifestation occurs through the cognition itself being dear...

No one would ever experience anything unpleasant; for knowledge, unlike external objects, does not have an occasional presence. If it is argued that even knowledge manifests as pleasant only in certain cases, then by what is this distinction made? If it is caused by habituation, then let that habituation apply only to external things. If it were independent of that, there would be no such distinction between proximity and distance for anyone.
There is no distinction in the fact that both are mental constructs (*manomātra*) serving as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

However, since [in the case of the real object] a specific species, such as a nimba tree, has been made the object of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), there is no over-extension of the principle. Even so, knowledge too is proximate only when it has the imagined nimba as its object; this is the distinction. If that is the case, then this follows: whatever thing...

An object is meditated upon (*bhāvyate*) by means of some particular form; it is that which is proximate to it which becomes manifest, not the object itself. Thus, for one meditating on a beloved woman (*kāminī*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that her father or another relative who is proximate to her becomes manifest, rather than the beloved woman herself. Now, is there some specific kind of proximity between the object and the cognizing consciousness (*jñāna*)? Even so, when the neem tree (*nimba*) is being practiced upon as something dear—

If that cognition manifests as something pleasant, then the neem tree and so forth would remain unpleasant as before. Therefore, just as the certain cognition of a snake or similar object—which is unpleasant—is itself pleasant because it serves as the basis for avoidance, yet the snake and so forth are not, so too is this case; thus, enough with such mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Or, is it your hypothesis that by the power of cultivation, a cognition having that [unpleasant] object arises in a purely pleasant form? If so, [then...]
If it is maintained that "the nimb-tree juice is imagined as pleasant," it follows that it is the very cognition of that object which is imagined as having the form of being pleasant.

Furthermore, its clarity arises from the immediate proximity of that object; for the cognition grasping it appears with the form of being pleasant without depending on any effort, [as soon as] that object is presented. (Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, 326)

Manifestation (*sphuraṇam*) is not the direct presence of an object that is not proximate. Thus, even when mountains and the like are meditated upon as momentary, it is the cognition of those objects itself that is meditated upon in the form of momentariness. Furthermore, its clear manifestation occurs through the arising of the aspect of momentariness in the cognizer when in proximity to the mountain and so forth; it is not the clear manifestation of the mountain and so forth, even though they are not proximate.
This is the state of being. Since this very cultivation of the object (*dharma-bhāvanā*) is grounded in the word and its meaning, there is no contradiction with the subject matter at hand.

In reality, however, "dearness" (*priyatva*) means the quality of producing pleasure. In that regard, when a person has the cultivation of dearness toward a particular object, that object—by taking as its material cause (*upādāna*) the mental continuum refined by that cultivation—produces pleasure as a cooperative condition (*sahakārī*).
In its established state, not everything is pleasant; rather, its quality of being pleasing is its very nature, and there is no fault in this, as it is perceived by everyone.

And that [nature] arises precisely from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). This should be applied similarly to mental qualities such as compassion (*kṛpā*) and the rest. Through the cultivation of the thought, "I shall rescue the sufferer," when one is in the presence of the object of that focus, that knowledge—which is clear, vivid, and corresponds to that [cultivation]—arises instantaneously.

It is the cause for the production of [the desired] performance. Thus, even in the case of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of a skull-bowl as pure, the manifestation of non-cruelty (*nairghuṇya*) should be understood as being like the approach of camphor; it does not arise simultaneously with either the relative itself or something else nearby.
As it has been stated in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*:
The excellence gained through awakening, compassion, and so forth does not require such effort when that object [of meditation] is present; rather, it unfolds spontaneously within each individual.
Therefore, even during the practice of the dharma of momentariness, as long as it has reached its peak, it must be experienced by this [yogi] to that extent.

It is indeed distinct from our perception and that of others, characterized by its lack of fragmentation. Just as for us, even regarding an object that is extremely similar [to another], there occurs an immediate perception and conceptualization that follows the distinction of different locations and degrees of clarity, or a corresponding practical application;

likewise, for the yogi, there are perception and conceptualization regarding two entities that differ in their momentary states. [This state] is unstained by the blemishes of passion and the like, which arise from the delusion of stability and so forth.
And "his mind" [is thus described]; such is the extent of its vivid manifestation.

But is this not merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) to say that its degree of excellence reaches only this far? To argue "because it has been observed so" is no answer. For even if it has been observed in this way, it cannot be maintained in the present case that its state is established by that alone; perhaps at some point—

As it is being refined, the excellence [of the meditation] would become manifest together with the object itself; thus, the previous fault is eliminated. If it is argued that even regarding [the qualities of] "dearness" and so forth, there might sometimes be a different ultimate state, we reply: let it be so. However, this gives rise to the suspicion of manifestation by means of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) which transcends the intended state. But for one who acts with foresight and is devoted to mental cultivation for the sake of their own goal or the goal of others, for them, that much alone [is sufficient].

Since the goal has been achieved, why would one enter into further exertion, given that it is purposeless and even harmful? This is just as when the desired cooking of food, medicine, and so forth has been attained; or as in this case, where although other forms of cooking might be possible, the desired result is already accomplished. Thus ends the determination of yoga.

The conventional usage of the term "culmination" (*prakarṣaparyanta*) refers to the limit of the process of maturation (*pāka*); since this is the case here as well, there is no fault whatsoever. Thus, although the manifestation of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the subject (*dharmī*) may be accompanied by non-correspondence due to the instability of the object, nevertheless, there is no room for such a suspicion regarding the cultivation whose scope consists of the aforementioned properties (*dharma*). If it is argued that the example of the passionate woman (*kāminī*) is therefore inappropriate, that is not a valid objection; for [it applies to] the cultivation...
This is because only the clarity of the illustration is intended; for this very reason, the Vārttika says:
"like aversion, dispassion, and passion."

In that case, is that yogic cognition different from sensory cognition or not? And what follows from this? On the position of non-difference, there would be no such thing as a distinct variety of perception called "yogic cognition," because it would be subsumed under sensory cognition alone. Nor can its status as a distinct variety be established on the grounds that it arises in a mental continuum refined by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for otherwise it would follow that even perceptions dependent on the refinement of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like would have to be established as separate varieties of perception. Furthermore, regarding the position of difference:

The claim that the knowledge which directly realizes momentariness arises from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and is thus distinct and otherwise [than sensory perception] is a sound purification [of the doctrine]; for if sensory perception itself were to realize instability in that state, there would be no need for yogic knowledge. Nor is its cognition of momentariness accidental; rather, that cognition arises from the clarity attained through meditative cultivation. Furthermore, this cultivation does not belong to sensory perception, but to the mental faculty (*manas*). Even without that [cultivation], [the following applies]:
Furthermore, if there were no direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), meditation (*bhāvanā*) would be useless.
Moreover, are these two [the object of meditation and its realization] at different times or at the same time? In that regard, being simultaneous is untenable;
for the momentariness of the substratum (*dharmin*) presented by sensory cognition must be directly realized through an experience arising from meditation.
Otherwise, for one who directly perceives the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) independently, a refutation based on the subject would be unavoidable;
this has already been explained.
Furthermore, the cultivation of a property does not have the function of directly perceiving the thing itself, unlike [the tasting of] a neem fruit and so forth.

Therefore, the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) is indeed superior to the domain of sensory cognition; thus, there is a fixed temporal distinction: first, sensory cognition apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*), and subsequently, mental cognition apprehends its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*). When there is a temporal difference, the latter lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to the former if they have the same object, because it would be apprehending what has already been apprehended. However, if they have different objects, [the subsequent cognition] operates upon something other than the domain of sensory cognition.
"Nor is there liberation from the aforementioned fault, because [the word] presents the subject (*dharmin*) independently.

To this we reply: first of all, in the first position, there is no refutation of the thing itself, because such a specific person, who is the probandum (*sādhya*), is already established. Nor is there a refutation of the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*), because such a specific state, precisely as a probandum, transcends the world—

Since it is described as distinct from the sensory cognition common to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) in order to demonstrate the specific means of accomplishing that state of being [the Buddha], the treatise does not achieve its purpose by a mere inclusion under the term "sensory cognition" (*indriyajñāna*), as if it were merely a refinement of the internal organ like the effects produced by elixirs (*rasāyana*). For this very reason, there is no description of it as distinct even when compared to the specific qualities produced by ointments and the like; it is [rather] transcendent of the world.

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, because there is no difference in their essential nature (*rūpa*), a distinction between types is indeed accepted even for those things that are generally subsumed under a single category, depending on the specific purpose; as, for example,

in the case of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), which— though included within the aggregate of formations associated with consciousness (*saṃprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*)— are distinguished by their conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).

This also applies to the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*) which has been subsumed [within the category of sensory cognition]. Therefore, there is no fault in the position that there is no difference between sensory cognition and the cognition of a yogi. That very same [cognition] is "sensory cognition" with respect to the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), and it is "yogi-cognition" with respect to the property (*dharma*); just as the perception of the substratum itself is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with respect to its negation.

Even on the view that [the object] is differentiated, there is no possibility of the objection based on the manifestation of stability and its opposite; for even by sensory cognition, which grasps the object in its entirety, only a fragmentary form is apprehended. Furthermore, the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) was previously difficult to obtain, but now it has been accomplished by the mind, which has attained proficiency by relying on the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the distinction.

But surely, since even the sense organ attains a state of unsurpassed excellence at that time, who can prevent the perception of distant or subtle objects, as in the case of an external yogi? For even animals occasionally perceive things in such a way due to some projection by karma. Furthermore, among existing moments, even a subtle dissimilarity must necessarily occur; otherwise, if there were similarity in every respect, [there would be] identity—

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Since the goal is accomplished by sensory cognition (*akṣavijñāna*) alone—which is capable of determining such subtle distinctions—yogic knowledge is useless.

By this, the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of suffering, non-self, and so forth, is also explained. Furthermore, [this applies] to one who possesses a human body, without [the aid of] sense organs.

"Let it be that the knowledge of a yogin is not to be produced because it is impossible [to attain]"; this too is incorrect. For a discerning person engaged in worldly activity, relying on the power of the eyes as presented by mere possibility, cannot abandon the path devoted to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or rather, since the accomplishment of such a sensory capacity is precisely assisted by the practice of that [path], the knowledge of a yogin is unavoidable.

Even if they are of equal status, there is no fault whatsoever in the case of sensory cognition. If it is argued that one of them is redundant, then which of these two— both of which possess the property of being brought together by their own causes— should cease its activity out of fear that its own function is superfluous,
as is the case with seeds and so forth when they have reached their final moment?

If it is argued that non-validity belongs to only one [of the two cognitions], then let there also be the state of being a non-cause for only one among seeds and the like. If it is asked, "Since all possess equal capacity, which single one can be established as the non-cause?", then why should one among the two cognitions—both of which possess the power of determination—not be rendered non-valid? If it is argued that, due to their mutual dependence, neither of the two should be considered valid, [we reply: ...

The same applies to seeds and the like: not even a single causal status can be established for them. As for the charge that [perception] would be "grasping what has already been grasped" (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), this does not exist at all. If it is argued that this is then a fault—no; for we accept that [status] based on a difference in time. Indeed, "grasping what has been grasped" is said to apply to what was already grasped, not to what is being grasped; just as one who performs what has already been done is not considered an agent, whereas one who performs what is currently being done is. Therefore, there is no distinction—
In the dark fortnight (*kālapakṣa*), this fault does not apply.
[This concludes] the section on the determination of yoga (*yoginirṇayaprakaraṇa*).

If it is argued that even so, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the manifestation of two forms, we reply: true; for first of all, the form of true knowledge (*satyajñāna*)—alas!—is indeed [present].

They occupy the same location, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] being an error. Therefore, who is capable of determining by what manner those two forms manifest as non-obstructive? Indeed, the range of the yogis is inconceivable.
[Pravā.
2.532]? Therefore, since there is no corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta), there is no occasion for either [the objection] "what is undesirable" or "what is not a fault.
If, then, they were simultaneous and thus independent of sensory cognition, how is the stated fault of independence to be avoided? [It is avoided] precisely by depending on the senses.
To say that it will avoid [the fault] is no answer; for in that case, even that would be nothing other than sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), since it follows the operation of those [senses].

There would be no such thing as "yogic cognition" at all. It would be better to accept only one [type of cognition]; thus, the position of a distinction [between them] is untenable. This is not so; for indeed, let there be no [fault regarding] the senses—

[Objection: But as for "looking" (*vīkṣaṇa*), just as [the visual organ] proceeds toward the production of its own cognition depending upon the presence of a suitable object in a fit location according to its own capacity, so too will the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) proceed; for the property of acting without reaching the object (*aprāpyakāritā*) is common to both, and because at that time the purposefulness of the mind is also accepted. However, the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does not possess such a power.

Since the mind (*manas*), like the eyes and ears, would produce cognition by obtaining an object situated in a suitable location according to such a spatial restriction, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, at that time, who is capable of determining the precise limit of the proximity of objects for the mind—just as it is for the ears and eyes? Only this much is said: as far as it is possible for it [the mind].
To be apprehended, an object capable of imparting its own form first becomes the range of that [cognition] by way of a nature that is distinct from and momentary compared to that of ordinary people.
This being the case, the form of the object is produced by the object itself and not generated by mental cultivation; thus, there is no suspicion of non-correspondence.

If it is argued that while the capacity of the eye and other senses is indeed observed in making superior objects their domain, the mind, however, does not transcend the senses to have everything as its object—[we reply: no, because of the possibility of [knowing] the minds of others and so forth. If it is argued that even this is not accepted by some—[we reply: no, because it is improper to reject something merely on the grounds of its being unobserved. If it is argued that there is a lack of means—[we reply: even in the absence of a means...

There is no means other than mere non-apprehension. Therefore, the point of this introduction is that if it were so, then there would be no resolution even for yogis under the view that the sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manojñāna*) are distinct. However, a resolution has already been shown in another way. And this being the case, there is no fault even under the view of a difference in time, provided that [the latter] is the first occurrence of the mental consciousness, if...
Its operation occurs by transcending the path of the sense faculties; however, the fact that sensory cognition lacks validity in relation to it does not cause any distress—enough of this prolixity.
(From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, 42)

Thus, in the cognition of a yogi, because it pertains to the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), the form of the object is produced by the object itself. However, through such cultivation, a certain extraordinary power is bestowed upon his mental continuum—just as a specific collyrium is applied to the eye—by which he possesses a vision not shared by other people. As was stated previously: "If, then, the cognition of a yogi were produced solely by the object, [how could there be] the thorough knowledge of the past and the future?"

What is the point? This is the result of not delving deeply into the context. For the introduction of the existence of the nature of things was made by way of the authority of a "partially omniscient" one (*upayukta-sarvajña*), and not with reference to the position of an "omniscient of all" (*sarvasarvajña*). Therefore, even the non-perception of the past and future does not constitute a contradiction, since the cessation of suffering is established by that much alone, and because it enables the introduction of unshakable teaching for others.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised against the knowledge of a yogin— claiming that it cannot be a direct realization because it is produced through the cultivation of the aspects of all things possessing those properties (the *dharmīs*) by means of cultivating the reality (*tattva*) of momentariness and so forth within the central circle (*kaṇikā*)—

that must certainly be disregarded, as it falls outside the arguments found in the *Vārttika*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other authoritative works. Otherwise, the very cultivation of [the truths] such as "all is suffering" and so on would be rendered purposeless.

And if it were intended that this [knowledge] bestows only the state of being omniscient in every respect, why would its refutation be set forth with effort in the Vārttika? [The author] maintains that satisfaction is found in the thought: "It is not possible for us to know [this]."

And so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* with these words. Furthermore, when that state is attained, for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is free from obscuration, there will arise—due to an excellence of compassion and a dedication to the aspiration for the welfare of others in every aspect—an acquisition of a particular means (*upāya-viśeṣa*) within a mind that ranges over the entire field of experience and in which enthusiasm has long been firmly rooted; by practicing which, [one perceives] everything pertaining to all objects, atom by atom, according to their respective place and time.

When a cognition arises that is more clearly imitative of its object, then there is neither non-correspondence caused by the deviation from the object, nor is there a lack of objective support (*nirālambanatva*), because it is the objects themselves that appear. Now,
if the determination of an objective support is based on both the mode of arising and the similarity [to the object], [then...]

If it is asked, "How can that which exists at a different time be apprehended? those who know the principles of logic understand that its very status as a cause is what makes it capable of imparting its form to the cognition.

Because of this statement [from *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.247], it follows that similarity (*sārūpya*) alone is ineffective; how, then, can the charge of being without an objective basis (*anālambanatva*) be avoided?
This is incorrect, for that definition is indeed intended with respect to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) regarding external objects, as occurring simultaneously with them—

This is intended to negate the apprehension [of an object] by a cognition that does not assist it, as is the context here. In reality, however, whatever appears therein is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*). For example, in sensory perception it is the external [object], while elsewhere it is its own form (*svākāra*), according to the force of appearance; this is from the *Yoginirṇayaprakaraṇa*.

For the commentary on the first chapter states: "The apprehension and non-apprehension of perception. In that context, what is called the "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*) of an external object is merely the arising of its form (*tadākāra*).

For it is simply from the experience of the arising of a form as if separated from the outside that the thought "this has been seen" occurs. Indeed, at the time of its conceptualization, no other arising is required, because that [arising] is to be determined only subsequently.

[This occurs] either through the attainment of the fruit or through repeated practice. Furthermore, that arising of the mental aspect [of the object] occurs, in the case of sensory perception, from the object; in the case of error, from a distortion; and in the case of conceptual construction, from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Among these, correspondence with the object exists in that which is produced by the object, while in other cases there is subversion, with respect to the external world. However, with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is a rule of correspondence everywhere. Therefore, in a cognition where there is correspondence with the intended [object], there can be neither correspondence nor similarity [to the object] without its being produced from that [object].

In that case, there is the request for its arising from that [object]. Therefore, validity consists precisely in having that form; and since similarity and arising from that [object] constitute the definition of the cognizable, both are non-contradictory.

However, where—by the power of a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone, through the sovereignty of a deity, as in a true dream—the form of the object appears according to the reality of the object, [that is another matter].
There is no intervening cognition; in that regard, nothing arises from it. As the *Vārttika* states:

"In this way, for those of impure intellect, there is the conceptualization of the apprehended and the apprehender regarding form and so forth and the mind; however, the state of the yogis is inconceivable."

Thus it is said. Therefore, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the persistence of an object of cognition occurs through both similarity and arising with respect to external things; for a yogi, however, it occurs even through mere similarity. As for its own nature (*svarūpa*), it occurs through mere fitness (*yogyatā*) alone—this is the logical principle. [Objection: "In that case, if there were a manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-sphuraṇa*) of what is yet to be or what has already passed, they would have to be present."
[Pravā.

2.532] Now, if it is argued that the object's own nature (*svarūpa*) is not present and that cognition itself takes on its form, such that [cognition] is necessarily without an objective support (*nirālambana*), that too is not the case. For even when an object is not present, if cognition conforms to its place and time through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), how could it be—?

What is the objective support (*ālambana*)? It is because, through a specific mode of manifestation, there arises the conceptualization of temporal distinctions; and because, due to the necessity of performing practice in accordance with that [conceptualization], its attainment follows. As the Bhāṣya states:
"Just as he was seen joined with the time of autumn and so forth, so too there is no sublation of that [perception]."

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, the determination of difference occurs precisely through reflection (*saṃcintya*) for the sake of perceiving the nature of an object that possesses temporal distinctions. As it has been stated:
"Whatever one indeed wishes to understand..."
[From the *Pravāha-bhāṣya* 2.615]:

"At the time of emergence from meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*), etc. However, knowledge that is effortless (*anābhoga*) is not contradictory when occurring in sequence; for there is no contradiction because mere knowledge truly manifests.

1. *Tattvasaṃgraha*, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, p. 19; 2. *Tattvasaṃgraha* 3628 (?)332, in Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Nibandhāvalī*, in the section on the "Occurrence of Presentness" (*vartamānatā-prasaṅga*), as [it states]: "Because in the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*), it is the very nature of the object (*vastu-svarūpa*) that manifests. And although...
Even in the case of the present, although it is only the form of the cognition that flashes forth, there is nevertheless a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it precisely as being present.

The same should be understood regarding the distinctions of distance, proximity, and so forth. In those cases, validity arises from the necessary correspondence with what is attained through such determination; otherwise, there is error, as in the case of a beloved woman in a dream and the like, or in the conceptual construction of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice as a means to attain heaven through intuition (*pratibhā*).

There is no concern at all because there is an absence of the manifestation of a future object in its distinct form. Furthermore, in that case, there is no certainty regarding the rule of attainment for a discerning person engaged in worldly activity.
If it is asked, "What certainty is there even in the present case?"—well, whose certainty is being considered here: that of the person [themselves] or of someone else?

Or [is it for someone else]? If it is for him [the ordinary person], then just as an ordinary person possesses a knowledge of the means [of cognition] in which all suspicion of error has been completely dispelled through practice, why should the manifestation of future, past, and other objects not likewise belong to the yogin due to extreme practice? If, on the other hand, it is for another [person], then this follows: as long as there is no realization of its validity for another, it is not a valid means of cognition; and as long as it is not a valid means of cognition...

In that case, since there would be no non-erroneous cognition of the validity of anything else, nothing at all would be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is not the case that [the opponent's position] follows from being under the sway of mere dogmatic attachment.

Consequently, because the specific distinction of the cultivation [of the path], which is accompanied by a particular means, does not manifest directly, there is doubt regarding the establishment of such [a state]; however, even if it were established, it cannot be undermined by defects such as the lack of a basis (*nirālambanatva*).

Furthermore, having raised the objection that even if an external object is not apprehended by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), it might nevertheless appear clearly as an object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), [the opponent] says: "That which is apprehended by inference and that which is determined—both are exclusions of others (*anyāpoha*) and not real entities (*vastu*), because if they were to penetrate the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression would be impossible. This too is incoherent. For instance, whether in this way or that, [it is argued] under the influence of the scent of the Buddhist tenets (*bauddhasiddhānta*).

In conventional practice, just as in the cultivation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the form of a beloved woman, it is impossible to prevent the eventual production of a pure moment of an apprehended object (*upādeya-kṣaṇa*), even from a momentary form. Furthermore, if you should attempt to establish that such a state of exclusion (*apoha*)—which rests solely upon the bed of momentary conceptual constructions—does not follow after the conceptual construction of a beloved woman and so forth, we shall accept it exactly as you have argued. Nor is the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) merely the negation of a non-entity.
For even in the view of Dharmottara, it is established that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of determinative cognition (*adhyavaseya*).

[Objection: But is not the form of determinative cognition "fire has been cognized by me"? And in that case, to claim that the particular characteristic flashes forth there is sheer audacity, because conceptualization and determinative cognition have the same object. [Response: True; however, that much does not mean that it flashes forth therein.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is said to be that which is determined (*adhyavasita*). If it does not manifest, then since there is no cognition, how can there be determination? If it does manifest, then this is merely an appearance (*pratibhāsa*); how then can it be a determination? Furthermore, appearance and determination do not have the same object. For appearance is direct manifestation; whereas determination is the making of something an object of activity even when it does not manifest, by virtue of the capacity to delineate a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
This is the view of the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*). Therefore, that performance which conforms to [the object] must be determined as being entirely non-penetrating of the form that appears.

And that [performance] is in some cases merely superimposed, while in other cases it is the actual nature of the thing (*vasturūpa*). Since the present context accepts the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is indeed the actual nature of the thing; so how can it be said that "only a negation, which is a non-entity, is determined"? Let this persistent argument, which was never begun, rest for now.
In the section on the Determination of Yogic Perception (*yoginirṇayaprakaraṇa*):

Even in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) of an excluded form (*vyāvṛttākāra*), and not of mere exclusion (*vyāvṛttimātra*), provided it conforms to experience. Otherwise, at all times, something or other—such as a *rākṣasa* or similar entity—might manifest. However, through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there occurs a transformation (*pariṇati*) into the form that has been determined (*adhyavasitākāra*).

In that case, there is a lack of objective support (*nirālambanatva*) only with respect to what is superimposed upon the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), which is itself unsublatable; however, when it exists, that very thing is the objective support, as has just been stated.

As for what you said— that the status of an object as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) with respect to consciousness is pervaded by its dependence upon a sense faculty (*indriya*), and that this [dependence],
being excluded from here by the perception of its own opposite, also excludes the object's status as an objective condition— therein, [you have stated] a non-pervasive contrary...

To clarify the attainment [of cognition] without first establishing, by means of valid proof, the relationship of pervasion between having an object as its condition and depending on a sense faculty— this is a great feat of ingenuity! If you say, "Because it is so observed," then indeed, observation is simply non-observation.

Let it be accepted as authoritative; what is the use of this obsession with adducing such a means of proof? Therefore, we see no contradiction if an entity were to assume the status of an objective support even without depending on the sense organs. Now, it has already been stated here that a particular kind of fuel is not the cause of smoke; thus, even without fire, it cannot produce smoke by means of a thousand refinements. Therefore—

Alternatively, if [cognition] were to arise from the object alone, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference based on the cause of all effects. Therefore, cognition also possesses the property of arising from an object that is dependent upon the sense faculty; this is its status as a supporting condition (*ālambana*).

If it is argued: "Since there is an absence of sensory activity, and since that [cognition] is established as being dependent on other causes—given that its existence is not present when those other causes are present—how can an object be known by itself without depending on the senses? This objection is also refuted by the possibility of knowing another's mind; for the Cārvākas accept those who know the minds of others.

For those other than the Mīmāṃsakas, there is no alternative but to admit doubt even for the Cārvākas and others. And when there is doubt, it is impossible to establish the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) with absolute certainty. [Objection: But surely, because the effect of cognition is necessarily dependent upon the sense organs, there can be no doubt regarding anything else, just as smoke is necessarily dependent upon fire. [Reply: If that were so, then the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) required for the cognition of color to depend upon the visual organ would not be the same as that required for a specific movement.

If [the capacity] depends upon the feet, it is diminished even by a fraction; how then was the example of smoke not capable of negating the movement of snakes and other creatures who are devoid of feet? Or else, how could the task of neutralizing poison and so forth—which for some is accomplished through a succession of forceful mantra-recitations involving the activity of hands and other limbs—be achieved by another through mere meditative absorption (*samādhi*) alone? Furthermore, smoke likewise does not exist anywhere without fuel.
Since an arising independent of fire is observed [in the case of smoke], one might suspect that it is likewise here;

therefore, external entities, which are perceived as existing in the relation of cause and effect, have such restricted modes of occurrence. However, for the mental continuum, there is a manifold manifestation precisely due to the power of the formative forces (*abhisaṃskāra*) of diverse karmas.
Therefore, it cannot be restricted that whatever degree of dependence exists for the effect based on that [external object] in one case, that same degree of dependence must exist in another;

so how could there be a total absence of the cognition of another's mind and so forth? Furthermore, if the sense organ were not the cause of cognition—just as fire is not the cause of smoke independently [of fuel]—then its own excellence, such as the proclamation, observation, and so on regarding its own object, would be utterly meager. For instance, [as stated] in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*: "To whatever extent [the range of] fire, fuel, and so forth..."

The means of cognition, such as smoke and so forth, that has been perceived is not capable of transcending space. Likewise, how could it produce [cognition] for vultures and others beyond the range of our own sensory perception after having produced it within that range? Or, if it were to produce it, the causal complex (sāmagrī) based on the mental continuum would not be able to sustain the status of fuel and fire, nor would the cognition be able to sustain the status of smoke.

Therefore, why could it not be possible for [the effect] to arise from some particularity, even when there is a deficiency of auxiliary conditions or an excessive interval? If it is argued that this distinction is produced by the genus (*jāti*) and not based on the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), we say no;
for even the genus has as its nature the production of diverse forms precisely through the sovereignty of diverse karma, and karma is nothing other than the mind.

This does not avoid the objection regarding the mind’s lack of a physical locus. Now, if it is argued that because the sense organ functions by reaching its object, the entire causal complex for the production of consciousness occupies a common location; even so, why is it that in some cases there is contact with a portion of the eye fixed upon an object situated at such a great distance, while in other cases it seems to rest as if nearby? What can be said here other than the sovereign power of karma (*karmādhipatya*)? Therefore:
The power of the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) which serves as their basis is indeed diverse;

for it is not possible even in the external world [to account for such variation]. Otherwise, between two lamps situated in identical locations, one might have a beam of rays that travels far, while the other’s would travel only nearby. Now, if [it is argued that this is due to] a mantra—

If it is argued that this might occur through the power [of the mantra] itself, and that it produces dullness by the sight of a crawling serpent, then that is indeed the power of the mental continuum alone. Even in the case of a mantra, it is produced solely by the greatness of the person. As determined in the *Vārttika*:
even though mantras are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), they possess no power independent of a person. Therefore, it is the person alone [who possesses the power].
It follows that by means of mantras and other such methods, one can subvert the established power of external objects; thus, what is impossible in the present case?
Just as the status of an object as a support is seen to depend upon the eye, and is therefore accepted as being restricted to it, so too is it seen to depend upon light;
consequently, owls and the like would not see in the dark. If you argue that there is no fault because this is indeed observed [in their case], then [the same applies] here.

You are defeated precisely because of the fact of being perceived. For instance, even though the eye and light are equal in their requirement of causal conditions, the observation that one transcends [the other] due to the inconceivable power of the mind casts suspicion upon and defiles the other as well. However, such a thing cannot be maintained in the absence of perception. Now, if it is argued that effects, although possessing the commonality of being cognitions, belong to different species and thus do not depend [on one another], [we reply: no.
It is said that these [cognitions] arise from a difference in the causal complex (*sādhanasāmagrī*).

But by what means have you been deceived into thinking that even this extraordinary knowledge under discussion shares the same genus (*jāti*) with the knowledge of ordinary people? If it is argued that there is no difference in genus because it is non-existent, then [we reply]: non-existence is not a difference in genus.

Because a restriction [of the object] is possible only through the existence of the sense organs, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, for people like us, who have arisen from common karma, the dependence upon sense organs— which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of being an objective support (*ālambanatva*) with respect to the distinction of experience— cannot, by its own cessation, act as a negator of mere experience (*anubhavamātra*), since the establishment of pervasion occurs only with reference to specific cases.

Now, if it is claimed that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by unifying mere experience alone, then, due to the absence of any sublation by the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka*), pervasion itself cannot be established as a basis for the yogic determination of the relationship between cause and effect; for the foundation of the restriction between cause and fruit is destroyed, since it is untenable for [pervasion] to be common to smoke and other such [inferential marks], given the manifestation of diverse karmas.

Because [the cognition] arises from a mental continuum possessing inconceivable power due to impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is mere experience; and since there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases when relying on a specific instance, that very fault called "possessing a specific property" remains. Furthermore, as he says: "And for a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is unreal, there is the production of a clear cognition even without dependence on an external object."

Since capacity is observed through the behavior of those afflicted by desire and the like, even a real object (*bhūtārtha*) is capable [of producing cognition] independently of that [object]; thus, it cannot be understood that the object possesses the status of being an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). In this regard, what is this independence from the object? Is it (1) not having the object as its domain, or (2) the non-appearance of the object directly, or (3) not having the object as its cause, or (4) deviation from the object? Regarding the first position:

To claim that it has both the nature of a real object (*bhūtārthatva*) and lacks an object (*aviṣayatva*) is contradictory; for, just as in the case of the inference arising from it, this [perception] also has that as its object insofar as it depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). If, however, one argues that it lacks that as its object insofar as it depends upon appearance (*pratibhāsa*), then let it be so; yet, since it is precisely the cognition produced by that [perception] which is intended to have that as its object, the second position is also untenable. The third position is impossible, because even that [inference], by way of the inference arising from itself, possesses the nature of a real object.

Because it is an effect; for this very reason, since deviation is also established, the fourth [alternative] is not tenable. Therefore, since there is a rule of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for the clear cognition arising from that [object], how could it be impossible to understand that the object is the objective support (*ālambana*)? Consequently, the objection is well-founded according to the ancient method, and the refutation is exactly as stated.

Furthermore, that effort made to deny the cognition of past and future entities—by arguing that for this [cognition], only those moments of objects immediately preceding it can logically be grasped, and not those further back in time, and so forth—that has already been refuted. However, in the case of the present position regarding the Omniscient One, as many things as produce a cognition and come within the range of His own knowledge, all those momentary, suffering, and selfless [phenomena]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.]
The proof of the thesis is established by this much alone: that there is recollection regarding things past that have been perceived, and mere possibility regarding things yet to come.

If it is asked, "If it is merely recollection regarding the past, how can there be a clear manifestation (*sphuṭībhāva*) of the aspects of the collection (*samudaya*)?"—the five aggregates themselves are the "collection" in relation to what follows. In that regard, this very clarity of the aspect of the collection occurs when [those aggregates] have become present before one.

In contrast, there is a certain mode of manifestation which, by its very nature, serves as the cause for the immediate production of corresponding conceptualizations and subsequent practices, through which one becomes distinguished from ordinary beings as before; and in the case of past objects, it likewise gives rise to a more vivid recollection. However, the realization of the Truth of Suffering through aspects such as momentariness occurs solely by means of the intrinsic nature independent of others. Now, [one might object] that conceptualizations are by their very nature incapable of arising simultaneously—

If it is argued that when there is a determination (*avasāya*) of the aspects of suffering (*duḥkhākāra*), there is no [simultaneous] determination of the aspects of origin (*samudayākāra*), and subsequently [the former] becomes devoid of its object—this is true; for even in the case of each individual Truth (*satya*), the conceptualization of its four aspects does not occur at one and the same time.
Nor is there any such deficiency; for direct perception (*sākṣātkāraṇa*) is precisely the mode of apprehension in which all the aspects have become manifest.

Because the manifestation of the sequence of intended conceptualizations occurs as scattered by the conceptualization of seeds. For instance, when a person perceives a blue, moving, blooming, and so forth, qualified lotus, there is no direct perception (*sākṣātkriyā*) of all the aspects of that object through a sequence of conceptualizations.
(Vācaspati in *Nyāyakaṇikā*, p. 146; cf. *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvali*, p. 10; *Nyāyakaṇikā*, p. 149).

10–11: "The contradiction [is as follows], and it should be inferred in the present case as well: moreover, for you, the moments are mutually [distinct] through their respective successive experiences directly..."

Conceptual constructions (vikalpa) proceed according to one's intention, consisting of the synthesis of what has been apprehended. It should be understood that the state of omniscience is established by experience alone. In this same way, it should be inferred that for the truths of cessation and the path as well, their cognition through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) applies to everything.

Furthermore, as for the objection that seeing only a few things implies the impossibility of seeing all things—on the grounds that all objects are somehow related to one another, whether directly or through a succession—that is already refuted by the very fact that such a relation is not admitted. However, if there were a conceptual synthesis (*saṅkalpa*) whose object is every single thing by way of its being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*), such a state might occur provided that there were the possibility of remembering a succession of births at that time; but [that is not the case].

We perceive a fault [in your position]. Just as for one who has practiced [meditation], upon seeing fire and so forth, there arises instantly the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that "this is fuel, the effect" and "this is fire, the cause," so too let there be clarity (*vaiśadya*) for those things grasped by conceptualization when their cultivation reaches its peak. However, we do not maintain that the perception of one thing results from the mere relationship [of association] with the perception of another. Or, even if there were no such clarity regarding all objects—

For one in that state, mere non-conceptual [cognition], being consistent, is sufficient for the task of omniscience. Alternatively: "The non-conceptual [cognition] has as its object only its own objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it is the cause of the determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of all things as qualified by their respective properties. Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, because its activity follows upon that ascertainment, it has all things as its object. As it has been said:
Those of great intelligence determine all aspects from a mere glance.

[Pravāraṇa-vārttika 2.107] Set aside this doubt: from where does this greatness of an experience—which takes only a few things as its object—arise, such that it results in the determination of all things? If you say it is due to the removal of obscurations such as passion (*rāga*), then [the objects] must be perceived exactly as they are.

One might see [the object], yet it would not be logical for this [person] to possess skill in the creative construction (*nirmāṇa*) of determinations regarding all things without exception. For while the obscuration of reality by impurities is easily found, there is no obstruction to the creative construction of mental verbalization (*vijalpa*).
Herein lies the challenge: when an object is being perceived, is it simply that no obstruction to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is observed? Or...

Or is it produced by afflictions (*kleśa*)? And that twofold [distinction] does not exist. For nowhere is there a conceptualization of all aspects as there is in direct experience (*anubhava*). Nor can there be such a deficiency in conceptualization (*vikalpa*) without afflictions. For when an object is seen as pleasant—even if it possesses faults—the non-conceptualization of those faults clearly indicates that passion (*rāga*) is the cause. Furthermore, when an object is unpleasant—even if it possesses qualities—the non-conceptualization of those qualities [indicates the same].

At that time, there is aversion. However, when there is no practice, the non-conceptualization of all things as having a real nature is produced solely by delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, this is not an obscuration like that of a blanket or similar objects; rather, it functions by instilling a defect in the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*). Therefore, to the extent that delusion and the rest are overcome, to that same extent, through effort and the removal of defects, when the cognitions become determinate (*vyavasāya*) regarding those various forms, finally, all [cognitions]— [...final sentence fragment omitted per instructions...]

In all things that are produced, there would be no contradiction if [the connection] were present; for even in the case of things seen through a succession of mental acuity and those remembered—according to the *Nyāyakaṇikā* (pūrvapakṣa, p. 150) and compare the *Ratnanibandhana* (p.

11)—since memory is possible and because birth is beginningless and endless, [the connection exists] in those being perceived due to the implantation of extremely firm impressions of memory within a single [stream of consciousness].

Furthermore, because the ascertainment of the cause has the nature of ascertaining everything of that same class, there is no fault resulting from the non-arising of conceptual constructions regarding all objects. This concludes the section on the Yogin’s Ascertainment. And as for what was said: "And that [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge, because it is produced by mental cultivation while possessing extreme clarity."

If it is argued that a cognition produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāja*) which possesses extreme clarity is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), just like the clear cognition of an object cultivated after it has been inferred, [we reply:
since it has already been demonstrated that there is no such meditative cultivation at all regarding fire once it has been inferred, the example is non-existent.

And as for this poetic elaboration of his: "here, the trunk of his body, sluggish due to the dullness produced by the weight of the cold, applies itself to the practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) with the conviction that there is fire [within]"; if, in that case, the arrival of the cultivation occurs through the mind's own absorption due to being afflicted by dullness, then what room is there for inference? For inference is sought as that which possesses the proficiency for purposeful action. Therefore—

Furthermore, if one is likewise incapable [of direct perception], what is the use of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? Or rather, let there be clarity (*sphuṭībhāva*) itself beforehand; what room is there for inference?

For it is not possible that a lover would fail to apply himself to cultivation as long as he has not inferred the beloved woman. Therefore, let there be merely a cognition of fire produced by cultivation for one afflicted by dullness.

As for the example, that too is refuted by the example of the beloved woman, as illustrated in one's own poetry. Furthermore, it is not a logical principle that because one cognition born of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is invalid due to its lack of correspondence with reality, another cognition—even one that is consistent—must also be invalid; for if that were so, it would follow that all sensory cognitions would be invalid, just like the illusory appearance of hair and the like.

Furthermore, regarding that which was elaborated to establish a rule of correspondence between the cause— characterized by the intensity of cultivation— and its two effects, such that the illustration and the illustrated are similar, do you not perceive there as well that the eye itself is the common cause for both the vision of two moons and the vision of one moon? If it is argued that the distinction between the two eyes is caused by the impairment or non-impairment of the cataract (*timira*), then [the same applies] to the two cultivations as well.

If it is argued that there is no distinction [between the two cognitions] because their objects are respectively real and unreal; or that in the case of the eye, some modification produced by a cataract (*timira*) is the differentiator, while in the case of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is some difference in the nature of the cognition itself even though the object is not different—[we reply: No.

Since a more powerful difference in capacity (*śaktibheda*) can be established on the basis of the causes being either corroborative or otherwise, what is the use of anything else? It is like the case of [two cognitions], one with an object and the other otherwise.

Furthermore, there is no distinction between the cognitions of color, taste, and vision, nor between the cognitions of the probandum (*sādhya*) arising from a true reason and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), nor between the activities produced by them.

Moreover, the objection that "there is no modification even in the eyes" is flawed, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of classifying even a modification produced by collyrium as a defect. Rather, [the distinction] is due to being a cause of error; thus, even in that case, the difference is established by capacity (*śakti*). Such is the nature of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

It is only the state of being clearly manifest through intensification (*prakarṣaṇa*) that is established here, not validity (*prāmāṇya*), for [if it were validity], there would be room for defects such as the unestablished nature of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*).

Validity, however, arises from correspondence due to its having a real object (*bhūtārthatva*), and its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) arises from being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*); by this much alone, it should be understood that the entire system corrupted by ignorance (*avidyā*) is refuted.
