Even for the author of the *Nyāyaprakīrṇaka*, Jñānaśrīmitra, perception of non-existent objects occurs precisely through the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth.

[The system] is expanded. And regarding what was stated concerning the conceptual nature of inference: "In that regard, everything presented by conceptual constructions is unreal, because it is associated with words. When that [unreal object] is cultivated, once the conceptual nature—which is caused by the apprehension of what is associated with words—is removed from the conceptual construction belonging to you (the opponent) through the cultivation of that [unreal object] until it reaches a state of clarity, then, upon the removal of that [conceptual nature], the [object] to be apprehended—"
[The object] ceases when conjoined with all [conceptual] words; therefore, it follows that even the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) of a yogin would be without an object.

In this regard, what is meant by "being without an object"? Is it a state of formlessness due to the loss of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*), or is it having another form, or perhaps, even while possessing that form, being unconnected to the nature of that object? First of all, the first position is impossible, because of the [nature] of cognition...

Because it is untenable for [cognition] to be formless, for we observe that through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of an object such as a beloved woman, its very form becomes vivid. For this very reason, the second position is also not tenable; as he himself has stated: "For even one afflicted by grief, when the activity of the senses is restrained, there would follow the appearance of a father or other [relative] through the cultivation of the image of his son. Furthermore, when this [object] is being cultivated in a state of conjunction, no other distinct form appears clearly.

To claim that "it exists" is a confused prattle. For by this [statement], the manifestation of the object in every respect is effectively denied; since meditation (*bhāvanā*) is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptual construction is impossible without association with words, where could there be any manifestation? Furthermore, for one who asserts that the appearance of the father and so forth would follow from the meditation on a son, the appearance of the son itself—[is not likewise denied?]—is not...

It is indeed known; otherwise, one might argue that even through the mental construction (*bhāvanā*) of a son, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the appearance of a son. However, a mere lack of desire does not suffice to negate what is perceived.
And thus, for a lover, the clarity of the form of his beloved—even in the form of a small particle—[is established] by the specific speech and gestures [of the lover].

[The author] strengthens [his position] through poetic composition. And how could he himself make such statements as "in the state of clarity produced by contemplation" meaningful? Therefore, it is correct to establish the distinctness [of the object] with respect to the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), on the grounds that the vivid manifestation of one thing does not arise from the contemplation of another. This is not the case, however, regarding the conceptual form (*vikalpa-rūpa*) and that which is intended as the objective domain (*gocara*), between which there is mutual [distinction].

This is due to the superimposition of identity upon those two. For even what is intended as "external" becomes manifest only through the emergence of a clear moment that is the material cause of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To that extent alone, there arises the conventional usage that "that object has been directly perceived by him. It has already been largely considered that a cognition bearing the form of an object is reliable only when the object exists, whereas it is unreliable when it does not.

For this very reason, the third alternative as well has been refuted; for it is impossible to describe any contact with the form of a real object by means of a cognition other than either correspondence or direct realization. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the cultivation of the son," what is the meaning of "cultivation of the son"? If you say it is the repeated placing of the son in the mind, then even the meaning of "placing in the mind" must be explained.

It is merely the conceptualization of that form. If this is so, then as for what he [the opponent] prattles—that when momentariness is to be meditated upon (bhāvya), it is superimposed (samāropita) [upon reality]—[this is refuted by the fact that] it is real (*vāstavam*). (Compare *Ratnagotravibhāga* p. 13; *Nyāyakaṇikā* p. 148; compare *Ratnagotravibhāga* pp. 9–10).
Regarding the section on the determination of the yogi:

if it is argued that momentariness alone is what appears to the cognition of the yogi—no, for even if one practices the meditation on the real and the unreal regarding a distinction consisting in the absence of identity between existence and non-existence, if there were an appearance of the real, then that [appearance] would likewise occur during the practice of the "sons of the Real" (*satyatanaya*). Furthermore, sound—
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that some other distinct entity called "son," due to its similarity [to the father], would appear as his own essential nature. Therefore,

the claim that even non-conceptual cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it arises from a practice whose object is unreal and lacks correspondence (*saṃvāda*), is also refuted, since there is no such thing as the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a superimposed object.

For just as there is the repeated conceptualization "son, son," so too, if there were the conceptualization "superimposed momentariness, superimposed momentariness," then there would be a cultivation of superimposed momentariness; but it is not so. Rather, [the thought is] "conditioned phenomena are momentary. Therefore, like a real son, actual momentariness itself is cultivated.

Alternatively, another aspect of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the son of truth must be stated. Since one does not touch the momentary particular (*kṣaṇika-svalakṣaṇa*) through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the momentary, how can that conceptual construction or its cultivation [be established]? This is the same even in the case of the conceptual construction of a son. Furthermore, the determination of it being a conceptual construction based on the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) is exactly the same. For even in the conceptual construction of a son, nothing other than the superimposed [object] appears. Therefore, this...

Even though there is a manifestation associated with the word superimposed upon the mental conception of a son, one who desires the clear appearance of an actual son rejects the subject at hand; what is this other than being swallowed by the great demon of delusion?
And this similarity to the contemplation of reality has been stated merely on account of its externality in relation to the superimposed [object] flashing forth in conceptual thought.

From an external perspective, however, the mental cultivation of a son by one afflicted with grief is indeed a cultivation of the non-existent (*abhūtabhāvanā*). For this very reason, that manifestation of the form of a son appearing before him is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) at that time, because such a son does not exist. On the other hand, the cultivation of momentariness (*kṣaṇikabhāvanā*), because phenomena always have that as their nature, has an existent object; therefore, the clarity produced by it is a valid cognition due to its non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādāt*). Now, as for the [object] of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) being non-substantial—
The thought remains in our hearts that even when there is the conceptualization of a son, the clarity (*vaiśadya*) attained regarding him as an object is indeed distinct; this is not our view.

Let that too simply perish within the heart. For this *Yoginirṇaya* has been commenced, and it suffers no harm by either [of these positions]. Since even for Apoha, clarity is observed only in that which is determined to be thoroughly purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what can be done here?

If it is asked: "Since there is no appearance of a real object (*vastu*) in inference, how can there be purification of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to it?"—this is a different topic. Furthermore, as for this:
"Moreover, habituation (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated placing of the object to be cultivated in the mind; and that..."

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and austerity (*tapas*), when practiced for a long time, continuously, and with firm ground, are held to produce the clarity of an indistinct conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, that cannot be firmly established by one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness (*kṣaṇikanairātmyavādin*). For instance, whatever kind of conceptual construction arises as the grasper of the object to be cultivated, it ceases without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*); and in that case—

Furthermore, when [the previous state] has ceased, a condition that arises again is produced as something entirely new (*apūrva*) of just such a kind. Thus, by this method, [this occurs] over a thousand eons. (Compare *Ratnagotravibhāga*, pp. 13–14, 340;
*Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*).

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the arising of what was previously non-existent, no impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [action]—which constitutes "practice"—is generated. By this, the production of a distinguished cognition as "practice" is also explained. For how could a preceding cognition, having ceased without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*), produce a subsequent state that is distinct? In every respect, it is only a form that persists through successive conditions that can be refined by them.

This is inconsistent. For there is no cause for determining the certainty of such a rule—that a subsequent cognition arises in exactly the same manner as the first cognition which apprehended the object and ceased without leaving a trace—other than the touch of a fierce deity.
If you argue that this is due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), then surely momentariness is contradicted by permanence, not by the arising of something dissimilar. For that [momentariness]...

Just as a preceding moment, though ceasing without leaving a trace, gives rise to a subsequent moment that is similar to it, so too, if it produces a subsequent moment characterized by even a slight degree of distinction due to a minute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), what harm is there? For we do not harbor the same aversion toward the momentariness of entities as you do. Moreover, here too there is a slight difference in the causal complex; for indeed, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary.

Thus, for one who applies themselves to meditative cultivation out of a desire to exhaust the suffering of *saṃsāra*—and not merely with a view toward verbal recitation—their resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is indeed distinguished.

That [resolve] too produces a result that is distinguished by even a minute degree more than before, until, through a sequence of increasing intensity (*taratamādika*), the final fruit is attained, just like a seed and so forth. However, if distractions and the like should intervene in the interim, there will be only a gradation of dullness and so on.
It may be so. As the commentary states:
"When the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is stronger, there is the cessation of distraction (*vyākṣepa*);
when distraction is stronger, the latent impression becomes turned away."
[From the *Pramāṇavārttikabhāṣya*, p.

2500] Thus it is said. If, then, destruction occurs without any continuity (*niranvayavināśa*), how could the second [moment] acquire a specific quality, given that the previous specific qualities do not transfer?

If this is so, then even in another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there ought to be such a specific quality, because these [qualities] do not transfer there either. Therefore, even though it is non-existent...

Just as that particularity arose by the power of its cause, so too has this one arisen. If it is argued that this [effect] is therefore identical to that, we say no; for because of the difference in the cause, a difference in the effect is unavoidable. To explain: the first particularity arose from something devoid of such a particularity, whereas this one [arose] from such a particularity—

How could there be identity [of the cause and effect] from the minister? For the continuity (*anvaya*) is simply unable to withstand scrutiny. For that portion which has been transferred from the cause, no other cause can exercise its operation; and that very operation was previously non-existent. Thus, when there is the cessation of a factor, there is no persistence of it, and for that which persists, there is no cessation. Therefore, how can cessation and arising coexist within a continuous series?

If it is argued that [the term "together"] is used because of co-existence (*sahavṛtti*), then by that logic, one would have to assume a state of inherence even with space (*ākāśa*). This is because there is no such thing as the meaning of "togetherness" (*saha-artha*) that is produced merely by persisting through both times. Furthermore, at the time when the destruction of the jar and its shards occurs, there is no intervening interval [in which they could co-exist]. (Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā, p. 19)

The section on the determination of the yoginī is refuted. As for the remainder, it is merely a proclamation of a methodological procedure that stands in opposition to valid means of knowledge; so what is the use of it? Furthermore, since the Self remains as stable as the foot of Hari (Viṣṇu), the application of excellence or deficiency is impossible; this has been explained many times, so let it rest for now.

Furthermore, as for what he said— that practice is undertaken to settle the mind in one-pointedness and to abandon distraction, yet for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), there is no such thing as a distracted mind because everything is one-pointed by virtue of being restricted to each respective object— that too is incoherent. For it is established by direct experience that for some, the mind brings a reality (*tattva*) into manifestation.

For one, there is the misconception (*viparyaya*) consisting of the mere reflection upon effects and so forth; for another, it is otherwise. In that regard, every mind that is turned away from the reality (*tattva*) of selflessness and so on is called "distracted" (*vikṣipta*). But what is not sufficient by this much—that according to the stated sequence, a mind fixed solely upon reality is "concentrated" (*samāhita*)? Why must one necessarily seek out a state where a single [mind] alone ranges over various objects? And yet, the reality—
Because it is possible to have a conceptual apprehension (*avagraha*) of a single form even prior to the time of direct realization, that [realization] exists in a conventional sense;

for since the destruction of my own defects is bound to occur, the engagement in the practice of the path remains unimpeded. Indeed, the intention toward what is to be attained is the motivator in all cases. If that [intention] exists, who can turn back one’s engagement, even if there is no actual correspondence with the reality of things? For by that—

If it is argued that [the practitioner] acts upon momentariness and so forth as they have been ascertained therein by means of inference, [we reply: because certainty has not yet become second nature, the mind—subjugated by the latencies of beginningless ignorance—engages in a conventional practice that is entirely inconsistent with such certainty. For this very reason, even when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has been attained, the necessity of relying on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) must be sought in the *Vārttika*. Therefore:
Practice prior to the attainment of that fruit is accomplished as if by ignorance; and from such practice, one becomes perfected and omniscient.

Furthermore, the refutation of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* from the perspective of the Yogācāra position is irrelevant, because its method of proof proceeds precisely by accepting external objects (*bahir-artha*). Even in that case, the sublation (*bādha*) raised against the position of universal omniscience is refuted simply by the fact that such [universal omniscience] is not accepted.
Moreover, that is not a true sublation at all, because it establishes only doubt. For instance, as for the claim regarding the status of past and future objects—

It was stated for the purpose of negation that there is no form whatsoever belonging to the non-existent; this is indeed true at present. Consequently, it is also true that there is no apprehension by the cognition produced from that [non-existent]. However, it has been shown that even though it is like a true dream and so forth, the possibility of its being otherwise cannot be denied. Furthermore, just as there is no form at present, so too there is none in other times, whether past or future. Thus...

If [the object] were non-existent, even its state of being past or future would not be possible, like the mane of a horse; furthermore, the absence of error and non-contradiction have already been considered above.

Furthermore, as for what you have said—that non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) is not tenable in your view—this is because, according to you, non-contradiction is intended to mean either the perception of an object that is subsequently attained, or the presentation of an object that is the locus of purposeful activity, or the accomplishment of the functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) as it appears.
None of this is possible for a cognition of past objects and the like; nor is it even tenable for a cognition of a present object under the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
1. Compare *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, p. 14. 2. Compare the same work, p. 19. 3. Compare the same work, p. 19. 4. Compare the same work, p. 14342; *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.

This too is merely the sway of envy, for it is devoid of logical justification. If you say that such a statement is made because there is a temporal separation between the future and the past, then the same consequence would apply to spatial separation as well; thus, even in a place suitable for activity, the indicator would be invalid. If you argue that "it exists at least for now," then other things—whether future or past—would likewise exist at that time.

If you argue that it does not exist [in the present], then it is the same for that which exists in that place: one could say it does not exist there either. Furthermore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is no different; just as it occurs when the object is present in that place, so too does it occur when it is present at that time. Even though the present moment is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is not undermined, because of the capacity for the superimposition of unity (*ekatvāropa*); this is due to the fact that there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) from the perspective of that [worldly] intention.
Because it is established.

Furthermore, the critique initiated by the followers of Kumārila (Kaumārilas) regarding an omniscient being— beginning with the non-perception of a cause for such a being, and then proposing the alternatives that its cause must be either sensory cognition, mental cognition, or born of the power of cultivation (bhāvanā), and further distinguishing whether that which is born of the power of cultivation is visual or mental— that critique merely serves to demonstrate the weakness of the possibility [of such a being]; it does not result in the definitive proof of his non-existence.

As was discussed in the investigation into whether [cognition] depends on the sense faculties or has an object, the non-perception of a cause does not result in uncertainty; for that very reason, even regarding the objects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it is impossible to deny the power of that which arises from the force of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, even according to the author of the *Kāśikā*, yogins do not possess a cognition in which merit and demerit appear as direct perceptions (*aparokṣa-pratibhāsa*), because of the lack of sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*).

The inference "because of existence, like ourselves and others" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is impossible to ascertain with certainty its exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, the phrase "knowledge of merit and demerit" refers merely to a thorough knowledge of the connection between actions and their fruits; and that is difficult to prevent when the recollection of past births (*jātismaratva*) is possible. Therefore, since such thorough knowledge is possible, when the cultivation [of that knowledge] reaches completion, this gold and so forth becomes thus...

What is untenable about the claim that this means, when being applied, would immediately give rise to a conceptual cognition and thus result in the arising of perception? This must simply be understood as applying to the recollection of past lives (*jātismṛti*). In that case, mere non-perception is not a valid means of proof;

therefore, it is not correct to state a total negation. For instance, even though there is the possibility of forgetting what has been practiced due to derangements of the humors (*sannipāta*) and so forth, [perception still occurs].
Even the recollection [of past lives] is observed in some; likewise, even due to the pain of dwelling in the womb, for someone whose intellect is exceptionally sharp,
through the arising of merit and the mildness of that suffering, the recollection of an immediately preceding birth occurs— this cannot be denied in any way by one who is not a Cārvāka.

Furthermore, since it is possible for this [mental cultivation] to take as its object many different births, there is no contradiction in the possibility of forming mental constructs regarding all objects in a gradual sequence; thus, the defect of the non-arising of cultivation caused by the lack of knowledge of those objects is avoided. Moreover, since cultivation is possible by correctly grasping the arrangement of the world through scripture (*āgama*), even if scripture is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless—

For one who possesses faith and demonstrates the correspondence with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) regarding what is profound, what might not be possible? Furthermore, once the non-falsity of that object of knowledge is established, the goal is accomplished. Indeed, it is observed that even a part becomes manifest through either a collective [perception] or a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, there is a gradual manifestation of the subtle and so forth.
5. Ślokavārttika, Kāśikā commentary, First Volume, p.
218, Yoginirṇayaprakaraṇa:

"By this, that too is refuted: [the claim] that one who has mastered a single treatise is incapable of [mastering] another, or that both [are impossible], or that many [treatises] are [impossible] in many ways."

The supreme human goal is manifested through words and so forth; there is no doubt about this. However, this further point exists: the effort required for the initial study of a treatise is not the same as that required for another subject with a different denotation. Thus, in the progression toward the excellence of proficiency, it may happen that someone attains such excellence regarding an unheard subject as another does not even regarding a heard one. Therefore, the possibility of recollecting [knowledge from] a previous birth arises.

Furthermore, because the processes of inclusion (*ūha*) and exclusion (*apoha*) are possible even regarding objects that have not been previously practiced through repeated cultivation, one will not remain in a state free from afflictions merely by that much, due to the capacity for acting for the sake of others. Alternatively, because all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*) are possible, yogins devoted to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) will manifest everything according to their own will. For this very reason, the objection raised against the position that [the Buddha] perceives everything—that meditative cultivation is useless—is itself pointless.
When the cultivation of the four noble truths has been perfected, since one can establish one's own will through the possibility of inference regarding all objects,
if one were to perceive that there is some other happiness or means for accomplishing the welfare of others in the direct perception of all things, it would not be through cultivation.

Exhaustion: someone might think that for one in such a state, it is easy for everything to become manifest; thus, even Mahodadhi has not said anything more than this, and by saying just that much, the objection has been answered. Therefore, however one reflects upon it, the presentation of objections against an omniscient being results in mere doubt; there is no absolute certainty regarding the refutation. But as for the proof of the omniscient being under discussion—

[It is] exclusively so. If it is argued that even there [in the case of the omniscient being], there is no restriction regarding place, time, or person—no, for the proof is not employed with reference to those [restrictions]. Indeed, this proof is directed against one who denies [the possibility of knowledge] in every respect; and that [proof] achieves its purpose even if there is no restriction of place and so forth. And thus, such a [proof] has been set forth by us in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.

||10|| The Chapter on the Drop of Non-duality (Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa).

In this context, for one who adheres to the existence of external objects, the mental conviction is that whatever is perceived in a certain way exists in that way—just as a blue lotus is established as being blue in form. And since jars and other such things are perceived as having a nature distinct from consciousness, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (reason based on essential nature). There is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) here, because [the object] is perceived as separated from the factor of the grasper and as being suitable for pointing out with the forefinger.
Because the form of the jar and so forth is embraced by both its manifestation and its conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) through a nature that stands before one;

for indeed, the cognition "this is a jar" or "this is not a jar" is self-evident to all persons—even those who have not learned linguistic conventions—and an internal cognition arises corresponding to that very [object], free from the explicit mention of specific names. Even an infant, upon seeing the breast as a means to pleasure...
By directing the tip of its hand toward that [object], it extends itself outward, accompanied by the faculty of determination (*avasāya*).

Consequently, the cognition of the form of a jar or the like as something distinct [from consciousness] does not set out upon the path of non-establishment (*asiddhi*), nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*) to the probandum (*sādhya*), since its occurrence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) has been demonstrated; for a contradictory reason is defined by its pervasion with the opposite of the probandum, and such is impossible here.

Therefore, there is neither uniqueness (asādhāraṇatva) nor doubtful positive concomitance (sandigdhānvayatva); and because it is not observed in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), it is not a common inconclusive reason (sādhāraṇānaikāntika). Nor should it be argued that even though one with jaundice perceives a conch shell as yellow, or a person with ophthalmia perceives floating hairs, no such [objective] determination occurs; therefore, the reason must be considered common (sādhāraṇa). For such perceptions are sublated by a sublating cognition (bādhaka).

Because it is erroneous, it lacks the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, in the case at hand, since there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) and error is thus unestablished, there is indeed the operation of direct perception. Nor can there be a lack of confidence based on the thought that "a sublater might arise here at some time," for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the operation of direct perception everywhere. Therefore:
When there is a subverting factor consisting of differences in place, time, or person, [the cognition] is not born of the senses;
however, the perception of the difference between a jar and so forth is perceptual because such a subverting factor is absent.

In that case, the objection—"What is the use of inference when perception is already functioning?"—is not to be raised, because what is intended is the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). For the possibility of dispute regarding the object of perception does not cease merely through the application of inference. In this regard, just as even when a cow is perceived, a deluded person who, due to some superimposition, fails to engage in its conventional usage [of "cow"] is [led to act] by means of the collection of dewlaps and so forth...

[Objects] are set into operation as having such a nature, or the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding non-existence is established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); likewise, even in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) is to be employed in linguistic usage based on its being perceived in that way according to other scriptures—thus there is no fault. And this linguistic usage is based solely on that [perception], for it is established simply by being set into operation once; for even in the case of a blue lotus and so forth, [there is no distinction between the blue quality and the substance].

In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, regarding conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), there is no other or additional cause for [action] besides appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), because it would follow that activity could not occur based on those alone. For even the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) is sought only upon the first instance of activity; as for repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), however—

This conventional usage is based solely on that [distinction]. However, in the case of the conventional usage of difference under discussion, it is observed everywhere that it is sustained by the proficiency of beginningless habituation. For it has been said:
"Even a child..."
And so forth.
Therefore, for one who is proficient in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), such practice is restricted solely to that which is perceived as such.

When that [conventional object] is to be proven, the state of being perceived as such is pervaded by the absence of dependence on anything else. And even if, in some case, there is perception as such...

In that case, there would be an absence of conventional usage; therefore, since it would depend on something other than that, the property of being perceived as such—which is negated by the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) in the absence of the probandum, namely the fitness for that conventional usage—is pervaded precisely by the fitness for such a determination regarding an object where sublation is absent. Thus, because the pervasion is established, there is also no "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance" (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva).

It is established that one does not approach the presence of a reason that has not been set forth; thus, it is proven that the distinction between cognition and the object of cognition—even regarding what is perceptually accessible—is an inescapable subject of the aforementioned inferential discourse.
To this, it is replied: What is this so-called "cognition" (vijñāna), such that its apprehension as distinct could establish such a conventional usage?

For if "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is defined as that by which something is known, or that which knows, in either case this definition is dependent upon an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Now, for those who deny the external world, no such thing called an "object of knowledge" is established, such that there could be a "knowledge" which serves as the means for its apprehension. Indeed, for a proponent of duality (*dvaitavādin*), the conventional usage that "this is knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge" must be based on a specific operation.

Or is it restricted by its nature? In the first case, does the operation of knowledge reside in the object of knowledge, or that of the object of knowledge reside in the knowledge, or do both reside in each other?

Even here, regarding the first case, there are further alternatives: is it a producer (*nirvartaka*) or a transformer (*vikāraka*)? Among these, first of all, it cannot be asserted that the operation of knowledge upon the object of knowledge is productive, because [the object] is an imperceptible entity.

Because this would entail the consequence of [the object] being destroyed [by the cognition]. Nor is it logical to accept that [destruction] occurs in that very way, since [the object] is seen by someone at that very time. Furthermore, if one accepts that [the object] is removed by that cognition, then even if it remains out of sight (*parokṣa*), its existence cannot be denied. Moreover, if that [object], being seen later by him, becomes the very remover of that cognition, it could not be the object [of that cognition]. It is not visible to that [cognition]; rather, something else is produced by that cognition.

If you say "yes," then the impossibility of [consciousness] having a single location follows. If it were non-obstructive (*apratigha*), then the nature of consciousness—which is luminous, self-evident, and not within the range of others—would merely be established by another name. If you argue that this is not so because it possesses the form of blue (*nīlarūpa*), [we reply: this is addressed in the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa*.

Furthermore, by whom has the negation of the arising of a blue form within consciousness been established, such that there would be the consequence of a failure to apply the means of proof for its establishment?
Therefore, it is not logical for the proponent of duality to claim that what is imperceptible is simply non-existent.

Nor is this even an accepted position of his; thus, there is no insistence on this point. This is so even for one who desires the non-existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*) in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is not intended that what is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) is non-existent in every respect; rather, even if it exists, it must necessarily be the object of some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), albeit at a slight distance. Otherwise, the statement "when there is contact with an existent object, a cognition arises for a person" would be impossible to maintain, because of the absence of an existent prior to the cognition. Furthermore, that admission is not logical; so what is the point of this mere [objection]?
Since this is what is intended to be said, enough with further elaboration.

However, regarding the position that [the object] is a transformation (*vikāryapakṣa*), if one were to establish the rule that "whatever object is the transformation of a particular cognition is its apprehended object," then even the sense organ—which is a transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) impaired by grief and so forth—would have to be the apprehended object; or else, the pallor of the face and the like? For that [pallor] is produced by suffering.

If it is argued that there is a transformation (*vikāra*), we say no; for nothing other than the perception of an impaired form is observed. This has been thoroughly examined in the treatise (*śāstra*), so enough of this effort. Now, if it is argued that such an excellence (*atiśaya*) does not belong to the object (*prameya*) through cognition, but rather that there is the production of something whose nature is illumination (*prakāśa*), then even in this position, that which has one as its object would have all things as its object. For upon the cessation of the cognition of that [object], there would be the cessation of its very form—[otherwise] there would be no difference [between the two].
There would be the undesirable consequence of [the object] being perceived while remaining in its state of being established [as a potentiality].

If it is argued that this is not the case because other things also possess the means for that [perception], then there would be the undesirable consequence of that [object] being manifested even when its cognition has ceased. Even if the form of that [object] does not cease when its cognition ceases, this very same fault remains; for [the form] is not [separate from the cognition] in the way that a pot is [separate] when the potter’s effort has ceased.

The state of being a jar belongs to the clay only in relation to that [specific effect]; or rather, due to fire, the absence of weight in the jar exists only in relation to that which is affected by the fire.

If this were so, then its nature as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) would also be common to all things, yet it is not so. Therefore, just as this [jar], though common in its aspect as a "jar," does not exist in its form as a causal agent, so too it would not exist in its form as luminosity (*prakāśa*); what kind of absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) is this?

[Objection: Is its capacity to assist specific recipients common to all? [Reply: Its luminosity, which depends on specific persons, is likewise common to all; thus the two cases are equal. [Objection: They are not equal. For "capacity to assist" (upakāritva) means either direct assistance or merely the state of being fit for activity.

Would it be acceptable? In that regard, there is no dispute concerning the mere capacity (*yogyatā*) which is common to all. However, regarding the first position, the meaning of the objection is as follows: "If its state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*)—characterized by the performance of an action consisting of assistance—is present in one case, why should it not be so in another as well? This is not a valid principle, because it depends upon factors such as the absence of an intervening interval. Therefore, [the cause] residing in the continuum (*santāna*) of the material cause (*upādāna*)—
[If] its own proximity [is the cause], and its assistance is directed toward that very [proximity], how could there be nourishment (puṣṭi) in the case of something remote and so forth?
Likewise, if even "illumination" were intended as a conventional usage by way of generating another effect, then this might indeed be the case. As some have said: [cf.
Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, ad Jaiminisūtra 1.1.4].

Its manifestation (*vyaktatva*) consists precisely in its being the producer of a manifestation characterized by cognition (*buddhi*). For in that case, that very [object] which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of a cognition—counted as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and not participating as another means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—is not logically manifest, because it lacks the provision of auxiliary causes (*sahakāra*).
Furthermore, we shall state another refutation regarding that point as well.

And this is not tenable, because we are currently considering the position that the object, being of the nature of light, arises from cognition itself. However, if the usage of the term "manifestation" (*vyakta*) is based on the mediation of another effect, then there is no damage to our present thesis, namely that it does not arise in that manner [directly] from that [cognition]. If it were to arise in such a way, the undesirable consequence of its being common to all would be unavoidable; for even the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) exists only as long as there is a distinction—

The capacity to produce pleasure and so forth within a continuum is indeed common in relation to that [continuum]. However, when the very nature of pleasure and so forth is admitted, who then is capable of denying its commonality? If it is argued: "Even so, that which is the pleasure of one is not the pleasure of another," [we reply: commonality and non-commonality are properties of the object; therefore, they do not apply to cognition.

It is logical that pleasure and so forth, being restricted to that [specific] self, are not common to others by virtue of their nature as favor and so on. However, if an external form is admitted—even though it is the effect of that [favor]—it is indeed common, because the favor consists in the nature of a subsequent moment that is to be appropriated by the consciousness of pleasure. In this very same way, there is both commonality and non-commonality.

Thus, for Maitra, that which is called "being the son of Caitra" is not some entity—such as fairness of complexion—that would be common to others; rather, it is precisely the fact of being produced by him that is designated as his "sonship. And that act of procreation belongs to Caitra alone and is not shared with anyone else. Likewise, the designation based on that [act] is also unique, just like the designation based on being produced by him. Fairness of complexion, however, although produced by him, is common to others.

It is not correct to argue that [the manifestation] is produced by that [cognition] alone because it is a different quality, for this is a common [property]; for he (the son) is fair not only due to his father, but also due to others.

Likewise, the manifestness of an object is not merely its being produced by cognition; rather, the accepted position is that there arises a form of luminosity (*prakāśa*) that excels it, since its form remains indistinct when obstructed and so forth. Otherwise, the object could not be said to be "manifest. Such is the linguistic usage.

That [external object] would be merely the cause [of the cognition], just as whiteness is for one who employs the term [“white”] based solely on its being produced by that [whiteness], or as it is for a Sautrāntika based on its being the producer [of the cognition]. And just as for him there is the consequence of [the external object] being the object of another, producing cognition, so too for this [proponent] there is the same consequence regarding the cognition that is produced; thus, nothing more than a transgression of the convention regarding the causal relationship between the object and the cognition is added. As for the avoidance of [the fault of] commonality, it applies to both [positions] alike. It is not [the case that one avoids it while the other does not].
However, the accomplishment of the production of objects in their manifested form is established from this [consciousness].
In the production of light, everything is capable of being illumined;
but if there were no production or illumination, not even a single thing would be so.
This is the summary.
For just as,
in the case of two jars— one raw and one baked— covered by dense darkness, [the distinction between them] consists solely in the fact that one has been produced by fire.

One who asserts manifestness (*vyaktatva*) is not truly able to resolve the objection regarding its incapacity for perception; likewise, this [manifestness] should be understood as being produced by cognition itself. However, if it is admitted that manifestation arises from cognition—just as light arises from a lamp or similar source—then [the following applies].
In that case, the error regarding this [object], such as a pot that is out of sight, would be established; however, the common defect remains difficult to avoid.
If it is argued, "In that case, even a pot manifested by a lamp would become manifest to everyone," [the reply is:

that manifestation produced by the lamp—which consists in the state of being free from darkness and the capacity to generate a cognition dependent on factors such as being situated in a suitable location—is indeed common [to all].
However, it is precisely through cognition that the determination [of an object] is established by means of conceptualization, memory, desire, and so forth, which bring about activity and the like.

If even that were to appear as something already accomplished, just like its luminosity, then alas, it would follow—as has already been largely stated—that it would be common to everyone as the means for activity and so forth, or for the pleasure and other experiences of that moment. Therefore:
For an external mass, there is no manifestation through cognition, whether that cognition occurs at the mere moment of arising or through some further excellence;
rather, manifestation occurs when that which is of the nature of light itself comes into being.
Otherwise, there would inevitably follow the consequence of [the result] being common to all.
Therefore, the operation of cognition is not based on the establishment of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

If it is argued that the object of knowledge possesses the status of being grasped (*grāhyatva*) because of its operation upon the cognition, we say no; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the sense organ (*indriya*) is also an object. Or, if the status of being grasped consists in producing a cognition with a similar form (*sārūpya*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya-viśeṣa*). Furthermore, the qualification "provided it is external" (*bāhyatve sati*) would only be appropriate for one who asserts that very [external] nature. Therefore, this position also is not tenable. Let it be so.
Let it be that the position of dual operation holds: cognition, arising from an object with a form similar to it, is the apprehender through its operation of realization.

In that case, because of the operation of the object, there is no apprehension of those [objects] that are not operative; and because of the reliance on the operation of cognition, there is no [apprehension] of the sense organ either.
If you argue that the operation of realization does not belong to the cognition in that regard, this too is not a valid principle. For that [realization]—

Is that which has the nature of the object of realization (adhigativiṣaya) something other than knowledge (*jñāna*) in its form, or another instance of knowledge? In the first case, since it is established just like the object itself, there is an absence of the operation of knowledge [upon it]. Alternatively, if the object likewise required the operation of knowledge, the aforementioned fault would follow. In the second case, however, it is contradictory to say that the operation of knowledge occurs within knowledge itself; for an operation is precisely—

This same refutation applies here to the notion of "going" as well, because the non-difference between the activity and its possessor is established. In this very same way, the conceptualization of [the activity] as a property of either the cognition or the object should be seen as rejected.

Furthermore, if the object were something distinct [from the cognition], what would happen to it? It would be like the sense organ; for it is not the case that when blue is seen, the sense organ is seen.

If it is argued that there is the attainment (*sādhigati*) of that [cognition], then what causes its connection with the cognition produced by knowledge? If it is argued that this is due to its own operation (*vyāpāra*), then, in that case, since the attainment of both is established through the operation of both, there would be either mutual objectivity (*grāhyatva*) or mutual subjectivity (*grāhakatva*). And in this way, the objection regarding the apprehension of the sense organ (*indriya*) is not avoided; for [the attainment] does not depend on the operation of the eye.
[Objection:

"There is apprehension (*adhigati*) of form through [the operation] of the sense-faculty; however, the operation of the sense-faculty is upon cognition itself, whereas for form, it is so even there [in cognition]. [Response:
Who indeed, other than one out of sheer dullness, would be capable of making such a distinction? For there is no separate entity distinct from both cognition and the object of cognition.

Only something in the form of an apprehension (adhigama) is perceived, wherein the operation of cognition alone might be postulated; yet even there, it belongs to the object and not to the sense organ—this is merely a desire for elegance. If it is argued that the relationship between the apprehended object and the object itself is characterized solely by the relation of object and subject (viṣaya-viṣayibhāva), [we reply: Is this very relation of object and subject not itself the operation?

It is examined by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And for one for whom that [construction] is not established in respect of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, how could it be established even in respect of the act of comprehension and its object? Or, if one were to arbitrarily accept that the object of comprehension possesses the status of being an object, how could one then reject [the existence of] knowledge? If it is argued, "This conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) certainly exists," we reply: it does exist; however, it is merely this that must be considered—what is its foundation?—namely, the non-confused...
Or is it the determination of the nature of characteristics, or the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the beginningless habituation to false conceptualization? Let it be;
if you ask what its seed is, so what of it? For we do not [assert anything] simply because another person does not understand it.
Thus, the definition of these two has been shown to be non-confused. By this, the postulation of [cognition] as a distinct entity from apprehension is refuted;

for, just like that [apprehension], its having that [object] as its domain is unestablished. And it is a great display of discernment to claim that an object is "known" by means of an apprehension that does not have that object as its domain. By this, [the opponent's view] is refuted, which—during the time of debate—does not effect or transform the object through the operation of cognition.

Nor is it the case that the term "object" refers to the cognition itself; rather, since [the term] merely extends to the act of apprehending that [object], the [opponent's] conceptual construction is refuted.
Therefore, it is established that this conventional usage of "cognition" and "object" does not occur by way of an intervening operation.
Nor is it restricted by genus (*jāti*), for [an object] is established as being knowable by someone, at some time, and in some place.

Because of this [fallacy]. For such a systematic arrangement does not exist for things like "cowness" (*gotva*), which are fixed by their very nature. Furthermore, even now, a distinction in characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) must necessarily be stated, yet it cannot be established; in its absence, if mere existence (*sattāmātra*) were the cause of the reality of either cognition or the object of cognition, then everyone would achieve the awareness of all objects—or, conversely, no one at all—since there would be no distance [between them]. But surely, it exists?

The proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the sense organs with their objects is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth; the cognition arising through the power of that [proximity] is established as restricted to its respective object and excluded from remote objects due to the absence of the sixfold contact (*ṣoḍhā-sannikarṣa*). Thus, how could there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? This too is trivial. For by this [proximity], one might establish a restriction on the *origination* [of cognition], but not a restriction on its being the apprehender (*grāhakatva*) with respect to any particular object.

Regarding consciousness: it may be granted that knowledge is produced by an object through the power of contact—such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth—and not by something lacking that [contact], such as a remote object; however, there is no certainty as to what its apprehender (*grāhaka*) is. If you argue that it is "that very thing by which it was produced," then the self, the mind, the sense organs, and their conjunctions would also be objects of apprehension, and thus the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is not avoided. For [the cognition] does not [apprehend] the objects—
Even if it were admitted [to exist], some utility for this [mind] in relation to the sense organs and so forth would have to be possible, by which a distinction in its apprehension could occur.
Alternatively, the production of determinate cognition or another operation has just been considered.
*Advaitabindu-prakaraṇam* (The Drop on Non-duality)

If it is argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because manifestation occurs only of that very [object], then we reply: while manifestation exists as something impossible to deny for the two parts conceived as the grasped and the grasper, if there is some basis for the powers of instrument and locus, let that be stated. Nor is mere simultaneous manifestation itself the basis, as in the case of two moons, or the mutual grasping of those very two.

This would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Or, in the case of blue and yellow, one moon would be false and the second part would be insentient; furthermore, because the mental faculty (*manas*) cannot have two functions simultaneously, such arguments are appropriate only within the framework of the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*). And it is for that purpose that this investigation is undertaken.
However, when even the two parts are not manifested together—since it is not accepted that a cognition can be experienced by another simultaneous cognition—then this [argument] as well...

There is no such possibility. However, if the adherence to a poorly formulated convention were not a hindrance, then one might consider the following argument: that the forms of joy, distress, and so forth, as well as the form of the moon and so on, are experienced simultaneously within the mind. Yet, even this basis for the argument is examined and found to be untenable;
thus it remains established that [the opponent's position] is not valid.

Thus [it is argued]. Furthermore, the fact that there is sensory contact with a jar and not with a camel must be determined from that very experience itself. And the status of this [experience] as an experience of that [object] is due to its arising through contact with that [object];
thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Alternatively, if the experience of that [object] were established by some other means, then [contact] would be redundant.

Because it would be redundant. Furthermore, if [the cognition] were an experience of that [object] simply because it arises through contact with it, then the experience of the object would have to be an indistinct manifestation established merely by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not a distinct one; this would result in the subversion of what is observed, just as Maitra’s sonship to Caitra or his fairness of complexion [are not experienced directly]. Therefore, this portion intended as the object, which manifests with clarity, [is so] because it is devoid of consideration regarding the operation of other causal factors.
One perceives the self as something known by itself, just like joy, distress, and so forth.
As for the one who thinks:
"But that very same prior causal complex [produces] the cognition of the object-moment,"
One should make it possess both light and form, so that there may be simultaneous perception.
If the manifest object is already produced by the causal complex, what is the use of cognition?
Furthermore, there would be the fault of commonality; nor, if it were unmanifest, could there be the appearance of clarity.
Since this is established merely by virtue of dependence on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
it follows that the sense organ (*indriya*) would also possess the nature of illumination (*prakāśatva*).

But if stability [of the object] is maintained, how could even a single object be produced by a single causal complex? And how could consciousness be experienced as flashing forth simultaneously with that object?
Now, if cognition were non-cognition, then even all that is well-spoken would be difficult to perceive externally today under the view that it is self-cognizable.
(Jñānaśrīmitra-nibandhāvalī 352)

If it is argued that the capacity [for cognition] belongs solely to the causal complex (sāmagrī), then the cognized object and the cognizer would be distinct; yet, since they have arisen with such a nature—just like taste and color—who could be questioned about it?
If the form of the object and the subject is determined and characterized,
then, in seeking its production, let it be called the power of the causal complex (sāmagrī).
When health is established in its own nature, then the power of the physician must be stated;
yet the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower has not even now been determined.
Therefore, when one's own true nature is to be stated, [employing] a change in the causal complex,
or speaking of something irrelevant, or behaving like a ḍiṇḍika is simply a pretense.
Therefore, there is no knower whatsoever, no object of knowledge, and no act of knowing;
rather, this world must be understood as self-luminous, existing independently of those [distinctions].
For blue and so forth appear, and there is nothing else that illuminates them;
thus, their self-luminosity is established, and for us, that alone is consciousness.
These are the intermediate verses.

This being the case, there is no such thing as "consciousness" that is established as distinct, by virtue of which the fact of the form of a jar and so forth being perceived as distinct could prove its difference from it; thus, the reason (hetu) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*) and is beset by the fault of being unproven (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, the intended probandum—the conventional usage of their difference—does not serve the purpose at hand precisely because the qualification is unestablished. For even if the jar were of the nature of consciousness, since...

Since difference is established even from another cognition, it is of no use to establish mere difference [in general]. Therefore, since difference must be proven with respect to a specific limit (*avadhi*), and you are unable to clarify that limit, your presentation is futile.

Now, [one might object]: "Even for the Proponents of Cognition (*Vijñānavādins*), there is the conventional usage of 'cognition'; whether that [usage] exists in such a way or otherwise, it is the same for us as well."

In that case, it will find refuge in the proof of its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, there exists in the world what is recognized as "some cognition"; it is from this very fact that we shall state the distinction. Our definition has no role here.
And if you argue: "In an inference that proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), there can be no conformity to convention (*samaya*)"?
For the Vijñānavādins, consciousness-ness is luminosity;
and that [luminosity] is the same for both parts designated as the apprehended and the apprehender.
In the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa*:
"Difference does not arise from knowledge, for distinctness follows from being manifest; that [distinction] is perceived only when these things, such as jars and the like, are separate."
Furthermore, there is the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), for jars and the like are indeed not unmanifest.
However, when the subject (*dharmin*) is something other than these [manifest objects], then the non-establishment of the property (*dharmāsiddhi*) is clear.

Furthermore, there is the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*) because [the object] is known through differentiation; moreover, for one who maintains that [consciousness] is self-luminous, there are further issues such as the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).
Therefore, that [argument] is not tenable with respect to the opponent's view.
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, this is described as "consciousness flashing within.
Consequently, there is a distinction between that [consciousness] and that which is of an unknowable nature.
What fruit is there even from faith?
If the establishment of the knower and the known were accomplished by means of their own forms,
then the conventional distinction between blue and its cognition would be a human fabrication.

If you are satisfied with the distinction between the ego and the pot— two things that possess the nature of self-luminosity yet lack the forms of the cognized and the cognizer, which are unique to each, and which touch upon internal determination and external determination respectively; (then you may hold this view).
Why is the establishment of the difference between two distinct continua not for your delight?
Furthermore, there is no manifestation for that which exists within the path of a different continuum;
even if it were to appear, would not the loss of the relationship between the object and the subject be observed?
If no one accepts the identity of two distinct continua,
yet someone were to accept it, even in that case [the refutation] would be effective by means of the proof of their difference.
Oh, what a great effort has been exerted by this external critic; it is indeed appropriate!
When the Vedāntins and others assert non-difference between two cognitions despite a difference in their mental continua,
they do not [assert] the unity even of two cognitions of blue.
Why then is there this persistent application to vice?

For even among the proponents of Vijñānavāda, there are various positions. To illustrate: in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, it is stated that the single mind appears in the world as if possessing the portions of the apprehended and the apprehender.

Or is this self-cognition divided into two—namely, the cognition of cold and so forth, and the cognition of pleasure and so forth? Or is the cognition of pleasure and so forth supreme here? Or is blue and so forth deposited within it by the power of ignorance?
Is it a single thing possessing variegated forms, or rather, is it entirely formless?

And what use now is the consideration of their relative strength and weakness for one who is engaged in establishing an external object through such an insistence on a formal proof? Therefore, since the form of the jar—which is of the nature of consciousness as described and established as being individually cognizable—is not distinct from that which is accepted by other [proponents of] consciousness, there is no fruit whatsoever in proving its difference; thus, the effort is futile. Now, it may be argued that it is not individually...

If it is argued that the form of the jar is the object of cognition because it is common to all, and therefore, although it is self-luminous, it is essentially an external object due to its commonality, and thus the cognition of it as non-different from the self is employed to establish linguistic usage—this is not so; for commonality has already been refuted previously. Indeed, that manifest form does not belong [exclusively] to those whose causal conditions are complete and who are in close proximity, as if it were their own.
Because it has been demonstrated that even for things that are remote, engagement and withdrawal cannot occur unless they are prompted [by a cognition].

If [the object] were not common [to all], then [prompting] would not occur even for those things that are proximate. Indeed, even for proximate things, that form is not one and the same; rather, it is of such a kind [as to be capable of prompting].

If there is indeed a difference [between the object and its cognition], then how can there be a single, unified apprehension? This is not a fault, because such [unified] apprehension is observed even in the case of distinct things like strands of hair.

If it is argued that this is not valid cognition (*pramā*) because a sublation (*bādhaka*) is seen in that case, then why is a sublation not perceived here as well—namely, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of activity and so forth occurring even toward something obstructed? Even if that were the case, the very fact of activity and so forth is the reason; it is simply that for such a manifestation alone—
To the question, "What is the cause here that some [beings] come into existence while others do not?", we reply: it is *vāsanā* (latent predisposition). What is this *vāsanā*?

It is merely the power of the material cause (*upādāna-śakti*) which has been transmitted through a beginningless succession of preceding cognitions; it is designated as if it were distinct by virtue of some particular perspective, though it is perceived as such. This has been analyzed elsewhere. Due to the similarity in the transformation of such seeds, some [beings] arise.

There is no fault here in the fact that such knowledge does not belong to others, because the succession of the relationship between material cause and its effect is fixed, like the hair and other objects seen by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Or rather, just like that [hair], there is also the determination of a single location due to its resistance (*pratighatva*); enough with this elaboration.
This is the summary:
Why is there one [cognition] when there are distinct [objects], by virtue of determination? If it is argued that this is not so because of sublation, then why is no sublation perceived now?

However, similarity is appropriate for cognitions to manifest because of the equality of their seeds in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*); furthermore, since they lack resistance (*pratigha*), there is no fault even if they occupy the same location.

From this, it is established that [the Self] is also knowable by each individual self (*pratyātmavedyatva*). If it is argued that hardness and so forth are not attributes of cognition (*jñāna*), we say:
no, because all things are cognition by virtue of having the nature of light (*prakāśa*). Furthermore, one cannot tolerate [the claim that] blueness is an attribute of cognition.

"Hardness," he says, is for one of dull intellect. If it is argued: "Is it not the case that whatever blue is perceived, that very same thing is experienced as hard? And this is not tenable in the case of consciousness"? [We reply: Even externally, for one who perceives through delusion, blue is merely color (*rūpa*) and hardness is touch (*sparśa*). There is nothing else besides these two that falls within the range of perception. This is because a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*).
If you say this, what is this "nature of being a quality" (*guṇatattva*)? If it is merely dependence (*pāratantrya*), then the reason is non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).

If, on the other hand, it is something else entirely due to a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), even so, because it is impossible to establish a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary, the reason suffers from the fault of having a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*). As for this [argument] which...
He recites: "That which rests in substance, possesses qualities, and is not a cause—independent [of other causes]—in conjunctions and disjunctions.
Even there, its status as a quality is established by its resting in substance.
And once the nature of being a quality (guṇatva) is established, there follows its having a substratum;
thus, these two would be mutually dependent.
Therefore, for this [proponent], his own logical system alone remains as his refuge.

It serves no purpose in debate for one who does not regard that [external object] as a valid means of knowledge; enough, then, with this chewing of what has already been chewed. Or, let there be some other external substratum for the two qualities; even so, if it is luminous (*prakāśa*), then it cannot exist without being included within cognition.

If it is non-luminous (*aprakāśatva*), the reason remains unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, the simultaneous determination of blue and hardness is nothing but an illusion (*bhrānti*). [This is because of] the subverting factor...

In the manner already described, there is indeed no inclusion of one cognition within another; furthermore, the seed of a cognition appearing as blue is the necessity of being the means for awakening the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a cognition appearing as hard, which depends upon [the prior] activity.
Thus, it is not like a jackal.
The cries [of the opponents] run toward the lion of the Yogācāra:

as for what was said—that there is the cognition "I am not a jar"—even in that case, for those for whom this "I-cognition" has the self (*ātman*) as its object, when it does not occur with respect to a jar and so forth, it would only negate the nature of being a self (*ātmatva*), not the nature of being consciousness (*jñānatva*). This remains true even if one takes the object of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the locus.

The notion of "I" does not belong to consciousness alone, because that would lead to the absurd consequence [of it] also applying to Caitra’s mind. If you argue that for Caitra it indeed exists there [in his own mind], then in considering why it does not exist for Maitra as well, one must conclude that the lack of habituation (*anabhyāsa*) toward other continua is the answer.

And that lack of habituation exists even with respect to the forms of jars and so forth, which appear directed toward external objects. Therefore, this is the exclusion of the ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*).
Even if it were established otherwise, it would not suffice to cause the affliction of being of the nature of consciousness.

(1. See Vaiśeṣikasūtra 1.1.16. Furthermore, it might be argued that whatever is consciousness necessarily becomes the object of either one's own or another's *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense); [but] it is not so.

If it is argued that the form of the jar is likewise [the object], we say no; for the pervasion of the object by the cognition, which is the subject, is unestablished. For the object is held to be distinct [from the cognition]; it is not an effect, though it might be the cause. And there is no necessity that the existence of an effect follows from its cause; thus, due to doubt regarding the exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, these proponents of externalism, having merely invoked the externality of the form— [70a] ...[the rest of the sentence is cut off in the source].

The procedure for proving difference imitates the account of heating gold and removing its knots; nor is mere non-existence the probandum, but rather—given the context—the distinctness from the illuminator of a jar or the like, which is already established as manifest through the operation of the illuminator despite being previously unmanifest.

Since such [distinctness] is not established [by the argument], the proof is futile; thus, the proponent’s statement constitutes the fallacy of stating what is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

[This constitutes] a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Or, even if it were not so, who could prevent the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) based on the appearances of those suffering from sleep or cataracts?
If it is argued that "in all cases, the external object exists as a support (*ālambana*), though its spatial and temporal characteristics may differ"?
In all cases, the cognition of the object of perception has a nature that is otherwise than the actual place and form [of the object].
Thus, it can also be said:
"How is there the grasping of one's own nature, and how is there the grasping of another? These are the intermediate verses.
How is there the grasping of one's own nature, and how is there the grasping of another?
Whether the intellect is distinct from the self or not, its lack of activity is the same.
And just as it appears elsewhere to be active, so too does it appear in itself;
like a lamp, this conventional usage cannot be denied by the intellect.

Therefore, just as there is the view that it is "misapprehension otherwise" (anyathākhyāti), so too, if one reaches a conclusion through oaths that "it is not cognition itself appearing, but rather something external that is not external, which is non-blue appearing in the form of blue."

What is the cause here for the failure of knowledge, even though its nature is that of an object? And what is the reason for its manifestation being restricted to a particular location? This objection applies equally to both [theories].
If an internal disturbance associated with a particular modification of the power (*śakti*) is present there,
why can it not be stated that this too is the cause in this case?
Furthermore,
in the *Advaitabinduprakaraṇa*,
it is said: "If that which is real appears otherwise, let that be the case due to a difference in location."
Otherwise, how could there be a manifestation as non-existence when there is a difference in time?
A living actor may indeed be known by another name, but one who is dead cannot;
therefore, it is the mind alone that is capable of appearing as something else in all circumstances.

Therefore, even in the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), there is no avoidance of the charge of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). If it is argued that, despite the difference in time, the object is not absolutely non-existent because it exists at its own time, [we reply: what utility does the mere existence of that object at another time have at the time of its appearance?

That which is useful to something by virtue of its own presence cannot be effective for that thing when it has long since passed away, just as a burnt seed or the sky is not capable of producing a sprout.

Or [it may be said] regarding blackness: the appearance of an object is established by means of its own existence (*svasattopadhānena*); thus, there is the perception of a contradiction (*viruddhopalabdhi*), because even for that which has perished, the possibility of causal efficacy (*śakti*) remains. "Utility by means of its own existence" constitutes two contradictory properties (*viruddhau dharmau*). Here, even a past seed situated in a granary is utilized indirectly (*paramparayā*), but not by means of its own existence; it is for this purpose that the qualification is employed.

An object that appears must be said to be utilized within the appearance precisely by the imposition of its own existence, not through a mediated succession. For the appearance would be either a property (*dharma*) or an effect (*kārya*) of that object. In the case of being a property, there is simultaneity; in the case of being an effect, there is a rule of immediate succession following its own existence.
Thus, even a single moment of interval cannot tolerate the absence of that state; therefore, the object’s utility within the appearance occurs only through the imposition of its own existence.
It is established that, due to the absence of that [object], the past cannot be manifested. Therefore,
this which is appearing is manifesting while being non-existent.
Because its own existence has passed away, due to the disappearance of its substrate.
Furthermore, even in the absence of that [object], if there is an appearance, then the appearance of a non-existent thing follows;
for by your own words, you desire that there be an appearance even in the absence of existence.
Therefore, even in the view that external objects exist, the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is difficult to avoid in the case of erroneous cognition.

Or, let there be the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*); in either case, it is merely a transformation of cognition (*jñānavivarta*), and since it is similar to that [transformation], it cannot be refuted by mere disapproval. Thus, because the pervasion is absent, the reason "being perceived as distinct" is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of difference.
[The opponent] says: "It is established. But even if this is the case for those who are deluded, what follows regarding experience?

If you argue that there is no inconclusiveness because the qualification 'provided it is non-delusory' is intended [in the definition], we say: no. For the status of being delusory is dependent upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), and since such a cognition is established here as well by the very sequence already stated. To explain:"
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*:
"From self-luminous cognition, by virtue of its unique nature..."
If there were a difference [between the object and consciousness], the object would be cognizable by another, and thus it would be common to all.
And such a restriction is not established by the reasoning already stated;
therefore, how could a jar be distinct from cognition, any more than hair and the like?
Since the establishment of a property does not occur in the absence of a certain thing,
the positive concomitance (anvaya) of that property excludes its difference from that thing.
Therefore, since this unique property of self-luminosity— which is the opposite of the common characteristic of externality consisting in non-self-luminosity—
is perceived in jars and other objects, it negates their [status as] external; thus, by the force of this sublation, such a cognition is indeed an error.

Furthermore, this very established fact is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and it is not based on mere conjecture; thus, there is no charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As for what the Vijñānavādin proves:
"Whatever appears is consciousness, like what is seen in a dream."
And this [argument]—that "blue and so forth manifest, and therefore they are self-existent causes"—is as follows:
Even then, let this continuous stream serve to establish the connection [between the two],
and let there be no room for doubts regarding the succession of cognitions from afar.

It is accepted that consciousness is self-luminous and unique; moreover, the pervasion of luminosity by that very nature [of consciousness] is established by others as being uncaused by anything else.
If blue and so forth manifest by themselves and not by another,
then why does one not likewise maintain that they manifest by themselves and not by something else?
