If even the operation of differentiation, though observed, is deemed inappropriate in the present case,
how then can you postulate an unobserved differentiation of the locus?
But surely, it is observed that "that which is itself a distinction of manifestation," and so forth;
even there, however, it is not said that the nature [of consciousness] is pervaded within the self.
In this same way, it should be understood that the intellect shines by itself,
just as emptiness shines by itself in the sky, because it precludes the activity of another.
Thus, the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa* and the supreme Śruti are for the purpose of destroying the delusion regarding the activity of the Self.
The mental state (*vṛtti*) does not exist by virtue of its own activity; rather, at that time, it takes on the very form of that [Self].
Just as space is untainted and self-luminous, so too is this [consciousness] unique;
this has already been established previously.

Consequently, that which is called "manifestness" (prakāśatā), having set aside [the notion of] commonality and other operations because it is equally defective in all cases, remains established [as the defining characteristic].
Therefore, through reasoning, a determination of their identity with those two [terms] is obtained by means of their contradiction;
consequently, when there is a contrary [conclusion], the reason cannot remain established because of that very contradiction.
Since luminosity is established, white and other colors are of the nature of cognition;
any hope for them to have an external form is merely a vain hope.
If the forms are the very nature of a single variegated cognition, how can there be a distinction [of parts] corresponding to each atom? Likewise, there would be no mutual awareness [of those parts].
Even so, whether [the cognitions] are mutually distinct or not, there is a loss of their defining characteristics, just as with external objects.
If this is the case even when they are distinct, how can those cognitions be connected with illumination?
Now, if the appearance [of objects] is likewise merely the cognition of one's own mental continuum by means of another cognition,
then what offense has the external world committed against this mass of false forms?
Furthermore, in the case of false cognition, there is neither manifestation nor anything else;
therefore, that reason, being common to both sides, establishes doubt.
This other exclusion (*vyāvṛttyantara*) has been described as "falsity and otherness";
even though it possesses doubt, its status as cognition remains established upon manifestation.
Thus, when it has been established that what is manifest is cognition, its status as awareness remains—
whether in some cases or everywhere— even if its unreality is asserted through debate.
Therefore, it is cognition alone that is real, whether it be true or false, and not the external;
or let there be an external object as well, yet let its nature be that of illumination, which is consciousness.
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*,
even the conceptualization of difference and non-difference does not subvert luminosity,
nor is it excluded from the pervasion with the aforementioned probandum; so what purpose would such [a distinction] serve?
For one who might imagine that another perceives another, the rest [of the argument] might indeed constitute a fault; however, we say that this is not the case even in a dream.

Because it is devoid of both unity and plurality, this insentient world is without intrinsic nature; just as it is, there is no such thing as "it. How, then, can there be existence for a single entity?
In this treatise, we state that the cause of cognition is whether the manifest blue and so forth are insentient or indeed non-insentient.
In that case, if the absence of being one or many were to impart some other property [to the object], what would be lost for us by that? For the insentience of blue and so forth remains unchanged.
Indeed, when existence has been established, whether [an object] be insentient or non-insentient,
things such as the horns of a horse— which are non-existent— are certainly not inferred in reality.
Nevertheless, this is irrelevant because it is devoid of any consideration of existence;
for it is only when existence is already established that a specific qualification is considered.
Even if there is doubt regarding existence, if that [object] exists, it must be cognition itself;
therefore, the designation "non-defect" applies to both the proof of non-existence and its sublation.
Since it possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its form as a mere conventional designation, it is not without a substratum;
otherwise, how could even the reason of "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) have a substratum?
If there were not mere non-existence in that [dream], and if there were here [in the waking state] mere cognition-only,
then the establishment of external objects would be contradictory to both positions.

If you say that what is to be proven here is "the state of being a cognition whose limiting adjunct is reality," then why is such a qualification introduced when the subject under discussion is merely "cognition-ness" in general?
If the state of being knowledge were not pervaded by the state of being a real entity, such that it could exist even in its absence,
then what fault would there be in [calling this] a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), or rather, let there be the state of being a real entity.
Furthermore, in the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa*: "Moreover, is existence intended to be negated as something other than the self that is mere luminosity,
on the grounds of its being devoid of intrinsic nature?"

In a negation, there is no exclusion of that which is distinct from the nature of manifestation; for if this [nature] itself were excluded, by what could it be excluded while appearing before the witness?
If inference, being a means of valid cognition, sublates something for someone, why should perception not likewise establish something for someone else, given that it too possesses that same status?
In the end, the validity of perception must necessarily rely upon inference;
however, that which is produced by the senses, being of the nature of mere manifestation, does not depend on inference.
Now, this [object] is the domain of inference and not of sensory cognition;
since it is of the nature of luminosity and is directly perceived, how can there be any occasion for inference?
Now, that which is established by direct perception cannot be refuted;
moreover, what kind of distinction in exclusion (vyāvṛtti) could there be here if [the object] were unable to withstand analysis?
Let it be a property of consciousness alone, while the external object is like the horn of a hare;
or, in the absence of the causal efficiency of an object, let that property belong to cognition itself.
Furthermore, the lack of causal efficiency and the inability to withstand analysis belong to cognition itself and not to external objects; what more than this can be said?
This reflection belongs to consciousness alone; for its scent does not exist externally at all.
Since its similarity to a serpent’s horn is thus established, is its purpose not thereby fulfilled?
The designation of a "heap of form" is applied to those things that appear externally like a cluster of reeds;
since formations (*saṃskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) are not distinct from it, why do you not consider them non-distinct?
The very root of non-manifestation is unstable because its existence cannot be established;
however, for that which exists in the form of manifestation, it is merely an uncontradicted attribute.
If, due to that same defect, even luminosity is far removed from existence,
then what else will non-luminosity prove regarding non-existence?
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*:
"Non-existence belongs only to that which does not manifest; it does not belong to manifestation by its own nature.
Therefore, it is said that non-existence [belongs] to that very thing, but this is not tenable in the case of a conceptual construction."
Furthermore, for that which is manifest, its reality arises solely from its manifestation;
whereas for even a hair, its non-existence is determined by a cognition whose nature is insentient.

For this very reason, even for blue and other objects accepted by the Prābhākara (Prakāśa), it is precisely causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that has been declared to be their reality; without that, there is no distinction between the two [the external object and its cognition].
Furthermore, consciousness is impermanent because it is invariably accompanied by activity;
however, when there is an absence of activity, its existence is primary indeed, because it manifests [independently].
At that time, neither its momentariness nor its existence is being contradicted; since existence consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that probans is not defective.
Nor can its impermanence be avoided by positing another state;
for it is that very moment which is cognized, otherwise there would be no distinction whatsoever.
If it is argued that this relation of cause and effect has thus arrived [as a reality], then indeed there is no negation here of the conventional; for even its momentariness is merely conventional.
If it were eternal in reality, it could not exist even conventionally;
if you say it is eternal because impermanence is negated, even so, how can there be any attainment?

One may speak of difference and non-difference by placing some entity in the foreground according to distinctions of space, time, and so forth; but what sequence could there be within one's own pure consciousness?
The nature of cognition neither unites with nor divides from other things;
for the distinction between self and other is merely a decoration borrowed by the intellect.
The so-called "ineffability" of anything else indicates the existence of its own intrinsic nature;
that very form is the reality, and it is established in non-duality.
For indeed, O learned one, that which is firmly established necessarily attains its result;
otherwise, by mere cognition alone, there is neither engagement nor cessation.
*Advaitabindu-prakaraṇam*
First, the aspect of the grasper differentiates itself from the grasped;
likewise, it does so from other grasped objects as well.
Otherwise, in the absence of non-duality (advaita), it would cut away all difference;
therefore, difference and non-difference are restricted to duality (dvaita) and not likewise in non-duality.
And as long as one reflects upon the distinction of time for the sake of awakening from sleep,
this [sleep] is swallowed by another mental construction through its own exhaustion, just like anything else.
Therefore, what is called "permanence" exists neither in reality nor even conventionally;
yet, even though it lacks the nature of momentariness, let it be apprehended just as inference is.
Even the conventional usage of "variegated" and "one" is considered to be intent upon the exclusion of difference;
for here, only the pure manifestation exists, devoid of both unity and plurality.
What can be achieved even by that which exists as pure luminosity if it is devoid of all power?
Since there would be no capacity for action, what could its own nature possibly become?
If even the nature of illumination cannot be found through investigation, we understand that investigation to be inference; it does not sublate direct perception.

If even the sense-organ produced [cognition] is sublated when there is a reversal such as that of the *guñjā* berry and fire, it is due to error regarding the external form; how could there be any delusion regarding its own nature?
"If you claim that valid cognition is invalid, the occasion for investigation has been lost;
for by so speaking, something must necessarily be either established or sublated."
In that case, what kind of praise could there be for one who speaks unreasonably in an assembly?
There is no reasoning superior to inference; what is established if that [inference] is disregarded?
If it is argued that there is an awakening by means of his cognition because she has been accepted by him,
then how can there be an awakening by means of his cognition when she herself has not been sublated by her own acceptance?
If it is argued that "there is nothing to be proven," then sublation (*bādhā*) itself must also be something to be proven.
To say "that too is not" is a useless statement; for what purpose would even such a question serve?
1. *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, p.
89: "If there is any fruit of speech, it is nothing other than that [which arises] from comprehension."
Words are capable of conveying meaning; the eye, smoke, and so forth are not beautiful [in that regard].
If the nature of cause and effect exists only conventionally, by whom could it be apprehended?
Certainly, the cognition of the cause arises from the effect; otherwise, vows and the like would be useless.
Even one who, upon feeling heat and so forth, reaches for sandalwood and not for fire—
To speak of anything without relying on cognition does not occur.
If arguments are set forth after having introduced some subject matter, why is there no taking of a position in the treatise? If not, by whom would that [subject] be grasped?
When asked about the path to liberation, if one were to explain the cultivation of emptiness,
thereby awakening [others] to emptiness, how could one then censure the grasping at a position?
Therefore, relying upon conventional reality, its probandum and its means of proof are unavoidable; thus, the acceptance of the means of valid cognition is itself unavoidable.
If you claim that pride is accepted within conventional reality, then this very analysis is also conventional.
If it is not accepted even within conventional reality, then one who speaks thus is a victor in every way.
Just as there is conventional consensus regarding cause and effect, so too is there consensus regarding cognition;
for one who desires inference, perception is not [the sole authority]—this is no small certainty.
If it is argued that there is dispute regarding self-awareness, we reply: no, because it is established by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Therefore, even though it is not ultimately real, cognition is accepted as the primary authority.

If it is conventional reality (saṃvṛti), what is the point of extracting [the ultimate]? Let the ultimate (paramārtha) be just that much. Furthermore, since [the ultimate] is itself conventional, how can the conventional be abandoned within conventionality?
If it is argued that the mental application of the term "existence" (sattā) is based on its connection with manifestation (prakāśa),
then how can there be any comparison with that which possesses neither manifestation nor the capacity for it?
Therefore, properties such as the inability to withstand analysis do not undermine its luminosity.
1. cf. *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, p. 89.
If the *Advaitabindu-prakaraṇa* is desired, let it be [the work] of Ceta alone; for the establishment of the mind (*manas*) is well-known from its luminosity (*prakāśa*).
That which is called the non-existence of the Light is stated only in relation to an existence imagined by oneself; thus, there is no contradiction.
But for the opponent, it is the Light alone that is the ultimately real entity.
Both [theories] are equal in being sublated by worldly consensus and established proof:
that which has the nature of manifesting what is non-existent is not real, nor is it existent; it is not one with the other, nor is it dual, nor is it non-dual with those two.
If the world were thus devoid of the four peaks [of existence],
what would be the difference between the views of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) and those of the Madhyamaka?
Even causal efficiency belongs only to those things whose very nature is luminosity;
yet for those [opponents] who maintain that such luminosity is itself negated,
let there be their difference— though it is naturally difficult to overcome.
"But for one who knows the Self, this path consists essentially of the burden of daring."
Thus, this incidental point has been introduced somewhat in accordance with the opponent's subsequent arguments; enough of this elaboration.
It is established that the three worlds are consciousness alone, by virtue of their being manifest.
Thus ends this treatise, the *Advaitabindu*.
[11] The *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.
[First Chapter] Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and vast, who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, and whose radiance flashes forth everywhere.
May the author of the commentary on the *Vārttika* to the *Munīndramata* live long—
he who is the stage-manager for the drama of the perspective establishing the existence of mental images (*sākārasiddhi*).
He possesses the glorious prowess that is difficult for all enemies to overcome, and which first humbles pride on the paths of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
This entire triple world exists as representation-only;
herein, the relative strength and weakness of its internal distinctions is now explained.
For instance, through the sequence of refuting external objects and so forth:
first of all, this external object is not [ultimately real], because it is of the nature of manifestation, and because it is necessarily perceived simultaneously [with consciousness].
Nothing else is possible here according to reasoning; even if it were possible, it would not possess the characteristics of an object of apprehension. Therefore, this is merely the mind.
The world possesses diverse forms, such as white, the *gāndhāra* note, sweetness, fragrance, delicacy, and the opposite of pleasantness, and so forth. Thus, it is said in the Sūtra:

"O Sons of the Conqueror, that which is called the triple world is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* strives through a succession of efforts to illuminate the doctrine of "possessing aspects" (*sākāravāda*) regarding external objects themselves. If one asks: "How then can this be said to be the original teaching of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)?"

Because it has been joined with other [arguments] from the perspective of formlessness (*nirākāra*), it is said that he has established [the object] as if it were established as mere existence (*sattāmātra*); however, this is not his own original invention.
Regarding this, others say: "Let white, pleasure, and so forth have the nature of being solely manifestation (*prakāśa*); [yet we maintain] their emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)."

But they are not able to transcend [this], even if the reasoning characterized by the absence of being one or many attempts to conceive of an external object that is impossible—[as stated] in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, 1.
pra. vā. 1. 1.

That [emptiness] does not fear white and other colors which possess the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the emptiness of all phenomena alone is superior, as has been proclaimed many times in the Āgamas. Also in the Vārtika:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, in that very way they fall apart."
"But the system of consciousness is merely conventional.
Regarding this, others offer this resolution: "Let the unreality of the mental aspects (*ākāra*) follow from their sublation; however, pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*) is real."

This is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*), because the cognition of that [light] cannot be erroneous, as it is a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since light has luminosity alone as its innate nature (*nija-rūpa*), that nature is not brought about by a distortion (*viplava*); therefore, the cognition of it cannot be an error. Blue, however, being a different form, may indeed be brought about by a distortion; thus, the cognition of it could be an error. Consequently, there is no room for a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) regarding blue and the like.
In the *Prakāśa*: "However, it should be understood that in all cases, what is negated are the imagined and the unreal."

Here it is considered: what is this so-called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) that is distinct from blue and the like? For if it were not distinct, there would be no removal of the fear of contradiction. Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for something distinct. First of all, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is impossible to perceive anything other than the blue object which is itself manifesting. Nor is it inference (*anumāna*), because [the manifestation] has never at any time been experienced as being perceptible.
Because the apprehension of a relation [between the word and its object] would be impossible for anyone;
furthermore,
luminosity is perceived within one's own mental continuum through inference.
What insult could be greater than this: to have as one's object of concern that which is beyond direct perception?

It is evident that this view of Śabarasvāmin has been adopted; what more need be said here? Therefore, this visible self, being unperceived as distinct from jars and other such objects, cannot be the object of the conventional usage of "existence," just like universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.
Otherwise, there would be no negation of those [universals] either.
If it is argued that [the self] is non-existent because it lacks succession and so forth due to the acceptance of its eternity, we reply:

no, for there is no absence of the pervader of validity [in the case of the self], since what is perceptible is simply not observed [therein], provided one does not disregard [the possibility of imperceptibility].

Or how could there be a negation of the qualities and actions of a horn? This [objection] is trivial. If you argue that when blue is perceived as having the nature of consciousness, the perception of both the blue and the consciousness-nature is impossible to deny, and thus non-perception is not established; then, when a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) is perceived, how can one who objects on the basis of the perception of both natures be refuted? [For they are] perceived separately.

If it is argued that the treatise on the establishment of the aspect (*sākārasiddhi*) holds that existence (*bhāva*) is common [to both], and that light and blue are spoken of as non-distinct due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), then the same would apply to qualities (*guṇa*) and substances (*dravya*). If there is such insistence on the negation of inherence (*samavāya*), is it because they are not perceived separately due to the power of ignorance, or because they simply do not exist?
Doubt is possible regarding both [theories]: that "that very thing is its perception" can be applied to objects such as karma, or even to a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass;
therefore, [doubt remains].
Furthermore,
if that form which has attained visibility is not seen separately,
how could it exist even when the blue object is scattered in a hundred ways?
Just as there are no universal properties (sāmānyaguṇa) and so forth, likewise there are none in the various [perceptions] of white and so on, which appear as partless.
Since other manifestations are likewise non-existent,
how could there be any possibility of non-sublation when white and other colors are sublated?
If the difference between the two appearances were as distinct as the difference between the self and the body, then a single cognition would perceive them as entirely separate;
for it is observed that even in the case of two objects, they are perceived by the same mind in such a manner.

For, due to the extreme similarity between a magical illusion and a ball, they are perceived as a single cognition even when occurring at different times; however, when they occur simultaneously in different locations, there is a sharp distinction in their appearance, which is inseparable from the ascertainment of their difference. Therefore, when there is a difference in location, the distinction in manifestation and its ascertainment occur without obstruction.
In a location, there is only a distinct form; there is no other form, nor another location.

If it is argued that there is indeed a difference in nature between wind and sunlight even when their location is not different, we say no; for these two arise as the forms of composite wholes (*avayavin*), and being solid and possessing resistance (*sapratigha*), they cannot occupy the same space. However, a collection of atoms (*paramāṇunikara*) does undergo intermingling.
It settles; and if that is so, why is the collection of wind, heat, and dust particles not considered to have distinct selves and distinct locations?

Therefore, just as there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too is there a difference in location (*deśa*); thus, what is called "location" is not something other than the essential form (*svarūpa*) itself. Consequently, when that [location] is non-different, the essential form itself is non-different, and this applies to manifestation (*prakāśa*) as well.
— *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*.
Likewise, if one accepts the aggregation of atoms, the same fault would apply;

or even if [the object] is gross, the fault remains exactly the same because of the distinction of spatial locations. Furthermore, pervasion here is otherwise terminated, as it appears differently in a fragmented [object].
Due to the power of that [attainment], there is the manifestation of white and other [colors], and from that, the persistence of light.

For as long as there is a spatial extent characterized by forms such as blue, so long—if there were an absence of pervasion—there would follow the consequence of a fragmented appearance of that blue and so forth, because of its being manifested separately by virtue of that [pervading entity]. Therefore, for as long as there is the manifestation of white and so on, there must exist that which is called "manifestation" itself. Consequently, even for that [manifestation] which pervades that same spatial extent, just as with the blue, when one considers it in terms of whether it is a composite whole or an atom:

Furthermore, there is no liberation from common defects; therefore, there is no persistence of anything in the negation of blue and so forth, because difference itself is absent and thus there is no difference in manifestation.

Now, just as the difference between two moments is established through a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) even though they appear to be non-different, so it is here as well. For just as the existence and non-existence of a specific effect—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—prove the difference between those two [moments], so too does the occurrence of a subverting argument prove the difference between manifestation (*prakāśa*) and blue (*nīla*). Therefore, if it is argued that manifestation, being unsublated, is indeed distinct from the blue object which is sublated, we reply: [The author] says:

Non-sublation (*abādhyatā*) is of two kinds, distinguished as *paryudāsa* (exclusion) and *prasajya* (absolute negation). Even *paryudāsa* may refer to the specific individual under discussion, as in the case of "one who is not to be touched" and so forth, which introduces another form of sublation; this is because it excludes a genus, like "non-Brahmin" [which implies a Kṣatriya].
If this so-called non-sublation is considered to be established by the force of valid cognition (*pramiti*), [then it is as follows].
Even the cognizer is capable of [establishing] a distinction within his own cognition, which is by nature diverse. Furthermore,
how could the absence of sublation— given its commonality when [the object] is non-existent— spread doubt regarding a locus, such that it might establish a distinction from that [cognition]?

For in the case of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the mere absence of the appearance of sublation constitutes non-sublation. And since that [absence of sublation] is the same even for that which has a doubtful existence—i.e., the unreal—how could it establish that the manifestation (*prakāśa*) has the nature of a distinct entity from blue and so forth?
If it is argued: "There is no doubt regarding the establishment of their distinct natures, because while blue and so forth are sublatable, the manifestation is unsublatable," we reply: not so.

Because non-contradiction consists merely in the non-appearance of a sublater, and because when there is doubt regarding existence, it is impossible to establish a distinct nature [for the object] even from a blue thing that has been sublated;
for this very reason, it was said, "of the doubt regarding the term.
However, in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), such an evasion is impossible due to the force of other sublaters. One should not harbor the hope of establishing such a fragile proof.

And it cannot be asserted here in this case in the same manner as there. For in that instance, the sequence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) may sometimes be perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in terms of gross time, as in the case of fetching honey or water; yet at other times, even if it is imperceptible in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*), its capacity remains [as established in] the *Sāmarthyāsākārasiddhiśāstra*.
If it were to undergo a change in its own nature, it would follow that it ceases to exist at the moment when all activity is exhausted, because what has already been done cannot be done again.
Thus, it is logical that this sequence of effects cannot transcend the sequence of causes; yet, such is not the case here.

Something accomplished solely through manifestation is established either through direct perception or by implication. Nor can a real distinction in essence—which is posited through the differentiation of effects by means of analytical abstraction—be truly applicable to that which appears as non-distinct all at once; such a distinction belongs only to conceptual construction, like the orange color of a lamp's light when it serves the purpose of illuminating the space where darkness has been dispelled. It is undivided...

And this reflection occurs regarding that which appears as such: there is no appearance of moments as being non-distinct, because if the manifestation of a form pervading all temporal divisions were to terminate in a single moment, it would follow that everything would be perceived simultaneously across the three times.
Nor can a difference in effects—which is not even subject to perceptual convention—bring about a difference in causes through its states of existence and non-existence, by treating them as one.

For in perception, whatever state— be it existence or non-existence— belongs to the effect at one moment, that very same state persists in the subsequent moment as well, due to the absence of any distinction. Therefore, just as its object is a producer [of cognition] by means of a form that lasts for only a single moment, so too is this sensory cognition.

The apprehender conforms to that [object] by means of that very form; however, the determinative judgment (avasāya) obscures its [the object's] operation. In this case, however, the manifestation itself is experienced as clearly non-different. Nevertheless, if one imagines a difference, what has been wronged by a thousand limiting conditions (*upādhi*)? And it has already been stated that there is no "warder-off" other than non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Therefore, this lack of sublation occurs when there is the possibility of the non-perception of the perceptible.
Being known by itself, it dissolves of its own accord and does not depend on another subsequent [cognition].
Furthermore, if there were a separate appearance of "sublation here" and "no sublation there," then both would exist;
but if there is no such appearance, how can there be a lack of proof for that which is a constituent part of it?
Even if a reason were established therein, it would be conceived as being capable [of proving the probandum];
yet surely it is not connected with the probandum, and therefore it is not competent even regarding its own form.
An object, by establishing its own nature or its cause without deviation,
does not cease to be that very nature even when it contradicts someone's argument.
But surely, for an embodied being, luminosity indeed appears within blue and other objects;
since there is no sublation regarding that alone, is it not sufficient that it is being manifested?
What is the point of stating that fire has the nature of blue light?
For this effort is not intended to express the absence of sublation for that very [fire] itself.
(Jñānaśrīmitra, *Nibandhāvali*, 372)
If the manifestation of blue were itself the manifestation, what more could be said?
Even if its manifestation were to arise from something else, it would be impossible to prevent.

If its manifestation does not come from anything else, yet its manifestation is something entirely other [than itself], then that blue object would not be manifested; for what does it have to do with the manifestation of something else?
And because the relationship itself is sublated, there is no syntactic connection (samanvaya) expressed by "his";
even if the genitive case is obtained, a confusion of forms is impossible in any way.

Therefore, its luminosity is undeniable from whatever source it may arise; and when that luminosity is not sublated, there is no result, nor is there anything at all consisting of that [luminosity] alone.
However, let that which is desired and well-established be stated with confidence;
for by this very means, even those reasons [previously cited] are cleared away as being unestablished in their substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).
If it is argued that the objects [of cognition] are established as being uncontradicted because they are produced by volition,
then that [volition] lacks validity in establishing [the object], since it is identical to the object itself.
If existence [is established] only through non-obstruction, then that [non-obstruction] is the cause for existence;
thus a circular argument (cakraka) arises, which excludes this very illusion (māyā).
Moreover, even if there is no sublation when sublation appears, it is set aside;
but in the absence of that [appearance], such a state is established as being merely a locus of doubt.
But if one relies on the property of the class (*vargadharma*), it does not transcend the circle of reasoning (*cakraka*).
Let there be a substratum; however, let the cause that effects the sublation be stated.
Or else, it has been shown that self-cognition itself does not exist separately.
Nor is it logical for you to maintain that there is even a cognition [of the object] as "self-cognition," since even when self-cognition occurs,
sublation may still assail the blue and other such objects.
If self-awareness does not belong to the blue object, why does it not manifest? To say "let it be manifested by another" is impossible in such a case.

Since the existence of another person's consciousness apart from one's own has been refuted at length elsewhere, if it is argued that [the other] does not exist because they are not "another," then let there be no "otherness. However, by the mere fact that "selfhood" is possible, the establishment of that [consciousness] through its own cognition is sufficient; therefore, no further treatise on the establishment of the forms of self-cognition alone is required.

If it is argued that there is no fault because its identity [with the universal] is merely imagined (*kalpita*) due to its nature as form (*rūpatva*), this is a deception of the ignorant. For the imagination of identity arises from appearance alone, while that appearance is produced by that very imagination; thus, mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident.
If it is argued that the imagination does not arise from mere appearance, but rather from the determination (*avasāya*) of the appearance, then that too—

The determination of the appearance (*pratibhāsāvasāya*) arises from the appearance; thus, there is a circular sequence: from the conceptualization of identity (*tādātmyakalpanā*) comes the appearance, from that comes the determination of it, and from that comes the conceptualization of it. If it is argued that the conceptualization of it does not arise from the conceptualization of identity, but rather from the identity that has been made the object of conceptualization, we say no; because that [identity] did not exist prior to the conceptualization. Otherwise, [the fault remains].

Because the status of being imagined is untenable. Furthermore, nothing that is imagined is ever observed to be employed in any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); for if it were so, its very reality would follow.
By this, the claim of its identity with the unreal is also refuted, because if it were to serve any purpose, even its unreality would be untenable.

Otherwise, since there would be no basis for negation in the case of a mere name, one might argue that it is not contradictory for something to be unreal even while it is useful and manifest, because it is sublated. To this we reply: since manifestation cannot be sublated, if the sublater does not sublate its utility in some respect as well, why must it necessarily be called a "sublater"? From where, then, could there be an identity with unreality?

Now, does it subvert the power of the object through its own capacity, rather than directly? Let it be; what is the point of insistence here? Since the subversion of the capacity is established, it remains that an unreal identity is of no use.
As for what is further said: "Consciousness itself, because its nature is luminosity, is manifesting, yet due to beginningless error—"

The claim that consciousness manifests through illusory forms such as blue and so forth due to the disturbance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like in dreams and the like—that too has been refuted by this very argument.
Since nothing called "consciousness" is perceived apart from blue and the rest, this is merely a proclamation of a theoretical construction. [To be proven—]

The example of a dream is also empty. Furthermore, since there is an absence of causal power due to its falsity, even when one intends to express a state of being such as "blue" and so forth, the meaning is merely a simultaneous appearance; thus, it has been clearly stated that there is an absence of being illuminated by that [appearance].
So, how is this?

[Objection: Is it not a transgression of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? [Reply: If it is argued that "it appears in such a way due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), and therefore it will simply be that which is manifested," then, this being the case, ignorance would be the cause [of its appearance] rather than its illuminator. Since that [consciousness], whose nature is luminosity, arises from that [ignorance] just as a lamp arises from its own cause, how could there be a destruction of its self-luminosity?

Even so, if the state of being illuminated by another were established, it would follow that even experience [would be so]; thus, nothing at all could be called self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Furthermore, because it is impossible, there is no proof of existence anywhere through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, this logic—that "self-cognition is the cessation [of the object] in relation to the cause that has the nature of illumination"—does not hold; for the same applies to blue and other objects as well. Thus, self-cognition is established.

If it is argued that because [the object] is not blue, it lacks the status of being an effect, and therefore there is merely a manifestation—whether by ignorance or by light—and that in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali* it is stated that because it is a real entity (*vastu*), it is simply produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)? That too is trivial. For even experience...

For indeed, by self-awareness alone, the object [is known]; therefore, the so-called unreality of the blue arises from its absence, and that absence follows from its unreality, as it is an obstacle to causal efficacy.

Moreover, whether blue be false or not, how can its status as an effect (*kāryatā*) be denied? For an entity is called an "effect" when it depends upon the operation of another for the completion of its own nature.
Its causality is established by the fact that it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatayā*).
"Existence or non-existence must be eternal, because [the effect] does not depend on anything other than the cause."

In this way, the lack of restriction regarding place and so forth should also be understood as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, there is nothing else that serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) apart from the dependence on another, which is established by the specific determination of place and time. Otherwise, let there be no such thing even for experience itself.
Thus, this talk of the birth of something that is merely an object of faith from such [an effect] is a non-origination of some other observed form based on what is seen.

Regarding the claim that [the opponent] "rejects" [this view], what can we say to it? By this, the argument that "even in the case of arising after non-existence (*abhūtvābhāva*), there is no status as an effect because of the absence of causal capacity (*śakti*)" is refuted, since causal capacity is established according to the sequence already stated. As for the object of mere faith (*śraddhāviṣaya*), let it be considered; for its non-perception does not invalidate the point. Even if causal capacity were absent, why would the status of being an effect—defined by its arising in dependence on others—not persist, given that the exclusion of what is not that (i.e., the definition) remains intact?

Now, if being an entity (*vastu*) is the property of an effect (*kāryatva*), and there is no such thing as being an entity without power (*śakti*), then let power also exist, since we observe "being an effect"—a property of an entity—which is pervaded by that [power]. If it is argued that "that very thing does not exist because of the absence of power," we say no, because that is unproven (*asiddhatva*). There is no doubt regarding its being an effect, just like any other effect. Therefore, if there is an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) between power and being an effect...
Let there be some capacity that is being inferred; it cannot be rejected by mere non-inference. However, in the absence of an obstruction, the status of being an effect is established.
Therefore, how can it be said that because blue is not an effect, self-awareness does not exist on account of the causes of mere manifestation?

Furthermore, if it were merely a manifestation of something by something else, this might still be expressible—like a jar and its light—on the basis of a determination of non-difference between preceding and succeeding moments, provided that no other unperceived material cause is possible. But what kind of misapprehension is this regarding that which is admitted to be unreal? For the arising of something unprecedented is not contradictory; it is simply [the case] that there is manifestation just as there is blueness. Let it be so.

Or, if there were causal efficacy in every respect, even then, given the necessity of dependence on another, there would arise the suspicion that it is revealed by something else. If, however, there were absolute independence in every respect, there would undoubtedly be an absence of self-awareness for all modes of appearance. And when sublation is observed in that case, the lack of confidence in its existence is established elsewhere as well. Alternatively, [the argument continues:]
1. *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (Pra.vā.), 1.181–2. *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*:
"If it is held that [the cognition] is distinct from the blue object because of sublation (*bādhā*), then from where does the removal of that sublation arise?"
Regarding the phrase "because of non-superimposition" (*anāropāt*): if the basis for mutual existence were something other than the result of non-sublation,
then since they say that only the sublated blue is superimposed, how could the state of being non-superimposed— which is itself the result of sublation— be capable of establishing non-sublation?
If it is argued that the very nature of consciousness is that [form], then why is it not so for that which has the nature of blue?

For just as it is said that the nature of light is indeed luminosity itself, and not something brought about by a distortion (*viplava*), so too the nature of blue is simply blueness; even if it were said that this is not brought about by a distortion of it, that would not cause one's face to turn away [in objection].

Furthermore, the operation of logic does not function through such a division, whereby one thing would be to be accepted (*upādeya*) and another to be rejected (*heya*). Now, there is no establishment of "blue" without manifestation (*prakāśa*), nor is there an establishment of manifestation without "blue. If it is argued that [manifestation] exists in the case of yellow, let it be so; however, it is not a property (*dharma*) of blue. If it is argued that this is because of the identity of the term "manifestation," then [we reply]: with respect to the manifestation of the property of yellow, even that which is devoid of [the manifestation of] blue [is established].
The persistence of blue is the object of negation;
since it exists precisely as non-superimposed, its very nature is that [persistence]. Thus, this conceptualization is not restricted solely to manifestation.

[The opponent replies: "There is confidence [in their difference] due to the absence of sublation. [The author rejoins: "In that case, let the difference between the two be established without effort, since they are mutually exclusive.

We recall the example of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), for it is impossible to point to a cloth and water [as a counter-example]. You yourselves are the authority here, given that no contradictory properties—characterized by persistence and displacement—have been perceived in the designated substrata."

Enough, then, with this persistence! For one who is to be trusted that "its form is precisely that," and who is focused solely on conceptual construction—if it appears in such a way [to him], why should it not be so?
The reality of the blue object consists merely in its manifestation as its own nature; its only further "offense" is the establishment of its existence.

Moreover, this is a novel means for the removal of sublation: that its very essence is its reality. For even that which is subject to sublation—such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the universal (*sāmānya*), and so forth—is likewise [established].

Whatever appears or is conceptualized in whatever form, that very form is its reality according to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Whether that [reality] be existent or otherwise, there is room for sublation (*bādhā*) in both cases; therefore, this applies to the blue or to the light. If, at most, there is a distinction in the occurrence of defects such as non-establishment (*asiddhi*) through a division [of the object], yet it is not that very [form] itself [which is sublated].

Considering it to be reality (*tattva*): furthermore, that which is superimposed and merely imagined is what is sublated; they say that which possesses manifestation is the sublated, while the unreal is the real (*tattva*). Therefore, [reality] must reside solely in the imagined. Otherwise, how could it not be restricted exclusively to the visible (*dṛśya*)? (Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Nibandhāvalī*, 11)

The state of being superimposed (āropitatva) is merely conventionally designated as such in relation to that which is sublated, like water [in a mirage]. However, they designate even that which is manifest, though sublated and false, as [superimposed], like a double moon. Therefore, if you must say that even the visible is superimposed, let it be so said. But how can it be that the visible itself is superimposed? Consequently, it is not a mere conceptual construction (kalpita) that is superimposed.

It is established by way of exclusion as being other than that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is only through valid cognition that establishment or sublation (*bādhā*) deserves to be determined; however, the arousal of sublation or establishment does not consist merely in the fact that "this is its very reality.
Thus, even when this distinction is made, blue and so forth are conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), because although they are perceived, they are subject to sublation.

Because [the latter] is a mere mental construction (*mānatvāt*). However, consciousness whose very body is light, appearing as blue and so forth, is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it cannot be sublated and because it possesses powers established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it appears as if grasped in the palm of one's hand. For if light were distinct from the blue, the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*)—namely, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—regarding the blue would not be set aside merely by a lack of desire; this has been stated previously.

Furthermore, what kind of sublation could there be for that which is intended to be manifest, simply because it does not manifest? Likewise, power (*śakti*) also has only form as its object, as will be explained immediately thereafter.
Moreover, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), like that between "produced" and "impermanent," appears to be brought about by mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā-mātra*), and not directly.

It is like a pair of *yamalaka* fruits, or like two moons. And when the substratum (*dharmin*) appears as distinct, it is possible to ascertain that "this property is possible here, and that one is not possible here. This is because, specifically in the case of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it is only a real property (*vastudharma*) that can be introduced [as the probans] through its contrapositive. Furthermore, every means of establishing difference is merely a means of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), for nowhere is there any [establishment of difference] without the association of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*).
Because their difference is unestablished. Otherwise, there would be no such thing as non-difference; nor can two contradictory properties be differentiated by mere conceptual construction alone.

Furthermore, they must be understood as having distinct substrates through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for if they were perceived as being without a substrate or as having the same substrate, there would be no operation of either of the two means of knowledge, nor would there be the establishment of contradiction. And if those two are established as having different substrates, what else remains?
The endeavor to establish a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*):

for this very reason, the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is based on cognition, which is the determination (*nirṇaya*). In that regard, the establishment of a difference in properties occurs in some cases through a difference in location, as with a physical sphere (*golaka*), and in other cases through a difference in time. It is with reference to this that it is said: "For this very reason, there is a difference in substance (*vastubheda*) between those two states."

Regarding the term "to be determined" (*niśceya*): for even there, one cannot point out that "this is the state of being in the granary" and "this is the state of being in the field. Since such a distinction cannot be demonstrated through the difference in time, the distinction must be shown through performance and non-performance of an action.
And since the establishment of the distinction is concluded by that much alone, the presentation of "action" and "non-action" serves merely as a means for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Where...

However, there is no delineation of difference by way of space and time; in that case, the only recourse is either a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*) or a difference in the sense faculties (*indriya*).

This is like the color, taste, and so forth of a beverage, or like the Cārvāka’s own admission regarding the intellect and the body. For he [the Cārvāka] must explain by what form the conceptualization of mountains and such differs from the body—which possesses the shape of hands, feet, and so on—if it were not cited as an example; otherwise, in what form would it possess the nature of being a conceptualization of mountains and the like?

How could the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* clarify this? However, where there is not even a trace of a difference in appearance, and [the object] is other than the form of conceptual construction, there is indeed an ontological non-difference, just as in the case of a blue lotus and so forth.
If sensation were non-distinct and thus a unity, then that [object] would indeed be established as possessing distinction;
for how could difference and non-difference have a basis if there is no means of proof?
This is an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).

Therefore, the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by sublation and non-sublation does not suffice for the linguistic usage of difference regarding a substratum (*dharmin*) without a difference in appearance. Merely establishing difference—because it takes the form of establishing existence—is not subject to the threefold fault.
It falls into the fallacy of infinite regress (*jāti*). As for what is also said:

"Whatever is neither one nor many in a certain form does not exist in that form, just as suffering [does not exist] in the form of pleasure; and since consciousness is neither one nor many in the form of blue and so forth, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*),"—that too is refuted by this very [argument] and is merely a matter of personal satisfaction. For it is not understood, or rather, it does not cognize.

The nature of consciousness is intended to be based on its activity (*vyāpāra*), since it is denied in other cases; however, its essential nature is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*). And that luminosity does not exist by way of that [activity]—thus, what is intended is not merely the denial of identity with it, but rather that it exists precisely by its own nature.

By this, it is also implied that, as in that case, no fault arises; otherwise, the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would not be achieved, because there would be the unwanted consequence of [the reason] being excluded even in the case of the son of a barren woman merely by way of exclusion. Therefore, since the distinction is established solely through the presence and absence of sublation (*bādhā*), no additional meaning is introduced beyond that; thus, this point is already covered by that very [argument]. Nevertheless, something further is said here regarding the form (*ākāra*).

In the context of proving a manifestation that is distinct [from the object], either manifestation must be established by inference while it is not appearing at all, or it must be established as something distinct from the form while it is indeed appearing. In either case, what occasion is there for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) within the section concerning the proof of a positive entity (*vidhisādhana*)? Even if it exists with a nature imparted by that [manifestation], if [it does not exist] in its own nature...
There would be no cessation of the suspicion of non-existence, as in the case of a horn; how, then, could the establishment of difference [between existence and non-existence] be achieved?

If, on the other hand, the non-existence of those two is intended to be of the very nature of another positive entity (*bhāvāntara-svabhāva*), then a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*) alone should be employed, because the dispute concerns a positive object. However, if someone were to doubt that [the effect] might still occur even in the absence of that [cause], [then a different argument is required].

In some cases, because another [instance] is non-existent, how can there be an example, or how can there be the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), given the absence of any other means of proof? Or, if that were the means of proof, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
— *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

And if it is argued that "light exists as having the nature of light," then at the time of the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), there is no avoidance of the objection regarding the irrelevant.

For the dispute is not over unity and plurality in terms of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); rather, it concerns whether there is difference or non-difference with respect to its forms (*ākāra*). Furthermore, how can the establishment of existence (*sattva*) belong to one who disputes unity and plurality? In that case, blue and so forth would simply be non-existent due to the absence of causal capacity (*śakti*).
Even if there were unity, what is the point of the effort to propose that? For even in its absence, existence is established through the power of exclusion (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
Otherwise, how could one establish it when there is doubt regarding it? And that [power] will be considered later.

Now, if "by that" means "the state of being one or many," that is, the state of being one or many by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then existence would be established by that very [nature]. Thus it is said:

If it is asked: "What then is its nature, by virtue of which there is a connection with both unity and multiplicity?"—if it is replied that "it is this very thing which is fit to be pointed out by the forefinger," then [the objection remains]: "This is not blue; therefore, cognition is neither one nor many"—thus this argument floats away.
If, on the other hand, it is something else, that is not established. Or, if it were established, what would be the use of this [forefinger]? And that same criticism remains in that state.
For a dispute occurs only regarding what is unestablished; once that [subject] is established, there is no occasion for the question of whether it exists even in the form of another.

Now, this subject (*dharmin*), which is manifestation itself, is indeed established; and when its non-existence in the form of blue and so forth is established, [its existence in its own nature] is obtained by implication.

If you argue: "There is indeed a difference, and since what is intended is established by that much alone, there is no need to conform to [the requirements of] a positive injunction; therefore, it is precisely the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) that is relevant to the present context," then this is a great display of cleverness! However, if even non-existence (*avidyā*), like blue and other objects, is a manifestation, yet it is non-existent even in its own form, then how can a difference be established? Surely, one might say, "there is no suspicion of its being non-existent because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*)."

Because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because there can be no error regarding its own nature (*svabhāva*). For dispute exists only regarding difference (*bheda*). If that is so, how could there be a sublation (*bādhā*) even of blue, given such an establishment? It has already been stated in passages such as "the very nature of manifestation is manifestation. And it is possible to say that "the very nature of the manifestation of blue is the manifestation of blue," and so forth. Therefore, even if difference is rejected...

Even if one’s own experience were to establish the existence of manifestation by leaving no room for sublation, what does that matter? Likewise, even if it lacks such power, what does that matter? For even in that case, since there is no relinquishing of the hand [of inquiry], difference remains unestablished because of the presence of "blueness" (i.e., the object). Now, if it is argued that manifestation is established as ultimately real for the opponent, yet the dispute concerns only its difference, then manifestation is indeed existent.

The probandum is not established by [the reason] "not having the nature of blue. In that case, your cleverness consists merely in the exhaustion of all possible means and the finality of logic. This deserves to be treated with ease according to the logic of establishing the selflessness of a jar for one who maintains a doctrine of self. Furthermore, in this proof, the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is the difference between the two aspects of experience which appear as non-different; the reason is the absence of being one or many in that form. And it is not as has been stated—

The positive concomitance with the probandum can be shown in the example; for even there, a luminosity distinct from the forms of suffering and so forth is unestablished. Even if it were established, one could not say "as the known by the unknown"; rather, it is logical that the experience of suffering possesses the form of suffering and so forth.
1. "Even in the case of resolve (*adhimokṣa*)," it says in the *Mātṛkā*.
This refers to the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*;
for otherwise, if a manifestation (*prakāśa*) apprehended by one form were to have its non-existence revealed by another form, it would be [only] in relation to that [other form].

There would be a distinction; and consequently, at the time of the probandum (*sādhya*), a distinction would be established because the blue form is experienced as distinct from the yellow. Therefore, if a distinction dependent upon self-luminosity cannot be demonstrated in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), how will it exist in the probandum either, given the total absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?

If it is argued that "that which is neither one nor many" is stated here as a general positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that is incorrect. For, even if not explicitly stated, the probandum (*sādhya*) is considered to be pervaded by the reason according to the [proponent's] intention, just as in the case of the argument for the existence of the self (*ātman*).

This point is also the same as in the proof of the eyes and other faculties being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), and so forth. Alternatively, [the formulation is]: "Whatever is neither one nor many..."

In this context, having raised the alternative as to whether what is intended by "that which appears as non-different" is "that by which [something] is manifested," or "in a general sense," [the response is:
if it refers to a particular, there is a lack of concomitance; if it refers to a generality, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

This is because, just as in the case of pleasure and pain, the experiences of blue and yellow are not of each other's nature; thus, through their existence in that [non-identical] form, a difference is established.

However, there is no impairment for perception, which grasps [objects] as non-different, in either case. The rest is as in our *Bṛhadīśvaravāda*. Furthermore, when the application of the reason is made on the basis of the position that "illumination (*prakāśa*) is neither one nor many, like blue and so forth," then what is this so-called "illumination"? Is it the act of illuminating (*prakāśana*), or that which "is illuminated" (*prakāśate*)? Or is it something else entirely, denoted by the word "illumination," which performs such functions as "illuminating" and so forth?
Is it because it has been refuted by being established in relation to that?
In the first case, regarding blue, yellow, and so forth as they appear, what is called "manifestation" is merely a property (*dharma*);
even though it appears as if distinct by excluding other differences, it remains indifferent to the dismantling of the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) in conceptual cognition.

Since it is capable of abiding [within itself], how can there be an establishment of difference in reality? For properties (dharmas) have no existence anywhere apart from the nature of the substratum (dharmin), just like qualities (guṇas), actions (karmas), and so forth. On the other hand, in the view that the agent is the means of accomplishment, it is blue and the like alone that manifest; therefore, as before, that very [blue] is empty of that form.

Furthermore, regarding the position that [the object] is a different entity (*arthāntara*), if the term "it manifests" (*prakāśate*) is taken as a positive concomitant (*sānvaya*), then even though that which is distinct from blue and so forth—which is sublated by the non-perception of the perceptible—is non-existent in that nature, there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*). Even in the position of total destruction without residue (*niranvayanāśa*), there is no establishment by means of valid cognition; and although the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) might be avoided by relying on a relationship of probandum and probans between two mere exclusions (*vyavacchedamātra*), it is still not [the case].

This is relevant to the present context. Now, this very manifest [object] that is cognized is the subject (*dharmin*). But surely, "cognized" means appearing, and that is precisely the blue itself; there is nothing whatsoever distinct from it.
If you ask: "Since this effort is directed precisely toward proving its distinction [from the cognition], why was that [distinction] not sought at the very outset?"

Whatever may be your objective, the substratum of that proof must be shown to have an established nature, provided that what is called "light" is accepted as a real entity (*vastu*) serving as the locus (*dharmin*). However, if— out of deference to the view that both the probandum and the proof consist merely of exclusions (*vyavaccheda*)— it is considered a non-entity...

Alternatively, if the subject (*dharmin*) is an entity whose ontological status is doubtful, then this rule does not apply; in that case, the establishment of the intended point is far off. Now, if—conforming to the establishment of the intended point—the subject is "manifestation" as an actual entity, then, being accepted as having a settled nature, it would necessarily be blue itself. In that case, it follows that "form is empty of the nature of form," yet even so, there is no establishment of the intended point. Nor can it be established by another [property] through its emptiness of that [blue].

The term "stability" (sthiti) refers to the expectation that there is no [intrinsic] form. This is so that there may not be the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—namely, that one thing is empty of another because it has a different nature; for even by that much, the purpose of the phrase "by that" (*tena*) is fulfilled.

Alternatively, according to the system that maintains the existence of forms (*sākāravāda*), it is a negation of the external object as it is conceptually determined, just as there is an emptiness of the form of two moons in the case of two moons seen by one with cataracts.

This [is the case], because negation occurs only with respect to that which has been superimposed everywhere, and for ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), there is always only a superimposition of externality upon their own internal form; otherwise, reality would be lost. Therefore, the intended proof is not established regarding the subject (*dharmin*) "blue. Now, what is the use of this restriction to a particular? "Luminosity" (*prakāśa*) is considered the subject in a general sense. And since the probandum is excluded by a restriction to a particular, the means of proof—
Because it would entail the consequence that there is an obstruction to the path. Furthermore, no one employs a means of proof without intending the probandum (*sādhya*).

Nor is a subject (*dharmin*) ever established as one from which the probandum has been excluded, like something already proven. Therefore, there is no emphasis on being restricted to a particular [instance].
Or, let there even be such restriction.
"This very one before us is indeed named 'Manifestation' (prakāśa), concerning whose distinction from Nīla you were in doubt;

let there be an end to this curiosity. Furthermore, the relationship between property and property-bearer has been observed through a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), just as in the case of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical reason:
one exclusion is the property-bearer, while otherwise their coexistence or distinction is the probandum; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. This too is inconsistent.
For the establishment of the probandum and the probans is based merely on their exclusion [from others];
however, it is the form of the property (*dharma*) as perceived through its distinction that is actually employed.

For since it is impossible to understand the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) without a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), the establishment of the reality of the probandum and the probans—which exist as floating forms—is based solely on their being grounded in the essential nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpa*). It is not, however, based on the mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) while the nature of the property (*dharma*) remains in a floating state; for this [reality] is not perceived through words such as "tree" unless the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is presented as "this is so. Exclusion...

Difference, however, is required for the sake of the conventional usage of difference, not for the sake of the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*); for if it were perceived as residing in a specific individual (*vyakti*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the substratum itself remains unestablished. Just as, even when a particular characterized by branches and so forth—a sound such as "pot" which is perceivable by the ear—is recognized as the substratum, there is no contradiction; thus, when there is doubt regarding the momentariness of a tree or similar matters, one proceeds according to the means of proof (*sādhana*). So too [in the present case].
There is no room for this in the present context. For, in the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*,
it is stated that as soon as this subject (*dharmin*), which is capable of being pointed out by the gesture of the index finger, is presented as blue, by that much alone—

Because the doubt regarding difference has been eliminated, there is no occasion for a formal proof (*sādhana*); for without that blue form, it is impossible for the manifestation (*prakāśa*) to be established as residing in a specific form. Indeed, the attainment of its own nature occurs when the mere exclusion of non-manifestation (*aprakāśavyāvṛtti*) is established in a particular instance, just like the exclusion of the non-verbal (*aśabdavyāvṛtti*), and not through the exclusion of each individual [non-blue]. Therefore, due to the presence of the suspicion of non-existence, a real property (*vastusaddharma*) is not established. Consequently...

When there is a requirement for a real entity (*vastu*), since every universal possesses the nature of a real entity precisely by way of its particular form (*viśeṣarūpa*) through its causal efficiency (*arthakāritva*), the process of investigating difference and non-difference culminates in the presentation of the blue subject (*dharmin*) itself; however, its momentariness and other such attributes would remain objects of doubt,
as they have not yet been excluded.

Furthermore, in this case, since the proponent himself has already demonstrated that this very subject (*dharmī*) appears as having the form of blue, what is there left for the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*) to ascertain? Or, is it not a fault if the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) is made later? It is indeed a fault; for even if it is stated later that "the manifestation is neither one nor many with the blue," the conclusion remains fixed precisely upon the nature of the blue, such that [one must still ask] "what is this manifestation? Thus, the fault persists.

Because it is impossible to demonstrate another distinction, and because, in the absence of a perceived particularity (*viśeṣa*), the substratum (*dharmin*)—which is of the nature of existence—cannot be established. And although, in the case of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), both [the property and the substratum] are entities excluded from what is not that nature, nevertheless, this [reason] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is not merely that; rather, it is also this [substratum]. Therefore, it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) by virtue of its commonality with the example, and not as the form of the substratum itself. Such is this [point].
Because it must be relied upon for the sake of engagement or withdrawal precisely in its unique form;

for this very reason, even regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the desire for further particulars is eliminated by means of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Let it not be that there is non-existence due to being devoid of all individuals; ultimately, even in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no absence of individuals because of its definition. These same [arguments] apply to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth as well.

[The following are] the divisions. However, by relying upon an imagined distinction (*kālpanika-bheda*), there exists the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) even when there is a real (*tattvataḥ*) exclusion of difference. Likewise, if the status of being a substratum (*dharmibhāva*) were also to exist through an imagined distinction, let it be; for if one accepts that its reality (*vastutva*) consists in that very form, what effort would there be to deny it? Or how could another [opponent] take it seriously, since [the opponent's position] is established merely by defining the nature of the substratum?

Is it refuted? Precisely for this reason, just as there is an effort toward the probandum (sādhya) for that person, so too for another who seeks the same probandum, there is likewise a search for the nature of the property (dharma). This [search] does not indicate a lack of discernment on the part of one who desires the production [of the result], just as one who is noble remains indifferent to it. Therefore, enough with that inference which is frustrated merely by the determination of the specific nature of the subject (dharmin) of the probandum.
Therefore, it is said:
"When the locus (dharmin) is established, a property (dharma) that is in doubt deserves to be proven;
but when the specific nature of the property is already settled, the [proponent] is defeated."
Even the rebuttal regarding the distinction established by convention applies to the subject (*dharmin*).
For if the subject is one whose specific characteristics are established by valid cognition (*pramā*), then such [conventional] impossibility constitutes a fault. (382)
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is stated: "Even though [the object] is established through inference, there is still a dependence on the knower of the relationship (*saṃbandhavid*)."
The form is accordingly conceived as distinguished in accordance with that [perception].

Likewise, even if [the object] were possible, since it is impossible to say that "this manifestation is also thus," the case remains as before: there is a sublation of what was accepted regarding the subject (dharmin) blue; nothing else is established, and what is accepted as real is in vain.
Just as it has been stated regarding the proof of the peacock's cry that there is no other means [of proof] than the very existence of its form; so too [is it here].

Furthermore, in the formulation beginning with "in whatever form," if the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) were not "by means of the cognition of blue and so forth, it is neither one nor many," then what fault would there be? Consequently, it is indeed possible to state it thus:
"In whatever form a thing is neither one nor many, in that form it is non-existent."
Just as pleasure is obscured by pain, so too is it obscured by darkness.
Just as in the case of blue, who can prevent the absence of gross and atomic forms from light as well, which pervades that same extent of space?
Therefore, blue exists, but not in the form of light; consequently, the establishment of a distinct, insentient form [for the object] follows. However, the nature of light is unreal (*alīka*).
And this is logical:
In some place, there is a certain illumination resembling a flash of lightning;
in relation to that, external light is considered stable, and therefore its unreality [is established] within that illumination.
Just as the capacity of cognition is held to exist for the production of a false blue,
so too is the capacity held to exist externally for the production of a false awareness.
It cannot be said that "this is not desired by you either," because my lack of desire for this arose from not knowing such a proof.
Nor is pure illumination ever perceived by anyone;
even pleasure and the like have the form of an object to be known, and therefore the intellect is superior to that.
The cognition of a reflection and so forth is pleasant even for one who is cold;
even when there is a reflection, the reflection appears as non-different from the cold object itself.

Is it not the case that the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* [is relevant here], and that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) lacks the power to apply to that [position]? If that were so, then suffering (*duḥkha*) would likewise be of the nature of luminosity itself, and thus could never be abandoned. Furthermore, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of reviving the [reality of] the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth.

Everything from the very beginning is shattered; therefore, no establishment of difference occurs within the appearance of non-difference. For this very reason, it has been stated that every cause of difference is merely a means for conventional usage.
As for those who say: "The subject (dharmin) appearing as duality, because it is erroneous, must necessarily be connected with reality, like the moon-image seen by one with ophthalmia..."

The hope that the appearance of duality is as it is perceived—that even for them, the manifestation of what is non-existent is an error—is thus refuted; and this very point also refutes the claim that the so-called "illusion" (*māyā*) is unreal, and so forth. Furthermore, no so-called "magician" is established as being distinct from the form of self-luminous cognition. And one cognition is held to arise from another cognition.
Thus [it is said].
