As for those who claim that difference exists by way of having both inclusive (anuvṛtta) and exclusive (vyāvṛtta) forms, for them too this is a mere conceptual construction; for, as was already largely stated in the discussion on cloth and water, there is no establishment of such a thing through any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), just as there is none for a universal (sāmānya). Therefore, this [is the case]:
The cognition "the light is blue" is based on distinct limiting adjuncts (upādhi), because it is a qualified cognition, just like the cognition of one who wears earrings.

This is the conclusion of the argument. Therefore, regarding the various manifestations such as blue, yellow, and so forth—which arise from their respective immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—that which is called "manifestation" has a nature established merely through the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*); it is a mere conceptualized property (*dharmamātra*).
That this remains unimpaired even when those [objects] are absent is a most gross delusion.

Now, if the relationship between the property and the substratum (dharma-dharmin-bhāva) is established as being reversed, even in that case there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for there exists only a misconception (viparyaya).
The distinction is this: the substratum is that which possesses direct experience, while the property is that which is conceptualized as genus and so forth.
But why is the reverse desired for faith and the blue?

It is only because this world, weak in discernment, relies upon mere positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to posit a difference, that it engages in conventional usage regarding difference and the reversal of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*), as in the case of clay and its particular forms; therefore, one should not be dogmatic about this. Furthermore, it is impossible to accept these two as having separate natures.
If blue and so forth are luminous, what need have you for another luminosity?

Or if blue and so forth are non-luminous, what need have you for another luminosity? Indeed, that which is not luminous by itself does not become luminous through another—this is because [the latter] is the very nature of the former, and so on. (From *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*)

Because of the [scriptural] statement. Now, if you think that this is not so because there is no other nature for that which conceives itself as unreal (*alīka*), then, precisely because it lacks any other nature, its nature must be mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*); what, then, is the use of another luminosity? To say that "that unreal thing appears as mounted upon [luminosity]" is equivalent to the doctrine of a self (*ātman*) that is the substratum of cognition and so forth. However, this is the distinction: for the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the self— [...is established... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly).

If it is argued that its existence as luminosity is not contradictory and thus requires another blow [of an external object], then even the act of utterance is not possible for that whose very nature is light; so what is the use of these fruitless and heavy efforts? Let there be no exclusion of self-luminosity in the case of unreality. Therefore, what offense has been committed by the external object in making manifest that which is not of the nature of the Self?
If its capacity were directed toward the false, how could it cause the real thing to cease? Therefore, Dharmottara’s desire is established without any obstacle.
If this [cognition] flashes forth as requiring assistance precisely with respect to the object,
then it is fitting that the object alone be the recipient of the conceptualization of identity.
And when there is the manifestation of a false distinction, the form does not reside [in the object] as its locus;
likewise, when an external distinction is revealed, what is the use of a [mental] form?
It is maintained that there is no single state of security or vulnerability for both the external and the other [the internal];
let sublation belong only to the external—how then could unreality [belong to both]?
Let there be an obstruction caused by the intellect, as if it were the establishment of an external object; yet this has been observed repeatedly as being consistent with reason.
Just as those with perfected intellects do not perceive external objects as they truly exist,
so too there is no sublation, nor does it destroy their own [realization], even though [the object] appears externally.
This is an intermediate verse.

Furthermore, since that which is false has the nature of non-existence, it possesses no causal capacity whatsoever; thus, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), which depends upon being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), collapses even if it was established with effort. This sequence is accepted for the purpose of introducing the system of Idealism (*vijñānanaya*). And therefore, it is as follows:

Furthermore, there is a unique insistence on establishing the existence of duality in the *Pramāṇavārttika*. Therefore, if it is maintained that cognition is in fact formless (*nirākāra*) in reality, let the establishment of the causality of forms be set aside for now; since the external object possessing form cannot be denied because it is perceived, how can the proof of "Cognition-Only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) be established? Thus, the attempt to prove that forms are unreal is like raising a weapon for one's own destruction.
The effort [to prove] the object has thus been established. However, when the form is undivided, the determination that "blue was seen, not yellow" arises from the specific nature of the form itself;

thus, according to the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, by the power of this proof, even in the absence of an external object, the conventional establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyavasthā*) is nonetheless achieved on the basis of mental imputation (*ābhimānikī*).

Therefore, for one who has begun this investigation, because the object of apprehension lacks any defining characteristic, its establishment as mere self-awareness is unimpeded. For this very reason, at the conclusion [of that investigation], it is said:
"This nature of his consists of blue and so forth, and that is experience."

One might look well-spoken saying such things as [Pramāṇavārttika 2.328]. Now, if your intention is that even so, you will later refute the reality of the external form— whether as a pervader or otherwise— and establish mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*), then why, from the very beginning, have you been protecting this demon of form?

By means of this continuous argumentation? Just as it is your own view that this cognition is formless while the external correspondence possesses form, so too, having introduced the non-perception of such a distinction, let there be the establishment of the result [of the proof]. Therefore, whence the consideration of the definition of the apprehended object (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*)?

Nor should two reasons be stated for the simultaneous perception with that which is manifesting, because of the fault [that would arise] by way of proving the existence of forms; for there is no pervasion.
And because attainment necessarily requires [an object], it is well established according to the intention of Dharmottara.
Therefore,
we see that these very three modes are the direct proof of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) for the Master in all cases.

The intent of the *samarthanā* (justification) is precisely this; however, regarding the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) as formulated by the former masters, it is merely an expression of agreement, because there is no refutation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) here as there was [previously] for gross objects. Therefore, if there is a lack of attention toward the rebuttal of atoms in the *Dharmottara*, we observe that the effort [to refute them] is absent primarily due to the statement, "Their form is neither one nor many," and thus [the refutation] is already established. Consequently, everything is in disorder.

The Master’s view is not intended here; nor is there any harm in that, provided it possesses even a trace of logic. Something has already been said on this point. Furthermore, do not think that because the external is known through manifestation it is unreal—by this very means, the status of the grasped and the grasper is presented in another way. And since [the external] would otherwise result in non-manifestation, self-luminosity finds its scope; so what [is the need for] manifestation?

[How could they exist] otherwise? Therefore, it is established that color, sound, and so forth are of the nature of cognition by virtue of being self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*), since we have already demonstrated in the refutation of external objects that their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) [is established]. Here too, one should not be afraid of this "terror for children"—namely, that mere self-cognition is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and that [self-cognition] as a reality (*tāttvika*) is unestablished (*asiddha*)—because a conceptualized [self-cognition] is untenable, and only the real [self-cognition] is [intended].
Since this has been established, there is no room for the two-fold dilemma.

For this very reason, when one proves that consciousness is unreal because it does not exceed its own form (*ākāra*), neither the charge of an unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) nor the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) can be leveled. Furthermore, as it is stated by way of the contrapositive (*viparyaya*): "Whatever form is unsublatable for something, that is its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*); for example..."

The argument that "the nature of all phenomena is awakening, and the indestructible form of the essence of awakening is existence; therefore, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason)"—that too is refuted by this very [point]: because a distinct subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished, and because blue is subject to sublation. —From the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, verse 386.
Since there is no functioning of cognitions apart from the distinction of their forms, victory belongs to the powerful Madhyamaka school which refutes that [distinction];
otherwise, this non-dual [reality] remains beyond reproach.
But for one who maintains that the mind is formless, what room is there for such diversity?
The first chapter, the Refutation of the Formless [Cognition], in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.
1. Tattvārthā-vibhaṅga-pañjikā, folio 529 [Second Chapter]: If, then, the mind that is devoid of form does not exist in reality, how can there be an establishment of affliction and purification?

There is indeed a total disruption; for the entire collection of forms is overwhelmed by delusion due to the apprehension of that which is not [the object] as being that [object]. Saṃsāra is precisely this delusion. When the mass of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) arising from it is completely eradicated, the affliction disappears, and what remains is the stainless, mere luminosity devoid of objective appearance—this is Nirvāṇa. Thus, there is no contradiction. Otherwise, however, [it would be so].
If the cognition possessing aspects were sublated, purification would be untenable;
if it were not sublated, however, one would fall into the undesirable position of establishing defilement [as real].
For if there were cognition of one's own nature as it truly is through those very manifestations, then error would be absolutely non-existent.

Consequently, all sentient beings would be eternally liberated and eternally perfectly awakened Buddhas. If it is argued that conceptual cognition is an error because it determines an object in its own manifestation despite the object being non-existent, then how is that [object] determined by it?

That object would not be manifest; or, if it were being manifested, how could it not be manifest within that [cognition]? If, on the other hand, it is indeed manifested, then it follows that the object is identical with it. Furthermore, if the object were non-existent, that [cognition] would not occur. There would be absolute certainty [in such cases] as: "Māndhātṛ existed," "Śaṅkha will exist," "The self exists," and "Sound is eternal. And [there would be certainty] regarding the word "cow" [as being the object itself].

Furthermore, it would manifest through its own distinct characteristic (svalakṣaṇa); and since a linguistic convention (saṃketa) is impossible with respect to a particular characteristic, that cognition would not be conceptual at all.
Therefore, the cognition of a cow arises through the universal "cowness" (gotva), which is common to all individual cows, by means of a false, verbalized distortion (viplava).

It must be accepted that its manifestation as "it appears" is the determination of the object as a cow; for in this way, these faults would not arise, since there is a mistaken determination of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) even though it does not appear [in the cognition]. And just as the unreal universal "cowness" has a manifestation and identity with the cognition of a cow, and because it is non-distinct from that [cognition], it possesses reality or non-superimposedness, so too is it with blue and the rest.

In the case of unrealities such as blue and so forth, their identity with manifestation is established simply by the establishment of their manifestation; for there is no contradiction between unreality and non-unreality residing in a single entity that possesses multiple forms. Furthermore, if "identity" alone were the reason when "being real" and "not being superimposed" are the properties to be proven, then it would be inconclusive due to [the presence of] "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like. If, however, "unsuperimposed identity" is the reason, then it is unestablished (*asiddha*).
To this it is replied: If the apprehension of something as what it is not— namely, error— is accepted by everyone,
then it is not tenable that this [apprehension] occurs even with respect to a false form, as if it were real.
1. *Tattvasaṃgrahapañjikā*, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, and Maṇimālā, p.

29: In common worldly usage, it is said that "the apprehension of water in a mirage is an error," and in the treatises, it is stated in many ways that "inference is erroneous because it proceeds by determining an object (*artha*) within its own appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), which is not the actual object. Thus, what is called "apprehending that in what is not that" (*atasmiṃstadgraha*) is...

Error has been understood. If it is untenable in the theory of "cognition with form" (*sākāravāda*), then consider how it could be tenable if the form were merely false (*alīka*). For cognition indeed arises with some form, whether real or false; as for the superimposition of an external object upon that form, it might be produced by that [cognition] itself or by something else. If it were produced by that [cognition] itself, then at that very moment, another operation would be required...
How then can there be a superimposition [of that form] upon it? And if it were non-existent at another time, whose operation would it be?

In the second case, even another cognition does not perform any action whatsoever toward an external object through any other operation, except by way of an origination associated with the grasping of its own form. Thus, even when this [subsequent cognition] makes the form of the earlier cognition its object, it is not [an external object].

It does not touch upon another operation that merely mimics a fraction of its form, because even the form of the word is included within its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, if there were another operation for the sake of external superimposition (*āropa*) that did not consist of a form, one would have to state it as a means (*sādhana*) even in the case of inference. If it is argued that this is a means for comprehension (*adhigati*) and not for superimposition—no, for [this applies] to the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-nirbhāsa*).

Since this is rejected in the case of inference (*anumāna*), it is merely a superimposition (*āropa*). If you argue that "superimposition" means having an unreal object, then surely the apprehension of form itself would be the accomplishment of inference. Therefore, "superimposition," "ascertainment" (*avasāya*), and "conceit" (*abhimāna*) are synonymous. The distinction between them, however, lies in their correspondence or lack thereof; for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It might be so.

Therefore, there is no operation of cognition other than its own form; and if that external object being superimposed appears in the intellect in its own nature, then this is merely a true perception—what, then, would be the purpose of the superimposition? Furthermore, if it were to appear [as such], there would be a second form.

There would be the consequence [of it being] a feeling (*vedanā*). If it is argued that its manifestation is nothing other than the manifestation of that [object's] form—no, because that [form] is the object of superimposition (*āropa*).

For the manifestation of a mirage is not itself the manifestation of water, even though they are unified with it. If it is asked, "What is the meaning of this 'unification' (*ekīkaraṇa*)?"—if it means being the cause for the attainment of oneness, then there would never be a state of oneness between the superimposed and the object.

From existence, non-existence itself [cannot arise]. For there is no cause whatsoever for a rabbit’s horn. Nor is it tenable for a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) to claim that what was previously manifold attains oneness; there might merely be the arising of a different entity, but even that is not within the range of perception, except as an object of superimposition (*āropa*). And even by that much, nothing happens to the object—so how could there be its superimposition? Or, if there is a single cognition...

What is meant by "unification"? Even so, it cannot belong to two things, because there is no experience of them as healthy (or distinct). Nor is superimposition merely the cognition of two things, like blue and yellow; and the claim that they are perceived as one due to the absence of even a trace of awareness of the object to be superimposed must also be rejected. For if an external object were to manifest, it would be logical for it to be perceived either as one or many, or as existent or non-existent.

If it is argued that this cognition is a "single cognition" because it occurs through the concealment of the object's nature in all its aspects, then, if its nature is concealed, it would not appear at all. If it is argued that this is not so because some part of it does appear— no, for [this contradicts] the *Niraṃśasākārasiddhiśāstra*.
Regarding whether an object appears in its entirety or does not appear at all, the treatise itself has explained this at length according to the opposing view.

If it is argued that [the object appears] through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), that too—being synonymous with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—has already been stated to know nothing of the external object beyond its own internal form. Or, if it is an apprehension as non-different [from the cognition], even now, under the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is an apprehension of identity.
It has already been stated and answered: even if there is merely a negation of cognition through distinction, it has not been stated that there is no cognition of the external object;

so how could there be its superimposition? Furthermore, the phrase "not by way of distinction" is useless, because there is an absence of a cognitive determination of identity through non-distinction, and because it is impossible to deny the mere cognition of the object of superimposition itself. For one who merely restates that [cognition], there is no special point.

Therefore, it has been said that as long as something is being conceptualized, there is no superimposition (āropa) because of the absence of contact with the object of superimposition. Thus, by whatever means,
and through the conventional designation of its appearance, when an error is established by means of such superimposition, it is as if false even though the form is real.

This is merely a logical restriction (*uparodha*); it does not, however, mean that its reality (*tāttvikatva*) has been asserted. If that is so, then since there would be no delusion even when its own nature appears, how could there be the status of being an error? It is not possible in any way, provided one respects critical inquiry (*vicāra*). Nevertheless, relying upon worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—which is pleasing only so long as it is not investigated and is established even among children—we employ the designation "person" (*pudgala*) and so forth, just like the conventional usage of such terms.
But when subjected to critical inquiry, they simply fall apart.

Just as the self [is established] through external [perception], and as there is valid cognition through verbal testimony, so too do the various misconceptions persist for those devoted to worldly convention.

In this regard, as long as there is conceptual investigation (*vicāra*), so long is there saṃsāra; and as long as there is the culmination of the discernment of one’s own true nature (*svarūpa-pariccheda*), so long is there nirvāṇa.
It is said that the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of existence itself is nirvāṇa;
such is the logical principle. How, then, is there the thorough knowledge of existence? Or how can there be activity and so forth through delusion regarding that which is non-existent in reality?

We shall explain this. First, let us consider how the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākāravādin*) establishes the status of error from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). In that case, let there be no error consisting of the imposition of something else (*parāroparūpā bhrāntiḥ*) upon that [consciousness]. Rather, error is simply the association with unreal forms (*alīkākārayoga*). What is improper about the removal of that [association] being security? First of all, this very [position] violates both common worldly experience and the treatises; for, in the case of a rope—
People employ the term "error" (bhrama) based on the superimposition of a snake; however, cognition does not touch the person in any specific form.

As for that superimposition of a snake, there is no effort to determine exactly how many categories it traverses, nor does another person have the power to carry it to its ultimate limit. For now, it is established that one employs this term "error" based on its defining characteristic.

In the treatise as well, activity through the determination of an object within one's own appearance is called "error" (*bhrānti*); it is not, however, because the appearance itself is devoid of an object. Likewise, this is precisely the meaning of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized; for here too, in the collection of Jñānaśrīmitra’s works, it is not merely that the conceptualized is false, but rather that it is so because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the perceived upon it. Even in non-conceptual [perception], two moons are seen as established.
Thus, because one's own activity is superimposed upon that very [object] through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it would be "delightful when not investigated.
Even in non-conceptual [cognition], there is the state of being an error; nothing further than that arises from conceptual construction.
Therefore, it is said that [the cognition] comes to rest in non-conceptual [perception] only after having settled in conceptual construction.

Therefore, since the persistence of error occurs everywhere solely through the imposition of something else [upon reality], what is improper in this? For is it not simply a case of being unable to resolve that [objection] and thus resorting to another technical definition (*paribhāṣā*)? Or, if the resolution is simply due to the impossibility [of the objection], then what fault is there in this?
If it is argued that this is because [the object] has been accepted [as such], then if that were so,
there would be these two intermediate verses.
There exists, at least for the sake of conventional practice,
an error which is sublated by inquiry;
this much alone suffices for the establishment of what is intended.
The remainder is the specific residue of dogmatic clinging.

For that conventional delusion is indistinguishable from the positions of either the real or the unreal; since I have already accepted that even the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is unreal, the attribution of "delusion" to it— lest it should persist in the ultimate sense— is a mere dogmatic insistence (*abhiniveśamātra*),
because both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are established otherwise as well.
As long as there is investigation, it is excellent that error should be dispelled;
but when [the truth] is realized as being present in every way, that is even more beautiful than the beautiful.
Therefore, it is appropriate to apply effort to investigation;
for even the wise might occasionally harbor doubt regarding the removal of what is real.

Therefore, what is the point of this claim that "error is the appearance of the unreal"? Even for one who does not accept that [definition], this is merely a failure to adopt the opponent's position; it is not a transgression of the observed principle of logic. As for the statement, "it is the exclusion of that [unreal] because of its impossibility," for one who perceives that impossibility, what kind of "logical vision" (yoga-dṛṣṭi) could there be such that error is defined as "the manifestation of the unreal"? For indeed, it is the appearance of the non-existent.
Is it intended [by you] that there is no manifestation of an unreal God or the like, or that the appearing form is unreal, or that some real thing does not manifest? Regarding this,
there is the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.
"How could that which has the manifestation of its own nature be non-existent?
If it is because of sublation, then is that sublation not also [subject to] perception and inference?"
If there is no confidence in perception in one case, what recourse is there in another? How then can inference, which is preceded by that [perception], be an object of trust?
Its status as direct perception arises from the direct realization of its own nature, and there is no other [criterion];
for this very reason, its being the ground for conceptual construction and error is indeed sublated.
If it were not perceived by direct perception, there would be no manifestation of its form at all;
therefore, the claim that God and so forth appear [to consciousness] while being non-existent is incoherent.
If its form were to appear as something truly existent,
then that which appears to you as non-existent would indeed be appearing as non-existent.

By this, the second position also should be understood as refuted; for since existence is established by the very appearance [of the object], there is no room for sublation. But surely, even in the case of the appearance of two moons and so forth, that which is perceived is indeed sublated?
Since it is observed [in experience], there is no lack of logical consistency; thus, what was previously stated is also incorrect.

That too is incorrect, because that which is sublated does not appear [in cognition], whereas that which appears is not sublated. For it is said: "The appearance of the form of the cognition is the sublation of the external object;
for while there is the appearance of the visible form itself, there is also the sublation of the tangible."
For that which appears as mere form is determined as a specific aggregate of color, taste, odor, and touch;

it is for this very reason that actions such as grasping with the hand are possible in the case of [illusory] hair and the like. Consequently, sublation (*bādhā*) also pertains only to that form which is accompanied by those [other qualities], not to form-in-general. Indeed, one who seeks a specific kind of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) attends only to the establishment or sublation of the means to achieve that [efficiency], and not to anything else.
For any eunuch, what is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a woman?

1. See *Ratnākaraṇḍa-nibandhana*, p. 125. 2. See the same work, p. 126. 3. See the same work, p. 125; the reading of the final quarter-verse there is: "even that which is known is sublated. 4. See the same work, p. 125. In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, it is stated that those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*) examine even universals (*sāmānya*) and the like for the sake of other purposes. In that regard:

When only the form (*rūpa*) appears, and the four concomitants are determined as being of the nature of a composite whole, people— due to a lack of discrimination— conceive of these two as non-different and engage in worldly discourse, saying "this is real" or "this is unreal. Therefore,
whatever affirmation or negation occurs here based on that very misconception has its ultimate conclusion in what is merely determined (*adhyavasita*), through the superimposition of something else.

Because its true nature is concealed, there is therefore no sublation of it in reality, just as in the case of the referent of a word. And it is established that for whatever complex [of factors] there is sublation, there is no appearance of it.
Therefore, even if sublation were to occur for that which appears merely through the power of conceit (*abhimāna*), let it be real; let it not be so.

There is no harm, for such diverse conventional [phenomena] are indeed experienced in the world; it is precisely for this reason that the inquiry into reality (*tattva*) is undertaken. However, if—as described above—that [reality] does not manifest, how can there be a determination of it? Thus, it follows that there is the manifestation of the non-existent. Likewise, regarding the conceit of non-difference (*abhedābhimāna*), the appearance of non-difference—which is non-existent—is a concealment through superimposition; yet even this cannot occur without the manifestation of something else.
There would be an emergence of a vast throat [of cognition]. In that case, if one were to close one's eyes and reflect, one would laugh at oneself;

for it has been stated that even for a determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is no manifestation of a specific form (*ākāraviśeṣa*). What is called "the manner of superimposing another" is not the appearance of a particular form. Nor is there a perception of what is not the self (*anātman*). Furthermore, neither is the negation of its own form intended by people, nor is it possible for the nature of the thing itself—

Because it would contradict their appearing [as such], that very form cannot belong to non-existent things like Īśvara and so forth, for that would entail the non-existence of non-existence itself. Therefore, what was asserted in the Sākāravāda— that eternal entities and the like must indeed be existent— has fallen back upon its own position.
If it is argued that there is sublation even when something appears, then existence cannot be attributed to non-existent things;
for there is no negation of those perceptions whose existence has not been refuted, precisely because their negation would itself be negated.
If that whose own nature appears [as real] is not real because of a sublater,
then what confidence can there be even in the sublater, since it too appears as having another nature?
The exclusion of its own nature occurs through the introduction of another nature;
yet even in that case, doubt arises because of the perception of a prior sublation.
If there is no sublation other than that which arises from non-apprehension, then let this [non-apprehension] be the very same as the former; for the manifestation of form is identical in both cases.
There is no proof for you that [cognition] does not manifest anything other [than itself],
since even when its own nature is manifest, there may be a sublation.
1. From the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Ratnākara*, and the *Nibandhana* (129): therefore, the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.
If it is argued that even when there is no appearance of its own nature due to the subversion caused by the purification of the cause,
there are likewise no subverters [of that cognition], then this would be a great subversion.
These are the intermediate verses.

Therefore, what further cause for laughter is there than this frantic effort to revive, by the mere hearing of words, that which has been in every way cast out as the manifestation of the non-existent— an indeterminate determination of an object? To revive again, by means of a word, that which has already been refuted by a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
It was like the wonder felt by one bitten by a serpent through the power of a mantra.

Therefore, it is correct that the wise, whether from their own perspective or that of others, concern themselves merely with investigating the basis for the application of terms such as "self" or "cowness," as well as the seed of that [application]. This is the ultimate truth here: due to various beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in a certain form—dependent upon a specific awakening condition—and while arising, it leads to outward-directed activity.

It produces a continuous stream of favorable purposive activity, such as memory and verbal expression. Consequently, for a person seeking purposive activity, there arise efforts toward engagement, avoidance, or indifference that correspond to external objects. This is because the causal nature of the moments of cognition within the mental continuum of an ordinary being is restricted in this way; even at the time of conceptualizing an object whose relation to reality is uncertain, there occurs an inclination toward determining its existence, non-existence, and so forth.
[This is] the production.

In that regard, when [the means of cognition] functions in both ways, its capacity as a means—which has come about through the power of its own causes—is precisely this superimposition (*āropa*) of the object upon the domain of activity, which is synonymous with "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*); just as, for example, in the case of the cognition of the moon, whether it be erroneous or non-erroneous, there is the perception of that [object].

The operation of apprehension (*grahaṇa*) is not merely the generation of a determinate judgment (*avasāya*). This is because, according to the principle that "this [apprehension] must be understood as being nothing other than the cognition of an object, as inferred from its effect," even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in a form such as "there is fire here" has as its external determination (*bāhyādhyavasāna*) precisely its capacity to impel purposeful action (*pravṛtti-ākṣepakatva*).
And just as for indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpa*), the very form of the moon and so forth is what effects the determination, so it is for the determinate judgment.

Moreover, it is precisely that [cognition’s] having such a form which serves as the means for the activity directed away from other objects. Consequently, even though the appearance of that form has no causal relation to an object not present at that time, it is established as if distinct—both as the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*) and as the cognition that superimposes (*āropyajñāna*). (See *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra-nibandhana*, p. 129).

If it is argued: "In that case, those same three [aspects] are established as non-existent, and since establishment is cognition, there is no release from the cognition of the non-existent," this is merely shifting the burden within the stream of argument. For it has been stated that the superimposition of something is nothing other than the implication of activity conforming to it; it is not some further "cognition" per se. Therefore, even now, the determination of the triad as non-existent is merely a conventional usage corresponding to that [determination].
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*,

there is no fault whatsoever in the view that the result [of the means of valid cognition] is the cognition in the form "this is non-existent," which is characterized by the state of disregarding the theory of the perception of the non-existent (*asatpratītivāda*).

In this way, one should infer similar minor disturbances elsewhere as well. This kind of error—consisting of the apprehension of something as what it is not among all conceptual constructions—is in accordance with experience. This very thing is designated as the "unification of the perceived and the conceptualized.

It is the capacity to engage with another object based solely on the awareness of its own internal appearance, and it is in dependence upon that [capacity] that one's own nature is concealed by the form of another.

This is the state of the gift (*dānasthiti*). However, with respect to appearance (*pratibhāsa*), it is said that the form of another (*pararūpa*) is concealed by its own form (*svarūpa*), because only that [own-form] is manifested.

Even though the external exists, it is in reality objectless (*nirviṣaya*) precisely because of its manifestation. Furthermore, because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) has the nature of the self (*ātmarūpatva*), and because there is no conceptual determination (*anadhyavasāya*), there are thus three ways: according to conceptual determination, according to appearance, and according to reality.
The stability of the body.
If that which is excluded from other classes (*vijātivyāvṛtta*) is what is denoted by words externally, then let it be a conceptualized form within conceptual cognition; furthermore,

my friend, since this has been established as a factor [of cognition], both [the external object and the internal image] are now determined through their appearance (*bhāsa*) by means of this primary cause (*nidāna*).

For if, due to the absence of an external object through its non-existence, there is an absence of appearance; and if there is an absence of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a form resembling a real entity excluded from heterogeneous things—which is produced by sound—then nothing at all would be denotable; what, then, exists in reality?
If it is argued that it is for the sake of exclusion (apoha), then this so-called "exclusion" is clearly nothing at all.

The connection [of the term] "the denotable" is as in the preceding sentence. This is the meaning: "exclusion (apoha) is the denotable" means that, in reality, there is a negation of exclusion regarding the denotable itself. Just as the statement "it becomes non-existence" means "it does not become existence.
Therefore, it is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the object of words.
Regarding the sūtra beginning with "by whatever dharma," and so forth:
how many sprouts could possibly emerge from such a root for those who propound negation (*apohavādin*)? There is no insistence on this point here, because:

The property of conceptual construction known as "ascertainment of the external" is established as having the characteristic of being the cause for activity directed toward the external; therefore, even if a determination of all aspects were to follow from that [single aspect], its nature would be established as being useful for activity corresponding to that [determination]. Furthermore, since it is not within the scope of experience that a conceptual construction which delineates only a single form possesses the power to engage with another form, how could there be [any validity] from other means of knowledge such as verbal testimony?

It is logical that the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* is the authority here. In that context, even though indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is erroneous, it is established as a grasper (*grāhaka*) by virtue of its clear manifestation.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), however, because its nature consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), functions independently of anything else; yet, because it delineates a single, non-clear exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is [classified as] an imposer (*āropaka*), and so forth.

It is the vessel for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even without touching anything external, is called "erroneous" because it functions as the cause for engagement with respect to something external—whether that external object exists or not. However, in the case of non-conceptual [perception], its status as an error is established as the connection with a form (*ākāra*) that contains within it the capacity to produce such a conceptual construction, even though no such [external object] exists.
Every conceptual cognition, though devoid of an external object, follows various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) and,
being fashioned with its own internal form, produces the recollection of perceived results and so forth;
thus, like perception, it incites the activity of people without depending on anything else.
This is called the superimposition of one thing upon another, like the superimposition of water upon the rays of light, as in the case of [mistaking] water for water.
Thus is the summary.

This being the case, that which was determined as having the form of an external collection and brought to a state of readiness for engagement according to the aforementioned sequence is sublated, yet there is no appearance of it; and it is established that the appearing aspect itself is not what is sublated.

For there is indeed no dispute regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). It is simply that a subsequent conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) arises following what is endowed with causal efficiency, and there is no impairment of that efficiency. Impairment, however, applies only to that [causal efficiency] which is to be accomplished by a specific collection of factors; thus, it is only that [specific efficiency] which is absent. Therefore, how can it be said that there is sublation (*bādhā*) of that which is appearing? And when one relies on the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), everything previously stated recurs.
Thus [it is said].
In the consideration of the absence of a pervader, there is neither a boat nor a long pepper;
yet, apart from defects, there is the examination of affliction and so forth within that which possesses aspects.

It has begun. In that regard, even though there is the experience of the true nature of things (*satyasvākāra*), no affliction arises because one relies on the fact that all cognitions possess a state of error—which, although established in worldly convention, is produced by seeds from beginningless time. Just as there is a conventional determination of error in some cases when external objects exist, so it is everywhere in the case of ascertainment; however, the error is not at all within the self, but is designated only with respect to outward-directed activity.
This is what is meant:
whatever form a cognition appears as, that indeed is its very nature.

Thus, because there is a determination of externality when words are joined [to the object], it is precisely therein that conceptualization and lack of clarity [arise] in relation to other cognitions.
Because, in comparison [to that], that very object remains alone and distinct; however, in the case of its own nature (*ātmarūpa*), such a form does not exist—
[as stated] in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, 396.
Because that cognition arises from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), how could there be such a fixed determination given the possibility of deviation?

Even when this very [cognition] is intended to be connected with another object by means of a word after having been made its object, even then the connection occurs only with respect to the other, not with respect to itself; thus the treatise (*śāstra*) must be considered here. Therefore, it would follow that it is not conceptual at all; [if you argue otherwise,] it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with respect to itself, whereas its status as conceptual with respect to another—
[This is said] by the power of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) established [by the cognition].

Now, if it is said thus solely by the power of the manifestation of the thing’s own nature (*vastusvarūpa*), this is a great boldness even to assert in the case of the theory of "cognition with form" (*sākāravāda*). If it is argued that [the thing] is drawn forth by the determination—no, because that [determination] has been established otherwise. For indeed...

The so-called "ascertainment" (*avasāya*) regarding its manifestation is nothing other than the apprehension of the appearance itself. Therefore, it is not tenable to argue that there is an ascertainment of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though it does not appear, due to error. If the cognition of that [particular] is touched by the ascertainment, what else could this be but an appearance?
It is not tenable to say it is because of indistinctness; for if there were a cognition of that form, that very [indistinctness] would be unestablished.
"Once born, the substrata are indeed mutually dependent," and so forth— let this be remembered.

And at that time, it cannot be an error, because it appears as the very form of a real entity (*vasturūpa*). If you argue that it is a false cognition (*alīkavitti*), how can that itself be the determination of an object (*arthādhyavasāya*)? If you say that "that itself is it," no; for one who knows "this is false," there is no established determination of an external object. If you argue that it is not a verbalization of the false, but rather the cognition of that [false thing] which constitutes the determination of the external, [we reply:]...

Even so, there would be a mere synonymy, and not a clarification of the intended meaning. For, insofar as it is said that "cognition has a false form" due to the absence of contact with an external nature, just as much is meant by saying "it is a determination. Therefore, no distinction whatsoever has been stated. And this being the case, just as "false-form cognition" cannot properly have a relationship with the external, so too "determination" cannot have a relationship with the external.
It would [be so]. For the genitive case is indeed dependent upon the conceit of having understood that; in its absence, how could it exist?
If that [object] of his is false because it has been handed down through tradition, then by that much alone there is no error;
for such a defect does not apply even when the object is not false.

Therefore, that which was asserted—that this "determination of an object by the intellect" is merely a specific manifestation capable of association with verbal expression—is refuted; for the connection [expressed] as "of the object" (*arthasya*) is untenable, and because there can be no error regarding cognition itself. Furthermore, let the determination simply be that "the manifestation is false"; what is the use of the qualification "capable of association with verbal expression"? [If it is argued that this is] for the purpose of excluding non-conceptual [cognition],...

If this is so, then even in the theory of non-falsity (*analīkavāda*), it is only cognition qualified by those specific attributes that is an error, not all cognition; thus, there is no total absence of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*viśuddhi*). For even when error ceases, it is only a particular class of cognition (*jñānajāti*) that is relinquished. Furthermore, in both systems, the connection with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsarga*) is dependent upon something else, so there is no fault. It is simply that in the absence of its perception, the determination (*vyavasthā*) of its conceptual ascertainment (*avasāya*) is...
This is a fault; and since it is common to both of us,
even one who runs far away from the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* [cannot escape], for without relying on cognition, external activity arises solely from a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*).

It must be accepted that the determination (*avasāya*)—which, by metaphorically grasping that [external object], connects with the external thing—abides within the function of the mental state (*vṛtti*).

At that time, there is no distinction as to whether the form (*ākāra*) is false or real. Furthermore, if the meaning of the determination is thus made manifest through the fact of being determined, then everything previously stated—that the identity of the object [with the cognition] exists while its non-existence and so forth apply when the object is unreal—is untenable.

The very fact that cognition proceeds toward an object without having seen it is itself the error. Therefore, since there is no contact with the actual object even when the exclusion (apoha) is the denotable content in the form of a conceptual construction, how can there be the fault of the consequence of determining all aspects?
Thus he says: "And the error regarding the universal-cognition is not thereby a flaw."
[Pravā.

3.169], because it implies activity toward that very object by way of having the form of the exclusion of others (*ekavyāvṛtti*). And since a person attains satisfaction with just that much, they do not analyze anything further. However, regarding the failure to obtain that alone, he states the contradiction: "And for that which, even though existing, does not appear in conceptual cognition..."

To say that something which is manifest belongs to that which is non-existent is far removed from reason; nor can there be non-existence for that which is being manifested. Therefore, how can the blue [color]—which is non-existent [in the absence of the universal]—be manifested by means of the example of "cowness," and how can there be a conceptualization of identity between them? By this, the argument beginning with "of those residing in various forms" is also refuted. Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that manifestation and non-existence belong to a single entity, because their contradiction has been established.

Since there is no real entity distinct from the manifestation (prakāśa) itself, there is no purpose in postulating a difference; for what is intended is merely the negation of one of two things. And this [negation] would occur either when one thing is manifest while the other is imagined—as in the case of "pot-ness" in relation to a cloth—or even between two things that appear as distinct, like a hare and a mosquito. However, it does not apply to those whose appearance is non-distinct.
Furthermore,
this principle is not established in any case for two things whose distinction is established merely through mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-mātra*);
it applies only to that which is distinct [in reality].
If it is argued that even though color and shape appear as non-distinct, the shape is nonetheless unreal—no;

for what is being negated there is merely a conceptualized shape known as the "conjunction of the arrangement of parts. But how could one negate the essence of color itself, which is denoted by the word "square" and arises as a state distinct from the conditions that fall within the scope of conventional usage such as "circular" and so forth? The same applies here to the distinct [shape].

Only that which is imagined can be negated; however, neither blue as the essence of manifestation nor manifestation as the essence of blue can be negated, precisely because they appear as non-distinct. Consequently, if one seeks to prove either its status as a real entity or its non-superimposed nature, it follows from the existence of blue.

Furthermore, with respect to the form of cognition that has become manifest, there is no absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). For the manifestation of the form of "cowness" is not a superimposition by anything else, because there is no superimposer distinct from it; rather, it arises as the manifestation of the very form of "cowness" produced by its own cause. Nor is there a superimposition of a thing upon itself, nor a superimposition of one thing by another; this is merely a matter of naming.
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, however, it would be as follows:

therefore, the nature of luminosity (*prakāśātmakatva*) is entirely non-superimposed (*anāropita*), and thus there is not even a scent of the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, that which is superimposed must necessarily be indistinct, like water and so forth; yet the luminosity of the blue is experienced as being most distinct.
But it is not as if there were a distinct manifestation of light, like a distinct blueness; for if light were manifest, its appearance would necessarily follow, just as [the quality] blue does.
Thus, wherever there is the cognition that something appears as unreal or false according to logic (*tarka*) or scripture (*āgama*), such is the understanding of the Commentator.

This is because, other than through manifestation, it is either with respect to what is determined therein or from the perspective of conventional intent. For he employs the term "unreal" (alīka) and so forth merely on the basis of the absence of external causal efficiency as imagined by that form. Following that [conventional] description, this is merely a negation of the external.
In reality, however, the non-existent is simply another kind of existent; and it is called "unreal" because it is other than what is intended. Nevertheless, it might be argued:

When cognition has a permanent form (*nityākāra*), then because it arises as pervading multiple times, it would follow that it must be both possessed of form and eternal; but this is merely a trifle. For its possession of that form is due to mere imitation (*anukāramātra*), and not through identity (*tādātmya*), since otherwise there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of burning from the mere conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of fire. Therefore, just as a banyan tree, though pervading a vast space, [is reflected] even on the surface of a mirror [which can be covered by] a mere leaf—
Just as [an eternal object] is imitated by a reflection due to some difference in form, so too an eternal [object] is [imitated] by a momentary form. And there is experience in this regard:

at the time of conceptualizing an eternal self and so forth, there is an imitation of that [eternal object] even without a pervasion of all time, which would otherwise obstruct the opportunity for another cognition [to arise].

For even if it is false, it need not necessarily possess light that extends over time in a permanent form; otherwise, it would lack the capacity to prompt activities such as the investigation of its existence or non-existence in accordance with that [light]. Therefore, it is logical that it imitates it even slightly, even without extending over time—just as a representation of an upright staff or the like is sometimes attended to. Below—

By means of its upper and middle parts, it demonstrates that for an eternal entity, there would have to be the production of all states simultaneously—characterized by past, future, and present forms—within a single [moment]. Likewise, there is no contradiction in the arising of even the intellect (*buddhi*) in a single moment while bearing those forms. Therefore, that which is non-existent does not manifest; rather, it would merely be the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavasita*), as was stated previously. And that which does manifest...
It is established that it does not exist by its own nature; therefore, the manifestation of the non-existent cannot be the definition of error, because such a thing is impossible.

For this very reason, the third alternative—that what exists does not manifest—is also not tenable, because existence is pervaded by manifestation, and non-manifestation is swallowed up by non-existence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that what is called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes an object? And yet, there is no absence of an object simply because the means of valid cognition has ceased to function. Furthermore, the essence of a real entity (*vastusattva*) consists in its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*), and this is not incompatible even with that which remains unmanifested. [Response: This is true within the framework of the theory of external objects (*bahirarthavāda*), since that [capacity] is admitted even for things that remain unmanifested; however, in the case of the appearance of [illusory] hair and so forth, the causal efficiency of the object as it is determined—
1. This means because of pervasion (*vyāpti*). 2. Compare *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī*, page 125, *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*:

"Because non-existence is established precisely through separation; for if there were an absolute absence of external objects, cognition would never fail to be luminous, and by that alone [the point is established]."
What is the use of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) regarding existence?
Furthermore:
"If its existence is not established by manifestation alone, how can it be other than non-existent?"
If even causal efficiency does not belong to everything for everyone, why is there no manifestation [of it]?
Even in the case of external objects, existence is accepted in reality as being their manifestation;
the determination of existence is established through the power [of cognition] according to the intention of the cognizer.
Since even a capacity cannot be established as existing without being manifested,
there would be no stability in discourse.
It is known through its effect that [the cause] possesses the power by virtue of another power; moreover, being an effect implies dependence upon something else.
Even if the power is not definitively ascertained, it exists if there is a distinct exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
If its capacity is not ascertained, how indeed can it have the nature of being an effect?
For the state of being an effect is the very nature of the thing itself, even though it possesses distinct exclusions (vyāvṛtti).
Otherwise, why is it that hair and the like do not possess the status of being an effect?
If you say they indeed have the status of an effect, then let "manifestation" itself be existence, because of its non-deviation [from existence].
If it is argued that superimposed things have no causal efficacy, why is it not the same for manifestation?
If manifestation is [causal] because of its unification [with the object], how can it be the same for causal efficacy?
Just as there is no member because of the absence of the fruit, so too there is no fruit because of the absence of the members;
therefore, when there is doubt regarding substantial reality, there is doubt regarding its being an effect and so forth.
Therefore, through the power of practice, there is a definitive certainty regarding that capacity:
luminosity itself is existence, or its effect is simply cognition.
Nor does its existence depend on another effect; rather, it is known through self-awareness (svasaṃvit), for a cognition never deviates from its own object.
If anyone has doubt regarding that matter, certainty arises from practice;
therefore, even externally, reality is established through manifestation alone.
1. *Tulana-ratnanirbhaya-puḥ* 125;
not found in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*.
Likewise, there would be the destruction of the momentary nature [of the object], because it is apprehended by cognition in a single moment; furthermore,
that cognition would be merely occasional, since the eternal power [of the object] would be exhausted.
And it is stated in the treatise that cognition is existence, while the non-existence of the perceptible is non-cognition;
this is independent of the loss of designation, purposeful activity, and so forth.
Moreover, incapacity in that regard is not a subverting factor;
furthermore, this much distinction has been stated: visibility and invisibility correspond respectively to existence and non-existence.
Sometimes, for someone, some manifestation exists through inference;
however, the absence of manifestation should be understood as false when there is outward attention.
Even in the absence of inference, there is the manifestation of conceptual construction itself;
let manifestation be of the same nature as the existence of such things.
Everyone seeking purposeful action attains the status of a real entity (vastu) precisely through the result;
and since one deposits the appearance right there [in that result], it is the locus of activity.
And thus there is no impairment of the commenced conventional measure;
therefore, power has been described, as well as existence and the pure intrinsic nature.

Therefore, even in the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda), although from the standpoint of conventional usage there is a twofold status: power (śakti) and existence-luminosity (sattāprakāśa) as the ultimate reality.
These are the intermediate verses.

Now, if it is argued that "existence" (sattva) is defined as "potency" (śakti) with the intention that existence should not belong to a form (ākāra) even if it appears, provided it is devoid of potency— even so, since there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for [proving] its distinctness from that [form], what kind of desired proof is this? Furthermore, it is not possible to deny that the form possesses causal efficiency (arthakāritva), because of the moment of the material cause (upādeyakṣaṇa), the determination (adhyavasāya), and the continuum (prabandha) initiated by it.
Furthermore, because it has been demonstrated that in the case of birth, there exists an invariably antecedent state— which persists even now and consists in the determination of existence,

non-existence, and so forth— otherwise, the causal relationship would not be established anywhere. If it is argued that the cause therein is a distinct, pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*), [we reply:]...
Through positive and negative concomitance, it is observed that the form possesses causal power;
that another [factor] attains the status of being the cause is the established rule of the royal court.
If [it is argued that] the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* is also a cause [of cognition], then the existence of an aspect (*ākāra*) cannot be denied;
for fire does not deny the causality of fuel with respect to smoke.
Furthermore, the agency of both [the agent and the object] depends upon one another,
due to the capacity for the persistence of their existence, just as in the case of fire and fuel.
If it is determined that a distinct manifestation, dependent upon blue, performs [the act of manifesting],
then it follows that a *piśāca* (demon) dependent upon fire is a constituent part of smoke.
For this very reason, ignorance alone cannot be established as a member [of dependent origination];
for no one is ever prevented from relying on a perceived collection of conditions.
Otherwise, the entire diversity [of the world] would be produced by karma alone;
there would be an elimination of other causes, and the fruit of human effort would not exist.
If there were no conformity with existence and non-existence, there would be no relation of cause and effect anywhere;
and if there were conformity with existence and non-existence, there would likewise be no relation of cause and effect anywhere.
And the determination of a blue perception does not arise from the seeing of a non-blue form;
for the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl occurs despite the absence of a deviation in color.

In the case of form, let there be the superimposition of another form upon that which is of the same class when charcoal is seen; or, by chance, let there be a perception otherwise even without such [superimposition].
In that case, the distinction between the types [of smoke] is to be inferred, like the smoke created by a yogin.
Because that [distinction] is not perceived when there is a confusion regarding the apprehension of difference.
Just as in the case of an external seed being accepted as the cause of a sentient being, so too,
when a cognition arises in the form of a sprout, one who rejects the external object and instead designates knowledge as its place [of occurrence], [does so] in that same manner.
It has been stated that "conditions arise and cease.
If its pervasive property were the cause, such as its being earthen and so forth, then let there also be illumination; yet there is no manifestation—this is a sound conclusion.
Likewise,
from that [work],
the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.
In that case, since the result of an external blue object is indeed observed,
whereas no such result is seen for the cognition of [illusory] hair and the like, the latter lacks the status of being a real entity.
In that case, let reality itself be negated due to the absence of its activity;
it is not the mere status of being a real entity that is precluded for something engaged in another activity.
As one emerges from the interior of a mountain cave into the illusion of a waterfall,
what is there in reality by virtue of the reality itself, since that action has been transcended? For when the action of discernment is lost, how can a person who seeks that object [attain it]?
In that very state, through the practice of existence, one should again declare the form of the intellect to be non-existent.

Therefore, in accordance with that [conventional consensus], the expressions "unreal appearance" and so forth are uttered for the purpose of negating that which is imagined within the perceptions regarded as non-erroneous.
For that [form] is not self-cognizable by that cognition; rather, it is something else, and that [other thing] is certainly not real.
Therefore, the universal "cowness" and so forth are indeed non-existent, since they do not manifest as the form itself.
Just as a pair of moons is not even a single moon, so too, by the very nature of what is to be understood, it is the same here; this is the general direction.

This is the conventional arrangement established according to mental determination; however, in reality, things such as hair-tufts are not universals, because they lack any objective referent upon which one could insist.

Thus he says: "But not because of being a non-object," and furthermore: "The appearance of clarity exists because, by virtue of having the nature of cognition, it is an object; however, the notion [of it being hair and so forth]..."

That which has a universal as its object, which appears as hair, and which is devoid of reality— though counted as sensory cognition— is non-existent because it determines an external object that does not exist.
If it follows that the universal is the object by virtue of having the nature of cognition,
there is no fault, because that is accepted; for its commonality consists in its having the nature of the object.
It has been stated more than once that the referent of a word is a phenomenon characterized by non-rejection;
and in the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*,
it was explained that this referent of a word is unreal, in accordance with how it is perceived.
In the commentary, it is stated that existence consists in being of the nature of cognition;
if existence is defined as appearing, then it must be according to how it appears.
That very existence [of cognition] is not a sublater even when it is externalized as knowledge;
there is no sublation because of the absence of a pervader, whereas incapacity and so forth are considered external.
It is logical that the meaning of a word is dependent [on cognition], because that form appears in verbal cognition;
and for embodied beings, there is a determination of their own internal form precisely as something external.
Therefore, just as the term "sentient being" is used for that which is not a sentient being in order to establish the truth,
so too the notion that the three realms are mind-only is considered to be a diverse [conventional] view.
This effort is indeed equal regarding all words such as "emptiness" and so forth;
that very mind, possessing an aspect, is described as appearing as the object.
For the negation of the external object as it is conceptualized has indeed been established by oneself;
moreover, its being afflicted by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) is held to be due to the arising of forms that are undesirable.

For one who has ascended to the pinnacle of non-duality, there is neither engagement nor withdrawal, since the internal capacity to give birth to the volitions that project worldly activity has been exhausted.
How could those very [states] be considered "saṃsāra" by one who knows them?
It is only through the misconception of the ignorant that a form is said to be seen in a mirror.
The prevention of superimposing that [externality] upon the forms of cognition; [this is the refutation of] externality within the forms of cognition.
Having thus restated the nature of sensation,
the existence of things in their true state is like that perceived by one with cataracts.
For those who have seen the moon, its moon-nature is non-existent;
furthermore, due to the separation from the concave surface, there is no oneness with the external object in the mirror.
The nature of consciousness is not perceived as distinct from the objects that enter within it— whether they be entities possessing resistance or those designated by mental images.
For this very reason, there is a separate statement regarding that which is reckoned as general cognition;
in common worldly usage, such cognition is well-established as if it were distinct, like the reflection in a mirror.
As it says:
"The remainder is the same. Or else, "beginning with... and so forth.
And likewise, in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, the *Ākārāḥ* states: "The appearance is a reflection; that which belongs to both is imagined, not real."
There is no identity between consciousness and external objects, because [the latter] results in the loss of its own essential nature.
There is no otherness because it has not been grasped as such, nor is there existence for that which is unmanifest;
and by the sequence of the King [the Self], it is devoid of both unity and multiplicity in the mirror.
And so forth.
Thus, it is either logical or not that phenomena are joined [together] like reflections in a mirror;
the yogin abides in the non-manifest, for manifestation is considered to be conceptual construction.

That which appears slightly as external within that [consciousness] through the exclusion of others (ekāpoha) is the manifestation of universal radiance, or it is the proliferation (prapañca) like a kadamba flower.
That which has ascended upon various conceptual constructions is to be abandoned, even in a mind that is variegated.
Even when the external object of apprehension is abandoned, one must prevent the persistence of the act of apprehension;
by abiding in the preservation of suchness, one transcends "mind-only."

"Lest, upon the removal of the superimposition, there also be the removal of the object of that superimposition— lest there be a fall of the eye of the doctrine of nihilism (ucchedadṛk)— there is the warding off of non-appearance."
In that regard, due to the absence of even one [of these],
"the diverse things remain just as they are in the world," so say the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
"For thus the wise discipline [the reality]; in this same manner, other [cases] are also to be inferred."
The *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* is proclaimed as being fully contained within the consciousness of the great elements and so forth; indeed,
when that [consciousness] is known, false conceptual constructions surely come to an end.
Therein, the conviction of non-existence, the cessation of objects, and [the realization] "it is known by that" occur in the heart consisting of reflection;
and the destruction [of defilements] occurs through the direct realization of the nature of knowledge.
There is no harm to the names, the causes, or the forms [of things] even when they are sublated;
let phenomena be mere names, or let them exist with an imagined nature.
Then, through the destruction of adventitious impurities, it is like the surface of space;
its equality with the object of knowledge is manifest by virtue of its non-distinction from that object.
This [consciousness] is mere luminosity, resembling the continuum of a lamp-flame;
for it lacks any non-luminous part, since its own form is not something separate from its luminosity.
Even for one who possesses no particle of luminosity, such a state was not possible even previously;
rather, the condition of being either defiled or stainless depends upon the persistence of delusion.
In that very [dependent nature], which consists of various forms dependent on causes,
that which is imagined— the act of grasping and the grasper— is non-existent. Of that [dependent nature], its form is the single essence consisting of the discernment of those two.
The prince spoke from all sides once it was completed.

Therefore, in the theory of the existence of mental aspects (*sākāravāda*), there is no contradiction whatsoever with the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or with the scriptures (*āgama*). Nor is there any unreality (*alīkatva*) of the aspects, because their causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*) has been established. Or, even if they were unreal, or merely designated as "error," there is nonetheless no connection to actual defilement (*saṃkleśa*) in reality, because there is no loss of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and because there is an absence of the imposition of something else (*parāropa*).

The notion that "all embodied beings are always already liberated" is an obstruction resulting from a long-continued stream of habitual practice. For once something has arisen from its own cause in the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it cannot be altered by anything else, even by one possessing power, let alone by what is considered false. Furthermore, when it arises as unified with its own cause, its nature is non-dual cognition; what need is there for repeated recitation of this point?

If [it is argued that it is so] because of a grasping [subject], then its arising in such a way from its own cause and its being experienced as having that nature would mean that identity has been accepted by entities; this causes great distress to the proponents [of other views]. (406)
Furthermore, from the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*:
If it is argued that [things] arise and appear as such due to ignorance, and therefore are not reality, this too lacks substance.
Let there be the birth of a cause from whatever source; what is the use of deliberating over a cause?
Even if something undesirable arises, it remains exactly as it is, regardless of its nature.
Thus, one must with great effort offer a final libation to the proponents of non-aspectarianism (anākāravāda),
provided that they accept the ultimate [reality] as something to be realized through faith, thinking that some distinction [between them and the Yogācārins] might eventually arise.

If it is argued that there is a perception of oneness like that of milk and water even though they arise as distinct entities, this is not so; for there is no perception of them as distinct, yet there is no misapprehension of the self by itself.
For just as the grasping of a self occurs by means of the self, so too is that [self] its own nature;
the manifestation of cognition, which depends on another, is a delusion consisting of a single conceptual construction.
If there were no sublation even in another [case], the occurrence of error would be impossible;
how much less so in the self-awareness where not even a trace of sublation exists?
If it is argued that there is a subsequent determination of non-difference, even that causes no harm;
for like indeterminate cognition, this too consists for self-awareness in nothing but the unreal.

Nor is there any superimposition of another [subject] therein; that [error] is false, yet it is self-cognized. What other peace is there than the cessation of the engagement with and withdrawal from that?
Even if it were merely false, it would certainly not act as an obstacle;
for if it were to act as an obstacle while being false, it would follow that falsity itself is false.
Movement to another sphere of experience is certainly not desired by anyone as a cause of bondage;
moreover, in the case of self-awareness, there is no bondage for it even by a hundred [such movements].
For if the insentient were bound by its own cognition and illumination were due to its own cause,
then— this being an untenable position— it would be impossible for there to be cognition even through identity with itself.

For it is not logical that this [consciousness], arising from its own cause as something whose nature is luminosity, should possess insentience (jāḍya) brought about by an obstruction to self-awareness through the power of false forms. Therefore, if that [consciousness] were to know itself as non-different from those [forms], then that false [form] would be real; thus [it is argued] in the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.

This also is not possible, precisely because of contradiction. For when one's own consciousness alone is being produced, its becoming otherwise—namely, the arising of a nature that is either that [consciousness] or not that [consciousness]—is contradictory.
If there is an obstacle to the awakening of one who is not yet a *tanmātra*, that very obstacle is itself a merit;
for it is he who, being himself non-existent, has assumed the form of a disciple.
If it is by way of an undifferentiated form, then there is an unshakable identity;
even if it is by way of a differentiated form, provided it is not perceived, there is no harm whatsoever.
For one who perceives the two— the false and the non-false— by way of their distinction,
if they see the false as having the form of the non-false, [then it is not so].
Therefore, there is no talk of the cognition of the unreal; the self is not made known by something unreal.
Whether one considers it in this way or that, if the superimposition of an external object is not admitted, [the cognition of the unreal is impossible].
For one who desires external objects as their goal, engagement in activity and so forth is not possible.
Since the mind is fixed upon its own cognition as unreal,
and because activity and cessation do not proceed from the superimposition of other unrealities,
why, O friend, should embodied beings exert themselves for the sake of liberation? It is already directly present.
Even if it remains in the form of a subtle manifestation during hearing, what harm is there?

Consequently, since all sentient beings would always be liberated, there would be no need even for perfect enlightenment (samyaksaṃbuddhatva), and thus no one would undertake the practice of skillful means (upāya).
