Therefore, if this delusion— characterized by the apprehension of that which is not [that]— which is by its very nature devoid of rational analysis, were not established as having the capacity to impel such activity, then there would be no fault even if it were merely a false appearance.
This is not a rebuttal by way of a counter-objection:
"If that which is false exists without implying an activity,
then see the audacity of the power of the non-false!"
Its activity proceeds through false appearances and never through real forms or qualities;
being thus devoted to the contrary, this Yogācāra is not ultimate.
In this world,
that which is of utility is merely false and illusory in nature;
elsewhere, the determination of such [utility] is refined by critical inquiry.
But that which is conceptualized through external, conventional usage is equal in both cases— whether it possesses a formal aspect (sākṛti) or lacks one (anākṛtimat).

How then is it that the minds of the most intelligent ones are habituated to an adherence to the "formless" (nirākāra) alone, by abandoning the "with-form" (sākāra), out of fear of losing the established distinction between affliction and purification?
If, however, there is an application of effort toward thorough investigation (parāmarśa)...
In the view that [cognition] possesses an aspect (sākāravāda), the establishment of the connection with causal capacity and so forth is logical;
however, in the view that it is aspectless (nirākāravāda), this applies to internal affliction and purification.

Thus, there is a great difference. For instance, if the form (*ākāra*) were a real entity, then an experience, by virtue of its identity with or its connection to that form, would perceive a particularity and produce a corresponding determination (*adhyavasāya*); and that determination, being informed by the particularity of the object, would give rise to purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
In this way, there would be no confusion of activities. For when a certain object, through the application of a particularity inherent in its own nature, brings about a distinction in action—
One should not assume [the existence of a mental image] merely because of a particular auxiliary cause, like something being blue or yellow, or like holding a lotus or a stone in one's hand.

Therefore, both identity (*tādātmya*) and the auxiliary cause are established as being necessarily connected to a real entity (*vastu*). Furthermore, if the form (*ākāra*) were not a real entity, there would be no distinction between the mind perceiving water and the mind perceiving fire; consequently, from the experience of water, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of fire.

In this way, from the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of fire, there would be an inclination toward one who desires to drink or bathe. One who thinks "there is no fire here" does not act out of a desire for a drink; so what difference is there between that and an experience which, due to its transparency, surpasses even the rays of a crystal gem, yet possesses an unreal form? For the crystal itself does not appear as such, setting aside the assistance provided by objects such as blue or yellow.

[Objection: "The cause for the distinction in activity is the difference in power (*śaktibheda*) resulting from the association (*saṃsarga*) with a form that, though non-existent, appears and thus partakes in worldly designation. [Response: That is incorrect;
for, if it is non-existent even while appearing, what kind of purpose could there be here in its association?
Even a false designation is not capable of negating the existence [of the object].

Therefore, for one who speaks thus, it would be equally worthy of belief that an object which is inherently of a single, undifferentiated nature becomes capable of plunging [into water] through its conjunction with a sky-lotus, yet becomes a source of burning and destruction through the proximity of an unexpectedly enraged son of a barren woman. If it is argued that even though those two (the sky-lotus and the son of a barren woman) are non-existent, there is a distinction because the form of the one is not perceived while that of the other is; we say no, because even when perceived, the non-existence of the latter brings about an obstruction to the effort toward assistance.
Because of this statement: "And for that which is non-existent and incapable of having any excellence added to it, no distinction whatsoever can arise from anything.

Nor is there any distinction of that [non-existent thing] from the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, nor is there any [distinction] of illumination (*prakāśa*) from it. Furthermore, the claim that "the form (*ākāra*) is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)" is also not coherent, because—

Since even the status of being a qualifier (*lakṣaka*) is possible only with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), as in the case of a crest (*śikhā*) and so forth; and since illumination (*prakāśa*), even when thus qualified, cannot by itself—due to its own lack of differentiation—be conducive to a distinction in action. If it is argued that such a power belongs to it through the efficacy of the object (*karman*), we say no, because an object does not [produce an effect] without depending on a perceived means (*dṛṣṭasādhana*).

Because no such power (*śakti*) is perceived. Nor is a distinction in function observed without a distinction in form; yet, if one were to postulate that [the self] possesses mere witnesshood (*sākṣitva*), it would follow that one must likewise postulate it for the cook and others in relation to cooking and so forth. Therefore, the form itself possesses an undeniable power therein. Furthermore, there is no seed for establishing a distinction between different experiences. Consequently, that which "shines forth" (*prakāśate*) is the form itself, which is the manifestation (*prakāśa*).
The established position is that "manifestation" (prakāśa) refers merely to its specific attribute, by way of excluding other distinct properties.
For external activity is indeed restricted to the form [of the object]; how could there be a state of error regarding it in the absence of that [form]?
Therefore, for one who holds the view that [the object] is not perceived...
This so-called "accomplishment of what has been undertaken" is merely a figurative expression for its complete rejection.

If that were so, then as long as there is awakening, there would be mental aspects (*ākāra*); and as long as there are mental aspects, there would be the persistence of the delusion created by external functioning. Thus, there would never be purification (*vyavadāna*). However, if mental aspects are unreal, then through the total destruction of the collection of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) from which they arise, when [the aspects] have utterly ceased, nothing but pure luminosity remains—devoid of appearances and resembling space; thus, there is purification.
[One] is liberated. If it is argued that this is difficult to achieve according to the view that the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is real, let it be so; what must such a person do?

For one who is greedy for the destruction of the *saṃbhogakāya*—a great undertaking—it is better that there be no false conceptualization at all, which is by nature unreal, or rather, no external activity. Or else, let even the mental aspect not be desired; [let there be] the state of the absence of specific mental aspects.

What fault could there be in the arising of a specific desired form through the power of one's application toward the accumulation of merit? Nor can there be a permanent restriction to that [specific form] simply because a fault is occasionally perceived in its appearance, for an absolute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is possible; otherwise, even the occurrence of the false would have to be eternal. Therefore:

The mind, which has reached a certain pinnacle of maturity through the abundance of practice in the radiant manifestation of hundreds of virtues, is variegated by the beauty of the primary and secondary marks;
it is a treasury of qualities whose essence is bound [to the self] and which is firmly established against unwholesome latent impressions.
It is devoid of a multitude of pure aspects, but it is not without aspects altogether.
If conventional reality were to cease, there would be the destruction of the *dharmakāya*;
and if its formal aspects were to cease, there would be the ruin of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
(Jñānaśrīmitra, *Nibandhāvali*, 410)
The persistence of the cognition of those who rule over the ten stages [of bodhisattvas] in that form is like the clear licking of a hand by leaving aside its mass.
When even the lords of the ten stages, who are like fully awakened Buddhas,
have their inner minds rendered utterly formless,
then what need is there to mention the licking of hands by a mere child?
And those wretched ones who perceive only emanations are even more miserable.
Through the sovereign power of the Buddha, such awakening of the ten worlds is the supreme gain;
it is like the removal of the burden of delusion for those who were wandering as minute atoms.
There is no happiness, especially not in that which is impure.

If it is argued that because of the direct realization of those dharmas, there is the vision of the *dharmakāya*, then while the vision of the *dharmakāya* would follow as a consequence, the vision of the *saṃbhogakāya* is not established for him.
Because it has that form, the intellect arises with that same form;
this experience of it by universal monarchs arises from the accumulation of merit.
The teaching of the Dharma, which is sharp and arises when pure worldly conceptualization is present before one.
Alternatively, even the knowledge of all things [is attained] through the ripening of the vow for upliftment, according to each respective purpose.

Even in the absence of an apprehended object and so forth, because correspondence regarding various objects is possible for those seeking those respective things, the establishment of omniscience is also merely the manifestation of the forms within one's own cognition. Alternatively,
it is like the variegated state of the experience of all embodied beings.

In all three times, through the maturation of his vows, the All-pervading Lord— whose every form conforms to those [beings]— manifests at the time of their arising with the splendor of his own nature, appearing as a single form through the intermingling of various manifestations.
This [world], covered by extremely subtle mango leaves, is perceived as its own true nature in its entirety by those ten stages who possess formless vision.
*Sākārasiddhiśāstra* (The Treatise Establishing Cognizant Form)
And therein they desire that this portion which is the object of the body be immovable and peerless; [so too] the remainder, without exception.
For instance:
by what is this rule established that a variegated thing is one?
And by what is this rule established that this piece of earth is one?
If that state is reached by means of conventional truth,
then this great excellence arises from the vast burden of the purity of knowledge.
And this collection of diverse forms,
which has the nature of an unassailable, real object,
cannot be subverted by misconceptions even if the intellect exerts effort, because of the intellect's inherent partiality toward that [object].

[Pravāhaṇa-vāda 1.292–3] Born from the practice of the accumulations, it is the ground of the radiance of the sky-like state— familiarized by the removal of adventitious manifoldness and established in the singular cognition that is the object of unsurpassed delight.

By whom could this portion of the world—whose mass of activities for the sake of beings never ceases through various multitudes of emanations—be abandoned, if indeed its emergence were considered appropriate? It is merely a conceptual construction.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the establishment of affliction and purification, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.

411 [Third Chapter] But how, when one abides solely in self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), can the relationship of cause and effect be established, so that the sequence of causes and effects under discussion may become an object of focused attention? For it is thus: there is no prior [cause], no subsequent [effect], nor even anything consisting of a synthesis produced by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of both.

The intellect (*buddhi*) is unable to enter into the conventional experience of the relation between cause and effect— which is inseparable from the apprehension of difference in the form "this [is] from that"—

because all cognitions consist solely of their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and thus it is impossible for them to have any acquaintance with the discourse of another. Although by the first cognition only the limit (*avadhimātra*) is apprehended and not the possessor of the limit (*avadhimat*), and by the subsequent cognition only the possessor of the limit is apprehended and not the limit, [this is so] through the synthesizing intellect (*anusandhāna-buddhi*).

But since it is not apprehended by even a single [cognition], who else could be the cognizer? Even the notion that "this is the limit" or "that is the limit" arises solely through the power of that [cognition]; for not even a single [external] object exists as such.
Consequently, the object of those two [cognitions] is also merely their own pure nature.
By this, the relation of priority and posteriority is refuted, because they are not grasped as prior or posterior in any way whatsoever, whereby they would consist of that [relation].

Thus, the fulfillment of the desire is that there exists a state of cause and effect. For perception has no operation here, since priority and posteriority are set aside when there is an absence of distinct cognitions. Nevertheless, it might be argued that because they arise sequentially, there is indeed a state of priority and posteriority;

therefore, the cognition of "prior" and "posterior" makes its own nature, which consists precisely of that prior and posterior form, the object of experience. However, due to the absence of a reflective form (*vimarśa*), the word [does not apply].

Thus it is set forth as supreme. Yet, by that much, there is no loss of the experience of the object; for indeed, "name" (nāma) is not the actual thing itself, yet it too proceeds subsequently through a conceptualizing cognition (*anusandhāna-buddhi*). Nor, by that much, is its self-awareness (*svavedana*) impaired;
for it is precisely through self-cognition that it brings about a sublation by means of the specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by each preceding moment.
And the cognition of cause and effect is precisely the cognition of a fixed sequence of prior and posterior states.
To this, it is replied:
At the time of the conceit of self-awareness as non-self, all this is fit for worldly transaction; however, when one is intent upon the awareness of one's own true nature, [all this ceases].
What connection could there be with the prior and posterior states of difference?
Just as there is mutual grasping by those of divided intellects regarding external objects, so too is there division in that [consciousness];
likewise, there is also the relation of prior and posterior, unless—
There is no external object at all, yet there is the perception of an external object.
In the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*:
"Just as there is a sequence of before and after for external objects,
so too is there the apprehension of cognition itself."
And memory, when it is consistent, is effective in both cases;
otherwise, experience would be of no use at all.
Therefore, that which was established by the intellect through subsequent reflection is indeed self-evident even for one who lacks valid cognition;
however, this is so only when there is the descent of valid cognition, not when the supreme [reality] remains unknown.
This state is clearly like a painting in the sky.
Nor can such a state be established even by the purification of the internal organ (*koṣṭha*),
since it has never been within the scope of practical realization; for it has never been seen by anyone at any other time.
If one can tolerate doubt that is not contradicted by valid cognition.
Therefore, even the sequence [of cognition] cannot exist without a method of determination; that too is like a blind man in perceiving another object.
Consequently, it is merely a distraction from the external and is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
There is no confusion within its own self; therefore, there is no succession.
Likewise, the sound itself is not established; thus, that which is perceived as being both prior and posterior is unreal.
For there is no cognition of another, nor is it an illusion of the self.
Even in the case of error, it is not intended by [the proponent] himself in that manner.

But surely, how can even you establish the negation of the relation between cause and effect, given the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For perception is not determinative because it is non-conceptual; nor is mere conceptualization [determinative] because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that the determination arising from perception or from a logical mark (*liṅga*) is determinative of its own cause—the object—due to an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), then [that determination itself] must be established by a means of valid cognition.
In that case, how could the relation of cause and effect be sublated?

That is incorrect; for in this way, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not demonstrated, because when perception is negated in its grasping of the relation of cause and effect, it implies a negation of its own operation. Furthermore, if one relies on the acceptance of another, there is no independent establishment of the *prasanga*.
Because it is a means of proof (*sādhana*). This presentation merely brings forward an obstruction to the opponent's negation.
And so, in *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*:
If there were sublation of the cause from some source, then the relation between cause and effect would remain;
but if that very cause does not exist, then the relation between cause and effect is not established.

By saying "there is no cause," he refers to [the argument] beginning with "it would have a cause" and so forth. Furthermore, once the negation of another's position has been established, one's own conventional usage of "existence" is not thereby proven. If it is argued that for the opponent as well, there is merely a blockage to the establishment of their own conceptualization, and that the relationship between cause and effect is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then [the opponent's claim of] non-existence is not...

If it is argued that this is established by circular reasoning (*hārasiddhi*), we say no; for the opponent has initiated the argument by assuming only that much [of the relationship]. Indeed, even the conventional usage of "existence" is established as dependent upon a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, if there were some means of valid cognition regarding the relation of cause and effect, that relation would exist;
but in its absence, how could this [relation] be? Thus, this relation of cause and effect is [only perceived] at certain times and in certain places through perception...
Devoid of cultivation, he maintains unerring loving-kindness toward external objects.
If it is argued that [the opponent's position] is not equal because other defects are also possible in the external [system],
then another refutation has been stated here by the author of the Bhāṣya as well.
Even though there was no entry by those who follow the Sūtras and Vārtikas,
the author of the Bhāṣya likewise reflected his own independence out of strength.
Or rather, why is this fault not considered to apply exclusively to the external as well?
Otherwise, how could there be an effort such as "if the external were experienced," and so forth?
Therefore, let this rule or prohibition established by his benevolence be heeded by the wise; what is the use of anything else?

But surely, even so, for one who concludes that "this follows from that reasoning," the reason (*hetu*) has already been discarded; moreover, one must ultimately resort to non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Thus, how can there be any presentation of logic (*yuktinyāsa*) without the reason? For such [a conclusion] is not...
In such a discussion, it is possible to remain silent.
When one speaks, something must necessarily be either established or refuted;
in that case, how can there be a cognition for one who asserts that [the act of speaking] is causeless, given that it pervades itself?
Therefore, this grasping of causes by the virtuous is indeed difficult to abandon.
Furthermore, the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* is contradicted by its own words, for from that very statement, the understanding of the meaning would arise for him.

How could one deny that the utterance of words is invariably concomitant with the acceptance of the relationship between cause and effect? Moreover, since all systematic arrangements are governed by the relationship between cause and effect, this doctrine would result in the total collapse of such order.
This too is inconsistent; for it is not the case that the relationship between cause and effect does not exist, even though it is established through conceptual determination.
In reality; therefore,
however,
as long as there is no cessation of conventional usage which is deluded by nature.
To that extent, the appropriation of causes in such and such a manner is not faulty.
Just as one accepts a reason for the sake of establishing merely one's own cognition,
so too does one accept its invariable concomitance when denying cause and effect.
If it is established by worldly convention, let the relationship between cause and effect remain; but if it is established by direct perception, then let self-awareness be accepted.

Indeed, it is not a matter for the respect of the wise that self-awareness—which is incompatible with the apprehension of a distinction pervading prior and posterior states—should persist while simultaneously cognizing the nature of causes and effects as being arranged in a sequence of before and after. Therefore, rather than tolerating such a direct apprehension of cause and effect, it is more appropriate to abandon this addiction to the doctrine of Vijñānavāda. Consequently, just as causes such as illumination are without an external object...

The means of proof (*sādhana*) are useful for reminding one of conventional usage by relying upon the relative truth (*saṃv�iti*); likewise, the statements of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vacana*) that establish causal capacities (*śakti*) are not contradictory. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is known by the person engaged in worldly convention (*sāṃvyavahārika*) as being preceded by the apprehension of difference.
Once direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that grasps non-difference has arisen, [the notion of difference] dissolves of its own accord; at times, it may not even grasp difference.
In that regard, as long as there is the manifestation of activity by both disputants, so much is well; for the dispute occurs only between those who abide in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
And in that case, how can there be talk of proof without a reason (*hetu*)? Well then, it is by means of a reason that the absence of a reason is to be proven.
The meaning would be that the reason negates itself; however, this is not a contradiction, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the reason itself does not exist.

Thus, even the dissolution of all established conventions (*vyavasthā*) is not a sublation, since it is precisely the cessation of the entire phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) that is auspicious (*śiva*).
For all connections between entities proceed by way of cause and effect;
yet, through self-awareness, one arrives at the partless state that is mere dependent origination.

But in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), even that which is a cause establishes that which is to be established, and the systematic arrangements (*vyavasthā*) remain intact. What accusation of self-destruction (*ātma-vadha-upālambha*) is there? (cf. *Madhyamakāvatāra-bhāṣya* p. 4, 11; *Madhyamakakārikā* 25.24).
Just as the external object, together with its preceding state associated with the grasped, exists, so too does another [moment] manifest itself as the memory that grasps it.
When one strives to investigate the root of things that are thus distressed, how can this variegated phenomenal world withstand such a denial?
Thus is the summary.

How, then, is the absence of a cause established by means of a cause? This is its meaning: in a conceptual construction that conforms to the form of ultimate reality as it has been introduced through the medium of a cause, the appearance of the absence of preceding and succeeding forms is itself the absence of the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect. Therefore, based on the fact that it is perceived as possessing activity, this self-appearance—though itself devoid of activity—is [designated as such].

It appears as if it possesses activity; therefore, that reason is renowned as the "reason for the absence of a reason. Furthermore, there is no means for attaining reality other than the specific manifestation of the form of conceptual construction. However, when one rests in the ultimate reality characterized by self-awareness alone, there is no dispute whatsoever for anyone, nor is there any application of proof or refutation. And even if that [ultimate reality] is far removed within the conventional world, it is somehow...
The mere manifestation of that form is itself the refuge.

For this very reason, for one who knows that "the cognition of an object must arise from words," the formal argument (prayoga) that "there is no cause" requires the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*). Thus, there is no contradiction; however, this fault would indeed occur if there were a total denial [of the causal relationship], as follows:

The statement that "word is not expressive" and "inference is not a valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇa) involves no contradiction whatsoever, because of the qualification "in reality" (tattvataḥ). Just like sensory perception, inference is a valid means of knowledge only from the standpoint of conventional usage (saṃvyavahārataḥ), not in reality, because it depends upon the apprehension of a relationship (saṃbandha) and so forth. Nor can that [relationship] be established by one who is immersed in mere self-awareness (svasaṃvedana-mātra); for even in the case of a reason based on essential identity (svabhāva-hetu), there is a positive concomitance (anvaya)...

Because the distinction between the two [affirmation and negation] is to be established through a difference in cognition, and because validity arises from correspondence (*saṃvāda*), yet there is no correspondence whatsoever regarding a distinct object; therefore, the validity of anything other than self-awareness is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Likewise, the conventional discourse of cause and effect is also merely conventional, since both are of a single nature of cognition.
Just as there is no valid cognition in another world, so too there is none in the cause and effect;
and just as there is cause and effect, so too there is valid cognition in another world.
On what basis, then, is the establishment of the mind asserted here?
Since, in reality, no other [external] object is established, its establishment is merely proving what is already established in conventional truth.
The intellect that is delightful only so long as it is not investigated is the conventional (saṃvṛti), as long as it is known by something else;
the reality (tattva) would be that which is apprehended by each successive cognition, up until the non-dual.
And [the principle] that "this is born from that," as well as the Sūtra and the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.
"The arising of this conceptual construction occurs for one who knows the supreme [reality] through a sign;
thus, this is merely conventional reality, and there is no such activity here for one who knows [reality] itself."
Likewise, even the intellect that performs synthesis would be mere conceit;
therefore, whatever is established from that mere conceit is merely conventional.
As long as there is conventional reality, the determination of causes and so forth remains stable;
and activity undertaken by avoiding what is undesirable is not faulty.

If [an entity] could not exist without causal capacity (*śakti*), then since that very capacity does indeed exist, the talk of its being "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) is false; what is the point of this difference in terminology?
It is not merely that the externality of cause and effect is acceptable;
rather, from a cognition in the form of a seed, this cognition in the form of a sprout arises.
For those two cognitions that know the relationship of cause and effect,
what is the use of a difference in words, since they are both simply cognitions that know an object external to their own differentiation?

In the absence of difference, there is no establishment of the relation of cause and effect due to the lack of duality; or else, those two cognitions themselves would be mutually contradictory because of their distinctness. There is neither a prior cognition nor a subsequent one, nor is there any other self that could be the grasper of them.
Afterwards, the conceptualization that "the grasper exists" will become a thorn that shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas.
If the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) is admitted, let there also be the apprehension of the external object; what is the use of shame here?
Or, if you desire liberation through the light of logic, then let there be the apprehension of the expressive power as well.
If it is determined that "it is seen," then this [object] exists even externally;
for the sublation of the external object resides precisely within self-cognition, and that same [sublation] applies to both the result and its constituent parts.
The cessation of causes and conditions is the negation of a [substantial] cause;
I declare that non-arising is the establishment of mind-only.
Manifested; "non-arising," according to the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*.
The negation of cause and effect: the very abiding in mind-only is the negation of cause and effect,
if its occurrence were by means of a cause alone.
As long as there is external determination, and as long as the notion of a self functions due to a lack of realization,
it does not proceed from anything else, unlike what occurs otherwise.
There is no certain determination apart from inference,
nor is there inference without supreme knowledge;
for that [ignorance] destroys both oneself and others.
So too are my own interests and those of others the causes for me.

Establishing inference—which arises from the means of valid cognition purified by the determination of the three marks of a reason, which by its very nature functions toward external objects, and which, though inseparable from the cognition of another, serves as a means for awakening others—by making it a proof for the sake of instructing others; and then, in a certain context, challenging that very restatement of its meaning with the fault of contradiction: what kind of logic is this? It is merely that ordinary people do not [accept] the validity of inference.
One is able to live by avoiding adherence to duality, as well as the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the truth established therein.

And that very conviction in the truth which consists in the mere realization of one's own perfected awakening is itself a repudiation of external inference and its objects. Nor can it be maintained otherwise, for if it were so, the goal would be accomplished at that very moment, which would entail the abandonment of the effort characterized by repeated practice.

Therefore, just as from the power of delusion there arises the mental resolve for a self and so forth, [so too] when direct realization is attained, the omnipresent *dharmadhātu* is established; thus, there is no returning once again to the position of inference, like ashes remaining even after the extinction of a fire whose fuel has been consumed. For this very reason:

The meaning is that the conceptualizing intellect, designated as conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), becomes tranquil when it is without an objective support (*nirālamba*). This very same point is reiterated in the context of the investigation into cause and effect;
nothing further is being prescribed. To the extent that there is external inference and mental apprehension, this alone constitutes cause and effect.

Acceptance [of that] occurs at that very time, because the mark (*liṅga*) which is its locus serves as a communicator regarding what is imperceptible, and acts as a causal factor (*kāraka*) in the cognition of it.

As for the subsequent subsistence in mere self-awareness (*ātmavedana*), that itself is the relation of cause and effect; so what is the point of this insistence? How, then, is the distinction between the causal and the communicative established by the author of the *Vārttika* in the Vijñānavāda? True, [this is] a secondary...

This is merely a conventional arrangement; therefore, the method of expression is that [the object] should be postulated by relying upon cognition. However, when the ultimate reality is being ascertained, the entire treatise on the establishment of the existence of mental forms (*sākārasiddhi*) is powerless.
[Pravāraṇavāda 2.4], and so forth.
This is the meaning: prior to the realization of non-duality, according to the distinctions between the dull, middling, and sharp intellects of the persons to be instructed, as follows...
Or rather, such a systematic arrangement may be made so that, through the gradual sharpening of the intellect, there arises confidence in non-duality which is not fixed in each respective stage.

For this very reason, although conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) possesses a multiplicity like that of successive ultimate realities (*paramārtha*), the entry into the relationship of cause and effect based upon it is precisely the reality (*tattva*) consisting in the possibility of the three kinds of perception and non-perception. This [system] is exactly the same as that starting from another conventional reality, lest there be deception regarding one's own intended position.

Conventional [cognition] is to be accepted; it is not, however, inferior simply because there is no distinction in the lack of adherence to the ultimate truth, for there is a distinction based on whether it accords with one's intention or not. Therefore, this is not even a subject for inquiry: how can the establishment of an object result from mere cognition that lacks a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), much less from that which is sublated by critical investigation? For in such cases, there is no establishment of an object other than mere personal satisfaction. Such as it is...

That very cognition is [itself] cognition; likewise, the non-establishment of an object is itself the establishment of the object—this is an offering corresponding to the spirit of the Yakṣa. If one follows the heart of the Noble Ones, then by our own heart everything exists; yet a discerning cognizer should understand it in such a way that he might be deceived even regarding mere satisfaction. Therefore, he says:
And this nature of the conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*) has been stated [in the passage beginning with] "it is said... and so forth.
Therefore, there is no fault of following a specific proof for the conventional; what thirst could there be for anything else?
Now, according to our own view, everything exists, whereas for those who have directly realized reality (*tattva-sākṣātkārin*), it does not exist—what state could that be?
True;
to one who has realized the truth, this world is like a dullard, a madman, or a ghost;
and even though he has realized the truth, he appears to the world like a dullard, a madman, or a ghost.
Therefore, in this regard, the autonomy belongs to Will.
If the world were a manifestation of what is non-existent, then its establishment would not be direct;
for there is no manifestation other than the conceptualization of its own appearance, nor [is there one] through causes and the like.

Therefore, although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) there is no relation of cause and effect, how could it be disregarded since it is impossible to avoid within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*)? The production of the result under discussion arises from a collection of causes; for one who seeks its accomplishment follows that [conventional] process precisely because it is merely conventional. However, for one who has directly realized ultimate reality (*tattvasākṣātkārin*), just as the establishment of the relation of cause and effect does not exist anywhere, so too [is it here].

Nor is there any [actual] performance [of an action]. If it is asked, "How can that which causes no benefit be real?"—we say no; for from our perspective, its continuity of performing the welfare of others has ceased at its own moment. But in reality, it has been established that luminosity alone is the actual existence (*sattā*) of the variegated form itself; thus the point is settled.
Now, even so, if it is argued that "that variegated thing is one," then this is even more variegated than that! [Pramāṇavārttika 2.200]
Furthermore, this mutual perception of difference is most extraordinary.

For "variegated" (*citra*) is defined as having various forms (*nānākāra*). Therefore, how can there be non-difference among these forms which are superimposed with mutually contradictory properties? If it is argued that even so, how can there be difference among those [forms] contained within a single cognition, given that they do not cognize one another—like distinct mental continua—and thus the consequence would be that only some single [form] appears? That is incorrect, because the superimposition of contradictory properties remains just as it was.

Therefore, this [cognition] is indeed manifold; however, because it is produced from a non-different material cause (*upādāna*), its nature consists in mutual perceptibility and the appearance of simultaneity. But there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cognitions arising in other mental continua (*santānāntara*), as they lack that state of having a non-different material cause.
Here, it is considered:
Does their having a single material cause eliminate their plurality?
And precisely because of that plurality, mutual cognition among them is not admitted.

For one consciousness does not enter into another consciousness. And it is precisely through the removal of the bolt of a single consciousness that the denial of mutual cognition between one's own and another's cognitions occurs; and since that [denial] remains unshaken even in the present case, there is no distinction. Now, if the appearance of simultaneity is to be established, what is the use of its entry into a single consciousness? For there is no harm done by that which contradicts the probandum even without it. But surely—

The term "sāhitya" (togetherness) is also known as a definition established merely by coexistence within a specific place and time. Furthermore, since their manifestation consists in the direct perception of their own respective natures, mutual cognition is not established—just as in the case of many men standing together in deep darkness. Therefore, it is only the penetration of one another's consciousness that serves the purpose of the conventional usage of "mutual cognition"; what is the use of "sāhitya" here?

Is it by way of a mere measure? Or, if the term "appearance of concomitance" (sāhityapratibhāsa) is intended to mean that there is indeed an appearance [of objects] everywhere for all [cognitions], then even when the appearance of concomitance is the probandum, the argument that "pervasion by a single universal consciousness" is contradictory is a hollow verbal formulation;
for in that sense, this is merely a synonym [for the same point].
If it is argued that there is no mutual determination within a single cognition, then upon the denial of that [determination], there would be no mutual perception at all;
this flaw regarding the object is here unbearable.

In the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, let it be that there is no assistance from the appearance of a literary composition; for if the appearance of one were for the sake of the appearance of another, even though they share a non-different substratum (*abhinnopādāna*), their distinction would not be negated. This is because, regarding the refutation that "one's own cognition does not enter into another's cognition," [the objection remains].
We do not know what has been made superior, since there is no nourishment of any distinction when merely enumerating synonyms.
Moreover,
even when they share a single substratum, those [cognitions] do not enter into one another's awareness even when combined; otherwise, what indeed would constitute their difference?
Immersed solely in their own consciousness, they do not touch upon the consciousness of another;
yet they perceive one another—this is truly a great wonder.

If it is argued that there is a thorough familiarity [of the mind] due to the non-difference of the causal conditions (*upādāna*), then it would be better that there be no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of the objects]; for even when [objects] are distinct, there is no such experience.
Likewise, if a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were capable of apprehending a restricted object, [it would follow that all objects are apprehended].
If one were to create that mind, what fear could there be? In either case, it is undermined by the defining characteristic [of being a creator].

This being so, there is no fear whatsoever regarding the refutation of that which possesses the characteristic of being an object (*grāhya*) by virtue of its arising and its similarity [to the cognition];

for for the proponent of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*), the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is easily established in quite another way. In that case, because there is no distinction in their material cause (*upādāna*), all [cognitions] experience one another, since they all have the nature of experience (*anubhavasvabhāvatva*). However, when produced by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrījanyatva*), the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the experience (*anubhava*) possess their respective restricted states of being the object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and the knower (*vedakatva*).

And [this] would be so; and because of that restriction, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Now, if it is asked: "Since even an insentient thing manifests at that time, how is there a fixed determination?"—the answer is: the object is that which has an insentient material cause (*upādāna*), while the other is the subject (*grāhaka*). If it is argued that this definition is over-extensive with respect to the sense organ (*indriya*)—we say no, because by the very power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is produced as the object of cognition specifically as blue.
Through being produced together, there is mutual assistance and inseparability,
as well as an identity that precludes any distinction between you two.

If it is argued that there is the fault of commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) regarding the arising of manifestation (*prakāśa*), [we reply: its arising is by way of being cognizable (*vedyatva*), not by way of being manifestation itself. If it is asked, "What is this 'being cognizable'?", [the answer is: the objection—"How can there be mutual cognition between two things known by themselves?"—is the same [for both sides]. Furthermore, if it is argued that "being cognizable" is nothing other than the arising of manifestation, even so, the fault of commonality will be avoided precisely through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Now, since an entity is of a single nature, just like its blueness, it cannot remain without manifesting—given that non-manifestation is likewise unique [to it]—unless it has first come into being. To this we reply: "It is indeed possible through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)," so let us remain silent on this point. [Jñānaśrīmitra, *Nibandhāvalī*] Now, if this matter is contradicted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what power of the causal complex could possibly be brought forward? As for that which...

Even its manifestation does not require [another], for in the determination of its own nature, it dissolves by itself; how then can there be a designation of non-difference between the substrate and the object?

For when two lights have arisen, one light is not illuminated by the other, nor does one appear to the other, nor is there any logical consistency in saying "in one. Just as the self-luminosity of a lamp is somehow known, and in accordance with that knowledge—

Just as it is understood [that one lamp does not illuminate another], so too no mutual illumination between lamps is ever observed; therefore, just as the notion that "one lamp is illuminated by another lamp" is an error, so too is the notion that "one cognition is known by another cognition. Consequently, for what purpose should there be an answer consisting of a single substratum?

By this, even the denial of the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda) regarding "self-cognition" is not rejected, provided that the avoidance of over-extension (ativyāpti) is easily achieved.
This too is refuted, because the very object of another's cognition remains unestablished.

If it is argued that the illumination of another is indeed observed, even that occurs only by way of generating a subsequent moment of light within that which was previously non-luminous; thus, there is no room for such an objection in the case of cognitions, lamps, and the like. As for the claim that even in those cases, the co-existent light is the illuminator of the cloth—
He [the opponent] also [claims] that the determination of reality does not occur through mere worldly convention (*lokādhyavasāya*).

If, in the inference that serves as the basis for the determination "this belongs to this," one were to depend upon the production of that cognition, then—given the acceptance that the object is revealed simultaneously with the cognition—the determination that "it does not exist" would be untenable. Now, is there parity here too with respect to the subsequent conceptual cognition (*pṛṣṭhajavikalpajñāna*)? If so, then this very [point applies].
"The former [the object] is not the grasper; this [the cognition], however, is simultaneous"—this is the entry point into the Sautrāntika doctrine.

Now, if it is argued that light does not possess the quality of being an illuminator merely by generating cognition, and that cognition likewise exists only as a co-existent factor—merely by virtue of arising simultaneously with its causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—then it would follow that the sense organs existing at that same time must also be illuminators, since they too [arise simultaneously]. Their...

If it is argued that [the lamp] is so because its nature is light (*prakāśa*), then let the light itself be light; but how can it be an illuminator? For blue cannot become yellow merely by being in the company of something yellow. Therefore, nothing that is ineffective can occupy a position within the framework of relationship. However, through the medium of assisting the cause, a lamp is seen to participate in the conventional usage [of "illuminating"] with respect to jars and the like, which are not of the nature of light.

Therefore, if one intends that the cognition of that [first] cognition is itself manifested by another cognition, and thus there exists a single understood material cause (*upādāna*), one might indeed refrain from using the genitive case;

however, this is not so with respect to its status as direct perception (*adhyakṣatā*). This is unlike the case of "Maitra is handsome for Caitra," where the genitive is used with respect to the understood quality of handsomeness, but not otherwise.
Direct perception [occurs] with respect to beauty, because the two beauties reside in a single substrate.

If it is argued that no one uses [the term] in this way, [we reply]: if he were a critic, how could he even use it, since the logic is the same? Thus, by the maxim of the blind man grasping at milk, this [objection] has already been disposed of, as it lacks the defining characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

This is the gateway to the non-dual means of the Leader of Logic (*nyāyanāyaka*). Nor is this logic [flawed]; so what is the point of this "shaking about" (*loṭana*) favored by Śubhagupta out of hatred for the Vārttikakāra? If it is argued: "In that case, what is the purpose of the cognition that cognitions appear both together and separately, like many lamps?"—[we reply: No, for they appear as "together" only in relation to a distinct perceiver.
This is the conventional usage. Now, even in the absence of that [external object], the manifestation of things when combined is not exhausted. This is true;

however, in the *Sākārasiddhi-śāstra*, there is no such thing as "one being the manifestation of another. Furthermore, since the nature of self-manifestation exists even for those [senses] covered by a blindfold, it is not [the case that manifestation depends on another].

The proof has been set forth. Therefore, it is only through the mutual inclusion within consciousness that the conventional usage of "mutual cognition" is established. For there is not even a rumor that lamps originating from a single source are themselves mutually illuminating.
In that case, the individual atoms are indeed distinct; if the living soul is even more dear [to the Lord], then it is clear that there is a unique, uncommon cause for such an unseen power (adṛṣṭa).
Moreover,
if it is argued that just as a lamp is seen to be self-luminous and yet manifold,
so too would their mutual manifestation be observed there due to the non-difference of the seed [of consciousness], then this is indeed well said.

Thus, this arising from a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī-sambhava*) may, by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), enable the inference of one thing upon the perception of another in certain cases; it does not, however, lead to the direct perception (*adhyakṣatva*) of the other, as is the case with taste, color, and so forth. Likewise, having a single material cause (*ekopādānatā*) would establish a further degree of homogeneity (*sajāyīyatā*), but not the manifestation of another [quality] which is to be proven through a confusion of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-saṅkara*). Otherwise, in some cases, one might even claim that one [thing] is insentient (*jaḍa*) while the other is not.

By this, the conceptualization that mutual manifestation consists simply in having a non-different material cause (*abhinnopādānatva*) is also refuted; for even insentient things (*jaḍa*) that share a single material cause would entail a mutual insentiency, since their insentiency—as well as their luminosity—consists in their very nature as self (*ātmarūpa*). Thus, the same applies to luminosity.
The existence of a thing is not established by way of producing a form;
likewise, let it be so according to convention through the state of having a single material cause.

For just as, according to the Sautrāntika, the state of being an object of cognition consists solely in the production of a similar form and not in its manifestation, so too the manifestation of one [color] would be the manifestation of another, and there would be no perception of a variegated [form]. Furthermore, even the fact of having a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*) must be understood here in its pure sense, because it is determined that in both the states of dream and waking, the cause is exclusively the variegated form itself. [The text continues: *vyākula-*...

Even at the same time, because conceptualization possesses multiple forms; and even when conceptualizing a single object, because its form is variegated according to the difference in spatial location.

Furthermore, regarding the production of an aggregate from an aggregate, if the causal capacity is attributed to only one [of the causes], then in some cases the fact that multiple things act as producers—which conforms to the presence or absence [of the effect]—is the same. This is because we observe the arising of a blue form even from a distinct blue form.

For one who asserts that a variegated [effect] arises from a non-variegated [cause], there is no state of deficiency or excess, because it is impossible to enumerate [the causal factors]. Furthermore, like a banyan tree,
even if there were deficiency or excess, something single might produce many.

But there is no single nature for that which is deficient; nor is it a wonder that the non-dual [is manifold]. In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*, it is stated that just as that cognition [arises], so too does another manifold [cognition] arise from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) through a distinct location immediately after states such as deep sleep. Or, let it be that at some time and in some place, [a manifold arises] from a single, coalesced form.

The existence of a variegated [cognition] occurs either successively or non-successively. First, when immediately following the waking state, for as long as one is not obstructed by torpor (*middha*) and so forth, there would be no mutual experience of moments other than those belonging to the first moment, because of the difference in their material causes (*upādāna*). If it is argued that this is due to their being awakened from that same [single] cause through a continuous succession, then, to the extent that there is an interval [between them], to that same extent...

Due to the gradation of intensity, there would be a mutual obscuration or destruction [of forms] at some distance; however, the non-destruction of variegated manifestation is experienced for many days through states such as waking, nor is there any gradation of intensity therein. It is not so in the case of the form of cognition.
If you say it is possible, how can it be possible for there to be the cognition of a distinct thing through a single-form cognition, unless there is non-difference of the material cause (*upādāna*),

since it is precisely the internal difference or non-difference that is the determining factor? Nor does the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) establish the actual state of affairs, because its conclusion is the opposite [of what was intended].
Furthermore,

if the apprehension of the derived [effect] occurs because of its connection with the material cause, why does the same not apply to the material cause itself? Thus, mere connection is not the determining factor.

For cognition is by nature remote from one another; yet, having transcended that limit, proximity reveals its own power, and that [proximity] is primary only in relation to the material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, just as in inference which depends on a single causal complex, the experience of a distinct co-existent entity would have to occur solely through the mediation of the apprehension of its cause. If it is argued that this is not the case because [the object] is past, [we reply: no, for there is no such thing as remoteness in terms of intrinsic nature or time.

There is some distinction. Now, regarding the material cause (*upādāna*), both of these [proximity and non-proximity] are merely a distance of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*) from the co-existent entity. In that case, proximity would be inferior here, whereas it is mature [or primary] in the material cause; thus, there is the "lizard-and-rabbit" logic (*godhā-śaśa-nyāya*). Furthermore, the persistence of perception is due to the power of proximity. If, then, there were a manifestation of the past, it would have to be present; how could it be past? Therefore, it is not past.

[Objection: Manifestation! If such a vision of reality were the case, then that which is being experienced by the supreme consciousness as its own self would be nothing other than one's own nature; how then could there be the cognition of another?

In that regard, let the proclamation of "contact" for one whose eyes are not yet opened apply elsewhere as well. Or rather, like a yogin, there may even be the grasping of what is beyond [the senses].

It might be so; yet, in such a continuous progression, there would be the consequence of perceiving every preceding moment, either until reaching a single material cause (*upādāna*) or until there is no limit at all.

Just as there is a gradation in the degree of separation, so too there is a gradation in the intensity of proximity. Thus, if there were the consequence of the appearance of even its own material effect, everything would be like that. Furthermore, if the variegated appearance were indeed a [single] distinct entity, then—just like blue and yellow—it would be [a single color], such as blue.

Since even the two parts [of a composite] are seen to be ultimately reducible to atoms, there exists nothing whatsoever that is perceived as a single entity which could have another thing as its material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, the entire world would fall into an unobstructed blindness. Nor does this doctrine conclude with the mere statement "nothing whatsoever.
This is the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.

If this is precisely what you intend to say, why this trivial prevarication? Let it simply be stated that, by a straightforward process, even the multiplicity of entities does not exist. If you argue that the unreality of forms is already accepted, even so, why this [argument] which fails to withstand scrutiny?
Moreover,
since mental aspects (ākāra) are not real entities, it is impossible for them to have a single material cause;
however, there is no such defect in the case of mere luminosity (prakāśamātra), even though it lacks internal differentiation.

Thus, there is a collapse of the established tenet (*siddhānta*). Consequently, even if this non-difference of the material cause (*upādāna*) is asserted independently of the Teacher, it cannot bring about the mutual experience and manifestation of these forms (*ākāra*) without implying a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, if a difference were admitted, one could not tolerate their mutual appearance.
But the patience regarding mutual manifestation is the supreme state of subject and object.
Therefore, what is the ultimate truth here? For if it is seen in this way, let it be seen; however, [it is seen] as non-different.
This deserves to be investigated whether it belongs to the seed or to its own self.
If there were unity, there would be an absence of variety; if there were plurality, this [absence] would be even more certain.
Neither unity nor plurality is logically tenable for cognitions.

If the various forms are indeed the very nature of the mind, how can it be manifold? Or rather, if that mind is manifold, how can its unity be maintained? Furthermore, O Sage, the intellect does not possess the form of atoms, nor is it capable of apprehending them when they are aggregated.
And they speak with mutual confusion; this must be some kind of illusory process.
This is what the wise declare as established by the power of reality:
in whatever way objects are analyzed, they fall apart in that very same way.
[Pravāraṇavāda 2.209] That form by which entities are determined does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold form is found among them. (426)
These [opponents], corrupted by the poison of their own investigations, do not maintain the constituent parts of Jñānaśrīmitra’s collection of treatises;
for it is better to disregard those things required [for the argument] while adopting the "closing of the eyes like an elephant" (ignoring them).

Thus, it is the emptiness of all phenomena—like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflection—that is established by reason; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, if one asks: "The present investigation was undertaken concerning the Blessed One; so is the Blessed Buddha, too, like an illusion or like a dream? To whom, then, is the reproach here directed? For it is the Blessed One himself who has manifested [reality] in that way.

Is it not because [the Buddha's speech] is illuminated by the Noble Ones with joy (*sollāsam*), and because suchness (*tathatā*) is accepted as being without distinction between a Tathāgata and an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), [he possesses] a specific profundity and magnanimity celebrated in the scriptures? But surely, since this is sublated by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), and since the forms of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are unreal, what is his magnanimity? Furthermore, there would be the consequence of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). [And] because its nature is a cognition in which the non-existent appears, it is delusive (*bhrānta*). How...
Regarding profundity: that is incorrect, for error is the apprehension of something as what it is not; any other kind of error has already been refuted.
Furthermore, one does not perceive the unreal by means of an unreal form.
The Tathāgata knows phenomena exactly as they abide;
even from the perspective of conventional designation, there is no delusion regarding this, because the seed [of such delusion] is absent.
Since engagement and withdrawal arise from conceptual construction, which is born of latent predispositions,
by uprooting those two along with their root, one abides in the state beyond modification.
In this view, the theory of the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is not undesirable,
because everything appears here as non-existent in its true nature, and nothing else exists that is not sublated.
Because this has already been refuted in detail previously;
nevertheless, this very point has been accepted as a constituent part of the path that leads to the higher Dharma.
The mind, whose internal forms such as water and so forth are devoid of external objects, vibrates within with pleasure, pain, and other sensations.
"It is said that no sublation can occur here because there is no spatial extension [of the object]; but even this is erroneous. For:
"Whether directed internally toward objects such as pleasure or externally toward objects such as cold, cognition takes on the form of each respective [object] and is indeed seized by sublation."

In the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, we understand that the form (*ākāra*) of cognition belongs exclusively to a specific individual. As for the absence of spatial extension (*deśavitāna*), would it be a smallness of space or its total absence? In that regard, even if the space were the size of an atom (*paramāṇu*), the same fault would apply; how much smaller could it possibly be?

The first position is not tenable. As for the second, it is impossible, because that which is possible must necessarily exist somewhere. If it were non-existent anywhere at all, its non-existence would be established as absolute. Furthermore, states such as suffering and mental pleasure are experienced as manifesting within the body, distinguished from external locations. Otherwise, they would be like light, [indistinguishable] from blue and other such objects.
If there is no distinction [between the atoms], the same fault applies.
Furthermore, what is the point of asking how much space they occupy within that body? Or what is this "having spatial extension"?
For even in the case of form (*rūpa*), nothing is perceived anywhere apart from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) that could be designated as "space. Nor is the locus itself the space.

Otherwise, it would follow that even wind and sunlight would lack spatial location. Furthermore, the operation of a sublation does not depend on that [spatial location], but rather on the intrinsic nature [of the object].

And just as the intrinsic nature, though partless, appears in the conceptualizing intellect as if surrounded by distinct, additional attributes, so too is "space" (deśa)—which is the opposite of the cognition that reflects upon time and form—conceptually constructed as the counterpart to the movement through space, such that one perceives "this is here."

It does not indeed enter into conventional usage; nor has it already been stated that this state [of consciousness] does not persist within feelings such as internal pleasure or mental ease, just as it does not persist in contact (*sparśa*) and so forth? Now, if the thought is that—unlike in the case of blue and other objects, where one perceives a very clear distinction between upper and lower parts, as well as their being delimited by measurements such as a *vitasti*, a *hasta*, an elephant, or a man—the same is not the case for pleasure and so forth, then:

What is the point in knowing merely their location? For in that case, it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things such as smell, taste, sound, and so forth—which do not possess tactile organs—would likewise lack a fixed location.
Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a specific location for fire and other such things when they are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).

Now, one might argue that since smell and taste are present in whatever fruit they occur within, it is possible to infer that the two [the universal and the particular] reside in a fixed location; however, this is not the case for others...

If it is argued that [the soul] is perceived at the time of grasping by means of its eastern part and so forth, and by the measurement of the remaining sense organs? Why then can pleasure and the like not also be apprehended by the measurement of the location within the body where they are experienced? Furthermore, non-pervasion is observed in the case of the perception of smell and taste in their effects.
If it is argued that the perceiver is perceived in a fixed location, even that [perceiver], which grasps gross objects, does not perceive the location as consisting of atoms in a restricted manner.
It is capable of measuring. Therefore, in this case, it is the same: it exists by pervading some extent of space.

Likewise, at the time of perception as well, there is indeed a determination of the specific restriction of that which is delimited by the location of the sense organ. This same principle applies even to pleasure and so forth; for even that which is produced from seeing or hearing—such as the eye itself becoming cool upon seeing a beloved after being scorched by the sight of what is unpleasant—is the same.

This is experienced by you. However, when one who is scorched by the hot rays [of the sun] plunges into a pond, there is a manifest distinction of magnitude or a sense of upper and lower parts. Even if one were to imagine the rising of another location there, it would still be that very same location. A restriction of magnitude is appropriate for kings upon their respective lands. And this alone is human happiness—that which is verbal cognition; thus, there is no proof of a difference.

Or [it is established] because of its clear appearance. As for mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), however, because it is mental in nature, even when its appearance is not clear, there is no obstacle to its general establishment here [in this context] as being possible in some particular location, following from that [pleasure]. Nor is there any insistence [on its necessity].
In that case, it would be useless, because it would follow that even the probandum (*sādhya*) would be conceptual (*vikalpaka*).

Furthermore, if there were no determination of a restriction of magnitude (*parimāṇa*), then while there might be a negation of spatial location (*deśavattā*) in some cases, let there not be a negation of temporal location (*kālavattā*) for anything at all, since it is impossible to determine the magnitude of a moment (*kṣaṇa*). It simply did not exist previously.
Furthermore, the more robust cognition that "it does not exist at the five [senses]" establishes its occurrence at a specific time.

Here too, the certainty remains established that pleasure and so forth do not exist outside the body, but exist only here within it. Moreover, the connection with time is indeed accepted for pleasure and so forth; otherwise, the sound reasoning that they would never occur at all would serve as a sublation, and that very same [reasoning] applies to their spatial location.
It brings [the object] near, because it is sometimes non-existent and at other times conjoined with existence. And that very place where it exists is the location;
whether that [location] is gross or subtle—what does this matter? As for time, the establishment of its restriction is made in view of another purpose.

Just as the restriction to a specific time is clearly evident, so too is the restriction to a specific location; however, this spatial restriction occurs either through minuteness or through excessiveness.
But in neither case is there an absence of contradiction, as is seen in the case of pleasure and the like.
What indeed is achieved by a refutation through mere words when there has already been a specific rejection?

Thus, since spatial existence is necessarily concomitant with mere existence, just like temporal existence, it cannot avoid the possibility of the non-perception of a pervader anywhere; nor can one say "let it not be so," for how else could the conventional usage of "existence" itself be established in the case of pleasure and the like?
If the distinction between the one and the many is not established, then even for you, the duality [of subject and object] cannot be established;
for, like a limited person casting aside the light of his own knowledge, [you must reject] either of the two—oneness or its opposite.

For just as, because pleasure and the like do not appear with a form situated before one like blue, it is impossible to ascertain their exclusion from being either unitary or manifold; likewise, for that very reason, the possibility of either of those two [unitary or manifold] is also [impossible], since the determination "this which shines before me is either one or many" is what is actually perceived. Even in the case of something imperceptible, if it were established in that way according to its observed nature, even though it does not shine before one—

Since spatial restriction occurs in accordance with the form appearing before one's eyes, let it be established that those two [space and time] are also absent—just like sparks from a fiercely blazing fire.
If it is argued that "that which exists must necessarily exist in some manner," we say no; for because they are all-pervasive, there is doubt regarding either one of them.

Because there is doubt regarding the very existence of a sentient being (*sattva*). As for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), however, cast away its power just as you would a white conch-shell; do not remain with hope for it.

Furthermore, since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even one who points out the "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) for another does not himself engage in the conventional usage of "existent. This is because, in the absence of both a proof and a refutation, doubt is logically established. And in the case of what is self-cognized...

In the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*, the very absence of any sublation (*bādhā*) regarding the mass of the intrinsic nature of cognitions such as blue is the powerful seed for this [position]. If it is argued: "In that case, let there be invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of self-cognition; however, in the absence of sublation, there is validity"—it is not so, because of non-perception...

Since non-existence is established by mere [non-perception], and because for one who has practiced [the observation] externally there is the possibility of a corroborating factor that is non-subverting, there is no other "non-perception of the perceptible. However, this discussion regarding non-subversion has already been considered in the *Śāstra*; let it rest for now.
In this same way, even stories and the like produced by the Vedas possess the status of valid cognition.
The claim that "validity is established by default" has also been swallowed up by subsequent arguments.
They know that even where validity is intrinsic, it is the fruit of repeated practice; for everything practiced externally is unreal, yet it is contemplated within.
If it is argued that the appearance of the mass of objective forms, though unreal, cannot be denied because of the power of the subjective form—
just as pleasure and so forth [cannot be denied]— we say no;
for both parts possess the nature of self-luminosity.
What could be the grasped or the grasper? For there is no manifestation of one thing by means of another.
Thus, since it has already been established that there is no external defect [in this view], the state of reality does not arise from mere conceit.

Furthermore, in this system, if the entire host of afflictions— attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, and so forth— is innate, by virtue of being of the nature of formless cognition just like suffering and the rest;
And what distinction could there be between the desirable and the undesirable, my dear friend, in the view that [the mind] possesses form? How, then, could there be detachment?

For you, the connection with the aspect of light (*ālokākāra*) is an error. Due to its absence, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [afflictions] would exist as the very nature of those dwelling in existence; for if they were unreal by way of their objective support (*ālambana*), it would follow that even pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth would be so. Therefore, the rejection of what is undesirable and the adoption of what is otherwise—this is precisely the position of the Sākāravādins stated in different words. [The text continues: "the visible portion of the circle of aspects (*ākāracakra*)."

However, this argument—that disagreement culminates in what is tangible—is of no consequence. Just as something may be abandoned by someone because it is undesirable even though it is an error, so too, let a particular form remain because it is desirable even though it belongs to the world; thus, there is no damage to the thesis. Furthermore, these [factors] such as pleasure are accepted as mental concomitants (*caitta*); the mind (*citta*), insofar as it grasps the object, has the nature of the form and is to be discarded, whereas the mental concomitant is that which persists in its state.

This contradicts scripture, for [the object] is not a factor associated with the mind (*saṃprayuktadharma*). Furthermore, if there is no difference [between the mind and its objects], they must be unreal just like the mind, or else the mind itself must be real just like them; how then can the probandum—the formless [mind]—be established?
Now, one might argue that whatever is meditated upon becomes clear in that very way, and thus the mind could be meditated upon even as having the form of space.
In that case, pride will become manifest; and since it lacks a well-established form, it is itself formless—so how can there be the establishment of the probandum?
No, because there is no purpose [in such a claim].
(Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī, 430)
If you desire to attain the state of space, you must cast off this physical body, which is untouched by the defects of saṃsāra and radiant with the primary and secondary marks of a great being.
Is it not true that this *saṃbhogakāya* is indeed accepted by the sons of the Arhats?
One who desires to attain the *dharmakāya* should worship the body that is like space.

If this is argued, then that [cognition] is not the probandum (*sādhya*), because the desired object is already fully established by what has been stated. Nor is it a means of proof (*sādhana*) for any object, since the establishment of any object from a formless [cognition] is unproven. It has already been stated that the establishment of an object for another [person] is likewise strictly bound to a specific form. Now, who could possibly maintain that the establishment of an object arises from the form itself, while it arises from something else—namely, the formless?

Could it possibly return from elsewhere than from the *syādvāda*? If you argue that this is so because of scripture (*āgama*), then what refuge can there be for a scripture when its meaning is contradicted by reasoning (*yukti*)? Since the capacity of an object is distinguished by a specific form conjoined with merit and knowledge, and since that [capacity] reaches its ultimate limit within itself, how could it be severed from that, or from anything else?
How could it be possible? For whom could such a cognition ever be impossible? Nor does the primary scriptural text (*āgama*) have such a meaning;

any recourse to another interpretation might occur through the boldness of one's reasoning, but that [boldness] has been exhausted—this is what was considered. Nevertheless, out of fear of contradiction (*bādha*), that very form must be accepted; and since it is not contradicted, let it also be established that it alone is capable of conveying the meaning, and for that very reason [it is authoritative].
If it is argued that even prior [to linguistic convention], the capacity of the object resides only in that which is connected to it, the connection is "just like that.
There is no such mode of convention whatsoever.

Wherever it is situated, no contradiction can strike it down. For instance, as for this sky which has the form of fire: if it were pervasive like space, then its refutation would be exactly like that of space itself.
Even when compared to moonlight, lightning, the radiance of jewels, sparks of fire, and so forth, [it remains unsurpassed].
How can that which has not been perceived either in its own nature or by way of an illustrative example be established as having a form, and by whom could it be compared to those very things?

Will it come to pass? For one who is dispassionate toward form, that knowledge arises from the very cultivation of the right path through the cognition of purity; it does not arise from the mere meditation upon that [object], for such a person is free from the danger of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Furthermore: in a composite [entity], there is the same fault as with its parts; in an indivisible [entity], there is the same fault as with an atom (*paramāṇu*).
There is no other entity here, for emptiness is all-consuming.

Therefore, the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* must be accepted even by one who fears the ruin caused by contradiction; yet it is impossible [to accept].
