If you argue that it must indeed be accepted because it was spoken in the *Pravacana*, then is this now like drinking salt water from a "father's well," or like [seeking] the source of the elements (*dhātu*)?

Is it not the case that the path of the Śrāvakas and others was not taught by him? And here, even that which is indicated as something to be abandoned is not abandoned because of ignorance; rather, it is due to the inclination and desire of those to be trained. For the Blessed One is an authority precisely because he teaches the way to heaven. Therefore, since there is no cognition of its utility [in that context], and since there is an absence of any demonstration of the transgression of a prohibition regarding what is not visible to oneself, [there is no fault].
From where could there be accomplishment born of cultivation? The culmination of activity lies precisely in the enjoyment (saṃbhoga);
its qualities are restricted solely to that, as is its inclination; its measure is likewise restricted solely to that.
The other [type of activity] is equal only through sublation.
Alas, those for whom the Victor is merely an external authority have lost even their own Teacher—
he who was grasped through the direct method and who shines with the characteristics [of the Dharma] derived from the scriptures.
Emptiness is nothing other than consciousness, and profundity resides within that [consciousness].
It has been deliberated whether that [profundity] pertains to all imagined phenomena.
Even in the scriptures, it is not heard by one's own words that a formless substratum possesses the nature of the Dharma-body; nor has any other explanation been made [to this effect].

If it is desired that the mind be partless because it lacks any observed parts, then let it indeed be entirely empty. If it is not entirely [empty], then there can be no analogy for something partless.
Is even renunciation not a lover of that which is dear?

For it was shown previously that the resemblance to space occurs precisely through the departure from adventitious stains and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, the comparison to space is made everywhere according to the very same correspondence (*sādharmya*) taught in the Mahāyāna-uttara-tantra, such as "free from conceptual construction like the sky," and so forth. Thus, it is not by way of a lack of form (*ākāra-viraha*). As for that which [was said]:
In that which is nothingness, without appearance, without support, and without basis;
even when the eye has transcended it, it is formless and invisible.
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, among the Buddhas, everything is seen, yet it does not exist in that way. (Jñānaśrīmitra-nibandhāvalī 432)

Thus it is said. In this regard, the qualification "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) and so forth is clearly intended to manifest the absence [of such qualities] even when the sky appears to have elevations and depressions caused by dust, clouds, and the like. Furthermore, the use of the locative construction "among the Buddhas" (*buddheṣu*) rather than saying "even in the Perfectly Awakened One" (*saṃbuddhe 'pi*) is an effort to employ a plural number that serves as a refutation. However, regarding the Blessed Sugata, there is indeed neither denial (*apavāda*) nor superimposition (*samāropa*) in the manner described.

What is intended here is merely this: that even when there is the perception of characteristics—such as depressions and elevations—there is no [intrinsic] existence. Or, let it be applied to the Blessed One as well by changing the grammatical gender of the statement. As stated by the venerable Master Vasubandhu in the *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*, in the section concerning the definition of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*): "Because it cannot be defined by means of the duality of the apprehended and the apprehender, it is formless (*arūpi*)."

It was distinguished [in the previous context] as being "without appearance" because it possesses an object; likewise, let it be so here when the term "Buddha" is employed. Its state of possessing nothing (*akiñcanatva*) is to be understood as the departure of adventitious passion (*rāga*) and the like. The remainder is not contradictory. Therefore, it is precisely within the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) that—
Since it is established that error consists in the non-manifestation of the innumerable [aspects] as the self,
it should be understood without confusion that manifestation has the sense of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

"Just as one might say, 'How do you see it? It appears and manifests in this way,' so too the expression 'it appears' (khyāti) is not contradictory even when applied to conceptual construction (vikalpa)."
And because [this] is very clear in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:
"If, however, manifestation were intended to be the appearance of a non-existent form,
then the enjoyment of the Sage would be like that of a crown prince or a king— which is impossible."
Why did he not state that its manifestation as something else occurs through its sovereignty?
For instance, he clearly distinguished the meanings of permanence and omnipresence.
Therefore, this determination is said to be the manifestation of the non-existent;
hence, out of fear of expending silver, let no heap of jewels be cast aside.
If this same principle applies even to the abandonment of the *dharmakāya* as spoken by him,
then who, indeed, would have gone for refuge to the Buddha by way of rejecting him?
The property of the entity, which is the nature of the subject, is its general characteristic;
it is considered to be the Dharma-body, known as emptiness, which delivers those who are timid.
This nature, known as the "essential" (svābhāvika), is proclaimed by such terms as emptiness, suchness, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the peak of existence (bhūtakoṭi).
The *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* proclaims that, according to the Yogācāra system, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) exists;
yet, through the non-existence of duality, universal emptiness is established on the Middle Way.
The revolution of the outflows is itself the untainted realm;
it is the reality and the ultimate truth, and because of the awakening to that, one is called a Buddha.
When a cognition has that ascertainment as its result, the qualities that depend upon its power cannot be denied,
just as [the qualities] of a distinct subject [cannot be denied].

For this manifold [world], which is necessarily manifesting, must be directly realized as emptiness; by that alone is enlightenment accomplished—what need is there for anything else? Nor is there any means of direct realization other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And that suchness (*tathatā*) is a quality of the mind common to both the states of affliction and purification; thus it is designated as "natural," "innate," and "the fundamental nature" (*prakṛti*).

Pride (*māna*) also, with respect to purification, is the sphere of the conventional designation "Dharmakāya. In that regard, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*), when cultivated without depending on specific mental aspects (*ākāra-viśeṣa*), will counteract whichever aspect happens to be present;

thus, it results in that very final aspect brought forth by the auxiliary cause of the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), which produces the specific characteristics and so forth of the subject (*dharmin*).

It acts as the basis. In that regard, in its prior state, that very dependent nature is called "variegated" (*citram*); it is also termed "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). But at the ultimate stage, because variegation itself is no longer the motivating factor for false conceptualization, it is not so designated; rather, it is said to be devoid of that form. Furthermore, even though there is the occurrence of mere dependence upon causes, in the absence of dependence upon the latencies of the unreal (*asadvāsanā*), [the dependent nature is no longer called "variegated"].

Nor is it called "dependent" (paratantra); rather, it is called "enjoyment" (saṃbhoga), because it is the enjoyment of the Dharma and because it is enjoyed by those on the ten stages. Or, from the perspective of ultimate reality, since there is no state of cause and effect, how could there be dependence? Therefore, the Dharmakāya is indeed of the nature of Dharma. Now, [one might object]:
The dharmas that are untainted and have attained purity in every aspect constitute the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature.

Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). How then can it be said that the nature described by others is a phenomenon called emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? That is incorrect. Indeed, no nature of phenomena other than emptiness is found within the path of the scriptures (*āgama*); rather, it should be understood according to one's inclination (*adhimukti*) through a distinction in its mode of existence. For instance:

Some understand selflessness (*nairātmya*) as being devoid of a creator god (*īśvara*) and the like; others [understand it] as the absence of an eternal self (*ātman*), even one that is inexpressible (*avācya*); and still some [understand it] as the conjunction with the luminosity of the insentient (*jaḍaprākāśya*).
(Jñānaśrīmitra-nibandhāvalī 434)

Furthermore, others [hold that the self] does not exist even as an external subtle body because it disappears; yet others, like those who maintain the dream-theory, hold that it does not exist even as its own cognition because it cannot withstand an investigation into its nature.
And because, through the process of reasoning and reflection, the mind gradually becomes solely inclined toward that [object].
For the establishment of the existence of things does not occur through either perception or inference;
rather, it is by means of these two alone that they are sublated, and thus the primary purpose of those two lies therein.

Nor do we say that the Dharma consists merely of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; rather, it is the nourishment and sustenance of all those modes of mind (*cittaprakāra*) which bear their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), whose nature is reckoned as body and intellect. Even that [nourishment] is mentioned as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), for the purpose of awakening to enlightenment by means of its relinquishment. And in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
The nature of those phenomena that have attained purity in all its aspects is such;
because this is taught as a general definition, there is no abandonment of the *saṃbhoga* [body], yet it is established as a distinct body (*kāya*).

Since it is enumerated up to the limit of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is counted separately. Therefore, having distinguished it by way of the relationship between property and substrate (*dharmin*), [it is so designated].

This is the establishment of two bodies. For that [body], there is a relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) with the Blessed One; for the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), however, it is a relationship of origination (*tadutpatti*).
But when that form is intended as being eternal and consisting of the aspect of all pure qualities (*śukladharma*), then even in that case, it is simply a matter of origination from him.
As it has been said:
"Qualities are characterized by the *dharmakāya*.
This being the case, although that [the *dharmakāya*] is indeed the means (*sādhana*), nevertheless, one does not pay regard to it merely as such;

rather, it is regarded simply as the reality (*tattva*). If it is asked why there is no end to the relationship between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), [the answer is: because of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality itself.

Because that [universal] alone is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because its cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there can be no abandonment or incapacity regarding those two [cultivation and the result] if it is not ascertained. Furthermore, since that [cultivation] achieves its purpose through the appearing subject (*dharmin*) itself, the search for a validating cognition (*pramāṇa*) that ascertains it remains the only remaining task; thus, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is complete. Moreover, that which is to be cultivated must indeed have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*), just like momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth.

Another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is established; and since the designation "Buddha" depends upon the realization of that [nature], that alone is the primary form of a Buddha, or he alone is called "Buddha," just as it is said, "The majesty itself is the king. For the *Uttaratantra* states that the variety of the [major] marks and so forth belongs to the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). Furthermore, even if some other entity were to exist in this way, it would serve no purpose whatsoever. Therefore, [it is] the *dharmakāya*—
Since this is merely a borrowed ornament for the sake of persuasion, there is no adherence whatsoever to the perception of formlessness. Therefore,
[95a] because it possesses the distinctions of body, enjoyments, and abode, from that...
And this being so, the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra* states:
"In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, situated above the Pure Abodes..."
The Perfectly Awakened Ones awaken there; how could it be otherwise in the formless realm?
The Lord, abiding precisely as the *saṃbhogakāya*,
has directly realized the *dharmakāya* through his own awareness;
for when there is a difference of ten [stages], that very [realization] is what is to be accomplished.
But when there is no object to be bound, various efforts are in vain.
Because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, consciousness is ultimately real;
yet, due to its lack of being either one or many, even consciousness is empty.
Even conventionally, that nature does not involve a turning back from the three realms; nor is such vastness desired, because it would transcend the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If you have endured momentariness, why should unreality not be endured? Or, if momentariness is indeed endured, how can death not be endured?
For one who has no fear of death, how could there be fear of anything else?
Indeed, every form of abuse is terrifying only because it culminates in death.
Better than death is perpetual weakness, for that alone is dear to us;
better is the non-attainment of a desired object than its attainment followed by separation.
Therefore, this very nature is not intended to be transgressed;
nevertheless, it is the established position that some excellence is desired to be attained.
Let space itself be [the example] for the sake of pacifying the notion of motion;

since it is common to both the momentary and the unreal, there is no fault whatsoever. Just as with momentariness, dependence on causes and so forth should also be understood in this way. Therefore, enough of this misplaced timidity. Moreover:
In the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*, [it is said]: "If there is no transgression of the nature of things, for the sake of removing the false stain from the surface of the sky."
This [argument] is the same even for one who holds that [the object] is false according to valid cognition.
The third chapter, the Entry into the Middle Way, from the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
[The Fourth Chapter] Or rather, what constitutes this falsity of that which has experience as its very nature, if it is due to sublation (*bādhaka*)? By what is what sublated?
[It would be sublated] by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) in the case of the mass of variegated forms. But this is like the guarding of a cow after it has already been sold.
Because it establishes the conventional [nature],
and because the commentary proves the contradiction with the "manifestation of the real" (satkhyāti) which is pervaded by that [conventional nature].

Furthermore, regarding the relationship between the sublated (*bādhyatva*) and the sublator (*bādhakatva*): first of all, cognition does not sublate itself, because self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is inherently powerful.

Could sublation occur through another [cognition], whether it shares the same object or has a different object, and whether it is simultaneous or non-simultaneous? In that regard, as for that which shares the same object...

And to say that "this sublates that" is incoherent. Even if they have different objects, what kind of sublation could there be? If you mean that it is merely by the presentation of its own object, then why would this not be a sublation of the other by that very same [presentation]? Nor can it be simultaneous; for when multiple things—whether of the same or a different class—appear at one and the same time, which could be sublated by which? But if there is a difference in time, there is all the more no room for such a claim, as is well agreed upon by the great authorities.
This would also apply by extension to Śrī Harṣa.

Now, if the demonstration that one cognition is objectless by means of another cognition were intended as a sublation (*bādha*), that sublation would not be contradictory between two cognitions occurring at different times. If that object appears in that cognition, then it must indeed exist; how, then, could there be sublation?

But if it does not appear at all, then it is non-existent by its very nature; what need is there for another negation? Or rather, it would not be said that there is a sublation (*bādhana*) directed toward that object.

If you argue that there is a negation of what has been superimposed (*āropita*), we reply: since it has been established that even superimposition is established merely through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), the sublation based upon it likewise does not transcend the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Now, just as the distinction of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)...

Error is characterized merely by the production of another cognition based on a certain support; likewise, the very arising of a cognitive form such as "it is thus and not otherwise" will constitute the sublation.
If this is so, it is established that there is no sublation in reality. This cognition has arisen through the apprehension of a certain form.

It is merely a name; nothing at all has been refuted or established by this, just as [the cognition of] sweetness follows immediately after the cognition of blue. If you argue that there is a distinction because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a refutation elsewhere, we reply: that which is established by mere determination is precisely what is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*).

Therefore, the demonstration of the emptiness of an objective support (*ālambana-śūnyatā*) does not have the purpose of refutation. Furthermore, this approach is possible only within a duality consisting of the distinction between that which possesses an objective support and its opposite.

It might be so; however, in the case of non-duality (*advaita*), it would be a great act of temerity to claim that cognitions—which, in their state of existence, culminate in a realization restricted solely to their own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—could mutually sublate one another. And as Jñānaśrīmitra has said: [438]...
"In the *Nibandhāvali*, it is stated that the cognition of [the self-]establishment of others' cognitions is not like that, nor is there any sublation [of it].
If it is argued: 'But surely the proof of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) also arises from another [cognition], and likewise, sublation will also occur [from another]'?"

This is without substance. For one established within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is not able to remain without relying upon inference; otherwise, one would not engage in any activity such as proceeding or desisting. And when inference is relied upon, the establishment of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) necessarily follows. However, there is no room for inference in the final determination of ultimate reality (*tattva*). Likewise, if contradiction is accepted only within the conventional, [then there is no fault].
Furthermore, if this [object] were to appear again as something established as external, then the sublation (*bādha*) would occur precisely there. This [objection] is trivial;

for whether it be cognition (*buddhi*) or an insentient thing (*jaḍa*), the establishment of sublation occurs right there. Even then, the operation of the proof (*sādhana*) does not proceed by transcending the form of the external object. Now, what is the use of this conceptualization?
By taking the manifold form of cognition itself as the subject (*dharmin*), the operation of the proof does not apply to the external object.
This resembles the story of one who has mounted a horse but forgets the horse.
With reference to any particular feeling, that which is external is indeed merely external;
and the inquiry as to whether that [external object] might be insentient knowledge is pointless.
Thus it is established that, in every respect, the sublation [of an object] is inseparable from the determination of external objects as graspable.
Now, if it is argued: "This very [determination] is considered the object of the sublation of blue and so forth;
therefore, the inquiry as to whether that cognition might be insentient is pointless."
Nor does the sublater [of an error] have the fear that "this is the form of a cognition," nor would there subsequently be a "dethroning" (utkīlana) of the capacity of that cognition.
Furthermore, there is no rule of dependence regarding the determination of an external object of apprehension;
for this [cognition] "this is blue" may be sublated whether it exists externally or as the mind.
Or let that distinction exist; nevertheless, there is still sublation of this [position]:
is a blow that causes death not inflicted upon a kinsman by one with a mind of enmity?

If this is argued, we reply once more: it is the established position that there is no room for a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the proof of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). In that case, when a subverting argument is established as being inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*) from the determination of the grasped and the grasper, nothing undesirable is entailed; for just as there is a distortion (*viplava*) regarding that [determination], so too is there one regarding the subverting argument, and thus the probandum is proven. Furthermore, it is impossible to avoid that inseparability.

Furthermore, there can be no sublation (*bādha*) of that which has not been made an object of cognition, because the determination of sublation takes the form: "this is sublated by that. And as for this making into an object, there are the following alternatives:

[the sublation occurs] by something other than the sublator, by the sublator itself, or by another [cognition] distinct from both. Regarding the first alternative—that it is by something other than the sublator—there is the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*.
If it is made an object by another [cognition], then it is certainly not sublated. Even if it is made an object by a sublating cognition, what room is there for sublation?

For making an object is the very manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*). If you argue that the manifestation of its own nature occurs precisely through being sublated, this is contradictory: "manifestation of its own nature" implies the existence of its own nature, whereas "being sublated" implies non-existence.

If it is argued that both [the cognition and its object] are sublated sequentially? No; first of all, there can be no sublation at the initial stage, because the related entity has not yet been cognized. If, on the other hand, there is the manifestation of its own nature, then by that alone its existence is established; where, then, is the sublation? Indeed, even if such sublation were to occur at a later time, it would not affect it, because at that time the object itself no longer exists. Or, if it were still present, nothing could be done even by a hundred sublaters. This applies to both cases.
But if it is made an object [of cognition], then there is simply the establishment of corroboration; where, then, is even a scent of sublation?

Nor is it logically possible for one thing to be made an object by that [other] or by anything else, since we have already begun this inquiry into the establishment of consciousness. Nor can it be [made an object] by itself.
There is room for sublation regarding the act of making [an object] an object,
when that which is manifesting by itself is made an object by another;
for a stronger sublater must strike down its own head.

Furthermore, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—whose operation terminates in its own mere form, thinking "this blue has been sublated by me through this reasoning"—does not even touch upon the matter of difference; nor is it a rash claim that, in the case of non-difference, it sublates that very self. Moreover, regarding the cognition of both self and other, there is simply consistency (*saṃvāda*), as before. If, however, one were to sublate what has not been made an object of cognition, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such as the sublation of the apprehension of external objects.

One might hope that even when liberation occurs and one is untouched by that [external world], once knowledge has arisen, there will be the conventional usage of "establishment" and "sublation" regarding it; however, that [usage] is a delusion within the state of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), and thus sublation produced by it is also merely a delusion. For when the determination of grasping external objects is overcome, everything is submerged in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); what action could then be performed by whom against what? Indeed, even then, it is not possible to say, "This is thus."
To do so would result in the re-emergence of duality. As they say:
"Even when one perceives that 'this is indeed consciousness alone,' by placing something before oneself, one does not abide in that state of pure consciousness."

Thus [it is said]. Now, if it is argued that even when there is certainty regarding reality (*tattva*), for one who has not yet attained direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), sublation (*bādhaka*) might find an opportunity—just as in the case of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth?

Even so, there is no fault. For just as this object is known, sought, or attained through innate ignorance (*sahajāvidyā*) solely within the domain of the external, so too would sublation descend upon that very summit. However, in the consideration of pure consciousness alone, all— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

This is the cessation of activity. Thus, this relationship between the sublated and the sublator is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*); it finds no occasion at the time when the true nature of reality (*tattvarūpa*) is being manifested. And at that time, although the means of proof (*sādhana*) likewise has no application, its non-application does not constitute a sublation, because the probandum (*sādhya*) has already been established. — *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*

If that [thesis] is not established, the other [refutation] cannot even arise; apart from merely satisfying the opponent, what purpose does it serve? If, then, the application of the subverting argument (bādhaka) depends upon the operation of a proof for that [thesis], then this fault indeed follows. But who would delay in this way? Let the application of the subverting argument come first! This is merely like rinsing the mouth out of fear. For when there is the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā)—

It is established that there is no entry of a sublation (bādhaka) against this [consciousness]. Therefore, since its application depends precisely upon the absence of identity with that [object], when consciousness is established as being nothing other than luminosity (*prakāśatā*) in dependence upon the determination of that [luminosity], the possibility of a sublation is dispelled; for such a sublation could only occur in the form "this is not consciousness. Consequently, as long as there is no sublation, [consciousness] exists only as having an external nature.

It is established that [the object] is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-rūpa*). If it is asked, "What fault is there in such a proof?"—it is not so; for since inference itself does not even arise when the state of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is established, what opportunity is there for proof or refutation? For instance, in the case of external cognition, inference and other means of knowledge do not exist within self-cognition alone.
But that which is established by one's own self-awareness arises from the very apprehension of that [object].
Nevertheless, if satisfaction is found in stating these defects,

then since the nature of the other [the probandum] is unestablished, and the nature of the locus and the reason are likewise unestablished, there is neither establishment nor pervasion; what, then, is not a defect?

Furthermore, this non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), or any other subverting argument (*bādhaka*) termed "investigation" (*vicāra*) and so forth, is not something distinct from inference that could serve as an object of possibility. For every statement advanced by one engaged in a dispute must, by manifesting the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), be useful to the subject at hand only by implying an inference. Therefore, within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), one must necessarily accept the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus has it been demonstrated by us in the *Advaitabindu*.

Otherwise, what kind of establishment of meaning could there be for anyone through mere restatement (*anuvāda*) in whatever way? Nor can inference be considered non-authoritative (*ayathārtha*) by disparaging perception, since it possesses a necessary utility, whether directly or indirectly, in the apprehension of relations and so forth.

Because it is produced by that very [cognition], even that [subsequent cognition] is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when the former is not a means of valid knowledge; this is merely a claim of noble birth for one whose progenitor is of ignoble lineage. Furthermore, since this awareness of the form [of the object] regarding its own nature is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—having cast away all erroneous conceptualization—how could there be any occasion for sublation?
If self-awareness alone is not the source of other means of knowledge, then what is the means of knowledge here?
Therefore, regarding those things established or sublated by it:
There is no power in anything other than sublation and proof.

Regarding the *Sākārasiddhiśāstra*: if it is asked, "At the time of establishing representation-only (*vijñapti*), how can there be a self-defeat of one's own position?"—it is not so; for when the probandum is established, even one's own [position] is defeated.
Just as a fire that consumes its own support burns its own branch when it is rubbed against it,
so too does the wealth of another [burn] oneself.
If [consciousness] were a destroyer, who here could commit an offense?
Indeed, the cognition of another, which is established by means of representation (*vijñapti*), does not hope for its own validity while subverting something else.
However, an investigation raised on the basis of the generality of cognizing another—just as fire is a burner for everyone and not just for some one—is [not applicable here].
This is a fallacy. As for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it cannot claim validity merely by disregarding perception; that is not logical.

However, the validity of the means of cognition that establishes representation (*vijñapti*) is limited precisely to the exclusion of the validity of another's experience. Furthermore, when one does not act accordingly because one fails to perceive—due to a lack of reflection—that which possesses existence as established by the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*), then at that time there is no [non-perception of the pervader].

The non-apprehension [of the object] is not a fault, because it does not invalidate [the cognition] itself; as for invalidation by another [cognition], that is equal [to the case of the opponent's argument], since the punishment [of falsity] is common [to both]. For there is no appearance of a capacity in self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). But when the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) alone is the leader [of the proof], then even another perception (*pratyakṣāntara*) is unable to undermine its validity, let alone self-cognition, which by its very nature has already cast far away any suspicion of error or conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
[This applies] to the stain. Therefore, there is no impairment from any source for that which is protected by consciousness.
But surely, just as there is no validity for the sense organ [in that case], so too there is no status as a means of valid cognition for inference?
Likewise, it can also be argued that if inference were not a valid means of knowledge, neither would sensory perception be.

When an inference arising from a mark (liṅga) that has been grasped as a constituent part [of the argument] is sublated, the fault lies in that very [mark]; for if it is not faulty, how could there be a sublation produced by it?
Therefore, even if both are valid means of knowledge, nevertheless,
let consciousness manifest its own persistence within itself, since error is impossible therein; however,
how can this cruel contradiction regarding its being both one and many be averted?

Because their continued existence is inseparable from that which is to be accomplished by them, who knows whose power is more exalted between these two— the one perceived directly and the one inferred— both of whom possess equal majesty and glory?
(Jñānaśrīmitra-nibandhāvalī 442)

That too is not relevant to the path [of the argument]. For let there be parity between the non-perception of the pervader—which is restricted solely to the cognition of another—and the perception of another that grasps the pervasion and so forth, since the validity of one is necessarily concomitant with the invalidity of the other. But self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the substratum for both and is not dependent on anything else; so how can it be placed on the same scale as that?
Furthermore, because inference has a remote object as its domain and does not apply to what is directly perceived, what room is there for considering their relative strength?
For this very reason, it is stated that a thesis (*pakṣa*) must not be contradicted by perception and the other means of knowledge.
But surely, even in the case of perception, inference is indeed accepted in order to bring to linguistic usage a particular nature (*svabhāvāntara*) that was previously unexpressed.

Furthermore, affirmation or negation does not apply to that which is merely appearing. For, when a specific arrangement such as a horn or a finger appears, the word "cow" or the like is applied; when only the bare ground is perceived, there is the conventional usage of negating a jar or the like; and when the form of two moons appears within cognition, there is the negation of an external pair of moons. But there is no affirmation of those very things that are appearing.

There are two negations. Likewise here, too, in the context of negation, let as many imagined properties as there are of the appearing form of blue and so forth be negated—be they such as self and other, the grasped and the grasper, the made known and the maker known, permanence and momentariness, unity and plurality, or [the categories of] substance, quality, and being composed of the three *guṇas*; or [properties such as] the accompaniment of other forms characterized by touch and so on, or atoms.
All things, from form down to the capacity for causal efficiency, are denoted by the term "proliferation" (*prapañca*), because they are all merely imagined.
Therefore, regarding a manifest substrate (*dharmin*), the negation or affirmation of another attribute that is not manifest occurs only in reliance upon conventional usage;
for even in the absence of verbal or other such usage, the capacity for it remains in a latent state within that which is capable of it. However, this does not apply to what is actually manifest.
There is no prohibition [against this], as it says: "The origin of logic.
When that non-apprehension of it is to be proven as not being based on an existent thing, [it is established].
Thus, the reason is not the non-existence of that very thing, because of the employment of words.
The reason is excluded from its locus.
[Pramāṇavārttika 3.205–6] [Pramāṇavārttika 4.91]

And so it is said: "If, then, affirmation and negation regarding that which appears are both useless and ineffective, and even for that which does not appear, that very negation is likewise ineffective and useless—what then is the function of words? None at all in reality; this is merely a conventional usage based on dependent origination, wherein by means of words something is either affirmed or negated. As it has been said:

For, by virtue of the convention "the tree exists," it is precisely the production of a conceptual construction that induces activity corresponding to that [tree] which constitutes the existence of the tree as expressed by the word.
(Compare *Nyāyabindu* 3.38;
*Sākārasiddhiśāstra*).

The procedure is as follows: the negation of a tree is simply the production of a conceptual construction that implies the exclusion of non-trees (tarthi). However, when the words "is" (asti) and "not" (nañ) are not employed, the mere production of a conceptual construction of a form possessing branches and so forth—which is incapable of either engaging with or withdrawing from the word "tree"—is what is called the non-performance of affirmation and negation. And when that [conceptual construction] is in proximity to the word "is," that very same branched object appears as if being augmented by existence.

"It appears" (*pratibhāti*) refers, in relation to what precedes it, merely to the delineation of a specific form. Even when joined with a negative particle (*nañ*), as in "it is as if being diminished," it is merely the delineation of a diminished form in relation to the experience of an affirmation; from that follows activity and so forth corresponding to that [form].

Likewise, in the case of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—such as the perception of smoke or clouds which are the manifestations of conceptual construction—it is [determined] by the necessity or otherwise of its correspondence [with reality].

This is the distinction. Thus, there can be no affirmation or negation regarding the manifest form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*), nor regarding the external object—which, though existing or non-existing in reality—is not manifest. Nevertheless, through the medium of the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the conventional practice of affirmation and negation applies solely to the external object as it is imagined;
for that which manifests directly before one cannot be negated even by a hundred "nots. And this conceptualization is distinct from the inward-turned awareness [of pure consciousness].

Because, in the conceptualization of a mere tree, there is an exclusion of the state of being attentive to the determination of its existence or non-existence. For this very reason, the form (*ākāra*) is said to be superimposed as an external reality, and it is called "exclusion" (*apoha*), since it is that alone which appears in verbal cognition. However, due to cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), it was previously explained that it appears as something external, excluded from those of a different class. Therefore:
In reality, there is no negation of either the form or the external object;
for while the external exists conventionally, the form does not exist even conventionally.

Likewise, because it is purposeless and because the world is by nature extroverted; and since there is no room for negation even regarding external objects when they manifest before one, how could there be any such room regarding one's own self? Therefore, there is no possibility of protection through logical reasons against that which has been rejected by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And that which is established by self-awareness is indeed established in reality.

Although the relationship between the probandum and the probans is purely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), nevertheless, it must be based upon a valid convention (*sat-saṃvṛti*). For if the establishment of the probans and so forth were different for each individual, everything would be established for everyone. Furthermore, there is no possibility of protection from refutation by reasons even for one who abides by a different convention. If there is any disagreement regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) on the part of others, [it is resolved] as follows:
And in that regard,

it has been definitively established in the treatise that it is not possible for the means of valid cognition to exist without self-awareness, just as the world cannot exist in the absence of a knower.

Therefore, since [the existence of the self] is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), any inference—such as the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—is rendered without scope; thus, the thesis is contradicted by direct perception.
